@{\tx_iso&(tx_iso|tx_iso)&test[1]/b[1] }" 800ns
102 E "/TOP/system/PD_tx_iso1" "/
@{\tx_iso&(tx_iso|tx_iso)&test[1]/b[1] }" 750ns 760ns "/TOP/
system/receiver/in1[2]" 750ns

Appendix G: Gate-level Debug Mode
* Overview and Usage
* Find Instances Pane
* Port List Pane
* Trace Results Pane

Overview and Usage
The Verdi platform gives you all the tools you need to debug large gate-level designs.
For very big designs, Verdi first imports the source code and then shows the flattened
schematic. After this step, you can use Verdi's features to start debugging.
Sometimes, your gate-level design is very large and flat, with over a hundred million
instances in one scope. In these cases, opening the full schematic takes a lot of time and
makes debugging difficult. Here, you may not need advanced debug features. Instead, you
need fast and simple tools, like searching for instance ports and tracing fan-in or fan-out
connections. Performance is most important.
To help with this, Verdi offers Gate-level Debug Mode. This mode does not show the full
source code or schematic. Instead, it gives you basic debug tools, such as searching
instance ports and tracing fan-in/fan-out connections quickly. You can use the fast search
to find instances and ports, and view partial schematics and waveform right away.
To use the Gate-level Debug Mode, add the -fastGate command-line option when
invoking the Verdi platform. You can apply this mode only to a gate-level netlist, so that
lots of syntax errors can be encountered if the -fastGate option is used with an RTL
design as follows:.
% Verdi -fastGate -f run.f &

After the Verdi platform is invoked, the Welcome page is displayed. Because the
-fastGate option is added and it can only be applied to a gate-level netlist, the Work
Modes icon is disabled, which means the work mode may not be changed. Click the Hide
button in the upper right corner to close this Welcome page.

Overview and Usage

Select the Do not show this page again option before hiding the Welcome
page so that it does not appear the next time the Verdi platform is invoked.
Figure 1033 Welcome Page

After hiding the Welcome page, the top window of the Gate-level Debug Mode appears.
The window contains the following four pane areas:
* The Find Instances pane in the left: This pane lists the matched instances.
* The Port List pane in the middle: This pane lists instance ports of the selected instance
in the Find Instances pane.
* The Trace Results pane in the right: This pane shows the trace fan-in and trace fan-out
results as a text grid.
* The nWave window in the bottom: This pane shows the related waveform from the
* The Message pane in the bottom: This pane shows the general messages (for
example, the import messages) in the General tab and shows the compilation error
and warning messages in the Compile tab.

The following sections explain how to perform gate-level debugging with these panes.

Find Instances Pane
The Find Instances pane is opened in the left side of the main window after the Verdi
platform is invoked, as shown in Figure 1034.
To search for a string, perform the following steps:
1. Enter the text you want to locate in the Find field.
2. Press Enter on your keyboard.
Or
Click Find button.
You can use wildcard characters in the Find field as follows:
* Use the asterisk (*) to match zero or more characters.
* Use the question mark (?) to match any single character.
* Use the backslash (\) to treat special characters as normal text.

Find Instances Pane

* Typing \*abc finds *abc, but not abc.
* Typing \a finds a.
Click the drop-down arrow beside the Find button. Two options are displayed: Match
Case and Match Substring.
Figure 1035 Find Options

* Match Case: When this option is turned on, a case sensitive search is performed. The
default value is on.
* Match Substring: When this option is turned on, the search is applied to all substrings.
The default value is off.
For example, if the Match Substring option is turned off and the system.i_cpu is entered
and a search is performed, only the instance system.i_cpu is found as shown in the
following figure.

off) and then a search is performed, all instances under system.i_cpu is found as shown
in the following figure. The instance under system.i_cpu.i_ALUB is not found unless the
string is specified as system.i_cpu.*.*.

Find Instances Pane Right-Click Options
Some options are provided after the instance is found. Select the instance of interest and
right click to display the options:
* Show Selected in Port List: Shows all ports of the selected instance in the Port List
* Schematic Flatten Window: Opens a new flatten schematic pane to display the
selected instance.
* Delete Selected: Removes the selected instance from the Instance List pane.
* Save: Saves all instances listed in the Instance List pane to a text file.
* Load: Loads the instance list from a saved file. A warning message is displayed if the
loaded instance cannot be found in the design.

Port List Pane
The Port List pane appears in the middle of the main window after the Verdi platform is
invoked as shown in Figure 1034. This pane shows the port list of the selected instance
in the Find Instances pane. To view the port list, double-click the instance and select the
Show Selected in Port List command right-click option, or drag and drop the instance
from other panes.

Port List Pane

A search mechanism is also provided in the Port List pane. Enter the string in the Find
field and then click the Find button to perform the search. A type filter is provided in the
pane to filter the port list by a specific type. Click the drop-down arrow beside the Find
button to display four types of filters: input, output, inout, and all. By default, the all filter
option is selected.
Figure 1040 Find Options

If the FSDB file is loaded, the FSDB value can be annotated to the Port List pane. Turn on
the View -> Active Annotation option in the main window and all values are annotated to
the right of the port list. The value is synchronized with the cursor time in nWave window.

Appendix H: Scope-Based Peak Activity Analysis
for Power Estimation Flow
The scope-based peak activity analysis for power estimation flow helps the user with
improved debug performance and reduced complexity. Several filter mechanisms are also
available to help the user to find the peak transition range with ease.
* No Design Mode
* Dumping Detailed Report into FSDB File
* Transition Type Filter
* Signal/Scope Name Filter
* Calculating Switching Activity Differences
* Tcl Options
* Batch Mode Support for Scope-Based Peak Activity Report

title: 1 and output X)
text:
No Design mode is a calculation mode that allows you to analyze switching activity without
loading a design but on providing an FSDB file as data input for analysis.
In this mode, same-net analysis is simplified. based on the following methods:
* Count transitions based on instances
If you dump the FSDB file with the detailed information of essential instances, this
mode counts the transitions on the output signal of all the leaf instances.
* Count transitions based on the FSDB signal
If you do not dump the essential instance information into an FSDB file, this mode
recognizes the same-net signals or the signals driven by same source signal. The
transitions will be counted on the most leaf scope.

Considering a case where four same-net signals exist; only the transitions on the output
port Q of top.a.b.Reg and top.a.Reg cells are counted in No Design Mode, because
these ports are the output ports of most of the leaf instances.
Figure 1044 Same Net Analysis in No Design Mode

Starting from the Verdi 2015.09 release, the default debug_access skips the cell
dumping. So, you need to enable cell dumping to use the No Design Mode. If cell dumping
is not enabled, then design would be required for this mode.

Use Model
For the No Design Mode, input files and output reports are as follows:
Input:
* FSDB file
* Filter configuration file
Output:
* Top-N transition count/time range with CSV format
* Full transition count/time range with FSDB format (optional)
* Signal/scope name filter report

Utility
To perform switching analysis - No Design mode in batch mode, you can use the
waveSwAnalysis wrapper command.
Syntax of the waveSwAnalysis command is as follows:
waveSwAnalysis fsdb_fname -time_window time [Options]

Here, [Options] can be any of the following:
* -parallel [number] specifies the number of processes in multi-process mode
where the time range is separated into [number] segments and switching analysis is
performed for each segment in parallel.
If [number] is less than or equal to 1, switching analysis runs in single process
mode. If you do not specify this option, switching analysis runs in single process
mode by default.
In the case of parallel mode, each process occupies one individual license. For
example, if you specify '-parallel 10', then switching analysis will require 10 licenses
to run.
The following output reports are generated:
CSV format report: Parallel mode automatically merges the CSV format report. It is
same as the original result.
FSDB format report: Parallel mode uses a virtual file to merge all the FSDB
reports as one FSDB file. For example, if the output file name is fsdbReport, a
directory named as waveSwAnalysisLog is created for separated file reports and
one virtual file named fsdbReport.vf.
-filter_mode [LeafInst|FsdbSig] specifies the same net filter mode. If user
does not specify this option, LeafInst is considered as the default filter mode.
LeafInst: In this mode, transitions are counted based on leaf instances output port.
FsdbSig: In this mode, transitions are counted based on the FSDB signal.
* -top "scopeName" specifies the scope. The scope name must be double quoted. If
user does not specify the scope, the top scope of FSDB is used by default.
* -include_sub includes all the scopes below the specified scope.
* -filter fileName specifies the filter options in the filter file. The following filter
options are available:
filter-out: specifies the signal/scope to be filtered-out.
filter-in: specifies the signal/scope to be filtered-in. If this option is specified, it
analyzes if the scope/signal meet the criteria.
filter.conf
filter-out:
*.clk.*
*.dut.cpu.output
filter-in:
top.dut.cpu.*

* -bt time specifies the start time of analysis. If this option is not specified, full
simulation time is used.
* -et time specifies the end time of analysis. If this option is not specified, full
simulation time is used.
* -delta time specifies the sliding delta of switching analysis. If you do not specify the
sliding delta, the sliding delta is 1% of the time window and the minimum size is 10.
* -o fileName specifies the file name of the switching analysis report. If you do not
specify this option, the report file is named as SwitchingReport.csv in the current
directory by default.
* -dump_waveform dumps the waveform file format report.
* -show_top_data number specifies the number of top-N high transitions to be
displayed in the output report. The default value is 10. Set 0 to show all data.
* -show_top_scope number specifies the number of top-N high transitions of scope to
be displayed in the output report. The default value is 1000. Set 0 to show all scopes.
* -hierarchical_levels number specifies the number of levels you want to dump into
the report file.
* -max_transition|-max_reduce_transition shows the positive/negative difference
of two consecutive time ranges.
* -time_window time specifies the time window of switching analysis.
* -v enables the verbose mode.
* -h prints the usage.
* To perform FSDB Switching Analysis with default settings, use the following command:
%waveSwAnalysis analysis.fsdb -time_window 100

* To perform FSDB Switching Analysis with the specified scope name and time window,
use the following command:
%waveSwAnalysis analysis.fsdb -top "top.dut" -include_sub
-bt 0 -et 10000000 -time_window 1000 -delta 50

Batch Mode
To enable No Design Mode,
1. Prepare the Tcl command file using the saCreateReport Tcl command.
saCreateReport -sameNetFilter 1 -scope scope_name -fsdb file.fsdb
-group time_window -param resolution -pivot scope

Here,
saCreateReport generates the scope-based peak activity report.
-sameNetFilter specifies No Design Mode (count transitions based on instances).
For No Design Mode, the number range can be 1 (transitions are counted based on
instances) or 2 (transitions are counted based on the FSDB signal).
-scope specifies the scope. If user does not specify the scope, the top scope is
used by default.
-fsdb specifies the FSDB file.
-group specifies the time window for switching analysis.
-param specifies the sliding delta of switching analysis.
-pivot scope enables scope-based switching analysis.
2. Execute the following command:
verdi -play command.cmd -batch

Transition Type Filter
The SA_X_FILTER environment variable is provided to allow the user to enable or disable
the transition type filter. The default value is 2.
The transition type filter can be used to filter out the transitions as follows:
* The transition is ignored in the following scenarios:
For state change from X/Z to 1/0 at the beginning and from 1/0 to X/Z at the end.
For state change from 1/0 to X/Z then to 1/0, if values between X/Z transition are
the same.
If the state changes from 1->X->1.
If the state changes from 0->X->0.
* The transition is valid in the following scenarios:
For state change from 1/0 to X/Z then again to 0/1, if the values are between X/Z
transition are different.
If the state changes from 1->X->0, count
If the state changes from 0->X->1, count
For state change from 1/0 to 0/1
By default, the transition type filter is enabled. To disable it, execute the following
setenv SA_X_FILTER 0

* 1: Specifies No design mode (transitions are counted based on instances)
* 2: Specifies No design mode (transitions are counted based on the FSDB signal)

Batch Mode Support for Scope-Based Peak Activity Report

For the "No design mode", user can also specify any other FSDB file instead of using the
primary FSDB file.
-fsdb Input_FSDB_File

Specifies the FSDB file to be used as input file.
Signal/Scope Name Filter Options
-filterFile Filename

Specifies the filter options in the filter file.
Top N High Transition Data Options
-showTopDataNo Number

Specifies the number of top-N high transitions to be displayed in the output report. The
default value is 10.
If user does not specify any report dumping option and triggers switching activity in noGUI
mode, the output report is dumped into a text file SwitchingReport.txt by default.
Usage Example
- saCreateReport -sameNetfilter 1 -filterFile <file name> -fsdb <input
FSDB> -fromTime 0 -toTime 100000 -dump_csv -filename ./report.txt

Inputs Files:
* FSDB file
* User defined time window size
Functions:
* Based on the -filterFile options, report the toggle windows.
Outputs:
* Report the top N time windows with the most toggle counts and toggle count in each
* Report the % of signals that has at least 1 toggle.

Batch Mode Support for Scope-Based Peak Activity Report
For scope-based peak activity report, you need to perform analysis on the FSDB files
which have large number of scope and long simulation time. In such a case, the analysis
process may take time more than expected. Therefore, it is recommended to run the
analysis in batch mode.

Batch Mode Support for Scope-Based Peak Activity Report

For No Design Mode, only the batch mode is supported.

Behavior Analysis Mode
To perform analysis in batch mode, execute the following steps:
1. Prepare the TCL command file.
debImport -sv "tb_srsn.sv"
debLoadSimResult srsn.fsdb

saCreateReport -scope {tb} -fromTime 0 -toTime 400 includeSub -group 100 -param 100 -pivot scope -dump_csv
-dump_waveform -filename ./report.fsdb
debExit

Preface
The Verdi Coverage User Guide and Tutorial discusses Verdi Coverage that provides
visualization for coverage data. Verdi Coverage provides a comprehensive visualization
environment for coverage data. It integrates with the design hierarchy display. You
can use it to get a summary of coverage results or details of various coverage types.
Verdi Coverage can display code coverage, covergroup coverage, and assertion
coverage. Furthermore, you can use the Exclusion Manager of Verdi Coverage to show
all exclusions and unresolved exclusions and edit exclusions. You can also use Verdi
Coverage to create a verification plan or verification plan components (.hvp files) and link
specifications (.pdf files). The interaction between the Verdi platform and Verdi Coverage
is also provided to debug with designs and the coverage report.

Introducing Verdi Coverage
(R)

The Verdi Coverage function in the Verdi Automated Debug Platform provides
visualization for coverage data. After you load simulation coverage results for a Verilog or
VHDL design, you can use Verdi Coverage. You can easily check the coverage report in
the Verdi platform.
Verdi Coverage provides a comprehensive visualization environment for coverage data. It
integrates with the design hierarchy display. You can use it to get a summary of coverage
results or details of various coverage types. Verdi Coverage can display the following
coverage information:
* Code coverage including:
Line Coverage: The statements that were executed during simulation.
FSM Coverage: The blocks of code that make up FSMs can be identified. FSM
coverage reports on the states, transitions, and sequences of states during
simulation.
Toggle Coverage: Whether the signals in the design toggle from 0 to 1 and 1 to 0
during simulation.
Condition Coverage: Conditions are expressions and sub-expressions that control
the execution of code or the assignment of values to signals. Condition coverage
tests whether both true and false states of these conditions were covered during
simulation.
Branch Coverage: Analyzes how if, case statements, and the ternary operator (?:)
establish branches of execution in your Verilog design. It shows vectors of signal or
expression values that enable or prevent simulation events.
* Covergroup Coverage: Coverage of SystemVerilog testbench coverage groups.

* Covergroup Coverage: Coverage of SystemVerilog testbench coverage groups.
* Assertion Coverage: Coverage of SystemVerilog cover properties or assert
properties. Low Power Coverage: Coverage of UPF low power coverage groups.
Furthermore, you can use the Exclusion Manager of Verdi Coverage to show all
exclusions and unresolved exclusions and edit exclusions. You can also use Verdi
Coverage to create a verification plan or verification plan components (.hvp files) and link
specifications (.pdf files). The interaction between the Verdi platform and Verdi Coverage
is also provided to debug with designs and the coverage report.

Chapter 1: Introducing Verdi Coverage

Currently, the supported simulator is VCS with version 2013.06 and later.

Prerequisites
Before you can begin using the Verdi Coverage capability, the following criteria must be
met:
* Your coverage database is generated by a VCS simulator with version 2024.09 or later.
* The coverage features must be enabled at compile-time and simulation time to include
them in the coverage database and view them in the Verdi platform by using the -cm
line+tgl+fsm+cond+branch+assert compile option and runtime option. For example:
> vcs -P $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/VCS/LINUX/novas.tab \
$VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/VCS/LINUX/pli.a \
-f file_list.vc -cm line+tgl+fsm+cond+branch+assert -sverilog
> ./simv -cm line+tgl+branch+fsm+cond+assert

If your design includes UPF file for power simulation, the -power=coverage
+dump_hvp compile option is needed to enable VCS power coverage features. For
example:
> vcs -P $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/VCS/LINUX/novas.tab \
$VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/VCS/LINUX/pli.a \
-sverilog <your design> -upf <your UPF power design> \
-cm line+tgl+fsm+cond+branch+assert -power=coverage+dump_hvp

* You have the Verdi license and the Verdi Coverage add-on licenses.
If the Verdi platform is invoked through Verdi Coverage, there is no need to
check another Verdi license.
* Output files generated by newer versions of the Verdi, VCS and VCS utilities are not
backward compatible with older versions
Recommendation: Always ensure the tool version is equal to or newer than the version
used to generate the output file.

1. For details on the compilation options, see the VCS User Guide.
2. For details on the compilation options, see the VCS User Guide.

If you change the location of a source file, you can map the path to the relocated file using
the -pathmap <file> option. The rule specified in the file relocates source files. For
example,
> verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb -pathmap <file> &

The syntax of the path mapping file is as follows:
<old_directory_path_name>:<new_directory_path_name>

## the content of the path mapping file
/home/work/src: ~local/files/source

The subsequent chapters discuss how you can use Verdi Coverage.

Showing Instance-Based Scores for Coverpoints and Crosses
An Instcov mode score (different from defalult or union mode) is computed by
calculating the average score of instances. This score applies only to definition-level
covergroup, coverpoint, cross, or bin hvp regions. Instance coverage must be enabled as
option.per_instance = 1.

How to Display the Instance-Based Scores Feature
To ensure the instcov mode score is dispayed, you must enable the -group
instcov_for_cp_score option explicitly. This option has the effect of -group
instcov_for_score showing the instcov mode score of covergroup. Refer to the
Instance Coverage Score Option section of the Verification ContinuumTM Coverage
Technology Reference Manual to learn more.
Enabling the -group instcov_for_cp_score option ensures the display of the instcov
mode score of covergroups through the following:
* The Summary and Coverage Detail panes ) display the instcov mode score for
definition-level coverpoint/cross.
* The HVP pane displays the instcov mode score for definition-level covergroup,
coverpoint/cross and single-bin regions.
Usage of the -group instcov_for_cp_score Option
Add the -group instcov_for_cp_score option in the Verdi Coverage command line as
given below:
%> verdi -cov -covdir <simv.vdb> -group instcov_for_cp_score

Switching the Coverage Score between Default Mode and Instcov Mode
With the -group instcov_for_cp_score option, you can toggle the preference item
View -> Compute Group by Instance to switch the coverage score between the default
mode and instcov mode in the Summary and Coverage Detail panes.

If you toggle the preference item for HVP regions scores, a dialog box pops up to enable
you to recalculate and view the new plan scores.

Using Verdi Coverage
This chapter provides information on how you can use the capabilities of Verdi Coverage
with its various coverage modes. It also describes each of the Coverage GUI tabs in the
following sections:
* Using the Summary Pane
* Using the Hierarchy Tab
* Using the Modules Tab
* Using the Groups Tab
* Using the Asserts Tab
* Using the Statistics Tab
* Using the Tests Tab
* Using the UPF Low-Power Coverage
* Using Application Preferences
* Using the Functional Code Coverage Auto Generation
* Example for User Reference

As shown in Figure Coverage Mode, when Verdi Coverage is invoked, the Coverage mode
is launched by default. The Summary, Coverage Source Code (CovSrc), Coverage Detail
(CovDetail), Message, and Exclusion Manager panes are displayed in the main window.
Figure 1

Coverage Mode

The Summary pane gives you the summary information for each type of coverage and
navigates to the required database. It consists of the Hierarchy, Module, Group, Asserts,
and Statistics tabs to show the summary of your design and coverage with different forms
of presentation. The Coverage Source Code pane shows the source code and covered
and uncovered highlights for specific coverage types in the Coverage Detail pane.
Verdi Coverage is a multi-window docking application with a flexible and easy-to-use
graphical user interface. Thus, the following general functions are introduced for easier
usage before describing the Verdi Coverage features:
* The layout of Verdi Coverage is flexible and you can resize, dock, and undock each
pane in Verdi Coverage.
* As shown in Figure Search and Filter, you can filter the content of each pages in the
Summary pane based on the string entered in the Filter field.
Figure 2

Search and Filter

* You can search the content of each pane in Verdi Coverage based on the string
entered in the Search field. You can also click the Search Option icon to add-on
search options. The Search field is hidden by default. Use the Show/Hide Search
Widget command in the right-click menu to show the field.
* The bindkey values and drop -down menu names and locations can be customized
through the Customize Menu/Toolbar form. Use the Customize Menu/Toolbar
command to invoke the form. For more information, see the User Interface chapter in
the Verdi User Guide and Tutorial.

Advanced Masking
In previous releases, Verdi provided quick filters to search items based on characters, for
example a covergroup name or an instance name.
Now, Verdi also enables you to filter the items based on coverage scores, exclusion
status, properties, and so on.
Verdi provides this advanced masking feature in the Summary pane, the Coverage Detail
pane, and the HVP pane.
This advanced masking does not result in recomputation of HVP scores, which behaves
differently from quick filters and modifiers.
With the advanced masking capabilities, you can filter by specifying a single condition as
well as multiple conditions.
For the single condition, you can use the following syntax for filtering:
[text filter][conditional_expression]

* [text filter] is a wildcard or regular expression that matches items by their name.
If the matched items also fulfill [conditional_expression], Verdi retains the items.
You can also retain the sub-items of the matched items, if you select the following
option from Preferences > Global:

However, if the sub-items of the matched items do not fulfill the condition, Verdi does
not show the items even if the above option is selected.
* [conditional_expression] is of the following format:
[column name][operator][Number/String]

[operator]refers to >, <, =, !=, >=, <=, and :. Here, : refers to =.
[Number] refers to int, float, or double.
[String] is only allowed with : and =. [String] with empty spaces should be
enclosed within "". If [String] includes "", use escaped characters.

To specify multiple conditions for filtering, use the following syntax:
[text filter][operator][conditional_expression1] [operator]
[conditional_expression2]

[text filter] and [operator] are optional. Also, if no operator is specified, then it is

AND by default.

Show Source Code and Coverage Detail
You can double-click a row under a column in the Hierarchy page for a specified scope
to see the corresponding information in the Coverage Source Code and Coverage Detail
panes (refer to Figure Figure 8):
* In the Coverage Source Code pane, the source code with annotation indicates the
covered type from the double-clicked column.
For example, refer to Figure Figure 8, double-click the jb1 row under the Line column.
The source code with annotation indicates a covered line in the jb1 scope.
You can also see the exclusion status icons shown in front of the line number. Macro
instances are collapsed in the Coverage source code pane by default.
You can click the expand/collapse icon in the line number widget to show/hide the
macro content.
* In the Coverage Detail pane, the selected page in the Coverage Detail pane displays
the coverage percentage for the specified coverage type.
For example, refer to Figure Figure 8, double-click the jb1 row under the Line column.
The line coverage details of jb1 scope are shown in the Coverage Detail pane in the
Figure 8

Check the Coverage Details

You can also change the coverage type in the highlighted source code by selecting a
different coverage page in the Coverage Detail pane.
For example, as shown in Figure Figure 9, the source code is shown and highlighted
based on the branch coverage.
Figure 9

Check Covered Source Code by Selecting Specific Coverage Type

The following steps describe how you can show the location of the corresponding source
code line automatically:
1. In the Preferences form (invoked using Tools -> Preferences), turn on the Auto-scroll
CovSrc when switching CovDetail metrics option in the Detail View page.
2. In the Coverage Detail pane, select a row in one page (for example, select a row in the
Branch page).
3. In the Coverage Detail pane, select another page (for example, select the FSM page).
4. The coverage type in the Coverage Source Code pane changes to the FSM coverage
type.
5. In the Coverage Detail pane, select the previous page that contains the previously
selected row (for example, select the Branch page).
The coverage type in the Coverage Source Code pane changes to the branch coverage
type.
In addition, the location of the corresponding selected item in the page is automatically
displayed in the Coverage Source Code pane (that is, the scroll is moved to the
corresponding location).

Expanding MDAs in the Coverage Detail Pane

single click using the Expand All option.

provides the Collapse All option to hide the details of MDA using a single click.

Configuring Computation Modes
You can configure the display of the Coverage report data based on the following
computation modes:
* Show Ratio for Detail
* Compute Group by Ratio
* Compute Group by Instance
* Show Condition IDs
* Line Coverage
* Toggle Coverage
* Using FSM Coverage
* Using Condition Coverage
* Using Branch Coverage
* Using Assert Coverage

These modes are available in the View menu and can be set/unset as shown in the
Figure 10

Computation Options in the View Menu

These modes are discussed in detail in the subsequent sections.

Show Ratio for Detail
As shown in Figure Show Ratio for Detail, you can use the View -> Show Ratio for Detail
command to show the actual counts in the Coverage Detail panes.
Figure 11

Show Ratio for Detail

Compute Group by Ratio
The score for a covergroup is calculated as the average of the percentages of individual
cover point scores by default.
You can use the View -> Compute Group by Ratio command to calculate the covergroup
scores and overall group scores as a ratio between the number of covered bins and the
total number of coverable bins.
Compute Group by Ratio shows the difference between the score calculation with and
without the ratio.

Figure 12

Compute Group by Ratio

Compute Group by Instance
You can use View -> Compute Group by Instance to calculate the covergroup scores
using the coverage of each instance for the covergroups with instance coverage.
Figure Compute Group by Instance shows the difference between the score calculation
with and without enabling this option.
Figure 13

Compute Group by Instance

Show Condition IDs
You can use View -> Show Condition IDs to view the condition IDs for an expression in
the Condition tab as shown in the Showing Condition IDs.

Figure 14

Showing Condition IDs

Toggle Coverage
The Toggle page in the Coverage Details pane displays the value transitions from 0 to 1
and 1 to 0 for each net and register.
Refer to Figure Check Toggle Coverage Details, for the following actions:
* Double-click a signal in the Details table and the signal is highlighted with its coverage
range in the Coverage source code pane.
* Select a signal in the Details table, and the bit list of the signal is displayed in the Bit
List table.
* The bits in the Bit List table can be compressed or uncompressed by selecting the
Compress Vector Bits and Uncompress Vector Bits commands in the right-click
menu or by double-clicking the bit.

Figure 18

Check Toggle Coverage Details

Using FSM Coverage
The default FSM page has two panes (see Figure Check FSM Coverage Details)
* The upper pane displays the state, transition, and sequence coverage for each FSM
with a percentage bar annotated with the total number of covered and uncovered
objects and the percentage of each.
* The lower pane displays transition or sequence results for all possibilities in a table or
list format.

Figure 19

Check FSM Coverage Details

Displaying Transition Details
Transition mode for the selected FSM displays all the possible transitions and indicates
whether the current state of the FSM made any of these transitions.
You can display the results in a table or list format. In the table format (opened by default),
select the States & Transitions mode in the Mode field.
In the list format, select the Transition mode in the Mode field.
Figure Check FSM Coverage Details shows the table view with states and transitions
displayed with covered transitions in green and uncovered transitions in red.
Transitions that are not possible are white with a dash.
To view the transition details in list format with coverage ranges, enable the Show as List
option.
Figure FSM Transition List shows transitions with the covered transitions displayed in
green and uncovered in red.
Transitions that are not possible are not listed in the table.

Figure 20

FSM Transition List

Displaying Sequences
Select the States & Sequences mode in the Mode field.
As shown in Figure FSM Sequence Table, the Sequences mode shows states and
sequences and their possible coverage numbers that an FSM can follow to go from one
state to another state.
Holding the cursor on a cell displays a tooltip showing the sequences and their coverage.
You must enable the sequences at compile-time with the -cm_fsmopt
sequence option to view sequences in the Verdi platform.
Figure 21

FSM Sequence Table

To view the state details in list format, enable the Show as List option.
Figure FSM Sequence List shows sequences with covered sequences displayed in green
and uncovered in red.

Figure 22

FSM Sequence List

Using Condition Coverage
The Condition page helps you monitor whether both true and false states of the conditional
expressions and sub-expressions in your code are covered.
See Figure Check Condition Coverage Details for the following actions:
* The Condition List pane expands to show coverage by possible vectors or subconditions, percent coverage, and the line number of the expression.
* Double-click an expression in the Condition List pane, and the expression is
highlighted with its coverage range in the Coverage source code pane.
* Select an expression in the Condition List pane, and the Expression Display pane
displays the selected expression above with possible conditions and their coverage
status below.

Figure 23

Check Condition Coverage Details

The Condition page also provides an observability feature to locate situations where a
certain part of the combinational circuit is controlling (and hence observable) the primary
output of the combinational circuit.
Certain vector combinations of a sub-expression is marked as covered only if that
combination is controlling the primary output in the context of the whole expression.
As shown in Figure Condition Coverage Observability, you can view the observability
expression in the Expression Display pane.
You must use the -cm cond and -cm_cond obs options at compile-time to
enable the observability based condition coverage and view the observability in
the Verdi platform.

Figure 24

Condition Coverage Observability

You can use the View -> Show Condition IDs command to show the condition names in
the Condition page of the CovDetail pane.
Figure 25

Showing Condition Names

Using Branch Coverage
The Branch page displays the coverage percentage for branch coverage. See Section
Check Branch Coverage Details for the following actions:
* The Detail List pane shows the items and branches of the selected scope.
Expand an item and select a branch, and then the value of the selected branch is
shown in the Value column of the lower pane.
* Double-click a branch to view the annotation in the Coverage Source Code pane for
the branch.

The corresponding statement in the source file is annotated to identify code that is
covered and that is not covered.
The source code lines are color-annotated according to their coverage values. You can
see only the line of branches as color-annotated and not the line of terms.
* The implied branches are shown in the Coverage source code pane only when you
view branch coverage or are analyzing the branch metric.
The implied branches of case and if statements are indicated by MISSING_ELSE and
MISSING_DEFAULT tags.

Using the Modules Tab
The Module tab displays coverage results by listing module definitions, variants for
parameterized modules and module instances and their total coverage score and
individual scores for line, toggle, FSM, condition, branch, and assert coverage. Click the
icon to the left of the module name to see the instances under it (see Figure Modules
Page).
Figure 28

Modules Page

The Modules page usage is the same as the Hierarchy page usage. Refer to the Using the
Hierarchy Tab section for details.

Hiding Module Variant Lines
The Modules tab of the Summary pane displays coverage results organized by module
definitions. For parameterized modules, a Variant level is introduced below each module,
grouping instances with different parameter values.
This structure can result in a deeply nested hierarchy, especially when there are many
parameter variations,
To address this, the Hide module variant items in module page option in there. When
enabled, this feature simplifies the view by hiding the variant-level items, allowing you to
focus directly on module definitions and their instances.
Steps to Enable
To enable this feature, perform the following steps:
1. Open Verdi Coverage and go to the Application Preferences dialog box.
2. Navigate to the Summary Table section.
3. Select the Hide module variant items in module page check box. This option is not
selected by default.

Using the Modules Tab

Figure 29

Application Preferences

4. After enabling the option, open your VDB file or reload it if already open.
Figure 30

Default Behavior

Figure 31

After Enabling Option and Reloading VDB

5. The Modules tab in the Summary pane hides module variant items for parameterized
modules. Only module definitions and instance coverage scores are displayed.

Filters in Cross Tables in the Coverage Detail Pane
Verdi has an advanced filter on bins in cross table for ease of analysis when there are a
large number of bins in a cross.
With the filter capability, you can easily search the bin items as per your requirements. It
also enables you to sort the items.
This capability is available in the CovDetail pane of Verdi Coverage.

and to filter based on s_HI, s_LO, and s_MID.
To sort the bins two options are available, that is Sort A to Z and Sort Z to A.

Determine Coverage by Test for a Coverpoint or Cross Bin
To see which tests have covered a specific bin of a coverpoint or cross, right-click the
bin in the CovDetail pane and select Show Associated Tests. This feature is especially
useful when you load a coverage database containing results from multiple tests, or a
merged database created using the -show tests option, into Verdi Coverage.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
For example, if you right-click the covered bin op2 of coverpoint B and select Show
Associated Tests, a list of all tests that have covered the op2 bin are displayed.

The list shows the test names (for example, simv.vdb/test1, simv.vdb/test3, and
simv.vdb/test4) along with their respective hit counts (for example, 22, 12, and 15).

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
If the -show tests option was not used when merging coverage databases, only the test
list of the merged database is displayed, along with the total hit count (for example, 49).

The Show Associated Tests feature is enabled only for covered objects. If the
"At Least" value is not 1 and a bin is uncovered (that is, Hit Count is less than
"At Least"), this feature is disabled.

Changing Coverage Aggregation Based on Metric Coverpoints
By default, coverage score is calculated based on the average coverage rate of a metric.
However, coverage metric with higher coverage points must impact coverage score
than the one with lower coverage points. Therefore, Verdi Coverage enables you to
automatically set weight according to metric coverpoints.

Setting Weight Based on Metric Coverpoints
To automatically set weight according to the number of coverage points, perform the
following steps in the Verdi Coverage GUI:
1. Select Tools > Preference to display the Application Preferences dialog box.
2. In the dialog box figure (Application Preferences), select the following check box from
the Summary Table category:
Automatically set weight according to metric coverpoints
This option is disabled by default.

(69.89%*641)+(50.66%*1662)+(43.82%*89)+(33.98%*462)+(57.77%*296)+(20%*

and Statistics tabs in the Summary pane. Other areas, such as URG, or Verdi Source

The Functional Code Coverage Auto Generation utility generates partial code to define
covergroups, coverpoints, and coverage cross coverpoints. This definition is based on a
configuration file provided to the utility in CSV format. The code generated with this utility

is pseudo code, but is very close to the actual SystemVerilog code. The following is the
covergroup definition from the SystemVerilog LRM:
Figure 56

Covergroup Definition in LRM

The following sections describe the CSV input file format.
They also cover command line and GUI usage, possible output and error messages, and
utility limitations:
* Format of the Configuration File
* Running the Functional Code Coverage Auto Generation Utility
* Limitations of Functional Code Coverage Auto Generation

Format of the Configuration File
The CSV configuration file used as input can support the following types of covergroups:
* Single and multiple class
* Single and multiple variable
* Mixed class and variable

Corresponding to the covergroups mentioned above, a CSV file can be composed of the
following three types of tables:
* Covergroup
* Var Type Covergroup
* Class Type Covergroup
Covergroup Table

var
class

Field

Input type for the covergroup.
var implies variable type, for example,
bit[4:0]. Class is a type that includes data and
subroutines (functions and tasks) that operate
on this data.

Required for the class type while it is optional for
the var type.

option

Implies the covergroup option and is optional.

Description of the Var Type Covergroup Table Fields

Field

The coverage specification name should start

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The utility supports bins, ignore_bins, illegal_bins, wildcard bins, and transition
bins. It recognizes the ignore_bins, illegal_bins, and wildcard bins by using
the #, ##, and ? symbols respectively. Four patterns, including =>, [, [->, [=
with parentheses added for the whole transition bins, are used to recognize
the transition bins. Cross bins support logic operators, including &&, ||, and !.
All these logic operators can be used separately. The ! symbol can be used
along with && or ||. The number of bins should be less than pow (2, type_limit
+ 1), for example, for val type bit[4:0], the upper limit of the number of bins

title: Verification ContinuumTM

Running the Functional Code Coverage Auto Generation Utility
This utility can be executed in both command line and GUI modes:
Running the Utility in Command Line Mode
code_gen -c cg_gen_multiclass.csv -f covergroup.sv

* code_gen is the executable code.
* .csv is the format of the input support configuration file.
* covergroup.sv is the default output file name. The output file name can also be
specified.

Running the Utility in GUI Mode
By default, the Generate Covergroupoption in the Tools menu is disabled. To enable
this feature, set VDCOV_GENERATE_COVERGROUP_ENABLE to 1. Then, perform the following
steps:
1. To display the covergroup generating dialog box, click Generate Covergroup
Figure 58

Covergroup Generating Dialog Box

2. To load the configuration file, click the Config File button.
Figure 59

Loading the Configuration File

The utility supports the CSV and JSON formats of the configuration file.

3. To add the configuration file in the Config table, select the file in the dialog box and
click Open. The content in the Config table is read-only and can only be updated by
loading a configuration file.

Messages Output
Messages, including errors, warnings and info are logged in the Message window. For
some critical messages, warnings are displayed to inform users immediately.

Limitations of Functional Code Coverage Auto Generation
The following are the limitations of functional code auto generation:
* The Functional Code Coverage Auto Generation utility does not support a mixed input
of class and interface.
This limitation applies to the autogen covergroup.
* Code_gen does not check the syntax correctness of the input CSV values. For example,
event, option, and bins cannot guarantee that the generated .sv file can compile
successfully
* The syntactical level (covergroup, coverpoint, or cross) in type options is not supported
yet.
* It is meaningless to use && along with || for cross bins.
Only the first logical operator && or || is recognized.
* A covergroup does not support multiple options.

Using Verification Planner
The Verdi platform also provides the Verification Planner feature to help you focus on a
hierarchical verification plan and manage the specification for higher coverage.
The verification planner (HVP planner) in Verdi Coverage allows you to create a specific
plan to measure what is important for each design. It also supports accountability, so that
what gets measured gets done. Plans should be created as early as possible to determine
the important metrics. As the design progresses, this helps ensure important plan features
are not forgotten. Verification plans can be saved into a readable format, for you to present
to management. This keeps everyone informed about the coverage plan.
In this chapter, you are able to:
* Associate a plan with multiple specs.
* Link a feature to multiple sections in the spec.
* Link a section in the specification with multiple features.
This chapter encompasses the following sections:
* Using the Layout

Auto-Saving Option for HVP Editor
Verdi Coverage provides an Autosave feature with the HVP editor that helps prevent data
loss if the tool crashes for some reason. Verdi performs an autosave in the background
every 5 minutes.
However, the original .hvp and .spc files does not change until you click Plan > Save.
Consider an example of a plan named MyPlan.hvp. If you choose the Recover option,
the tool loads the HVP data from .MyPlan.hvp and .MyPlan.hvp.spc. Verdi Coverage does
NOT modify the original MyPlan.hvp until you perform Plan > Save.

Preference Setting for AutoSave
You can use the preference setting shown in Figure Autosave Preferences to enable or
disable Autosave and also modify the Autosave interval.

Autosave Preferences

Recovering/Discarding Data From an Autosave
Consider an example where you are editing MyPlan.hvp. If you exit Coverage without
saving it or if there is a crash, Verdi created the files .MyPlan.hvp and .Myplan.hvp.spc
automatically in the background.
When you open this plan the next time, Verdi checks whether the .MyPlan.hvp file exists; if
the file exists and the modified date of the hidden file is later than the file MyPlan.hvp, the
following warning message is shown:
Figure 70

Recover/Discard/Cancel Autosaved Data

In this scenario, you can:
* Click the Recover button to load the Autosave data.
* Click the Discard button to discard the Autosave data and load MyPlan.hvp.
* Click the Cancel button to cancel the opening of the HVP file.
After you select an option and confirmed, the .MyPlan.hvp file is deleted.

Save Behavior
The plan is saved in the definition order by default. A dialog box opens when you try to
save the plan that is sorted in the ascending or descending order.

The sorted column and order are not saved in the configuration file, novas.rc, which
saves only the default column width and position.
The current sort order is saved in the bookmark and in the session file, novasLog/
vdCov_autosave.ses, which saves the column width, position, the name of the sorted
column, and the sort order.
You can restore the information by reopening the session file.

Limitation
The following operations in the ascending and descending orders are not supported for the
undo and redo functions:
* Drag and drop
* Copy, cut, and paste
* Delete item
* Add item
* Move up or move down
If the current sort order is ascending or descending, and if the undo and redo
commands are not supported in this order, the HVP list view disables the undo
and redo operations.

Disabling Default Expansion
When you open a plan through the Plan Explorer (DB mode), the Plan menu (file mode),
or by refreshing a project to reload plans in DB mode, the plan tree displays in an
expanded state by default. The tree expands down to the first level of items, showing
features and subplans immediately.

Figure 76

Expanded Plan Tree

This default behavior eliminates the need to manually expand the plan tree after each
open or refresh operation, allowing you to begin reviewing plan content immediately.
However, if you prefer the plan to open in a collapsed state, you can disable the default
expansion behavior by performing the following steps:
1. Open the Verdi Coverage preferences by selecting Tools > Preferences.
2. Navigate to the Plan View section.
3. Enable the option to keep the legacy collapsed behavior on plan open.
Plan View Scoring Options
The Plan View category also provides the following scoring preferences. After you change
either preference, click the Recalculate icon in the Hvp pane to refresh scores.
* Level Score column -- Displays an optional Level Score column by default before
the Score column. At plan and feature levels, Level Score is the average of child Level
Scores. See Displaying the Level Score Column in Plan View.
* Include test.percent.pass metric into Level Score/Score -- Includes the
test.percent.pass metric in Score and Level Score calculations. See Including
test.percent.pass in Score and Level Score.

Expanding to a Specific Hierarchy Level
Verdi Coverage provides context menu options and keyboard shortcuts for controlling
the expansion level of the plan tree in the Hvp pane. These options allow you to quickly
expand or collapse the tree to a specific hierarchy level without manually expanding each
node.

You can expand the entire plan tree to a specific hierarchy level by right-clicking in the Hvp
pane and selecting one of the following context menu options:
Table 5

Plan Tree Expansion Options

Context Menu Option

Expand Plan To Feature Level

Expands the plan tree to the feature level. Any expanded measure
and source items are collapsed. This provides a feature-oriented
overview of the plan.

Expand Plan To Measure Level

Expands the plan tree to include measures under each feature,
providing visibility into the coverage metrics associated with each
feature.

Expand Plan To Source Level

Expands the plan tree fully to include source items under each
measure, showing the complete hierarchy of the plan.

Figure 77

Plan Tree Expansion Options

Expanding a Selected Node by Levels
You can expand a specific selected node in the plan tree to a given depth using the
Expand Node by Levels context menu option. This applies the expansion only to the
selected node and its descendants, rather than to the entire plan tree.

Keyboard Shortcuts in Verdi Coverage
This section provides the keyboard shortcuts that are available when working with plans
in the in the Hvp pane and related views in Verdi Coverage. For example, Ctrl+S saves a
plan and Ctrl+F shows or hides the search widget (unified find), matching Verdi debugger
behavior for search.
If you used earlier releases, note that Ctrl+S no longer toggles the search
widget. Use Ctrl+F instead. Shift+F no longer creates a new feature; use Ctrl
+H.
Some shortcuts apply only when plans are stored as local .hvp files (file-based mode),
only when plans are managed on a Verification Management System (VMS) server

(server-based or DB mode), or in both situations (mixed mode). The following modes
determine which plan shortcuts are active:
* File-based mode (default): plans are local .hvp files.
* Server-based (DB) mode: plans are stored on a VMS server, for example when
SNPS_HVP_VMS_ENABLED is set or -vms is used on the command line.
* Mixed mode: both file-based and server-based plan operations are available; shortcuts
for both groups are enabled.
The bindkey values and menu names can be customized through the Customize Menu/
Toolbar command. For more information, see the User Interface chapter in the Verdi User
Guide and Tutorial.

Displaying Source Patterns as a Column
You can display source information directly in the plan tree by enabling the optional
Source Patterns column in the Hvp pane. This column shows the source patterns
associated with each measure, providing quick visibility into source mapping without
expanding individual nodes.

Figure 79

Source Patterns Column

Enabling the Source Patterns Column
The Source Patterns column is disabled by default. To enable it, click the corresponding
toggle button (

) in the Hvp view toolbar.

When enabled, the column appears in the plan tree view and is configurable (for
example, you can resize or reposition it). The column is read-only and its content updates
automatically when the plan is updated or refreshed.

Source Patterns Column Content
The Source Patterns column displays source information only at the measure level. Cells
at other hierarchy levels (plan, feature, subplan) remain blank.
Each source entry uses the format <source_type> : <pattern>. The following are
examples of source pattern values:
* instance : top.fifo
* cover group : tb_top::mod1.cg1

When a measure has multiple sources, each source is displayed on a separate line within
the cell. You can use the Wrap Text option for the column to display the full content of
cells with multiple sources.
Figure 80

Wrap Text of the Source Patterns Column

If a source pattern is too long to display in the available column width, the value is
truncated with an ellipsis (). You can hover over the cell to view the full source pattern
in a tooltip.
If a measure has no valid source, the cell remains empty.

You can add features in a planner from the compiled result in the Verdi platform. You
can also add them from the coverage database or directly from design to strengthen
the current coverage. When the database is loaded into Verdi Coverage, the status of
current coverage is displayed in the Coverage mode. Verdi Coverage provides a method
to directly add the weak sources to a planner.

You can also link to spec-based PDF files for features in the HVP planner. This populates
the plan in the Hvp pane with a requirement specification already written by the designer.
You can then link the specification with the feature. This ensures that requirements in
the design specification are not forgotten or lost. They are incorporated in the verification
plan. After the feature setting in the Hvp pane is complete, you can link a requirements
specification for the feature. Use the spec-linking feature of Verdi Coverage.
Additionally, the explicit structure of Hvp hierarchy is also provided. After you add a feature
or sub-plan, the numbering of added item is automatically numbered.
The following sections describe these methods to add features:
* Adding Features From Coverage Database
* Adding Features From the Design
* Specification Linking in Planner
* Running a Specification Review
* Configuring the Linked Feature
* Measure Concealment in Reports

Adding Features From Coverage Database
When the coverage database is loaded into Verdi Coverage, you can use the following
method to add features:
* Drag an item (source) from the tabs in the Summary pane and drop to the planner row
in the Hvp pane.
As shown in Figure Create a New Feature from Summary, a new feature is created
with its numbering, the measure and source.
Figure 81

Create a New Feature from Summary

* Select the plan in the Hvp pane. Select a source in the Modules, Groups, or Asserts
tabs of the Summary pane and use the Add to Plan command in the right-click
command menu.
* Select the plan in the Hvp pane. Select a source in the Hierarchy pages of the
Summary pane and use the Add Instance to Plan or Add Tree to Plan commands
in the right-click command menu to add the instance or the entire hierarchy of the
selected source to the plan.
* Drag a named object from the Line, Toggle, FSM, and Condition tabs of the CovDetail
pane and drop to the row of the plan in the Hvp pane.
For example, you can drag a named line from the Line page or a variable from the

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
selected source to the plan.
* Drag a named object from the Line, Toggle, FSM, and Condition tabs of the CovDetail
pane and drop to the row of the plan in the Hvp pane.
For example, you can drag a named line from the Line page or a variable from the
Toggle page and drop it to the selected plan in the Hvp pane.
Alternatively, use the Add Tree to Plan right-click command to add the selected object
to the Hvp planner.
For the UPF power plan, you can drag a Covergroup or a Coverpoint from the
CovDetail pane and drop to the row of the plan in the Hvp pane.
If the source is a group or assert, Group or Assert is automatically specified as the metric
of the new measure.
If the source comes from the Hierarchy tab, the Modules tab or the Verdi platform, all code
coverage metrics included in the database are automatically specified for the measure.
When multiple sources are dragged and then dropped to a planner, sources are combined
under the measure (refer to Figure Select Multiple Sources).
Figure 82

Select Multiple Sources

You can use the Rename command in the right-click menu of the Hvp pane to rename the
plan, feature, measure, or source names.

Additionally, the numbering of each feature can be modified using the commands in the
right-click menu (see Figure Numbering Setting):
* Restart at 1: Set the numbering starting from 1.
* Continue Numbering: Reset the numbering to automatic setting.
* Set Numbering Value: Specify a numbering.

a New Feature icon, Verdi inserts the feature as the last child feature item of the
selected parent item (plan/feature).

created. With the new Create Sibling Feature icon in the Hvp pane, there is no need to
reselect the parent feature for each new sibling feature.

Adding Features From the Design
You can also create features and add them to a plan directly from instances, modules,
groups, and asserts directly from the design. You can select an instance sub-tree, create
features in a plan based on that sub-tree and then map them.

Creating a New Feature and Sibling Features
You can create a feature tree mapping of a selected leaf instance or instances included
in the tree under the leaf instance, using the following steps. The order of selection in
summary table and plan does not affect the result.
1. Select an instance for which you want to create a feature in the plan, in the Hierarchy
tab and right-click on it as shown in Figure Selecting the Level of Sub-Instances. If you
want to select all the instances included in the tree under the leaf instance, then select
the menu item Select by Levels -> All.
You can also select multiple instances using the Ctrl or Shift keys.

Figure 84

Selecting the Level of Sub-Instances

2. After you have selected the instance(s) in the Hierarchy tab, select the plan into which
these features should be added in the Hvp tab. In this case, the features should be
added to the plan named New_Plan.
3. After both the plan and the instances are selected, right-click on the selected
instance(s) and select either the Clone Hierarchy to Features or Clone Hierarchy to
Sibling Features menu options.
The Clone Hierarchy to Features menu option creates a new feature under the
plan New_Plan that measures selected coverage items. The Clone Hierarchy to
Sibling Features menu option creates a new sibling feature of the selected feature
that measures selected coverage items.

The following sections describe the position, order, and naming of the features created:
Position of the New Feature(s)
* Create Features: The newly created features are the last child of the parent (selected
item).
* Create Sibling Features: The newly created sibling features are the closest sibling of
the selected item. This is also applicable for multiple selection support.
Order of the New Feature(s)
The order of new features is the same as the order in which you select the instances using
the Ctrl key. When you select multiple instances using the Shift key, the resultant features
are ordered top-to-bottom.
Naming of New Features
By default, the name of a new feature is the name of the instance from the design
hierarchy. However, if the name is a keyword in the HVP language such as test
or feature, it is renamed by adding a suffix _renamed. For example, if a feature is
created from an instance named feature, the feature that is created from it is named
feature_renamed. You are notified of this change with warning message similar to the
following one, in the message window.

'feature' is a keyword and cannot be used as a feature name. It is
renamed to 'feature_renamed'.

Specification Linking in Planner
Verdi Planner enables you to track a verification project and ensures that all its verification
goals are achieved. It allows you to create a hierarchical verification plan to measure what
is important for each project.
A linked and executable verification plan ties every part of the original written specification
and test plan documents to their corresponding verification goals.
The following figure shows how the verification specifications, plans, and data come
together to track progress and status of the verification project:

Links to the specifications ensure that every feature in the specification has a
corresponding feature in the plan.
Links to verification data ensure that anything below target (low coverage, tests failing, and
so on) is presented and linked to the corresponding features to highlight needed actions.

Specification Linking Count
Verdi Coverage provides a set of link count attributes with the spec_link_count prefix.
These attributes identify all linked specifications with a plan. These attributes show the
number of links to a feature or sub-feature from a given specification document. These
attributes are automatically created when you associate specifications with the plan. You
can link the plan with more than one specification.
The number of associated specifications determines the number of spec_link_count
attributes in the plan. Each specification generates only one spec_link_count attribute.

The initial value of this attribute is zero. It gets updated when a plan feature links to or
unlinks from the specification. You cannot edit this attribute. It is automatically populated
when the specification is linked with its associated text.
When you associate a specification file with a plan, Verdi Coverage generates the
spec_link_count_<filename> attribute. This attribute counts the number of links in the
specification from the plan. The type of this attribute is integer. Its propagation is set to no.
The value does not propagate to the child node. The attribute is available in the Hvp pane
and in the Attributes section of the HvpDetail pane as shown in the following figure:

You can use the spec_link_count attribute for quick filtering and for creating modifiers,
like any other integer-valued attribute. To use the spec_link_count attribute, filter only
the features that link to a specific specification. For example, consider the following filter
statement:
remove feature where spec_link_count_my_doc == 0;

In the example, the statement creates a filtered plan with only features that link to the
my_doc specification.
For details on filters and modifiers, see the Using Modifiers section.

Excluding Ignore Sections From the Specification Coverage
Computation
Computing specification coverage for all features in the specification requires them to be
verified against the corresponding features in the verification plans. Normally for SoClevel testing, it is not required to verify IP-level features; therefore, these features of the
specification are not relevant for calculating specification coverage. Using specification
linking, you can search for these irrelevant sections in the entire specification and mark
them as ignored.
Previously, specification total lines were used as a denominator for calculating
specification coverage as follows:
Denominator = Total Lines
Uncovered Lines = Total Lines - Linked Lines - Todo Lines - Ignored Lines

Now, specification linking can exclude ignored sections from the specification total lines
and use its result as a denominator for calculating coverage as follows:
Denominator = Total Lines - Ignored Lines
Uncovered Lines = Total Lines - Linked Lines - Todo Lines - Ignored Lines

Color Settings of a Verification Plan
Verdi enables you to update the color settings of verification plans, their sub-plans,
specification linking colors, and coverage colors. To update the color settings, perform the
1. Click Tools > Preferences to open the Application Preferences form.
2. In the Plan View Category, select Spec Colors or Plan Colors as per your
requirement:
Select Spec Colors to update the color settings of Linked, Ignore, and Todo text
of top and sub plans in a PDF document.
Select Plan Colors to update the color settings of sub-plans, inactive cells, warning
and error messages, and an invalid score of an item in the Hvp pane.
3. To change spec-linking colors, select Spec Colors to show the following list:

An example of the PDF document after setting its color using Spec Colors is shown in
the following figure:

4. To change plan colors, select Plan Colors to show the following list:

An example of plan colors is shown in the following figure:

You can also change coverage colors to update the color settings of uncovered, partially
covered, and covered objects. Also, you can update the color settings of excluded and
covered, excluded and uncovered, and unreachable objects. To change coverage colors,
select the Coverage Colors category from the Application Preferences dialog box as
shown in the following figure:

Specification Linking With Coverage-Based Color Coding
The coverage-based color coding feature in Verdi Coverage enhances the visualization
of linked sections in specification documents. This feature assigns distinct colors to linked
sections based on the coverage score of the associated feature, making it easier to
identify uncovered, partially covered, and fully covered sections.
Follow these steps to enable and configure coverage-based color coding in specification
linking:
1. Click Tools > Preferences to open the Application Preferences dialog box.
2. In the Plan View category, select Spec Colors. Select the Enable color coding for
linked sections check box. By default, it is deselected.

Figure 100

Color Coding for Linked Sections

3. Set the Threshold score(%) to define the boundary between partial coverage levels.
For example:
Uncovered: 0.00% coverage.
Partial Covered #1: Coverage between 0.00% and T.
Partial Covered #2: Coverage between T and 100.00%.
Fully Covered: 100.00% coverage.
4. Assign colors to each coverage level. Use the color picker in the Application
Preferences dialog box to select your preferred colors.
5. Click OK to save your preferences.
This feature is useful for quickly identifying the coverage status of individual features and
their linked sections in the plan view. The annotated overall score for each HVP feature
is divided into four levels 0.00%, (0.00%, T), (T, 100.00%), and 100.00%. If the plan does
not have an overall annotated score, the feature is ignored, and all linked sections use the
default color scheme. Sections linked to multiple features or overlapping linked sections
display an accumulated color. For example, overlapping light green sections appear as
dark green.

Figure 101

Overlapping Colors

Limitations

Running a Specification Review
When you have an updated specification, you can update and review the linked
specification in the Spec Review Window.
There might be some mismatched and missing sections of the linking features between
the new and linked specifications. In these cases, unresolved sections have to be
reviewed.

The following sections describe how you can use this feature to perform the specification
review.

Using the Specification Review Flow
To start reviewing a specification, select a plan in the HVP tab and perform the following
steps:
1. Select the linked specification you want to inspect and review it in the Spec Files tab of
the HvpDetail pane. Refer to Figure Select a New Specification.
2. Click the
icon and select the specification file you want to compare in the invoked
Choose a spec file dialog box.
3. Click the Open button.

Select a New Specification

4. The Spec Review Window form opens with the comparison between the current and
the new specifications. An example is shown in Figure Spec Review Window.

Spec Review Window

The status field of the selected current specification is changed to Updating.
Figure 104

Status Field

The Current spec and New spec fields show the paths of the current and new
specifications.
The Review Summary field (as shown in Figure Review Summary) in the Spec Review
Window shows how many unresolved sections need to be reviewed, including mismatched
and missing ones.

Review Summary

The matched, unmatched, new, or missing sections or lines are identified. The current
specification is annotated for the unresolved section links and the new specification is

Reviewing Specifications
In the Spec Review Window, you can click the Previous or Next button to find out and
check the previous or next unresolved section.
After checking it, you can use the Accept or Reject buttons to accept or reject the
mappings of the mismatched section links from the current specification to the new one.
For missing sections, you can only use the Reject button to reject it.
You can also use the Accept All and Reject All buttons to accept and reject all
unresolved sections.
After you accept or reject a mapped section, the Review Summary field is also updated
accordingly to show one less unresolved section.
After all the unresolved sections are reviewed and either accepted or rejected, the
Matched number in the Review Summary field displays 0 and disappears to signify that
there are no more updated sections to review.
You can click the Close button to stop review in the invoked Spec Review form.
When your review has no remaining conflicts, the following dialog box opens.

If you want to accept the updates during the review, click the Accept button. The linked
specification in the HVP planner is updated to the new one.
If you want to cancel updating the specification, you can click the Revert button to cancel
all decisions (accepted or rejected) made in this reviewing.
The linked specification remains the original one. The status is changed to `Linked' after
clicking either Accept or Revert the buttons.
Figure 109

Linked Status

Click Cancel to return to the review window.
When a review still has some unresolved sections, the following dialog box opens.

Click the Close button to close the review first and click the
later.

icon to continue the review

Click the Revert button to stop the review and revert the linked specification to the
previous version. You can also click the Cancel button to return to the current review. You

can click the review undo icon in the Hvp pane to undo the following actions during the
review:
* Start a specification review with a new specification
* Review all unresolved sections.
* Complete the review and the old specification is replaced by the new one.
Limitations of the Specification Review Flow
Only text in a document can be selected manually. This excludes text that cannot be
selected in tables. Images can also not be selected manually.

Measure Concealment in Reports
Currently, HVP provides the flexibility to create multiple measures and metric sources
within features. Though this flexibility is useful for many HVP use models, it might produce
complex reports for simple models. HVP is now enhanced to simplify usage and reporting
for portions of the plan that follow a simplified pattern of a single source for each feature.
This is referred to as a 1:1:1 feature because one feature contains one measure and one
source.

You can conceal a measure in a report if a feature qualifies the 1:1:1 compression. Verdi
can infer from the structure of the feature whether it is qualified for the 1:1:1 compression.
To qualify for the compression, the feature should meet the following criteria:
1. The feature is a leaf feature, that is, it does not contain any subfeature.
2. The feature contains exactly one measure.
3. The measure contains exactly one source.
4. The source name should not contain wildcard and regular expressions.
For example, the following feature is qualified for the 1:1:1 compression:
feature cd;
Metrics = "Line, Cond";
measure test Measure_1;
source = "cd";

The HVP planner cannot store items that it does not recognize. The following are the
various ways to generate XML files which can be loaded to Verdi:
* Use the command Save As to save an XML file without the skipped contents. See
Saving the Plan.
* Use the command hvp genxls -plan <plan_file> to generate an XML file without

* Use the csv2hvp_DPTX.py utility to convert a CSV verification plan to Excel XML and

You can also generate a report in the XML Spreadsheet 2003 format from an existing HVP
file by using the Plan -> Report command. The generated report is for viewing purposes
only, it cannot be loaded into Verdi Coverage as an HVP file.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The csv2hvp_DPTX.py utility converts a CSV verification plan into an XML Spreadsheet
2003 file for use with Verdi Coverage and Verdi Verification Management System (VMS).
When VCS_HOME is set, the utility also runs hvp annotate to produce an HVP plan file that
can be loaded in Verdi Coverage.
This methodology converts a verification plan into the HVP format supported by Verdi
VMS. The utility generates the Excel XML plan and hvp annotate converts that XML
to HVP. Loading the plan into Verdi Coverage or uploading it to VMS is a separate step.
For details on annotation and loading Excel XML plans, see User Data As a Spreadsheet
Worksheet and Generating the HVP Excel XML Plan With Report.
The output is a standard Excel XML plan, not the extended loadable report format
produced by hvp genxls -report or Verdi Coverage save-report with Loadable set to
Yes. For details on the loadable report format, see Generating the HVP Excel XML Plan
With Report.
* Prerequisites
* Running the Utility
* Plan Data CSV Format
* Attribute Definition CSV (Optional)
* Attribute Name Sanitization Rules
* Output Files
* Limitations
* Loading the Generated Plan in Verdi Coverage

Prerequisites
Before running the utility, ensure that the following prerequisites are met:
* Python 3.x
* VCS_HOME environment variable set. This is required only for automatic .hvp file
generation. When VCS_HOME is not set, only the .xml output is produced.
For VCS and Verdi Coverage version compatibility when loading generated plans, see
User Data As a Spreadsheet Worksheet.

Running the Utility
Run the utility from the command line as follows:
python3 csv2hvp_DPTX.py \
-input_file_path <plan_csv_file> \
-output_dir <output_directory> \
[-attr_def_file_path <attribute_definition_csv_file>]

The following table describes the command arguments:
Table 11

csv2hvp_DPTX.py Arguments

Argument

Required

Yes

Path to the input CSV file
containing the verification plan
data.

-output_dir

Yes

Directory where the output
.xml (and .hvp if VCS is
available) files are written.
The directory is created
automatically if it does not
exist.

-attr_def_file_path

No

Path to a CSV file containing
attribute type definitions. If
omitted, all attributes are

Example (Linux)
python3 csv2hvp_DPTX.py \
-input_file_path /home/user/plans/dptx_plan.csv \
-output_dir /home/user/plans/output \

Example (Windows)
python3 csv2hvp_DPTX.py \
