Viewing the Hold Time Pair for a Fault
In Verdi-Coverage, you can use the keyboard shortcut key Shift+Ctrl to select multiple
faults and click the Update hold-time-pairs button on the detail fault GUI to see the hold
time of faults.
For the display of Hold Time Pair (HTP) for the fault, the following points should be
considered:
* Open the nWave window and load the FSDB file.
* You can open multiple nWave windows but only the Primary nWave window shows
HTP. The primary waveform is annotated with a red square on the lower-right corner of
the waveform window. By default, the first nWave window to be invoked is the primary
window.
* You can open multiple FSDB files in same nWave window but only one file is active. To
view the active file, choose nWave > File > Active File. The HTP displayed in primary
nWave window is cleared, if you change the Active file.
The following are the steps to display HTP in the nWave window:
1. Double-click a module in the FaultSummary frame to open the FaultDetail View.
2. Open the nWave window and add a signal, for example, cmp[31:0].
3. Select a fault and click the RMB option Display HTP in nWave Window.

4. You can view the HTP in the nWave window.

5. Begin-end time range on the waveform can be seen in the waveform as follows:
The solid line denotes start time (inject time) and the dashed line denotes end time
(release time). The line uses the fault-status color. Long dash orange line means
more than one event (inject or release) occurring at the same time.
Number labels denote lines (Hold Time Pair) that can be overlaid together.
Shade color is used for background, fault-status color for non-overlap range, gray
color for the overlapped range.

The ability to compare FSDB files is imperative in being able to validate the data being
generated by the dumper/FSDB file. Verdi supports comparing the FSDB data generated
through new methods with FSDB files generated by existing features, and also to be able
to detect potential differences when code is updated or fixed.
nCompare provides the following features:
* Command line option to specific faultId which needs to be compared
Syntax
nCompare [-wave waveform_file1 [-wave waveform_file2] [-faultId
fault_id1 [-faultId fault_id2]]

Displaying Error in nWave
The pattern of diverge range and mismatch range are the same, which results in the
inability to distinguish the diverge range and mismatch range. So the diverge range pattern
is changed to "SLANT_RIGHT" when signal need to show mismatch.
* Second signal:
FM pattern: ID_RED5, SLANT_RIGHT
Mismatch pattern: ID_RED5, SLANT_LEFT
* Golden signal:
FM pattern: ID_RED5, SLANT_LEFT

Limitation
When the golden FSDB file and the second FSDB file are the same, only the second FM
value can be displayed in nWave.

There are %d pairs having no FM in golden signal, %d pairs having no FM in
secondary signal, %d pairs having no FM in both signals.
Displaying Error in nWave
The pattern of diverge range and mismatch range are the same, which results in the
inability to distinguish the diverge range and mismatch range. So the diverge range pattern
is changed to "SLANT_RIGHT" when signal need to show mismatch.
* Second signal:
FM pattern: ID_RED5, SLANT_RIGHT
Mismatch pattern: ID_RED5, SLANT_LEFT
* Golden signal:
FM pattern: ID_RED5, SLANT_LEFT

Limitation
When the golden FSDB file and the second FSDB file are the same, only the second FM
value can be displayed in nWave.

Overview

Overview
An FSDB file might contain the following three types of information:
* Design Hierarchies
* User-Defined Data Types
* Value changes
The FSDB Reader reports design hierarchies and user-defined data types to your
application through a tree callback function. It reports value changes through a valuechange traverse handle, which lets you move forward and backward through value
changes.
Your application typically implements the tree callback function. It must accept the
following three parameters:
1. Callback type indicating callback data
2. Client data registered by the application using the ffrOpen() or ffrOpen2() call
3. Callback data
Cast the callback data to the structure that matches the callback type so you can read the
correct values.

Design Hierarchies
After you traverse design hierarchies in a tree callback function, the FSDB Reader does
not keep them in memory as well-defined data structures. Your application must store
them in memory if you need them later.
In FSDB, each unique variable has a unique id code. Keep the id code for each variable
because it is the key for value-change traverse. In general, store all id codes your
application needs.

User-Defined Data Types
FSDB supports user-defined data types mainly for VHDL. VHDL lets you define
enumeration types, physical types, and similar constructs.
FSDB stores each data-type definition and assigns it a data-type id code. Each variable
has an associated data-type id code so your application knows how to display value
changes for user-defined types.
The FSDB Reader reports user-defined data types to your application through the tree
callback function.

Opening the FSDB File

For FSDB version 1.x, user-defined data types are stored within design hierarchies. For
version 2.x, FSDB stores them separately. If you use FSDB 2.x, call the appropriate API to
read user-defined data types.
To traverse value changes for a variable, you need its id code. Create a value-change
traverse handle using that id code. Then use the traverse functions on the handle to move
forward and backward through value changes.

Value changes
Your application can create more than one value-change traverse handle with the same id
code. Each handle provides a different view of value changes for the same variable.
Each value-change traverse handle has an internal index that points to the current time
and value change. Move this index forward or backward to traverse value changes.

Opening the FSDB File
To open an FSDB file, use ffrOpen or ffrOpen2. The difference between ffrOpen
and ffrOpen2 is that ffrOpen activates the registered tree callback function during
the call, whereas ffrOpen2 does not activate the function. From FSDB version 2.0,
the FSDB Reader supports the reading of scope hierarchies and variables. Therefore,
ffrOpen2 is mainly for the FSDB file in version 2.0 or higher, and the application can
call ffrReadScopeTree to read scope hierarchies and ffrReadVarByLogUOff to read
variables.

Traversing Design Hierarchies

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
pe hierarchies and variables. Therefore,
ffrOpen2 is mainly for the FSDB file in version 2.0 or higher, and the application can
call ffrReadScopeTree to read scope hierarchies and ffrReadVarByLogUOff to read
variables.

Traversing Design Hierarchies
Design hierarchies are read using the tree callback function. The application defines
the tree callback function and notifies the FSDB Reader where it is by calling ffrOpen
or ffrOpen2 (this is called "registration"). During the call of ffrOpen, the FSDB Reader
activates the registered tree callback function to notify the application what it has read.
This is done via the two parameters: callback type and callback data. The mapping
between the tree callback type and the tree callback data can be referenced at Appendix
B. During the call of ffrOpen2, the FSDB Reader does not activate the registered tree
callback function. Instead, the application must call the specific API to activate the tree
callback function, such as:
* ffrReadScopeTree: To know scope hierarchies.
* ffrReadScopeVarTree: To know both scope hierarchies and their signals.
* ffrReadDataTypeByBlkIdx: To know user-defined data types.

Multiple Tree Issues

The following code example describes the above feature:
bool_T MyTreeCBFunc(fsdbTreeCBType cb_type, void *client_data, void
*cb_data)
{
switch (cb_type) {
case FSDB_TREE_CBT_BEGIN_TREE: break;
case FSDB_TREE_CBT_SCOPE: {
fsdbTreeCBDataScope *scope =(fsdbTreeCBDataScope*)cb_data
//Access scope definition through the "scope" pointer
}
case FSDB_TREE_CBT_VAR: {
fsdbTreeCBDataVar *var = (fsdbTreeCBDataVar*)cb_data;
// access var definition through "var" pointer
}

}
}
int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
ffrObject *obj = ffrOpen("sample.fsdb", MyTreeCBFunc, NULL);
}

The application defines its tree callback function as MyTreeCBFunc and notifies the FSDB
Reader where the function is by calling ffrOpen (registration). During the call of ffrOpen,
the FSDB Reader notifies the application what it has read by calling the tree callback
function defined by the application, that is MyTreeCBFunc.

Multiple Tree Issues
Sometimes simulators have some limitations and cannot dump all signals into a single
tree. Such usage might cause multiple trees in an FSDB file. For example, a Verilog
dumper and a SystemC dumper in the same process might have to dump their data into
the same FSDB file. In this case, there are at least two trees: one for Verilog and one for
SystemC. The tree callback function of the application takes this issue into consideration
and does not assume that all signals are in a single tree.
Possible scenarios of the multiple tree usage are as follows:
* Multiple trees but scopes do not overlap.
This is the most common case. Two FSDB dumpers dump their data separately and
just share the same FSDB file. Such trees are as follows:
Scope A
Signal A1

Traversing Value Changes

Scope B
Signal B1

* Multiple trees and scopes overlap.
This is also possible scenario. An FSDB dumper is unable to query all signals in a
scope and needs to reenter the same scope to dump additional data later. It often
happens in testbench dumping. Such trees are as follows:
Scope A
Signal A1
Scope A
Signal A2

* Multiple trees and scopes/signals overlap.
This should not happen. A signal should have a unique copy of the definition. However,
some FSDB dumpers might go wrong and generate such FSDB files. This cannot
be prevented by the FSDB writer. The FSDB Reader ignores such signals if they are
detected. Such trees are as follows:
Scope A
Signal A1
Scope A
Signal A1

Traversing Value Changes
Traversing value changes is done via the value-change traverse class defined by the
FSDB Reader. The ffrVCIterOne class contains numerous member functions to traverse
the value changes back and forth. In the tree callback function, the application knows
the id code of each variable. These id codes are important because when the application
traverses the value changes of a variable, its id code is the key to create a value-change
traverse object associated with it. By supplying the id code, the application calls the
ffrCreateVCTrvsHdl API to create a traverse object and points the pointer at it, which is

Traversing User-Defined Data Types

called "traverse handle." After that, the application can call the member functions with that
traverse handle, such as ffrGotoXTag, ffrGotoNextVC, and ffrGetVC, to traverse the
value changes back and forth. Here is the code segment.:
ffrObject *fsdb_obj;
fsdbVarIdcode var_idcode;
ffrVCTrvsHdl vc_trvs_hdl;
byte_T *vc;
fsdbTag64 time;

The code segment creates a value-change traverse object associated with a variable,
whose id code is represented by var_idcode, and creates a traverse handle,
vc_trvs_hdl. With this traverse handle, it first calls ffrGetMinXTag to query the minimum
time where the value has changed. Then, it moves the internal index to that time by
calling ffrGotoXTag. Finally, it calls ffrGotoNextVC to move the internal index forward
repeatedly until there is no value change.

Traversing User-Defined Data Types
User-defined data types are traversed through a tree callback function. For FSDB version
1.x, user-defined data types and design hierarchies are stored together. However for
FSDB version 2.0, user-defined data types, scopes hierarchies, and variable definitions
are stored separately. As a consequence, the way to traverse user-defined data types
between FSDB version 1.x and FSDB version 2.0 is different.
For FSDB version 1.x, all user-defined data types are known in the tree callback function
after the tree callback function is activated. For FSDB version 2.0 or higher, the application
that activates the tree callback function to notify the application all user-defined data types
must call ffrReadDataTypeDefByBlkIdx.
* ffrReadScopeTree(): Notifies the application about scope hierarchies.
* ffrReadVarByLogUOff(): Notifies the application that all variables belonged to a
specific scope.

Selecting Variables By Their Id Codes

* ffrReadScopeVarTree(): Notifies the application about both scope hierarchies and all
variables in each scope.
* ffrReadDataTypeDefByBlkIdx(): Notifies the application about all user-defined data
types.
To determine FSDB version 1.x and FSDB version 2.0, call ffrHasScopeTree(). If it
returns FALSE, then the version is 1.x. If it returns TRUE, then the version is 2.0. The
application can call ffrHasDataTypeDef() to notify whether an FSDB file contains userdefined data types.

Selecting Variables By Their Id Codes
Before loading value changes onto memory, the application must notify the FSDB Reader
about variables through ffrAddToSignalList.

Loading Value Changes for Variables Into Memory
Once the required variables are selected, the value changes for the variables are loaded
onto memory by calling ffrLoadSignals(). Value changes of unselected variables are
not loaded onto memory.

Creating Value-Change Traverse Handles for Variables
To traverse value changes of a variable, the application must create the value-change
traverse handle associated with it. Then, the value changes can be traversed back and
forth via the member functions of the traverse handle. Each traverse handle has its own
internal index to point to a current time and value change. The value-change traverse is
done by increasing or decreasing the internal index.
The application can create more than one traverse handle associated with a variable. In
that way, the application can traverse the value change at different times simultaneously
via these traverse handles.

Traversing Value Changes Using Traverse Handles
The traverse handle is a pointer that points to a traverse object, and the value changes are
traversed via the member functions of the traverse object.

Closing the FSDB File

Here are the descriptions of each member functions:
* ffrGotoXTag: Moves the internal index to the proper position based on the time
specified by the application.
* ffrGotoPrevVC: Moves the internal index to the previous time and value change.
* ffrGotoNextVC: Moves the internal index to the next time and value change.
* ffrGetXTag: Returns the current time based on the internal index.
* ffrGetVC: Returns the current value change based on the internal index.
* ffrGetSeqNum: Returns the sequence number of the current value change at the
current time. This API is valid only when the FSDB file contains the sequence number
information.
* ffrGetMinXTag: Returns the minimum time where the value change occurs.
* ffrGetMaxXTag: Returns the maximum time where the value change occurs.
* ffrHasIncoreVC: Notifies the application whether this variable has value changes.
* ffrFree: Frees the data structures of the traverse handle. However, the value changes
of the associated variable are not freed.
* ffrGetBitSize: Returns the bit size of the associated variable.
* ffrGetBytesPerBit: Returns bytes per bit of the associated variable.
* ffrGetVarType: Returns the variable type of the associated variable.

Closing the FSDB File
To close an FSDB file, call ffrClose()to perform cleanup tasks. ffrClose() might
not actually close the FSDB file, as the FSDB Reader keeps a reference count for each
FSDB file. This value is increased if the file is reopened and decreased if closed. When
ffrClose() is called, the FSDB Reader first decreases the reference count. If, as a result,
it equals to zero, then the FSDB Reader closes the FSDB file. If not, the FSDB Reader
does not close the file.

Scope Tree
Scope tree is supported from FSDB version 2.0 to reduce the time it takes to traverse
design hierarchies. The result is that the time to open an FSDB file and draw design
hierarchies is shortened. Scope tree refers to scope hierarchies and does not include the
variables in each scope. Therefore, when ffrReadScopeTree() is called, it notifies the
application about scope hierarchies, but not about the scope of each variable.

Scope Tree

In the tree callback function, if the callback types are begin tree, scope, up-scope, or end
tree, the application can receive a logical unsigned offset from the callback data. This is
the key data when the application likes to get signals for that scope. For example in Figure
1, the root scope is called top and has two sub-scopes named system and mem. The top
scope has a variable named t, the system scope has a variable named s, and the mem
scope has a variable named m.

If the application has called ffrReadScopeTree and keeps the logical unsigned offset

Jump Behavior
Jump behavior describes how the ffrGotoXTag() function works. The application
specifies a time to which it would like to jump, but the specified time might or might not
have value changes. The FSDB Reader aligns the return time, if necessary.
In Figure 2, the whole simulation run is from time 0 to time 65, and a variable has value
change at time 15 and 50.
Figure 2

Jump Behavior

If you create a value-change traverse handle associated with this variable and try to jump
to a different time, the result is determined as follows:
* Jump to 5; jump fails; return time is not changed; return glitch number is 0.
* Jump to 10; jump fails; return time is not changed; return glitch number is 0.
* Jump to 15; return time is 15; return glitch number is 2.
* Jump to 65; return time is 50; return glitch number is 1.
* Jump to 30; return time is 15; return glitch number is 2.

Recording Dumpoff and Dumpon

* Jump to (-1); jump fails; return time is not changed; return glitch number is 0.
* Jump to 50; return time is 50; return glitch number is 1.
* Jump to 70; jump fails; return time is not changed; return glitch number is 0.
When you jump to a time with a value change, the traverse handle updates to that time.
The return time equals the jump time.
If there is no value change at the jump time, but the time is within the simulation range, the
return time moves forward to the next value change.
If the jump time is less than the minimum simulation time, the jump does not work. The
return time stays the same, and the glitch number is 0.
If the jump time is greater than the maximum simulation time, the jump does not work. The
return time stays the same, and the glitch number is 0.
The ffrGotoXTag() function can also show the glitch number for the return time.

Recording Dumpoff and Dumpon
Now, time range from dumpoff to dumpon is recorded into an FSDB file. Both the
FSDB Writer and Reader provide APIs for the application to specify and query time
range between dumpoff and dumpon. Note that dumpoff and dumpon are file based. It
means when one of them is activated, it is applied onto all signals. It cannot be applied
onto a single signal or partial signals. For details on reading dumpoff ranges, see
ffrObject::ffrHasDumpOffRange and ffrObject::ffrGetDumpOffRange.

Getting Support Information in the FSDB File
To get support information in the FSDB file, see the description of
ffrObject::ffrHasSupportInfo and ffrObject::ffrGetSupportInfo.

Traversing Value Changes in Time-Based Fashion
Traversing value changes in time-based fashion using the ffrTimeBasedVCTrvsHdl class.
This class is different from ffrVCTrvsHdl, as ffrVCTrvsHdl is signal-based traversal and
ffrTimeBasedVCTrvsHdl is time-based traversal.
When the application needs to traverse several signals in an FSDB file without
ffrTimeBasedVCTrvsHdl, it has to create ffrVCTrvsHdl for each signal, traverse a signal
from the first value change to the last one, and switch to another signal to repeat the steps
above. This is called a signal-based value change traversal.

Traversing Value Changes in Time-Based Fashion

The selected signals can be normal signals or transaction signals, but the signal type
cannot be mixed. The signal type in ffrTimeBasedVCTrvsHdl should be the same. If
ffrTimeBasedVCTrvsHdl has different signal types, ffrTimeBasedVCTrvsHdl cannot be
created.
With ffrTimeBasedVCTrvsHdl, the application might choose to create a time-based
value change traverse handle for all selected signals and traverse their chronologically
ascending order.

Although the example above uses ffrVCIterOne::ffrGetTransVal to get transaction
values, it is recommended to use ffrVCIterOne::ffrGetTransInfo in future as it is
easier to extend. ffrVCIterOne::ffrGetTransInfo is supported from FSDB version 2.3.
ffrTransInfo filled by ffrVCIterOne::ffrGetTransInfo contains the returned value of

a transaction. Below is the description of each field in it:
Field Name

Description

trans_id

Specifies id of the transaction

Transaction Traversal

Field Name

Description

label

Specifies label of the transaction

begin_time

Specifies begin time of the transaction.

end_time

Specifies end time of the transaction.

status

Specifies the status of the transaction. Its possible values
are as follows:
* FSDB_TRANS_STATUS_UNKNOWN: Shows that the
transaction encounters unexpected errors.
* FSDB_TRANS_STATUS_PENDING: Shows that the
transaction is started but did not end yet.
* FSDB_TRANS_STATUS_FINISHED: Shows that the
transaction is finished successfully.
* FSDB_TRANS_STATUS_CANCELLED: The
transaction is canceled. This value is not yet supported.

attr_count

Specifies the number of attributes of the transaction.

attr_hdl_arr

Specifies an array of attribute handles. Its size is equal
to attr_count. It is used to interpret the values of
attr_val_arr.

attr_val_arr

Specifies an array of attributes value pointers. Its size is
equal to attr_count. It is interpreted by the handles in
th
attr_hdl_arr. If the i attribute in attr_val_arr is an
array of strings, the application must treat its value as an
array of string pointers that is arranged as:

//
// OpenFsdbFileForWrite()
//
void
__OpenFsdbFileForWrite(ffwObject **fsdb_obj, char fname[],
fsdbFileType file_type)
{
// Open fsdb file
*fsdb_obj = ffw_Open(fname, file_type);
if (NULL == *fsdb_obj) {
fprintf(stderr, "Fail to open a fast file object File
name = %s.\n", fname);
exit(FSDB_RC_OBJECT_CREATION_FAILED);
}

}

// Use handle scheme for tree creation
ffw_CreateTreeByHandleScheme(*fsdb_obj);
ffw_SetScaleUnit(*fsdb_obj, "0.01p");

ffrResetSignalList

//
// OpenFsdbFileForRead()
//
fsdbRC
__OpenFsdbFileForRead(ffrObject **fsdb_obj, char fname[])
{
//
// Check and open FSDB file
//
if (FALSE == ffrObject::ffrIsFSDB(fname)) {
fprintf(stderr, "%s is not an FSDB file.\n", fname);
return FSDB_RC_FAILURE;
}
*fsdb_obj = ffrObject::ffrOpen2(fname, NULL, NULL);
if (NULL == *fsdb_obj) {
fprintf(stderr, "ffrObject::ffrOpen2() failed(%s).\n",
fname);
return FSDB_RC_FAILURE;
}
}

return FSDB_RC_SUCCESS;

An extended VCD value change includes a state (value), a strength0 value for the port
(signal), and a strength1 value.
Extended VCD FSDB files encode these value changes specially. Call
ffrVCIterOne::ffrGetVC() to get a signal value change. Then call this API to decode the
state and two strengths. Call ffrObject::ffrIsEvcd() to check whether the FSDB file is

FSDB_BT_EVCD_L to FSDB_BT_EVCD_f.
*ret_s0

Strength0 specification for the port. fsdbStrengthType is defined in fsdbShr.h.
*ret_s1

Strength1 specification for the port. fsdbStrengthType is defined in fsdbShr.h.

This API always returns success. Call ffrObject::ffrIsEvcd() first to avoid unexpected

ffrOpen
static ffrObject* ffrObject::ffrOpen (str_T fname, fsdbTreeCBFunc tree_cb_func, void
*tree_client_data, ffrOpenOption opt = FFR_OPEN_OPT_DFT);

Opens an FSDB file, creates an FSDB Reader object, and returns it. ffrOpen lets you
register a tree callback function and tree client data to traverse the design hierarchy.
During the open session, the FSDB Reader reads the design hierarchy. If tree_cb_func
is not null, the FSDB Reader calls tree_cb_func to notify you of each element it reads. In
tree_cb_func, identify what the FSDB Reader returns (scope, signal, upscope, and so on)
using the callback data type. Then cast the callback data accordingly. The FSDB Reader
reads the entire design hierarchy during the open session.
Pass user-defined data to tree_cb_func through tree_client_data. You can also use it as a
buffer between tree_cb_func calls.
Synopsys recommends ffrOpen3 instead of this API.

fname

Pointer to the FSDB file name string.

Tree callback function from your application. fsdbTreeCBFunc is defined in fsdbShr.h.

Tree client data passed back to the tree callback function.
opt

Open option for Novas only. It has a default value; you can ignore it.

ffrObject::ffrOpen3

text:
Opens a compressed FSDB file in gzip or bzip2 format. Only the process that opens
the compressed file uses this option. Other processes must not open the temporary
decompressed file. The decompressed file is not shareable because a hidden temporary
file is created in the specified directory.
Available only on LINUX and LINUX64 platforms.
isSharedObj

Specifies whether the same reader object address is returned when you open the same
FSDB file multiple times in one job. When isSharedObj is set to 1, this API behaves like
ffrOpenNonSharedObj.
For multi-threaded use of FSDB Reader objects, use ffrObject::ffrOpenNonSharedObj.

static ffrObject* ffrObject::ffrOpen3 (str_T fname);

Opens an FSDB file. See ffrObject::ffrOpen2 for details.
ffrObject::ffrOpen3 is similar to ffrObject::ffrOpen2. tree_cb_func and tree_client_data
are NULL. Set them later by calling ffrObject::ffrSetTreeCBFunc. This API is convenient
when you perform basic operations without traversing the design hierarchy.
Synopsys recommends this API over ffrOpen and ffrOpen2.

ffrObject::ffrOpenNonSharedObj is similar to ffrObject::ffrOpen3. It returns a different
reader object address each time you open the same FSDB file in one job.
Use this API for multi-threaded programming on FSDB Reader objects.

fname

ffrOver2GIdcode
bool_T ffrOver2GIdcode() const;

Checks whether the number of id code in FSDB is over 2G or not.

True when the id code is over 2G, False when the id code is not over 2G.

ffrReadDataTypeDefByBlkIdx
fsdbRC ffrObject::ffrReadDataTypeDefByBlkIdx (uint_T &blk_idx);

Read the data type definitions in the FSDB file. In FSDB, all data type definitions are
stored in data type blocks. The argument blk_idx means data type block index. It is usually
zero, which means to read from the first data type block to the last one. If it is not zero, say
1, it means to read from data type block 1 to the last one. At the end of this call, argument
blk_idx is updated to indicate the biggest block index it has read so far, which is useful
information when the FSDB file is still growing.

blk_idx

When calling the API, the application needs to supply a value (usually 0) to indicate which
data type block to begin to read data type definitions. After the API finishes, it contains the
biggest index of data type block the FSDB Reader has read so far.

Detect if the FSDB file has new data coming in under interactive mode and read it if any.

The ffrTimeBasedVCIterOne class provides an iterator for traversing value changes
across multiple signals in time-based order. Unlike signal-based traversal (which reads all
value changes for one signal at a time), time-based traversal interleaves value changes
from multiple signals in chronological sequence.
To use time-based traversal:
1. Create a traverse handle by calling ffrCreateTimeBasedVCTrvsHdl with an array of
signal idcodes. All signals must share the same type.
2. Call ffrGotoNextVC to advance to the next value change in time order.
3. At each step, use accessor methods such as ffrGetVarIdcode, ffrGetXTag, and
ffrGetVC to retrieve the signal idcode, time tag, and value of the current change.
4. Call ffrFree when traversal is complete to release resources.
The following table summarizes the member functions:
Function

Description

ffrGotoNextVC

Advances to the next value change in time order.

ffrGetVarIdcode

Returns the variable idcode of the current value
change.

ffrGetXTag

Returns the time tag of the current value change.

ffrGetVC

Returns the value data of the current value change.

ffrGetSeqNum

Returns the sequence number of the current value
change.

ffrGetVarIdcodeXTagVCSeqNum

Returns the idcode, time tag, value, and sequence
number in a single call.

ffrGetBitSize

Returns the bit size of the current signal.

ffrGetByteCount

Returns the byte count of the current signal value.

ffrGetBytesPerBit

Returns the bytes-per-bit encoding of the current signal.

ffrGetVarType

Returns the variable type of the current signal.

ffrGetGlitchNum

Returns the glitch number at the current time tag.

ffrIsItPropVar

Returns true if the current signal is a property variable.

ffrIsItStreamVar

Returns true if the current signal is a stream variable.

ffrFree

Frees the iterator and releases associated resources.

void ffrOEMInit
void ffrOEMInit (int argc, char *argv[], void *xt_ap_context, ffrOEMFuncTbl
*ret_oem_fun_tbl, ffrInsertOEMComputedVC insert_oem_computed_vc);

OEM can compute value changes and insert the result into Novas so that the result could
be displayed on the waveform window. ffrOEMInit is used to initialize this scheme. It is
called inside Novas, not in OEM products.
After this function is called, when actions defined in ret_oem_fun_tbl is invoked in Novas,
OEM-defined callback functions are called and they can respond to these actions.
insert_oem_computed_vc is used to insert value changes into the FSDB reader memory.
Whether invoking this scheme or not is determined when Novas is built. It is not invoked in
normal releases of Novas. OEM needs to cooperate with Novas for this scheme to work.

Deprecated
This function has been replaced by ffrOEMInit2(). Although the ffrOEMInit function still
works, it is not enhanced in the future.

argc

FAQs
This chapter addresses frequently asked questions about FSDB Reader API usage.
Because combining multiple APIs can be complex, each FAQ provides a focused
explanation with code patterns and best practices.
* Load on Demand
* ffrCreateTimeBasedTrvsHdl() & ffrResetViewWindow()
* ffrGetVC()

Load on Demand
Question 1: In the current Verdi flow, essential signals in a fan-in cone are collected and
loaded together. Does this still need to done in the new FSDB file, or the FSDB Reader
decides which ones to load?
Answer 1: It is not necessary to do so, although it is more efficient. When the value
changes of several signals occur in the same block and several signals are loaded at the
same time, the block is only decompressed for a time. If the signals are loaded separately,
the block is decompressed many times. Of course, the former is more efficient.
Question 2: When the simulation time window is large, the signals is divided by time
slots?
Answer 2: No, ffrSetViewWindow() must be called to enable partial loading.
Question 3: When time 0 was passed to ffrGotoXTag, the memory usage suddenly
increased 150 MB. It is a clock signal, so the decompressed size was expected to be large
if the entire signal is loaded. Does the new FSDB reader read the entire signal or just a
time slot of it?
Answer 3: If the value change of the clock signal was not loaded and ffrGotoXTag() was
allowed to load them, only the value change at the specified time step is loaded. When the
first LoadSignal API is called, the FSDB reader builds a navigation database for all signals
in the FSDB file if the estimated navigation database size is smaller than 200 MB. The 150
MB most likely comes from here. 200MB is a trade-off number. It speeds up later value
change traversal, but it does not slow down the first LoadSignal API too much.

Chapter 4: FAQs
ffrCreateTimeBasedTrvsHdl() & ffrResetViewWindow()

Question 4: Clock signals seems to be memory monsters because of their regular value
changes. Can clock signals be kept in the compressed format (or a formula to recalculate
waveform), and traversed in a special way?
Answer 4: From past experience, special encoding of clock value changes does not save
much space in ordinary FSDB files as clock signals are always 1-bit and an FSDB file
usually does not have many clock signals. Special encoding complicates the FSDB Writer/
Reader; therefore, it is not included in FSDB files.

ffrCreateTimeBasedTrvsHdl() & ffrResetViewWindow()
Question: Sometimes it is necessary to rewind to time 0 (and read again until the end,
and repeat it again and again), and sometimes it is necessary to rewind to the start of
some view window. What is the best sequence of calls to make and parameters to pass?
Is it necessary to ffrFree() and create a new time-based handle or is there an easier
way for rewinding to 0? Is it good enough to have ffrObject::ffrResetViewWindow()
repeated calls to rewind the FSDB file for rereading or is using:
ffrFree()
ffrCreateTimeBasedVCTrvsHdl(uint_T num, fsdbVarIdcode sig_arr[])

better?
Answer: A new time based traverse handle must be regenerated when the view window is
changed. For example:
ffrSetViewWindow();
ffrCreateTimeBasedTrvsHdl();
// do something
ffrResetViewWindow()
ffrFree();
ffrCreateTimeBasedTrvsHdl();
// do something

ffrGetVC()
Question: Can a value change pointer returned by ffrGetVC() be stored and used later?
Answer: When using ffrGetVC() to get value changes of a signal, remember to copy the
returned value to the buffer or use it immediately. Do NOT store the returned pointer and
use it later. It is not guaranteed that the pointer always points to the correct value change.
For example, if an integer signal has value changes at:
(0 0) 32
(0 20) 4567890

Preface
The Verdi FSDB Reader Summary provides detailed information of the FSDB Reader
updates which occurred in different Verdi versions.

Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and answers to
frequently asked questions about Synopsys tools. The SolvNetPlus site also gives you
access to a wide range of Synopsys online services including software downloads,
documentation, and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
If prompted, enter your user name and password. If you do not have a Synopsys user
name and password, follow the instructions to sign up for an account.
If you need help using the SolvNetPlus site, click REGISTRATION HELP in the top-right
menu bar.

Contacting Customer Support
To contact Customer Support, go to https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com.

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary
language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also
includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working

FSDB Writer
This chapter contains the following topics:
* Overview
* Bit Size and Bytes Per Bit
* Write Design Information
* Write Value Change
* Glitch and Glitch Number
* Sequence of Value Changes

* Value Change Memory Limit

Overview
An FSDB file contains three types of information: design hierarchies, user-defined data
types, and value changes.
* Design hierarchies include the hierarchies between each scope (design entity) and the
variables that each scope holds.
* User-defined data types include enumeration type, physical type, integer type, and so
on. VHDL and SystemVerilog drive the capability to have user-defined data types.
* Value changes are the waveform data from the simulator. Each value change includes
a time and a value.

Overview

This section includes the following topics:
* Creation Mode
* Schemes

Creation Mode
To write information into FSDB, the FSDB Writer provides the "creation mode" concept.
The FSDB Writer supports two types of creation modes, which are tree creation mode and
value change creation mode. Under the tree creation mode, the application calls FSDB
Writer APIs to create design hierarchies and user-defined data types. Under the value
change creation mode, the application creates waveform data. The application can switch
between these two modes at any time. However, FSDB Writer usually enters tree creation
mode first because some signals exist. Then the FSDB Writer enters the value change
mode. The tree creation mode begins from FSDB Writer as "begin tree call" and ends in
FSDB Writer as "end tree call". After this, the mode is switched to value change creation
mode.
The FSDB Writer gives each unique variable an idcode, and uses it to identify the unique
variable. The idcode of a variable is the key data for most FSDB Reader APIs. Under tree
creation mode, the application must choose a scheme it likes to use to create the trees.
The FSDB Writer supports two schemes for tree creation: idcode scheme and handle
scheme. In the idcode scheme, the application generates an unique idcode for each
unique variable. It ensures that all these idcodes are positive integer and continuous from
the smallest to the largest one.

Schemes
The FSDB Writer allows to you create value changes using the following methods:
* Signal-Based Method
* Time-Based Method
With the signal-based method, the application records all value changes for one variable
before moving to the next. With the time-based method, the application checks each time
when value changes occur, finds all variables that change at that time, and records their
changes. This repeats until the simulation finishes.
It is recommended to use the time-based method. FSDB files made with the signal-based
method do not support partial loading when you read them.
To help the application find the number of unique variables, use the handle scheme. In this
scheme, the application keeps a handle for each variable, and the FSDB Writer assigns
an idcode. The handle is usually a pointer to an object in memory, and each object has a

Bit Size and Bytes Per Bit

unique address. The FSDB Writer uses this address to create a unique idcode for each
variable.
Variables can have more than one name, called aliases. For example, a variable with
idcode 3 might be called "bus" in one scope and "data_bus" in another. Both names
point to the same variable. You can create aliases by using the variable creation API with
different names but the same handle.
The default tree creation method is the idcode scheme, but the handle scheme is easier
and recommended for most users.
An FSDB file may have no design hierarchy, one hierarchy, or several. The design
hierarchy works like a tree, with each node as a scope. Scopes can contain other scopes
and variables, allowing for nested structures.
To build and move through the design hierarchy, use the "current scope" concept. The
current scope is the node you are working in. Some APIs let you change the current
scope, which helps you organize the hierarchy. When you create a variable, it is added to
the current scope.

current scope is the node you are working in. Some APIs let you change the current
scope, which helps you organize the hierarchy. When you create a variable, it is added to
the current scope.
Sometimes, you may need to know the order of value changes at the same time. This
is called the sequence number. By default, the FSDB Writer does not record sequence
numbers. To enable this, call a special API. When enabled, the FSDB Writer starts a
counter for sequence numbers. The counter resets to one at each new time and increases
for each value change. Recording sequence numbers adds more data to the FSDB file,
which can make the file larger.

Bit Size and Bytes Per Bit
This section describes the bit size and bytes per bit defined by FSDB. FSDB uses bit size
to determine if a variable is a scalar or bus signal. If the bit size is 1, then the variable is
a scalar signal. If the bit size is greater than 1, then the variable is a bus signal. FSDB
calculates the bit size by the formula:
ABS(lbinum - rbitnum) + 1

Where,
* ABS: specifies absolute value.
* lbitnum: specifies left bit number (the most significant bit index).
* rbitnum: specifies right bit number (the least significant bit index).
FSDB uses bytes per bit to determine that one bit is represented by how many bytes. If
there are less than 257 values in the value set, then you can use one byte to represent
one bit since one byte can represent 256 values. If there are less than 65537 but more
than 256 values in the value set, then use two bytes to represent one bit.

Write Design Information

The bit size and bytes per bit information are very important to value change creation.
When the application creates one value change of a variable, the application passes an
address indicating where the value is to the FSDB Writer. The FSDB Writer calculates how
many bytes it should copy from that address by using the following formula:
bit size * numner_of_bytes_to_represent_one_bit

After that, similar steps are performed on the triangle variable. The application should
notice that once all the value changes of a variable have been created, the time must be
rewound.
However, if there is no special reason, it is not recommend to use signal-based scheme in
the application. One reason is that partial load functionality (FSDB Reader's functionality)
does not work for those FSDB files created by signal based scheme.

Time-Based Scheme
To create value change by time-based scheme, the application stops at a specific time
where value changes occurred. Then it figures out what variables have value changes at
that specific time. Finally, it creates the value changes of those variables at that specific

Glitch and Glitch Number

time. The same steps repeat until it reaches the maximum time of the simulation run. Here
is the example to demonstrate time-based value change creation:
struct MySignal _sig;
fsdbTag64 xtag;
unsigned char val;
xtag.H = 0; xtag.L = 5;
val = (unsigned char) FSDB_BT_VCD_0;
val = (unsigned char) FSDB_BT_VCD_Z;
xtag.L = 17;
val = (unsigned char) FSDB_BT_VCD_X;
xtag.L = 23;
val = (unsigned char) FSDB_BT_VCD_1;

In the above example code, the application finds out time 5 has value changes, then it
creates a xtag at time 5. After that, it figures out that both the circle and triangle variables
have value changes at that time, so it creates their value changes. The application goes
further to find out the next time where has value changes. Therefore, it finds time 17,
creates a xtag at time 17, then it figures out that the triangle variable has one value
change, but circle variable does not. So it just creates the triangle variable's value change
at that time. The application keeps going further, creates a xtag at time 23, creates the
triangle and circle variables' value changes at that time.

Glitch and Glitch Number
If a variable has more than one different value changes at a specific time, then we say
it has glitch at that specific time. In order to reduce the extra data brought by glitch, the
FSDB Writer provides two ways to determine which glitch should be stored.
* API: ffw_SetGlitchNum
* Environment Variable: FSDB_ENV_MAX_GLITCH_NUM
The maximum glitch number for the FSDB Writer is 255. Another words, the
argument "number" in ffw_SetGlitchNum (ffwObject *obj, ushort_T number)
cannot exceed 255.

Sequence of Value Changes

Take Figure 2 as an example. A variable has five value changes: 0, 1, 0, x, and z, at time
t. If the application sets glitch number as zero, then all of the five value changes are stored
into FSDB. If the application sets glitch number as one, then the last value change is
stored into FSDB. If the application sets glitch number as n (n >= 2), then the first (n-1)
value change(s) and the last one are stored into FSDB.

If glitch number is 0, then (0,1,0,x,z) are stored into FSDB.
If glitch number is 1, then (z) is stored into FSDB.
If glitch number is 2, then (0, z) are stored into FSDB.

If glitch number is 5, then (0,1,0,x,z) are stored into FSDB.
The FSDB Writer has default value for glitch number, and the default value varies with
FSDB version. The current default value can be found in the ffwAPI.h header file.

Sequence of Value Changes
In some cases, the application might want to know the sequence of value changes
occurred at the same time. therefore, the FSDB Writer supports sequence dumping, which
records the sequence of value changes occurred at the same time. After the sequence
dumping is enabled, the FSDB Writer starts a counter to record sequence number. The
counter is set to one when a time (a xtag) is created, it is increment by one after a value
change has been created. Take the following figure as an example: there are two signals,
denoted by circle and triangle respectively. They all have value changes at time t1 and

Duplicate Value Change

t2. If sequence dumping is enabled, then sequence of each value change is shown as
follows:
Figure 3

Sequence of Value Changes

Since sequence dumping introduces extra data into file, therefore, it is not enabled
by default. The application must call ffw_DumpSeqNumTurnOn to enable sequence
dumping.

Duplicate Value Change
For all the value changes of a variable, regardless of the time, if the adjacent values are
the same, then the second one is a duplicate value change. Duplicate value changes
might cascade, so there might be a series of the same value. For most digital signal types,
the FSDB Writer automatically filters the duplicate value changes. For analog signal types,
the FSDB Writer does not filter duplicate value changes. For example, if the signal is of
memory range type or voltage type, the FSDB Writer does not filter its duplicate value
changes. If the signal is of digital type, and it has value z at time 5, 15, 20, and 25, then
the FSDB Writer filters the value at time 15, 20, and 25, and only keeps the value change
"z" occurred at time 5.

Value Change Memory Limit
When a value change has been created, the FSDB Writer keeps it in memory. If certain
amount of value changes has been accumulated, the FSDB Writer flushes all the value
changes into a file, and then recycles the memory. This operation is called a "flush

General Writing Steps

session," while the amount of value changes is the so-called "value change memory
limit". The flush session is usually performed by the FSDB Writer automatically, but
in some cases, the application might take control. Calling ffw_Sync API forces the
FSDB Writer to perform the flush session. The value change memory limit can be
altered by calling the ffw_SetVCMemLimit API or setting the environment variable
FSDB_ENV_WRITER_MEM_LIMIT.
Based on the design size and VC count, the writer memory limit is increased automatically
at runtime if the runtime is not specified. The increase helps to reduce FSDB size and
speed up dumping and FSDB reading. A message (for example. "For performance
reasons, the Memory Size Limit has been increased to 128M.") is shown when the size is
changed.

General Writing Steps
* Open an FSDB
* Set scale unit and other information
* Choose tree creation scheme
* Initialize data type creation if necessary
* Create the design hierarchy
* Create the value changes
* Close the FSDB

Open an FSDB
Call the ffwOpenFile2 API to open an FSDB. Specify the file name and file type.
The file type tells the FSDB Writer the source of the information. Define it as fsdbFileType
in the fsdbShr.h header file.
After the file opens successfully, the API returns a pointer to an FSDB Writer object. Pass
this pointer to most FSDB Writer APIs.

Set Scale Unit and Other Information
If the simulation has a scale unit, set it with ffw_SetScaleUnit. If it does not, the default is
1ns.

General Writing Steps

Simulation date and simulator version are optional reference information. Use these APIs
to set them:
* ffw_SetScaleUnit
* ffw_SetSimulationDate
* ffw_SetSimulatorVersion

Choose Tree Creation Scheme
Choose a tree creation scheme by calling ffw_CreateTreeByIdcodeScheme or
ffw_CreateTreeByHandleScheme. The default is the idcode scheme if you do not call
either API.

Initialize Data Type Creation If Necessary
If your design includes user-defined data types, call a data type creation API so the FSDB
Writer can initialize the data structures it needs to store data type definitions.
Call ffw_GetDataTypeCreationReady for this step. Most designs do not include userdefined data types. By default, the FSDB Writer assumes none are present.

Create the Design Hierarchy
Build the design hierarchy by calling tree creation APIs:
* ffw_BeginTree -- Creates a top scope with no name.
* ffw_CreateScope2 -- Creates a child of the current scope and moves the current
scope down to the new one.
* ffw_CreateUpscope -- Moves the current scope up to its parent scope.
* ffwCreateVarByIdcode2 or ffwCreateVarByHandle2 -- Creates a variable in the
current scope.
* ffw_EndTree -- Completes the design hierarchy.
An FSDB file might contain none, one, or multiple design hierarchies.

Create the Value Changes
Conceptually, a value change is composed by a pair: a time and a value. The time is
created by calling ffw_CreateXCoorByHnL, while the value is created by calling the
ffw_CreateVarValByIdcode or ffw_CreateVarValByHandle API.

Memory Dumping

Close the FSDB
Call ffw_Close to close the FSDB. This API flushes necessary in-core data and temporary
files to the FSDB file. It then performs cleanup tasks and completes the FSDB file.

Memory Dumping
Memory is a two-dimensional viewpoint of a group of value changes. It comprises two
kinds of variables: memory range variable and memory variable. A memory range variable
indicates the boundary of memory, which is defined by the name of the variable. A memory
variable indicates each element within the memory. For example, to define a block of
memory consisting of 4 words of 8 bits each, you could specify the name of the memory
range variable as
my_mem[0:3]
and the name of the memory variables as
my_mem[0]
my_mem[1]
my_mem[2]
my_mem[3]

prerequisites when creating attributes:
1. An attribute must be created between a ffw_BeginTree() and its corresponding
ffw_EndTree() since it is part of a tree
2. ffw_GetDataTypeCreationReady() must be called before the first attribute is created.
Of course, ffw_GetDataTypeCreationReady() needs to be called only once.
Although an attribute is created within a tree, it could be used to create transactions
owned by streams in other trees.
This API returns the same attribute handle if and only if all properties of the attribute
(including name, data type, larridx, rarridx, and hidden) are the same. If any one of the
arguments is different, FSDB Writer returns a new handle even if the name is the same.
An attributes is not bound to any stream or transaction. Once an attribute is created, it
could be used to create any transaction of any stream.
An attribute could be an array of elements of data_type. Specifying the arguments larridx
and rarridx does this. If it is a scalar, set the two arguments to the same value.
If the attribute is an array of strings, its creation might look like:
fsdbAttrHdl attr_hdl;
fsdbAttrHdlVal attr_val;
char *str_val[3] = { "string1", "string2", "string3" };
attr_hdl = ffw_CreateAttr(ffw_obj, "string_attr",
FSDB_ATTR_DT_STRING, 0, 2, TRUE);
attr_val.hdl
= attr_hdl;
attr_val.value = (byte_T*) str_val;

ffw_CreateAttr2() is recommended, instead of using this API, since this function is not
extended in the future.

extern fsdbVarIdcode ffw_CreateMemoryRangeVarByIdcode (ffwObject *obj,
fsdbVarIdcode var_idcode, fsdbVarType var_type, str_T var_name);

Creates a memory range var by idcode. The application supplies the idcode. A memory
block is a two-dimensional value matrix. It consists of a memory range variable and
memory variables. The memory range variable defines the block boundary by name. For
example, a block of 4 eight-bit words can be defined as:
my_mem[0:3]
my_mem[0]
my_mem[1]
my_mem[2]
my_mem[3]

The memory range variable my_mem[0:3] indicates 4 memory variables named
my_mem[i]. Index i runs from 0 to 3.

Idcode for the var.
var_type

Var type. See fsdbVarType in fsdbShr.h. Set to FSDB_VT_VCD_MEMORY_RANGE or
FSDB_VT_VHDL_MEMORY_RANGE.

Dumps a memory range value change at the current xtag. The change applies to the
var for var_idcode. Use start_mem_idx and close_mem_idx to bracket memory variable
indexes with value changes.
For example, if the memory range variable is my_mem[1:10] and my_mem[3],
my_mem[5], my_mem[6], and my_mem[9] have value changes, set start_mem_idx to 3
and close_mem_idx to 9. start_mem_idx need not be less than close_mem_idx.
If the memory range variable is my_mem[10:1], set start_mem_idx to 9 and
close_mem_idx to 3. Match the index direction in the variable name.

ffw_CreatePropVarByHandle

Pointer to a property variable argument, ffwPropVarArg. See ffwAPI.h for details. Brief
field description follows.
// Argument passed to the API format
struct ffwPropVarArg {
ffwIdcodeOrHdl u; /* var idcode or var handle */
str_T name; /* var name */
byte_T type; /* var type */
byte_T not_used[3];
str_T assoc_clk_name; /* associated clock name */
char **assoc_var_name; /* associated variable name */
uint_T count; /* count of assoc_var_name */
str_T text_description;
};
typedef struct ffwPropVarArg ffwPropVarArg;
//Detailed description of the fields above
ffwIdcodeOrHdl: An unsigned integer or a pointer which points to a void
type object.
var_name: A string pointer representing full hierarchy name or plain
name.
var_type: For a property variable, it's variable type can be either one
of the following:
FSDB_VT_PROP_ASSUME /* Property assume(similiar to
** assert but shown in different way) */
FSDB_VT_PROP_RESTRICT /* Property input constraint */
FSDB_VT_PROP_COVER /* Property cover clause */
FSDB_VT_PROP_LOCAL_MEMORY /* Property local memory clause */
FSDB_VT_PROP_LOCAL /* Property local clause */
FSDB_VT_PROP_EVENT /* Property event clause */
FSDB_VT_PROP_BOOL /* Property bool clause */
FSDB_VT_PROP_ASSERT_FORBID /* Property assert forbid clause */
FSDB_VT_PROP_ASSERT_CHECK /* Property assert check clause */
FSDB_VT_PROP_ASSERT /* for backward compatible */
For details, refer to fsdbVarType defined in fsdbShr.h.
assoc_clck_name: Pointer to a string representing associated clock name.
The assoc_clk_name can be a slice of a vector signal.
(Format: assoc_clk_name_string[lbitnum, rbitnum] )
**assoc_var_name[]: An array of pointers pointing to associated variable
names.
The assoc_var_name can be a slice of a vector variable.
(Format: assoc_var_name_string[lbitnum, rbitnum] )
count: the number of assoc_var_name strings.
text_description: Pointer to a string describing the property var.
With predefined formats, the text_description string can be used for
special purposes.
[Known special uses of text_description]
Associate "failure message" with a property variable.
[Format]
%__DESC__% normal descriptions %__FAIL_MSG__% failure message.
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^delimiter ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^delimiter
When the associated variable has assertion failures, failure message
(string behind delimiter
"%__FAIL_MSG__%) is shown on nWave like the graph below.

to FSDB.
//
char *prop_sig_assoc_var_name[] = {

};

typedef struct PropSignal PropSignal;
PropSignal prop_sig1 = {

ffw_CreateTreeByHandleScheme
extern void ffw_CreateTreeByHandleScheme (ffwObject *obj);

Set tree creation scheme as handle scheme, which means the application does not
need to worry about making idcode for each signal, it leaves that job to the FSDB Writer.
ffw_CreateTreeByHandleScheme also enables the FSDB Writer to set up necessary
data structures for subsequent var creation, such as hashing table, and so on.

ffw_CreateTreeByIdcodeScheme

ffw_CreateTreeByIdcodeScheme
extern void ffw_CreateTreeByIdcodeScheme (ffwObject *obj);

Set tree creation scheme as idcode scheme, which means the application takes the
responsibility to make an idcode for each signal, and it must guarantee each idcode is
positive integer, and all idcodes are continuous from the smallest to the biggest one. The
default scheme for tree creation is idcode scheme.

ffw_CreateTriggerPointVarByVarIdcode
ffwVarMapId ffw_CreateTriggerPointVarByVarIdcode (ffwObject *obj, str_T var_name,
fsdbVarIdcode var_idcode);

Create a trigger point signal. This is a special kind of signal only used by some third party
vendors for marking trigger time of a simulation.
* The values of trigger time are stored in a trigger point signal.
* An FSDB file could contain at most 1 trigger point signal. If more than one is created,
only the first one is visible in nWave.
* Basically, trigger times are value changes of the trigger point signal. Therefore, no
limitation is imposed on the number of trigger times.
* Trigger points are only visible in Debussy.qds.
Procedures of creating trigger point signal and trigger time:
Creating a trigger point signal is like creating ordinary variables. Only the API name is
different.
ffwObject *obj;
obj = ffw_Open("test.fsdb", FSDB_FT_VERILOG);
ffw_BeginTree(obj);
ffw_CreateTriggerPointVarByVarIdcode(ffw_obj, "trigger_point",
trigger_point_idcode);
ffw_EndTree(obj);
A trigger point signal might contain several trigger times during
simulation. A trigger time should be recorded at the time step it
happens. For example, if a trigger time is 300,

ffw_CreateVarByHandle
extern ffwVarMapId ffw_CreateVarByHandle (ffwObject *obj, fsdbVarType var_type,
fsdbVarDir var_dir, void *data_type_hdl, int lbitnum, int rbitnum, void *var_hdl, str_T
var_name, fsdbBytesPerBit bpb);

Create a var by handle. The handle is usually a pointer to an object. Since the virtual
address of an object is unique, the application can take advantage of this to represent a
unique var by the virtual address of an object.

This function has been replaced by ffwCreateVarByVarHdl2(). Although the
ffw_CreateVarByHandle function still works, it is not enhanced in the future.

Var_type

Var type. Refer to fsdbVarType defined in fsdbShr.h.
Var_dir

Var direction. Refer to fsdbVarDir defined in fsdbShr.h; if the direction is unknown, then
specify it as implicit.

ffw_CreateVarByHandleAndPath

Data type handle is a void pointer type cast on fsdbDataType or a handle given by the
application. Refer to fsdbDataType defined in fsdbShr.h.

Left bit number.

Right bit number.

Var handle, usually a virtual address of an object which can identify a unique var.

Pointer to a string that represents the var name.
bpb

An enumeration value which means how many bytes it takes to represent a bit of the var.

Non-NULL if successful; NULL if fail; where ffwVarMapId is defined in ffwAPI.h.
If users would like to put '/' in signal names for files in Epic format,
'\' (backslash) must be added as the leading character of the signal name. The
'\' works as an "escaped character" and won't be shown in the Get Signals form
and the signal pane of the nWave window.

ffw_CreateVarByHandleAndPath
extern ffwVarMapId ffw_CreateVarByHandleAndPath (ffwObject *obj, fsdbVarType
var_type, fsdbVarDir var_dir, void *data_type_hdl, int lbitnum, int rbitnum, void
*var_hdl, str_T var_name, fsdbBytesPerBit bpb, str_T full_path_scope_name, str_T
scope_separator)

ffw_CreateVarByHandleAndPath

Creates a var by handle, full path scope name, and scope separator. The handle is usually
an object pointer. Each object's virtual address is unique. Use that address to identify a
unique var.

Replaced by ffwCreateVarByVarHdlAndPath2(). ffw_CreateVarByHandleAndPath still
works but will not receive future enhancements.

var_type

Var type. See fsdbVarType in fsdbShr.h.
var_dir

Var direction. See fsdbVarDir in fsdbShr.h. If unknown, set to implicit.
*data_type_handle

Data type handle cast to void from fsdbDataType or supplied by the application. See
fsdbDataType in fsdbShr.h.

Left bit number.

Right bit number.

Var handle. Usually an object's virtual address, which identifies a unique var.

Pointer to the var name string.
bpb

Bytes per bit for the var.

ffw_CreateVarByIdcode

Pointer to the full path scope name for the var.

Pointer to the scope separator string.

Non-NULL on success; NULL on failure. ffwVarMapId is defined in ffwAPI.h.

Do not call this API between
ffw_CreateArrayBegin()
/ffw_CreateArrayEnd()
ffw_CreateRecordBegin()/ffw_CreateRecordEnd()
ffw_CreateStructBegin()/ffw_CreateStructEnd()
It may create scopes inside the pair and produce the wrong hierarchy.

ffw_SetDumpLimit
extern void ffw_SetDumpLimit (ffwObject *obj, uint_T size);

Set dump limit of an FSDB file in mega bytes. Once dump limit is turned for an FSDB
file, you cannot turn it off. When dump limit is turned on and the size of the FSDB file
reaches the specified limit, the FSDB Writer recycles the space from the beginning of this
file and the value changes in the recycled space is no longer exists. Because dump limit
is only for value changes, the file size is not exactly the same with the specified size. It
might be slightly larger or smaller. The minimum value of size is 32 on all platforms. The
maximum value of size is 1800 on 32-bit platforms because a file cannot exceed 2GB on
these machines. As for 64-bit platforms, there is no such limitation. You should avoid using
dynamic trees (that is, trees created after any value change is created) when dump limit
is turned on. Otherwise, the FSDB file immediately grows to the specified dump limit size
because such trees are placed in the end of the file, even if there are no value changes in
between. Notice that when you use dump limit, there is slight performance penalty and you
also loose recycled value changes.

text:
Set LIFO (last in first out) dump limit of an FSDB file in mega bytes. The main difference
between this API and its counterpart ffw_SetDumpLimit() is - When FSDB file reaches

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
ffw_SetLockingScheme

the specified limit, ffw_SetLifoDumpLimit() leads the FSDB Writer to discard the
following value changes (LIFO) while ffw_SetDumpLimit() leads the FSDB Writer to
recycle space of the early value changes for the newly created value changes (FIFO).
Once dump limit is turned on for an FSDB file, you cannot turn it off, and LIFO dump limit
cannot be used with ffw_SetDumpLimit() and auto switch file at the same time.
When LIFO dump limit is turned on and the size of the FSDB file reaches the specified
limit, the FSDB Writer does not start to discard value changes immediately. Instead,
it first writes all the values currently stored in the memory buffer (size of the memory
buffer can be set by ffw_SetMemLimit, ffw_SetVCMemLimit and environment variable
FSDB_ENV_WRITER_MEM_LIMIT). Likewise, if the LIFO dump limit is reached while
writing a dynamic tree, the FSDB Writer writes the whole dynamic tree into FSDB, then
start to discard the following values. As a result, file size is not exactly the same with the
specified size. It might be slightly larger or smaller.
The minimum value of size is 32 on all platforms. The maximum value of size is 1800
on 32-bit platforms because a file cannot exceed 2GB on these machines. As for 64-bit
platforms, there is no such limitation.

size

Dump limit size in mega bytes.

ffw_SetVCMemLimit
extern void ffw_SetVCMemLimit (ffwObject *obj, uint_T mem_limit)

Specify the memory limit which the FSDB Writer uses to determine when to flush in-core
value changes to disk file. If the total memory size of in-core value changes exceeds
the memory limit, the FSDB Writer flushes all in-core value changes to disk file so the
FSDB Writer can recycle the memory. Multiple FSDB Writer objects are supported so
the application can write multiple FSDB files simultaneously; this is why this API has a
parameter pointing to the FSDB Writer object.

mem_limit

ffw_SwitchFile

The memory limit, unit is mega bytes. Valid values are from 4 to 2048. The default writer
memory limit follows:
64MB if var_count < 5M,
128MB if 5M <= var_count < 10M,
256MB if 10M <= var_count

Flush in-core value changes to FSDB even though the memory limit has not been hit. The
FSDB Writer has memory limit for in-core value changes, it is the criterion to determine
when the in-core value changes have to be flushed to disk file. If the application would like
to force the FSDB Writer to flush in-core value changes to disk file, no matter the memory
limit has been hit or not, then just call this API.

ffwCreateMDAVarByIdcode
extern fsdbVarIdcode ffwCreateMDAVarByIdcode (ffwObject *obj, ffwMDAVarArg *arg);

Creates an MDA (Multiple Dimension Array) var by idcode.
Set the idcode with arg->u.idcode = your_var_idcode.
MDA uses sparse arrays to store memory signals. Compared with
ffw_CreateMemoryRangeVarByIdcode, this API has several advantages:
1. It scales better. To create
reg [0:7] mem[0:1023]

ffw_CreateMemoryRangeVarByIdcode needs 1024 signals to represent the memory.
This API needs only 1 signal. This saves memory when creating an MDA with many
cells.
2. It supports multi-dimensional array signals. ffw_CreateMemoryRangeVarByIdcode
supports only 2D signals.
ffwMDAVarArg has fields that need special attention:
dim: Dimension of the MDA signal.
packed_arr_begin_pos: Begin position of the packed array for the MDA signal,
starting from 0. SystemVerilog calls dimensions declared before the signal name
packed_array. See the example below.
left_idx_arr: Array of lbitnum values for all dimensions.
right_idx_arr: Array of rbitnum values for all dimensions.
init_val_a_bit: Initial value of the signal. Use FSDB_BT_VCD_X for Verilog
signals. If you pass FSDB_BT_VCD_X for mem[0:1023][0:7], all 1024 cells initialize
to XXXX_XXXX.

extern fsdbRC ffwCreateScopeByPath (ffwObject *obj, ffwScopeArg *scope, str_T
scope_separator);

Creates a scope hierarchy by parsing the name field in *scope.
Provide a full path scope name. The API splits the name into tokens using
scope_separator. It builds the scope tree from those tokens in order.
If you specify a module name in *scope, the API associates it only with the leaf of the
scope path.

*scope

Pointer to the scope separator string.

FSDB_RC_POINTER_IS_NULL if rec->name is NULL.

FAQs
This chapter addresses frequently asked questions about FSDB Writer API usage.
Because combining multiple APIs can be complex, each FAQ provides a focused
explanation with code patterns and best practices.
This section includes the following topics:
* Creating Two-Dimensional Memory Signal or an MDA Signal
* Create a Digital/Analog Mixed FSDB File

* Create Var by Var Idcode APIs
* Ctrl-C in FSDB-enabled Simulators
* ffw_Close() does not Free Memory

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Creating Two-Dimensional Memory Signal or an MDA Signal
Question: How should a two-dimensional memory signal or an MDA signal be created?
Answer: The following two methods are available:
1. With memory depth and memory type signals -> for two-dimensional memory only.
2. With array begin and array end -> for general multiple dimensional arrays.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
With Memory Depth and Memory Type Signals
Use the following syntax to create a two-dimensional memory signal:
reg [0:7] macroram [0:15];

One of the following two methods, creating signals or creating values, can be used.
A memory signal acts as a memory cell. A memory depth signal acts as a bounding box
to include all memory cells that have value changes at a time step. For better viewing
performance, do not include redundant cells that do not have value changes.

Creating Two-Dimensional Memory Signal or an MDA Signal

// Create signals
//
ffw_CreateMemoryRangeVarByHandle(ffw_obj,
(void*)&mem_range, FSDB_VT_VCD_MEMORY_RANGE, "macroram[0:15]");
ffw_CreateVarByHandle(ffw_obj, FSDB_VT_VCD_MEMORY,
FSDB_VD_INPUT, FSDB_DT_HANDLE_VERILOG_STANDARD, 0, 7, (void*)&mem_cell_0,
"macroram[0]", FSDB_BYTES_PER_BIT_1B);
ffw_CreateVarByHandle(ffw_obj, FSDB_VT_VCD_MEMORY,
FSDB_VD_INPUT, FSDB_DT_HANDLE_VERILOG_STANDARD, 0, 7, (void*)&mem_cell_1,
"macroram[1]", FSDB_BYTES_PER_BIT_1B);

ffw_CreateVarByHandle(ffw_obj, FSDB_VT_VCD_MEMORY,
FSDB_VD_INPUT, FSDB_DT_HANDLE_VERILOG_STANDARD, 0, 7,
(void*)&mem_cell_14,
"macroram[14]", FSDB_BYTES_PER_BIT_1B);
ffw_CreateVarByHandle(ffw_obj, FSDB_VT_VCD_MEMORY,
FSDB_VD_INPUT, FSDB_DT_HANDLE_VERILOG_STANDARD, 0, 7,
(void*)&mem_cell_15,
"macroram[15]", FSDB_BYTES_PER_BIT_1B);
// Create values
//
// time 10: cell_1 and cell_2 have value changes.
// Set start_mem_idx to 1 and close_mem_idx to 2 to include // cell_1 and
cell_2.
//
ffw_CreateXCoorByHnL(ffw_obj, 0, 10);
ffw_CreateMemoryRangeVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, &mem_range, 1, 2);
ffw_CreateVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, (void*)&mem_cell_1, value);
ffw_CreateVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, (void*)&mem_cell_2, value);
// time 20: cell_1, cell_3, cell_13, cell_15 have value // changes
// Since the cells are sparse, use two ranges to include the // four
cells.
//
ffw_CreateXCoorByHnL(ffw_obj, 0, 20);
ffw_CreateMemoryRangeVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, &mem_range, 1, 3);
ffw_CreateVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, (void*)&mem_cell_1, value);
ffw_CreateVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, (void*)&mem_cell_3, value);
ffw_CreateMemoryRangeVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, &mem_range, 13, 15);
ffw_CreateVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, (void*)&mem_cell_13, value);
ffw_CreateVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, (void*)&mem_cell_15, value);

When dumping memory signals, the following rules should be followed:
1. The memory range signal must be created before any related memory signal is
created. That is, the memory range signal should be created as:
macroram[0:15]
macroram[0]
macroram[1]

macroram[15]

Creating Two-Dimensional Memory Signal or an MDA Signal

The following creation does not work:
macroram[0]
macroram[0:15]
macroram[1]

macroram[15]

2. The name of the memory range signal must include a starting and closing memory
signal index. That is, the name of the memory range signal should be created as:
macroram[0:15]
macroram[0]
macroram[1]

macroram[15]

The following creation does not work:
macroram[0:13]
macroram[0]
macroram[1]

macroram[15]

3. The value of the memory depth signal only covers the minimum possible range of the
memory cells that have value changes at that time step, instead of covering all memory
cells. Take the code snippet above for example, if only cell_1 and cell_2 have value
changes, use the following syntax:
ffw_CreateMemoryRangeVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, &mem_range, 1, 2);

instead of:
ffw_CreateMemoryRangeVarValueByHandle(ffw_obj, &mem_range, 0, 15);

The second usage directs nMemory to update value changes of all memory cells. This
is not an error but should be corrected for lack of efficiency.
4. This mechanism does not work for computed signals whose value changes are
generated on the FSDB reader side at runtime. Use the second method, "With array
begin and array end" to create memory.

With Array Begin and Array End
An array such as `an_array[0][1][0:31]' is called an MDA (multi-dimensional array).
An MDA signal with two dimensions is a special case of MDA, because it is recognized
as a two-dimensional memory signal and can be viewed with nMemory. MDAs cannot be
created by specifying its variable name as MDA.

Create a Digital/Analog Mixed FSDB File

Instead, "array begin" and "array end" must be used to create each dimension of the array
in a nested fashion. For example, `an_array[0:1][0:2][0:31]' must be created in the
following method:
ffw_CreateArrayBegin("an_array[0:1]", 2)
ffw_CreateArrayBegin("an_array[0][0:2]", 3)
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[0][0][0:31]")
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[0][1][0:31]")
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[0][2][0:31]")
ffw_CreateArrayEnd()
ffw_CreateArrayBegin("an_array[1][0:2]", 3)
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[1][0][0:31]")
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[1][1][0:31]")
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[1][2][0:31]")
ffw_CreateArrayEnd()
ffw_CreateArrayEnd()

If it is created as:
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[0][0][0:31]")
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[0][1][0:31]")
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[0][2][0:31]")
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[1][0][0:31]")
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[1][1][0:31]")
ffw_CreateVar("an_array[1][2][0:31]")

nWave treats each variable as an independent variable, instead of grouping them into an
MDA signal called an_array[0:1][0:2][0:31].

Create a Digital/Analog Mixed FSDB File
Question: How should a digital/analog mixed FSDB file be created?
Answer: Refer to the epic.cpp file in the FSDB Writer for examples. The point is:
1. Set the file type to FSDB_FT_EPIC.
2. Use FSDB_VT_EPIC_LOGIC as the variable type of digital signals.
3. Use the following State Number as the value of digital signals. `character" is the value
string shown in nWave.
Character

State Number Meaning

`0'

logic ZERO (strong drive)

`1'

logic ONE (strong drive)

Create VHDL enum Values
Question: How should VHDL enum values be created?
Answer: There are 4 cases to consider.
Case 1: 0< literal count <= 255 (signal is 1 Byte)
<create signal>
bytes_per_bit

= 0
= 0
= FSDB_BYTES_PER_BIT_1B

<create value change>

b;

b = 3;
ffw_CreateVarValueByIdcode(obj, idcode, &b)

Case 2: 0< literal count <= 255 (signal is 2 Bytes)
This case is not recommended, because of compatibility issues.
Since the literal count <= 255, the value change might be held with 1 byte. Although it is
fine to use 2 bytes to hold the value change, one byte is wasted. Therefore, this method is
not recommended.

Create VHDL enum Values

If this case must be used, remember to use "unsigned short" instead of "byte_T" as the
value change placeholder. If "byte_T" is used to hold the value change, the result is
sometimes be wrong depending on machine endians.
<create signal>
bytes_per_bit

= 0
= 0
= FSDB_BYTES_PER_BIT_2B

<create value change>
/*
** Since the signal is 2B, don't use byte_T as the
** vc placeholder.
** byte_T b;
*/
unsigned short
u;
u = 3;
ffw_CreateVarValueByIdcode(obj, idcode, &u)

Case 3: 255 < literal count <= 65535
Because the maximum value change (65535) needs to be held with 2 bytes, use
"unsigned short" as the value change placeholder.
<create signal>
bytes_per_bit

= 0
= 0
= FSDB_BYTES_PER_BIT_2B

<create value change>
unsigned short

u;

u = 3;
ffw_CreateVarValueByIdcode(obj, idcode, &u)

Case 4: 65535 < literal count
Since the maximum value change (2^32-1) needs to be held with 4 bytes, use "unsigned
int" as the value change placeholder.
<create signal>
bytes_per_bit

= 0
= 0
= FSDB_BYTES_PER_BIT_4B

<create value change>

Create Var by Var Idcode APIs
Question: Why are there three "create var by var idcode" APIs? What are the
differences between ffw_CreateVarByIdcode, ffwCreateVarByVarIdcode, and
ffwCreateVarByVarIdcode2?
Answer: They work the same and exist for backward compatibility.
ffw_CreateVarByIdcode
extern fsdbVarIdcode

Ctrl-C in FSDB-enabled Simulators
Question: How should Ctrl-C be handled in FSDB-enabled simulators?
Answer: The simulator must treat calling the FSDB writer APIs as a critical section and
must not interrupt it. If it receives a Ctrl-C when running in a critical section, it should
remember it (got_ctrlc = TRUE) and return the control to the normal flow instead of just
closing the FSDB file. After leaving this critical section, the simulator should check if there
are any signals caught previously in the critical section. If yes, handle it.
The flow is shown as follows:
< Normal flow >

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
< Signal Handler >

is_critical_section = TRUE
[begin] call fsdb writer APIs
got Ctrl-C
-----------> if (is_critical_section == TRUE) {
got_ctrlc = TRUE
return;
}
else
handle_ctrlc_signal();
[end]
call fsdb writer APIs
is_critical_section = FALSE
if (got_ctrlc == TRUE)
handle_ctrlc_signal();

Of course, there are additional details to be handled. For example, when Ctrl-C is caught
during ffw_BeginTree(), if the simulator has just closed the FSDB file, however, the
design tree does not go into the FSDB file because ffw_EndTree() is not called. These
details should be handled.

ffw_Close() does not Free Memory
Question: Does ffw_Close() free memory after closing a writer object?

ffw_Close() does not Free Memory

Answer: No, it does not. The memory is freed after a new writer object is created. The
reasons are:
1. The FSDB dumper (PLI) needs the variable map in the writer object to delete the
registered value change callbacks.
2. In ffw_SwitchFile(), some data in the old writer object needs to be assigned to new
writer object. This is done with an assignment after ffw_Close(). For example:
__CreateAndSwitchToNewObj()
{

ffw_Close(old_obj);

}

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
new_obj->head_tree = old_obj->head_tree;
new_obj->tail_tree = old_obj->tail_tree;

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text: In conclusion, the memory in ffw_Close() cannot be freed.

Verdi 2023.12
Starting from this release, you can migrate to NPI Waveform Model/Writer, which is
the latest FSDB Reader/Writer to seamlessly read FSDB. The following data types are
supported only with NPI Waveform Model/Writer:
1. Modport/interface port
2. Virtual file
3. The FSDB which includes power signals
4. Packed mode dumping

Verdi 2017.12
* Starting from this release, the FSDB is upgraded from version 5.5 to version 5.6.
* The fsdbVarIdcode is enlarged from int to int64 so that larger designs (over 2G
idcode) can be handled with ease in the future.

Verdi 2016.06
Starting from this release, functions and tasks can be dumped to FSDB. By default, they
are not dumped for performance consideration. You can use one of following methods to
dump them to FSDB during runtime (simulation)
1. Using the FSDB_FUNCTIONS environment variable:
For example: setenv FSDB_FUNCTIONS 1
2. Using the +fsdb+functions runtime option:
For example: simv +fsdb+functions

Introduction
In this chapter:
* Overview
