Overview
More designs now contain embedded processor cores. Validating these designs often
requires code that runs on the embedded cores. Test code development is also part of the
overall validation strategy.
Hardware debug works at the hardware level. The hardware state appears as signals.
Embedded code is written at the Assembly or C level. This creates a gap in abstraction
levels.
Bridging the gap requires a solid understanding of how the embedded core works. Teams
often develop ad hoc scripts to refine captured trace data to the assembly level. Returning
to the C level often requires tedious manual work.
(R)

The Verdi Automated Debug Platform with the Verdi Hardware Software Debug (HW/SW
Debug) Solution supports embedded software debugging. The embedded processor core
is an HDL model that is part of the simulated design.
As illustrated in the following figure, the SoC design includes CPU cores, memory models,
and I/O peripherals. The compiled C image file loads into the memory model for core
execution.
The Verdi platform with HW/SW Debug integrates debug features between HDL and
software. You can debug the design at the hardware level. The Eclipse program connects
a Verdi plug-in to debug embedded code at the Assembly or C level. C/Assembly code, C
variables, and the stack are visible. Hardware and software debugging stay synchronized
in time. You can debug designs with multiple cores simultaneously.

Overview

Figure 1

HW/SW Debug Overview

You can view behavior at the C or Assembly application source level. This makes it easier
to understand how the software application interacts with the hardware design.
Verdi HW/SW Debug supports all ARM Cortex cores out-of-the-box. Custom
cores can often be supported as well. For details, contact the Synopsys Support
Center (verdi_support@synopsys.com).

Supported Platforms
The Verdi HW/SW Debug Solution is only supported on Linux RedHat and SUSE
platforms on 64 bit hosts. Solaris is not supported.

Requirements
To start running the Verdi HW/SW Debug Solution, Verdi_HwSwDebug license is
required.

Compilation Phase
The CPU log file generated from the design (executing embedded C code) is used as an
input by Verdi HW/SW Debug Solution. For details on generating this file, refer to your
CPU vendor instructions.

The embedded application image file (ELF file) is created by armcc, gcc, or any other
compiler. This ELF file is taken as an input by both the gdb engine and the Verdi HW/SW
Debug Solution to retrieve information about the initial memory state. To enable the
compiler to generate debug information, such as, function name/memory address
mapping, variable name/memory address mapping, file name and line number/memory
address mapping, add the -g debug option to the compiler command, as follows:
gcc -g
armcc -g

Compiler Optimizations
Verdi HW/SW Debug Solution supports all C compiler optimization levels (-O0, -O1, -O2,
and-O3). The default optimization level for gcc compiler is -O0 and for armcc compiler is
-O2.
It is recommended to use -Og or -O1 optimization option to improve the debug
experience. However, all -O optimization levels (-O0, -O1, -O2, -O3) are
supported.
The following sections show the sample code and the effect of using optimization options
on this sample code.
Sample Code with -O0
In the sample code, each C source code line maps to many disassembly opcodes. With
the -O0 option, all the values are written to memory, and nothing is removed. This is also
illustrated in Figure 3.

Simulation Phase
Enable log file dumping in the design before starting simulation. See CPU Vendor
documentation for details.

Converter Phase
The hwsw_debug_convert tool directly converts one or multiple CPU log file(s) to an FSDB
file containing data for the HW/SW Debug engine, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 8

HW/SW Debug Converter Flow

The configuration of the log file names, ELF file names, and CPU types is completed on
the command line or in a design .xml file read by the hwsw_debug_convert tool.
The supported features of the hwsw_debug_convert tool are as follows:
* Read in one or multiple log files in configurable format.
* Write out data in an FSDB file.
* Support multi-core and multi-cluster designs.
(R)

(R)

* Support the log file format produced by all ARM Cortex cores. Log files produced by
other CPUs are supported with minimal effort.
* Read in FSDB files for debugging purposes.
* Write out log file in generic format for debugging purposes.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Usage
To use the hwsw_debug_convert tool, specify the hwsw_debug_convert command in the
command line, or create a .xml file that is read by the hwsw_debug_convert tool.
The following are examples of using the hwsw_debug_convert command to convert log
files into FSDB files.
The parameter arguments (that is, arguments without a dash) of HW/SW Debug
Converter must be specified before the options (that is, arguments with a dash).
* Converting a log file from an ARM Cortex-M3 processor into an FSDB file:
hwsw_debug_convert cpuType=Cortex-M3 exeFile=test.elf \
-i tarmac.log -o hwsw.fsdb

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
* Converting a log file from a four-core (ARM Cortex-A53), single-cluster system run in
AArch64 mode into an FSBD file:
hwsw_debug_convert cpuType=Cortex-A53-64 exeFile=test.elf \
-num_cores=4 -i ca53_tarmac.0.0.%d.log -o hwsw.fsdb

* Converting a two-Cortex-A53, two-Cortex-A7, mixed-cluster system into an FSDB file:
hwsw_debug_convert cluster0.cpuType=Cortex-A53 \
cluster0.exeFile=test0.elf \
cluster0.traceFileName=ca53_tarmac.0.0.%d.log \
cluster1.cpuType=Cortex-A7 \
cluster1.exeFile=test1.elf \
cluster1.traceFileName=tarmac_cluster1_cpu%d.log \
-num_cores=2,2 -o hwsw.fsdb

Alternatively, this could be done in a design .xml file which is read in by the
hwsw_debug_convert tool:
<cluster>
<name/>
<cluster>
<name>cluster0</name>
<core>
<name>cpu0</name>
<cpuType>Cortex-A53</cpuType>
<configName>AArch64</configName>
<exeFile>test0.elf</exeFile>
<traceFileName>ca53_tarmac.0.0.0.log</traceFileName>
<cpuId>0</cpuId>
<clusterId>0</clusterId>
</core>
<core>
<name>cpu1</name>
<cpuType>Cortex-A53</cpuType>
<configName>AArch64</configName>
<exeFile>test0.elf</exeFile>
<traceFileName>ca53_tarmac.0.0.1.log</traceFileName>
<cpuId>1</cpuId>
<clusterId>0</clusterId>
</core>
</cluster>
<cluster>
<name>cluster1</name>
<core>
<name>cpu0</name>
<cpuType>Cortex-A7</cpuType>
<exeFile>test1.elf</exeFile>
<traceFileName>tarmac_cluster1_cpu0.log</traceFileName>
<cpuId>0</cpuId>
<clusterId>1</clusterId>
</core>
<core>
<name>cpu1</name>
<cpuType>Cortex-A7</cpuType>
<exeFile>test1.elf</exeFile>
<traceFileName>tarmac_cluster1_cpu1.log</traceFileName>
<cpuId>1</cpuId>
<clusterId>1</clusterId>
</core>
</cluster>
</cluster>

Then, execute the following:
hwsw_debug_convert -load_design design.xml -o hwsw.fsdb

Note that each cluster contains one or more cores and has its own memory space. In
addition, each cluster launches a separate gdb (GNU Debugger).
Log Files
The log files are line-oriented text files and typically include information for instructions,
register assignments and memory transactions. See the following for more details:
* Instruction information should include the program counter, and may also include
timestamp, operation code and disassembly code.
* The register information should include the register specification (name or ID) and the
value stored in the register.
* The memory information should include the address, data, data width and access type
(read/write access).
The format of the log files depends on the model of the HDL processor. The following is an
example of the log file:
10245 ns Ins
Mem
10975 ns Ins
11445 ns Ins
Reg
11445 ns Ins
Reg
11445 ns Ins
Reg

00000000 [e59ff018]
Read4 @(00000020)=0000003c
0000003c [ea000011]
00000088 [e3a00000]
R0=00000000
0000008c [e3a01000]
R1=00000000
00000090 [e3a02000]
R2=00000000

Following is the list of required options:

Pattern Files
The log file format is specified using trace patterns which are available in the Verdi release
package at $VERDI_HOME/share/hwsw_debug/patterns location.
For example, for a Single Core R7,
% hwsw_debug_convert cpuType=Cortex-R7 exeFile=test.elf \
-i cpu.log -o hwsw.fsdb

The pattern files (.pat files) describe how the hwsw_debug_convert tool should read in the
log files, in other words, the .pat file defines how a log file should be parsed.
Pattern files for supported ARM cores and other cores are supplied with Verdi
HW/SW Debug. You should write a custom pattern file only for custom cores.

During parsing, each line in a log file is matched against all lines of the pattern file. If a line
matches, the fields in the line is used to extract the data. The order in which the patterns
are checked is not determined.
Each line of the pattern file is a regular expression, namely a Portable Operating System
Interface (POSIX) extended regular expression.
For matching data, the lines also contain fields. The fields are identifiers which are
enclosed by the '%' characters (such as %PC%), and determine the location of significant
data for the hwsw_debug_convert tool.
The following is an example of the pattern file:
#PARAMETERS: configName=ARMv7
# Instructions:
%TIME% %TIMEUNIT% Ins %PC% \[%OPCODE%\]( : %DISASM%)?
# Registers:
Reg %REGNAME%=%REGDATA%
# Memory:
Mem %RW%(ead|rite)%MEMSIZE% @\(%VADDR%\)=%MEMDATA%

Viewing Conversion Progress
The converter tool allows you to view the conversion progress using the progress bar. The
progress bar is displayed when you run the convert command interactively from a terminal
and if the conversion takes longer than a second. The progress bar is not displayed
when the output of the hwsw_debug_convert tool is redirected to a file. You can use the
-progress yes|no|auto option to force the progress bar on, or off.

Converting Cycle Counts into Time Values
If a CPU log file contains cycle count instead of time, you can use the following method to
convert cycle counts into a time value:
* If the clock of the core is running at the same rate all the time, you can specify the
frequency using the clockPeriod and clockOffset parameters.
* If the clock frequency of the core changes, or if the reset time is not constant, you
cannot specify the clockPeriod and clockOffset parameters for conversion. In this
case, you can use the following method to convert cycle counts into a time value:
During the run, the cycle counter signal of the core must be dumped into an FSDB file (for
example, design.fsdb file).You must specify the design.fsdb file during the converter
run. You must also specify the cycle counter signal using the cycleCounterSignal
parameter as shown in the following example.
Example:
hwsw_debug_convert -hw_fsdb design.fsdb
cycleCounterSignal=top.dut.cluster0.cpu0.cycle_

counter_signal

Debug Phase
HW/SW Debug solution provides a synchronized view for embedded software debugging
in Eclipse and HDL hardware design debugging in Verdi. Eclipse uses C source files, ELF
file and FSDB file as input files whereas Verdi uses the design FSDB file as an input.
For example, use the following commands to debug your design:
% hwsw_debug -ssf hwsw.fsdb
% hwsw_debug -ssf hwsw.fsdb -verdi_args "-lib -ssf design.fsdb"
% hwsw_debug -ssf VirtualFile.vf

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
To create a Virtual File using Verdi, perform the following steps:
1. Open the design.fsdb file.
2. In the nWave window, select the File -> Edit Virtual File command.
3. Add the hwsw.fsdbfile to FSDB File list using the Add button. Click OK.
The VirtualFile.vffile is created. This virtual file can then be used for future invocations of
Verdi or hwsw_debug.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Invoking HW/SW Debug
The Verdi platform with HW/SW Debug provides the following flows to invoke HW/SW
Debug:
* Hardware-Centric flow
* Software-Centric flow
In the Hardware-Centric flow, the HW/SW Debug window can be invoked from the Verdi
platform to debug the design with both the hardware circuit and the embedded software.
In the Software-Centric flow, the HW/SW Debug window can be directly invoked to focus
on the high-level embedded software of interest. If deeper investigation is needed for
detailed hardware behavior, the Verdi platform can be invoked on demand.
The following sections describe how to invoke HW/SW Debug in hardware-centric and
software-centric flows:
* Invoking HW/SW Debug in Hardware-Centric Flow
* Invoking HW/SW Debug in Software-Centric Flow

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The following steps illustrate how to invoke the HW/SW Debug window from the Verdi
platform. Refer to the Demo Examples section for an actual example.
1. Invoke the Verdi platform with the FSDB file:
> verdi -ssf hwsw.fsdb &

For complete debug of the HDL, the design files can also be loaded into the Verdi
platform. Refer to the Demo Examples section for an example.
Select Hardware Debug Mode in the Welcome page. After loading the simulation
results of the design including the ARM core into the Verdi platform, Eclipse with
HW/SW Debug can be opened using the Tools -> Invoke HW SW Debug command.
The Workspace Launcher form appears.

The Eclipse specified in the HW/SW Debug page of the Preferences form
(invoked by using the Tools -> Preferences command) is executed. The
default value is $VERDI_HOME/bin/eclipse.
2. Specify a workspace directory to store the Eclipse debug project and click the OK
button.

Workspace Launcher

3. The Debug Configurations form appears. Main, Architecture and Advanced tabs are
provided in this form for setting the debug session configuration.
Select the Main tab in the Debug Configurations form to configure HW/SW Debug
session.
Select the Architecture tab to configure the viewing layout of the whole system under
debug session. All the clusters and cores are listed in the Architecture tab. You can
enable or disable particular clusters/cores for the debug session. The disabled clusters/
cores are not considered for the corresponding HW/SW Debug session.
Select the Advanced tab to specify additional options. The options are sent to HW/SW
Debug as the default value of advanced usage.
For details regarding the various tabs and options available in the Debug
Configurations form, refer to the Debug Configurations Form section.
4. a. After specifying the debug configurations, click the Debug button in the Debug
Configuration form. As shown in Figure 10, when Eclipse starts for the first time,
a confirmation dialog appears asking whether the Synopsys HW SW Debug

perspective should be made the default perspective in Eclipse. Click the Yes button
to confirm the perspective switch.

Starting with the 2018.09 Verdi release, the version of Eclipse used with the HW/SW

Debug Configurations Form
The Debug Configurations form can be used to view and change all the parameters
that affect the running of HW/SW Debug session. It contains Main, Architecture, and
Advanced tabs and the following basic buttons on each of the tab:
* Apply
It triggers the standard apply mechanism in Eclipse. Additionally, it saves the
architecture description to the architecture file specified in the Architecture tab in the
Debug Configurations form.
* Revert
It triggers the standard revert mechanism in Eclipse. All changes in the Debug
Configurations form are reverted.
* Close
It closes the Debug Configurations form and eventually prompts the user to save the
changes. It does not affect the running debug session.
* Debug/Continue
Debug starts a new debug session.
Continue proceeds with the currently running session. If the user has changed
something in the debug configuration, it prompts the user to save the changes. This
does not affect the running debug session.

Main Tab
The Main tab is used to set the most important parameters of the HW/SW Debug
configuration. The user can set the location of the FSDB file, specify the path to the
HW/SW Top Instance in the design, and the run location of the simulation. The initial
conditions of the HW/SW debug session can be controlled by choosing if the start should
be at the current time from Verdi, go to a certain function, address in code on a certain
core, or just run to the first instruction.
In case Verdi is not present in the system, then the Use Current Time from Verdi option
is disabled and greyed-out.
The following sections are present in the Main tab:
* Design: Specifies the location of the FSDB file and the path of the HW/SW Top
Instance in the design in the FSDB file and HW/SW Top Instance fields respectively.
* Simulation Run Location: You can specify the path where the simulation is executed
by selecting one of the following toggle options: Use FSDB Path, Current Working
Directory, or Path.

* Initial Time: Specify the initial conditions of the HW/SW Debug session by selecting

Use Current Time from Verdi: The debug session starts at the current time of Verdi.
Go to Function/Address: The debug session goes to the specified function or

Go to First Instruction: The debug session starts at the first instruction.

Architecture Tab
The layout of the whole system under debug can be viewed in the Architecture tab. The
information displayed in the Architecture tab is a superposition of the information about
the hierarchical organization coming from the FSDB file and the hierarchical information
contained in the architecture file. The information in the architecture file always takes
precedence, thus allowing the user to customize the hierarchical information.
The Cluster/Core parameters listed in the Architecture tab are read-only.
To make changes in the parameters, re-run the conversion step using the
hwsw_debug_convert tool.

To enable or disable particular Clusters/Cores for the debug session, check/uncheck the
check boxes in front of the Cluster/Core names. The disabled Clusters/Cores do not take
part in the corresponding HW/SW Debug session.
To display the hierarchical organization of the clusters and their cores check the Show
only Cluster/Core hierarchy option. This would help you to get a better overview of the
architecture and to be able to quickly enable or disable whole clusters or single cores.

Options field in the Advanced tab. For example, the values for parameters that require

values can be specified here. The specified additional parameters override the default
startup parameters of Eclipse upon launch.

Invoking HW/SW Debug in Software-Centric Flow
The following steps illustrate how to invoke HW/SW Debug in the Software-Centric flow.
Refer to the Demo Examples section for an actual example.
1. Invoke HW/SW Debug with the FSDB file using the hwsw_debug command:
hwsw_debug -ssf hwsw.fsdb &

2. As mentioned in Step 2 of the Invoking HW/SW Debug in Hardware-Centric Flow
section, the Workspace Launcher form appears. Follow the Steps 2 to 7 in the Invoking
HW/SW Debug in Hardware-Centric Flow section to invoke the HW/SW Debug tool
only.
Optionally, you can invoke the Verdi platform by clicking the
toolbar, as illustrated in Figure 18.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
icon in the HW/SW Debug

Invoking HW/SW Debug in Software-Centric Flow

Figure 18

Invoke Verdi from HW/SW Debug Toolbar

The -ssf <FSDB_file> option is automatically applied when launching the Verdi platform
(that is, the FSDB file is opened in the nWave window as the active FSDB file).
You may also load a design.fsdb file into Verdi using the following command:
hwsw_debug -ssf hwsw.fsdb -verdi_args "-ssf design.fsdb"

With Hardware Debug section for time synchronization button details).

Using HW/SW Debug
Eclipse includes a customized Synopsys HW SW Debug perspective tailored to the
HW/SW debug solution. When you start Eclipse, this perspective becomes active
automatically.
The HW/SW Debug tool provides a programmer's view of C/Assembly code executed
on HDL CPU code. As demonstrated in Figure 19, the core contents appear in separate
views. You can add, reorganize, or remove views. Drag a view by its title to reposition it.
Figure 19

Programmers View of Code on HDL CPU

The following sections describe HW/SW Debug features in Eclipse. They also explain how
to synchronize embedded software debugging with HDL hardware design in the Verdi
platform.
* Software Debug
* Multiple Cores Debug
* Synchronization With Hardware Debug

It is possible to debug embedded code in Eclipse using breakpoints, stepping, and running
through the code. This means that debugging embedded software closely resembles the
way software debugging usually works. In addition, HW/SW Debug provides the option
to run and step backward in time. This enables easy answer to questions that frequently
occur when debugging code, like "how did the program get here", "where does this value
come from" or similar. So, going back to the call of the current function can be achieved
with a single click.

Debugging Views
The location where the execution is currently stopped can be shown with a mark in the (C
or Assembly) Source Code window during debugging (see Figure 19). The disassembly
code is also shown with the current instruction marked in the Disassembly view. The
general purpose registers of the core and their values are shown in the Registers view.
The Variables view shows the values of C code variables. As demonstrated in Figure 20,
memory contents as seen by the core at that point in time are displayed in the Memory
View.

are two fields showing time value and time unit. Current simulation time is the product of

the value in the Time Value field gets automatically re-calculated. However, the current

Debug Commands
The standard debug commands can be issued by clicking one of the icons on the debug
toolbar or using the corresponding menu items available under the Run menu. Reverse
Resume, Reverse Step Into, Reverse Step Over, and Uncall commands are additionally
provided in the debug toolbar to run or step backward in time.
* Reverse Resume: Run backward in time until a breakpoint condition is met.
* Reverse Step Into: Run backward in time until the next instruction or source line.
* Reverse Step Over: Run backward in time until the previous source line is reached.
Skip over any subroutine calls encountered.
* Uncall: Run backward in time until the point where the current subroutine is called.

Instruction Stepping Mode
Usually the stepping commands are executed based on source lines in C/C++ or
Assembly files. This means that stepping advances the simulation until the next or
previous source line is reached. During debug, sometimes no source code exists, so
debugging has to be done based on the disassembly code. In this case, normal stepping
skips over the code for which no source code exists.
HW/SW Debug provides an instruction stepping mode to support debugging by stepping
into instructions. In the debug view, click the

icon on the debug toolbar to enable

Multiple Cores Debug

instruction stepping mode. After instruction stepping mode is enabled, the stepping
commands are executed based on single assembly instructions.
Figure 28

Instruction Stepping Mode Icon

Multiple Cores Debug
HW/SW Debug solution provides support for debugging complex designs having multiple
CPUs or multiple clusters wherein each cluster further comprises of multiple cores.
HW/SW Debug solution provides programmer's views into multiple clusters and cores
simultaneously and the debug view shows call stack for multiple clusters and cores. In the
Debug View, the clusters are assigned a separate debugger process and the related cores
are each assigned a separate debugging thread of the debugger process.
Figure 29 illustrates debug view for a multi-cluster multi-core design that has two clusters
and each cluster contains four cores.
Figure 29

Multi-Core Debug View

Active Core and Switching to Different Active Core
When debugging a multi-core design, at any given moment, exactly one core is the active
core and only this core is able to receive the debugging commands issued by the user. As
shown in Figure 30, the active core is the one that has a debugging window selected in the
Debug view.

Multiple Cores Debug

Figure 30

Active Core

The currently active core is the one that provides necessary information for the other views
in Eclipse, such as, Registers view, Memory view, Variables view and so on. In other
words, these views display the corresponding information related only to the currently
active core, except when the given view is pinned to a given core.
Selecting a debug window from another core within the Debug view can simply switch to a
different current view. Immediately after switching the active core, all views in Eclipse that
are not pinned to a specific core get updated with the information coming from the new
active core.

Thread Local Breakpoint Checking Mode
Usually, breakpoints are active on all cores for which a matching source line exists.
Whichever core hits a breakpoint first initiates the interrupt. When a breakpoint is hit on a
core while stepping in another core, the step is interrupted and the focus changes to the
icon on the
core where the breakpoint is hit. To solely focus on one core, click the
debug toolbar of the debug view to enable thread local breakpoint checking.

Synchronization With Hardware Debug

After the thread local breakpoint checking mode is enabled, only breakpoints on the active
(currently focused) core are checked if they are hit. This also means that when stepping in
one core the focus never changes to another core.

Synchronization With Hardware Debug
The views of Verdi platform and Eclipse are synchronized regarding time. When the time
cursor in the nWave window is changed, the information displayed in the views of Eclipse
is also updated. When the Eclipse view is changed by stepping or running to a breakpoint,
the Verdi views are also updated to the same time. Breakpoints do not have an impact on
this operation.
As demonstrated in Figure 31, the called function is marked in the Debug view and
the contents in the Registers view are also flushed for the current cursor location. The
execution lines in Disassembly and Source Code view are also marked.
Figure 31

Set Cursor and Eclipse Views Synchronized

The synchronization is also done in the alternate direction. As soon as the current
execution location is changed in Eclipse (after some run command), the time cursor in
the Verdi platform is updated to reflect the simulation time where the current line of the
C/Assembly source code is executed in the simulation (refer to Figure 32). When the value
in the Time Value window of the Eclipse toolbar is changed, the Verdi windows also get
updated to the same time.

Synchronization With Hardware Debug

Figure 32

Step Into Source Code and nWave Synchronized

toolbar:
* Click the

icon to enable synchronization from software to hardware.

* Click the

icon to enable synchronization from hardware to software.

By default, synchronization in both directions is enabled.

Performance Profiling
Profiling allows you to measure where your program spent its runtime and allows you
to learn which functions called which other functions during execution. This information
allows you to trace and correct the parts of your program which are slower than you
expected.
The HW/SW Debug solution allows you to measure the runtime performance of the
software (SW) running on an embedded processor core. You can use the gprof option as
an argument to the HW/SW converter to generate profiler reports detailing where time was
spent by an embedded software application during execution.
The performance profiler report lists the following information for a function:
* Percentage of time spent in that function
* Average time spent in that function per call
* Which functions called it, and how often
* How often was the function called
* Which functions it called
This information allows you to quickly figure out the following:
* Portions of your code that cause slowdown

text:

* Which functions called it, and how often
* How often was the function called
* Which functions it called
This information allows you to quickly figure out the following:
* Portions of your code that cause slowdown
* Portions of your code that you should spend effort to optimize runtime performance
This feature allows you to get performance-related information without modifying the
application code.
The following sections describe this feature in detail:
* Generating Performance Profiler Reports
* Generating Assembly Listing Annotated with Execution Times
* Limitations

Use the hwsw_debug_convert command along with the gprof option in the command line
to generate profiling information. Following is the syntax:
hwsw_debug_convert -load_design design.xml gprof -o hwsw.fsdb

Where, the design.xml file contains the configuration of the log file names, ELF file names,
and CPU types.
If hwsw.fsdb file already exists, use the following syntax to generate profiling
information: hwsw_debug_convert -i hwsw.fsdb gprof
The hwsw_debug_convert command processes information in the CPU log file or an
existing hwsw.fsdb file and writes the profiling information into a profiler file with the format
filename .gmon.out (for example, cluster1.gmon.out).
If the design contains multiple clusters, a separate profiler file is generated for each
cluster. The hwsw_debug_convert command automatically selects distinct names, such as
cluster0.gmon.out, cluster1.gmon.out, and so on.
You can view the profiling information in Eclipse or generate the profiler report in text
format using the gprof tool, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 34

Viewing Performance Profiler Reports

format. Following is the syntax:
gprof <elf_file> filename.gmon.out > filename.log

Where, filename.log is the text file to which the profiling information is written.

Viewing Profiler Reports in Eclipse
To view profiler reports in Eclipse, perform the following steps:
1. Select a Cluster in the Debug View, as shown in Figure 1-2.
2. Click the Show Profiling Data icon

in the HW/SW Debug toolbar.

Eclipse searches for the ELF and gmon.out files of the current selection in the Debug
View, and if both are found, it automatically opens the Gprof View with the related profiling
data, as shown in Figure 35. Eclipse generates single profiler report for each cluster, if you
select multiple clusters in the Debug View, Eclipse displays profiling information for all of
them.

Figure 35

Viewing Profiler Information in Eclipse

If Eclipse is not able to locate any or both of the ELF and gmon.out files, it displays
the Gmon File Viewer dialog box, as shown in the following figure, which allows you to
manually specify those files.

Figure 36

Gmon File Viewer Dialog Box

After the files are specified, the version of the Binutils is checked to see if it meets the
minimum recommendations before opening the Gprof View. If the version of the Binutils
does not meet the minimum recommended version, a warning dialog box is displayed as
follows:
Figure 37

Binutils Version Dialog Box

Click the OK button in the Binutils Version warning dialog box to open the Gprof View.
To resolve the Binutils warning message, make sure that the Binutils are picked
up from the QSC compliant tool chain.
Alternatively, you can also perform the following steps to open the Gprof View:
1. Click the File > Open File command.
2. Select a gmon.out file in the Open File dialog box, as shown in the following figure,
and click the OK button.

Figure 38

Open File Dialog Box

3. Click the File System button in the Gmon File Viewer dialog box as shown in
Figure 39.
Figure 39

Selecting a Binary File

4. Select a binary file in the Open Binary File dialog box and click the OK button.
5. Click the OK button in the Gmon File Viewer dialog box to open the Gprof View with the
related profiling data.

Generating Assembly Listing Annotated with Execution Times
You can also create profiling information by creating an assembly listing annotated with the
execution times.
To create an assembly listing annotated with the execution times, you must first create a
disassembly listing. This depends on the tool you use:
* For gcc/binutils, use the objdump -d <ELF_FILE> command
* For clang, use the llvm-objdump -d <ELF_FILE> command
* For RVDS/ARMCC, use the fromelf -c <ELF_FILE> command
To create a disassembly listing, the output must be written into a.disfile (for example,
myapp.dis). You can then create an annotated disassembly listing using the following
command:
hwsw_debug_prof -d myapp.dis -g filename.gmon.out

% objdump -d ./test_sw/test.elf > myapp.dis
% hwsw_debug_prof -d myapp.dis -g file.gmon.out -o test.dis.log

disassembly file.

Limitations
Following are the limitations of this feature:
* If you want to view line-based profiling information, enable debug information when you
compile your application. Debug information maps addresses to source lines.
This does not conflict with the requirement to support optimized code. Most compilers
can generate debug information for optimized code.
* The time consumed by the assembly instructions is calculated based on the data of the
instruction log. This time might be inaccurate due to certain effects, depending on the
complexity of the architecture.

Coverage Support
The following sections describe HW/SW Coverage support in detail:
* Line Coverage Support
* Coverage Exclusion Support

Verdi HW/SW Debug supports line coverage for the C/C++ or Assembly application code
which is run on an embedded processor core part of a design. This feature generates
metrics for total coverage of lines that tell you how much of your code is actually executed
by the tests. Verdi HW/SW Debug uses the new hwsw_debug_coverage tool to generate
line coverage information.
Line coverage shows which lines of code are exercised, and which ones are not, by the
application tests during a simulation run. Line coverage also produces annotated listing
that identify the lines of code that are not exercised.
The following topics describe this section in detail:
* Generating Coverage Information

* Example of Text Report Containing Coverage Percentage per Function
* Generating Annotated Source Files with Line Coverage Information

text:
Use the hwsw_debug_convert command along with the gprof option in the command line
to generate coverage information. Following is the syntax:
hwsw_debug_convert -load_design design.xml gprof -o hwsw.fsdb

Where, the design.xml file contains the configuration of the log file names, ELF file
names, and CPU types.
If the hwsw.fsdb file already exists, use the following syntax to generate
coverage information: hwsw_debug_convert -i hwsw.fsdb gprof
The hwsw_debug_convert command processes information in the CPU log file or an
existing hwsw.fsdb file and writes the coverage information into a file with the format

filename.gmon.out (for example, cluster1.gmon.out). The gmon.out file contains

information to compute coverage.

You can also merge gcov JSON software unit coverage into the final source-level
coverage result by using the -merge_gcov_json option of hwsw_debug_coverage.
This option merges gcov JSON line coverage with HW/SW Debug line coverage and
propagates the merged result to .covdb, text reports, annotated source files, and .info
output.

Options Supported by the hwsw_debug_coverage Tool
The following table lists the options supported by the hwsw_debug_coverage tool:
Option

-l, -elf_file FILE

The ELF file for which the coverage information should be
generated.

-g, -gmon_files FILE

The input data file produced with the gprof option of
the hwsw_debug_convert tool containing profiling and
coverage information. If there are multiple gmon.outfiles
(for multiple tests), you must separate them with commas.
The results are the total coverage with the sum of the
coverage from the individual files. The option defaults to
gmon.out if no gmon files or file-lists are specified.

-f, -gmon_list FILE

A file with a list of gmon files (one file per line) produced
with the gprof option of the hwsw_debug_convert tool
containing profiling and coverage information. The results
of all gmon files are merged (summed up). You can also
provide multiple gmon file lists separated with commas.

-d, -disassembly FILE

Annotates the given disassembly file.

-o, -annotated_disassembly FILE

The output file that contains the content of the disassembly
file annotated with the coverage information. Using "-" as
filename writes the output on the STDOUT. Defaults to the
name of the disassembly source file extended with ".cov".

text:
Generates coverage report into the given file. If
no filename is given, writes coverage report to the
"coverage_report.txt" file.

title: 0.00 0.00 1/1 init_libc [32]
text:
Annotates source files with coverage information in gcov
format. If no output directory is given, a directory named
"src_coverage" is created.

title: 0.00 0.00 1/1 init_libc [32]
text:
Adds one or multiple paths to search source files in.
Searches in the sub-hierarchy given. Multiple paths must
be separated by ":".

Option

title: 0.00 0.00 1/1 init_libc [32]
text:
Changes the name of the file generated with coverage
information for displaying in Eclipse. The default name is
based on the name of the gmon.out file.

title: 0.00 0.00 1/1 init_libc [32]
text:
Generates coverage information in the format compatible to
lcov .info file. The default name is based on the name of the
gmon.out file.

-no_inlined_calls

Does not add coverage for the lines containing inlined
function calls . That is, inlined calls are displayed without
code (there is no 'call' instruction due to inlining). The

Merging Coverage Data
To collect the coverage data for multiple tests, perform the following steps:
1. Run the simulation/emulation with the first test
2. Use the hwsw_debug_convert tool to generate a gmon.out file for the first test. For
example, test1/gmon.out
3. Run the simulation/emulation with the next test
4. Use the hwsw_debug_convert tool to generate a gmon.out file for the next test. For
example, test2/gmon.out
5. Repeat the last two steps (3 and 4) for each test in the test set.
6. Provide a comma separated list of all gmon files when running the coverage tool to
generate the desired merged coverage information for all tests.
hwsw_debug_coverage -gmon_file test1/gmon.out,test2/gmon.out

The application ELF file must be the same for all runs. This is checked by the
coverage tool.
When running an application on a multi-core processor, code executed on any of the
cores is added to the coverage. This is equivalent to merging the coverage data calculated
separately for each of the cores.

Requirements on ELF File
To generate annotated source, the ELF binary must contain debug information which
allows to map code addresses back to source lines.
Optimizations might optimize certain code lines. The optimized code lines do not appear
as covered/uncovered, just like other lines which did not result in any code, for example,
comment or empty lines.
If there is no debug information, you still have the option to generate a disassembly based
coverage report.

Viewing Line Coverage Information in Eclipse
The .covdb file containing coverage information is generated by the
hwsw_debug_coverage tool. This file is meant to be read and displayed by the HW/SW
Debug Coverage Eclipse plug-in.
Following is the syntax to generate the .covdb file containing coverage information:
hwsw_debug_coverage -l test.elf -covdb hwsw.covdb
hwsw_debug -ssf hwsw.fsdb &

You can also merge gcov JSON software unit coverage into the final
source-level coverage result by using the -merge_gcov_json option of
hwsw_debug_coverage. This option merges gcov JSON line coverage with
HW/SW Debug line coverage and propagates the merged result to .covdb, text
reports, annotated source files, and .info output.

The tool adds the line coverage counts from the gcov JSON file or files to the existing
HW/SW Debug line coverage data and writes the merged result to the selected output
format.
Examples
* Generate a merged coverage database for Eclipse:
hwsw_debug_coverage \
-elf_file test.elf \
-g cluster0.gmon.out \
-merge_gcov_json unit1.gcov.json.gz,unit2.gcov.json \
-covdb merged.covdb

This command merges source-level line coverage from the gcov JSON files with
HW/SW Debug coverage derived from cluster0.gmon.out, then writes the merged
result to merged.covdb. You can open merged.covdb in the Eclipse Coverage View.
* Generate annotated sources from merged coverage:
hwsw_debug_coverage \
-elf_file test.elf \
-g cluster0.gmon.out \
-merge_gcov_json test.gcov.json.gz \
-add_source_path src \
-annotate_sources merged_src_cov

text:
This command generates annotated source files that reflect the merged line coverage
result.
How the merge works
The tool reads line coverage information from the gcov JSON input and merges it with
the existing HW/SW Debug source-level line coverage. For each valid source file and line
number:
* The tool adds the gcov execution count to the current line count.
* If the line does not exist in the HW/SW Debug dataset, the tool creates a new line
coverage entry.
* The tool recomputes file coverage and function coverage from the merged line
coverage result. It does not merge file-level or function-level execution counts directly
from the JSON input.

Partial coverage handling
gcov can mark a line as partially covered when the line has execution count greater than
zero (count > 0)and some basic blocks on that line did not execute (unexecuted_block

== true). During merge, the tool keeps the partial coverage flag if either gcov or HW/SW

Debug reports the line as partially covered.

Because the merge happens at source-line granularity, the tool cannot determine whether
partial coverage from different sources collectively covers all basic blocks on that line. As
a result, a line can remain marked as partially covered in the merged output even when
different tests cover different execution paths.

Function Declaration Lines
gcov can report an entry count on a function declaration line. hwsw_debug_coverage
tracks coverage on lines that map to executable instructions. To keep the merged result
consistent, the tool maps a declaration-line function entry count to the first executable line
in that function.

Viewing Merged Results in Eclipse
Generate a .covdb file from the merged coverage result, then open it in the Eclipse
Coverage View. The Coverage View displays the merged source-level line coverage as
file-level and function-level statistics. Double-click a function to open the corresponding
source and review covered, uncovered, and partially covered lines.

Requirements and Compatibility
This feature supports gcov JSON coverage data that follows the JSON format
documented for GCC gcov. The implementation targets GCC 12.3.0 and JSON format
version 1. The tool can read newer JSON output versions, but it processes only the fields
defined in version 1 and ignores any additional fields.

Warnings and Error Handling
The tool validates the JSON structure before it merges any data. If required fields are
missing or invalid, the tool skips the affected JSON file, file entry, or line entry and reports
a warning. Examples include:
* Missing or invalid files array in the JSON file.
* Missing or invalid file entry inside the files array.
* Missing or invalid lines array for a source file.
* Missing or invalid line_number or count in a line entry.
* Source file path in the JSON file does not match any source file found by the tool.

Limitations
The following are the limitations of -merge_gcov_json:
* The tool merges line coverage only from gcov JSON input. It does not merge branch,
condition, or block coverage.
* Function coverage and file coverage are derived from the merged line coverage. The
tool ignores function execution counts from the JSON input.
* File matching depends on source file name and line number correspondence.
Mismatches can lead to partial merges or skipped files.
* If you use -mixed together with -merge_gcov_json, source line counts can differ from
disassembly counts. Source lines include merged gcov and HW/SW Debug counts, but
disassembly counts reflect HW/SW Debug data only. The tool reports a warning in this
case.
* You cannot use -merge_gcov_json together with -basic_block_based. gcov JSON
input is line-based, so the tool reports an error when both options are specified.

Generating a Text Report
Following is the syntax to generate a text report with line coverage information:
hwsw_debug_coverage -elf_file test.elf -report report.txt

Generating Annotated Source Files with Line Coverage
Information
Following is the syntax to generate annotated source files with line coverage information:
hwsw_debug_coverage -elf_file file.elf -annotate_sources <new_dir>

Example:
%> hwsw_debug_coverage -elf_file ../coremark.elf -add_source_path
test_sw/ -annotate_sources ann_path

You can generate a folder with annotated source files. For each source file an annotated
copy of the source file is created under the respective path. The lines containing code are
prefixed with the number of times they were executed (covered lines). The lines which are
not executed (uncovered lines) are prefixed with "#####". The lines which did not result
in any code are prefixed with "-". The lines which do not produce any code (for example,
comment lines or variable declarations) are not counted as uncovered lines.

Generating Annotated Disassembly File with Line Coverage
Information
To generate annotated disassembly file with line coverage information, you must first
create a disassembly listing. This depends on the tool you use:
* For gcc/binutils, use the objdump -d <ELF_FILE> command
* For clang, use the llvm-objdump -d <ELF_FILE> command
* For RVDS/ARMCC, use the fromelf -c <ELF_FILE> command
To create a disassembly listing, the output must be written into a .dis file (for example,
myapp.dis). You can then use the following syntax to generate annotated disassembly file
with line coverage information:
hwsw_debug_coverage -elf_file file.elf -disassembly file.dis
-annotated_disassembly ann_file.dis

Example:
%> hwsw_debug_coverage -elf_file ../coremark.elf -disassembly myapp.dis
-annotated_disassembly after_myapp.dis

The lines containing assembly instruction are prefixed with the number of times they were
executed (covered lines). The instructions which are not executed (uncovered lines) are
prefixed with "#####". The lines which did not result in any code are prefixed with "-".

Coverage Exclusion Support

Coverage Exclusion Support
Coverage data is collected over multiple tests and simulations. Analyzing the accumulated
coverage results uncovers parts of a design that have not been exercised and validated.
These uncovered parts are called coverage holes. Some coverage holes can be excluded,
such as debug code, because part of the design functionality will not be used in valid
scenarios.
Verdi HW/SW Debug supports specifying coverage exclusion with an exclusion file.

Specifying Exclusions
You can use the following command to specify exclusion (text only) patterns in a file:
% hwsw_debug_coverage -exclusion_file <FILE>

This command allows you to specify a text file containing exclusion patterns to be
excluded from coverage statistics. For a description of the syntax of an exclusion file, use
the -help exclusion command as follows:
% hwsw_debug_coverage -help exclusion

A coverage exclusion file (FILE) is a line based text file where each line describes one
exclusion. The following forms of exclusions are supported:
* Any line starting with a # is a comment, and is ignored.
* The following pattern excludes all source files named dhry_1.c.
dhry_1.c:

* The following pattern excludes line 300 in all source files named.
dhry_1.c: 300

* The following pattern excludes the range of lines starting with 200 and ending with 220:
dhry_2.c: 200-220

* The following pattern excludes all coverage points in function Proc_6 of file dhry_2.c:
dhry_2.c: Proc_6

* The following pattern excludes one line in function Func_2 relative to the function
header:
dhry_2.c: Func_2 +26

Coverage Exclusion Support

* The following pattern excludes range of lines in function Func_2 relative to the function
header:
dhry_2.c: Func_2 +32-34

* The following pattern excludes all functions named Proc_5, in all files:
: Proc_5

* The following pattern excludes all coverage points in .c files matching the name
dhry_*.c:
dhry_*.c:

* The following pattern excludes all files in the sub-folder drivers/other:
drivers/other/*:

* The following pattern excludes any source file in the folder drivers, or any sub-folder:
drivers/:

Adding a Custom Core
This chapter describes the procedures to customize the Synopsys HW/SW Debug
environment to work with your custom processor.
Customizing the HW/SW Debug environment involves the following three steps detailed in
this chapter.
* Create a configuration file with the names of all CPU registers
* Create a pattern file to parse your CPU log file
* Validate your CPU Core in the HW/SW Debug environment
The following sections describe this feature in detail:
* Prerequisites
* Creating the HW/SW Debug Configuration File
* Creating the Log-Pattern File
* Testing and Debugging

Prerequisites
The following topics describe the prerequisites:
* Software Development Tool (Compiler)
* Debugger (GDB)
* HDL Simulator

Software Development Tool (Compiler)
The software compile tool for your processor must generate the executable file (also
called the application file). The file must use a format that the GDB used for this integration
accepts.

Creating the HW/SW Debug Configuration File

The application file is loaded into GDB during the HW/SW Debug session. The HW/SW
Debug server loads the application content into its memory for viewing in the Eclipse
environment.

Debugger (GDB)
A GDB (GNU Debugger, http://sourceware.org/gdb) retargeted for your processor
architecture is required. It is recommended to use the latest version available for your CPU
core, and the GDB version must be v7.0 or later. GDB must be able to connect to a target
using the Remote Serial Protocol (RSP) over a TCP/IP connection (via the command
target remote :port). Normally this should not be an issue, however, for some heavily
customized versions of GDB, it might be.

HDL Simulator
The Verdi tool suite works with all simulation vendors. The hwsw_debug_convert
application parses the CPU log file, so there is no dependency on the simulator used. The
simulator must generate an FSDB file for any design signals displayed in Verdi.

Creating the HW/SW Debug Configuration File
The Synopsys HW/SW Debug requires a configuration file in XML format to specify the
registers available for your custom processor. You can find the processor registers using
the GDB debugger used for this integration. You can use the registers specified in the
configuration file to map the registers specified in the FSDB file to the registers in the
GDB.
The registers are mapped using the internal GDB register numbering order. To find the
register names and numbers in the GDB, you can run the GDB executable with one of
the following commands. You can use the help internal command to get help on the
command format for your GDB.
% custom-gdb \ --ex "maintenance print remote-registers" \ --ex "quit" |&
tee log
% custom-gdb \ --ex "maintenance print registers" \ --ex "quit" |& tee
log

The above command prints the register information similar to the following:
Name Nr Rel Offset Size Type
zero 0 0 0 4 uint32_t
r1 1 1 4 4 uint32_t
r2 2 2 8 4 uint32_t
more GPRs register
pc 32 32 128 4 uint32_t
status 33 33 132 4 uint32_t

Creating the Log-Pattern File
estatus 34 34 136 4 uint32_t
sp 35 35 140 4 uint32_t
more Control/Flags registers

From the above register names and the Rel and Nr columns, you can create the following
configuration file with the syntax given below. A Perl script is available to translate the
GDB log into the XML syntax.
% hwsw_reg_to_xml.pl archname logcore_name.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<esw_debug_configuration>
<architecture name="MyCore">
<reg name="zero" bitsize="32" path="core_regs[0]"/>
<reg name="r1" bitsize="32" path="core_regs[1]"/>
More GPRS info here
<reg name="pc" bitsize="32" path="pc" is_pc='1'/>
<reg name="status" bitsize="32" path="ctl_regs[0]"/>
<reg name="estatus" bitsize="32" path="ctl_regs[1]"/>
More Control/Flags register here
<mem name="mem" addrsize="28" path="memory_access"/>
</architecture>
</esw_debug_configuration>

The Verdi HW/SW Debug tool must know which register is the program counter. The Perl
script tries to detect this (any register called pc). Check that this is correct. Edit if needed,
so that you have one is_pc='1' tag, and it is attached to the PC of your core as follows:
<reg name="pc" bitsize="32" path="pc" is_pc='1'/>

Testing and Debugging
This final step validates the configuration file which you created earlier in the process. This
step involves testing the register configuration file and log pattern file along with the GDB
integration.

Validating the Converter Pattern File
The converter can be executed on a sample CPU log file, FSDB file, or generated text
file. It is recommended to initially generate a text file output as this is easier to manually
validate the results of a short test.
% hwsw_debug_convert \
cpuType=MyProc \
patternFile=MyProc.pat \
configName=MyProc \
exeFile=test.elf \
gdbPath=custom_gdb \
clockPeriod=1ns \
-C pwd \
-i cpu.log \
-o output.txt

The Register definition file is specified by configName, and hwsw_debug_convert
searches for MyProc.xml in the current directory (or the directory specified by the -C
argument).
The clockPeriod is required if your CPU log has cycle counts. This parameter should be
removed if you have ns or ps (or other time units) in the log file.
The output format is Verdi FSDB if the .fsdb extension is specified. Any other extension
generates a text file that allows you to see the result of the conversion.

Testing and Debugging

If any lines do not match a pattern from the log pattern file, then an error is issued. You
can use these errors to debug the line that does not match any pattern.
If register names do not match, then review the MyProc.xml file to see if the register
names are correct.
It is useful to view the original CPU log file and the generated output.txt file together and
perform some basic manual checking for some program counter values, register values,
and memory read/write transactions. Just a few of these lines should be checked to
ensure that the data was parsed correctly. Note that a single pattern with ".*" matches all
lines but does not extract data from the CPU log.
Rerun the conversion, and specify -o hwsw.fsdb to generate an FSDB file for validation.

Invoking Verdi HW/SW Debug Tool
Start by invoking Verdi HW/SW debug from the eclipse side. It is easier to debug any
simple issue with this invoke method. If required, invoke from the Verdi tool later.
% hwsw_debug -C pwd -ssf hwsw.fsdb

If the Eclipse environment does not invoke or fails to invoke GDB, you can troubleshoot as
follows:
1. Register-Configuration File Not Found
Specify the path to the directory containing the register configuration file
% hwsw_debug -C config_directory
% hwsw_debug -config_path config_directory

Check if the name of the configName parameter during conversion is correct. Verdi
automatically adds ".xml" to the end of this name.
2. GDB not found
Invoke your custom_gdb from the PATH environment variable.
Check if the gdbPath=custom_gdb name is correct during the
hwsw_debug_convert step.
Ensure that the custom_gdb is on your path:
% which custom_gdb

3. Other Errors

Testing and Debugging

Check the Verdi console for any error message and correct the problem
Check for any GDB connection error message in the $cwd/hwswDebugLog/
HwSwDebug.log

Check if the .gdbinit files under $cwd or $HOME exist, and if they are correct.
If the Eclipse and GDB tools do not invoke, contact Synopsys for further assistance.

Integration Test
In this test, each register is loaded with a specific value and various memory read/write
statements are executed. This allows you to test the basic functionality that the Eclipse
environment uses to show complex C data and other data types. If possible, run a short
test that loads each register with a fixed value and convert the log to FSDB. Then step
through the code in Eclipse one opcode at a time:
* Switch to instruction stepping mode (select the "i" icon in the Debug view)
* Check if the PC value is correct and the disassembly matches the CPU log file
* Check that the time displayed in Eclipse matches the time in the CPU log file
* Check if the register value updates after each step matches the disassembly
* Check if stepping over a store instruction updates the memory view
If you see behavior you do not understand, contact Synopsys for further assistance.

Known Issues and Limitations
The following known issues exist in the HW/SW Debug feature:

counter signal from an FSDB to calculate timestamps, when the timestamps are based
on cycle counts of an unfixed core clock.
* The hwsw_debug_convert tool does not support the interactive use model.
* It is not possible to alter the embedded core's state (registers, memory, and program
flow) in Eclipse.

Information
Following is the syntax to generate annotated source files with line coverage information:
hwsw_debug_coverage -elf_file file.elf -annotate_sources <new_dir>

Coverage Exclusion Support

Coverage Exclusion Support
Coverage data is collected over multiple tests and simulations. Analyzing the accumulated
coverage results uncovers parts of a design that have not been exercised and validated.
These uncovered parts are called coverage holes. Some coverage holes can be excluded,
such as debug code, because part of the design functionality will not be used in valid
scenarios.
Verdi HW/SW Debug supports specifying coverage exclusion with an exclusion file.

Specifying Exclusions
You can use the following command to specify exclusion (text only) patterns in a file:
% hwsw_debug_coverage -exclusion_file <FILE>

This command allows you to specify a text file containing exclusion patterns to be
excluded from coverage statistics. For a description of the syntax of an exclusion file, use
the -help exclusion command as follows:
% hwsw_debug_coverage -help exclusion

A coverage exclusion file (FILE) is a line based text file where each line describes one
exclusion. The following forms of exclusions are supported:
* Any line starting with a # is a comment, and is ignored.
* The following pattern excludes all source files named dhry_1.c.
dhry_1.c:

* The following pattern excludes line 300 in all source files named.
dhry_1.c: 300

* The following pattern excludes the range of lines starting with 200 and ending with 220:
dhry_2.c: 200-220

* The following pattern excludes all coverage points in function Proc_6 of file dhry_2.c:
dhry_2.c: Proc_6

* The following pattern excludes one line in function Func_2 relative to the function
header:
dhry_2.c: Func_2 +26

header:
dhry_2.c: Func_2 +32-34

* The following pattern excludes all functions named Proc_5, in all files:
: Proc_5

* The following pattern excludes all coverage points in .c files matching the name
dhry_*.c:
dhry_*.c:

* The following pattern excludes all files in the sub-folder drivers/other:
drivers/other/*:

drivers/:

Adding a Custom Core
This chapter describes the procedures to customize the Synopsys HW/SW Debug
environment to work with your custom processor.
Customizing the HW/SW Debug environment involves the following three steps detailed in
this chapter.
* Create a configuration file with the names of all CPU registers
* Create a pattern file to parse your CPU log file
* Validate your CPU Core in the HW/SW Debug environment
The following sections describe this feature in detail:
* Prerequisites
* Creating the HW/SW Debug Configuration File
* Creating the Log-Pattern File
* Testing and Debugging

Prerequisites
The following topics describe the prerequisites:
* Software Development Tool (Compiler)
* Debugger (GDB)
* HDL Simulator

Software Development Tool (Compiler)
The software compile tool for your processor must generate the executable file (also
called the application file). The file must use a format that the GDB used for this integration
accepts.

Creating the HW/SW Debug Configuration File

The application file is loaded into GDB during the HW/SW Debug session. The HW/SW
Debug server loads the application content into its memory for viewing in the Eclipse
environment.

Debugger (GDB)
A GDB (GNU Debugger, http://sourceware.org/gdb) retargeted for your processor
architecture is required. It is recommended to use the latest version available for your CPU
core, and the GDB version must be v7.0 or later. GDB must be able to connect to a target
using the Remote Serial Protocol (RSP) over a TCP/IP connection (via the command
target remote :port).

core, and the GDB version must be v7.0 or later. GDB must be able to connect to a target
using the Remote Serial Protocol (RSP) over a TCP/IP connection (via the command
target remote :port). Normally this should not be an issue, however, for some heavily
customized versions of GDB, it might be.

HDL Simulator
The Verdi tool suite works with all simulation vendors. The hwsw_debug_convert
application parses the CPU log file, so there is no dependency on the simulator used. The
simulator must generate an FSDB file for any design signals displayed in Verdi.

Creating the HW/SW Debug Configuration File
The Synopsys HW/SW Debug requires a configuration file in XML format to specify the
registers available for your custom processor. You can find the processor registers using
the GDB debugger used for this integration. You can use the registers specified in the
configuration file to map the registers specified in the FSDB file to the registers in the
GDB.
The registers are mapped using the internal GDB register numbering order. To find the
register names and numbers in the GDB, you can run the GDB executable with one of
the following commands. You can use the help internal command to get help on the
command format for your GDB.
% custom-gdb \ --ex "maintenance print remote-registers" \ --ex "quit" |&
tee log
% custom-gdb \ --ex "maintenance print registers" \ --ex "quit" |& tee
log

The above command prints the register information similar to the following:
Name Nr Rel Offset Size Type
zero 0 0 0 4 uint32_t
r1 1 1 4 4 uint32_t
r2 2 2 8 4 uint32_t
more GPRs register
pc 32 32 128 4 uint32_t
status 33 33 132 4 uint32_t

Creating the Log-Pattern File
estatus 34 34 136 4 uint32_t
sp 35 35 140 4 uint32_t
more Control/Flags registers

From the above register names and the Rel and Nr columns, you can create the following
configuration file with the syntax given below. A Perl script is available to translate the
GDB log into the XML syntax.
% hwsw_reg_to_xml.pl archname logcore_name.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<esw_debug_configuration>
<architecture name="MyCore">
<reg name="zero" bitsize="32" path="core_regs[0]"/>
<reg name="r1" bitsize="32" path="core_regs[1]"/>
More GPRS info here
<reg name="pc" bitsize="32" path="pc" is_pc='1'/>
<reg name="status" bitsize="32" path="ctl_regs[0]"/>
<reg name="estatus" bitsize="32" path="ctl_regs[1]"/>
More Control/Flags register here
<mem name="mem" addrsize="28" path="memory_access"/>
</architecture>
</esw_debug_configuration>

The Verdi HW/SW Debug tool must know which register is the program counter. The Perl
script tries to detect this (any register called pc). Check that this is correct. Edit if needed,
so that you have one is_pc='1' tag, and it is attached to the PC of your core as follows:
<reg name="pc" bitsize="32" path="pc" is_pc='1'/>

Creating the Log-Pattern File
The Verdi HW/SW-Debug tool requires information about each opcode executed during
the test so that you can re-create the CPU state at any point in time for post-process
debugging. During simulation, a CPU log file is typically created, and you must convert this
text information into a binary FSDB file for use by Verdi HW/SW Debug.
A converter tool is included in the Verdi package to perform this conversion. The converter
requires a log pattern file with regular expression syntax to allow easy parsing of your
specific log file format.

Testing and Debugging
This final step validates the configuration file which you created earlier in the process. This
step involves testing the register configuration file and log pattern file along with the GDB
integration.

Validating the Converter Pattern File
The converter can be executed on a sample CPU log file, FSDB file, or generated text
file. It is recommended to initially generate a text file output as this is easier to manually
validate the results of a short test.
% hwsw_debug_convert \
cpuType=MyProc \
patternFile=MyProc.pat \
configName=MyProc \
exeFile=test.elf \
gdbPath=custom_gdb \
clockPeriod=1ns \
-C pwd \
-i cpu.log \
-o output.txt

The Register definition file is specified by configName, and hwsw_debug_convert
searches for MyProc.xml in the current directory (or the directory specified by the -C
argument).
The clockPeriod is required if your CPU log has cycle counts. This parameter should be
removed if you have ns or ps (or other time units) in the log file.
The output format is Verdi FSDB if the .fsdb extension is specified. Any other extension

The output format is Verdi FSDB if the .fsdb extension is specified. Any other extension
generates a text file that allows you to see the result of the conversion.

Testing and Debugging

If any lines do not match a pattern from the log pattern file, then an error is issued. You
can use these errors to debug the line that does not match any pattern.
If register names do not match, then review the MyProc.xml file to see if the register
names are correct.
It is useful to view the original CPU log file and the generated output.txt file together and
perform some basic manual checking for some program counter values, register values,
and memory read/write transactions. Just a few of these lines should be checked to
ensure that the data was parsed correctly. Note that a single pattern with ".*" matches all
lines but does not extract data from the CPU log.
Rerun the conversion, and specify -o hwsw.fsdb to generate an FSDB file for validation.

Invoking Verdi HW/SW Debug Tool
Start by invoking Verdi HW/SW debug from the eclipse side. It is easier to debug any
simple issue with this invoke method. If required, invoke from the Verdi tool later.
% hwsw_debug -C pwd -ssf hwsw.fsdb

If the Eclipse environment does not invoke or fails to invoke GDB, you can troubleshoot as
follows:
1. Register-Configuration File Not Found
Specify the path to the directory containing the register configuration file
% hwsw_debug -C config_directory
% hwsw_debug -config_path config_directory

Check if the name of the configName parameter during conversion is correct. Verdi
automatically adds ".xml" to the end of this name.
2. GDB not found
Invoke your custom_gdb from the PATH environment variable.
Check if the gdbPath=custom_gdb name is correct during the
hwsw_debug_convert step.
Ensure that the custom_gdb is on your path:
% which custom_gdb

3. Other Errors

Testing and Debugging

Check the Verdi console for any error message and correct the problem
Check for any GDB connection error message in the $cwd/hwswDebugLog/
HwSwDebug.log

Check if the .gdbinit files under $cwd or $HOME exist, and if they are correct.
If the Eclipse and GDB tools do not invoke, contact Synopsys for further assistance.

Integration Test
In this test, each register is loaded with a specific value and various memory read/write
statements are executed. This allows you to test the basic functionality that the Eclipse
environment uses to show complex C data and other data types. If possible, run a short
test that loads each register with a fixed value and convert the log to FSDB. Then step
through the code in Eclipse one opcode at a time:
* Switch to instruction stepping mode (select the "i" icon in the Debug view)
* Check if the PC value is correct and the disassembly matches the CPU log file
* Check that the time displayed in Eclipse matches the time in the CPU log file
* Check if the register value updates after each step matches the disassembly
* Check if stepping over a store instruction updates the memory view

Demo Example 1
This demo uses the dhrystone example located in the $VERDI_HOME/demo/
hwsw_debug/dhrystone directory. This example demonstrates how to invoke Eclipse from
the Verdi platform to debug the design.
Perform the following steps to run the demo:
1. Copy the test case to your local directory:
%> cp -r $VERDI_HOME/demo/hwsw_debug/dhrystone.

2. Import the design with the recorder module library and load the generated FSDB file to
the Verdi platform:
%> gmake hwsw_debug

The following command displays the list of available targets and the description:
%> gmake help

3. Enter Hardware Debug Mode:
In the Welcome Page, click the Work Mode icon.
Select the Hardware Debug Mode option.
Click the Go to Work button to enter Hardware Debug Mode.
4. Invoke HW/SW Debug using the Tools -> Invoke HW SW Debug command. Click the

to store the debug project the first time HW/SW Debug is invoked.

The design consists of two clusters, each with two cores and each core runs different

Known Issues and Limitations
The following known issues exist in the HW/SW Debug feature:
* The hwsw_debug_convert tool does not support specifications of reference cycle
counter signal from an FSDB to calculate timestamps, when the timestamps are based
on cycle counts of an unfixed core clock.
* The hwsw_debug_convert tool does not support the interactive use model.
* It is not possible to alter the embedded core's state (registers, memory, and program
flow) in Eclipse.

Preface
IDX enables reusing waveforms to avoid continually re-creating and re-running stimulus.
A waveform (usually FSDB) records the values each signal or bus contains throughout the
simulation run.
It is a good source to replay those values as stimulus in a simulation.

Customer Support

Accessing SolvNetPlus

frequently asked questions about Synopsys tools. The SolvNetPlus site also gives you
access to a wide range of Synopsys online services including software downloads,

To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary
language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also
includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working
environment, including terms that are embedded in our software and IPs. At the same
time, we are working to ensure that our web content and software applications are usable
to people of varying abilities. You may still find examples of non-inclusive language in our

software or documentation as our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are
currently under review to remove exclusionary language.

Introduction
SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) describe legal or illegal behavior.
Simulation or formal verification can observe this behavior at the point of insertion. The
tool then flags the behavior as passed or failed. The benefits of assertions fall into the
following categories: reducing verification time, catching errors earlier, focusing the design
effort, and pinpointing sources of error.
Assertion IPs (AIP) have pre-built assertions that help to verify and signoff the IPs in
System on Chip (SoC) designs.
They can significantly reduce verification effort and improve design quality. They monitor
a target design without modifying the corresponding RTL. You can apply them in either
simulation or formal verification.
In the simulation environment, it is quite complex to compile the Testbenches and the RTL.
Therefore, once the existing simulation environment is ready, applying the SVA/AIP
afterwards become a challenge.
The following figure illustrates three issues that you need to overcome:
* The SVA/AIP must be bound to the DUT; an additional bind file must be provided.
* The recompilation is needed after applying the SVA/AIP and the bind file.
This may introduce unexpected errors due to the complex existing simulation
environment.

Chapter 1: Introduction

* The simulation runtime performance may be downgraded due to the additional SVA/
AIP checkers.
Figure 1

Three issues to Overcome

Setting Up the Environment
You need to run the following command in the C (CSH) shell environment before running
IDX:
% setenv VERDI_HOME <verdi_installation_path>
% setenv PATH $VERDI_HOME/bin:$PATH

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The following figure illustrates the flow of IDX assertion verification acceleration:
Figure 3

IDX Assertion Verification Acceleration

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
As the flow illustrates, IDX assertion verification acceleration flow consists of the following
two steps:
Step 1: IDX assertion testbench compilation.
IDX contains two usage flows for this step. You can choose any one of the flows to fit your
requirement.
* idx -compile_sva flow
* idx -compile_aip flow
Step 2: IDX waveform replay simulation
The differences between the idx -compile_sva and the idx -compile_aip flows are:
* Whether DUT (compiled KDB) is required:
AIP, as the name suggests, does not contain the external reference (XMR) inside.
Therefore, IDX can generate the assertion testbench without considering the DUT.
The idx -compile_aip flow does not require the compiled KDB of the DUT.
SVA modules can contain the XMR. In the idx -compile_sva flow, to successfully
compile the SVA modules, IDX requires the compiled KDB to extract the types and
the signals in the DUT.
* Whether specifying the bind file is required:
The idx -compile_aip flow requires you to specify the bind file to let IDX
understand the connections between AIP and the DUT.
The idx -compile_sva flow does not require you to specify the bind file. IDX can
extract the bind information from the KDB.
The table below outlines the differences between the idx -compile_sva and the idx
-compile_aip flows to generate the assertion testbench:

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Preparing the Inputs
The IDX requires four inputs to enable the AIP verification flow:
1. The waveform
2. The SVA/AIP source file and the corresponding VCS compilation script
3. (For the idx -compile_aip flow) The bind file that is used to bind the AIP to the
simulation environment; only one bind file is allowed
4. The configuration file for IDX assertion verification acceleration flow

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The Waveform (FSDB)
IDX allows to read the waveforms, that is, FSDB generated by any of the tools:
Note:
The assertions are not necessary to be included in the source waveform used
for assertion debug.

SVA/AIP Source File and the Corresponding VCS Compilation
Script
The SVA/AIP source files should be provided. An alternative is to specify these files with
the -f option. In addition, the corresponding VCS compilation script is necessary. Some
SVA related options like -assert enable_diag are strongly suggested to add to the
script.

The Bind File
The bind file means, a SystemVerilog file which contains the "bind" statements to bind
the SVA/AIP to the design. Here the design hierarchies and the design signals must
be existent in the waveform. Note that only one bind file is allowed in the IDX assertion
verification acceleration flow.
The syntax for bind statement is as follows:
bind <inst_name | module>
[SVA_ports]

SVA_module

#[SVA_parameters]

SVA_inst_name

The <inst_name> is the design full hierarchical name in the waveform. The <module>
is the module definition name. IDX supports only one <inst_name | module> in a bind
statement.
For example, given the design below:
module top ();
DUT u_dut_01 ( .*);
DUT u_dut_02 (.*);

TEST u_test ();

title: Verification ContinuumTM
Verification ContinuumTM
text:
endmodule

IDX supports the bind file with below description:
// bind <module>
bind DUT SVA_MOD #(.p(1'b0))
(.clk(clk_i), .rst, .addr);

u_sva_checker

or
// bind <inst_name>
bind top.u_dut_01 SVA_MOD #(.p(1'b0))
(.clk(clk_i), .rst, .addr);

u_sva_checker

The following// is not supported:
bind top.u_dut_01, top.u_dut_02
(.clk(clk_i), .rst, .addr);

SVA_MOD

#(.p(1'b0))

u_sva_checker

// not supported
bind DUT, TEST SVA_MOD #(.p(1'b0)) u_sva_checker
(.clk(clk_i), .rst, .addr); multiple bind instances or modules are not
supported:

Refer to Limitations and Known Issues for more limitations about the bind file description.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
IDX Assertion Verification Acceleration Configuration File
IDX requires a configuration file to describe the above inputs.
Compile SVA Flow (idx -compile_sva idx_sva_comp.cfg)
Below is the format of the idx_sva_comp.cfg configuration file in the idx -compile_sva
flow:
//waveform file abs. path.
WAVEFORM
= $PWD/novas.fsdb
//SVA source files and the compilation script
SVA_FILE
= -f $PWD/checker_file.f

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
//Specifying the -f file in the configuration file moves the running
directory. Therefore, it becomes necessary to provide either the
absolute path or the root directory along with the relative path.
COMPILE_OPT = +define+DUT_TOP=system.i_cpu.i_ALUB -sverilog
-timescale=1ns/1ns -assert enable_diag -kdb -debug_acc+all
//SVA top scope
SVA_BIND_SCOPE
SVA_TOP_MOD
SVA_TOP_INST

used in the DUT hierarchy
= system.i_cpu.i_ALUB
= alu_checker
= u_checker

//run time simulation options
SIMV_OPT
= -l replay_aip.log -assert report=sva.report
+fsdbfile+replay_aip.fsdb +fsdb+sva_success +fsdb+sva_vacuous
//waveform dumping Tcl commands. Use semicolon to separate tasks
(Optional)
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK = fsdbDumpvars +all; fsdbDumpSVA

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Note:
The SIMV_OPT and WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK attributes are the placeholder
for IDX runtime simulation. To enable the assertion verification in the VCS
simulation, the VCS runtime options like -assert success are suggested to be
used. Similarly, to enable the assertion debugging in Verdi, the FSDB dumping
command fsdbDumpSVA is also suggested.
Compile AIP Flow (idx -compile_aip idx_aip_comp.cfg)
Below is the format of the idx_aip_comp.cfg configuration file used in the idx
-compile_aip flow:
//waveform file abs. path.
WAVEFORM = $PWD/novas.fsdb
//bind file abs. path.
BIND_FILE = $PWD/bind.sv
//SVA/AIP source files and the compilation script
COMPILE_OPT = -sverilog -f $PWD/../src/run.f -assert enable_diag -kdb
-debug_acc+all
//run time simulation options
SIMV_OPT = -l replay_aip.log -assert success+report+summary+vacous
+fsdbfile+replay_aip.fsdb +fsdb+sva_success +fsdb+sva_vacuous
//waveform dumping Tcl commands. Use semicolon to separate
tasks (Optional)
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK = fsdbDumpvars +all; fsdbDumpSVA

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Note:
The attributes SIMV_OPT and WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK are the placeholder
for IDX runtime simulation. To enable the assertion verification in the VCS
simulation, the VCS runtime options like -assert success are suggested to be
used. Similarly, to enable the assertion debugging in Verdi, the FSDB dumping
command fsdbDumpSVA is also suggested.
Attribute

Description

+in

Maps the input ports of the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +in

+out

Maps the output ports of the scope.
For example, AUTO_MAP = +out
