Highlighted Signals Impacted by Safety Rules

You can also set up the addition of a safety mask through Preference>Waveform > View
Options > Waveform Pane.

Figure 44

Preference Option

On this page, users can specify the color and pattern for the safety mask. The default
color and pattern as follows:
Figure 45

Default Color and Pattern for Safety Mask

After the SSF design is imported, nWave masks the mismatched range for the signal
impacted by a rule depending upon the masking option selected in the Safety menu in the

nWave window. For example, refer to the following figure for the options selected in View
> Safety in the nWave window:
Figure 46

Safety Menu

Based on this setup, the safety mask is displayed for a signal impacted by a register rule.
Refer to the following figure:
Figure 47

Register Rule Mask

Also, tips are displayed for safety masks if the waveform tip is configured to be on. The
tips show the detailed information of the safety rule that impacts the signal. For example,
the following screenshot shows the tip format of the register rule, including the rule name,
compare error signal name, and replication number.

Figure 48

Tip for Register Rules

Similarly, tips are displayed for core, safe-fsm, and error-correction rules. When multiple
rules impact an RTL signal, the tip content is separated by lines. Refer to the following
screenshot:
Figure 49

Tip Format for Multiple Rules

Viewing the Signals in the Signal Pane
When you import an SSF design, nWave adds six new filter types for safety rule impacted
signals. These include all safety signals, register , core, safe-fsm, error correction, and
compare error rules.

Figure 50

Signal Pane Filter

Viewing the Context Menus for Safety Rules
The Safety menus in the source view enable users to debug for safety purposes.
Figure 51

Safety Context Menu in the Source View

If an RTL signal is impacted by a safety rule, the context menu corresponding to the
safety rule is enabled by type. For example, if the RTL signal is impacted by a Core rule,
the Core Rules context menu and its sub-menus are automatically enabled. Similarly,
the context menus for register, safe-fsm, and error correction rules are enabled if the
signal is affected by these rules. If the RTL signal is not impacted by any safety rules, the
corresponding context menus are disabled.

Tcl Command Reference for SSF in nWave

Locating the Source View for the Safety Policy Declaration
The Locate *** Command menus enable you to locate the SSF source view for safety
policy declarations, highlighting the entire line. If the RTL signal is impacted by multiple
rules, the SSF source view is located for the first rule and is highlighted.
Adding Error Signals to the Waveform
The Add Compare-Error Signal to Waveform options in all menus help to add the
corresponding compare error signals into a sub-group under the RTL signal. The sub
group name format is [RTL signal full name]#[rule type]#Error_Signal. For example, /
system/top/q#Register_Rule#Error_Signal
Adding Instrumented Signals to Waveform
The Add Instrumented Signals to Waveform options helps to add all the corresponding
instrumented signals into the waveform. This is a sub-group with the name format
[RTL signal full name]#[rule type]#Instrumented_Signal. For example, /system/top/
q#Register_Rule#Instrumented_Signal.

The display of the upper annotation strings on signals impacted by safety rules is
controlled by the Preference > Safety Aware > Annotate Safety Aware Design
Object(s) option. The following table shows the rule impacting the RTL signal and the
corresponding annotation strings displayed in the source view:

The Safety Specification Format feature in Temporal Flow View (TFV) provides users
with visual and contextual cues about RTL signals impacted by safety rules. This feature
enhances the debugging process by making safety-related information easily accessible
through the GUI, including toolbars, tips, right mouse button (RMB) menus, and color
coding. By leveraging these visual indicators, users can quickly identify and analyze the
signals affected by safety policies, improving both safety verification and overall design
quality.

Utility
The following sections describe the LCA features supported by Utility as part of this
release:
* The tracediff Utility
* Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression
* The nCompare Utility
* Utilities for Performance Improvement
* FSDB Utilities

Temporal Flow View (TFV) traces multiple mismatches of signals using the trace
mechanism in batch mode manually. The tracediff utility is provided in Verdi, which
traces mismatches of signals using the trace mechanism in batch mode automatically,
collects the root causes, and provides a trace report. You must import the design
completely, or the utility does not get invoked.
The tracediff utility provides two ways of tracing the mismatches. They are manual
mode and automatic mode as follows:
* Manual mode: A configuration file must be provided which describes the signals to
trace. With -signal_list in the command line, tracediff works in manual mode.
* Automatic mode: A configuration file is not required to be written but can still trace
signal mismatches. All the inputs needed in this mode are design, target waveform
file, and reference waveform file. The tracediff utility invokes nCompare with default
settings and extracts the mismatches from the target waveform file and reference
waveform file. Without -signal_list in the command line, tracediff works in
automatic mode.
After tracing mismatch for the signal list, a report is generated in the tracediffLog/
under the current directory by default. If a report file is not specified while executing the
command, the report is stored in tracediffLog/under the current working directory with
the default name tracediff_report.txt.

* Saving the Traced Path of the Batch Utility in a Database

Syntax for the tracediff utility is as follows:
tracediff -target_waveform <fsdb_file_name> -ref_waveform
<fsdb_file_name> [Verdi option] [tracediff option]

Command Options

-compare_scope
<full_hierarchical_sco
pe>

Specifies the top scope to compare signals. Only signals in
the scope and its sub-scopes are compared. Scope delimiter
must be a slash /.The default value is top scope, which is not
specified.

text:
Specifies if the tracediff utility compares X values. The
default value is 1.

title: Appendix 877
text:
Specifies if the tracediff utility compares Z values.
The default value is 1, that is by default tracediff utility
compares Z values.

-dut

Checks if the root cause is in the DUT or testbench so that
tracediff utility can annotate a root cause with the accurate
reason. It is optional and need not be specified.

-gen_list

It is provided for running auto mode and stop once the
signal list is dumped. You can revise the file and then reboot
tracediff manual mode with the revised signal list.

-ignore_signal
<signal_list_file_name>

Specifies the location of the file which contains the list of
signals to ignore tracing. Each line contains a signal pattern
and the pattern can be one of the following:
- signal#time: ignore tracing the signal at specified time.
- signal: ignore tracing the signal at any time.
This option can be used if any signal causes tracediff utility
to not function in the auto mode and it is ignored for auto
mode to work. It can also be used in manual mode.
Default is NULL and no signal is ignored.

-jmp_to_earliest

Jumps to the earliest point in time while tracing in the batch
mode.

title: Appendix 877
text:
Specifies the hierarchy level limit for the module to be
compared. For example, /top/a is compared but /top/a/b is
not compared if -compare_scope is /top and -max_level is
1 because /top/ais 1 level but /top/a/bis 2 levels from /top.
When n is 0, all signals in the hierarchy starting from the
specified module are compared.
Default value is 0 if not specified.

-auto_max_
sample_per_signal <n>

Specifies the maximum number of mismatches for each
pair of signals, starting from the earliest mismatch until
the maximum number is reached. When the maximum is
reached, the remaining pairs of signals are not compared.
When n is 0, there is still a limit of 2097152 mismatches for
each pair of signals due to the limitation of nCompare.
Default value is 1 if not specified.

-auto_max_
err_cnt_number <n>

Specifies the maximum number of mismatches in a
comparison. When n is 0, there is no limitation on the number
of mismatches.
Default value is 1000 if it is not specified.

-ncompare_opts

Specifies nCompare input options. The format is tracediff
[tracediff options] -ncompare_opts "[nComapre
options]. When -ncompare_opts is used, nCompare

options that are originally supported in tracediff auto mode
are unavailable.Waveform files set up in -ncompare_opts
is ignored. You have to specify what are the target and
reference waveforms for tracediff.
-out_file reportFile.txt Sets the name of the output report file.
-out_format
[plain|smlog]

Sets the format of the output file.If this option is not specified,
the default format of the output file is smlog. If the smlog
option is specified, you can open the output file with Smart
Log to analyze it.

-ref_waveform

The secondary waveform file used to compare signals. This is
a mandatory option in both manual and automatic mode.

-signal_list

Specifies signals that need to be added to the signal list.

-target_waveform

Specifies the target waveform. This option imports the
design of the target waveform as the fundamental design for
comparison.

Report Format
After tracing the mismatch for the signal list, the tracediff_report.txt report is
generated in tracediffLog/ under the current directory by default.
As illustrated in the following figure, the configuration settings are recorded at the top
in the report. The root causes are listed and followed by the mismatch signals that they
affect.
Tracediff transforms the given time unit into the time unit used in the target waveform. This
is the reason that in the following figure, tb.fout2#600 instead of tb.fout2#600000ps is
dumped.
The tracediff utility categorizes signals into the following four types and the meaning of
each type is available at the end of the report:
* Root Cause Found
* Root Cause Not Found
* No Mismatch
* Non-Existent Signals
If any duplicated signals are available in the signal list, then these signals are available in
the Duplicated Signals section in the report. However, these duplicated signals are not
counted in report summary. Instead, a warning message is issued which mentions that
some signals with the same tracing times are listed in the input signal list.

when using the tracediff utility.

Saving the Traced Path of the Batch Utility in a Database
The save/restore trace path feature is supported for traceX/tracediff batch mode. For
traceX/tracediff batch mode, you can use trace utilities in batch mode and get the trace
report. The option -load_trace_report is used to load report in verdi and show the trace
path by invoke traceX/tracediff to trace signal again. However, this behavior might cost a
lot of time to redo Behavior Analysis and tracing.
This project provides mechanism to save the trace path of utility tracing result and restore
them back in GUI mode, therefore, you don't need to redo Behavior Analysis and tracing
while restoring the trace path.
For traceX utility, you need to save the tracing path and traceX result table into the
database. When -load_trace_report option is reported back to Verdi and when you
click on the signal entry, the trace path is restored back to Temporal Flow View.

Figure 62

TraceX Flow

Verdi provides you the capability to open the report file in SmartLog and view the report in
human readable format. You can view or replay the trace path using the SmartLog file.
The -load_trace_report option is supported which opens the SmartLog and
automatically displays the report file provided for tracediff utility. However, this option
should not be used with -target_waveform option and if the signal needs to be traced
again then it takes a lot of time to redo the Behavior Analysis and trace the signal again.
verdi -load_trace_report tracediff_report.txt

Starting with this release, a database is supported which stores the tracing information into
the database and then restores the trace path without tracing the signals again.
Syntax for the database which stores the tracing information is as follows:
tracediff -target_waveform 1.fsdb -ref_waveform 2.fsdb -tdb -tdb_dir
traceDiff.tdb

This command outputs the database file into the traceDiff.tdb directory.
Command Options
Reason

-tdb

Enables you to dump trace results into trace
database.

-tdb_dir
<directory_path_name>

Specifies an alternative name and location for
the trace database directory. If this option is
not specified, then the default directory name is
tracediff.tdb.

Report Format
After tracing the mismatch for the signal list, the configuration details are saved in the
database tracediff.txt report that is generated using the following command:
tracediff -target_waveform 1.fsdb -ref_waveform 2.fsdb -tdb -tdb_dir
traceDiff.tdb

The configuration settings are recorded at the top in the report and the trace database
information is available in the result file as illustrated in the following figure:
Figure 63

Trace Database Available in the Result File

The tracediff utility categorizes the Configuration details into the following details as
* Input file
* Output file
* Target file
* Reference file
* Trace database
* Delimiter
* JumptoEarliest
Restore Trace Path
You can reload the trace result with following command:
%verdi -load_trace_report tracereport.txt

After the trace report is loaded again in SmartLog it loads the trace path from database
instead of trigger tracing path again on the SmartLog entries.

title: Appendix 877
text:
Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression
Starting with this release, if there are any failed tests during regression, Verdi finds the bug
and fixes it before allowing any new changes.
Verdi first takes the file to determine the debug entries. Debug entries are monitored
signals in the DUT that have mismatches between the failing and passed waveform. Then
it traces back to find the root causes, and summarizes it in a text file report. This report is
then loaded into Verdi to see the detail trace path from debug entry to root cause.

The following sub-sections provide the details of the use model:
Determining the Bug Entry
The debug entries are read from a .rc file. There are three types of tags in the .rc file:
* Signal: If the tag is Signal, each line must include the full hierarchical name and
a timestamp. These signals are scanned and they become the debug entries if the
values of this signal at the specified time is different within the two waveform files. For
example,
top.memory.nROutstanding#123
top.mySig1#1000
top.mySig2#50

* Scope: If the tag is Scope, each line must include a list of scope names and a
timestamp. Boundary signals within these scopes are scanned and those signals
become the debug entries if the values of this signal at the specified time is different
within the two waveform files. For example,
top,top.myScope1#200
top.myScope2#300
top#100-200

Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression

* Assertion: If the tag is Assertion, each line must include an Assertion name and a
timestamp. Signals that are associated to that assertion are scanned and become the
debug entries if the values of this signal at the specified time is different within the two
waveform files. For example,
top.memory.eos#160390000

The follow error message is an example on how to specify an assertion failure as debug
entry:
Error: "token.v", 144439:top.memory.eos : at time 160390000
ALL_DONE_EOS: All write transaction addresses must have been
matched with corresponding write response.
nb_cycles: 16040
Executing Axi End Of Simulation checks

here, ALL_DONE_EOS is the name of the assertion and 160390000 is the time.
Analyzing Root Cause
The root cause is analyzed by running the TraceDiff utility in Verdi. The following are the
enhancements to TraceDiff for root cause:
Trace Multiple Root Cause
For root cause, TraceDiff searches all fanins with mismatch on every level.
Trace Database
For root cause, TraceDiff saves the trace results in a trace result database that can be
efficiently and accurately replayed.
Ignore Mismatches on Waveform Time Boundaries
For root cause, TraceDiff does not trace signals with mismatches on the time boundary
only, because the mismatch may be due to inconsistency in the simulation evaluation
order. This helps to filter out false alarms.
Ignore Shifted Sequence
For root cause, TraceDiff ignores mismatches caused by delay shift.
Trace through Design Changes
For root cause, TraceDiff trace through minor design changes.

Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression

Data Input and Output Format
Data Input Requirements
The following is an example of the configuration file for root cause:
[Test]
DEBUG_ENTRY_TYPE = Signal
DEBUG_ENTRY = signal.list
REFERENCE_WAVEFORM = golden.fsdb
TARGET_WAVEFORM = cycle.fsdb
SIMV_DAIDIR = NA
IGNORE_MAX_TIME = 1
VC_SEQUENCE = 1
MULTI_ROOT_CAUSE = 1
JUMP_TO_EARLIEST = 1

* DebugEntryType can be set to Signal, Scope or Assertions
* When SIMV_DAIDIR is specified, the design is loaded from the given path instead of
directly from TARGET_WAVEFORM. If you want to load from TARGET_WAVEFORM, leave
SIMV_DAIDIR empty or specify the value as `NA'.
* IGNORE_MAX_TIME corresponds to the tracediff option -ignore_max_time.
* VC_SEQUENCE corresponds to the tracediff option -vc_sequence.
* MULTI_ROOT_CAUSE corresponds to the tracediff option -multi_root_cause.
* JUMP_TO_EARLIEST, when set to 1, each level will snap back to the earliest mismatch
before continuing the trace on the preceding level.
The design (simv) must be compiled with the option -kdb=common_elab.
The waveform files for both reference and target design must be run with the
+fsdb+gate=0 option.
Data Output Format
The final output of root cause is a text file report and the associated trace database.
The following is an example of root cause report using Signal or Scope DebugEntryType:
[RCA Results]
Configuration:
Reference Waveform:/remote/reference/test.fsdb
Target Waveform: /remote/target/test.fsdb
Tracediff Database:/remote/rcaLog/tracediff.tdb

Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression

IgnoreMaxTime: 1
VCSequence: 1
MultiRootCause: 1
JumpToEarliest: 1

Root Causes:
#138990000 /top/memory/Match[5:0]@1
--module: Axi
--location: token.v:145060
--debug_entries: /top/memory/sub/check/out[5:0]#138990000@1

The following is an example of root cause report using Assertion DebugEntryType:
[RCA Results]
Configuration:
Reference Waveform: /remote/reference/test.fsdb
Target Waveform: ~/remote/target/test.fsdb
Tracediff Database: ~/remote/rcaLog/tracediff.tdb
IgnoreMaxTime: 1
VCSequence: 1
MultiRootCause: 1
JumpToEarliest: 1

Root Causes:
#160390000 /top/memory/Match[5:0]@1
--assertion: top.all_done_eos
--module:
Axi
--location:
tokens.v:145060
--debug_entries: /top/memory/Match[5:0]#138990000@1
-/top/pc/NumError1#124810000@1
#0 /top/u/jcb/rsp/fifo@2
--assertion:
sample_top.all_done_eos
--module:
mali_jcb
--location:
tokens_lib.v:19710
--debug_entries: /top/u/jm/jcn_if/monitor_cb/rspcredit#10000@2
-/top/u/jm/jcn_if/rspcredit#0@2

The nCompare utility compares two FSDB files using a defined rule file and reports the

Following are the batch mode options in which it is mandatory to specify the -lca option
and set the VERDI_PARALLEL_COMPARISON environment variable.
Options

Explanation

signal_count
comparison. The error report file (*.nce) is updated
each time for each comparison. This option is only
supported without name mapping and with one
cmpSetSignalPair command. The default value is
100,000.
-proc process_number Specifies the multiple process numbers. This option
is only supported with the cmpCompare command.
-thread thread_number Specifies multiple thread numbers. The maximum
thread number is 16. This option is supported only
with the cmpCompare command.

title: Appendix 877
text:
Utilities for Performance Improvement

Utilities for Performance Improvement
Verdi supports the following two features or utilities for performance improvement:
* Prerequisites
* Trace Cache Utility
* Scan Utility

Prerequisites
To use these functionalities,
1. Set the VERDI_TRACEX_ENABLE environment variable as follows:
setenv VERDI_TRACEX_ENABLE

2. Specify the -lca option while invoking Verdi.

Trace Cache Utility
Verdi supports the trace cache feature that saves tracing time on the traceX utility. If a
signal is already traced, the trace engine stops at the cached signal and uses cached
traced results. The trace cache feature is enabled by default.You can disable/enable this
feature using the TFV_ENABLE_ROOT_CAUSE_CACHE environment variable.
To disable this feature, use the following command:
setenv TFV_ENABLE_ROOT_CAUSE_CACHE 0

To enable this feature, use the following command:
setenv TFV_ENABLE_ROOT_CAUSE_CACHE 3

Here, the default value is 3.
The trace cache feature is only supported for -cause_count 1. If you set this option with
number greater than 1, trace cache is turned off.

Scan Utility
Verdi provides the scan functionality or utility to scan signals with an X value. The following
options are available to help you to get the X signal list:
[-max_x_per_signal number] [-max_total_x number]
[-max_analysis_level number]

title: Appendix 877
text:
Specifies the maximum number of analysis X levels. If no analysis scope is specified, it
counts from the root scope. When the number is 0, all signals are analyzed. Its default
value is 0.
-max_total_x number

Specifies the maximum number of X for tracing. If the number is 0, it is unlimited. Its
default value is 1000.
-max_x_per_signal number

Specifies the maximum number of X for each signal. When the maximum is reached, the
remaining value changes of the signals are no longer analyzed. Here, 0 signifies no limit.
Its default value is 1.

Verdi supports the following utilities for FSDB:
* Support for Converting an FSDB File With Gate to an FSDB File Without Gate
* Support for Waveform Utility

Support for Converting an FSDB File With Gate to an FSDB File
Without Gate
In previous releases, the FSDB Reader takes more memory and CPU time to read an
FSDB file with gate when compared to reading an FSDB file without gate.
Starting with this release, Verdi supports the use of a utility, parallelWaveExpand, to
convert an FSDB file with gate to an FSDB file without gate. You can use this utility to
perform a one-time process to retrieve an equivalent FSDB from an FSDB with gate
enabled. Also, the FSDB Gate in the converted FSDB file is disabled. The FSDB contains
all the value changes so that an FSDB reader does not need to perform any reconstruction
of values.

You can also use the converted FSDB file to replace the original file in the remaining
debug flow. Therefore, you can reduce the consumption of memory and time. You need
to enable the environment variable VERDI_PARALLEL_WAVE_EXPAND for this feature along
with the -lca command line option.
parallelWaveExpand <input fsdb file> -t <number of threads> -o <output
fsdb file name>

<input fsdb file name> - represents an FSDB file with FSDB Gate enabled to be

converted.

<number of threads> - represents the number of threads to be used in this conversion.
<output FSDB name> - represents the output FSDB file name.

When using 8 threads to convert novas.fsdb to full_dump.fsdb, use the following
command:
parallelWaveExpand novas.fsdb -t 8 -o full_dump.fsdb

Support for Waveform Utility
Verdi supports a waveform utility tool called waveutils. It enables extracting, reporting,
VCD converting, and converting to SAIF features on waveform file. This utility tool
provides the following:
* Scalability of performance
* Capability of memory usage
* Capacity to handle large designs
Support for Multi-Process for Extract
The waveultis utility supports multi-process (Common Distributed Processing Library
(CDPL)) on extract. This tool uses the multi-process technique for extracting features
to share the jobs with multiple machines, which results in reduced runtime and memory
consumption on each machine.
To enable the multi-process on waveutils in Verdi, you must set up the

CDPL-related environment as follows:
* setenv VERDI_CDPL_ENABLE 1
* setenv VERDI_CDPL_HOST_FILE $HOST_FILE
The following syntax shows the content of $HOST_FILE:
<enabled> | <hostname|empty if it's grid> | <#slots> | <tmpDir|empty> | <mode> |
<command>
Each field is terminated by "|" except the last field. A space must be present for an empty
field. The descriptions for each field are as follows:
* <enabled>: 1 means the host is enabled. Anything else indicates it is disabled
* <hostname>: specifies 1 host name. This field is ignored for SGE and LSF modes
* <slots>: specifies the number of worker slots on this host (rsh and ssh), or farm (lsf
and sge); -1 indicates unlimited
* <tmpDir>: [optional] the temporary work directory
* <mode>: RSH|SSH|LSF|SGE
* <command>: the remote command for the corresponding connection mode
Example of RSH Connection Mode:

title: 1 | org-gup-0560 | 8 | /remote/tmp | RSH | rsh
text: 1 | org-gup-0560 | 8 | /remote/tmp | RSH | rsh

title: 1 | org-gup-0560 | 8 | /remote/tmp | RSH | rsh
text: 1 | org-gup-0560 | 8 | /remote/tmp | RSH | rsh

title: 1 | org-gup-0559 | 8 | /remote/tmp | SSH | ssh
text: 1 | org-gup-0559 | 8 | /remote/tmp | SSH | ssh

title: 1 | org-gup-0559 | 8 | /remote/tmp | SSH | ssh
text: 1 | org-gup-0559 | 8 | /remote/tmp | SSH | ssh

title: 1 | | -1 | /remote/lsf/tmp | LSF | bsub -q test -R
text:
"rusage[mem=1000] affinity[core(4)]"

Example of SGE Connection Mode:

title: 1 | | -1 | /remote/lsf/tmp | LSF | bsub -q test -R
text: "rusage[mem=1000] affinity[core(4)]"

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0

Support for SAIF Conversion
Verdi supports converting to SAIF in waveform utility using the waveutils --tool=2saif
option.

To enable and use the waveutils utility with tool=2saif in Verdi, you must specify the
following:
* Specify the -lca option during compilation.
* Set the environment variable VERDI_WAVEUTILS. For example,
setenv VERDI_WAVEUTILS

The following is use model to enable this feature:
waveutils --tool=2saif fsdb_file_name [options]

[Options] can have following options as described in the following table:
Options

Description/Options

[Options]

[-scope <scope_name>][-o
<saif_file_name>][-to_stdout][-bt
time[unit]][-et
time[unit]][-vhdl][-flatten_genhier][-to_vhd
l_presto][-h|-help][-keep_task][-merge_same_
scope][-slash_deli][-thread_number n][-proc
n][-disable_gz_saif]

-scope
<scope_name>

Specifies the scope and its sub-scope to convert to
the output SAIF file. This option cannot be used to
specify a signal name. Wildcards are not supported.

-o
<saif_file_name>

Specifies the output SAIF file name.

-to_stdout

Redirects the content of the output SAIF file to stdout
and the generation of the output SAIF file is disabled
even if option -o is specified.

-bt time[unit]

Specifies the start time of the translation. If omitted,
the start time of the FSDB is used. The time unit can
be Ms|Ks|s|ms|us|ns|ps|fs. If not specified, the default
time unit is ns.

-et time[unit]

Specifies the end time of the translation. If omitted,
the end time of the FSDB is used. The time unit can
be Ms|Ks|s|ms|us|ns|ps|fs. If not specified, the default
time unit is ns.

-flatten_genhier

Eliminates blocks created by generate constructs and
appends the block name into the signal name as a
prefix.

Options

Description/Options

-vhdl

Converts 9 MVL to 4 states value as follows instead
of skipping VHDL signals.
U X 0 1 Z W L H - (9 MVL)
X X 0 1 Z X 0 1 X (4 states)

-to_vhdl_presto

Converts fsdb file into saif file in VHDL presto
elaboration form.

-h|-help

Displays the help information.

-keep_task

Ignores the
vcd_task/vcd_function/vhdl_procedure/vhdl_function
scopes and their subscopes and signals. This option
does not support ZWD related files.

-merge_same_scope

Merges the duplicated scopes and signals. This
option does not support ZWD related files.

-slash_deli

Replaces the scope delimiter by slash character.
Default scope delimiter is '.'.

-thread_number n

Specifies the thread numbers to convert SAIF file,
n is the number of threads; it can be 1 to 4. By
default, multi-thread is enabled with waveutils
--tool=2saif utility, the default thread number is 4.

-proc n

Specify the multi-process number for the SAIF
conversion.
You must set the following environment variables
before using this option:
* VERDI_CDPL_ENABLE
* VERDI_CDPL_HOST_FILE
For more information on the above environment
variables, see Support for Multi-Process for
Extract section.

-disable_gz_saif

Disable the generation of SAIF files in gzip format.
The gzip SAIF are automatically generated with the
-proc option

Examples
The following are the examples of this feature:
* Convert FSDB to SAIF file.
%waveutils --tool=2saif verilog.fsdb -o verilog.saif

* Convert FSDB to SAIF file with 9 MVL to 4 states conversion for VHDL signals.
%waveutils --tool=2saif verilog_and_vhdl.fsdb -vhdl

* Convert FSDB to SAIF file with time range.
%waveutils --tool=2saif verilog.fsdb -bt 10ps -et 1000ps -o
verilog.saif

* Specify the scope name to convert.
%waveutils --tool=2saif rtl.fsdb -scope "/system/i_cpu" -o rtl.saif

The waveutils utility has the following limitations:
* Supports only input file version equal or greater than 2.0.
* Supports only fully array/struct/record.
* Does not support formbus.
* Does not filter user interested scope without any signals.
* Does not support information with sequence.
* Does not support "?" in -scope, -exclude_scopeand -sig.
* The unmatched scope/sig/exclude_scope message is printed only on console.
* The output waveform file from waveutils --tool=extract is signal based waveform
file.
* The output waveform file from waveutils --tool=extract is dumped by cheetah
technique.
* The thread number cannot be one when a multi-process is opened.
The memory limit flow cannot work with the multi-process flow.

Comparing VDBs Based on Plans
Verdi Coverage enables you to differentiate (or diff) VDBs based on mapped regions in an
HVP file and generate their reports. If an HVP file is not specified while differentiating (or
diffing) two VDBs, the database difference report shows all the difference between both
the VDBs. To limit displaying information pertaining to the HVP file, specify the HVP file
while diffing VDBs.
This feature applies only to functional coverage (covergroups and assertions)
and not to code coverage.
* Related Notes

Comparing VDBs Based on Plans

To diff VDBs based on plans, perform the following steps:
1. Click Tools>Diff Databases to display the following Database Diff dialog box:

2. In the Database Diff dialog box, load Database 1 and Database 2 . For example,
d1.vdb and d2.vdb are loaded in the figure above.
3. Upload the HVP file using the Load button in the Mapping Plan group box and click
OK. Note that it is not mandatory to upload the HVP file. However, it is required to diff
both the VDBs based on mapping regions specified in the file. For example, p2.hvp is
loaded in the figure above and its contents are as follows:

=========

endplan

4. Select one of the following Compare Types:
Shape - Reports items with different shapes.
Score - Reports items with the same shape but different coverage status.
Hit Count - Reports items with the same shape but different hit counts.

Creating a New and an Existing Plan

Group
Point/Cross

Only covergroup and assert metrics are supported for the Diff Databases
command.
Related Notes
The difference between two VDBs is implemented as explained here:
* For Group Metric
If a group or group instance is available in the plan, then the difference is applied
to the group and all its children coverpoints, crosses, and bins. Note that group
instances are not children of Variant or Definition.
If a coverpoint or cross bin is available in the plan, then the difference is applied to
the coverpoint and cross bin and all their children bins.
If a crossbin is available in the plan, the difference is applied to the bin.
* For Assertion metric
The difference is applied to show the elements which are mapped to the plan.
* This feature is not compatible with HVP modifiers.

Strict Exclusions Mode
In strict exclusions mode, excluding a covered object is not allowed. If you load an exclude
file in strict exclusions mode, only the uncovered objects in the exclude file are excluded.
Objects that are covered are not excluded even if they are listed in the exclude file.
When a region such as a module, module instance, or covergroup was excluded in
previous releases and had only uncovered objects in it, the region was excluded and an
exclusion for it could be saved to an exclude file. If a region contained both covered and
uncovered child objects, exclusions for uncovered child objects were not created and
they could not be saved. Starting with this release, when a region is excluded in strict
exclusions mode and it contains both covered and uncovered objects then its uncovered
child objects are excluded properly and those exclusions can be saved to an exclude file.
Note that if annotations are set on the region's exclusion, then those annotations are
automatically propagated to these uncovered child objects when the parent object is
excluded in strict mode.
This feature is now supported for the following exclusions:
* Module/Instance-level exclusions
* Covergroup definitions/instance-level exclusions
* Example

Union Merge of Cover Properties
Verdi enables you to merge databases that contain different cover properties/assertions
in their module instances. If some assertions are defined in an input database and
not in a base database, these assertions are retained in the merged database while
merging. These assertions are not linked to any module definition or instance in the design
hierarchy of the base database. However, Verdi displays these assertions in the Asserts
tab in the Summarypane and enables you to mark exclusions on them, if required.

Union Merge of Cover Properties

To display cover properties/assertions of a merged database in Verdi, perform the
following steps:
1. Load a merged coverage database using the following command:

Two-Dimensional Visualization of Covergroup Crosses
Verdi enables you to select any two coverpoints from an n-dimensional cross and project
the cross coverage data into a two-dimensional projection table with those two coverpoints
as the X and Y axis.
This feature helps in identifying coverage holes in the cross, such as when no bins are
covered, when a given coverpoint has a specific value.
For each cross, Verdi provides a list of projection tables and arranges the tables using the
following ranking criteria:
* Rows or columns that are completely uncovered
* Cells that are uncovered in table cells
* Low-coverage cells in table cells
Note that a low-coverage cell is a cell whose score is less than a tenth of the overall score
of a cross.
Also, projections with the same coverage for every cell are considered as least interesting
projections.

Two-Dimensional Visualization of Covergroup Crosses

To generate two-dimensional projection tables for an n-dimensional cross, click the Cross
2D Proj button in the CovDetail pane in the Verdi GUI.
Consider a cross of the coverpoints: X, Y, and Z in the following figure:

In the table, the red color represents Not Covered and the green color represents
Covered. This table shows the details of entire cross coverage.
It becomes difficult to find coverage holes from the table.
To generate two-dimensional projection tables for a cross of X, Y, and Z, click the Cross
2D Proj button in the CovDetail pane in the Verdi GUI.
When you click the Cross 2D Proj button, Verdi projects the cross coverage data into twodimensional tables as X x Y, X x Z, and Y x Z using the ranking criteria mentioned above.

cells.
This projection is given the second ranking (2/3). The projection X x Y contains only two

From Projections Y x Z and X x Z, you can interpret that all the cross products that contain
the bin circle of Coverpoint Z are not covered at all.

In previous releases, Verdi provided a unique feature ID for each plan and feature. This

In Verdi Planner, various functional coverage objects such as covergroups, covergroup
instances, coverpoints, crosses, and bins may be used as sources for data in a plan
feature.
These are connected to plan features by name. As these functional coverage objects were
explicitly created to collect coverage, it is helpful to know if any object was created but left
out of the plan.
Starting with this release, Verdi Coverage provides a new feature that enables you to
find functional coverage objects that are not referenced by any feature in the plan "unmapped" objects - and report them in an .hvp file.

To find unmapped objects in a plan, invoke the Report Unmapped Objects form using the
Plan -> Report Unmapped Objects command.

The following figure shows the Report Unmapped Objects form:
Figure 79

The Report Unmapped Objects Form

In the Report Unmapped Objects form, you can specify the plan to report from the list of
plans.
Also, you can specify the type of unmapped objects that you need to map. The types of
objects are as follows:
* Definition/Variant, Instance
* Point/Cross
* Bins
To generate the report for covergroup instances, for example, select the Cover Group
Instance check box in the Report Unmapped Objects form.
In the form, you can select the following different strategies that determine the number of
objects to be reported:
* High
This strategy considers a definition/variant and an instance as separate entities. If a
definition/variant is mapped but its one or more instances are not mapped, then the
instances are considered as unmapped.
For example, consider cg_var as a variant having coverpoints, cp1 and cp2, cross
cr1, and instance cg_inst. If cg_var is mapped, cg_inst is not mapped, and High
is selected as a strategy to determine the number of reported objects, cg_inst is
reported as unmapped.

* Medium
This strategy reports instances as mapped as long as their corresponding variant is
mapped. For example, consider cg_var as a variant having coverpoints cp1 and cp2,
cross cr1, and instance cg_inst.
If cg_var is mapped, cg_inst is not mapped, and Medium is selected as a strategy to
determine the number of reported objects, cg_inst is reported as mapped.
* Low
This strategy reports a coverpoint/cross as mapped if bins are mapped. For example,
consider that coverpoint cp1 has coverbins: bin1, bin2, and bin3.
If bin1 is mapped and Low is selected as a strategy to determine the number of
reported objects, cp1 is reported as mapped.
The object types, such as definition/variant, instance, coverpoint, cross, and bins, follow
certain rules to report unmapped objects. These rules are as follows:
* Definition/Variant, Instance
1. If a variant is mapped, all its instances are considered as mapped. The rule is
applied only when Number of Objects in the Report Unmapped Objects form is set
as Medium or Low and not as High.
2. If all instances of a variant are mapped, the variant is reported as mapped. The rule
is applied only when Number of Objects in the Report Unmapped Objects form is
set as Medium or Low and not as High.
* Point/Cross
1. If all coverpoints/crosses of a variant are mapped, the variant is reported as
mapped.
2. If all coverpoints/crosses of an instance are mapped, the instance is reported as
mapped.
3. If a coverpoint/cross in all instances of a variant is mapped, the coverpoint/cross in
the variant is reported as mapped.

all its instances is reported as mapped.
The rule is applied only when Number of Objects in the Report Unmapped Objects
form is set as Medium or Low and not as High.

mapped.

This section explains how VC Formal coverage is integrated with the Verdi coverage
reporting flow.
The two primary links between Verdi and VC Formal are displaying VCS Formal results in
Verdi, and linking VC Formal results into your verification plan using Verdi Planner.

The section describes how Verdi coverage is used to display and link to VC Formal
results. This section consists of the following subsections:
* Collecting VC Formal Results in the Coverage Database
* Measuring VC Formal Assert Status in HVP

Collecting VC Formal Results in the Coverage Database
To display VC Formal results in the coverage report, you must first have set the
VC_STATIC_HOME environment variable. For example:
setenv VC_STATIC_HOME /tools/synopsys/vcst

Here, VC_STATIC_HOME is an environment variable that is set to point to the installation
directory for VC Formal.
To start the VC Formal tool, use the following command:
vcf -f test.tcl -verdi

vcf is a command to start the VC Formal tool with an interactive shell. The vcf shell is a
new shell that calls vc_static_shell internally.

The vcf shell supports all the options that vc_static_shell supports. The vcf shell
automatically runs in the 64-bit mode, unless you explicitly specify the -mode32 option.
For details on vc_static_shell, see the VC Formal Verification User Guide. -f indicates
your VC Formal execution script
You provide your own Tcl script to run VC Formal. To enable collection and display of
coverage data in Verdi, include the following two commands in the script:
1. The command to run VC Formal must include the -cov all flag. If you wish assertions
to be targeted (not just cover properties), you should also include -cm assert as a flag
to VCS:
read_file -cov all -format verilog -sva -top $top -vcs "-cm assert
-sverilog $testDir/test.v -sva"

2. You must include a command to save the results to the coverage database, for
example, my_covdb:
save_covdb -name my_covdb -cov assert+cover

Figure 83

The VC Formal information is displayed in the Assert tab in the columns: FVtype,
FVstatus, and FVdepth.
This information should be same as the VC Formal results. The green color represents
Proven or Covered, the red color represents Falsified, Uncoverable, or Vacuous, and the
yellow color represents Inconclusive.
FVtype indicates the usage field. The value in this column can be either Assert, Cover, or

Assume.

FVstatus indicates the run status of VC Formal. Its possible values depend on FVtype:

* If FVtype is Assert, the value of FVstatus can be Proven, Inconclusive, Falsified, or
Vacuous.
* If FVtype is Cover, the value of FVstatus can be Covered, Inconclusive, or
Uncoverable.
The FVdepth column is interpreted as follows:
* If FVstatus is Proven, Vacuous, or Uncoverable and its value is -1, it represents
infinite depth.
* For other FVstatus, N>=0 represents the depth of the trace.

Measuring VC Formal Assert Status in HVP
VC Formal results can be annotated automatically onto features in your verification plan.
Using these results, you can measure your expectations with FVstatus.
The figure below shows VC Formal results in a verification plan with attributes and metrics.
Figure 84

VC Formal Results in HVP

To measure the VC Formal Assert status in HVP, perform the following steps:
1. Set the expected FV Assert status with FV attribute values using
fvassert_expected_status.
feature f_default;
//These values are same as default value, no need
//assignments again here.
//
fvassert_expected_status = proven;
//
fvassert_expected_mindepth = -1;
//
fvcover_expected_status = covered;
//
fvcover_expected_maxdepth = 0;
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: fsm.*";
feature f_expected_assigned;
fvassert_expected_status = inconclusive;
fvassert_expected_mindepth = 50;
fvcover_expected_maxdepth = 50;
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: fsm.a2", "property:
fsm.a_loop_break", "property: fsm.c2";

2. Add measures with property type sources and reference the FV Assert metric.
The new FV Assert built-in metric is added to keep the score of the FV Assert status
against users' expectation.
If FVstatus is same as fvassert_expected_status, the score becomes 1/1,
otherwise, the score becomes 0/1.
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: top.a1*";

3. Calculate FVAssert metric scores
After finding the matching region in the coverage database, the covered/coverable
status is extracted from that database and added as a ratio for the FVAssert metric
score.
For the FVAssert metric, you can get FVstatus from FV annotations in the coverage
database and compare fvassert_expected_status, which is set in fvassert*
attributes.
If FVstatus is same as fvassert_expected_status, then the assertion/property is
considered to be covered.

For example, the matching property top.a11: FVtype=assert and
FVstatus=Proven. If the expectation is fvassert_expected_sthe tatus
= Proven, the FVAssert metric score becomes 1/1. If the expectation is
fvassert_expected_status = inconclusive and fvassert_expected_depth =
60, the FVAssert metric score becomes 0/1.
For example, consider the following figure that shows six cases to measure the VC
Formal Assert status in your verification plan:

Case1: fsm.a2: FVtype is assert, FVstatus is falsified, FVdepth is 6 and it is
excluded. In the top.f_default.m1 feature, the property: fsm.* source matches
the excluded property, therefore, no score is added.
Case2: fsm.a_loop_break: FVtype is assert, FVstatus is inconclusive, and FVdepth
is 70. In the top.f_expected_assigned feature, fvassert_expected_status is
inconclusive and fvassert_expected_mindepth is 50 which are set by users. It is met
with users' expectations and the FVAssert metric score becomes 1/1.
Case3: fsm.a_trans: FVtype is assume. In the top.f_assume feature,
fvassume_status is reviewed which is set by users. The FVAssert metric score

becomes 1/1.

Case4: fsm.c_blk_cnt: FVtype is cover, FVstatus is covered, and FVdepth is 1. In
the top.f_default feature, with default attribute values, fvcover_expected_status
is covered and fvcover_expected_maxdepth is 0. Compare FVstatus to expected
attributes values and if the expectation does not meet, the FVAssert metric score
becomes 0/1.
Case5: fsm.c_trans, no FV annotation. In the top.f_default.m_no_fv_ann
measure, matching fsm.c_trans without FV annotation, the FVAssert metric
becomes 0/1 because the FVAssert metric is referred explicated in measure.
Case6: dummy source. In the top.f_default.m_dummy measure, for all metrics for no
matching region, the score becomes all 0.

Verdi Coverage provides plan diff tool that lets you easily find out differences (added,
deleted and changed features/measures/source regions/subplan/attributedef/metricdef/
spec) of two plans.

To find the difference between two plans, perform the following steps:
1. Choose two plans and configure them with different options.
2. Run the Plan Diff function.
It presents the Statistic View.
3. Open the Diff Detail View to review the details.
The subsequent sections describe these steps in detail
Choosing the HVP Plans
To view the difference, first select the two HVP plans that needs to be differentiated.
Choose the HVP files you want to differentiate on the Choose HVP Files dialog box. You
can do so by either typing in the HVP file paths or browsing the existing files.

selection.

Choosing the Plan Diff Configuration
You can compare the two plans by defining how deep the tool should look into the plan
structure. The settings are as follows:
* Feature/Sub-plan: Only the name, attribute and metric are considered. Measures are
NOT considered.
* Measure: Only name and metric selection are considered. The source in it is NOT
considered.
* Source: The source is considered.
Additionally, you can find differences for sub-plan definitions, attribute definitions, metric
definitions and whether it is a spec or not.
You can use the option Into Sub-plan to differentiate inside sub-plans
You can invoke the Diff Configuration dialog box from the main menu Plan->Diff
Plan Diff Rules
The tool shows the following three types of differences:
* "?" (modified)
* "<<" (added)
* ">>" (deleted)

various types of differences:

The Item order within a level of hierarchy is NOT considered. For example,
consider a scenario where in P1, the top level features are A, B, and C. In P2

Verdi Verification Planner: Derived Test Metrics
Verification Planner for Verdi supports the following additional built-in derived test metrics
to track verification progress:
* Percent Metric for Test Metric
* Test.completion Metric
Using these derived metrics, you can gather the percentage of tests with different status
and test completion percentage in a verification plan.

Percent Metric for Test Metric
In previous releases, the built-in test metric of enum type reports integer count for submetrics test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.unknown, and test.assert. For example,
test = 6;
test.pass = 3;
test.fail = 3;

In previous releases, the test metric reports the basic number of tests with status pass,
fail, warn, unknown, and assert in the HVP annotated report. It does not display the
percentage of these scores.

Verdi Verification Planner: Derived Test Metrics

Verification Planner for Verdi reports percentage score for each enum value of the test
metric. This enables you to get the percentage of tests with status pass, fail, warning,
unknown, or assert. The following is the list of the derived percent sub-metrics:
* test.percent.pass
* test.percent.fail
* test.percent.warn
* test.percent.unknown
* test.percent.assert
The score of a percent metric is the percentage of each enum's value of the test metric
against the total number of tests in that feature.
For example, if a is the integer count of the built-in test metric enum value and b is the
integer count of the total number of tests, then the percentage metric is computed as
(a / b)*100

For example, if
test.pass = 8
test.fail = 2
test = 10

then the value of test.percent.pass = 8/10 and is reported as 80%.
The following is the example for the usage of percent metrics:
feature f1;
test.percent.pass = test.percent.pass > 60%;
measure test, test.percent.pass m1;
source = "testname*";

Consider the following example,
feature parent:
test:6[pass:3 fail:3 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass:50.00%
feature block1
test:5[pass:3 fail:2 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass:60.00%
feature block2
test:1[pass:0 fail:1 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass: 0.00%

Verdi Verification Planner: Derived Test Metrics

In this example, the test.percent.pass score in feature parent is calculated from the test
score of:
feature parent test:6[pass:3 fail:3 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0] 50%

which is equal to 3/6. The total test score of feature parent is the sum of the test scores of
feature block1 and feature block2.
The following figure shows the derived sub-metrics displayed by Verdi coverage:
Figure 128

Viewing Percent Metric in Verdi Coverage

Test.completion Metric
The test.completion metric allows you to measure the progress of tests being written
against the number of tests expected to be written.
The score of the test.completion metric is the ratio of total integer count of all sub-metrics
of the test metric (test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.assert, test.unknown) and the
expected number of tests in a plan/feature. The expected number of tests should be set
using the test.expected attribute.
Where,test.completion=total_test_count/test.expected and
total_test_count=test.pass+test.fail+test.warn+test.as sert+test.unknown
Test.expected Attribute
You can use the test.expected built-in attribute assignment, as shown below, to set the
expected number of tests in feature/plan scope.
test.expected = <number>;
The expected number is like an annotation value kept in feature/plan node. The default
value of test.expected is 0.

Figure 129

Viewing test.expected in Verdi Coverage

The test.completion metric can be calculated only after setting the
test.expectedattribute.
The following example illustrates the usage of the test.completion metric:
feature Goal_pass;
test.expected = 2;
test.percent.pass = (test.percent.pass >= 0.5);
measure test, test.percent.pass, test.completion Measure_1;
source = "test3";

Examples for Image Selection

The following are examples that describe how sections containing images are handled
during spec-linking.
Consider the following two cases for a linked section containing images:
* A section contains images and text as well.
* A section contains image(s) only
These two cases are handled different ways during review and updating the section to a
new document during spec-linking.
Case 1: Section contains both images and text
In this case spec-linking follows the following process:
* Review and update the text to the new section in the new document.
* Find the images in the updated section in the new document.
* Generate a new section based on the text section and images, the decision table below
lists all the possibilities and review results.
Table 10

Image Text Matching

Missing

Missing

missing

The review result for an image depends on the updated text section in the new document.
There can be three results for image comparison: Matching, Missing, New. The result
conflict is not applicable for images.
* Matching: The image in the old document is found in the new document and it is
present by the updated text section.
In this case, image is found means that the image in the old and new documents are
the same.

* Missing: The image is not found in the new document, or it is found but it is NOT in the
updated text section.
* New: The image is in the updated text section but not in the old document. In Verdi
New is treated as a Conflict.
The image and text works as an entire link in the review process, so whatever actions
(accept, reject) that you choose to apply, the action is applied to both the image and the
text.
You may not be able to treat the text or the image as separate review-able objects.
Case 2: A section contains only image(s)
Without considering in the text in the review process, the search scope of an image is not
limited to the updated text section in the new document. The whole document is within the
search scope.
For example, if an image at page 10 was selected and linked as a section in the old
document, Verdi spec-linking feature searches the image at page 10 then around page 10,
that is page 11, page 9, page12, page 8 and so on, until the image is found.
If the image is found, then it is marked as matching, otherwise it is marked as missing.
The review result types new and conflict are not applicable in this case.

Difference Between Masks and Filters
As discussed, Verdi Planner supports two ways to customize the features displayed:
masks and filters. Though they appear to operate in a similar way, there is a distinct
difference in the way that they behave. Filters not only remove features from the displayed
plan view, they also disable the effect that those removed features' scores have on the
remainder of the plan. For example suppose a feature A with a score of 50% has 2 child
features A1 (0%) and A2 (100%). If you filter out feature A1 then its 0% score no longer
affects the parent feature A and A's score becomes 100%.
Masks are different because they simply hide rows based on the masking criteria. The
hidden rows' scores continue to affect scores. In the same example if A1 is masked, its
parent feature A's score remains at 50%.
In addition to this, the key differences between quick filters and masks are as follows:
* Any changes applied to a quick filter also affects scores; masks do not affect scores.
* Operations on quick filters can be saved as a modifier file that can be reloaded again;
masks cannot be saved as a modifier file.
* For quick filters, the filter icon
is displayed only when you click on the Quick Filter
icon; the mask icon
is always displayed on the right of Result columns.
* Quick filters are for attribute columns; masks are for Result columns.
Quick filters and masks can exist at the same time. However, quick filters have higher
priority than masks.

Transformation Rules of User Data to HVP Annotation
The following are the transform rules of User Data while annotating to HVP:
* Scientific notation with 'e' notation use cases (when the Format in SI Prefixes
preference option is disabled):
For numbers with more than 5 decimal places.
Any number greater than or equal to 1,000,000 or less than or equal to -1,000,000.
All the other use cases are represented using normal notation with 5 decimal
places.
* SI Prefixes use cases (when the Format in SI Prefixes preference option is enabled)
The following values are represented in SI Prefixes:
Numbers greater than or equal to 1000 and less than or equal to -1000.
Numbers in between -0.01 and 0.01, except 0.
* Floating point precision:
Scientific notation with 'e' notation: 6 decimal places
SI Prefixes: 6 decimal places
Normal Notation: 5 decimal places
* Display format for Scientific notation with 'e' notation:
Trailing zero: "." should be followed by "0" when there is no mantissa (for example,
1.0e+09).
Leading zero: A minimum of 2 digits are required for notation presentation. That is,
leading zero is displayed if the exponent is less than 3 digits.
* Display format for SI Prefixes:
Trailing zero: No trailing zero is used in the SI Prefixes. For example, 1M.

The following section describes the enhancement to the CRDB utility LCA feature
supported by Verdi as part of this release:
* Enhancement to the CRDB Utility

Enhancement to the CRDB Utility
In the previous releases, the RTL design had encrypted IP blocks because of which CRDB
could not be directly extracted from the FSDB file for the RTL design.
Starting with this release, the -RTL_FSDB option is added in the CRDB utility. This option
can be used to extract the CRDB from the FSDB file for the RTL design. The -RTL_FSDB
option is an alternative option to extract the RTL design.

The flow of CRDB is as follows:
1. Extract the gate level design
2. Extract the RTL design and
3. Perform the correlation.
The syntax for -RTL_FSDB option is:
crdb -RTL_FSDB RTL_FSDB_name

Here,
RTL_FSDB_name - Specifies the user-defined FSDB file name.
crdb -RTL_FSDB RTL_FSDB -GATE "-f gate.f" -impSVF "block1.svf block2.svf"
-expMap mapping.gz -allreg

Chapter 6: Correlation
Enhancement to the CRDB Utility

The syntax to extract gate level design and RTL design to perform the correlation is as
crdb -RTL_FSDB RTL_FSDB_name -GATE "<gate level import & BA options>"
-crdb <output CRDB name> <correlation options> [export mapping options]

If you extract RTL CRDB from FSDB more than once, then the previous
database extracted is overwritten with the latest extracted database. -append
option is not supported if you extract CRDB from FSDB. It issues an error
message and aborts the CRDB generation.

The -RTL_FSDB option in the CRDB utility has the following limitations:
* If the FSDB is written by a third party tool instead of FSDB dumper, some information
may be incorrect or missed due to wrong usage of FSDB writer by the third party tool.
The input FSDB requires a module name for each instance. If a module name is not
written into FSDB, then the extraction does not create a model for that instance.
* The following design information which can be extracted from the RTL design may not
be extracted from FSDB.
Register information is not available in FSDB.
Equivalent net or inverted equivalent net is not available in FSDB. That is, if some signals
are originally correlated through an equivalent net, it may not become correlated when
extracting it from FSDB.

FSDB Command Line, Environment Variable, and Dump
Command Options
The unified FSDB dumper supports three methods for specifying options. The methods
are:
1. Specify an option on the simulator command line. Refer to the FSDB Dumping
Command Line Options section for details on the command-line options.
2. Specify an option using an environment variable. Refer to Appendix A in the Verdi and
Siloti Command Reference Manual for details on the environment variables.
3. Specify an option in an FSDB dumping command. Refer to the FSDB Dumping
Command Option table for details on using options with the dump commands.
If the same option is set using more than one method, the resolution is: Method 1 >
Method 2 > Method 3.
For example, the FSDB dump file name can be set using one of the following methods:
1. Specify the file name on the simulator command line:
> simv +fsdbfile+high.fsdb

2. Specify the file name using an environment variable:
> setenv NOVAS_FSDB_FILE mid_prio.fsdb

3. Specify the file name in an FSDB dumping command:
$fsdbDumpvars("+fsdbfile+low_prio.fsdb");

This means that in this example, the resolved FSDB file name is high.fsdb.

Some options control related behavior. For example, NOVAS_FSDB_MDA enables
or disables MDA signal dumping, while NOVAS_FSDB_ALL enables or disables all
supported signal types. NOVAS_FSDB_ALL is a superset of NOVAS_FSDB_MDA.
When you set related options through different methods at the same time, the dumper
applies both settings. It does not use the usual priority order (command line, then
environment variable, then FSDB dumping command). Instead, it combines the effects:
1. Resolve each option's value using the standard priority: simulator command line, then
environment variable, then FSDB dumping command.
2. Apply the union of all resolved settings.
Example 1
1. Specify the environment variable to enable dumping MDA signals:
setenv NOVAS_FSDB_MDA 1

2. Specify the option in an FSDB dumping command to enable dumping all supported
signals:
$fsdbDumpvars("+all");

These options differ, so priority resolution does not apply. The dumper combines both
settings and enables dumping of all supported signals.
Example 2
1. Specify the option on the simulator command line to enable dumping packed MDA
signals:
simv +fsdb+packedmda

2. Specify the environment variable to enable dumping MDA signals:
setenv NOVAS_FSDB_MDA 1

Both +fsdb+mda and +fsdb+packedmda resolve to on. The dumper combines them and
enables dumping of all MDA signals.
Example 3
Specify the options on the simulator command line to filter all dumper messages, warning
messages, and error messages:
simv +fsdb+no_warning +fsdb+no_error +fsdb+no_all_msg

The dumper combines all three options and filters all dumper messages.

Dumping Class Objects by Level
You can use the $fsdbDumpClassObject dumping command to dump the value change in
object to the FSDB file.
Following is the syntax when specified in the design:
$fsdbDumpClassObject( class_name_or_object_name [, option]*)

Following is the syntax when specified on the simulation UCLI command line:
fsdbDumpClassObject class_name_or_object_name [option]*

Where, class_name_or_object_name is the class name or object name in full hierarchy
format that is specified to dump.

Dumping Dynamic Class Objects

When you invoke VCS to compile the design, you must use the -debug_access
+class or -debug_access+ckbd options at the compile command line.
To dump the expandable class pointer signal, set the following environment variable:
setenv FSDB_ENABLE_EXPAND_CLASS 1

Following are the options supported for the $fsdbDumpClassObject dumping command:
+object_level=depth: Keyword to identify the number of levels of hierarchy to dump for
the subsequent objects. The default value of depth is 1.

Where, depth can have the following value:
N: N level sub-object under the current object or object instantiated from the current class
object.
0: All sub-objects under the current object or objects instantiated from the current class
object.
Note: It is recommended not to set +object_level to 0 as it costs more with a complex
testbench and limited resources.
+fsdbfile+<filename>: Specifies the FSDB file name. If not specified, the default FSDB
file name is novas.fsdb.

Note: An environment variable can be used as part of the filename string argument.
When an environment variable is defined and then embedded into the option, the FSDB
dumper replaces the environment variable with the given definition.
Examples
$fsdbDumpClassObject("top.simple1.simple_class@1");

Dump the first object of class simple_class at scope: top.simple1.
$fsdbDumpClassObject("top.simple1.simple_class@3");

Dump the third object of class simple_class at scope: top.simple1.
$fsdbDumpClassObject("top.simple1.simple_class");

Dump all objects instantiated from class simple_class at scope: top.simple1.
$fsdbDumpClassObject("top.simple1.simple_class", "+fsdbfile+my.fsdb");

Dumps all objects from class simple_class to the specified FSDB file, my.fsdb.
$fsdbDumpClassObject("top.simple1.simple_class", "+object_level=3");

Dump objects below the class simple_class up to the depth specified for the depth
variable.

Encrypted IP
Debugging is complicated when dealing with encrypted IPs due to limited knowledge and
visibility. This leads to time-consuming back-and-forths between SoC and IP teams. To
tackle these challenges, new verification, debug capabilities, and robust methodologies
are required.
An encrypted IP block is a secured version of the RTL source code or its gate-level netlist,
processed through an encryption algorithm. This encryption allows certain tools to operate
on the code, but prevents users from viewing the source. The most versatile encryption
scheme is the IEEE-P1735 standard, widely adopted for interoperability among IP and
EDA vendors.
The objective is to serve IP suppliers and the design teams in the following ways:
* IP Supplier: Protects the security of the IP in the design flow across different EDA
tools.
* IP Users: Ensures the interoperability of the IP across different EDA tools and vendors.

Encrypted IP

The IEEE-P1735 uses the following two levels of encryption to generate an encrypted IP:
1. The first level of encryption creates a random session key that is used to encrypt the
source code into a data_block using a symmetric encryption algorithm such as AES.
2. The second level of encryption uses the public keys of the EDA tool vendor to encrypt
the session key into a key_block using an asymmetric encryption algorithm such as
RSA.
The decryption flow that resides in the EDA tools applies the same process in the reverse
order as follows:
1. The tool scans the key-block searching for its own key; once located, the tool uses its
own private key to decrypt the key-block thus obtaining the symmetric session key.
2. The session key is then used to decrypt the data-block allowing the tool to compile
the original source code.
The following figure illustrates the IEEE-P1735 encryption and decryption flows:
Figure 201

IEEE-P1735 Encryption and Decryption Flows

An encryption envelope is the preamble to the IP block in the source code. An IP supplier
must prepare an encryption envelope containing the public keys for each EDA tool that
is to be given access to the IP block. The encryption envelope consists of pragmas that
provide information such as encryption scheme, encoding type, key owner, key name, and
key method.
The following figure illustrates an encrypted IP containing multiple key-blocks, each
corresponding to a tool or vendor to be given access to the IP. One of the advantages
of the P1735 scheme is that the data block is common to all tools. Therefore, the same

Encrypted IP

encrypted IP block can be delivered to all the IP users and supporting various tools and
flows. The session keys are automatically generated, therefore, they are not known to
anyone and do not need to be safeguarded; only the private decryption keys must be
safeguarded by the respective tools.
Figure 202

An Encrypted IP with three key-blocks

The P1735 standard enables IP reuse across applications, addresses IP security and
interoperability. However, it does not dictate how IP distribution is controlled, what
information a tool can reveal, or how to protect IP contents. Each tool must implement its
own policies to safeguard IP content.

Encrypted IP Policies
The policies that govern Synopsys' simulation and verification tools have been developed
over a period of time to satisfy the needs of IP integrators as well as the security concerns
of IP suppliers. Since the compilers are able to decrypt encrypted IPs, they have access to
the full source code, including the original names of all the objects in the IP. Therefore, the
decryption tools must be carefully devised to avoid mistakenly disclosing any information
deemed proprietary. Specifically, the VCS compiler has been enhanced to safeguard the
private decryption key as well as the data contained in an encrypted IP block.
Error and warning messages issued by the compiler have been carefully designed to
reveal only information known to the IP user but sufficient for the IP supplier to identify the
source of the problem. In particular, any error triggered by an encrypted IP component
includes only three pieces of information: a description of the error or warning, file name,
and the line-number of the offending code - the names of objects in the IP are not
disclosed. The information issued is typically enough for the IP user to report the problem
to the IP supplier.
During simulation or a debug session, all introspection into encrypted IP blocks is
disallowed. This includes actions such as using wildcards through the hierarchy of
encrypted blocks or attempt to use a VPI iterator to traverse the content of the IP, which
would effectively allow IP users to decompile encrypted blocks. Likewise, the simulator
prohibits disclosing the hierarchical names or the values generated by an encrypted
IP block during simulation: The waveforms associated with an encrypted IP cannot be
dumped into an FSDB.

Debugging Standalone IP

There are a few exceptions to the strict IP protection provided to by the tools. An
encrypted IP is allowed to divulge design information. For example, assertions triggered
by an IP block contain the same information as if the assertion was in clear text. Similarly,
if the IP includes statements that print text (for example, $display), the statement is
allowed to execute undisturbed. The rational for this rule is that the IP owner is explicitly
including such code in the IP so it's not the responsibility of the tools to prevent such
actions from divulging internal information. Finally, knowledge of the hierarchical name of
an object inside an encrypted IP block grants an IP user access to that object, to either
examine or change its simulation value or to dump its waveform. The rationale for this rule
is that the only way the IP users knows the name is because the name was disclosed by
the IP owner. This capability is sometimes used by IP suppliers to deploy a workaround
that changes the behavior of the IP or to issue some information that may help diagnose a
problem while running at the IP user site.
Although the simulator does allow IP users to manipulate the behavior of a
signal internal to an encrypted IP block by specifying its hierarchical name,
this type of external manipulation of the behavior of the IP block is highly
discouraged and should be used rarely and in extreme cases. Instead, all
interactions between the design and an encrypted IP component should occur
through the IP's hardware interface, that is, top-level ports. Forcing signals in
lieu of a proper hardware reset or an initialization or configuration sequence can
cause the IP to malfunction and create problem that is difficult to debug.

Debugging Standalone IP
Debugging a potential IP problem while running a full chip test is challenging not just
due to lack of IP visibility; SoC or system-level simulations are large and compile and
run much slower than standalone IP tests. This situation is exacerbated when IP owners
incrementally request additional data from IP users to analyze a problem; the IP user must
typically recompile and rerun a lengthy simulation to generate the additional information.
To enable effective IP reuse, the debug problems associated with encrypted IP need to be
addressed.
Encrypted FSDB, is a proposal enabled by an asymmetric encryption scheme to protect
not just the source code (as enabled by P1735) but also the simulated waveforms.

Encrypted IP Waveform
When an encrypted IP includes unpredictable constructs or its internals are manipulated
beyond its I/O ports, IDX may not replicate a system level issue at the IP level. For
debugging, the IP supplier requires waveforms of all signals, which can be done using
Verdi alone. However, due to encrypted IP policies, an IP user cannot dump the internal
waveforms unless the IP supplier discloses all internal names, which is impractical. To

Debugging Standalone IP

solve this, the IP supplier can allow the dumping of waveforms during system level testing,
which are then encrypted for confidentiality. The IP user can generate the encrypted FSDB
but can't view the waveforms unless given the decryption key.
The Encrypted IP Waveform is a mechanism for securely exporting encrypted FSDB
files that can only be decrypted by IP suppliers using their private decryption key. The
Encrypted IP Waveform feature changes several aspects of the IP creation as well as the
simulation and debug flows. The Encrypted IP Waveform feature proceeds in the following
IP Supplier
1. Obtains an asymmetric RSA key pair.
2. Adds the public key to the IP and encrypts the IP.
IP User
1. Compiles the design with the new IP, which contain the public key.
2. Runs the system level simulation with a new option.
3. Specifies the design instances whose waveforms are to be dumped.
4. Ships the resulting FSDB to the IP supplier.
Finally, the IP owner uses the private key to load the FSDB waveforms into Verdi and
begin the IP debug session.
The encrypted IP waveform overall flow is illustrated in Figure 203. Each of the steps are
covered in detail in the next sections.

Debugging Standalone IP

Figure 203

Encrypted IP Waveform Flow

Although the Encrypted IP Waveform capability introduces changes to the IP preparation
and encryption flow, these changes are required to safeguard the IP. Other options such
as a post-encryption option to add the public key would give someone other than the IP
owner the ability to tamper with the IP. Encrypting the public key with the rest of the source
code ensures that no one other than the simulation tool use the key. It thus provides the
same security as the encrypted IP flow itself.
IP users are responsible for safeguarding their own data. VCS honors a request by an IP
user to dump the waveforms of nonencrypted design blocks - albeit all the waveforms
are encrypted using the IP owner's public key. Therefore, the IP owner can view all the
waveforms in the encrypted FSDB, even those that are not part of the IP. To avoid this, IP

Debugging Standalone IP

users must be careful to only dump non-proprietary data or limit the waveform dump to
only the IP of interest.
VCS protects the encrypted IPs that have different public keys. If instructed to dump
the waveforms of IP blocks with different public keys, VCS issues an error and does not
generate the FSDB. This means that if different IP owners need to debug a failure, multiple
simulation runs are needed; one run for each IP owner - or one for each public key.
1. Obtaining RSA Keys
There are many ways to obtain an RSA private/public key pair. You can use
fsdbEncKeyGen to generate RSA key pair or use official RSA website to generate it.
2. Adding the Public Key and Encrypting the IP
IP owners can use the new option -fsdb_public_key to have the -ipprotect
option of the VCS compiler to automatically add the public key attribute as part of the
encryption. The fsdb_key attribute is only relevant for the top-level module of the IP,
VCS automatically extends it to encompass the full hierarchy of the IP. The fsdb_key is
disregarded if specified anywhere else in the hierarchy of the IP block. In addition, only
one fsdb_key attribute should be specified in the IP.
vcs -full64 -sverilog -ipopt=noincludeprotect -ipprotect
encryption_header -fsdb_public_key public.pem ip.v

Specifying the fsdb_key to all the files causes VCS to add the fsdb_key
attribute to every module, which, as stated above is functionally immaterial
and increases the size of the encrypted data.
3. Compiling the Design
To enable the waveform dumping capabilities, the IP user must specify the
-debug_access and -debug_region=encrypt options to the VCS compile command
vcs top.v ip.vp -debug_access -debug_region=encrypt

This command generates a simv executable that is capable of generating an encrypted
FSDB.
4. Running the Simulation
To enable Encrypted IP Waveform for a simulation run, IP users need to add the +fsdb

+public_key_ip simv option when running the executable, as follows:
simv +fsdb+public_key_ip

5. Specifying Instances to be Dumped

Encrypted IP Waveform Flow Summary

IP users designate the design instances to be dumped using the $fsdbdumpvar task.
If any of the design instances specified to $fsdbdumpvars is an encrypted block that
includes a fsdb public key then the entire FSDB is encrypted using the public key.
As noted earlier, attempting to dump waveforms for encrypted IPs with different fsdb
keys result in an error and the dump is aborted. Similarly, adding instances in multiple
$fsdbdumpvars commands and any of the instances have a different public key results
in an error and the dump is aborted, even if a dump has already started.
6. Loading an Encrypted FSDB
The IP owner can load an encrypted FSDB into Verdi by specifying the private key
through the environment variable FSDB_DECRYPT before running Verdi.
setenv FSDB_DECRYPT private.pem
verdi -ssf novas.fsdb

If the private key is incorrect or it is not specified the FSDB fails to load. An encrypted
FSDB is rendered useless to anyone without the private decryption key. One of the
advantages of the Encrypted IP Waveform flow is that the IP owner does not need to
run the simulation. The encrypted FSDB contains all the simulation data as it executed
in the system level test.

PyVerdi Python Package
Verdi provides a Python package PyVerdi, which supports the following two APIs:
* callCommand
* addCallback
Before you execute Python inside Verdi, Verdi automatically imports both APIs, letting you
to directly write callCommand and addCallback inside your Python script without the need
for from PyVerdi import *.
PyVerdi.callCommand
The callCommand API is used to run Tcl commands. This API returns both Tcl return value
(integer) and the result (string) as a tuple.
Syntax: callCommand(tclString: str) -> tuple[int, str]
PyVerdi.addCallback
The addCallback API is used to register the Python function as an event callback
function, like addEventCallback in Tcl. This API returns true if the callback is registered
successfully; otherwise, it returns false. If you register both the Python callback and the Tcl
callback for the same event reason, only the Python callback gets triggered.
Syntax: addCallback(callbackReason: str, callbackFunc: callable[[str],
any]) -> bool

Replay Python Script
Using Command Line Interface:
Like Tcl replay flow, you can type verdi -playPy /path/to/<script>.py to replay a
Python script. Note that if you specify both -play and -playPy in command line option,
the -play (Tcl playback) is executed first, and then the -playPy (Python playback).
The Python output is shown in the Console window, including the executing error.
