EDR (Electronic Debug Record) is a feature that allows you to create, save, and load a
Verdi session, which may contain texts, screenshots, Tcl scripts that are used to reproduce
or solve an issue in Verdi. A common usage scenario would be that an R&D wants
to share his Verdi debug session with another R&D. He can create and save an EDR
session that contains the necessary steps to reproduce an issue. Then the other R&D can
reproduce the Verdi debug session quickly with a single click.

* Setting up the EDR Client
* Saving EDR
* Replaying EDR

Prerequisites for Installing the EDR Server

the EDR Server installation.
To ensure stable operation of the EDR server, verify that the machine meets the minimum
hardware requirements:

* RAM: Minimum of 8GB
* Disk: Minimum of 20GB

Saving EDR
Before invoking Verdi, set the VCS_HOME and VERDI_HOME environment variables using the
following commands respectively:
setenv VCS_HOME <vcs home directory location>
setenv VERDI_HOME <verdi home directory location>

Set the VERDI_ENABLE_ELECTRONIC_DEBUG_RECORD environment variable to 1 to enable

Once Verdi is opened, navigate to Tools -> Save to EDR to save the EDR.
The Save EDR dialog opens as shown in the following example figure:
Figure 213

Save EDR Form

* Run_Mode: This field supports Session mode and TCL mode. Session mode saves
a Verdi session skipping the reproduced steps, and TCL mode saves the command
history and enable you to see how the debug record is reproduced.
* Title: This field automatically set the string as <user>_<app>_<date> to help users
distinguish different records. The app can be Verdi or formal or static. You may add
more app names later.
* Category: A predefined list of error characteristics. The default value is Unknown
Issue.
* Tags: You may add one or more Tags (separate by comma) to the record.
* Permission: The permission drop-down list contains Public and all Linux groups
of the current users. The default value is public. Once permission is set to group,
enable_case_extration is disabled. If an EDR has public permission, all users can
access it. If an EDR has group permission, only users who have the corresponding
Linux group permission can access it.
* Description: You may add the description of the debug record to capture the main
purpose of the session.
* Other Setting:
Environment Setting: The environment setting does not add all user environments
to the record; however, only the important ones are added. The users can add other
environment settings to the record as needed.
Data Preparation: This tab enables you to set the batch mode commands to
prepare the data for Verdi debug. Default Commands are the pre-defined batch
mode commands by EDR. You may change it if needed. Once you write your own
data preparation commands, Enable Case Extraction check box is disabled.

Save EDR - Data Preparation

Data Path

For FSDB, EDR automatically gathers files that are opened with the wvOpenFile or

* Advanced: This field shows the advanced features that enables you to set multiple
checkpoints in the record, and Case Extraction. You may click "+" to add the
checkpoint. A checkpoint contains the command history executed so far (from last
saved checkpoint or from beginning) with a snapshot and checkpoint notes. You may
also use Update Snapshot to update from the current active window. If multiple views

edrSearch
The edrSearch utility allows you to search through EDRs.
Input
A search string that follows the rules below.
Supported Search key:
"session_name"
"session_description"
"session_sig_catg"
"session_creator"
"session_id"
"session_workmode"
"session_group"
"time_range"
"path.KDB"
"path.FSDB"
"path.simulation_log"

Supported Logical Operators
"AND"
"OR"

Supported Match Operators
"="
"~"

For example, the following string queries the EDRs whose session_name contains verdi
and session_creator is jack.
edrSearch "session_name ~ verdi AND session_creator = jack"

Note that time_range is a special key and it only supports three value: week, month,
quarter.
For example, the following string queries the EDRs that are created in last seven days and
session_description contains debug.
edrSearch "time_range = week AND session_description ~ debug"

Output:
One or more matched EDR session IDs, if not found, the output is "No matched records in
database."

Overview
Synopsys Memory VIPs are based on Synopsys SystemVerilog Technology (SVT)
infrastructure. The infrastructure includes SystemVerilog classes and Memory Server.
The Memory Server is one of the key elements of SVT Memory VIP infrastructure. Actual
memory values are stored in the Memory Server, rather than in a SystemVerilog array.
The primary advantage of this approach is performance independence. The Memory
VIP does not rely on each simulator's sparse array server implementation. For multi-GB
memories, the simulation typically accesses only a small portion of the overall address
space. In addition, this approach supports virtual patterns. These patterns enable memory
initialization without significant memory or performance overhead.
In a Memory VIP, protocol-level transactions and memory actions are stored in an FSDB
file. The Memory Server can be configured to record all memory actions to the same
FSDB file. You can then view the memory-related data in the Verdi Memory Protocol
Analyzer. With the information recorded by the Memory Server, you can determine any
memory address value at any time during simulation.
The SVT Memory Server has been enhanced to store the memory actions associated with
the server in an FSDB file as transactions. The streams of these transactions are tagged
with hidden attributes. The Verdi environment recognizes the memory instances and

Overview

displays them in the new Memory Array browser. In addition, you can view the memory
actions of the Memory Server in Transaction Table View or Transaction and Protocol
Analyzer windows.
For performance considerations, each instance of a Synopsys Memory VIP must be
configured to dump data to the FSDB file. By default, this capability is not enabled.
Synopsys Memory VIPs provide controls for dumping protocol-level transactions. They
also dump the status of internal state machines and the memory actions performed by the
Memory Server.

Cache Model Representation in AMBA ACE VIP
The general structure of the cache data model for AMBA ACE protocol, which is recorded
in the FSDB file to display cache data is illustrated in the following figure:
Cache Data Model

Coherent Transaction
* This transaction indicates AXI master is initiating a transaction which involves cache
coherency.
* This information is captured per address on a given cache line.
Snoop Transactions

Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer (Cache Mode)

* This transaction indicates the snoop transactions performed by the interconnect based
on the coherent request initiated by a master.
* This information is captured per address on a given cache line.
* Each snoop transaction has a predecessor/successor relationship with the coherent
transaction.
Cache/Cache Line Operations
* Any update made in cache memory happens on a cache line.
* The cache line information is recorded in the Cache and Memory Browser as explained
below.
The cache data is maintained each time the cache memory is accessed, which results in
the recording of a cache operation. The cache operation data is composed of the following
attributes and is represented as a transaction within the FSDB file with these attributes:
* Time
* Address
* Action
* State
* Data

Synchronization With Verdi Transaction and Protocol Analyzer
Verdi provides the capability that lets you synchronize the Cache pane with Verdi
Transaction and Protocol Analyzer and other transaction views, which provides a better
debug experience.
In addition to creating a cache operation transaction, relationships are established
between various transactions, which are used to display appropriate information in the
cache view and aid in the debug process. The predecessor/successor relationship is
illustrated as follows:

The VIP captures information related to the cache memory into a separate scope called
cache. This scope is present inside the same hierarchy as the master instance. The scope
contains a scope attribute, which indicates that this scope contains cache related data.
This data can be read by and displayed in the Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer:
Cache view.
The following two scopes are created below the cache scope:
* The info scope, which is used to store general information about the cache, such as the
width of each cache line and the number of lines in the cache.
* The operations scope, which is used to store the cache operation transactions.
When a cache operation is recorded, a predecessor/successor relationship
is established between each coherent transaction and the associated

Synchronization With Verdi Transaction and Protocol Analyzer

snoop transactions. If appropriate, this relationship is also established with
the slave transaction. Additionally, a predecessor/successor relationship
is established between each snoop transaction and the cache operation
transaction.

Improved Waveform Drawing Performance for FSDB-GATE
Signals
Describes nWave performance enhancements for FSDB-GATE signals: pixel-based
drawing (SNPS_VERDI_PIXEL_BASED_DRAWER), multitasking dense drawing, optional
red X highlighting (Waveform > View Options > Waveform Pane > Show X Color in
Multitasking Dense Drawing), docked/undocked progress display, default vs NeedX mode,
and limitations (unfinished files, auto-update, virtual files, anyall/real signal).
This feature improves the speed of drawing waveforms in nWave when working with
FSDB-GATE signals. FSDB files can contain many signals that are marked as secondary,
meaning their value changes are not dumped directly but reconstructed during reading.

This reconstruction can slow down nWave operations, especially for gate-level FSDBs with
many value changes. The new solution speeds up waveform drawing and makes the user
interface more responsive.
* Enabling Pixel-Based Drawer for nWave
* Enabling and Using X Color Display in nWave Multitasking Dense Drawing
* Limitations of Multitasking Dense Drawing and Pixel-Based Drawer for nWave

Enabling Pixel-Based Drawer for nWave
The pixel-based drawing feature in nWave improves how waveform data is displayed,
especially when handling large datasets. This feature changes how dense pixels and
'X' (unknown) values appear in the waveform view.
Setting Environment Variables
To activate the pixel-based drawer feature, set the following environment variable before
launching Verdi and nWave:
setenv SNPS_VERDI_PIXEL_BASED_DRAWER 1

Using the Feature
* Open nWave as usual after setting the environment variables.
* nWave polls the FSDB reader and update the waveform incrementally.

* The interface remains responsive; you can scroll, click, and view signal tips even while
data is loading.
* Unfinished waveform data appears as blue pixels. These pixels update as more data
loads.

nWave now draws green pixels to represent areas with enough value changes, instead of
checking each value change one by one. This speeds up rendering for large datasets. The
following figure illustrates the old behavior:

The following figure illustrates the new behavior:

Enabling and Using X Color Display in nWave Multitasking Dense
Drawing
The X Color Display in nWave Multitasking Dense Drawing is a feature that helps users
quickly identify unknown (X) values in waveforms when working with large FSDB (Fast
Signal Database) files. This feature is especially useful when debugging gate-level
simulations, as it visually highlights X values in dense waveform regions, making it easier
to spot issues without zooming in on every signal.
When you load a large FSDB file in nWave, the tool uses a dense drawing mode to speed
up waveform rendering. In this mode, nWave summarizes many value changes (vc) into
a single pixel. By default, X values might not be shown in red unless you zoom in. The
"NeedX" mode allows you to display X values in red even in dense drawing, but might
impact performance.

* Default Mode: Fast drawing, X values might not appear in red unless zoomed in.
* NeedX Mode: Precise X detection, X values appear in red in dense drawing, but might
slow down performance.

Enabling X Color Display (NeedX Mode)
Follow these steps to enable the X Color Display in nWave:
1. Go to Waveform > View Options > Waveform Pane > Show X Color in Multitasking
Dense Drawing in the nWave preferences.
2. Set the option to On.
When enabled, dense drawing shows "X" values in red for more accuracy.
When disabled (default), "X" values are not shown in dense mode, but appears
when you zoom in.
Viewing Progress and Status
* Undocked nWave Window: The progress bar appears in the toolbar when data is
loading. Hover over the bar to see tips.

* Docked nWave Window: The progress bar appears in the banner area, and a busy
status is shown in the tab area.

Limitations of Multitasking Dense Drawing and Pixel-Based
Drawer for nWave
* The "Show X Color in Multitasking Dense Drawing" option applies only to GATE FSDB
dense drawing.
* Enabling NeedX mode might impact performance, especially with large files.
* In default mode, "X" values might not be shown in red unless you zoom in.
* In default mode, "X" values are not shown in dense drawing unless NeedX mode is
enabled.
* Only the smallest range of value changes per pixel is reconstructed, which might affect
accuracy for some signals unless zoomed in or NeedX mode is enabled.
* This feature is not supported with unfinished files.
* Not supported with auto-update feature.
* Does not support virtual file (except auto-switch).
* Does not support anyall-related feature and real signal.

Verdi Low Power Import Performance Improvement
Profiling shows that Verdi low power import takes a long time to traverse all UPF
commands from the power database. To resolve this issue, run a batch mode executable,
lpcom, in parallel with VCS compilation.
lpcom processes the power database and serializes it into an archive. During Verdi bring

up, Verdi automatically picks up the archive and transforms it into the Verdi database.
This support is now enabled at compilation using the -kdb=lpcom compile option.
Following is the usage example:
% vcs design.v -sverilog -upf file.upf -lca -kdb=lpcom
% verdi -dbdir simv.daidir

When you use this option, Verdi imports resolved power KDB (PW-KDB) directly instead of
building Verdi Power Model.
You can use the following environment variable to disable -kdb=lpcom:

The following section describe the UVM-Aware Debug LCA feature supported by Verdi as
part of this release:
* Instant Recall Flow for UVM Debug

Instant Recall Flow for UVM Debug
When you debug a UVM error or fatal event in Verdi interactive mode, you need to rerun
the simulation to reach the error point after starting Verdi.
The Verdi Instant Recall feature lets you save the error point as a debug session during
batch-mode simulation. The UVM error message report helps you find error types, group
them, and plan your next steps for debugging with Instant Recall.
After you save the simulation session for a UVM error or fatal event, you can use Verdi to
restore the session in interactive mode. This saves time because you do not need to rerun
the simulation.
To enable the Instant Recall flow, use the -instantRecall VCS runtime option. The
Instant Recall flow enables the following:
* Record the simulation session at the first UVM error or fatal, and then use Verdi to start
debugging from the point where the simulation session was recorded.
* Stop the simulation at the first UVM error or fatal, print out the error message, create
checkpoint information of debug point, save the session, and then exit the simulation.
You can know at which UVM_ERROR is the checkpoint saved and identify that the test failed
with UVM_ERROR.
UVM error message report helps you to identify error types, group them, and perform the
next step for debugging with Instant Recall.
You can continue to perform debugging by using the -i -cprestore [saved_session]
Verdi command line option to restore the simulation session to Verdi in interactive mode.

Instant Recall Flow for UVM Debug

The following sections describe this feature in detail:
* Enabling Instant Recall Flow in VCS and UCLI
* Debugging in Verdi With Instant Recall Flow
Enabling Instant Recall Flow in VCS and UCLI
* You can enable Instant Recall flow in VCS using the -instantRecall runtime option.
For example, simv -instantRecall.
For compilation, you must specify the -kdb and -debug_acc+reverse options to
enable this feature.
* The -instantRecall option auto-generates a default instant recall script named
.synopsys_ucli_instant_recall.tcl under the run directory. The following are the
key points to note:
The instant recall script enables reverse debug (config reversedebug on), saves
debug point on the first UVM error or fatal, and then saves the session.
The saved session is the simulation session, not the Verdi session.
Simulation sources this Tcl script before sourcing your -do/-i script.
By default, .synopsys_ucli_instant_recall.tcl is overwritten for every instant
recall run.
To modify this script, you can add a header in this Tcl file to keep the current Tcl
version by adding/removing comment, so that your modification can take effect in
later instant recall runs.
The session can be overwritten if it exists.
Provide default session name. You can also define session names in the
.synopsys_ucli_instant_recall.tcl file.
* If the restore session fails, UCLI exits.
Debugging in Verdi With Instant Recall Flow
* The session is saved under the run directory. You can execute from the Verdi
command line as follows to restore the session from the time point where the first UVM
error or fatal happened.
% verdi -dbdir ./simv.daidir -i -cprestore [checkpoint_session]

You can specify the simulation session name to restore. If no file is specified, the
default session file is restored.
* If the restore session fails, UCLI exits and Verdi closes the interactive debug mode.

Specifying FSDB File Name for UVM Enabled Features

* From the Verdi command line, the restore session should not be used with -do/-i.
Example: verdi -dbdir ./simv.daidir -i -cprestore sess -do myScript
Verdi issues a warning message and skips -do/-i.
The following is the limitation of this feature:
* When Verdi is invoked with the -i -cprestore option, it may not consider some
runtime options of the Restart simulation command. This can happen as the Verdi
behavior is the same as the restore mechanism. That is, Verdi may not extract some of
the runtime options applied to simv.
You can use one of the following workarounds to avoid this limitation:
1. If an FSDB file is dumped for the simulation with the -instantRecall option, you
can invoke Verdi using both the -i -cprestore option and the FSDB file together.
The simulation options are saved in the FSDB file and can be reused while invoking
Verdi.
Example:%> verdi -ssf novas.fsdb -i -cprestore
2. If no FSDB is dumped, you can add the runtime options manually in the Verdi
command line as follows:
Example:%> verdi -dbdir simv.daidir -i cprestore -simDelim
+UVM_TEST_NAME=test_2m_4s // runtime options are used in the simulation
3. If no FSDB is dumped, you can add the runtime options after invoking Verdi and
before performing Restart.

Specifying FSDB File Name for UVM Enabled Features
By default, UVM data is dumped into the default FSDB file. You can use the
+uvm_fsdbfile=<filename.fsdb> runtime option to specify the FSDB

file for the UVM debug features enabled by the +UVM_TR_RECORD and
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE runtime options.

The following options can be specified with the +UVM_TR_RECORD and
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE:
UVM_AWARE, HIER, TLM, TLM2, IMP, RAL, FAC, COMPWAVE, RALWAVE, or MSG.

If filename.fsdb is not specified, then the file name is set to uvm.fsdb

Native UVM Dumping Support

automatically. If only filename is specified without .fsdb, then .fsdb is appended to the
file name automatically.
When the +uvm_fsdbfile=<filename.fsdb> option is specified, the +UVM_VERDI_TRACE
related dumping option dumps UVM components into the specified FSDB file, similarly, the
+UVM_TR_RECORD related transactions are recorded into the specified FSDB file.
If the +fsdbfile+<high.fsdb> and +uvm_fsdbfile=<uvm.fsdb> options are
used together, the resolution is +fsdbfile > +uvm_fsdbfile. That is, the
resolved FSDB file name is high.fsdb.
If the +uvm_fsdbfile=<uvm.fsdb> option is specified and $fsdbDumpvars
is called without specifying fsdb_name, uvm.fsdb only includes uvm items
as described in this section. The $fsdbDumpvars system task still generates
novas.fsdb as the default FSDB file for the specified scope in the function call.

Native UVM Dumping Support
VCS dumps the transactions and messages natively, thereby allowing seamless
integration without requiring modifications to customer libraries. It helps avoid unexpected
compile-time errors, ensures backward compatibility, and facilitates debugging using the
Fast Signal Database (FSDB).
To enable the native UVM dumping support feature, use the following compile-time and
runtime options. You can also use the compile-time options in the command file and
compile the design using the -f, -F, or -file option.
Compile-Time Options (vlogan and vcs)
-native_uvm_dumping uvm-1.1|uvm-1.2|uvm-ieee|uvm-ieee2020: Enables native

transaction dumping for specified UVM versions.
Runtime Option (simv)

-native_uvm_dumping: Enables +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=HIER+TLM

automatically.

Generating Coverage Reports in HTML Format

Generating Coverage Reports in HTML Format
Verdi HW/SW debug supports generating coverage reports in HTML format using
the -lcov_capture FILE option (where FILE specifies the filename) of the
hwsw_debug_coverage tool. This option generates coverage information in a format
compatible with the LTP GCOV extension (LCOV) .info file. The default name is based
on the name of the gmon.out file. This information is input to the genhtml tool to generate
an HTML report. LCOV is an open-sourced GNU toolset, and genhtml is one of its tools.
LCOV can consolidate multiple .info files and generate the merged HTML report.
Figure 298

Verdi HW/SW Debug: Generating Coverage Reports in HTML Format

In the above figure, the blue part is an open-source solution. The purple part is the
HW/SW Debug flow to generate coverage report. The yellow part is enabled using the
-lcov_capture FILE option to generate the .info files.
The following are the key points to note:
* If you specify the file name, the result is saved in the given file name.
* If the file name is specified as .gz file, the saved file is compressed in gzip format.
* If the file name is not given, the default name is based on the name of the gmon.out
file or the hwsw.info.gz file.
The following is the limitation of this feature:
* Branch coverage is not supported.

Interactive Simulation Debug
The following section describe the Interactive Simulation Debug LCA features supported
by Verdi as part of this release:
* New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug
* Controlling the Display of Console Command Output Messages
* Adding a Variable Name to the Watch Window Manually
* Selectively Adding Class or Members From the Source View to the Watch View

New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug
You can use the VERDI_NEW_UNIFIED_TCL environment variable as follows to enable the
new unified Tcl mode LCA feature in Verdi interactive debug:
setenv VERDI_NEW_UNIFIED_TCL 1

The new unified Tcl mode is applied in the following usages:
Launch Verdi with interactive debug mode together:
* simv -verdi
* verdi -I
* verdi -ssr [interactive_session_file]
* In simv UCLI mode, launch start_verdi
If interactive debug with new unified Tcl mode is exited to post-simulation mode, Verdi
switches to original unified Tcl flow.

New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug

The following figure shows the process flow of Tcl commands:
Figure 299

Process Flow of Tcl Commands

The following points describe the process flow:
* Verdi interactive debug is launched using the simv -verdi or verdi -simBin simv
-i commands.
* UCLI Tcl interpreter is used as default interpreter. Initially, all Tcl commands and
procedures are sent to UCLI Tcl interpreter for processing.
* UCLI Tcl interpreter sends all Verdi commands to Verdi for execution.
* After enabling new unified Tcl mode, Verdi updates views once after script execution
is completed. Verdi does not update the views after executing each command in the
scripts.

New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug

Pausing Script Execution During Simulation
In the new unified Tcl mode, Verdi allows you to pause script execution during simulation.
Verdi displays the following Stop dialog box when you click the Stop button during script
execution:
Figure 300

Stop Dialog Box

* Abort: Aborts script execution.
* Pause: Pauses script execution. If the script is paused, you can use the resume
command on console to continue script execution, or you can use the abort command
to abort script execution. Verdi displays the Busy dialog if the script is not paused.
When the Busy dialog is displayed, you can click the Abort button to cancel the pause
request.
* Cancel: Closes the Stop dialog.

Following are the limitations of this feature:
* The native Tcl commands set, rename, and alias in the NOVAS_AUTO_SOURCE script
file are expected to be used in Verdi, but not in UCLI, so you should not use these
variables or settings in the NOVAS_AUTO_SOURCE script to UCLI.
In interactive mode, the native Tcl commands set, rename, and alias are expected
used in UCLI, not for Verdi. Therefore, these variables/settings in UCLI do not sync to
Verdi.
* After script execution is completed, Verdi views are updated by simulation status even
if the script is not related.
* If you request to pause the script or add signal to waveform, simulation first completes
the execution of the current command and then performs pause.
* Dynamic object is not support for adding to waveform while simulation is running for the
executing script.

Controlling the Display of Console Command Output Messages

Controlling the Display of Console Command Output Messages
Verdi allows you to control the display of script commands and their output in the Console
pane.You must use the following environment variable to enable this feature:
setenv VERDI_TBV_ECHO_DISPLAY 1

You can use the following simulation command in the Console pane to control the display
of script commands and their output messages:
do [-echo [on|off]] <filename>

* filename - Tcl file. This file contains the script commands to be evaluated.
* -echo on - Displays the output (both command and its result) of all the evaluated
commands on the Console. By default, echo is on.
* -echo off - Displays only the result of the evaluated commands that requires
reporting.
Examples
Example-1: Behavior of do -echo on
Verdi> do -echo on test.tcl
Verdi> puts siga
siga
Verdi> next
sec.vhd, 135 : wait for 6 ns;
Verdi>step
sec.vhd, 162 : if (clk = '0') then
Verdi>stop -relative 1

Example-2: Behavior of do -echo off
Verdi> do -echo off test.tcl
siga
sec.vhd, 135 : wait for 6 ns;
sec.vhd, 162 : if (clk = '0') then

Controlling the Display of Console Command Output Messages

You can also control the display of the console command output messages when
executing the scripts using the View -> Enable Script Echoing option in the Console
menu bar, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 301

Enabling Script Echoing From Console Pane

By default, theEnable Script Echoing option is enabled. This option is valid for both
source and do commands, and the behavior is same as adding -echo on for the do
command.

Displaying the Result of Multiple Commands Inline on the
Console
When multiple commands are present on the same line in the script file, Verdi displays
the result of all the commands if you use the VERDI_TBV_ECHO_DISPLAY 1 environment
variable. By default, Verdi displays only the result of the last command.
set a [get b]

In this case, Verdi displays the result of all the commands present on the same line, for
example as follows:
Verdi> set a [get m_pkt.is_dir]
'b1 // value of a
Verdi> get m_pkt.is_dir; stop -relative 1

This feature applies only to functional coverage (covergroups and assertions)
and not to code coverage.

Related Notes
The difference between two VDBs is implemented as explained here:
* For Group Metric
If a group or group instance is available in the plan, then the difference is applied
to the group and all its children coverpoints, crosses, and bins. Note that group
instances are not children of Variant or Definition.
If a coverpoint or cross bin is available in the plan, then the difference is applied to
the coverpoint and cross bin and all their children bins.
If a crossbin is available in the plan, the difference is applied to the bin.
* For Assertion metric
The difference is applied to show the elements which are mapped to the plan.
* This feature is not compatible with HVP modifiers.

Strict Exclusions Mode
In strict exclusions mode, excluding a covered object is not allowed. If you load an exclude
file in strict exclusions mode, only the uncovered objects in the exclude file are excluded.
Objects that are covered are not excluded even if they are listed in the exclude file.
When a region such as a module, module instance, or covergroup was excluded in
previous releases and had only uncovered objects in it, the region was excluded and an
exclusion for it could be saved to an exclude file. If a region contained both covered and
uncovered child objects, exclusions for uncovered child objects were not created and
they could not be saved. Starting with this release, when a region is excluded in strict
exclusions mode and it contains both covered and uncovered objects then its uncovered
child objects are excluded properly and those exclusions can be saved to an exclude file.
Note that if annotations are set on the region's exclusion, then those annotations are
automatically propagated to these uncovered child objects when the parent object is
excluded in strict mode.
This feature is now supported for the following exclusions:
* Module/Instance-level exclusions
* Covergroup definitions/instance-level exclusions

Two-Dimensional Visualization of Covergroup Crosses
Verdi enables you to select any two coverpoints from an n-dimensional cross and project
the cross coverage data into a two-dimensional projection table with those two coverpoints
as the X and Y axis.
This feature helps in identifying coverage holes in the cross, such as when no bins are
covered, when a given coverpoint has a specific value.
For each cross, Verdi provides a list of projection tables and arranges the tables using the
following ranking criteria:
* Rows or columns that are completely uncovered
* Cells that are uncovered in table cells
* Low-coverage cells in table cells
Note that a low-coverage cell is a cell whose score is less than a tenth of the overall score
of a cross.
Also, projections with the same coverage for every cell are considered as least interesting
projections.

Two-Dimensional Visualization of Covergroup Crosses

To generate two-dimensional projection tables for an n-dimensional cross, click the Cross
2D Proj button in the CovDetail pane in the Verdi GUI.
Consider a cross of the coverpoints: X, Y, and Z in the following figure:

In the table, the red color represents Not Covered and the green color represents
Covered. This table shows the details of entire cross coverage.
It becomes difficult to find coverage holes from the table.
To generate two-dimensional projection tables for a cross of X, Y, and Z, click the Cross
2D Proj button in the CovDetail pane in the Verdi GUI.
When you click the Cross 2D Proj button, Verdi projects the cross coverage data into twodimensional tables as X x Y, X x Z, and Y x Z using the ranking criteria mentioned above.

Enhancement to Specification Linking

The following figure shows the two dimensional tables: X x Y, X x Z, and Y x Z with their
ranking:

The projection Y x Z contains one empty column with three zero cells. This projection is
given the first ranking (1/3). The projection X x Z contains one empty column with two zero
cells.
This projection is given the second ranking (2/3). The projection X x Y contains only two
zero cells and is ranked as third (3/3).
From Projections Y x Z and X x Z, you can interpret that all the cross products that contain
the bin circle of Coverpoint Z are not covered at all.
This feature has the following limitation:
* An n-dimensional cross that contains user-defined bins, ignore bins, or illegal bins
cannot be projected into two-dimensional tables.

In previous releases, Verdi provided a unique feature ID for each plan and feature. This
feature ID is globally unique and supports concurrent edits in the same .hvp file. However,
its length makes it cumbersome for people to read and use in other documents.
Starting with this release, Verdi provides a new built-in string attribute, HVP_FEAT_ID,
which is short, user-friendly, and easy-to-manage ID. Note that this new HVP_FEAT_ID
is not globally unique and is only unique within the HVP file. Moreover, it enables only a
single user to edit any .hvp file at a time to avoid conflicts.

Generating HVP_FEAT_ID for a Top-Level Plan
To generate HVP_FEAT_ID from the Verdi GUI, perform the following steps:
1. Click Tools ->Preferences to display the Application Preferences dialog box.
2. In the Application Preferences dialog box, select Plan View>Enable HVP_FEAT_ID

Once the Enable HVP_FEAT_ID option is selected, Verdi generates unique and short
IDs when a feature or subplan is created. For example, the following figure shows
HVP_FEAT_ID for the top plan and its feature, f1:

If you load an exiting plan without enabling HVP_FEAT_ID, the plan does not
display HVP_FEAT_ID for features and subplans in the plan. In this scenario, you
need to reload the plan. Therefore, it is recommended to enable HVP_FEAT_ID
before loading any existing plan to display HVP_FEAT_ID.

As the IDs are generated by Verdi, you cannot change its value using the Verdi GUI. When
a new feature is added, Verdi increments the value of HVP_FEAT_ID of the existing feature
and assigns it to the new feature. For example, when f2 is added, Verdi increments the
value of f1 and assigns this value to f2 as shown in the following figure:

Verdi assigns feature ID in the order in which the feature is created in the Verdi GUI. In the
HVP file, you can assign the IDs as per your requirement. For example, you may specify
IDs to the features in the HVP file for the top plan as follows:
plan top;
HVP_FEAT_ID = "0";
feature f1;
HVP_FEAT_ID = "1";
feature f2;
HVP_FEAT_ID = "2";
feature f3;
HVP_FEAT_ID = "6";
endplan

Applying Operations on a Top-Level Plan and Subplan
If you copy and paste a feature in a top-level plan or a subplan, HVP_FEAT_ID of the
feature gets changed. For example, if you copy the f1 feature and paste it as a subfeature under another feature f3, HVP_FEAT_ID of f1 under f3 gets changed from 1 to 11,
as shown in the following figure:

On the other hand, if you cut-and-paste or drag-and-drop a feature in a top-level plan
or a subplan, HVP_FEAT_ID of the feature does not get changed. Consider the following
figure that shows that if you move the f11 sub-feature and its subplan sub1 from f1 to f2,
HVP_FEAT_ID of f11 and sub1 does not change:

If you delete a feature in a top-level plan or a subplan, its HVP_FEAT_ID cannot be reused.
For example, if you delete the f1 feature whose HVP_FEAT_ID is 11 and then create
another feature Feature_1, Verdi assigns HVP_FEAT_ID of Feature_1 as 12 as shown in

Creating a Custom Compound ID Attribute
As HVP_FEAT_ID conveys information only about feature ID, you can create a custom
compound ID attribute that may convey additional information about a feature, such as
its project number and block number along with HVP_FEAT_ID. This custom attribute, say

FULL_ID, can be created using the HVP file and the Verdi GUI. In the HVP file, use the
following syntax to construct FULL_ID:
attribute string PRJ_ID = "P1";
attribute string BLK_ID = "B1";
attribute string FULL_ID =
"${PRJ_ID}_${BLK_ID}_${HVP_FEAT_ID}";

In the Verdi GUI, perform the following steps to create the FULL_ID attribute:
1. In the HvpDetail pane, click the Create an attribute
Attribute dialog box.

icon to display the New

2. In the New Attribute dialog box, specify identifier, type, and default value of FULL_ID

3. Click OK.

Verdi enables you to save the current configuration of the panes in the GUI using
bookmarks. Bookmarks provide quick access to these saved views and enable you to
easily toggle between them.
Bookmarks are useful when you need to analyze multiple sections of a design or views of
different coverage results. Consider a scenario in which you perform several operations to
select a particular scope, configure Verdi panes, apply a Plan filter, and so on.
The bookmark feature allows you to save such setups and return to them in the future by
selecting the saved bookmark.
Bookmarks enable you to save pane configurations, pane dock and undock status, scroll
bar locations, expand/collapse status, column configurations, sorting, filtering, and so on.
However, it does not save information such as which database, user data, HVP files,
exclusions/elfiles, specifications, and modifiers files are loaded, so that you can use the
same bookmark for different data sets.
This section discusses the following topics:
* Creating Bookmarks
* Editing Bookmarks
* Saving and Loading Bookmarks

Saving and Loading Bookmarks
You can save bookmarks using File-->Save Bookmarks(see the figure below). A saved
bookmark file has .bk as its default suffix. Bookmarks are independent of the specific
coverage database or design that is loaded when they are created.
Thus, you can create a bookmark while viewing one design and reload that bookmark to
return to the same view/configuration but with different data.
To load a bookmark, use File --> Load Bookmarks(see the figure below).

covergroup, view the bins of a coverpoint z, and scroll both Summary and covDetail
panes.

Then, you notice that certain bins, such that no[0e:0f], are not hit and you decide to
improve the test. Now, you can create a bookmark for this view and save it for future use
(see the figure below).

After improving the test, you collect coverage in simv_v2.vdb, which has the same shape
as that of simv_v1.vdb.
Now, loading the saved bookmark instantly takes you to the bins that were previously not
hit and should be hit with the improved test. For example, the no[0e:0f] bin is now hit
with the improved test (see the figure below):

To load a bookmark file on the Verdi command line, use the -bookmark
<bookmark_file.bk> option as follows:
verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb -bookmark <bookmark_file.bk> &

Bookmarks may not restore the following information correctly:
* Toggle signal vector compressed and expanded bits are not preserved.
* Covergroup expanded bins and the bins shown by "Show More" in crossbin tables are
not preserved.

In Verdi Planner, various functional coverage objects such as covergroups, covergroup
instances, coverpoints, crosses, and bins may be used as sources for data in a plan
feature.
These are connected to plan features by name. As these functional coverage objects were
explicitly created to collect coverage, it is helpful to know if any object was created but left
out of the plan.
Starting with this release, Verdi Coverage provides a new feature that enables you to
find functional coverage objects that are not referenced by any feature in the plan "unmapped" objects - and report them in an .hvp file.

To find unmapped objects in a plan, invoke the Report Unmapped Objects form using the
Plan -> Report Unmapped Objects command.

The following figure shows the Report Unmapped Objects form:
Figure 79

The Report Unmapped Objects Form

In the Report Unmapped Objects form, you can specify the plan to report from the list of
plans.
Also, you can specify the type of unmapped objects that you need to map. The types of
objects are as follows:
* Definition/Variant, Instance
* Point/Cross
* Bins
To generate the report for covergroup instances, for example, select the Cover Group
Instance check box in the Report Unmapped Objects form.
In the form, you can select the following different strategies that determine the number of
objects to be reported:
* High
This strategy considers a definition/variant and an instance as separate entities. If a
definition/variant is mapped but its one or more instances are not mapped, then the
instances are considered as unmapped.
For example, consider cg_var as a variant having coverpoints, cp1 and cp2, cross
cr1, and instance cg_inst. If cg_var is mapped, cg_inst is not mapped, and High
is selected as a strategy to determine the number of reported objects, cg_inst is
reported as unmapped.

* Medium
This strategy reports instances as mapped as long as their corresponding variant is
mapped. For example, consider cg_var as a variant having coverpoints cp1 and cp2,
cross cr1, and instance cg_inst.
If cg_var is mapped, cg_inst is not mapped, and Medium is selected as a strategy to
determine the number of reported objects, cg_inst is reported as mapped.
* Low
This strategy reports a coverpoint/cross as mapped if bins are mapped. For example,
consider that coverpoint cp1 has coverbins: bin1, bin2, and bin3.
If bin1 is mapped and Low is selected as a strategy to determine the number of
reported objects, cp1 is reported as mapped.
The object types, such as definition/variant, instance, coverpoint, cross, and bins, follow
certain rules to report unmapped objects. These rules are as follows:
* Definition/Variant, Instance
1. If a variant is mapped, all its instances are considered as mapped. The rule is
applied only when Number of Objects in the Report Unmapped Objects form is set
as Medium or Low and not as High.
2. If all instances of a variant are mapped, the variant is reported as mapped. The rule
is applied only when Number of Objects in the Report Unmapped Objects form is
set as Medium or Low and not as High.
* Point/Cross
1. If all coverpoints/crosses of a variant are mapped, the variant is reported as
mapped.
2. If all coverpoints/crosses of an instance are mapped, the instance is reported as
mapped.
3. If a coverpoint/cross in all instances of a variant is mapped, the coverpoint/cross in
the variant is reported as mapped.
The rule is applied only when Number of Objects in the Report Unmapped Objects
form is set as Medium or Low and not as High.
4. If a coverpoint/cross in a variant is mapped, the corresponding coverpoint/cross in
all its instances is reported as mapped.
The rule is applied only when Number of Objects in the Report Unmapped Objects
form is set as Medium or Low and not as High.
* Bins

1. If all bins of a coverpoint/cross are mapped, the coverpoint/cross is reported as
mapped.
2. If a bin of a coverpoint/cross is mapped, the coverpoint/cross is reported as
mapped.
The rule is applied only when Number of Objects in the Report Unmapped Objects
form is set as Low.
The mapped status is aggregated in the upward direction. For example, if a
node is mapped, all its ancestors are considered as mapped.
In the Report Unmapped Objects form, if Types of Objects is set as Bin and Cover
Group Instance is selected, Verdi Coverage reports covergroups as follows:

Specification Coverage Merge

Specification Coverage Merge
Verdi Coverage provides the specification coverage for each PDF in a plan. Previously, if
the same PDF was linked to different plans, you needed to select each plan separately.
You could view the specification coverage for the PDF in each plan. There was no way to
see the total coverage for a PDF from all linked plans.
The specification coverage feature now provides an overall summary of the specification
coverage for the PDF with the specification coverage from different plans.

To merge the specification coverage for a PDF from different plans, the toggle button
added in the Spec Files view of the HvpDetail pane.

This section explains how VC Formal coverage is integrated with the Verdi coverage
reporting flow.
The two primary links between Verdi and VC Formal are displaying VCS Formal results in
Verdi, and linking VC Formal results into your verification plan using Verdi Planner.

The section describes how Verdi coverage is used to display and link to VC Formal
results. This section consists of the following subsections:
* Collecting VC Formal Results in the Coverage Database
* Measuring VC Formal Assert Status in HVP

Collecting VC Formal Results in the Coverage Database
To display VC Formal results in the coverage report, you must first have set the
VC_STATIC_HOME environment variable. For example:
setenv VC_STATIC_HOME /tools/synopsys/vcst

Here, VC_STATIC_HOME is an environment variable that is set to point to the installation
directory for VC Formal.
To start the VC Formal tool, use the following command:
vcf -f test.tcl -verdi

vcf is a command to start the VC Formal tool with an interactive shell. The vcf shell is a
new shell that calls vc_static_shell internally.

The vcf shell supports all the options that vc_static_shell supports. The vcf shell
automatically runs in the 64-bit mode, unless you explicitly specify the -mode32 option.
For details on vc_static_shell, see the VC Formal Verification User Guide. -f indicates
your VC Formal execution script
You provide your own Tcl script to run VC Formal. To enable collection and display of
coverage data in Verdi, include the following two commands in the script:
1. The command to run VC Formal must include the -cov all flag. If you wish assertions
to be targeted (not just cover properties), you should also include -cm assert as a flag
to VCS:
read_file -cov all -format verilog -sva -top $top -vcs "-cm assert
-sverilog $testDir/test.v -sva"

2. You must include a command to save the results to the coverage database, for
example, my_covdb:
save_covdb -name my_covdb -cov assert+cover

Verdi GUI for VC Formal
To display the Verdi GUI for VC Formal (see the figure below), use the vcf command with
the -verdi option.

The properties are categorized according to usage fields in VC Formal as:
* assert: The property specifies an assertion to be solved. Its values are proven,
inconclusive, vacuous, and falsified.
* assume: The property specifies as a constraint.
* cover: The property specifies as a cover property. Its values are covered, inconclusive,
and uncoverable.
* unused: The property is disabled.
VC Formal Coverage in Verdi
To load the coverage database generated with VC Formal in Verdi, use the following
command:
verdi -cov -covdir my_covdb.vdb

-cov: Starts Verdi in the coverage mode
-covdir: Opens the coverage database
my_covdb.vdb: The name of the coverage database that gets opened. This is specified in
the test.tcl script with the save_covdb command.

The command generates the following pane:
Figure 83

The Verdi Coverage Assert Pane

The VC Formal information is displayed in the Assert tab in the columns: FVtype,
FVstatus, and FVdepth.
This information should be same as the VC Formal results. The green color represents
Proven or Covered, the red color represents Falsified, Uncoverable, or Vacuous, and the
yellow color represents Inconclusive.
FVtype indicates the usage field. The value in this column can be either Assert, Cover, or

Assume.

FVstatus indicates the run status of VC Formal. Its possible values depend on FVtype:

* If FVtype is Assert, the value of FVstatus can be Proven, Inconclusive, Falsified, or
Vacuous.
* If FVtype is Cover, the value of FVstatus can be Covered, Inconclusive, or
Uncoverable.
The FVdepth column is interpreted as follows:
* If FVstatus is Proven, Vacuous, or Uncoverable and its value is -1, it represents
infinite depth.
* For other FVstatus, N>=0 represents the depth of the trace.

Measuring VC Formal Assert Status in HVP
VC Formal results can be annotated automatically onto features in your verification plan.
Using these results, you can measure your expectations with FVstatus.
The figure below shows VC Formal results in a verification plan with attributes and metrics.
Figure 84

VC Formal Results in HVP

To measure the VC Formal Assert status in HVP, perform the following steps:
1. Set the expected FV Assert status with FV attribute values using
fvassert_expected_status.
feature f_default;
//These values are same as default value, no need
//assignments again here.
//
fvassert_expected_status = proven;
//
fvassert_expected_mindepth = -1;
//
fvcover_expected_status = covered;
//
fvcover_expected_maxdepth = 0;
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: fsm.*";
feature f_expected_assigned;
fvassert_expected_status = inconclusive;
fvassert_expected_mindepth = 50;
fvcover_expected_maxdepth = 50;
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: fsm.a2", "property:
fsm.a_loop_break", "property: fsm.c2";

2. Add measures with property type sources and reference the FV Assert metric.
The new FV Assert built-in metric is added to keep the score of the FV Assert status
against users' expectation.
If FVstatus is same as fvassert_expected_status, the score becomes 1/1,
otherwise, the score becomes 0/1.
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: top.a1*";

3. Calculate FVAssert metric scores
After finding the matching region in the coverage database, the covered/coverable
status is extracted from that database and added as a ratio for the FVAssert metric
score.
For the FVAssert metric, you can get FVstatus from FV annotations in the coverage
database and compare fvassert_expected_status, which is set in fvassert*
attributes.
If FVstatus is same as fvassert_expected_status, then the assertion/property is
considered to be covered.

text:
For example, the matching property top.a11: FVtype=assert and
FVstatus=Proven. If the expectation is fvassert_expected_sthe tatus
= Proven, the FVAssert metric score becomes 1/1. If the expectation is
fvassert_expected_status = inconclusive and fvassert_expected_depth =
60, the FVAssert metric score becomes 0/1.
For example, consider the following figure that shows six cases to measure the VC
Formal Assert status in your verification plan:

Case1: fsm.a2: FVtype is assert, FVstatus is falsified, FVdepth is 6 and it is
excluded. In the top.f_default.m1 feature, the property: fsm.* source matches
the excluded property, therefore, no score is added.
Case2: fsm.a_loop_break: FVtype is assert, FVstatus is inconclusive, and FVdepth
is 70. In the top.f_expected_assigned feature, fvassert_expected_status is
inconclusive and fvassert_expected_mindepth is 50 which are set by users. It is met
with users' expectations and the FVAssert metric score becomes 1/1.
Case3: fsm.a_trans: FVtype is assume. In the top.f_assume feature,
fvassume_status is reviewed which is set by users. The FVAssert metric score

becomes 1/1.

Case4: fsm.c_blk_cnt: FVtype is cover, FVstatus is covered, and FVdepth is 1. In
the top.f_default feature, with default attribute values, fvcover_expected_status
is covered and fvcover_expected_maxdepth is 0. Compare FVstatus to expected
attributes values and if the expectation does not meet, the FVAssert metric score
becomes 0/1.
Case5: fsm.c_trans, no FV annotation. In the top.f_default.m_no_fv_ann
measure, matching fsm.c_trans without FV annotation, the FVAssert metric
becomes 0/1 because the FVAssert metric is referred explicated in measure.
Case6: dummy source. In the top.f_default.m_dummy measure, for all metrics for no
matching region, the score becomes all 0.

Verdi Coverage now offers a tool/GUI that differentiates cover groups and assertions while
comparing two VDBs so both are equally important.
Consider two databases A.vdb and B.vdb with updates. The Group/Assertion
Differentiation Support now lets you see whether an assertion exists in A.vdb and not in
B.vdb. If it exists in both databases, whether it is passed in A.vdb and failed in B.vdb.
(passed means that the number of matches is > 0. All other cases are considered failed).
The purpose of the differentiation GUI is to highlight the objects that differ, giving the
option to get the full details of the differentiation on demand.
The following three types of differentiation are supported:
* Shape Differentiation
* Coverage Differentiation
* Hit Differentiation

To perform GUI differentiation between two databases, use the following steps:
1. Launch the differentiation tool from the Verdi Coverage GUI.

2. Select the two databases to differentiate (see the figure below).

Metric Options: Both Assertion and Coverage Groups are selected by default.
Group Compare Option: Shape, Score, and Bin are selected by default. If you do not
select the Coverage Group metric, then all Group Compare Options are disabled.
Shape: Performance shape comparison is done and only items with different shapes
are reported.
Score: Comparison done between items with the same shape and only items with
different score statuses are reported.
Hit Count: Comparison done between items with the same shape and only items with
different hit counts are reported.
Compare Level - Group, Point/Cross, Bin: The default option is Bin. For a large
design, the complete compare may take very long time, so the Level option is provided

Verdi Coverage provides plan diff tool that lets you easily find out differences (added,
deleted and changed features/measures/source regions/subplan/attributedef/metricdef/

To find the difference between two plans, perform the following steps:
1. Choose two plans and configure them with different options.
2. Run the Plan Diff function.
It presents the Statistic View.
3. Open the Diff Detail View to review the details.
The subsequent sections describe these steps in detail
Choosing the HVP Plans
To view the difference, first select the two HVP plans that needs to be differentiated.
Choose the HVP files you want to differentiate on the Choose HVP Files dialog box. You
can do so by either typing in the HVP file paths or browsing the existing files.

If some HVP files are already opened, the combo-box for Plan1 and Plan2 lists them for
selection.
Figure 107

Choosing HVP Files

Choosing the Plan Diff Configuration
You can compare the two plans by defining how deep the tool should look into the plan
structure. The settings are as follows:
* Feature/Sub-plan: Only the name, attribute and metric are considered. Measures are
NOT considered.
* Measure: Only name and metric selection are considered. The source in it is NOT
considered.
* Source: The source is considered.
Additionally, you can find differences for sub-plan definitions, attribute definitions, metric
definitions and whether it is a spec or not.
You can use the option Into Sub-plan to differentiate inside sub-plans
You can invoke the Diff Configuration dialog box from the main menu Plan->Diff

Figure 116

Deleting a Server

Once you click OK to confirm, the related server pane is closed automatically, if currently

Deleting a server breaks the existing association between the server and the plans linked
to it.

Managing Issues in Verdi HVP
Once you have configured and connected to the Redmine servers, you can access the
issue data using the Issue Management pane.
The Issue Management pane is a web page based flexible pane that hosts the third web
page. It provides following extending features besides the capability of hosting the third
party tool:
* List Issues - Shows issues matching a given criterion in the pane.
* Filter Issues - Filters issues based on the filters provided by the third part tool.
* Show Issue Details - Shows the issue details in the Issue Details page.
* Link Issues - Link selected/checked issues to the currently selected feature in the HVP
plan.
* Create an issue and link it to a feature.
This functionality is described in detail in the following sections:
* Finding, Creating, and Filtering Issues
* Displaying Linked Features of an Issue
* Creating Bug Metric and Adding Source Regions From Issues
* Linking a Feature to an Issue
* Unlinking a Feature from an Issue
* Linking the Plan to Projects in Server
* Linking to a Third-Party Issue Server
* Syncing With Issue Server
* Displaying Bug Details
* Creating a New Issue From the Selected Feature

leave the Issue Details page, the small icon disappears as well.

Unlinking a Feature from an Issue
You can use the following three ways to unlink a feature from an issue.

1. In the Issue Management pane, open the Issue Details page and click the button
Unlink with Feature to remove the linkage between the issue and the features.
2. In the HVP plan, use the CSM Unlink Issue to remove the linkage. After this action,
refresh the page in the Issue Management pane to get the latest data.
3. Open the issue within the third party tool via Verdi and remove the feature_id and
feature name in the Issue Edit page.

Linking the Plan to Projects in Server
A plan must be linked to some projects in the servers before you can add issues to it. To
do that, open the Link to Issue Server dialog box using the CSM Link to issue servers>Select Servers/Projects.
The dialog box lists all the available servers currently configured in the Verdi session. If
the plan is already managed by the server, the project is selected. De-selecting the server/
project removes the linkage between the plan and the server. You can select multiple
projects and servers.
Click the Sync with server(s) button to sync issues from the issue servers immediately
after you click Finish.

Figure 124

Selecting Servers/Projects to Link

Linking to a Third-Party Issue Server
The linkage between the plan and the associated issue server is maintained by the server
Id in the <plan>.hvp.bug file.
This file contains the possible status of issue in third-party tools, the linked issues from the
third-party tool and their feature Id.
After the plan is linked to a server, the server Id, and the server URL are saved to the
.hvp.bug file.
The server Id is also a part of issue_id whose format is <server_id>:<third party

issue id>.

The server URL in the .bug file is the only key that lets the HVP planner find the correct
server to link in Verdi.

The server Id is also a part of issue_id whose format is <server_id>:<third party

The server URL in the .bug file is the only key that lets the HVP planner find the correct

* If you link a plan to an issue server, the server Id and server URL is saved to the .bug
file.
* If open a plan created by another user and if server_URL in plan is not found in the
existing Verdi server list, Verdi prompts you to configure a new server with the server Id
and server URL in the plan.
The new created server configuration is saved in <user.home>/.vedi/
server.config and is listed in the Server pane.
* If server_URL is found in the existing server list, Verdi uses the existing server to
connect to the third party tool. Verdi internally creates a mapping from the server Id of
the existing server to the server Id defined in the .bug file.

However, if you want to replace server_id in the bug file with the one of the existing
server, you can save it as another plan using the Save as option.
In the Save as dialog box, select the Override Server Id option to replace the server Ids
in the .bug file.

It is suggested that you define a server with the same Server Id for a project or
a team.
Syncing With Issue Server
The HVP planner provides a way to automatically link a feature in plan with issues,
provided that these issues have a field named verdi_plan_feature_id and its value
matched feature_id.
If an issue satisfies this above condition, a bug source region is added to the measure
source list of the feature.
You can use the CSM item Sync Issues to refresh these bug source regions once you
add or delete some related issues in the third party issue management tool.
Select the feature(s) for which you want to create bug source regions. If no feature is
selected in the plan, all features in the plan are affected.

Each bug status belongs to one of the two categories Open or Closed. If the category is
not given it is set to Open by default.
Displaying Bug Details
The HVP pane provides the CSM Show Bug Details that shows the issues related to the
current feature or bug measure source in the plan correspondingly.

Creating a New Issue From the Selected Feature
Once a plan is connected to the issue servers, you can select a feature in the HVP plan
and use CSM Create an Issue to open the New Issue page in the Issue Management
tool.
If there is more than one server connected to the plan, a sub level menu is available to list
all servers.

After the New Issue page is loaded, you can drag the feature to the desired text field. The
full path of the feature and the feature Id in the plan is appended to the text fields.

Verdi Verification Planner: Derived Test Metrics
Verification Planner for Verdi supports the following additional built-in derived test metrics
to track verification progress:
* Percent Metric for Test Metric
* Test.completion Metric
Using these derived metrics, you can gather the percentage of tests with different status
and test completion percentage in a verification plan.

Percent Metric for Test Metric
In previous releases, the built-in test metric of enum type reports integer count for submetrics test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.unknown, and test.assert. For example,
test = 6;
test.pass = 3;
test.fail = 3;

In previous releases, the test metric reports the basic number of tests with status pass,
fail, warn, unknown, and assert in the HVP annotated report. It does not display the
percentage of these scores.

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
Verification Planner for Verdi reports percentage score for each enum value of the test
metric. This enables you to get the percentage of tests with status pass, fail, warning,
unknown, or assert. The following is the list of the derived percent sub-metrics:
* test.percent.pass
* test.percent.fail
* test.percent.warn
* test.percent.unknown
* test.percent.assert
The score of a percent metric is the percentage of each enum's value of the test metric
against the total number of tests in that feature.
For example, if a is the integer count of the built-in test metric enum value and b is the
integer count of the total number of tests, then the percentage metric is computed as
(a / b)*100

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
For example, if
test.pass = 8
test.fail = 2
test = 10

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
then the value of test.percent.pass = 8/10 and is reported as 80%.
The following is the example for the usage of percent metrics:
feature f1;
test.percent.pass = test.percent.pass > 60%;
measure test, test.percent.pass m1;
source = "testname*";

Consider the following example,
feature parent:
test:6[pass:3 fail:3 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass:50.00%
feature block1
test:5[pass:3 fail:2 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass:60.00%
feature block2
test:1[pass:0 fail:1 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass: 0.00%

title: 1 | | -1 | | SGE | qsub -P bnormal -V -l os_version=CS7.0
text:
In this example, the test.percent.pass score in feature parent is calculated from the test
score of:
feature parent test:6[pass:3 fail:3 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0] 50%

which is equal to 3/6. The total test score of feature parent is the sum of the test scores of
feature block1 and feature block2.
The following figure shows the derived sub-metrics displayed by Verdi coverage:
Figure 128

Viewing Percent Metric in Verdi Coverage

Test.completion Metric
The test.completion metric allows you to measure the progress of tests being written
against the number of tests expected to be written.
The score of the test.completion metric is the ratio of total integer count of all sub-metrics
of the test metric (test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.assert, test.unknown) and the
expected number of tests in a plan/feature. The expected number of tests should be set
using the test.expected attribute.
Where,test.completion=total_test_count/test.expected and
total_test_count=test.pass+test.fail+test.warn+test.as sert+test.unknown
Test.expected Attribute
You can use the test.expected built-in attribute assignment, as shown below, to set the
expected number of tests in feature/plan scope.
test.expected = <number>;
The expected number is like an annotation value kept in feature/plan node. The default
value of test.expected is 0.

Figure 129

Viewing test.expected in Verdi Coverage

The test.completion metric can be calculated only after setting the
test.expectedattribute.
The following example illustrates the usage of the test.completion metric:
feature Goal_pass;
test.expected = 2;
test.percent.pass = (test.percent.pass >= 0.5);
measure test, test.percent.pass, test.completion Measure_1;
source = "test3";

Figure 130

Viewing test.completion Metric in Verdi Coverage

Verdi provides a capability that lets you synchronize the Coverage and Debug display.

Before you perform the synchronization, the communication between Coverage and

Specification Linking Coverage
Verdi Coverage provides a measurement of the percentage of a spec that has been linked
to the verification plan. For example a spec that has 50% spec coverage means that half
of the spec is linked and the other half is not.
A spec with 100% spec coverage is completely linked to the verification plan. The

Note that Verdi uses the following rules to consider what text would be part
of the selection: Verdi draws a rectangle box from the start point to the end
point. - The selection is char based not word based. - Chars out of the box
are excluded in the selection. - Chars complete in the box are included in the
selection. - Chars partly included in the box (their boundary has intersection
with the outline of box) are excluded from the selection.

The following are examples that describe how sections containing images are handled
during spec-linking.
Consider the following two cases for a linked section containing images:
* A section contains images and text as well.
* A section contains image(s) only
These two cases are handled different ways during review and updating the section to a
new document during spec-linking.
Case 1: Section contains both images and text
In this case spec-linking follows the following process:
* Review and update the text to the new section in the new document.
* Find the images in the updated section in the new document.
* Generate a new section based on the text section and images, the decision table below
lists all the possibilities and review results.
Table 10

Review Results for Text and Image Selection
Image Text Matching

Missing

New

Matching

matching

Conflict

Missing

missing

New

The review result for an image depends on the updated text section in the new document.
There can be three results for image comparison: Matching, Missing, New. The result
conflict is not applicable for images.
* Matching: The image in the old document is found in the new document and it is
present by the updated text section.
In this case, image is found means that the image in the old and new documents are
the same.

* Missing: The image is not found in the new document, or it is found but it is NOT in the
updated text section.
* New: The image is in the updated text section but not in the old document. In Verdi
New is treated as a Conflict.
The image and text works as an entire link in the review process, so whatever actions
(accept, reject) that you choose to apply, the action is applied to both the image and the
text.
You may not be able to treat the text or the image as separate review-able objects.
Case 2: A section contains only image(s)
Without considering in the text in the review process, the search scope of an image is not
limited to the updated text section in the new document. The whole document is within the
search scope.
For example, if an image at page 10 was selected and linked as a section in the old
document, Verdi spec-linking feature searches the image at page 10 then around page 10,
that is page 11, page 9, page12, page 8 and so on, until the image is found.
If the image is found, then it is marked as matching, otherwise it is marked as missing.
The review result types new and conflict are not applicable in this case.

Choosing Annotation Level and Metrics for Coverage Calculation
You can create features and add them to a plan directly from instances, modules, groups
and asserts directly from the design.
You can select an instance sub-tree, create features in a plan based on that sub-tree and
then map them.
For more information on this feature, see section Adding Features from the Design in the
Verdi Coverage Tutorial.
For the K-2015.09-SP2 release, there is no option to choose the level of annotation (the
created source type: tree/feature) on an instance and also the metrics that needs to be
calculated for coverage.
By default, the annotation level is set at the tree-level, which means that if you select a
leaf instance, the leaf instance as well as the instances under the tree of the selected leaf
instance are annotated.
Also, by default, coverage for all metrics (line, cond, FSM, toggle, branch and assert) is
calculated.

The following are the error scenarios for this feature and way Verdi handles these error
scenarios.
* Scenario: No value statement in result the definition:
result overall_status;
endresult

Error/Warning: Issues an error; result value for overall_status is not calculated. The
result is skipped.
* Scenario: Only default value statement in result definition.
result overall_status;
value.In_Progress = default;
endresult

Error/Warning: Issues a warning and the overall_status value is always assigned to
In_Progress.
* Scenario: No default value in result definition.
result overall_status;
value.Not_Started = ((SnpsAvg <= 0) && (test == 0) && (bug == 0));
value.Done = ((SnpsAvg >= 100%) && (test.failure == 0) && (bug.open
= 0));

Reporting of Subplans in Excel as Separate Sheets

Difference Between Masks and Filters
As discussed, Verdi Planner supports two ways to customize the features displayed:
masks and filters. Though they appear to operate in a similar way, there is a distinct
difference in the way that they behave. Filters not only remove features from the displayed
plan view, they also disable the effect that those removed features' scores have on the
remainder of the plan. For example suppose a feature A with a score of 50% has 2 child
features A1 (0%) and A2 (100%). If you filter out feature A1 then its 0% score no longer
affects the parent feature A and A's score becomes 100%.
Masks are different because they simply hide rows based on the masking criteria. The
hidden rows' scores continue to affect scores. In the same example if A1 is masked, its
parent feature A's score remains at 50%.
In addition to this, the key differences between quick filters and masks are as follows:
* Any changes applied to a quick filter also affects scores; masks do not affect scores.
* Operations on quick filters can be saved as a modifier file that can be reloaded again;
masks cannot be saved as a modifier file.
* For quick filters, the filter icon
is displayed only when you click on the Quick Filter
icon; the mask icon
is always displayed on the right of Result columns.
* Quick filters are for attribute columns; masks are for Result columns.
Quick filters and masks can exist at the same time. However, quick filters have higher
priority than masks.

Support Scientific Notations for Real Metric Values in the HVP
View
Verdi HVP view supports Scientific notation with 'e' notation and SI Prefixes for the
sim_min and sim_max values. That is, the expression `e' and unit are now supported for
the real metric values in the HVP view.
You can use the Format in SI Prefixes (International System of Units preference)
option in the Plan View page of the Applications Preferences dialog (Tools ->
Preferences -> Plan View) to switch between the Scientific notation with 'e' notation and
the SI Prefixes. By default, the values are represented in the Scientific notation (`e'). You
can select the Format in SI Prefixes check box to view the values as SI Prefixes. You can
either click the Apply or OK to view the changes.

Support Scientific Notations for Real Metric Values in the HVP View

Transformation Rules of User Data to HVP Annotation
The following are the transform rules of User Data while annotating to HVP:
* Scientific notation with 'e' notation use cases (when the Format in SI Prefixes
preference option is disabled):
For numbers with more than 5 decimal places.
Any number greater than or equal to 1,000,000 or less than or equal to -1,000,000.
All the other use cases are represented using normal notation with 5 decimal
places.
* SI Prefixes use cases (when the Format in SI Prefixes preference option is enabled)
The following values are represented in SI Prefixes:
Numbers greater than or equal to 1000 and less than or equal to -1000.
Numbers in between -0.01 and 0.01, except 0.
* Floating point precision:
Scientific notation with 'e' notation: 6 decimal places
SI Prefixes: 6 decimal places
Normal Notation: 5 decimal places
* Display format for Scientific notation with 'e' notation:
Trailing zero: "." should be followed by "0" when there is no mantissa (for example,
1.0e+09).
Leading zero: A minimum of 2 digits are required for notation presentation. That is,
leading zero is displayed if the exponent is less than 3 digits.
* Display format for SI Prefixes:
Trailing zero: No trailing zero is used in the SI Prefixes. For example, 1M.

Support for Changing Fonts
Verdi Coverage supports changing the font and the font size globally. You can edit the
application font and the monospaced font.
The application font applies to the menu bar, toolbar, dialog boxes, and all Coverage views
except those where the monospaced font is applied.
The monospaced font applies to the content in the source view.
To change the font and font size, perform the following steps:
1. Click Tools > Preferences to open the Application Preferences form.
2. In the Global category, select Appearance.

Verdi Coverage supports the Tcl command gui_set_pref_value for setting the

The following section describes the enhancement to the CRDB utility LCA feature
supported by Verdi as part of this release:
* Enhancement to the CRDB Utility

Enhancement to the CRDB Utility
In the previous releases, the RTL design had encrypted IP blocks because of which CRDB
could not be directly extracted from the FSDB file for the RTL design.
Starting with this release, the -RTL_FSDB option is added in the CRDB utility. This option
can be used to extract the CRDB from the FSDB file for the RTL design. The -RTL_FSDB
option is an alternative option to extract the RTL design.

The flow of CRDB is as follows:
1. Extract the gate level design
2. Extract the RTL design and
3. Perform the correlation.
The syntax for -RTL_FSDB option is:
crdb -RTL_FSDB RTL_FSDB_name

Here,
RTL_FSDB_name - Specifies the user-defined FSDB file name.
crdb -RTL_FSDB RTL_FSDB -GATE "-f gate.f" -impSVF "block1.svf block2.svf"
-expMap mapping.gz -allreg

Chapter 6: Correlation
Enhancement to the CRDB Utility

The syntax to extract gate level design and RTL design to perform the correlation is as
crdb -RTL_FSDB RTL_FSDB_name -GATE "<gate level import & BA options>"
-crdb <output CRDB name> <correlation options> [export mapping options]

If you extract RTL CRDB from FSDB more than once, then the previous
database extracted is overwritten with the latest extracted database. -append
option is not supported if you extract CRDB from FSDB. It issues an error
message and aborts the CRDB generation.

The -RTL_FSDB option in the CRDB utility has the following limitations:
* If the FSDB is written by a third party tool instead of FSDB dumper, some information
may be incorrect or missed due to wrong usage of FSDB writer by the third party tool.
The input FSDB requires a module name for each instance. If a module name is not
written into FSDB, then the extraction does not create a model for that instance.
* The following design information which can be extracted from the RTL design may not
be extracted from FSDB.
Register information is not available in FSDB.
Equivalent net or inverted equivalent net is not available in FSDB. That is, if some signals
are originally correlated through an equivalent net, it may not become correlated when
extracting it from FSDB.

FSDB Command Line, Environment Variable, and Dump
Command Options
The unified FSDB dumper supports three methods for specifying options. The methods
are:
1. Specify an option on the simulator command line. Refer to the FSDB Dumping
Command Line Options section for details on the command-line options.
2. Specify an option using an environment variable. Refer to Appendix A in the Verdi and
Siloti Command Reference Manual for details on the environment variables.
3. Specify an option in an FSDB dumping command. Refer to the FSDB Dumping
Command Option table for details on using options with the dump commands.
If the same option is set using more than one method, the resolution is: Method 1 >
Method 2 > Method 3.
For example, the FSDB dump file name can be set using one of the following methods:
1. Specify the file name on the simulator command line:
> simv +fsdbfile+high.fsdb

2. Specify the file name using an environment variable:
> setenv NOVAS_FSDB_FILE mid_prio.fsdb

3. Specify the file name in an FSDB dumping command:
$fsdbDumpvars("+fsdbfile+low_prio.fsdb");

This means that in this example, the resolved FSDB file name is high.fsdb.

Some options control related behavior. For example, NOVAS_FSDB_MDA enables
or disables MDA signal dumping, while NOVAS_FSDB_ALL enables or disables all
supported signal types. NOVAS_FSDB_ALL is a superset of NOVAS_FSDB_MDA.
When you set related options through different methods at the same time, the dumper
applies both settings. It does not use the usual priority order (command line, then
environment variable, then FSDB dumping command). Instead, it combines the effects:
1. Resolve each option's value using the standard priority: simulator command line, then
environment variable, then FSDB dumping command.
2. Apply the union of all resolved settings.
Example 1
1. Specify the environment variable to enable dumping MDA signals:
setenv NOVAS_FSDB_MDA 1

2. Specify the option in an FSDB dumping command to enable dumping all supported
signals:
$fsdbDumpvars("+all");

These options differ, so priority resolution does not apply. The dumper combines both
settings and enables dumping of all supported signals.
Example 2
1. Specify the option on the simulator command line to enable dumping packed MDA
signals:
simv +fsdb+packedmda

2. Specify the environment variable to enable dumping MDA signals:
setenv NOVAS_FSDB_MDA 1

Both +fsdb+mda and +fsdb+packedmda resolve to on. The dumper combines them and
enables dumping of all MDA signals.
Example 3
Specify the options on the simulator command line to filter all dumper messages, warning
messages, and error messages:
simv +fsdb+no_warning +fsdb+no_error +fsdb+no_all_msg

The dumper combines all three options and filters all dumper messages.
