Adding Comments of Excluded Items From Coverage View
You can add a justification comment to each excluded item in the Coverage view. The
comment records why you excluded the item. The Exclude Comment column shows the
comment for each excluded item.
To add or edit a comment, perform the following steps:
1. Mark the item for exclusion.
2. Double-click the Exclude Comment cell of the excluded item. The Exclusion
Comment dialog box opens.
3. Enter the reason for the exclusion. For example, enter Add exclusion comment
here.
4. Click OK to save the comment. To discard the comment, click Cancel.

Figure 290

Exclusion Comment Dialog Box

Note the following behavior:
* HW/SW Debug saves comments to the exclusion file with the exclusion entries. It also
loads the comments from the exclusion file. Authors and reviewers can see why you
excluded each element without maintaining separate documents.
* The cell shows a long comment on a single line. To view the full comment, hover the
mouse pointer over the cell. The full text appears in a tooltip.
* Only items with the exclusion status Excluded or To be excluded respond to a
double-click. Double-clicking the Exclude Comment cell of an Included or To be
included item has no effect.

Generating Coverage Reports in HTML Format

Generating Coverage Reports in HTML Format
Verdi HW/SW debug supports generating coverage reports in HTML format using
the -lcov_capture FILE option (where FILE specifies the filename) of the
hwsw_debug_coverage tool. This option generates coverage information in a format
compatible with the LTP GCOV extension (LCOV) .info file. The default name is based
on the name of the gmon.out file. This information is input to the genhtml tool to generate
an HTML report. LCOV is an open-sourced GNU toolset, and genhtml is one of its tools.
LCOV can consolidate multiple .info files and generate the merged HTML report.

Interactive Simulation Debug
The following section describe the Interactive Simulation Debug LCA features supported
by Verdi as part of this release:
* New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug
* Controlling the Display of Console Command Output Messages
* Adding a Variable Name to the Watch Window Manually
* Selectively Adding Class or Members From the Source View to the Watch View

New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug
You can use the VERDI_NEW_UNIFIED_TCL environment variable as follows to enable the
new unified Tcl mode LCA feature in Verdi interactive debug:
setenv VERDI_NEW_UNIFIED_TCL 1

The new unified Tcl mode is applied in the following usages:
Launch Verdi with interactive debug mode together:
* simv -verdi
* verdi -I
* verdi -ssr [interactive_session_file]
* In simv UCLI mode, launch start_verdi
If interactive debug with new unified Tcl mode is exited to post-simulation mode, Verdi
switches to original unified Tcl flow.

New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug

The following figure shows the process flow of Tcl commands:
Figure 299

Process Flow of Tcl Commands

The following points describe the process flow:
* Verdi interactive debug is launched using the simv -verdi or verdi -simBin simv
-i commands.
* UCLI Tcl interpreter is used as default interpreter. Initially, all Tcl commands and
procedures are sent to UCLI Tcl interpreter for processing.
* UCLI Tcl interpreter sends all Verdi commands to Verdi for execution.
* After enabling new unified Tcl mode, Verdi updates views once after script execution
is completed. Verdi does not update the views after executing each command in the
scripts.

New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug

Pausing Script Execution During Simulation
In the new unified Tcl mode, Verdi allows you to pause script execution during simulation.
Verdi displays the following Stop dialog box when you click the Stop button during script
execution:
Figure 300

Stop Dialog Box

* Abort: Aborts script execution.
* Pause: Pauses script execution. If the script is paused, you can use the resume
command on console to continue script execution, or you can use the abort command
to abort script execution. Verdi displays the Busy dialog if the script is not paused.
When the Busy dialog is displayed, you can click the Abort button to cancel the pause
request.
* Cancel: Closes the Stop dialog.

Following are the limitations of this feature:
* The native Tcl commands set, rename, and alias in the NOVAS_AUTO_SOURCE script
file are expected to be used in Verdi, but not in UCLI, so you should not use these
variables or settings in the NOVAS_AUTO_SOURCE script to UCLI.
In interactive mode, the native Tcl commands set, rename, and alias are expected
used in UCLI, not for Verdi. Therefore, these variables/settings in UCLI do not sync to
Verdi.
* After script execution is completed, Verdi views are updated by simulation status even
if the script is not related.
* If you request to pause the script or add signal to waveform, simulation first completes
the execution of the current command and then performs pause.
* Dynamic object is not support for adding to waveform while simulation is running for the
executing script.

Controlling the Display of Console Command Output Messages

Controlling the Display of Console Command Output Messages
Verdi allows you to control the display of script commands and their output in the Console
pane.You must use the following environment variable to enable this feature:
setenv VERDI_TBV_ECHO_DISPLAY 1

You can use the following simulation command in the Console pane to control the display
of script commands and their output messages:
do [-echo [on|off]] <filename>

* filename - Tcl file. This file contains the script commands to be evaluated.
* -echo on - Displays the output (both command and its result) of all the evaluated
commands on the Console. By default, echo is on.
* -echo off - Displays only the result of the evaluated commands that requires
reporting.
Examples
Example-1: Behavior of do -echo on
Verdi> do -echo on test.tcl
Verdi> puts siga
siga
Verdi> next
sec.vhd, 135 : wait for 6 ns;
Verdi>step
sec.vhd, 162 : if (clk = '0') then
Verdi>stop -relative 1

Verdi allows you to add a variable name manually to the watch window. To enable this

setenv VERDI_DISPLAY_STL_ELEMENTS 1

* Class object id and the member (for example, classA@1)

Verdi Intelligent Coverage Optimization
VCS Intelligent Coverage Optimization (ICO) is a major step toward fully automated CRV
coverage closure. Figure 1-1 shows the high-level flow of its operation. ICO fits seamlessly
into your VCS regression environment running in the grid or cloud.
When enabled, ICO carries out intra-simulation learning across randomization within
a test. It also carries out inter-simulation learning across tests for effective coverage
optimization. ICO updates and shares a global learned database (cdb).
ICO uses AI/ML techniques to optimize stimulus generation efficiently. This improves
diversification and the quality of randomly generated stimulus. You can hit challenging
coverage properties more quickly and significantly reduce coverage regression turnaround
time (TAT).
Figure 310

Constrained Random Verification With ICO

ICO analytics provide testbench stimulus visibility, diagnostics, and root cause analysis.
They help you debug testbench issues. ICO detects potential over-constraints that may
limit generated tests. These constraints may not provide enough focused stimulus to hit
challenging coverage properties.

ICO also helps expose and triage hard-to-find bugs and cover rare scenarios. This applies
even after testbenches are deemed stable and mature. You can deploy ICO at all stages
of development, including before functional coverage is specified.
Refer to the VCS Intelligent Coverage Optimization User Guide for more information.
This document describes the Verdi debug support for ICO and visualization of ICO report
in the following sections:
* Quick Start
* Visualization of ICO Data
* Generating Verdi SDB
* Loading ICO CDB
* Bin Clustering
* Bin Exclusion
* Command Line Options

Loading ICO Data in Verdi
You can use Verdi GUI to open the cdb database. The following topics describe how to
load ICO data to Verdi GUI:
Generating CDB Database
You can use Verdi GUI to open the cdb database. Perform the following recommended
steps to generate cdb/kdb databases and to open Verdi GUI for ICO debug:
1. Compile command:
% vcs -sverilog -kdb test.sv -full64

2. Initialize the shared directory (record) once before regression using the following
command:
% crg -dir shared_record -shared init

3. Launch the concurrent simv (simvs running concurrently in background, updating the
shared record) using the following commands:
//for i in 1..100; do #run simv in parallel
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=2 \
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<shared_record> \
+ntb_solver_bias_wdir=<wdir> \
+<runtime_options> &
//done

Refer to the VCS Intelligent Coverage Optimization chapter in the VCS ICO
User Guide for more information on ICO runtime options and CRG options.
4. Generate sdb from cdb for viewing in Verdi:
% crg -dir <shared_record> -sdb <sdb>

5. After simulation, use the following commands to open Verdi GUI:
% verdi -apex -lca

Verdi ICO requires apex license.

Intelligent Constraint Debugger
Finding the root cause of test failures such as UVM_ERROR, SVA failures, and checker
failures is laborious. It requires several trial-and-error cycles.
These cycles slow the verification process and make it harder to achieve verification
closure on time.
The Intelligent Constraint Debugger (ICD) feature allows you to automate the localization
of the failure-inducing randomization constraints and reduces the manual debugging effort.
The architecture of ICD is shown in the following figure:
Figure 362

ICD Architecture

The ICD module is part of the VCS framework. The Constraint Solver solves
randomization problems generated by the Problem Generator based on the given
Constraint Random Testbench (CRT).
ICD uses AI/ML technology to identify minimal stimulus trigger conditions. These
conditions let the constraint solver reproduce the simulation failure. The Monitor checks
whether the current set of reduced stimulus trigger conditions triggered the simulation
failure.

ICD Use Model
ICD provides a unified executable with an intuitive interface that automatically runs the
process and generates comprehensive reports. The following is the use model:
% icd icd_config.json

The icd utility is available under the VCS installation at $VCS_HOME/bin/icd. It takes a
configuration file icd_config.json as input. It invokes ICD and generates reports.
.
Following is the use model:
Compilation:
vcs [compile-time options]

Simulation:
simv [runtime_options] ico_options

Debug with ICD:
% icd icd_config.json
% cat icd_config.json
{
"SIMV_CMD" : "simv <run_opt>",
"ICD_REGEX" : "<failure_regular_expression>",
"ICD_RECORD" : "ICD_DBG",
"ICD_REPORT" : "ICD_RPT"
}

SIMV_CMD: Specify the simulation command or a JSON list of commands with runtime

options that expose the failure.

ICD_REGEX: Specify regular expression of the failure message. For example, "ASSERT
FAILED. *ReqHighUntilAck_A".
ICD_RECORD: Specify the record directory to store intermediate results.
ICD_REPORT: Specify the report directory to store RCA reports.

The ICD flow iteratively minimizes stimulus trigger conditions required to reproduce the
simulation failure. It produces a failing test and a passing test with minimal differences in
constraint random variable values.
The report is dumped in the <ICD_REPORT>/icd_rca.json file.

License Requirements for ICD
ICD requires VCS APEX and VT_VCS_VERDI_ICD license keys.

LLM Prompt to Leverage ICD Analysis
To enhance ICD usability and enable agent-based debug workflows, ICD generates a
text-based prompt. You can use this prompt directly with Large Language Model (LLM)-
enabled tools such as Cursor, Copilot, and similar environments.
This prompt aggregates relevant context and debug information from the ICD flow. It helps
you perform root cause analysis (RCA) and identify potential fixes for simulation failures.
This feature does not alter the existing ICD usage model or execution flow. ICD continues
to identify the closest passing and failing simulations. It also produces standard RCA
reports and artifacts.

ICD is invoked in the usual manner:
% icd icd_config.json

As in the existing flow, ICD generates analysis outputs under the directory specified by
the ICD_REPORT parameter. These outputs include failure-inducing stimulus differences,
randomization context, and trace information.
With this feature, ICD additionally generates the following file:
<ICD_REPORT>/icd_rca.prompt

This file is automatically produced as part of the standard ICD report generation process.

LLM Prompt File Description
The icd_rca.prompt file contains structured instructions intended for direct use within
the chat interfaces of agent-enabled IDEs. The prompt is not a static template. It is
automatically populated with data specific to the detected simulation failure.
The prompt includes the following information:
* Failure message, matching regular expression, log file, and failure location.
* Reference passing iteration and reduced failing iteration identified by ICD.
* Minimal set of stimulus and randomization variables required to reproduce the failure.
* Pass and fail values for each failure-inducing variable.
* Randomization sequence and hierarchical context
* References to ICD-generated trace and RCA artifacts

Intended Use
The generated prompt guides an LLM agent to perform the following tasks:
* Interpret the failure scenario using the embedded simulation and debug context.
* Analyze ICD-derived RCA findings.
* Identify likely failure sources, such as testbench stimulus, design logic, or checkers.
* Propose potential fixes or debugging actions based on failure-specific data.
The file can be copied and pasted directly into an LLM chat interface. ICD does not
execute or validate the responses generated by the agent.

* The prompt is informational and advisory.
* Fix recommendations must be reviewed and validated by the user.

Aborting Diverging Traces
The +ntb_solver_bias_debug_abort_divergence runtime option allows you to
optionally terminate the diverging runs but with a clean exit so that the ICD database is
updated while the diverging run is deemed to be passing. This option exits the runs when
divergence from the original trace is seen during ICD debug thereby speeding up the ICD
overall runtime as those runs do not contribute to reach convergence of the results.
This option can be passed at runtime through the configuration file using the ICD_OPT
parameter. By default, it is set to 2 to allow aborting divergent runs only after first passing
iteration as opposed to value 1 to allow aborting after the first iteration.
* You can use the +ntb_solver_bias_debug_abort_divergence option
during debug_replay.
* A diverging run may eventually lead to the same failure message but
terminating earlier can miss it. However, such a trace indicates a different
failure trace with the same failure message.
* If +ntb_solver_bias_debug_abort_divergence=1|2 and the run is
diverging, then the Note-[ICD-DO] message is reported, simulation stops,
and a clean exit happens.

Debugging Non-Monotonic Traces
If the simulation traces are non-monotonic during debugging, iteration stops and an
ICD-NMT warning message is issued. This can occur when there are multiple diverging

Debugging Multi-Staged Simulation

simulation traces with failure messages accepted by the specified regex. That is, NMT
corresponds to a failing trace where there is a divergence in the simulation path from
the original failing trace during ICD iterations. Such a trace breaks the monotonous
assumption in ICD and limits the use of ICD. To avoid this, you can specify a regex with
more information such as simulation time to search for a specific failure trace.
This option can be passed at runtime through the configuration file using the ICD_OPT
parameter. By default, it is set to 1 to let ICD handle the debugging of NMT traces.
* At iteration 1, a hidden file with extension .nmt.ddb is generated in the
<ICD_RECORD> directory when the following conditions are met:
ICO-enabled debug is performed
Iteration 1 fails with an error message in the simulation log
NMT support is enabled using +ntb_solver_bias_debug_nmt=1
This debug data is used in the subsequent iteration. Rest of the files are
generated normally.
* The ICD-NMT warning message is issued when
+ntb_solver_bias_debug_nmt=0 and following conditions are met:
Iteration >= 1
Simulation has a failure message, but diverges from the original failure
trace
* The value of +ntb_solver_bias_debug_nmt used in iteration=0
is used in subsequent iterations and debug replay for all iterations
irrespective of what you specify. Therefore, even if you change the
+ntb_solver_bias_debug_nmt option in any iteration > 0, the change is
ignored.

Debugging Multi-Staged Simulation
A multi-stage simulation consists of multiple sequential simulation runs. Each stage
consumes data generated by the previous stage.
Failures in later stages may depend on conditions or data from earlier stages. Debugging
these failures requires identifying failure-inducing conditions in preceding stages.
The Intelligent Constraint Debugger (ICD) supports this capability through its multi-stage
simulation flow. Set the SIMV_CMD parameter in the ICD configuration file to a JSON list of
simulation commands (one for each stage).

Intelligent Simulation Replayer (ISR)
In a Constraint Random Verification environment, reproducibility of runs is not guaranteed
even with the same seed. Other variables include command line options, testbench (TB)
changes, DUT changes, and version or patch changes.
The Intelligent Simulation Replayer (ISR) helps replay a simulation in a best-effort manner.
It accounts for design and testbench changes.
Resimulation lets you match generated stimulus values modulo testbench changes. This
feature helps reproduce rare observations, such as failures in a modified testbench.

Verdi Intelligent Coverage Optimization
VCS Intelligent Coverage Optimization (ICO) is a major step toward fully automated CRV
coverage closure. Figure 1-1 shows the high-level flow of its operation. ICO fits seamlessly
into your VCS regression environment running in the grid or cloud.
When enabled, ICO carries out intra-simulation learning across randomization within
a test. It also carries out inter-simulation learning across tests for effective coverage
optimization. ICO updates and shares a global learned database (cdb).
ICO uses AI/ML techniques to optimize stimulus generation efficiently. This improves
diversification and the quality of randomly generated stimulus. You can hit challenging
coverage properties more quickly and significantly reduce coverage regression turnaround
time (TAT).
Figure 310

Constrained Random Verification With ICO

ICO analytics provide testbench stimulus visibility, diagnostics, and root cause analysis.
They help you debug testbench issues. ICO detects potential over-constraints that may
limit generated tests. These constraints may not provide enough focused stimulus to hit
challenging coverage properties.

ICO also helps expose and triage hard-to-find bugs and cover rare scenarios. This applies
even after testbenches are deemed stable and mature. You can deploy ICO at all stages
of development, including before functional coverage is specified.
Refer to the VCS Intelligent Coverage Optimization User Guide for more information.

in the following sections:

Intelligent Constraint Debugger
Finding the root cause of test failures such as UVM_ERROR, SVA failures, and checker
failures is laborious. It requires several trial-and-error cycles.
These cycles slow the verification process and make it harder to achieve verification
closure on time.
The Intelligent Constraint Debugger (ICD) feature allows you to automate the localization
of the failure-inducing randomization constraints and reduces the manual debugging effort.
The architecture of ICD is shown in the following figure:
Figure 362

ICD Architecture

The ICD module is part of the VCS framework. The Constraint Solver solves
randomization problems generated by the Problem Generator based on the given
Constraint Random Testbench (CRT).
ICD uses AI/ML technology to identify minimal stimulus trigger conditions. These
conditions let the constraint solver reproduce the simulation failure. The Monitor checks
whether the current set of reduced stimulus trigger conditions triggered the simulation
failure.

SIMV_CMD: Specify the simulation command or a JSON list of commands with runtime

options that expose the failure.

ICD_REGEX: Specify regular expression of the failure message. For example, "ASSERT
FAILED. *ReqHighUntilAck_A".
ICD_RECORD: Specify the record directory to store intermediate results.
ICD_REPORT: Specify the report directory to store RCA reports.

The ICD flow iteratively minimizes stimulus trigger conditions required to reproduce the
simulation failure. It produces a failing test and a passing test with minimal differences in
constraint random variable values.
The report is dumped in the <ICD_REPORT>/icd_rca.json file.

License Requirements for ICD
ICD requires VCS APEX and VT_VCS_VERDI_ICD license keys.

file with default values and required/optional fields for each parameter. This file can also
be obtained by invoking the icd command (that is, without any argument).

purpose only"
},

exposing the failure",

(see also: REGEX_MLINE)"
},
"optional" : {

simulation run",
"SIMV_LOG" : "Specify the simulation log file",
"ICD_RECORD" : "Specify the record directory to store
iteration results",
"ICD_TIME_LIMIT" : "Specify the time limit (in sec)",
"ICD_ITER_LIMIT" : "Specify the iteration limit",
"ICD_ICO_FAIL" : "Specify 0/1 to indicate non-ICO/ICO

LLM Prompt to Leverage ICD Analysis
To enhance ICD usability and enable agent-based debug workflows, ICD generates a
text-based prompt. You can use this prompt directly with Large Language Model (LLM)-
enabled tools such as Cursor, Copilot, and similar environments.
This prompt aggregates relevant context and debug information from the ICD flow. It helps
you perform root cause analysis (RCA) and identify potential fixes for simulation failures.
This feature does not alter the existing ICD usage model or execution flow. ICD continues
to identify the closest passing and failing simulations. It also produces standard RCA
reports and artifacts.

As in the existing flow, ICD generates analysis outputs under the directory specified by
the ICD_REPORT parameter. These outputs include failure-inducing stimulus differences,
randomization context, and trace information.
With this feature, ICD additionally generates the following file:
<ICD_REPORT>/icd_rca.prompt

This file is automatically produced as part of the standard ICD report generation process.

LLM Prompt File Description
The icd_rca.prompt file contains structured instructions intended for direct use within
the chat interfaces of agent-enabled IDEs. The prompt is not a static template. It is
automatically populated with data specific to the detected simulation failure.
The prompt includes the following information:
* Failure message, matching regular expression, log file, and failure location.
* Reference passing iteration and reduced failing iteration identified by ICD.
* Minimal set of stimulus and randomization variables required to reproduce the failure.
* Pass and fail values for each failure-inducing variable.
* Randomization sequence and hierarchical context
* References to ICD-generated trace and RCA artifacts

Intended Use
The generated prompt guides an LLM agent to perform the following tasks:
* Interpret the failure scenario using the embedded simulation and debug context.
* Analyze ICD-derived RCA findings.
* Identify likely failure sources, such as testbench stimulus, design logic, or checkers.
* Propose potential fixes or debugging actions based on failure-specific data.
The file can be copied and pasted directly into an LLM chat interface. ICD does not
execute or validate the responses generated by the agent.

* The prompt is informational and advisory.
* Fix recommendations must be reviewed and validated by the user.
* The effectiveness of the analysis depends on the LLM and its access to the
relevant codebase.

Files Generated by ICD
The following table lists the files generated under the <ICD_RECORD> directory:
Table 27

Files Generated by ICD

File Name

Hidden?

Use

.dbg.ddb

Yes

Generated at iteration 0. The data is used in subsequent
iterations.

.dbg.state

Yes

Current debug search state. This is updated after every
iteration and sets up the search parameter for the next
iteration.

dbg.state.<k>

No

This is needed to replay the kth debug iteration.

dbg.trace.<k>

No

Simulation trace (randomization, stimulus values) of the kth
debug iteration.

dbg.rca.<k>

No

Partial simulation trace (randomization, stimulus values)
of the kth debug iteration containing information of only
those random problems which were biased by ICO of the
simulation and lead to trace with <fail_msg> outcome.
This file is not generated if the iteration does not have
<fail_msg> outcome.

dbg.status

No

Status line per iteration.

Format of Non-Hidden File
The following is the format of a non-hidden file:
% cat dbg.status
iter

status
PASS
PASS
PASS

rca_size_min

rca_size_max

iter_est_max

..
..

PASS

DONE

The following table describes the columns of the dbg.status file:
Table 28

Columns of the dbg.status File

Column

iter

Debug iteration number.

status

FAIL or PASS depending on if <fail_mesg> outcome is

rca_size_min

Potentially minimum number of problems that require
biasing at this iteration.

rca_size_max

Potential maximum number of problems that require
biasing at this iteration.

iter_est_max

Potential maximum iteration required. This can be DONE
or STOP.
When parameter "ICD_ICO_FAIL" is set to "1":
* If DONE, then it found the minimal failure-inducing
biasing causes.
* If STOP at iteration 0, then it is unable to continue as
there is no <fail_msg>. Warning ICD-PNF is issued.
* If STOP at iteration 2, then it is unable to continue
as the run has <fail_msg> without any biasing.
Warning ICD-PNB is issued.
* If STOP at iteration is > 2, then the trace is NMT
(non-monotonic trace). Warning ICD-NMT is
issued. NMT corresponds to a trace where there is
divergence in the simulation path during recreating
failing/passing traces with fewer biasing.
When parameter "ICD_ICO_FAIL" is set to "0":
* If DONE, then it found the minimal failure-inducing
non-biasing causes.
* If STOP at iteration 0, then it is unable to continue as
there is no <fail_msg>. Warning ICD-PNF is issued.
* If STOP at iteration 1, then it is unable to continue
as the run has <fail_msg> with biasing. Warning
ICD-PB is issued.
* If STOP at iteration >1, then the trace is NMT
(non-monotonic trace). Warning ICD-NMT is issued.

found or not found.

Error/Warning/Note Messages
The following are the error and warning messages related to this feature:
Error-[ICD-RM] Debug regex missing
Debug regex missing in the command line.
Please specify regex with '+ntb_solver_bias_debug_regex=' option.
Error-[ICD-LM] Log file missing
Log file missing in the command line.
Please specify log file with '-l' option.
Error-[ICD-RF] Debug regex not well-formed
Debug regex '^ASSERT.*FAILED.[*06' is not well-formed.
Please specify a valid debug regex.
Error-[ICD-DIF] Debug record init failed
Debug record directory
'/remote/newTestCases/debugSaveRestore/ICO_DBG1'
could not be initialized due to 'Permission denied'.
Please make sure the debug record directory is created and is
accessible.
Error-[ICD-SRF] Debug record state read failed
The debug record state
'/remote/newTestCases/debugSaveRestore/ICO_DBG/.dbg.state.5'
could not be read due to 'No such file or directory'.
Please provide a valid debug record.
Error-[ICD-DRF] Debug record db read failed
The debug record db
'/remote/newTestCases/debugSaveRestore/ICO_DBG/.dbg.ddb'
could not be read due to 'No such File'.
Please provide a valid debug record.

Error-[ICD-OM] Debug option missing
Some needed debug option(s) missing.
Specify these options also: '+ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config,
+ntb_solver_bias_replay=1, +ntb_solver_bias_debug_record,
+ntb_solver_bias_debug_regex, -l'.
Warning-[ICD-PNF] Debug regex pattern not found
The debug regex pattern not found, nothing to debug.
Please make sure the run to debug has the pattern.
Warning-[ICD-PNB] Debug regex pattern found without biasing
The debug regex pattern found even without biasing, unable to debug.
Please make sure the run to debug has the pattern with biasing only.
Warning-[ICD-NMT] Non-monotonic trace found during debug
The debug trace found to be non-monotonic, unable to debug further.
Add runtime option +ntb_solver_bias_debug_nmt=1 for nmt traces.
Note-[ICD-DO] Divergence from the original run observed
This run is diverging from the original run, hence aborting it.
Use +ntb_solver_bias_debug_abort_divergence=0 to not abort.

The following message is generated in a non-ICO ICD flow:
Warning-[ICD-PB] Debug regex pattern found with biasing
The debug regex pattern found even with biasing, unable to debug.
Try with a different biasing option on the run to debug.

Debugging ICO Runs
For a simulation failure exposed with ICO, use the "ICD_ICO_FAIL" : "1" parameter.
The following note message is issued when ICD is enabled to debug ICO exposed
simulation failure:
Note-[CNST-ICO] ICO Enabled
VCS Intelligent Coverage Optimization is enabled with AutoBiasIntra +
Prognosis + Replay + Debug feature(s).

The following note message is issued when a particular ICD iteration is replayed to debug
ICO exposed simulation failure:
Note-[CNST-ICO] ICO Enabled
VCS Intelligent Coverage Optimization is enabled with AutoBiasIntra +
Prognosis + Replay + Debug(R) feature(s).

Debugging Non-ICO Runs
For a simulation failure exposed without ICO, use the "ICD_ICO_FAIL" : "0" parameter.

The following note message is issued when ICD is enabled to debug a non-ICO exposed
simulation failure:
Note-[CNST-ICO] ICO Enabled
VCS Intelligent Coverage Optimization is enabled with RecordOnly + Replay
+ Debug
feature(s).

The following note message is issued when a particular ICD iteration is replayed to debug
a non-ICO exposed simulation failure:
Note-[CNST-ICO] ICO Enabled
VCS Intelligent Coverage Optimization is enabled with RecordOnly + Replay
+ Debug(R)
feature(s).

When debugging non-ICO failures, ICO_OPT is optional. You can use different biasing if
you get the ICD-PB warning message.

Aborting Diverging Traces
The +ntb_solver_bias_debug_abort_divergence runtime option allows you to
optionally terminate the diverging runs but with a clean exit so that the ICD database is
updated while the diverging run is deemed to be passing. This option exits the runs when
divergence from the original trace is seen during ICD debug thereby speeding up the ICD
overall runtime as those runs do not contribute to reach convergence of the results.
This option can be passed at runtime through the configuration file using the ICD_OPT
parameter. By default, it is set to 2 to allow aborting divergent runs only after first passing
iteration as opposed to value 1 to allow aborting after the first iteration.
* You can use the +ntb_solver_bias_debug_abort_divergence option
during debug_replay.
* A diverging run may eventually lead to the same failure message but
terminating earlier can miss it. However, such a trace indicates a different
failure trace with the same failure message.
* If +ntb_solver_bias_debug_abort_divergence=1|2 and the run is
diverging, then the Note-[ICD-DO] message is reported, simulation stops,
and a clean exit happens.

Debugging Non-Monotonic Traces
If the simulation traces are non-monotonic during debugging, iteration stops and an
ICD-NMT warning message is issued. This can occur when there are multiple diverging

Debugging Multi-Staged Simulation

simulation traces with failure messages accepted by the specified regex. That is, NMT
corresponds to a failing trace where there is a divergence in the simulation path from
the original failing trace during ICD iterations. Such a trace breaks the monotonous
assumption in ICD and limits the use of ICD. To avoid this, you can specify a regex with

Iteration >= 1

Debugging Multi-Staged Simulation
A multi-stage simulation consists of multiple sequential simulation runs. Each stage
consumes data generated by the previous stage.
Failures in later stages may depend on conditions or data from earlier stages. Debugging
these failures requires identifying failure-inducing conditions in preceding stages.
The Intelligent Constraint Debugger (ICD) supports this capability through its multi-stage
simulation flow. Set the SIMV_CMD parameter in the ICD configuration file to a JSON list of
simulation commands (one for each stage).

text:
Debugging Multi-Staged Simulation

Include the runtime options that expose the failure. The following example illustrates this
setup.

Multi-Staged Simulation Debug Example
Consider the following simulation executables:
simv_write: Writes randomly generated configurations in a config.txt file.
simv_read: Reads configurations from config.txt and generates random stimulus. The
error Bad Stimulus is issued for a certain stimulus value.

Figure 363

2-Stage Simulation - simv_read Consumes `config.txt' Generated by simv_write

To debug the "Bad Stimulus" error in simv_read, configure the SIMV_CMD parameter as
a JSON list of simulation commands for each stage, as shown in the following example:
Example 1
{

}

icd_config.json

"SIMV_CMD" : [
"simv_write +ntb_random_seed=123",
"simv_read +ntb_random_seed=200"
],
"ICD_REGEX" : "Bad stimulus",
"ICD_ICO_FAIL" : "0"

In the following JSON configuration file, setting "REGEX_MLINE": "1" enables the regular
expression check to span multiple lines instead of being limited to a single line:
Example 2
{

}

icd_config.json

"SIMV_CMD" : [
"simv_write +ntb_random_seed=123",
"simv_read +ntb_random_seed=200"
],
"ICD_REGEX" : "Bad.*Bad.*stimulus",
"ICD_ICO_FAIL" : "0"
"REGEX_MLINE" : "1"

Hierarchical Layering and Sequence Partitioning
Debugging CRT test failures caused by complex randomization constraints is difficult and
time-consuming. It slows verification.
Intelligent Constraint Debugger (ICD) can use the hierarchical structure of randomization
components to reduce debug time. Set the parameter "ICD_HIER" : "1" and parameter
"ICD_PART" : "1".
The following example configuration file shows enabling the Hierarchical Layering and
Sequence Partitioning features:
Figure 364

Enabling Hierarchical Layering and Sequence Partitioning

Hierarchical Layering and Sequence Partitioning

In the following example, the highlighted randomization components are failure-inducing:
Figure 365

Failure-Inducing Randomization Components

The hierarchical ICD enables faster localization of the failure-inducing hierarchical
components. That is, class foo (blue arrow) at iter:2, class instance test.sv:10 (yellow
arrow) at iter:3, and randomization serial randomize_3 (red arrow) at iter:4.
* Convergence order is CLASS, INST, SERIAL, and DONE.
* If multiple layers converge at the same iteration, only the highest layer is
shown.

Intelligent Simulation Replayer (ISR)
In a Constraint Random Verification environment, reproducibility of runs is not guaranteed
even with the same seed. Other variables include command line options, testbench (TB)
changes, DUT changes, and version or patch changes.
The Intelligent Simulation Replayer (ISR) helps replay a simulation in a best-effort manner.
It accounts for design and testbench changes.
Resimulation lets you match generated stimulus values modulo testbench changes. This
feature helps reproduce rare observations, such as failures in a modified testbench.
The following sections describe ISR in detail:
* Simv Runtime Option
* Example
* Error/Warning/Note Messages
* Recommended Use Model

The following is the use model of ISR support for Non-ICO and ICO enabled runs:
Compilation
% vcs [compile-time options]

This feature does not require any change in the compilation.
Simulation
Enables ISR in the record mode.
% simv [vcs_runtime_options] [ico_runtime_options]
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=1 +ntb_solver_bias_isr_record=<isr_record> -lca

Intelligent Simulation Replay

+ntb_solver_bias_isr_record=<isr_record> -lca

+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=<0|1|2|3|4>

Table 30

Enabling ISR

Value

Default

Enables the ISR restore feature using cache to speed up the
subsequent replays.

+ntb_solver_bias_isr_record=<isr_record>

Specifies the ISR record where the simulation run information is stored and restored from.
It consists of the following files:
Table 31

ISR Record Files

Value

Saves the simulation information (binary file) with
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=1.

restored.rdb

Saves the simulation information after

+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=3. This file is required
with +ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=4.

report.txt

Reports the confidence score of matching values with
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=2|3.

Maps the serial numbers of replayed to original with
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=3.

* By default, +ntb_solver_bias_replay=1 is enabled automatically when
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=2|3|4. However, you can change it to
+ntb_solver_bias_replay=2, but not to +ntb_solver_bias_replay=0.
* The <isr_record>/saved.rdb file is generated with mode_isr=1,
and <isr_record>/restored.rdb is generated with mode_isr=3.
Both saved.rdb and restored.rdb files are required for
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=4.
* The scope, focus, soft ignore, and sbin files should be passed in replay
modes without any change. The replayer automatically maps these old
variables specified in the file to the new variables internally.
* The *.rdb files are not backward compatible across internal versions. You
may have same internal versions across various VCS streams. If the internal
version is different between different VCS streams used to save and restore,
VCS issues the ISR-RRF (incompatible versions) error message. However,
if the internal version is same between different VCS streams used to save
and restore, the ISR-RVM (version mismatch) warning message is issued.

The following section describe the SystemC Debug LCA feature supported by Verdi as

Simulator Support for OSCI
SystemC Debug supports post-processing features such as viewing the SC Design
Hierarchy, Extended SC Dumping, and so on. Only the post-processing flow (FSDB and
RIDB) is supported and interactive debug features are not supported in this release. All the
feature support that is available for IUS, VCS, and ModelSim is also available for OSCI:
* Full FSDB Dumping: SC ports, signals, plain vars (Source code must be compiled
with debug info (gcc -g)), sc_fifo, user-defined data type (for example, structure/union/
class) ( Source code must be compiled with debug info (gcc -g)), enum, and so on.
* RIDB Dumping: view SC hierarchy in Verdi hierarchy pane, signal list; double-click
opens src file ( Source code must be compiled with debug info (gcc -g))

Configuring the Simulator
Ensure that a working installation of Verdi is available and execute the following
commands:
Set the following environment variables:
% setenv VERDI_HOME <path to Verdi Installation>

It is necessary to set the LD_LIBRARY_PATH such that libfsdb_osci.so can be found:
% setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/OSCI/$PLATFORM

Activating the FSDB Dumper
You need to add a single statement to the SystemC source code which activates the Verdi
dumper and defines how much to dump. The statement must be called after the SystemC
elaboration is complete. For example, within sc_main after an sc_start(0) call.
#include <fsdb_osci.h>

int sc_main(int,char*[])
{

sc_start(SC_ZERO_TIME);
ridbDump("default.ridb");

}

fsdbDumpvars(0, NULL);
sc_start();

The fsdbDumpvars and related functions are declared in the C++ header file fsdb_osci.h
that is shipped in the Verdi image at $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/OSCI/$PLATFORM
% gcc -g -c -I$VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/OSCI/$PLATFORM -Isystemc/include/
main.cpp

It is not necessary to recompile all the SC source files; the existing object files
and libraries can be used without recompiling.
Linking and Running the Simulation

VC AutoTestbench
Verdi provides the VC AutoTestbench tool for testbench generation using the information
extracted from DUT IP-XACT file, VIP IP-XACT files and other configuration files provided
by users. VC AutoTestbench allows you to customize various aspects of a testbench,
such as, topology, interface and signal-level connections, clock or reset connection, and
so on. This tool enables easy and rapid generation of a testbench, which is usually a
time consuming and an error-prone process and it gates the actual testing for simulation,
acceleration, or emulation.

The VC AutoTestbench tool uses a licensing mechanism that is enabled by the
following license switches: VC-AUTO-TESTBENCH-VERDI-PLUGIN VC-AUTOTESTBENCH

Prerequisites

This chapter contains the following sections that provide details about VC AutoTestbench:

Prerequisites
The following are the prerequisites for using the VC AutoTestbench tool:
* AMBA-specific Protocol IP-XACT files are included in the Verdi installation under the

IP-XACT Overview
The IP-XACT standard describes an XML Schema for metadata documenting Intellectual
Property (IP) used in development, implementation, and verification of electronic
systems. This schema provides a standard method to document IP that is compatible with
automated integration techniques.

IP-XACT Overview

The IP-XACT standard is an electronic databook of all the IPs on the chip with their
configuration details. It contains the block-level information with details on how the
components are configured, such as,
* Modes of operation
* Register maps
* Address space
* Interface configuration
* Language and more details
It uses the XML standard to represent the data. For details, see http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/
document/6898803/.

Protocol IP-XACT
Protocol IP-XACT defines the notion of a bus definition whose attributes comprise of the
Vendor, Library, Name, and Version (VLNV) signature. This signature determines which
other IP is connected to the bus interface.
Each bus definition from Accellera, other vendors (such as ARM), or Synopsys
consists of two separate XML files. One XML file defines a construct designated by the
spirit:busDefinition XML tag. The other XML file defines a construct designated by
the spirit:abstractionDefinition XML tag.
The AMBA-specific protocol IP-XACT is present in the Verdi installation. You can point the
tool to the following path:

DUT IP-XACT
The DUT IP-XACT file defines an IP-XACT component definition. The IP-XACT
specification defines an IPXACT component as follows:
An IP-XACT component is used to describe the meta-data associated with any IP that can
be instantiated in a design.
For determining the overall structure of the testbench, the DUT IP-XACT defines a
collection of bus interfaces to which other blocks can be connected. In the case of VC
AutoTestbench, these DUT bus interfaces are connected to one or more VIPs.

IP-XACT Overview

The DUT IP-XACT component describes all the bus interfaces that can be connected to
VIP instances. For the tool to enable connections between the DUT and one or more VIPs,
the bus interfaces that are referenced by the DUT IP-XACT must be standard protocol bus
interfaces that are known to be compatible with the VIPs that are available to the user.
Further, VLNV for each of the DUT-specified bus interfaces must exactly match VLNV of
at least one VIP to make a legal connection between the DUT and a VIP. The IP-XACT
standard specifies this strict matching requirement.
You must generate the DUT IP-XACT while generating the RTL/Verilog files for the DUT.
If you are using ARM tools, or Synopsys Core tools or Arteris tools and so on to generate
the RTL, you must also generate the IP-XACT file for that DUT from the tool.

VIP IP-XACT
The VIP IP-XACT files describe VIPs with bus interfaces. The following are the two types
of Port-Level VIP IP-XACT definitions:
* Port-level IP-XACT descriptions correspond to single port VIPs. Examples include AHB
master, AXI slave, and CSI2.
* System-level IP-XACT descriptions correspond to system VIPs. Examples include AHB
system and AMBA system. These VIPs consist of port-level VIPs and other systemlevel VIPs.
System-level VIPs can include port-level VIPs and other system-level VIPs. The systemlevel IP-XACT descriptions reference the port-level IP-XACT descriptions. They also
reference other system-level IP-XACT descriptions.
Port-level and system-level VIPs are building blocks for system-level VIPs. Likewise, portlevel and system-level IP-XACT descriptions are building blocks for other system-level IPXACT descriptions.
To summarize, port-level VIP IP-XACT definitions describe stand-alone VIPs or VIP
building blocks. These blocks specify bus interfaces that can connect to DUT bus
interfaces. They can also connect to other testbench components in theory. The section on
Port-Level VIP IP-XACT definitions describes how this connection is determined.
You must set the DESIGNWARE_HOME variable to the VIP installation to get the VIP IP-XACT
files.
In the VC AutoTestbench flow, the VLNV must exactly match between the DUT IP-XACT
and the Protocol IP-XACT. This match is required to connect a DUT interface to a VIP
interface. If there is a mismatch, you cannot connect a VIP on that DUT bus.
Following are the steps to resolve this problem in Verdi:
1. Create a rc file with the name vcatb_protocol_alias.rc

The content of this file looks like:
============================
@verdi rc file Version 1.0
[busType]
amba.com,AMBA3,AXI_1,r2p0_0 = amba.com,AMBA3,AXI,r2p0_0
amba.com,AMBA3,AXI_2,r2p0_0 = amba.com,AMBA3,AXI,r2p0_0
[abstractionType]
amba.com,AMBA3,AXI_rtl_1,r2p0_0 = amba.com,AMBA3,AXI_rtl,r2p0_0
amba.com,AMBA3,AXI_rtl_2,r2p0_0 = amba.com,AMBA3,AXI_rtl,r2p0_0
============================

The LHS is the VLNV used in the DUT IP-XACT.
The RHS is the VLNV of the protocol in the protocol IP-XACT library.
1. The VC AutoTestbench tool searches for vcatb_protocol_alias.rc in the following
order:
a. Set the environment variable VCATB_PROTOCOL_ALIAS_FILE. It must point to the
absolute path of vcatb_protocol_alias.rc
b. ./vcatb_protocol_alias.rc
c. ~/vcatb_protocol_alias.rc

VC AutoTestbench is enhanced to visualize the memory map information and map

Memory Map Details in the IP-XACT File
The following sections are present in the IP-XACT file that contain the memory map
information:
* busInterfaces
It contains the list of bus interfaces. This list is used by VC AutoTestbench to derive
Initiator and Target values. All the slave bus interfaces are represented as Initiators and
all the master bus interfaces are represented as Targets.
* addressSpaceRef (Master busInterface), baseAddress
The addressSpaceRef section resides on a master bus interface. It provides a
reference of an addressSpace element that can be viewed by the master. Some of the
Master busInterface provides baseAddress, which is the base address reference.
* memoryMapRef (Slave busInterface)
The memoryMapRef section resides on a slave bus interface (Initiator). It provides a
reference of the memory map view of that element.
* addressSpaces
It shows the addressSpace viewed by a master bus interface (Target).
* memoryMaps
It mainly represents the following two areas:
Subspace elements that consist of masterRef and/or segmentRef attributes and it
consists of the base address for that memory.
Address blocks and register maps for that component.

Memory Map Terminologies
The initiators (slave interface) and targets (master interface) are derived from the IPXACT file. The memory map information across each initiator target can be represented as
* Local Address
At Initiator: The localAddress is the start address (base address) of the
addressSpace that an Initiator can access. From IP-XACT perspective,
localAddress is same as globalAddress, since IP-XACT does not differentiate
between both of these.
At Target: The localAddress is the base address of the target device
* Global Address
At Initiator: The Global Address is the start address (base address) in the system
memory, which gets actually mapped to the Initiator's local address. From IP-XACT
perspective, they are same at Initiator.
If the memory represented is a sparse memory, that is, segments, the
initiator always shows the least address. For example, if the memory is
sparse, like, 0x0 0x100 0x200 0x300, then the global address is 0x0. The
Range is the complete range specified by the addressSpace in the IP-XACT
file.
* At Target: The Global Address is the start address (base address) in the system
memory, which gets mapped to the target device's local address.
* Range
At Initiator: This is the total address range an initiator can access in its address
space starting from the baseAddress.
If the memory represented is a sparse memory, that is, segments, the
initiator always shows the least address. For example, if the memory is
sparse, like, 0x0 0x100 0x200 0x300, then the global address is 0x0.
Range is the complete range specified by the addressSpace in the IPXACT file.
At Target: Ranges are specified in the sparse memory based on how an initiator
can access this target.

Example: An Initiator CPU0 can access a target SRAM0 at the following sparse
locations:
Address, Range: 0x0, 0x1000
Address, Range: 0x2000, 0x1000

localAddress, globalAddress = 0x0
Range = 0x3000(Complete range from start to end)
Mask = 0x2FFF
Target = SRAM0

___________________________________________________________
The target has the following sparse information:

localAddress, globalAddress = 0x0
Range = 0x1000
Mask = 0xFFF
Source = CPU0
localAddress, globalAddress = 0x2000
Range = 0x1000
Mask = 0xFFF
Source = CPU0

_______________________________________________________________
* Mask
At Initiator, Target: The Mask information is usually Range -1 from the IP-XACT
perspective. The Mask is more useful when you add a new row and want to specify
interleaving between two slave devices. Each Mask bit represents one addressable
bit (A0, A1, A2 An).
A Master CPU0 can access 1GB DDR0 and 1GB DDR1 interleaved at 4K starting
at address 0x0. This would need addressable space of 2GB in total at CPU0. This
would need Interleaved 4K up to 1GB for DDR0 and DDR1

Creating Project for Large Designs
For creating projects for large designs, the following are the best practices:
* Ignore any specific modules having the given names.

To create a bus interface for a project, perform the following steps:

2. In the Create Bus form,

The following rules are used to calculate the possibility of matching and locate the
most possible physical signals for the selected bus logical signal:
If the direction of the physical signal matches the direction of the logical signal
If the width of the physical signal is the same as the width of the logical signal
If the physical signal name includes the bus name or includes a substring that is
similar to the bus name
If the physical name includes the logical name or includes a substring that is
similar to the logical name
g. In some cases where the DUT port signals names are not related to the bus and the
logical signal name, the rules may not work as expected.
h. Use the Auto Connect button to automatically connect all logical signals to the
most possible matches from DUT port signals.
i. Use the Connect button to connect the selected bus signal to the selected DUT
port signal.
j. Use the Disconnect button to disconnect a connected bus signal.
k. Use the Reset button to clear all connections.
l. After all connections are assigned, click the OK button to create the bus.

Replace and Connect Functionality
The generated testbench supports replace and connect functionalities. When a component
is selected as a replaceable component, you can decide if you want to use the bus
interface as an active VIP or a passive VIP. While using the generated testbench, you can
choose to use one of the following modes:
* Connect Mode (Passive Connect)
This mode enables you to connect the buses of a component or an internal instance to
specified VIP instances. When an actual RTL (original RTL instance) is connected to
the bus interface, the VIP is connected as passive mode. This passive VIP can then be
used to monitor traffic across that connection.
* Replace Mode (Active Replace)
This mode enables you to set a component or an internal instance as replaceable.
When there is no RTL connected to the interface, an active VIP gets connected to that
interface as a replacement for the original RTL instance. You can then use the VIP
capabilities to drive traffic at that interface.
The prerequisite for both active replace or passive connect is that in addition
to supporting an SV interface, the VIP must support a corresponding SV bind
interface.
To enable Passive Connect and Active Replace modes, perform the following steps:
1. Set your internal connection, that is, connect a component internal to the DUT with a
VIP in the AMBA system environment.
a. In the DUT Connections tab, select the component that you want to replace, and
select the Set Replaceable right-click option.
b. Click the '+' next to the component to view the internal components.
c. Select the item and use the Connect to VIP right-click option to connect to the
desired VIP.

2. Use the same defines for CONNECT as present in the output_dir/dut_wrapper/
dut_wrapper.sv file and the gmake command to enable Passive Connect mode. For
example:
gmake clean sanity_test CMDLINE_COMP_ARGS='+define+<CONNECT Define
present in the dut_wrapper.sv>'

3. Use the same defines for REPLACE as present in the output_dir/dut_wrapper/
dut_wrapper.sv file and the gmake command to enable Active Replace mode. For
example:
gmake clean sanity_test CMDLINE_COMP_ARGS='+define+<REPLACE Define
present in the dut_wrapper.sv>'

The name for CONNECT and REPLACE define present in the
dut_wrapper.sv file is based on the path to the instance being connected
or replaced combined with the DUT busRef name. For example, for
the following design XML, the resulting define for CONNECT would be
VCATB_CONNECT_SUBSYSTEM_A15_CCI500_I_CORTEXA15_1_AXI4MASTER

and the resulting define for REPLACE would be

VCATB_REPLACE_SUBSYSTEM_A15_CCI500_I_CORTEXA15_1_AXI4MASTER
<spirit:name>Subsystem_A15_CCI500</spirit:name>

<spirit:interconnection>
<spirit:name>i_cortexA15_1_AXI4Master</spirit:name>
<spirit:activeInterface
spirit:componentRef="i_cci500_large_fixed" spirit:busRef="S5"/>
<spirit:activeInterface
spirit:componentRef="i_cortexA15_1"
spirit:busRef="AXI4Master"/>
</spirit:interconnection>

The define's suffix contains a string to uniquely identify
the interface being connected or replaced, such as,
+define+VCATB_CONNECT_<unique_suffix>or +define
+VCATB_REPLACE_<unique_suffix>

Demo Examples

Support for PHY Integration
Point-to-point controller IP requires the use of a PHY to drive the physical signaling. The
controller IP provides a parallel bus interface, which is connected to the PHY simulation
model. The PHY model is typically provided separately from the IP model, and you must
connect the IP controller to the PHY model.
The VC AutoTestbench flow identifies situations where a PHY is required and generates
a testbench with a PHY Shell module that is connected to the DUT and to the VIP. To
complete the testbench integration, you must replace the PHY shell module with a module
that wraps your PHY simulation model.

Prerequisite
PHY integration requires a protocol IP-XACT description for both bus interfaces. You
need one for the parallel PHY bus interface and one for the serial PHY bus interface. If a
standard protocol IP-XACT is not available, develop it and ship it with the appropriate VIP.
If DUT IP-XACT does not support the required protocol IP-XACT, then an adjunct file
must be developed that exposes these bus interfaces and allows them to be connected to
testbench elements.

Serial Interface From DUT Side
If DUT IP-XACT exposes a serial PHY bus interface, this implies that a PHY model
is integrated into the DUT and is connected to the IP Controller. In this situation, the
testbench element is connected directly to the exposed PHY serial bus interface in the
DUT.

Parallel Interface From DUT Side
If DUT IP-XACT exposes a parallel PHY bus interface, this implies that a parallel PHY bus
interface connection is required. Some VIP titles support a direct connection to the parallel
PHY bus interface. Therefore, VC AutoTestbench provides you an option to select either
the VIP's parallel PHY bus interface or the VC ATB PHY shell module.
If you select the VIP's parallel PHY bus interface, then the VC ATB connects to it directly.

Support for PHY Integration

If you select to use the PHY shell module, then the VC ATB creates and connects a
compatible PHY shell module in the generated testbench. In this case, you also need to
choose one serial bus from the available serial bus list.

If you choose to use the PHY shell module, then the VC ATB creates and connects a
compatible PHY shell module in the generated testbench.
The following points characterize this feature:
* VC ATB identifies the compatible VIP by recognizing the parallel PHY bus interface in
DUT IP-XACT.
* VIP IP-XACT defines a serial PHY bus interface (or bus interfaces in the case of
multiple lanes) that is associated with the parallel PHY bus interface.
* VC ATB supports n-to-1 or 1-to-n ratios of parallel-to-serial interfaces for the PHY shell
module.
* If there are multiple serial PHY bus interfaces that map to a parallel PHY bus interface,
VCATB allows you to select which serial PHY bus interface must be used.
The PHY shell module is composed of a parallel bus interface and one or more serial bus
interfaces. The PHY shell module is non-functional. It defines a Verilog module with the
appropriate port interface to represent a PHY model.
For VIPs that support a parallel PHY bus interface connection, you can connect the VIP
to the parallel PHY bus interface of the PHY Shell module. This enables the generated
testbench to be functional.
For VIPs that do not support a parallel PHY bus interface, you must replace the PHY Shell
module with your PHY simulation model.
The parallel PHY bus interface of the PHY shell module is defined by the DUT IP-XACT.
The serial PHY bus interface (or bus interfaces in the case of multiple lanes) is identified
by the VIP IP-XACT. VCATB uses these bus interfaces to determine the signals required
by the PHY shell module. It connects the PHY shell module to DUT and VIP appropriately.
These signals are communicated to the template engine using Tcl variables. This allows
the PHY Shell module can be generated. The signal connections are communicated using
Tcl variables. This enables the PHY Shell module can be instantiated and connected in the
DUT Wrapper.
After the testbench has been generated, you must replace the PHY Shell module with
your simulation model. You can use the VC ATB User Extension feature and make use
of Verilog 2001 configuration capabilities to accomplish this. This can be done without
modifying the generated testbench..

Support for PHY Integration

In GUI mode, you can select whether you want to directly connect to the VIP provided
parallel PHY interface or use the PHY Shell module at the VIP selection step. If the
PHY shell module is selected, then VC AutoTestbench shows this in the testbench
hierarchy. The PHY shell module is presented like any other testbench element. It allows
for signal connection overrides in both the GUI and the config.ini file. After the testbench is
generated, you must replace the PHY Shell module with your simulation model.
Connecting to VIP
For a DUT PHY bus, you need to select not only the VIP to connect, but also how to
connect to the VIP. You can use PHY shell connection (serial) or direct connection
(parallel). For the PHY shell connection, you need to select which serial interface must be
used.
The Add New VIP right-click option lists all combinations of the possible selections. For
example, for the PCIE bus, the matched VIP is svt_pcie_device_agent. It supports both
parallel and serial connections. For serial connection, two different versions of serial
interfaces are available. Therefore, there are total of 3 different kinds of connections
supported. For each of them, the connection type and VLNV are displayed in the menu
title.

If you choose to connect a PHY bus through serial connection, the tool generates a PHY
shell module that is connected to the DUT and to the VIP. The PHY module is listed in the
TB Connections tab as a new section - PHY Module. For each module instance, all the
port signals are listed.

User Extensions

For details on the batch mode use model, see Support for PHY Integration.

User Extensions
User extensions allow you to develop and maintain your own extended codes. You can
modify the testbench and can keep the modified files under the user created user_env
and user_tests directories. By default, the extensions use the term 'user' in their file
names, variable names, object names, and so on.
The following sub-sections explain the available extensions.

Name and Location Alternatives
* Naming
You can optionally specify a prefix value to be used for file names, variable
names, object names, code elements and so on. This can be done either in the
GUI or in the [USER EXTENSIONS] section of config.ini. The specified prefix
replaces the default prefix - user in all the code references. However, this does not
apply to the "Makefile Only" controls, such as, USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR and
USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR. For example, if you specify proj1 as the prefix,
then every user in the name is proj1 instead, such as, proj1_vcatb_base_test.sv,
proj1_vcatb_env.sv, and so on.
If no prefix is specified, the default prefix - "user" is used.

User Extensions

* Directory Locations
You can specify the path/value of environment directory and/or test directory. This
can be done either in the GUI or in the [USER EXTENSIONS] section of config.ini.
Set the USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR value in Makefile.cfg to env_dir and the
USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR value in Makefile.cfg to tests_dir. User-provided
environment files and test files are pulled from the specified env_dir and tests_dir
directories respectively.
In order to incorporate user extensions, you must specify either the env_dir value or
the tests_dir value. If neither of these values is specified, the user extension support
is disabled.

Extending the Top Level Testbench
This feature allows you to insert content into the module defined by the vcatb_top.sv file.
There are two following two insertion points:
* Content provided in the user_top_includes.sv file which is inserted before the
vcatb_top module is declared. This allows for additional files to be included.
* Content provided by user_top.sv file is inserted at the end of the vcatb_top module.

User Extensions

Both files must be placed in the $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR directory. If these files are
present then they are automatically included by the generated testbench.
Based on its placement, this code can reference vcatb_top.sv content, if necessary. This
should be done sparingly, however, to avoid dependencies on specific naming, content,
and so on.

Extending the Testbench and Test Management
The testbench management can be adjusted by providing environment and test
implementations for different methodology-defined phases. To support this create
user versions of vcatb_base_test.sv (that is, $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/
user_vcatb_base_test.sv) and vcatb_env.sv (that is, $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/
user_vcatb_env.sv) files which include the desired adjustments.
If the files are available, these are included automatically and the Auto Testbench versions
of these files are extended from their user counterparts. For example,
* class vcatb_base_test extends user_vcatb_base_test;
* class vcatb_env extends user_vcatb_env;

Support for Additional Tests
To provide additional tests using the user extension flow, the additional tests must
be placed in the $USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR directory. You must also create a
user_test_package.sv file located in the $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR directory. This
file should be modeled after the vcatb_test.pkg file and contain include directives for
all the additional tests. The actual file names (such as, ts.my_test.sv) can be used here,
without any directory prefix, as the $USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR directory is added as
an incdir by the Makefile.
The generated Makefile provides additional support for this capability by including
$USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR in the list of directories it searches to identify valid test
names.
The generated testbench includes these additional tests by including
$USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/user_test_package.sv in vcatb_test.pkg
automatically, if available. This automatically includes all of the test files included in the
user_test_package.sv file.
User tests must also adhere to the basic testcase design criteria so that they work properly
in this flow:
* Test classes must extend from vcatb_base_test
* Test files must follow 'ts.*.sv' test file naming convention

User Extensions

Examples of correctly specified testcases can be found in the list of generated test files
located in the tests_dir directory.

Support for Additional Files
In addition to the user test management and user test files , you might have other files
which they need to include into the system. These files are included automatically if they
are specified in a file list stored as $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/user_file_list.f.
This file list can include VLOG or SV files, packages or programs, other file lists (file lists
prefaced with the -f option), and so on. The only requirement is that the paths which are
specified in the file list are hard paths. For example, if additional files are stored locally
in $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR, you need the $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/ prefix. If
stored elsewhere on the network, you must specify the files with a relative path or a hard
path.

Extending Build Management
As indicated in the previous sections, there are some build extensions which are built
into the Makefile. In addition, you can also add your own Makefile extension. Create
$USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/Makefile containing any additional settings you want
to add. The $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/Makefile file is included by the top level
Makefile after all of its variables are specified and before any rules are defined.
This can be used to modify any of the top level Makefile variables that are referenced in
the subsequent rules.

Initial User Extension Development
It is recommended to use the GUI or the config.ini process to enable your extensions.
Create user environment and/or test directories, set the appropriate prefix, env_dir, and
tests_dir values in GUI or config.ini, and generate the testbench with this information.
The benefit of following this process is that every regeneration includes all the user
extensions added previously.
During the initial user extension development, however, it might be necessary to forego
some of these steps. For example, you might want to take an existing testbench area,
incorporate some extensions, get them working, and then go back and make them official.
Set env_dir and test values in the original testbench description. You can accomplish
this by modifying the Makefile.cfg file in the generated testbench. You can specify
USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR and/or USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR values. Specifying
either of these values results in enabling the user extensions features and incorporating
the user extensions in the testbench.

User Extensions Flow

Delaying this decision to the `compilation' phase is only supported for the env_dir and
tests_dir settings. It is not supported for the prefix setting. Implementing this support
manually, that is, by modifying Makefile.cfg, also implies that these changes are not
picked up on subsequent testbench generation. That is, env_dir and tests_dir settings
not included in the testbench description are not included in the generated testbench.

User Extensions Flow
* Enter the Testbench features, including the identification of user_env and user_tests
directories.
* Generate original Testbench
Links are automatically established to user_env and user_tests.
* Regenerate the testbench
Links are automatically established to user_env and user_tests.

Support for Execution Manager Integration
The generated testbench that the VCATB application creates includes a basic
configuration file at <output>/eman/eman/vcatb_eman.emc, which can be used with
Execution Manager. This provides basic rules for compiling the generated testbench and
running tests. The generated configuration file can be included by another user-created
configuration file, and the build rules and test execution rules can be reused.

To simplify batch-mode operation, a basic "wrapper" is created to encapsulate the required
Verdi VC AutoTestbench capabilities into an easy-to-use batch mode tool.
Use the following command to invoke the wrapper:
vcatb -dut_ipxact/-d <dut_ipxact_file_to_be_processed>
-config/-c <ini_files_to_be_processed>
-protocol_ipxact_dir/-p
<protocol_ipxact_file_directories_to_be_processed>
-output_dir/-o <output_directory>

The following are the user-specified parameters for the wrapper:
* The -dut_ipxact or the -d option specifies the location of the DUT IP-XACT file to be
processed.
If the specified DUT IP-XACT (XML) file does not exist or cannot be read by the tool,
the tool issues an error.
* The -config or the -c option specifies the user input files to be processed.
Multiple user input files can be specified, separated by a space. If any of the specified
input files do not exist or cannot be read by the tool, the tool issues an error.
* The -protocol_ipxact_dir or the -p option specifies one or more directories where
Protocol IP-XACT files can be found.
Multiple directories can be specified, separated by a space.
* The -output_dir or the -o option specifies the directory to which output files and
directories should be written.
If the specified directory does not exist, the tool creates the directory. If the specified
directory already exists, the tool overwrites the files in that directory.
In addition to the DUT IP-XACT file, the templates require access to other IP-XACT
files that specify information about the various VIPs that are involved in the testbench
generation process. A template file can include Tcl code to open and read a VIP IPXACT (XML) file (that is located in the $DESIGNWARE_HOME directory structure).
Since the DUT IP-XACT file is specified on the command line, that file is automatically
read by the tool (as an XML file).

INI File Contents
The following are the sections that can appear in a user-specified INI file:
* Recipe Selection
The tool uses the simulation.uvm.vcs.xml recipe which generates a UVM simulation
testbench suitable for running with VCS. Different recipe files can be selected using
the following section in the INI file. The recipe selected must be present in the Verdi
installation or it must exist in the directory pointed to by VCATB_TEMPLATE_PATH.
;Recipe File selection
[RECIPE]
file = simulation.uvm.reg.vcs.xml

Lines that start with a semicolon in an INI file are comments.
* Clock Generators
The information for a clock generator can be specified with the following section. Note
that, only a single clock is supported.
;Clock generator attributes
[CLOCK_GENERATOR]
name = SystemClock
cycle = 200
initial_value = 0

* Reset Generators
The information for a reset generator can be specified with the following section. Note
that, only a single reset is supported.
;Reset generator attributes
[RESET_GENERATOR]
name = SystemReset
cycle = 150
initial_value = 0
clock_source = SystemClock

* VIP Environment
VIP environment values can be specified using the following section in the INI file. The
third_party_vip_home setting is possible with VIP environment.

;VIP environment attributes
[VIP_ENVIRONMENT]
designware_home = /<path>/dw_home
design_dir = /<path>/design_dir
third_party_vip_home = /<path>/third_party_vip_home

* Memory Map
The memory map format is given below. The memory map is related to IP-XACT DUT
components like AXI fabric and so on. It consists of the following information:
The comments section shows the actual IP-XACT information for the Initiator for that
target.
initiator_bus: Consists of Component and Bus interface.
initiator_global_addr: This is derived from Initiators baseAddress from IPXACT.
initiator_local_addr: This is derived from Initiators baseAddress from IP-XACT.
initiator_mask: This is derived from Initiators range
target_global_addr: This is same as Initiators baseAddress instead of targets
baseAddress.
target_local_addr: This is derived from targets baseAddress from IP-XACT.
target_mask: This is derived from targets range
The above local_addr, global_addr, and mask information are similar to
those used in VIP.
[MEMORY_MAP]
;Initiator
;Name: Structure_inst.CPU0
;Base Addr: 0xFFE0000
;Range: 0x1000
;Target
;Name = Structure_inst.RAM0
;BaseAddr = 0x1000
;Range = 0x1000
initiator_bus = Structure_inst.CPU0
initiator_global_addr = 0xFFE000
initiator_local_addr = 0xFFE000
initiator_mask = 0xFFF
target_bus = Structure_inst.RAM0
target_global_addr = 0xFFE000
target_local_addr = 0x0
target_mask = 0xFFF

[MEMORY_MAP]
;Initiator
;Name: Structure_inst.CPU1
;Base Addr: 0xAAAA00
;Range: 0x1000
;Target
;Name = Structure_inst.RAM0
;BaseAddr = 0x1000
;Range = 0x1000
initiator_bus = Structure_inst.CPU1
initiator_global_addr = 0xAAAA000
initiator_local_addr = 0xAAAA000
initiator_mask = 0xFFF
target_bus = Structure_inst.RAM0
target_global_addr = 0xAAAA000
target_local_addr = 0x1000
target_mask = 0xFFF
