Support for Execution Manager Integration
The generated testbench that the VCATB application creates includes a basic
configuration file at <output>/eman/eman/vcatb_eman.emc, which can be used with
Execution Manager. This provides basic rules for compiling the generated testbench and
running tests. The generated configuration file can be included by another user-created
configuration file, and the build rules and test execution rules can be reused.

To simplify batch-mode operation, a basic "wrapper" is created to encapsulate the required
Verdi VC AutoTestbench capabilities into an easy-to-use batch mode tool.
Use the following command to invoke the wrapper:
vcatb -dut_ipxact/-d <dut_ipxact_file_to_be_processed>
-config/-c <ini_files_to_be_processed>
-protocol_ipxact_dir/-p
<protocol_ipxact_file_directories_to_be_processed>
-output_dir/-o <output_directory>

The following are the user-specified parameters for the wrapper:
* The -dut_ipxact or the -d option specifies the location of the DUT IP-XACT file to be
processed.
If the specified DUT IP-XACT (XML) file does not exist or cannot be read by the tool,
the tool issues an error.
* The -config or the -c option specifies the user input files to be processed.
Multiple user input files can be specified, separated by a space. If any of the specified
input files do not exist or cannot be read by the tool, the tool issues an error.
* The -protocol_ipxact_dir or the -p option specifies one or more directories where
Protocol IP-XACT files can be found.
Multiple directories can be specified, separated by a space.
* The -output_dir or the -o option specifies the directory to which output files and
directories should be written.
If the specified directory does not exist, the tool creates the directory. If the specified
directory already exists, the tool overwrites the files in that directory.
In addition to the DUT IP-XACT file, the templates require access to other IP-XACT
files that specify information about the various VIPs that are involved in the testbench
generation process. A template file can include Tcl code to open and read a VIP IPXACT (XML) file (that is located in the $DESIGNWARE_HOME directory structure).
Since the DUT IP-XACT file is specified on the command line, that file is automatically
read by the tool (as an XML file).

INI File Contents
The following are the sections that can appear in a user-specified INI file:
* Recipe Selection
The tool uses the simulation.uvm.vcs.xml recipe which generates a UVM simulation
testbench suitable for running with VCS. Different recipe files can be selected using
the following section in the INI file. The recipe selected must be present in the Verdi
installation or it must exist in the directory pointed to by VCATB_TEMPLATE_PATH.
;Recipe File selection
[RECIPE]
file = simulation.uvm.reg.vcs.xml

Lines that start with a semicolon in an INI file are comments.
* Clock Generators
The information for a clock generator can be specified with the following section. Note
that, only a single clock is supported.
;Clock generator attributes
[CLOCK_GENERATOR]
name = SystemClock
cycle = 200
initial_value = 0

* Reset Generators
The information for a reset generator can be specified with the following section. Note
that, only a single reset is supported.
;Reset generator attributes
[RESET_GENERATOR]
name = SystemReset
cycle = 150
initial_value = 0
clock_source = SystemClock

* VIP Environment
VIP environment values can be specified using the following section in the INI file. The
third_party_vip_home setting is possible with VIP environment.

;VIP environment attributes
[VIP_ENVIRONMENT]
designware_home = /<path>/dw_home
design_dir = /<path>/design_dir
third_party_vip_home = /<path>/third_party_vip_home

* Memory Map
The memory map format is given below. The memory map is related to IP-XACT DUT
components like AXI fabric and so on. It consists of the following information:
The comments section shows the actual IP-XACT information for the Initiator for that
target.
initiator_bus: Consists of Component and Bus interface.
initiator_global_addr: This is derived from Initiators baseAddress from IPXACT.
initiator_local_addr: This is derived from Initiators baseAddress from IP-XACT.
initiator_mask: This is derived from Initiators range
target_global_addr: This is same as Initiators baseAddress instead of targets
baseAddress.
target_local_addr: This is derived from targets baseAddress from IP-XACT.
target_mask: This is derived from targets range
The above local_addr, global_addr, and mask information are similar to
those used in VIP.
[MEMORY_MAP]
;Initiator
;Name: Structure_inst.CPU0
;Base Addr: 0xFFE0000
;Range: 0x1000
;Target
;Name = Structure_inst.RAM0
;BaseAddr = 0x1000
;Range = 0x1000
initiator_bus = Structure_inst.CPU0
initiator_global_addr = 0xFFE000
initiator_local_addr = 0xFFE000
initiator_mask = 0xFFF
target_bus = Structure_inst.RAM0
target_global_addr = 0xFFE000
target_local_addr = 0x0
target_mask = 0xFFF

[MEMORY_MAP]
;Initiator
;Name: Structure_inst.CPU1
;Base Addr: 0xAAAA00
;Range: 0x1000
;Target
;Name = Structure_inst.RAM0
;BaseAddr = 0x1000
;Range = 0x1000
initiator_bus = Structure_inst.CPU1
initiator_global_addr = 0xAAAA000
initiator_local_addr = 0xAAAA000
initiator_mask = 0xFFF
target_bus = Structure_inst.RAM0
target_global_addr = 0xAAAA000
target_local_addr = 0x1000
target_mask = 0xFFF

* VIP Compile Options
Most VIPs support a set of compile-time options and macro constants which control
various features of the VIP. These are applied during the compile phase using the
+define+<option>=<value> syntax. Values which are supplied in this section are
checked to validate that the option provided are recognized by the VIP.
; Set a VIP compile-time option
[VIP_DEFINES]
UVM_DISABLE_AUTO_ITEM_RECORDING = 1

UVM_PACKER_MAX_BYTES = 1500000
SVT_AXI_MAX_ADDR_WIDTH = 32

* Compile Directives
General compile-time options can be provided in this section. Each value is applied
as-is on the compile command.

title: 1 2012 in default config
text:
tion
[VIP_DEFINES]
UVM_DISABLE_AUTO_ITEM_RECORDING = 1

UVM_PACKER_MAX_BYTES = 1500000
SVT_AXI_MAX_ADDR_WIDTH = 32

* Compile Directives
General compile-time options can be provided in this section. Each value is applied
as-is on the compile command. This section is not name/value pairs like the other
sections. No checking is performed on these values.
; Set a general compile-time option
[COMPILE_DIRECTIVES]
-kdb=common_elab
-quiet
+define+ENABLE_DUT_DEBUG=1

* Elaboration Directives
General elaboration-time options can be provided in this section. Each value is applied
as-is on the elaboration command. This section is not name/value pairs like the other
sections. Checking is not performed on these values.
; Set a general elaboration-time option
[ELABORATION_DIRECTIVES]
-debug_access+pp
-P pli.tab
msglog.o

* Runtime Directives
General run-time options can be provided in this section. Each value is applied as-is on
the elaboration command. This section is not name/value pairs like the other sections.
Checking is not performed on these values.
; Set a general run-time option
[RUNTIME_DIRECTIVES]
-cm line

* Ad Hoc Signal Declaration
There may be a need to declare ad hoc signals in the DUT wrapper. The following INI
section can be used to declare a single signal.
[SIGNALS]
name = ad_hoc_signal0
type = bit
value = 1'b0

The name and type entries are required. The value entry is optional, if it is not provided
then the signal is declared and not initialized to any value. For example, the entry
above results in the following signal declaration in the dut_wrapper:
bit ad_hoc_signal0 = 1'b0;

The following is the entry:
[SIGNALS]
name = ad_hoc_signal1
type = logic [3:0]

This results in the following signal being declared:
logic [3:0] ad_hoc_signal1;

* VIP Signal Connection Override
The tool attempts to automatically connect VIP signals to DUT signals. There may be
some situations where you want to override the automated connections. The following
INI section can be used to achieve overrides for VIP signal connections:
[VIP_SIGNAL_CONNECTION_OVERRIDE]
name = ahb_if_0.slave_if[0].hsel
value = ad_hoc_signal0

The value provided to the 'name' entry should be the hierarchical path to the VIP
interface signal to be assigned. The hierarchical path should begin with the VIP
interface instance. Since the instance name of this interface is not known when the tool
is first invoked, these connections likely need to be declared in the INI file used by a
second invocation of the tool.
The value provided to the 'value' entry could be an ad hoc signal that was previously
declared, or it could be a constant value. The tool uses the value that is provided as a
string.
* DUT Signal Connection Override
The tool attempts to automatically connect VIP signals to DUT signals. There may be
some situations where you want to override the automated connections. The following
INI section can be used to achieve overrides of DUT signal connections:
[DUT_SIGNAL_CONNECTION_OVERRIDE]
name = Structure_inst.CPU1_HSel
value = ad_hoc_signal0

The value provided to the 'name' entry should be the hierarchical path to the DUT port
to be assigned. The hierarchical path should begin with the DUT instance. Since the
name of this instance is not known when the tool is first invoked, these connections
need to be declared in the INI file used by a second invocation of the tool.
The value provided to the 'value' entry can be an ad hoc signal that was previously
declared, or it can be a constant value. The tool uses the value that is provided as a
string.
* DUT Parameter Override

The tool attempts to populate DUT parameters with default values from DUT IP-XACT
file. However, the default value in the DUT IP-XACT file may not match actual value in the
DUT file. The following INI section can be used to override a DUT parameter value:
[DUT_PARAMETER_OVERRIDE]
name = cci400_inst.AWUSER_WIDTH
value = 2

The value provided to the 'name' entry should be the hierarchical path to the DUT
parameter to be assigned. The hierarchical path should begin with the DUT instance.
Since the name of this instance is not known when the tool is first invoked, these
connections need to be declared in the INI file used by a second invocation of the tool.
The value provided to the 'value' entry is a constant value. The tool uses the value that is
provided as a string.
* DUT Files
The DUT IP-XACT may contain information about how to load the DUT, but the
information is optional and therefore this information may not be present. The following
INI section can be provided which causes the dut_files file to be populated with the
provided values:
[DUT_FILES]
path_to_dut_file1
path_to_dut_file2
17.18UVM REG

To support UVM REG, the tool assumes that you have already run ralgen and
generated the uvm_reg_block extension for their DUT. The name of the file that
contains the register model and the name of the model itself must be provided through
the INI file.
[UVM_REG]
file = ral_MemoryMap_MCU.sv
model = ral_sys_MemoryMap_MCU
ralgen_options = -uvm -t MemoryMap_MCU dut.ralf
enabled = true

* PHY_CONNECTION
If the DUT exposes the parallel interface of a PHY, then the DUT Connection section
allows you to select whether the generated testbench should include a PHY Shell
Module or if the testbench should instead connect the VIP directly to the parallel
interface (if the VIP supports this). The busdefs are identified using the VLNV, and if
any of the settings are not specified, then it is treated as a wildcard situation for that
setting.
To set up for a specific bus type identified by VLNV:
[PHY_CONNECTION]
parallel_busdef_vendor = synopsys.com
parallel_busdef_library = busdef.phy
parallel_busdef_name = pipeV4
parallel_busdef_version = 4.1
serial_busdef_vendor = synopsys.com
serial_busdef_library = busdef.phy
serial_busdef_name = pcie-txrx-phy
serial_busdef_version = 2.0
direct_connect = [0|1]

To set up for a specific bus instance:
[PHY_CONNECTION]
dut_bus_name = ddr4_dfi_if_inst.DWC_ddr_umctl2_dfi

serial_busdef_vendor = synopsys.com
serial_busdef_library = busdef.phy
serial_busdef_name = pcie-txrx-phy
serial_busdef_version = 2.0
direct_connect = [0|1]

* COMPONENT_CONTROL_OPTIONS
You can select the control options in this section. Each section instance defines
settings that are to be applied to an individual component or component view. To
differentiate controls associated with different component versions, the component is
represented by its VLNV value. If any of the VLNV settings is not specified, then it is
treated as a wildcard situation for that setting. If the view value is not specified, then the
settings are applied to all of the component's views.
[COMPONENT_CONTROL_OPTIONS]
vendor = arm.com
library = Cores
name = CORTEX15
version = r4p1_0
view = verilog
use_file_list = [0|1]
use_y = [0|1]
add_file_based_incdir = [0|1]
add_includes_to_file_list = [0|1]
add_synopsys_sim_ver = [0|1]
add_v2k = [0|1]
add_vhdl87 = [0|1]

* DUT_PARAMETER_OVERRIDE
VC AutoTestbench attempts to populate DUT parameters with the default value from
DUT IP-XACT file. However, the default value in the DUT IP-XACT file may not match
the actual value in the DUT file.
The following INI section can be used to specify overrides for the DUT parameter
value:
[DUT_PARAMETER_OVERRIDE]
name = cci400_inst.AWUSER_WIDTH
value = 2

The value provided to the name entry should be the hierarchical path to the DUT
parameter to be assigned. The hierarchical path should begin with the DUT instance.
Since the instance name of this instance is not known when the tool is first invoked,
these connections likely need to be declared in the INI file used by a second invocation
of the tool.
The value provided to the value entry is a constant value. The template uses the value
that is provided as a string.

* TESTBENCH_TOP
In case you want to use your own DUT wrapper instead of using the one generated by
the tool, you must specify the module name of the provided wrapper and the full path of
the DUT inside the wrapper module.
[TESTBENCH_TOP]
module = testbench_top
dut_path = user_dut_inst

* VIP Version
The latest version of the VIPs in the DESIGNWARE_HOME directory (and the directories
specified using the VC_VCATB_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH environment variable) are scanned
by the tool for possible VIP matches.
* Unmatched "VLNV" Signatures
You can indicate that unmatched DUT VLNV signatures can be ignored using the
following section in the INI file.
; Ignore unmatched DUT VLNV signatures.
[unmatched_dut_VLNV]
ignore = 1

Support for DUT Parameters (Batch Mode)
VC AutoTestbench populates DUT parameters with the default value from the DUT IPXACT file. However, the default value in the DUT IP-XACT file may not match the actual
value in the DUT file.
To override the DUT parameter values, add the [DUT_PARAMETER_OVERRIDE] section in
the config.ini file.
[DUT_PARAMETER_OVERRIDE]
name = cci400_inst.AWUSER_WIDTH
value = 2

The value provided to the name entry is the hierarchical path of the DUT parameter to be
assigned. The hierarchical path must begin with the DUT instance. Since the instance
name of this instance is not known when the tool is initially invoked, these connections
need to be declared in the .ini file used when the tool is invoked later.
The value provided to the value entry is a constant value. The template uses the value
that is provided as a string.

Component Fileset Settings (Batch Mode)
VC AutoTestbench provides you the component fileset setting to specify more information
to build a component.
You can define settings for an individual component or a component view in the
[COMPONENT_CONTROL_OPTIONS] section of the config.ini file.
To differentiate controls associated with different component versions, the component is
represented by its VLNV value. If any of the VLNV settings are not specified, it is treated
as a wildcard situation for that setting. If the view value is not specified, then the settings
are applied to all of views of the component.
An example of the [COMPONENT_CONTROL_OPTIONS] section, where, 0 corresponds to
disabling the option and 1 corresponds to enabling the option:
[COMPONENT_CONTROL_OPTIONS]
vendor = arm.com
library = Cores
name = CORTEX15
version = r4p1_0
view = verilog
use_file_list = [0|1]
use_y = [0|1]
add_file_based_incdir = [0|1]
add_includes_to_file_list = [0|1]
add_synopsys_sim_ver = [0|1]
add_v2k = [0|1]
add_vhdl87 = [0|1]

You can specify additional -y, +incdir, general options, and files for use with a specific
component or component view in the [COMPONENT_COMPILE_DIRECTIVES] section. Each

add_synopsys_sim_ver = [0|1]
add_v2k = [0|1]
add_vhdl87 = [0|1]

Overriding the Testbench Top (Batch Mode)
If you want to use your own DUT wrapper instead of using the one generated by the tool,
you need to specify the module name of the provided wrapper and the full path of the DUT
inside the wrapper module.
You can specify your own module and the DUT path in the [TESTBENCH_TOP] section in
the config.ini file as follows:
[TESTBENCH_TOP]
module = testbench_top
dut_path = user_dut_inst

Support for PHY Integration (Batch Mode)
If the DUT exposes the parallel interface of a PHY, you can select whether the generated
testbench must include a PHY shell module or the testbench should connect the VIP
directly to the parallel interface (if the VIP supports this) using the [PHY_CONNECTION]
section in the config.ini file. The busdefs are identified using the VLNV, and if any
settings are left unspecified, then it is treated as a wildcard situation for that setting.
Example to set the PHY connection for a specific bus type identified by VLNV:
[PHY_CONNECTION]
parallel_busdef_vendor = synopsys.com
parallel_busdef_library = busdef.phy
parallel_busdef_name = pipeV4
parallel_busdef_version = 4.1
serial_busdef_vendor = synopsys.com
serial_busdef_library = busdef.phy
serial_busdef_name = pcie-txrx-phy
serial_busdef_version = 2.0
direct_connect = [0|1]

Support for Verdi Machine Learning Library
Starting with this release, Verdi provides you an unified platform to collect data from EDA
tools and allows you to access data for machine learning applications. This platform
includes three abstract layers, such as table, model, and application.Each layer can read
and write from the database of APIs.
In the table layer, the tables are constructed using both C++ and Python. In this layer, you
can construct your own tables and extract specific data by any utility. You can also read
these tables using Python.
In the model layer, pre-defined types and properties can be selected to extract data from
the database by different utilities. These tables can be read using Python as well where
pre-defined relations between types are resolved. Currently, only 'waveform' model is
In the application layer, both the data collection and access methods are provided in the
'Database' class of the 'verdilearn' package in Python. You can take the tables as an input
to their machine learning applications.
These tables provide information about the C++ and Python APIs.

WISIM Replay Block Stimuli on SoC
All the ports are dumped to the FSDB file in a block-level simulation with block-level
testbench. Then, the captured block-level stimuli are applied on the SoC simulation
environment. During the SoC simulation, the block inputs are overwritten by the captured
block-level stimuli. At last, the two FSDB files dumping from block and SoC simulations
are compared. You can specify the stimuli and compare mapping files or it can be
generated automatically.
Figure 409

Use Model of WISIM Replay Block Stimuli on SoC

The concept of time-frame is depicted in the following figure. You can specify the time
range (Begin_Time and End_Time) for replay simulation and applying FSDB stimuli. While

WISIM Replay Block Stimuli on SoC

running the simulation with WISIM Testbench until Begin_Time (replay), block-level stimuli
from Begin_Time (stimuli) is applied to the SoC-TB. In other words, the FSDB stimuli are
shifted. After the maximum time of FSDB stimuli, the Replay simulation may continue
running until End_Time (replay).

To use WISIM to replay block stimuli on SoC, perform the following steps:
* Preparation (for VCS three-step flow):
Analyze the SoC design using vlogan and vhdlan for SystemVerilog and VHDL design,
respectively, and prepare the corresponding script for the analyzed library. Prepare the
configuration file and the corresponding scripts.
* Extract:
Generate WISIM testbench using the -replay_extract option. With Auto_Map and
Auto_Compare_Map, the automatic mapping files are generated in this phase. When
the mapping files or configuration are modified, you can add the -remap option after
-replay_extract to run the remap flow. You can skip generating the design by setting
the environment variable WISIM_SKIP_CG to 1, if you use VCS three-step flow. Then,
load designs from library (analyzed with -kdb=common_elab) with -lib options with
-replay_extract.
* Compile:
Compile the SoC design and WISIM testbench, using the -replay_compile option.
If you compile in the SoC environment, add wi_test.sv during compilation (two-step
flow) or analyze wi_test.sv into witbLib and add WI_TB_TOP (three-step flow) during
elaboration in compile script.
* Simulate:
Run simulation for the SoC design by applying FSDB stimuli under WISIM
testbench, using the -replay_sim option. With Compare_Map or Auto_Compare_Map,
wi_result.fsdb is automatically compared with the block-level one. It is able to
re-compare the same FSDB files with different options (Compare_Option) or signal
mapping (Compare_Map and Auto_Compare_Map) by adding the -recompare option
after -replay_sim.

PureLog Interface
PureLog includes three types of windows:
* SmartLog: The SmartLog window is mainly used to navigate certain log and is opened
by default with the binary PureLog. You can also open a new SmartLog window
through the SmartLog menu (Tools > New SmartLog) or the SmartSheet menu (Tools
> New SmartSheet).
* SmartSheet: The SmartSheet window is mainly used to navigate PureLog DB and is
opened by default with the binary PureLogDB. You can also open a new SmartSheet
window through the SmartLog menu (Tools > SmartSheet).
* nWave: The nWave window is used to visualize log messages through query
conditions that can help you comprehend log messages efficiently.

The SmartLog engine can be used to read and traverse log files in a readable view.
SmartLog loads a log file with a specific format that shows a structured presentation of the
log contents, thus providing a flexible and convenient use model for debugging.

The connection between the log file and the Verdi platform is built according to the
hyperlink rule files and the partitioning rule files.
For more information about SmartLog, refer to the SmartLog Tutorial chapter of Verdi User
Guide and Tutorial.
In addition to the classical functions, PureLog adds many advanced features to SmartLog.

Cross Log Probing
In some cases, you need to cross-reference multiple logs. The following are the two use
model examples:
* One simulation run generates two logs with time information. While checking these two
logs, many cross references are required.
In this scenario, you can use the log-probing by time feature.
* Open one log twice in two tabs as follows:
The first one is kept as full log without any filtering.
The second one is planned to be filtered.
While checking these two logs, many cross references are required between the
full-text-log and filtered-log.
In this scenario, you can use the log-probing by line feature.
To open the Log Probing dialog box, use the highlighted option on the toolbar.

The probing is mutual mapping. For example, if Log1 is set to probe Log2, then Log2 is

The probe mapping is broken once any mapping log is changed to "none-probing" status.
The breaking is also in mutual way. The probing includes two factors: <Time>
and <Line>.

Traverse Related Message Search Mechanism
PureLog traces 1000 blocks upward or downward from the starting block that you rightclick. A block is a group of messages with the first line matched by the partitioning rule, for
example, UVM header.
PureLog analyzes the first three lines of each block because:
* The key-value attributes are most likely to sit in the first few lines.
* It can speed up the searching.
Key and value are matched by the exact match mode by default.

Searching Messages With Fuzzy Match Options
1. Click the search settings icon to open the search settings dialog box.
Figure 440

Search Settings Icon

2. In the Matching Modes tab, change the matching mode of Key and Value to
FuzzyMatch.
Figure 441

Set the FuzzyMatch Option

3. In the Fuzzy Match tab, customize the fuzzy match settings of both the string and the
value match text. The type is automatically determined; for example, addr is the string
type and 0x2000000001a2a740 is the value type.

Figure 442

Customize the FuzzyMatch Settings

Higher String > Max Distance allows more fuzziness when searching the string.
If the Value > Max Value Difference mode is enabled, it is considered a fuzzy
match only when the difference between the trace and the match attribute is not
greater than the entered number.
If the Value > Max Number of Bits Difference mode is enabled, it is considered
a fuzzy match only when the number of bits difference between the trace and the
match attribute is not greater than the entered number.
4. Click OK and save the modified RC file.

When debugging the log, you may want to compare the error log with the golden log to
see the differences. However, sometimes there are a lot of differences at a certain point
that make it hard to get clues from it.
Figure 469

Compare Error Log With Golden Log

The general solution is to dump the waveform, but it requires rerunning the simulation that
takes a lot of time. In addition, the design verification engineers might not know a design
very well and may put in extra efforts to pick signals from the design under test (DUT).
PureLog provides a way to dump the waveform from the log directly. The advantage of this
feature is that you do not need to rerun the simulation and also do not need to pick signals
from the DUT. You only need to know the log well. In the log, you can show messages

a way to dump the waveform from the log directly. The advantage of this
feature is that you do not need to rerun the simulation and also do not need to pick signals

about interface connection, such as UART transaction, Ethernet Tx/Rx transactions, and
so on. You can pick some of them and dump to the waveform for observation.

Signal Type of Log-to-Wave
The following are the rules for log-to-wave to determine a signal type:
* Contains only a positive integer or a value string (for example, 0x123) : bit-vector
(digital)
* Contains a floating point number or a non-positive integer : analog
* Contains non-numerical data : enum

The PureLog DB enables you to keep the information of logs through the logCompile
script. Whenever you need to check a log for debugging, you can access it through APIs
or by using the simple UI query system. Some PureLog features also rely on the PureLog
DB. Generally, the PureLog DB can be written by the daily regression script at night and
can be accessed by you or PureLog in daytime.

Benefits of PureLog DB
The PureLog DB has the following benefits:
* Better performance: Most PureLog features can have better performance with the
PureLog DB.
* Less memory consumption: Most PureLog features can have less memory
consumption with the PureLog DB.
* AI technology: AI-related features of PureLog rely on the PureLog database.
* Customized application: You can access the PureLog DB through APIs or by using the
query system UI. Based on APIs and query systems, it is easy to develop a customized
application. It means that you can have your own debugging way.

Overall Flow in Simulation Application
Figure 480

Flow in Simulation Application

Setting Up the PureLog DB Server
Before saving or reading logs from the PureLog DB, you need to launch the server.
PureLog provides the msgdbControl utility to start or stop the server.

Starting the Server
Run the following command:
msgdbControl -start_server -storage_path <database storage path>

After starting the server, you can compile logs by logCompile and debug on DB debug
platform.

Stopping the Server
Run the following command:
msgdbControl -stop_server -storage_path <database storage path>

Remember to stop server:
* When you finish debugging.
* Before you want to clean up the DB storage.

Restarting the Server
You can restart the server under the same DB storage path. The compiled logs are
preserved.
msgdbControl -stop_server -storage_path <database storage path>

%> msgdbControl -start_server -storage_path <database storage path>
%> logCompile <opts> # compile/debug
%> msgdbControl -stop_server -storage_path <database storage path>
%> msgdbControl -start_server -storage_path <database storage path> #
restart server

Compiling Logs Into the PureLog DB
PureLog provides the logCompile utility to compile log information into the PureLog DB.
The utility supports CSV format and customized format.

CSV Format
(-log_type="csv")
logCompile
[-log_type="csv"]
-storage_path="<database_storage_path>"
-project_name="<project_name>"
-log_list="<log.ls>"
-separator=','
[-comment='#']
[-none_regexp='-+']
[-quotechar='"']
[-escapechar="\"]
[-hyper_rule="<hyper_rule_path>"]
[-date ="date"]

In case of CSV format, logCompile removes leading and trailing whitespace for each cell
and skips a blank line.
The CSV file list is specified in -log_list="<log.ls>".In this input file, each line includes
two sections. The left side is the input file path, and the right side is the database file path
to be saved.
Example log.ls file
./trace1.csv user_case/trace1.log
./trace2.csv user_case/trace2.log
./trace3.csv user_case/trace3.log

Customized Format
(-log_type="user_defined")
logCompile
[-log_type="user_defined"]
-storage_path="<database_storage_path>"
-project_name="<project_name>"
-log_list="<log.ls>"
-attr_rule_list="<rule.ls>"
[-hyper_rule="<hyper_rule_path>"]
[-date="date"]

For customized logs, logCompile requires the -attr_rule_list option whose input is
the list of SmartLog partition rules. All features extracted from partition rules are saved into
the PureLog DB. It is recommended to use the SmartLog UI to develop partition rules first
to ensure that all features are extracted correctly.
Example rule.ls file
attr_rule_general.rc
attr_rule_dramc.rc
attr_rule_mcard.rc

The file list is specified in -log_list="<log.ls>". In this input file, each line includes two
sections. The left side is the input file path, and the right side is the database file path to
be saved.
Example log.ls file
./sim_all.log proj/case1/sim_all.log
./sim_dramc.log proj/case1/sim_dramc.log
./sim_mcardlog proj/case1/sim_mcard.log

simWLogCompile
simWLogCompile is a wrapper that enables you to run simulation and compile the
generated simulation log with logCompile simultaneously. This approach helps to reduce

the time required to generate the Log Database.

Wrapper Options
All the options that contain %> simWLogCompile -h except -virtual_path and
-central_storage_path are passed to logCompile.

The simWLogCompile wrapper is used to execute simulation and compile logs
simultaneously through the following steps:
1. Use msgdbControl to start the local Log Database server at the beginning and stop it
at the end.
2. Collect and remove the options which are used by logCompile.
3. Start local DB server.
4. Launch VCS or simv with remaining options.
5. Launch logCompile with collected options to compile target log specified by the -l
option or -incr_log option.
Ctrl+C kills VCS or simv and logCompile.
6. Stop the local DB server when both the simulation and logCompile is completed.
The following specifies the options for the simWLogCompile wrapper:
Must Have Option for Wrapper
* -incr_log <TARGET_LOG> : Specify the log to be generated by the simulation and
compiled by logCompile. This option does NOT pass to the simulation.
* -l <TARGET_LOG> : Specify the log to be generated by the simulation and compiled by
logCompile. This option passes to the simulation.
When both -l and -incr_log are present simultaneously, the value of
-incr_log is prioritized.
Primary Options for Wrapper
The primary options for wrapper are optional.
* -storage_path <STORAGE_PATH>:
Path to local storage path.
Default: ./simWLogCompileDir/db_storage
* -project_name <DB_NAME>:
Database name.
Default: defaultProjectName

* -virtual_path <VIRTUAL_PATH>:
Specify the virtual path to be stored in the database.
Default: simWLogCompileDir/<TARGET_LOG>

<TARGET_LOG> is specified by -l or -incr_log option.

* -num_process <NUM_WORKS>: Number of logCompile worker processes for parallel
compilation.
Default: 1

Types of Simulation
The simWLogCompile wrapper consists of following types of simulation:
One Step Simulation
* %> simWLogCompile vcs -debug_access+all -lca -sverilog

-ntb_opts uvm-1.1 -timescale=1ns/100ps +incdir+$SVTB_PATH
+incdir+$RTL_PATH $DUT_LOAD -R +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM
+UVM_TESTNAME=test_r8_w8_r4_w4 +ntb_random_seed=1 +UVM_NO_RELNOTES
+FSDB_ON +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_LOG_RECORD +fsdbfile+verdi_i.fsdb
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE="UVM_AWARE|RAL|TLM|MSG|HIER|PRINT" -l
simv_verdi_i.log -storage_path ./db_storage -project_name project1
-virtual_path "case1/sim.log" -attr_rule_list "./rule.ls"

Two Step Simulation
* %> vcs -debug_access+all -lca -sverilog -ntb_opts uvm-1.1

-timescale=1ns/100ps +incdir+$SVTB_PATH +incdir+$RTL_PATH $DUT_LOAD

* %> simWLogCompile ./simv +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM

+UVM_TESTNAME=test_r8_w8_r4_w4 +ntb_random_seed=1 +UVM_NO_RELNOTES
+FSDB_ON +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_LOG_RECORD +fsdbfile+verdi_i.fsdb
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE="UVM_AWARE|RAL|TLM|MSG|HIER|PRINT" -l
simv_verdi_i.log -storage_path ./db_storage -project_name project1
-virtual_path "case1/sim.log" -attr_rule_list "./rule.ls"

Compile with -incr_log option
* %> vcs -debug_access+all -lca -sverilog -ntb_opts uvm-1.1

-timescale=1ns/100ps +incdir+$SVTB_PATH +incdir+$RTL_PATH $DUT_LOAD

* %> simWLogCompile ./simv +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM

+UVM_TESTNAME=test_r8_w8_r4_w4 +ntb_random_seed=1 +UVM_NO_RELNOTES
+FSDB_ON +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_LOG_RECORD +fsdbfile+verdi_i.fsdb
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE="UVM_AWARE|RAL|TLM|MSG|HIER|PRINT"
-storage_path ./db_storage -project_name project1 -virtual_path
"case1/sim.log" -attr_rule_list "./rule.ls" -incr_log "./simv.log"

Attributes in the PureLog DB
The attributes can be kept in the PureLog DB as string type or numeral type. You can
impose only numeral query on numeral attributes through APIs or the DB debug platform.
If you expect the attributes to be saved in numeral type, here is the summary of the
supported format:
* Number with decimal point (example, 1.6)
* Verilog integer literal constants (size <= 64)
* 0x (example, 0x1200)

Batch Mode APIs
General flow to use batch mode API is as follows:
* Write a python script for querying Database.
For example, demo.py.
* Execute the python script with "pureLogDBPython"
%> pureLogDBPython demo.py

import configparser
from verdilearn.msgdb_query.log_database import LogDatabase
# Get db_uri from config file
config = configparser.ConfigParser()
config.read('./db_storage/conf/msgdb.conf')
db_uri = config['database']['uri']
db = LogDatabase(db_name="demoDB", db_uri=db_uri)
# print all logs in database
print(db.get_logs())
# get key of log "demo/riscv.log"
log_name = "demo/riscv.log"
keys = (db.get_key(log_name))
print(keys)
# get attributes of 1st error messages
df = db.get_attr(log_name,
find={'Severity':'Error'},
cursor={"limit":1})
print(df)
# found that the addr is not expected
# traverse upward with "addr" attributes
df2 = db.get_attr(log_name,
column=['Code','Severity','Reporter'],
find={"Time":{"$lte":1210565000}, "addr":"0x2000000005b6a780"})
print(df2)
# try to traverse downward with "addr" attributes
df3 = db.get_attr(log_name,
column=['Time','Code','Severity','Reporter'],
find={"Time":{"$gt":1210565000}, "addr":"0x2000000005b6a780"})
print(df3)

Unified PureLog Database

Unified PureLog Database
PureLog provides internal partition rules for VCS logs. These include compile logs and
run-time logs.
Users can apply these internal rules in file-based debugging and DB-based debugging.

File-Based Debugging
You can open logs with the following TCL command.
Use the new -SNPSLog VCS option to apply internal VCS rules instead of the original
-parRuleFile option as below:
* viaLogViewerOpenLog -file {./compile.log} -hyperRuleFile
{Generic_rule.rc} -SNPSLog VCS

Afterwards, you can see the vcs compile or simulation logs with essential attributes.
Figure 481

Logs

DB Based Debugging
You can compile the essential VCS log information into a PureLog database and then
apply the PureLog DB APIs to leverage it for data mining or data telemetry.
To do so, you can call logCompile with a new -SNPS_log VCS option instead of the
original -attr_rule_list option as shown below:
logCompile user_defined
-storage_path='./db_storage' \
-project_name='vcsLog' \
-log_list='sim_log3.ls' -SNPS_log='VCS' \
-date='2023-08-25'

Afterwards, all essential attributes are kept in the PureLog DB.

Assume that you keep saving log information in the PureLog database and one day
there is a need to debug a testcase failure. In this case, you can import the logs from the
PureLog database into the DB debug platform.
The platform helps you check message (or transaction) protocol and cross reference
multiple logs with customized queries.

Launching DB Debug Platform
From the SmartSheet menu, choose File > Open Database and open the corresponding
toolbar as shown below.
Figure 482

The File > Open Database Command

To save time to open SmartSheet, you can use the following command options to start
PureLog with the SmartSheet window:
pureLogDB
pureLog -plog_db

Opening the Database Dialog
The first page of the dialog box enables you to set the database storage path. This is
where your MessageDB files are saved.
By default, the path is stored in the ~/.messagedb.rc file. You do not need to enter the
path again next time.
Make sure the PureLog DB server is running. If it is not running, start it using the
msgdbControl command. In some cases, you can also click the Restart Server button in
the dialog box.
Figure 483

The Open Database Dialog Box (Step 1)

The second page is to specify the log list that you want to import. You can select multiple
logs of a certain case even on different dates.

Figure 484

The Open Database Dialog Box (Step 2)

Outlook of DB Debug Platform
The top window is the visualization view and the bottom one is the overlaid table view.
Figure 485

DB Debug Platform Windows

The following figures show how to open the log display setting window.
Figure 486

Log Display Icon

Figure 487

Log Display Setting Window

In the log display setting window, you can see that there are three logs opened and each
log is represented by a certain color.
PureLog collects log information from these three logs and puts them in the overlaid table
view in time sequence.
Each message has a specific color in the head of the row that helps you to know the
source of the message easily.
The visualization window has one default channel that means the overall message count
of each log. Similarly, each individual log has its own signal color that can help you to
understand the source easily.
In this case, you can see that there is one message at time 11000 coming from red log
user_case/all.log. Also, at time 11040, there is one message coming from orange log
user_case/dramc.log.

Log Display Setting
The window shows a list of logs with their dates. During debugging, you might want to
temporarily hide some logs to focus on others.
You can bring back the hidden logs later if needed. Use the Log Display Setting to adjust
which logs are visible. Select or clear the check box to show or hide messages from a log.
This setting affects both the table view and the visualization view.
For example, if you hide the orange log user_case/dramc.log, its messages and signals
do not appear in the table or visualization views. The result is shown below.

Figure 488

Log Display Settings

It is easy to see the message again just by selecting the check box.

Overlaid Table View
This section contains the main features of the table view.
* SmartSheet: The table view belongs to the read-only SmartSheet tab; so it includes
SmartSheet read-only functions. You can refer to the SmartSheet section for more
information.
* Configure Columns: You can decide to show/hide the column sequence by this
feature. The following figure shows how to open the Configure Columns dialog box.
Figure 489

Configure Columns Icon

In the Configure Columns dialog box, you can use the Up and Down buttons in the
Show Columns section to refine the sequence of the columns.
Figure 490

Configure Columns Dialog Box

* Message Visualization: You can visualize certain attributes by right-clicking a table
cell. The menu looks like the following:
Figure 491

Message Visualization Menu

* Add Count of $Attribute=$Value to Waveform: This option generates the message
count with query condition $Attribute=$Value.
For example, you want to generate a signal with query condition Sender=DMA. To do
this, select a cell with Sender=DMA and then click this option.
Figure 492

The Add Count of $Attribute=$Value to Waveform Option

The new channel is generated based on query condition Sender=DMA.

Figure 493

Signal Generated Based on Query Condition

* Add Value of $Attribute to Waveform: This option generates the signal to reflect
attribute value.
For example, you want to generate a signal to reflect the attribute value of Status. To
do this, select a cell of column Status and then click this option.
Figure 494

The Add Value of $Attribute to Waveform Option

The new channel is generated to show the value transition of attribute Status.
Figure 495

Signal Generated to Reflect the Attribute Value

* Add All Message Events to Waveform: The overall query is to show the default
overall channel that represents the message count without any query condition.
Sometimes, you may delete the default channel but want to show it later. In this case,
you can use this option to show the overall default channel.

Visualization View
The overall default channel and channels generated from the overlaid table are discussed
in the previous sections. However, you need a more flexible way to generate a channel
with customized query condition.
PureLog provides the way to input customized query condition based on a certain channel.
You can generate a new channel from the default overall channel as follows:
1. Right-click the signal pane and choose PureLog Operations > Add Log Signal from
Query of Selected.
Figure 496

PureLog Operations > Add Log Signal from Query of Selected

The Query Setting dialog box opens.
2. In the Query tab of the Query Setting dialog box, fill in the query condition.

Figure 497

Query Setting Dialog Box (Query Tab)

3. In the Y-Value tab, configure the Y-Value settings.
Figure 498

Query Setting Dialog Box (Y-Value Tab)

In the Y-Axis section, you can choose what is the meaning of the Y-Axis. There are two
selections. It can be the Message Count or the Attribute Value.

For Message Count, the default setting is the Separate mode. In this mode, the message
count is calculated by each log like the default overall channel as shown below:
Figure 499

Message Count in Separate Mode

If you want to get the sum of messages from all logs, you can switch the mode to
Accumulate and get the channel as shown below:
Figure 500

Message Count in Accumulate Mode

There is only one signal in the channel that shows the message count from all logs.
* For Attribute Value, you can pick a value that you want to show from the drop-down
list.
* In the Empty Cells section, you can choose to ignore empty cells or take an empty
cell as certain value. It is useful if the empty cell means some specific value in your log
attribute.
You can mute or unmute channels to narrow down or resume your debug scope. The mute
function is helpful when you want to focus on specific channels.
The unmute function lets you resume the debug scope smoothly. The mute or unmute of
channels also impact the overlaid table view. It means that both the windows have the
same debug scope.
The following example shows the mute or unmute flow. It includes three channels, as
shown below:
1. The first one is the default overall channel without any query condition.
2. The second one is the message count with query condition Sender=DMA.
3. The third one is the message count with query condition Sender=MEM_CARD.

Figure 501

Mute/Unmute Flow

Now, you can right-click the signal pane and choose PureLog Operations > Mute Log
Signal and its Query Data to mute the overall channel.
Figure 502

PureLog Operations > Mute Log Signal and its Query Data

You can see that the overall channel is grayed out and also the overlaid table view shows
only those messages that have Sender=DMA or Sender=MEM_CARD.

Figure 503

Grayed Out Overall Channel

Similarly, to resume the overall channel, right-click the signal pane and choose PureLog
Operations > Unmute Log Signal and its Query Data.
Figure 504

PureLog Operations > Unmute Log Signal and its Query Data

In the end, both the overall channel and the message in the table view come back.

Support Multiple SmartSheet for Cross Reference of Multiple Log
Sets
In some cases, you might want to open two log sets in different SmartSheet windows but
visualize them in one nWave window.
To do so, perform the following steps:
1. Click Tools -> New SmartSheet in the SmartSheet window to open another
SmartSheet window.
2. Open the database as usual for another log set.

Bind Design Signals to Log Message
PureLog can visualize log message in event/transaction/signal terms without re-run
simulation. There are the following two typical scenarios:
* Debug only based on log message signals, which are generated from log messages.
* Debug based on log message signals, which are generated from log messages along
with real fsdb signals generated from simulation.
The issue with the second scenario is that not all end users know the fsdb signals
related to this log message. Furthermore, adding related fsdb signals into the
waveform view is routine work and it is better if these signals are added automatically.
The solution is to allow users to specify related dumped signals to log message
signals. It is a one-time effort, which means you just need to specify the signals

Bind Design Signals to Log Message

once. Afterward, every user can visualize log message signals and all related binding
dumped signals show up automatically. There are two typical use models introduced in
following sections.

Bind Related Signals to Attribute
The solution is to apply the SmartSheet-customized click function. Users can specify the
click function of a certain column through a TCL script. The following is a sample to show
log-to-event signals along with related signals:
1. Prepare the TCL script as a click function:
========= File: ClickFunc1.tcl =========
## remove existed waveform group
if { [wvIsGroupExist $LineText] } {
wvSelectGroup $LineText
wvCut
}
## Generate Log-to-Event signals
set QueryCond \{"TargetAttribute":"$LineText"\}
smartSheetAddMsgCountToWave -queryCond $QueryCond
wvRenameGroup $QueryCond $LineText
## Open dumped fsdb file
wvOpenFile -win $_nWave3 {sim.fsdb}
wvSetActiveFile -win $_nWave3 {sim.fsdb}
## Add related signals
if { $LineText eq "AttrValue1"} {
wvAddSignal -win $_nWave3 -group "$LineText
{/scope1/hier1/related_signal_1}"
} elseif { $LineText eq "AttrValue2" } {
wvAddSignal -win $_nWave3 -group "$LineText
{/scope1/hier2/related_signal_1}"
wvAddSignal -win $_nWave3 -group "$LineText
{/scope1/hier2/related_signal_2}"
}

2. Specify the click function in the PureLog command option:
purelogDB -click_func_header "<header1> <header2> <headerN>"
-click_func_file "<file1> <file2> <fileN>"

In the command option, the click function of <header1> is described in <file1>,
the click function of <header2> is described in <file2>, and the click function of
<headerN> is specified in <fileN>.
3. Click the hyperlink on certain attributes values.

Bind Design Signals to Log Message

The event signal of this attribute value and its related fsdb dumped signals show up
automatically.
Figure 519

The TCL script can be specified by experienced users. All other end users just
need to click the script to get things done.

The PureLog timing violation solution helps you find and fix timing violations in your design
more intelligently and efficiently.
The major features are as follows:
* Summarize the timing violations based on components.
Easy to dispatch task to the right owner.
* Prioritize timing violations in different scenarios wherein, you can pick the best one for
the particular scenario.
The corrupted flip-flop with the higher number of violations.
Active drivers associated with a higher number of violations.
* Support waive or unwaive operations effectively.
Waive conditions are saved or restored for the next run.
All waiver justifications are logged into the database for projectlevel review.
* Enable rapid debug workflows for timing violation analysis.
Oneclick access to related signals, violation messages in the simulation log, and
TFV trace results.
* Selectively compile simulation logs from large regression trees using path include and

More Details of Time Check Enable
Some timing violations happen before the reset stage. You can ignore these violations.

Open or Check Timing Violation Report
To open or check the Timing Violation Report, perform the following steps:

Save or Load wavied result of current opened report

Regression Debug Automation (RDA)
The following sections describe the LCA features supported by RDA as a part of this
release:
* Static Bug Finding Root Cause Analysis (SBRCA)
* RDA Integration With Verdi VMS

During RTL simulation, Dynamic SDC Verification in VCS detects domain crossing and
glitch issues, such as reset domain crossing (RDC) or glitches. Static bug finding is a part
of RTL sign off and saves weeks of efforts in a project cycle.
Debugging violations found by static bug finding can be difficult, especially when RDC
bugs appear in large numbers, such as during MCP verification. RDA offers a Static Bug
Finding Root Cause Analysis (SBRCA) solution that automatically organizes violations into
fewer groups. This solution connects violations to waveform, source code, and simulation
log for further debugging and uses Verdi for analysis.
* Technology Overview
* SBRCA Usage
* Smart Waiver

Technology Overview
SBRCA helps you to debug the static bug findings using Verdi. VCS complies with the
SDC commands containing RDC/Glitch property. After completing simulation with VCSSDC, SBRCA checks the results of VCS-SDC and helps in finding out the violations.
SBRCA extracts details of a violation message and displays the information in a binstructured report.
RDA provides Verdi GUI to review SBRCA reports generated after analyzing violations
from the log file. Use the Verdi GUI to continue debugging in the source code, logs, and
waveform.

SBRCA Debug Flow

The VCS compilation runs with the dynamic SDC verification infrastructure in the static
bug finding mode and VCS-MCP mode. However, they are implemented with different
mechanism and cannot be executed in the same way. Therefore, SBRCA has a different
configuration template from VCS-MCP. The following figure displays the flow from VCSSDC to :

* Run simulation. The property can pass or fail.

Grouping
The Grouping feature is a core part of SBRCA. It helps to review all the violations grouped
into bins with different information, which means that the same bin might have the same
bug.
You can group violations using the following grouping rules for RDC and Glitch:
RDC
* signal_to: Group by the same signal(TO) names
* signal_from: Group by the same signal(FROM) names
* signal_both: Group by the same signal(TO) and same signal(FROM) names
* reset: Group by the same reset signals name
* sdc_command: Group by the same SDC command

Glitch
* signal_to: Group by the same signal(TO) names
* signal_from: Group by the same signal(FROM) names
* signal_both: Group by the same signal(TO) and same signal(FROM) names
* sdc_command: Group by the same SDC command

Loading RDA in Verdi VMS
You need to use RDA plugin to load RDA in Verdi VMS. To invoke the RDA plugin, perform
the following steps:
1. Add RDA plugin to synopsys_eman.setup.
plugins:
- rda:
<VERDI_HOME>/platform/linux64/bin/rcaIntgrFlow/python38/rca_plugin.so

where <VERDI_HOME> is the full path of Verdi.
2. Load the RDA plugin in your .emc file.
plugins:
- rda

3. Register a load RDA report template using the following command:
vms admin register_custom_template -t $VERDI_HOME/share/autoRCA/
python38/etc/vms/web_template/load_rda_report.emd -a

The Open RDA report button is added to the Verdi VMS GUI.

Enabling RDA Binning
RDA binning is always enabled in the RDA plugin.

Enabling Debug Facilitator/RCA
Define the debug engines Debug Facilitator and DUTRCA. Enable these engines for the
error patterns that you want to analyze.
Debug facilitator is defined by default; you need to include DF.emc as shown in the
following command:
include:
- $VERDI_HOME/share/autoRCA/python38/etc/vms/engine_template/DF.emc

However, you need to define DUTRCA as shown in the following commands:
debug_engines :
- name: DUTRCA
cmd: $current_dir/dutrca_debug_engine_cmd.sh
log_file: $${EMAN_TEST_NAME}_dutrca_debug_engine.log
run_dir: $current_dir/DUTRCA/$$EMAN_TEST_PATH
custom_values:
REF_CL_WORK_DIR: $$EMAN_REF_FIND_CL_WORK_DIR
DUTRCA_CONFIG: $current_dir/dutrca.yaml

TARGET_SCOPE: minsoc_tb_top.minsoc_top_0
REPORT_PATH: $current_dir/DUTRCA/$$EMAN_TEST_PATH/dutrca_report.xml

After defining the debug engines, enable them for the specific error patterns. In the
following example, DF and DUTRCA are enabled for the uvm_error error pattern:

Reference Finder
The Verdi VMS feature, Reference Finder, allows connecting Verdi VMS to any source
control. For each failed test, you can find the most recent changelist where the test passed
and use this changelist as the reference for the test.

The following figure displays the flow that it follows for DUTRCA:
Figure 580

Reference Finder Flow

The Target for DUTRCA is generated using the following command in the Regular Debug
Test: debug_run_cmd
The Reference for DUTRCA is generated using the following command in the Reference
Debug Test: ref_debug_run_cmd
The debug engine DUTRCA needs a reference, so you need to define a reference finder
for a build. You can define a reference finder by adding the following scripts to your Verdi
VMS configuration file:
* init
[Optional] Specifies a script or command to initialize the reference finder. If this
command is defined, it is executed only after you start using the reference finder.
* list_cls
[Required] Specifies a script or command to get the list of changelist IDs. If this
command is defined, it is executed once at the beginning to allow loading these
changelists later. After the script is executed, its log file is parsed for getting the
changelist IDs.

* load_cl
[Required] Specifies a script or command that defines how to load a specific changelist.
It is called every time a changelist is required.

Applying Incremental Binning on Verdi VMS Parallel Debug
The Verdi VMS feature, Parallel Debug, allows you to run debug tests immediately after
the test fails in its custom failure category. Parallel debug provides the following benefits:
* Overlapping of the regular run and the debug run saves the overall turnaround time.
* Analyzing the RDA report and debugging before the regular run finishes.
The following figure displays the difference when you enable and disable the parallel
debug feature:
Figure 581

Difference Between Parallel Debug Off and On

* Incremental Binning
* RDA Behavior After Enabling Parallel Debug
* Requirement for Incremental Binning

Incremental Binning
The Once Binning feature allows categorizing all tests together and provides enhanced
clustering results as all the tests are considered. Once binning always provides the same
clustering results. However, it does not support the Verdi VMS Parallel Debug feature.
Incremental binning categorizes tests one by one and supports the Verdi VMS Parallel
Debug feature. The Bucket ID of a test remains unchanged after it is decided. Therefore,
incremental binning and once binning might have different clustering results. For example,
in the following figure, before test4 finishes, test3 is kept in bucket2. After test4 finishes,
the test3 stays in bucket2.
Figure 582

Difference Between Once And Incremental Binning

RDA Behavior After Enabling Parallel Debug
After the Parallel Debug feature is enabled, you can notice the following RDA behavior:
1. When Verdi VMS identifies the first failed test and sends the test to RDA for binning,
RDA report is created. You can open the RDA report using RCA Manager as shown in
Figure 583

RDA Report

2. RCA Manager checks every minute whether the report is updated. When the report is
updated, it displays the New Update Available! information in the toolbar, as shown in
Figure 584

RCA Manager Displaying "New Update Available"

3. Click File > Reload to reload the report in the RCA Manager. When you click Reload,
RCA Manager displays the latest updates. The New Update Available! information
in the toolbar disappears until the next update becomes available, as shown in the

* New action buttons include:

Post-sim mode button when the Debug Facilitator finishes.
Interactive mode button when the Debug Facilitator finishes.

Requirement for Incremental Binning
The following are the requirements for incremental binning:
* Enable the Parallel Debug feature using the following Verdi VMS command line option:
-parallel_debug.
* RDA categorizes tests using the Once Binning feature by default. The following
command is used:
% eman.

* To enable the Incremental Binning feature, run the following command:
% eman -parallel_debug

DesignDiff
The DesignDiff feature introduces a GUI to compare the source code of two designs:
the reference design and the target design. You can analyze the comparison results.
DesignDiff shows differences between the two designs based on the semantics of the HDL
code, rather than the text of the HDL code. The DesignDiff feature includes the following
functions:
* Integrates the RTL difference (XML format) into DesignDiff.
* Adds the difference functionality.
* Displays the number of design changes in the nTrace hierarchy.
* Allows you to click each scope to view related design changes.
* Shows the target source code in Verdi.
The DesignDiff feature provides options to calculate and display the number of design
changes in the Instance View pane and ignore any module or source code file.
This section provides details on the following topics:
* DesignDiff Requirements
* Enabling DesignDiff
* Reviewing DesignDiff
* Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files
* DesignDiff Limitations

DesignDiff Requirements

DesignDiff Requirements
The following are the requirements for the DesignDiff feature:
* The RTL difference generates the DesignDiff report only when the VSO folder is
available; otherwise, it throws errors.
* You must provide the target and reference designs as two versions of the same
design. It allows DesignDiff to generate meaningful reports for review and analysis. To
generate the target and reference design directories, refer to the Generating Required
Directories section.

Generating Required Directories
The DesignDiff feature requires simv.daidir and ref.daidir directories for the current
and reference designs, respectively. To generate these directories, use the following
compile options for the respective simulator:
* VCS
When VCS is used for simulation, compile the design using the -kdb=designdiff
compile-time option, as shown in the following command:
% vcs -kdb=designdiff -lca [other_options]

Where, [other_options] are the other compile-time options.
* VCS with VSO.ai
When VCS is used with VSO.ai, compile the design using the -vso cso -kdb option
along with other compile-time options, as shown in the following command:
% vcs -vso cso -kdb -lca [other_options]

After compilation, the *.vso folder is generated along with *.daidir in the same
directory.
You must save these two files at the same directory level.
* Third-Party Simulators

Enabling DesignDiff

For third-party simulators, elaborate the design using the -useius=adv -designdiff
or -usemti=adv -designdiff option along with other compile-time options, as shown
in the following command:
For IUS flow,
% elabcom -useius=adv -designdiff [other_options]

For MTI flow,
% elabcom -usemti=adv -designdiff [other_options]

Enabling DesignDiff
After generating the target and reference design directories using the compile-time options
provided in the Generating Required Directories section, enable the DesignDiff feature
using the designdiff command.
Use the following syntax to compare the two simv.daidir design directories:
% designdiff -dbdir <target_simv.daidir> -refdir <reference_simv.daidir>
[other_options]

Where, [other_options] are the DesignDiff runtime options. You can add the following
DesignDiff runtime options:
* -diffreport <filename>: Specify the file name for the report. By default, the file
name is designdiff_report.xml.
* -ignore_module <filename>: Specify the file name that contains the list of module
names to filter out. For more details on the -ignore_module <filename> option, refer
to the Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files section.
* -ignore_file <filename>: Specify the file name that contains the list of source code
files to filter out. For more details on the -ignore_file <filename> option, refer to
the Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files section.
* -with_score: Calculates the design change score for the report. For more details,
refer to the -with_score section.
For example, % designdiff -dbdir ./target/simv.daidir -refdir ./reference/
ref.daidir.
The designdiff command analyzes the design difference details and generates the
corresponding report in an XML format, designdiff_report.xml.

To view the generated report, designdiff_report.xml, in Verdi, run the following
command:
% verdi -load_trace_report <generated_xml_report>, or
% designdiff -load_report <generated_xml_report>

You must load Designdiff reports using the command line; the GUI Load RDA
Trace Report option is not supported for DesignDiff reports.
For example, % verdi -load_trace_report designdiff_report.xml

Sorting Source Code Changes
You can sort entries in the following ways:
* Click the File, Module, and Syntax headers to sort the columns.
* The comparison includes several elements, such as the File column, the Module
column, and the source code changes (add, delete, or edit). It also displays the target
begin and end lines, and the reference begin and end lines.
* The following priority is used for comparison:
File column = Module column > Source code difference (add, delete, edit) > begin line

> end line.

* The following priority is followed for sorting when Syntax is available:
1. Syntax
2. File
3. Edit mode
4. Begin line
5. End line
If two items match on one sorting element, use the next element to decide the order.
* You can sort entries alphabetically by file name or module name.
* If the file name or module name is the same, entries are sorted based on differences in
the source code. Entries that are not deleted appear before entries that are deleted.

Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files

* When comparing two deleted items, Verdi uses the following order of priority:
1. Target view begin line
2. Target view end line
3. Reference view begin line
4. Reference view end line
* When comparing two items that are not deleted, first compare the target view begin
line. If these lines match, compare the target view end line next.
* Sort keys are case-sensitive.
* The initial view sorts by the File column.
* The Line column does not support sorting.

DesignDiff Limitations

DesignDiff Limitations
The following are the limitations of the DesignDiff feature:
* Supported versions
The DesignDiff feature is supported for the following VCS release versions:
V-2023.12-SP2-8, W-2024.09-SP2-3, and later.
* File location requirements
The simv.vso folder must be saved in the same place as the simv.daidir.
* Unsupported languages and features
SystemC, Unified Power Format (UPF), Testbench, and VHDL languages are not
The scores of unnamed statements might not be accurate.
The Source View pane displays differences where a MACRO is used but not
defined.
DesignDiff cannot identify the exact changed line within an encrypted (protected)
block. It can only highlight the first line of that block as the changed location.
* Design reloading
To reload a design, you must run the srcDiffView -on Tcl command; otherwise,
Verdi cannot read the reference design.
* Scroll bar synchronization
When you select the SyncScrollBar check box, you can synchronize only from the
target view to the reference view, and not vice versa.
* Reference view limitations
Most of the reference view options, such as setting the active view, the right-click
options, and the drag option, are not available.
The reference view does not support the parameter annotation.
Non-manual scroll bar options, such as the srcGotoLine Tcl command, are not
When you jump to the target file line in the target design, the target line does not fall
in the range of a valid scope. The reference view does not get refreshed because of
the outdated data.
* Unsupported compilation flows

DesignDiff Limitations

VCS compilation is not supported with the -preserve_path option and in the
Scalene and PCH flows.
The -kdb=only and -kdb=common_elab:off flows are not supported.
The Verdi full-load mode is not supported when the design is compiled using the
-kdb=postelab flow.
* Design change detection
Any change in value format is treated as a design change. For example, if 3'b001
changes to 1'h1, the tool considers it as a design change.
A change in the order of the sensitive list is considered a design change.
A difference in the initial value in a declaration is not considered a design change.
Modules with different parameterizations cannot be combined for comparison.
DesignDiff does not detect modport changes within interfaces. Changes to modport
declarations, such as adding or removing signals from a modport, are not identified.
DesignDiff maps blocks at the process level (initial, always, final). When
multiple sequential blocks exist within the same process, DesignDiff does not map
sibling blocks individually. To ensure accurate mapping, place each sequential block
in a separate process.
* Scope of analysis
DesignDiff checks for differences in the Design Under Test (DUT). It does not check
the testbench for differences.

Verdi Formal Navigator
This chapter contains the following topics:
* Overview of Verdi Formal Navigator
* Launch Verdi Formal Navigator
* Setting Up Verdi Formal Navigator

Overview of Verdi Formal Navigator
As designers, you want to perform what-if analyses to test hypothetical scenarios and
observe the potential effects of specific changes without the need to rerun an entire
simulation. This approach saves time and allows you to quickly assess the impact of a
design change. It helps you make informed decisions and identify potential issues before
you progress in the verification process. You can leverage the Navigator feature of VC
Formal in Verdi for waveform manipulation, plotting, and design exploration, without
requiring detailed knowledge of how to use the complete VC Formal tool.
The Navigator feature is designed to enhance waveform analysis for design verification.
The Navigator view enables you to do the following:
* Generate Waveforms From Design Signals: To understand how the design signals
interact and confirm that the design operates as intended under various conditions, you
need to visualize the signal behavior over time. This feature offers a clear, graphical
representation of signal transitions and interactions by generating waveforms from the
design signals. Thus, you can spot any unexpected behavior in the design.
* View Specific Properties: This feature enables you to view specific properties, such
as assert or cover properties for targets and assume properties for constraints. By
doing so, it enables you to track the fulfillment of these properties during simulation.
* Add, Modify, or Delete Constraints and Targets: You often need the flexibility to
adapt your verification environment to different scenarios by adding, modifying, or
removing constraints and targets. This feature helps you to test the design under
various conditions and ensures comprehensive coverage.
* Edit Signal Values in a Waveform: You may want to perform what-if analyses by
adjusting signal values to observe the impact of these changes on the design. This

Launch Verdi Formal Navigator

feature enables you to edit signal values directly within the waveform and visualize the
effects of hypothetical adjustments. You can also generate a new waveform based on
these changes.
* Generate Counter-Example Waveforms for Failing Properties: This feature
generates counter-example waveforms and shows how and why a SystemVerilog
Assertions (SVA) property fails.
In addition to the above-mentioned tasks, you can experiment with different verification
scenarios without changing the testbench and recompiling to run the simulation again,
thereby increasing productivity.
After you load the design into Verdi and launch Navigator, VC Formal runs in the
background automatically. When the VC Formal engine is ready, the Navigator window
opens in Verdi, allowing you to generate waveforms without a testbench.
You can edit the signal values in a waveform cycle-by-cycle, plot the waveform again, and
generate a new scenario, or extend the current waveform for additional cycles. If you write
SVA, you can also independently create SVA assert and cover properties. It allows you to
generate a waveform to verify whether assert properties fail or cover properties are met.

Verdi Assistant
Verdi Assistant is an AI-powered feature that integrates a Large Language Model (LLM)
into the Verdi environment. It provides a chatbot interface for conversational debugging.
This feature allows you to interact with Verdi by using natural language. As a result, you
can find commands, execute them, obtain documentation or answers to usage questions
easily. Verdi Assistant automates command execution and provides instant support. It
reduces the learning curve for new users and increases productivity of experienced users.
Verdi Assistant provides the following benefits:
* Simplifies command discovery and execution through natural language prompts.
* Reduces the need to consult documentation or application engineers for common
tasks.
* Supports both new and experienced users by streamlining workflows.
* Executes multiple commands with a single prompt, saving time.
* Provides context-aware assistance based on the current GUI state.
* Offers feedback mechanisms to improve the responses generated by the assistant.

Understanding the Chat History Database
This section describes the chat history database, which stores all Verdi Assistant
promptresponse interactions in an SQLite3 file. This file also includes the configuration
of the Verdi Assistant directory, file name, data format, and the fields recorded for each
conversation turn.
This section contains the following topics:
* Database File Configuration and Format
* Data Stored Per Prompt

Database File Configuration and Format
This section explains how the Chat History Database file is configured, including how the
directory and file name are determined through environment variables. The database is
stored in SQLite3 format for easy access and compatibility.
* File Directory
Set the VERDI_ASSISTANT_CHAT_DB_DIR environment variable to specify the database
directory.
If you do not set this variable, the directory defaults to your home directory under
.verdi (for example, ~/.verdi).
* File Name
Set the VERDI_ASSISTANT_CHAT_DB_NAME environment variable to specify the
database file name.
If you do not set this variable, the file name defaults to chat_<username>.db, where
<username> is your operating system username.

* File Format
The database uses the SQLite3 format. Access the database by using SQLite3 scripts
or any SQLite3-compatible browser.

the Chat History Database. Each row includes the following columns, with a composite

The Waveform Agent is an intelligent sub-agent in Verdi Assistant. It uses AI-driven
agentic techniques to enhance waveform analysis.

The new capabilities are specifically designed to streamline the analysis of complex user
waveform files with enhanced precision and efficiency. These capabilities help users
identify potential issues earlier and ensure faster, more reliable design verification.
You can submit natural-language queries to request detailed information about a waveform
file. The agent processes these requests and retrieves relevant data.
In GUI mode, you interact with both a chatbot and a waveform view. This mode is also
called Waveform-Viewer-Integrated mode.
It enables contextual queries and visual signal analysis. You can reference items in the
waveform view using phrases such as "the selected signals," "the cursor time," or "the
waveform".
The waveform view updates based on the chatbot's responses. This provides instant
visual confirmation.

You can compile the essential VCS log information into a PureLog database and then

A message within a log is supposed to follow certain rules. For example, users expect
that the message "B" shows up after message "A". This kind of a rule is like a message

Bind Design Signals to Log Message
PureLog can visualize log message in event/transaction/signal terms without re-run
simulation. There are the following two typical scenarios:
* Debug only based on log message signals, which are generated from log messages.
* Debug based on log message signals, which are generated from log messages along
with real fsdb signals generated from simulation.
The issue with the second scenario is that not all end users know the fsdb signals
related to this log message. Furthermore, adding related fsdb signals into the
waveform view is routine work and it is better if these signals are added automatically.
The solution is to allow users to specify related dumped signals to log message
signals. It is a one-time effort, which means you just need to specify the signals

Bind Design Signals to Log Message

once. Afterward, every user can visualize log message signals and all related binding
dumped signals show up automatically. There are two typical use models introduced in
following sections.

Bind Related Signals to Attribute
The solution is to apply the SmartSheet-customized click function. Users can specify the
click function of a certain column through a TCL script. The following is a sample to show
log-to-event signals along with related signals:
1. Prepare the TCL script as a click function:
========= File: ClickFunc1.tcl =========
## remove existed waveform group
if { [wvIsGroupExist $LineText] } {
wvSelectGroup $LineText
wvCut
}
## Generate Log-to-Event signals
set QueryCond \{"TargetAttribute":"$LineText"\}
smartSheetAddMsgCountToWave -queryCond $QueryCond
wvRenameGroup $QueryCond $LineText
## Open dumped fsdb file
wvOpenFile -win $_nWave3 {sim.fsdb}
wvSetActiveFile -win $_nWave3 {sim.fsdb}
## Add related signals
if { $LineText eq "AttrValue1"} {
wvAddSignal -win $_nWave3 -group "$LineText
{/scope1/hier1/related_signal_1}"
} elseif { $LineText eq "AttrValue2" } {
wvAddSignal -win $_nWave3 -group "$LineText
{/scope1/hier2/related_signal_1}"
wvAddSignal -win $_nWave3 -group "$LineText
{/scope1/hier2/related_signal_2}"
}

2. Specify the click function in the PureLog command option:

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
$LineText eq "AttrValue2" } {
wvAddSignal -win $_nWave3 -group "$LineText
{/scope1/hier2/related_signal_1}"
wvAddSignal -win $_nWave3 -group "$LineText
{/scope1/hier2/related_signal_2}"
}

2. Specify the click function in the PureLog command option:
purelogDB -click_func_header "<header1> <header2> <headerN>"
-click_func_file "<file1> <file2> <fileN>"

In the command option, the click function of <header1> is described in <file1>,
the click function of <header2> is described in <file2>, and the click function of
<headerN> is specified in <fileN>.
3. Click the hyperlink on certain attributes values.

Bind Design Signals to Log Message

The event signal of this attribute value and its related fsdb dumped signals show up
automatically.
Figure 519

Event Signal and Related FSDB Dumped Signal

The TCL script can be specified by experienced users. All other end users just
need to click the script to get things done.

Abnormal Analysis
When a log file includes enormous lines and messages, it becomes very difficult to find
the abnormal points. The Abnormal Analysis feature of PureLog sums up the abnormal
points in a log. You only need to feed PureLog with some golden logs that are related to
the current error log.

Launching Abnormal Analysis
To launch Abnormal Analysis, set the following environment variables:
setenv PYTHONPATH
setenv VL_VERSION TD
setenv PYTHONPATH $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/
python:$PYTHONPATH
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/lib/linux64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

Abnormal Analysis

Using Abnormal Analysis
1. Keep daily record in the database.
For example, if you have case1, case2, and case3 in your daily regression, you can
use PureLog every day to save the record of each testcase in the database through
the PureLog TCL process. The high-level features extracted by partition rules are also
saved in the database for abnormal analysis.
The database used by abnormal analysis is not integrated into the PureLog
database. In other words, abnormal analysis uses its own database that is
different from the PureLog database.

The PureLog timing violation solution helps you find and fix timing violations in your design
more intelligently and efficiently.
The major features are as follows:
* Summarize the timing violations based on components.
Easy to dispatch task to the right owner.
* Prioritize timing violations in different scenarios wherein, you can pick the best one for
the particular scenario.
The corrupted flip-flop with the higher number of violations.
Active drivers associated with a higher number of violations.
* Support waive or unwaive operations effectively.
Waive conditions are saved or restored for the next run.
All waiver justifications are logged into the database for projectlevel review.
* Enable rapid debug workflows for timing violation analysis.
Oneclick access to related signals, violation messages in the simulation log, and
TFV trace results.
* Selectively compile simulation logs from large regression trees using path include and
exclude filters.
You need to set environment variable

PURELOG_ENABLE_TIMING_VIOLATION_REPORT = 1
