text:
Tcl Command
Use the following Tcl command to set the original data type and data unit for metric
columns:
perfSetColumnType -protocol <protocol_name>
-column <column_to_be_set>
-type <type_string> // column type
-unit <unit_string> // column unit

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
GUI Mode
To set the original data type and data unit for a column in the GUI mode, perform the
following steps:
1. In the Metrics tab, select an instance and click the Set Column Datatype right-click
option to open the Set Column Type and Unit dialog box.

2. In this dialog box, select the column for which you want to specify data type and data
unit in the Column field. Select Type and Unit in the respective fields and click Apply.

The specified data type and data unit for the column is displayed in the Details view and
Report view after you regenerate the report.
In the Details view, the data unit is displayed in the header section of the list view, as
illustrated in the following figure:

In the Reports view, the data unit is displayed in the axis label as illustrated in the following
figure:

Data type and unit settings are associated with a metric. In other words, if the
data type is set for the column of a metric, that setting is applied to all instances
of the same metric and column. If the original data type or unit is changed for a
metric, the change takes effect when the next performance report is generated.
Data type and unit configurations are saved during session saving. These
configurations can be restored during session loading.

Setting the Display Unit
You can set the display unit for a performance report by either using the perfColumnUnit
Tcl command or using the GUI mode. The display unit setting only changes the display
unit of a column. The datatype of the column does not change. This setting is applied to
the performance report immediately.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Tcl Command
Use the following Tcl command to set the display unit for metric columns:
perfColumnUnit -protocol <protocol_name>
-column <column_to_be_set>
-type <type_string> // column type
-unit <unit_string> // set the column display unit as the
given unit string
-instance <instance_to_be_set> // optional, to apply the
setting to the specified instance, all instances are not specified

GUI Mode
To set the display unit for a column (data or bandwidth columns) in the GUI mode, perform
the following steps:
1. Select a column in the Details view. Right-click Set Display Unit option to open the Set
Display Unit dialog box.

2. The Set Display Unit form opens. In this form. Select the unit to be displayed for the
column and click Apply.

If the display unit is changed for a column, the change takes effect immediately on the
current performance report, however, the display unit setting is not retained when the
report is generated again. Additionally, the filter on that column is removed.
If the display unit is changed for the y axis column, the constraint value remains the same
and is compared with the value in the original unit. In the chart, the constraint line is
adjusted according to the new display unit.
For both CSV and HTML format reports, the display unit setting is not used; the
original type and unit is used in the saved report.

After you enable synchronization (as explained above), if you select a row in the Details

Windows
You can use the View --> Sync with Waveform menu option to synchronize Performance
Analyzer with the nWave window. You can either synchronization with a new nWave
window or an already opened nWave window. This is illustrated in the following figure:

Synchronization With Waveform

Synchronization Between Performance Analyzer and nWave Windows

Once you enable synchronization (as explained above), markers are added inside the
nWave window at the location that corresponds to the value of the time that is associated
with the item selected inside the Details tab of Performance Analyzer.
Synchronization can only be performed for metrics whose results include time columns.
Note that some metrics include only a single time in their results, while other metrics might
contain two or more time columns.
* If there is only one time column, then only one marker is drawn inside the nWave
window. For example, if the time of the selected row is 1000, then a marker is drawn at
time 1000 inside the waveform viewer using a marker whose name is the same as the
time column name.
* If the metrics contains two time columns, then two markers are drawn inside the
waveform viewer with the two values matching those of the two time columns.
For example, if the metric has two time columns (called request_time and
response_time), and the value of request_time is 1000 and the value of
response_time is 3500, then the request_time marker is drawn at time 1000 and the
response_time marker is drawn at time 3500 inside the waveform viewer.
The Details tab does not allow multiple selections manually. Certain metrics that use the
rate function contain values that are calculated using multiple events. For these values,
all the events are highlighted when you select the value in the chart. In this case, the tool
shows two markers inside the waveform viewer, which indicates the time of the first event
as the start prefix column name and the end prefix column name as the last event in the
list. The tool auto-detects the time column(s) to facilitate synchronization. If a metric does
not contain any time columns, then there is no synchronization between Performance
Analyzer and nWave windows for those metrics. The selection synchronization icon
does not have any impact on nWave and Performance Analyzer when enabled or
disabled.
If there are more than two time columns, the values of the first two columns
whose name ends with time are used to add markers in the nWave window.

Limitations
The following limitations apply to the synchronization functionality in Performance
Analyzer:
* You cannot enable Performance Analyzer and nWave windows synchronization and
TNPA and nWave window synchronization at the same time. If you have enabled any
one of these synchronizations and attempt to synchronize the other window, then a
dialog box appears asking if you want to switch between the two synchronization types.

Cross-Instance Relationship

If you select the Yes option, the synchronization is switched from one to another.
If you select the No option, then the current synchronization remains.
For example, if you have already enabled synchronization between Performance
Analyzer and nWave, and then attempts to synchronize from TNPA to the same
nWave window, the Question dialog box appears that shows the message - Do you
want switch synchronization from Performance Analyzer and Waveform to TNPA and
Waveform?. Based on your choice, the synchronization is enabled accordingly.

Cross-Instance Relationship
Some performance analysis needs to be measured from transactions across multiple VIP
instances. For example, the analysis may cover Initiator (master) - Target (slave) pairs.
This requires a way to associate the master transaction(s) with the corresponding slave
transaction(s).
As the parent-child relationship can be used to associate transactions within one VIP
instance, the predecessor-successor relationship is used to associate transactions across
different VIP instances.
In addition, the master/slave cross-instance performance analysis metrics is built based on
predecessor-successor relations. The predecessor-successor relation is added by the VIP.
It is assumed that for the same master-slave pair, there are three different scenarios of the
predecessor-successor relations:
* One predecessor to one successor
* One predecessor to many successors
* Many predecessors to one successor
When the performance analysis metrics are written, the SQL query statement only
references the predecessor or successor when it is single and unique.
In other words, for the following three scenarios,

text:
successors
* Many predecessors to one successor
When the performance analysis metrics are written, the SQL query statement only
references the predecessor or successor when it is single and unique.
In other words, for the following three scenarios,
* One Predecessor to one successor - The SQL statement can query either predecessor
or successor.
* One predecessor to many successors - The SQL statement can only query the
predecessor.
* Many predecessors to one successor - The SQL statement can only query the
successor.

Cross-Instance Relationship

Many predecessors to many successors scenario is not supported.
When translating the FSDB file streams into SQL tables, Verdi Performance Analyzer
provides the following two extra columns:
* The pred_event column - Records the single unique predecessor.
* The succ_event column - Records the single unique successor.
When a transaction has 0 or more than 1 predecessors, its pred_event entry is null.
When a transaction has 0 or more than 1 successors, its succ_event entry is null.
This is illustrated in the following figure:

In a SQL query statement, pred_event and succ_event can be used to link two
transactions.
If transaction A is the single unique predecessor of transaction B, B.pred_event =
A.event are used.
If transaction B is the single unique successor of transaction A, A.succ_event = B.event
is used.
Following is an example of a metric:
perfCreateMetric -protocol "AMBA_SVT AXI_SVT"
-name "cinst_concurrent_write_response_count"
-type "multi_instance"
-definition {SELECT COUNT(*) AS
concurrent_write_response_count
FROM $inst__Bus_Activity AS activity_resp,
$inst__Transaction AS axi_transaction
WHERE axi_transaction.type_path =
'Transaction.Write'
AND activity_resp.type_path =
'WRESP.WRESP'
AND activity_resp.pred_event =
axi_transaction.event }
-description "Multiple slaves are trying to send BRESP
to the same master in B channel."

Support for Instance-Based Constraints
The Performance Analyzer allows you to set constraints for each performance metric on
an instance-by-instance basis. You can define minimum and maximum constraints for the
instances of the selected metrics in Min and Max columns of Results tab. This allows you
to set the constraints before the results are shown in the Results tab.
Note that,

instances.
* If you set the Min/Max constraint in the Results tab for a single instance (or multiple
instances) for a metric (or multiple metrics), the constraint settings in the Metrics tab
are overridden by the value(s) specified in the Results tab.

Improving Debug Messages for SQL Flow

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Improving Debug Messages for SQL Flow
It is difficult to debug the SQL flow in the tool. To solve this problem, tool debug messaging
has been enhanced for all the SQL/NO SQL errors written out in a separate log file and
this log file is stored with other Verdi logs.
The errors are captured and categorized with the unique code.
The following is the log path:
./verdiLog/verdi_perf_err.log

The following are the error examples:
* [SQL_ATTR_NOT_FOUND_ERROR] -> This error is flagged in the log file under this
category if any attribute is missing in SQL schema. This error can be resolved by hitting
"Resolved Attribute action".
For example, [SQL_ATTR_NOT_FOUND_ERROR] has no such column:
ace_transaction.total_byte_count in SQL
* [SQL_GEN_ERROR]-> Any generic SQL error is flagged in the log file under this
category. This error can be resolved as per the description given for the error.
For example, [SQL_GEN_ERROR] has no such table:
env.axi_passive_system_env.master_0_ace_trans_read_latency in SQL
This log contains all the errors occurred during the analysis.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Resolving Missing Attributes
Following is the use model for this feature:

Use Model
The red error icon, as shown in the following figure, is added to the metric node if the error
is of type No Attribute Found (NAF). You can right click on metric to get the RMB menu
and click on the action Resolve missing Attribute Errors. After regenerating the report
errors are resolved.
If the error is not resolvable then those attributes are the dumped part of ./verdiLog/
verdi_perf_err.log under macro (PERF_FSDB_MISSING_ATTR_LIST) file for user
reference.
Invalid attributes are not resolvable.

Resolving Missing Attributes

You need to create a json file for all the resolved attributes. Json file can be copied to
the path $PA_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH/performance/metrics/. This path is used for future
reference.

Batch Mode Operation
This chapter discusses about the batch mode support available for Verdi Performance
Analyzer in the following sections:
* Batch Mode Use Model
* Batch Mode Tool
* Batch Mode Commands

Batch Mode Use Model
The Performance Analyzer application in Verdi offers the functionality to calculate
performance metrics as a batch operation. This allows you to include performance
measurement and validation in a regression (or a similar automated validation)
environment. You can calculate performance metrics and check those metrics against
desired minimum or maximum constraint values.
Considering the highest level, the batch mode use model comprises of the following three
steps:
1. Write the command files [optional].

Batch Mode Tool
Performance Analyzer in Verdi comprises of an in-built wrapper that encapsulates the
required capabilities into an easy-to-use batch mode tool. The basic environment in which
this tool can be used is illustrated in the following figure:
Figure 41

Batch Mode Tool Environment

The wrapper has three types of input data and one type of output data.
It can be invoked using the following command:
verdi_perf -fsdb/-f
-instance/-i
[ -start/-s <start_time> ]
[ -end/-s <end_time> ]

-fsdb/-f

The -fsdb or the -f option specifies the FSDB file to be processed. The FSDB file is
the output of a simulation that contains all the protocol-related simulation data that is
required to perform the desired performance metric calculations. This means that FSDB
dumping must have been enabled for all VIP instances of interest. The FSDB file needs to
be specified either through the -fsdb option or in the command file specified by the -cmd
option.
-instance/-i

The -instance or the -i option specifies the instances on which the performance
evaluation is done. The instance needs to be specified either through the -instance
option or in the command file specified by the -cmd option.
-start/-s

The -start or the -s option specifies the start time for performance evaluation.
-end/-e

The -end or the -e option specifies the end time for performance evaluation.
-cmd/-c

The -cmd or the -c option specifies a list of one or more command files to be processed.
These command files can contain Tcl commands. You can use these commands to define
custom performance metrics. They can also enable or disable performance metrics. You
can set or clear constraint values, perform metric calculations, and specify the location and
type of results to produce.
-output/-o

The -output or the -o option specifies the name of the output file.
-format/-m

The -format or the -m option specifies the format of the output file: html for HTML format,
and csv for CSV format.
-session/-n

Batch Mode Tool

The -session or the -n option specifies the condition/option to save the current session.
The saved session can later be opened in the Performance Analyzer GUI.
The various options to save a session are as follows:
* on - Save the session always.
* off - Never save the session.
* fail - Save the session if there is any constraint violation.
The default option to save a session is fail.

Protocol Extensions
The Protocol Extensions defined for the Verdi Transaction and Protocol Analyzer
also apply to the Verdi Performance Analyzer. They are present at the same location
as pre-defined performance metrics. In addition to the Synopsys VIPs that are
located in the DESIGNWARE_HOME directory, any directories that are specified using the
PA_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH environment variable are also analyzed for protocol definitions and
any associated pre-defined performance metric definitions.

Batch Mode Processing Flow
The following two flows exist for batch mode processing:
1. Write the operations in a TCL command file, and specify the TCL command through
the -cmd/-c option.
2. Use other command line options to specify the FSDB file, instances, and so on.
The -cmd/-c command line option is mutually exclusive with other
command line options. You need to choose to use either the command file
or the command line options, but not both.
If no command files are specified, the Verdi Performance Analyzer applies the pre-defined
performance metrics to the VIP instances found in the design. It produces a report using
the default output format, which is CSV.
If the command file is specified, the command file can contain one or more of the TCL
commands mentioned in Batch Mode Commands section.

text:
Aggregate Performance Analysis
Verdi Performance Analyzer can also generate an aggregate performance analysis report
for all the FSDB files generated from multiple simulation runs for the same design. For
multiple FSDB files, the performance analysis report includes results for the merged
data from all the FSDB files and results for data from every single FSDB file. Therefore,
you can get a summary of performance results for all runs and also the statistical result
distribution/difference among every FSDB file.
This chapter explains about how to generate and view an aggregate performance analyzer
report in the following sections:
* Prerequisites
* Generating Aggregate Performance Analysis Report
* verdi_perf Utility
* Viewing Aggregate Performance Analysis Report in GUI
* Examples to Demonstrate Merged Results for Multiple FSDB Files

Prerequisites
The following are the prerequisites for aggregate performance analysis:
* Each FSDB file generated by a regression or by multiple runs must have a unique
identifier. This can be used by Verdi to organize, indicate, add or remove the test
results associated with a specific test. The FSDB full path (generated from the tests) is
used as the unique identifier.
* The FSDB files generated from different tests must have similar VIP instantiation
hierarchies. This merges the performance analysis results.
Some FSDB files may contain more instance hierarchies, while some may have
fewer instance hierarchies. However, only the results from the same VIP instantiation
hierarchy path are merged.

Generating Aggregate Performance Analysis Report

Generating Aggregate Performance Analysis Report
To generate an aggregate performance analysis report, perform the following steps:
1. Generate the result database (in Batch Mode)
Execute the verdi_perf command to initialize a result database (that is. a directory)
to save the performance results, and configure the metrics and constraints for the
performance analysis on multiple results.
Performance analysis on multiple test results share the same metrics and
constraints configuration.
2. Add or remove FSDB files to/from the database (in Batch Mode)
Run simulations for multiple tests, with Protocol Analyzer dumping enabled to dump the
FSDB file with protocol data. After each test, execute the verdi_perf command to run
performance analysis on the generated FSDB file.
The result is saved in the result database directory.
If there are constraints violations, the verdi_perf command issues error messages.
The FSDB file can be deleted after the file has been added to the result database;
aggregate results will not be affected.
In many regression systems, multiple tests are run at the same time. The verdi_perf
command can also run in parallel to analyze the dynamically generated FSDB files and
write the results to the result database.
You can also execute the verdi_perf command to override or remove an existing
analysis result from the result database.
3. Generate and view the aggregate performance analysis report (in Batch Mode)
a. Execute the verdi_perf command with -db/-d, -format/m, and -output/-o
options to generate HTML or CSV format analysis results.
b. View the report in a web browser (HTML format) or in an excel sheet (CSV format).
You can also view the aggregate performance report in Verdi GUI mode.
For details, see Viewing Aggregate Performance Analysis Report in GUI.

Generating Aggregate Performance Analysis Report

Consider the following axi.cfg configuration file:
perfSetTimeRange

The following is an example to generate an aggregate performance analysis report using a
configuration file:
1. In the first phase, an empty database directory needs to be created with the specified
protocol, instances, and configurations. This is an example to generate multiple FSDB
file result database for the svt_axi protocol with the preceding configuration file as
follows:
verdi_perf -protocol "amba_svt axi_svt" -cmd axi.cfg -db axi.dbdir

2. In the second phase, with the created empty result database directory (axi.dbdir),
execute the verdi_perf command multiple times (in parallel, if desired) to analyze the
performance of the FSDB files (generated from each test) into the result database.
verdi_perf -add axi01.fsdb -db axi.dbdir
verdi_perf -add axi02.fsdb -db axi.dbdir

You can remove an FSDB file from the database as follows:
verdi_perf -remove axi02.fsdb -db axi.dbdir

verdi_perf Utility

3. In the third phase, with the created result database directory, and FSDB files added
into the database, use the verdi_perf command to generate an HTML or a CSV
format report.
verdi_perf -db axi.dbdir -format html -output axi_html
verdi_perf -db axi.dbdir -format csv -output axi.csv

verdi_perf Utility
Verdi Performance Analyzer comprises of an in-built wrapper which encapsulates the
required capabilities into an easy-to-use batch mode tool. It can be invoked using the
verdi_perf utility to generate an aggregate performance analysis report.
Following is the list of valid options for generating an aggregate performance report:
verdi_perf
[
[
[
[
[
[
[
[

-instance/-i
-protocol/-p <protocol> ]
-cmd/-c <config_file_name> ]
-db/-d <database_name>]
-add/-a <fsdb_name> ]
-remove/-r <fsdb_name> ]
-force/-w <fsdb_name> ]
-output/-o <ouput_file_name> ]
-format/-m <output_file_format> ]

-instance/-i

The -instance or the -i option specifies the instances and scopes on which the
performance evaluation is done. The instance needs to be specified either through the
-instance option or in the command file specified by the -cmd option. The value of an
instance is a list of nodes where a node could be an instance or a scope.
-protocol/-p <protocol>

The -protocol or the -p option specifies the protocol to be processed for performance
evaluation. All the instances for the specified protocol are evaluated. This option is
required for database initialization.
-cmd/-c

The -cmd or the -c option specifies the metrics/constraints configuration file. The
configuration file syntax and format is the same as the one used for single FSDB file
processing. For example, the Tcl command for adding or changing metrics or setting
constraints could be added into the configuration file.
-db/-d <database_name>

verdi_perf Utility

The -db or the -d option specifies the name of the result database directory. This option
is mandatory for generating an aggregate performance report. If this option is not added,
Performance Analyzer enters the single FSDB mode.
-info

The -info option shows information about the specified aggregate database. The
information includes a global environment, which contains the FSDB file list, protocol, and
instance names. If the number of FSDB files is more than sixteen, only the first sixteen file
paths are displayed in the output. The output format is as follows:
General information for dbdir: <dbdir>
Protocol: "<protocol>"
Instance: <instance>
Number of instances: n
<instance1>
<instance2>
Number of fsdb files: n
<fil1>
<file2>
-add/-a <fsdb_name>

The -add or the -a option adds the specified FSDB file into the database.
-remove/-r <fsdb_name>

The -remove or the -r option removes the specified FSDB file from the database.
If neither -add nor -remove option is added, and either -instance or -cmd
option is specified, the verdi_perf command performs database initialization.
The -add and the -remove options can not be added at the same time in the
command.
-force/-w <fsdb_name>

The -force or the -w option overwrites the FSDB file with the same name in the database.
-output/-o

The -output or the -o option specifies the name of the output file. This is an optional
parameter.
-format/-m

The -format or the -m option specifies the format of the output file: html for HTML format,
and csv for CSV format. This is an optional parameter.

Viewing Aggregate Performance Analysis Report in GUI

If neither -add nor -remove is added, and neither -instance nor -cmd option
is specified, the verdi_perf command generates the report for the specified
database. If the -add option is added, the verdi_perf command adds the
FSDB file into the database.
You can use the following Tcl command to view information about the aggregate database
in batch mode:
verdi_perf -db <dbdir>
-info

The output format is as follows:
General information for dbdir: <dbdir>
Protocol: "<protocol>"
Instance: <instance>
Number of instances: n
<instance1>
<instance2>
Number of fsdb files: n
<fil1>
<file2>

Viewing Aggregate Performance Analysis Report in GUI
The results from multiple FSDB files are merged and appended in the aggregate
performance analysis report with an extra column to indicate the FSDB file where the
result originated.
To view the aggregate performance report for multiple FSDB files, you need to use the
Performance Analyzer view in GUI mode as follows:
1. Invoke the Verdi GUI with the Transaction Debug work mode.
2. Click the Menu -> Tools -> Transaction Debug -> Performance Analyzer menu
command to invoke Performance Analyzer.
3. In the Performance Analyzer pane, click the File -> Load Database command. Choose
the performance analysis aggregate result database from the Load Database form.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Viewing Aggregate Performance Analysis Report in GUI

4. Select the required files in the Files tab of the Hierarchy Tree pane.

5. Click the Show Report
icon in the toolbar or click the Show Report right-click
command for the selected files.

Click the Show Report icon in Performance Analyzer which also displays a progress bar
to notify users that the report generation is in progress. The progress bar is illustrated in
the following figure:

For aggregate performance databases, the Reload menu command is always
disabled. If any FSDB files are added to or removed from the aggregate
database, you must close the current aggregate database and open the same
database again.

Viewing Aggregate Performance Analysis Report in GUI

If any FSDB files inside the aggregate database are changed, the aggregate
performance report is not updated automatically to include the change; you
must add the same FSDB file to overwrite the previous FSDB file.

Files Tab for Multiple FSDB Files Database
If multiple FSDB files are opened in Performance Analyzer, the Files tab is available in the
Hierarchy Tree pane, which displays the list of all the FSDB files present in the database.
You can select any of the FSDB files by checking the check-box to view its performance
report and perform other operations.
The Files tab is illustrated in the following figure:

The following right-click commands are available in the Files tab:
* Check All: Selects/checks all the files
* Uncheck All: Deselects/unchecks all the files
* Show Report: Displays the performance report for the selected files
* Show Report in New Window: Displays the performance report for the selected files
in a new window
* Show Report for Single File: Displays the performance report for the selected file
(single file) in a new window. This also opens the FSDB file in a new window
This command is enabled only if the FSDB file exists.

Hierarchy Tree Tab for Multiple FSDB Files
* The Hierarchy Tree displays only the instances. The stream nodes are not displayed
since there are multiple FSDB files for the database. They may have different streams
in the same named instance.
* The Hierarchy Tree displays a union of instances. For example, if 1.fsdb has
VIP.env.axi_system_env.master_0 as an instance but 2.fsdb does not have this
instance and 2.fsdb has VIP.env.axi_system_env.master_3 as an instance but

Viewing Aggregate Performance Analysis Report in GUI

1.fsdb does not have it, then both of the instances appear in the hierarchy view of the
merged database.
* The transaction count is not displayed since the transaction counts may be different for
the same instance in different FSDB files.
* If the option to check an instance is disabled, that is, if the aggregate report is
displayed for all the available instances. To view the report for different instances as the
current aggregate database, re-generate the database with the new instance list.
The following figure illustrates the Hierarchy Tree tab for multiple FSDB files

Metrics Tab for Multiple FSDB Files
All the metrics are read-only because the metrics configuration is decided based on the
results for the FSDB files that were added to the results database. You can not change/
add or disable/enable the metrics,
* However, you can still use the Metrics view to change other settings which trigger
recalculation, such as constraints, chart types, and so on.
* You can add/change constraints for metrics.
* You can set/change the chart type for metrics.

Results Tab for Multiple FSDB Files
Multiple instance metrics are evaluated on the merged instances from all FSDB files.

Performance Report Pane for Multiple FSDB Files
For some of the metrics (mostly instance based and multiple instances based metrics), the
result for a single FSDB file is present in a single row. This result is displayed as a label.
However, for a result database with multiple FSDB files, the result is presented in a tabular
form. It is displayed as a line or a bar chart with the x axis as the name of the FSDB and

the y axis as the result of that FSDB. Therefore, you can easily view the summary of the
result distribution in different FSDB files.

Details Tab for Multiple FSDB Files
The Details tab for a result database with multiple FSDB files is similar to the single FSDB
details pane. The difference between them is that, there exists an extra column to indicate
the FSDB file to which the result is related. This is illustrated in the following figure:

Performance Report pane is supported.
For aggregate databases, synchronization between Performance Analyzer view
and other views (like protocol views) is not supported, since there are multiple
FSDB files involved. To synchronize with other views, you must open a single

This chapter provides you an insight into computation and visualization elements that
comprise a performance metric, which helps you to understand the design considerations
and the operation of previously-written performance metrics. This information is also
a prerequisite to designing and implementing custom performance metrics (either by
modifying a previously written performance metric or creating a new performance metric
entirely from scratch).
This chapter helps you to understand the following concepts in detail:
* The elements that comprise a performance metric and how they are utilized
* The computation and visualization elements that comprise a performance metric
This chapter also explains how to perform the following tasks:

to create a new custom performance metric.
* Modify the visualization element of a pre-defined metric provided with a Synopsys VIP
to create a new custom performance metric.
This chapter primarily focuses on the portion of the metric creation process that is utilized
to extract information from transactions in the FSDB file and assumes a basic operational
knowledge of Protocol Analyzer and Performance Analyzer.

Elements of a Performance Metric

Elements of a Performance Metric
The following three elements comprise a performance metric:
1. Performance metric definition: Defines how to extract the desired performance data
from the VIP transaction data in the FSDB file.
2. Data or column type specifications: Indicates the units associated with each piece of
data extracted from the FSDB file for each performance metric.
3. Visualization attributes associated with each performance metric: Defines how the
resulting data must be presented.
Both elements of a performance metric are used in interactive mode and batch mode.
The following figure illustrates the meaning of these three elements:
Figure 42

Elements of a Performance Metric

A performance metric definition is characterized by the following attributes:
* Name of the protocol for which the performance metric is defined
* Name of the performance metric
* Description of the performance metric
* Expression to use to calculate the metric
* Type of metric being defined (instance or multi-instance)
* Metrics on which the metric depends (if any)
The first three items in the above list are relatively self-explanatory.

The last three items are explained in the following sections.
The visualization of performance metrics is discussed in a separate section.

Performance Analyzer SQL Database
Internally, Performance Analyzer constructs an SQLite database that contains all the
protocol transaction information that is captured during simulation. This database
enables the creation of SQL expressions to extract the data necessary to calculate each
performance metric. While this chapter is not intended to be an SQL tutorial, basic SQL
expressions are discussed using examples.
An SQL database contains a collection of tables. Each table can be thought of as an
Excel spreadsheet, with rows and columns. One or more tables are created for each VIP
instance in the design. For each table, each row contains information about an individual
transaction and the each column represents the individual attributes for each transaction.
Since the metric expressions are written in SQL, knowledge of the SQL database structure
is required to understand how the metric expressions need to be written and how those
expressions are evaluated.
The general structure of the SQL database that is associated with a protocol instance is
derived from the object types in the protocol extension definition that is associated with
that instance. If performance metrics are created for a custom protocol, the details of
the object types protocol extension definition are defined during the VIP instrumentation
process. For Synopsys VIPs, this information is understood by examining the results of a
simulation in Protocol Analyzer (which is shown in detail below).

The protocol transaction information is used to construct the SQL database in the following
manner:
* Each top-level object type in the protocol extension definition is mapped to a separate
table in the SQL database for each instance. The name of the table is constructed from
the name of the instance and the name of the top-level object type display name. As it
appears in the Protocol Analyzer hierarchy tree).
* Each attribute that is defined for an object type in the protocol extension definition is
mapped to a column in the table in the SQL database that is associated with the object
type. The name of the column is the same as the attribute display name. As it appears
in the Protocol Analyzer hierarchy tree.
* For object types that define an object sub-type in the protocol extension definition and

As previously mentioned, the name of the tables that are created in the SQL database are
constructed from the name of the VIP instance and the name of each top-level object type.
The format of the table name is as follows:
<instance_name>__<top_level_object_type_name>

For Synopsys VIPs, the protocol extension definition is provided as part of the VIP.
However, the object type hierarchy can be easily understood by examining the protocol

transactions that are created during simulation in Protocol Analyzer, as illustrated in the
following figure:
Figure 44

Protocol Transactions Created During Simulation

The above figure shows the transactions recorded during the simulation of an AMBA AXI
system. Although not all the instances are visible, the design contains multiple AXI master
and AXI slave VIP instances.
The figure focuses on a VIP instance named master_0. On expanding the
hierarchy tree for this instance, the top-level object types are easily visible. For this
protocol, there are three top-level object types: Transaction, Bus_Activity, and
svt_axi_port_configuration.
There are object sub-types for two of the top-level object types. For example, the
Transaction object type has two sub-types called READ and WRITE. Each of those object
sub-types have additional object sub-types. Taken together, these define an object type
hierarchy. When looking at the object type hierarchy in Protocol Analyzer, it is important
to note the following: Only the object types for the transactions that were created in the
specific simulation are displayed. The protocol extension definition may define other object
types. However, if transactions of those types are not created during the simulation, they
do not appear in the Hierarchy Tree.
In addition to the columns that are associated with object type attributes (the information
that is displayed in the Details tab in the previous figure), each table in the database that is
associated with an object type has the following additional columns:
Column Name

begin_time

This column stores the begin time of the transaction.

end_time

This column stores the end time of the transaction.

Column Name

event

This column stores the unique identifier associated
with a transaction. While the value of this identifier
is not particularly useful to an end user, it is used to
enable selection synchronization between Performance
Analyzer results and Protocol Analyzer.

parent_event

This column stores the unique identifier for the parent
transaction (if the transaction has a parent transaction).
The value for this column is NULL for transactions that
do not specify a parent transaction.

pred_event

This column stores the unique identifier for the
predecessor transaction (if the transaction has a
predecessor transaction). The value for this column is
NULL for transactions that do not specify a processor
transaction.

succ_event

This column stores the unique identifier for the
successor transaction (if the transaction has a
successor transaction). The value for this column is
NULL for transactions that do not specify a successor
transaction.

type_path

This column stores a string that represents the
complete object type path. If the transaction object
type is a top-level object type, then the value for
this column is same as the object_type column.
For object sub-types, the format of the path
is:<top_level_object_type>.<object_sub_type>.<object_
sub_type>

channel

This column stores the name of the channel if any
protocol-related transactions specify a channel (such as
Rx or Tx).

label

This column stores the label associated with a
transaction. This value corresponds to the value of the
attribute $label, which is shown in the Details tab of
Protocol Analyzer.

All protocol related transactions are converted into an SQL database, based on the
database schema described earlier. During this conversion process, each transaction is
added as a record (that is, a row) in one of the database tables, based on the object type
transaction's. This database can then be used to evaluate the metric expressions that are
defined for each performance metric. These metric expressions are written using SQL
syntax to extract the required performance information.

Examples of a Performance Metric Definition
This sub-section analyzes a basic performance metric definition using the following two
examples:
Example 1
In this example, the performance metric definition calculates the latency of specific
transaction types. It is one of the pre-defined performance metrics that is provided with the
Synopsys AMBA ACE VIP. Even though this metric definition is specific to the Synopsys
AMBA ACE VIP, the calculation of transaction latency is common to almost every protocol.
Thus makes it a particularly useful metric to examine in detail.
Each performance metric definition is described using the perfCreateMetric Tcl
command, which has the following syntax:
Figure 45

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Syntax - perfCreateMetric

The six arguments to the perfCreateMetric Tcl command correspond to the six elements
that comprise a performance metric definition. The methods by which predefined or
custom metrics are loaded into Performance Analyzer is discussed in the following
sections.

The following figure illustrates the definition of the predefined metric called
ace_trans_read_latency:
Figure 46

Predefined Metric Definition

This performance metric computes the time taken by an ACE Read transaction to
complete (that is, the latency of each ACE Read transaction).
This definition illustrates that most the work required to define a performance metric is
constructing the appropriate SQL expression to extract the desired data from the SQL
database. The SQL expression is shown separately in the following figure:
Figure 47

SQL Expression

While SQL expressions can be quite complex, they all have the general structure that is
shown by the labels in the previous figure. Specifically, the SQL expression defines what
data is to be retrieved, where that data is to be retrieved from (that is, which database
tables) and the conditions that the table data must satisfy to be included in the results.
To understand this performance metric,
* It is easiest to first consider the FROM portion of the SQL expression.

For this performance metric, it is necessary to analyze data from two tables:
$inst__Transaction and $inst__svt_axi_port_configuration.
As discussed earlier, Transaction and svt_axi_port_configuration are the names of two
of the top-level object types that are defined for this protocol. Also, database tables are
created based on the names of the instances in the design.
Since performance metrics are intended to be used for any design, the names of the
specific instances in the design cannot be required when defining metrics. To satisfy
this requirement, the $inst string is used when defining performance metrics. When the
performance metrics are evaluated, Performance Analyzer automatically replaces $inst
with the name of the instance for which the metric is being evaluated. For example,
if this performance metric is being evaluated for the instance named master_0, the
$inst string is replaced with master_0 and the tables called master_0__Transaction and
master0__svt_axi_port_configuration are queried by the tool.
This portion of the SQL expression includes the SQL keyword: AS, which allows a
table to be locally named to make the rest of the expression easier to understand.
For example, the table called $inst__Transaction can also be referred to as
ace_transaction in the rest of the SQL expression. In other words, this creates an alias
for the table.
* Next, consider the WHERE portion of the SQL expression.

For this performance metric, the transactions in the database must satisfy two
conditions to be included in the result.
The first condition that must be satisfied is that the value of type_path must be
equal one of the two specified strings. As mentioned earlier, the type_path database
column is automatically populated by Performance Analyzer. It represents the
complete object type path for each transaction. Note that, the table alias is used to
reference the type_path database column (that is, ace_transaction). This means
that this condition only applies to the database tables whose top-level object type is
Transaction.
For the Synopsys AMBA ACE VIP, there are two READ transaction object types
(one type is used if the VIP is configured to operate as a master; the other type is
used if the VIP is configured to operate as a slave). Since this performance metric
is intended to be applicable for both master and slave ACE VIPs, both values are
included in the SQL expression.
The second condition that must be satisfied is that the value of axi_interface_type
must also equal one of the two specified values. This portion of the condition also
uses a table alias. So, this condition only applies to the database tables whose top-

level object type is svt_axi_port_configuration. This additional condition is included
in this metric, because the Synopsys AMBA VIP is very flexible. It can be configured
to represent one of the several different AMBA protocols, including ACE or AXI.
This additional condition ensures that this metric only applies to instances of the
Synopsys AMBA VIP that are configured to operate as ACE masters or slaves.
The following figure shows how FROM and WHERE portions of the SQL expression
correlate to Protocol Analyzer:
Figure 48

SQL Expression Correlation With Protocol Analyzer

* Finally, consider the SELECT portion of the SQL expression.

This portion of the SQL expression defines the information to be extracted from the
database and placed in the Results table for this performance metric.
As mentioned earlier, this performance metric is intended to calculate the latency
values for ACE Read transactions. The latency of a transaction is calculated by
subtracting the end time of the transaction from the begin time of the transaction.
This is the first value that is calculated for the performance metric. The AS portion
of the expression allows you to specify a name for the calculated result. If a name is
specified, that name is used for the column in the results table when the performance
metric is evaluated.
The next two values that are extracted from the transaction database are the begin
time and end time for the transaction. As mentioned earlier, begin_time and end_time
columns are automatically added to the transaction database tables by Performance
Analyzer. These two values are included in the results table for two reasons. The first
reason is for graphing. When this performance metric is graphed, the goal is to use the
latency value for the x-axis and the request_time (that is, begin_time of the transaction)
for the y-axis. Visualization definitions for performance metrics is described in detail in
a later section of this document.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
graphed, the goal is to use the
latency value for the x-axis and the request_time (that is, begin_time of the transaction)
for the y-axis. Visualization definitions for performance metrics is described in detail in
a later section of this document.

The final value that is extracted from the transaction database (and placed in the
Results table) is the transaction event. This is the unique identifier that is associated
with a transaction. While this value is not particularly useful to an end user, it enables
selection synchronization between Performance Analyzer and Protocol Analyzer.
For example, assume that the latency of a transaction violates a maximum constraint
value specified by the user. If the event value is included in the metric result, the
offending transaction can be selected in Performance Analyzer. The same transaction
gets selected in Protocol Analyzer (note that the windows must have synchronization
enabled to utilize this capability).
The names that are specified in the SELECT portion of the SQL expression (using the
AS SQL keyword) define the column names in the result table that is generated when
the performance metric is evaluated. For this example, there are four columns in the
Results table with the names latency, request_time, response_time and event.
The following figure shows the result data for this performance metric in the
Performance Analyzer GUI:
Figure 49

Result Data for Performance Metric

Since the event data is used internally by Verdi, the event values are not displayed in
the data that is presented to the user.
Example 2
In this example, the performance metric definition calculates the number of bytes
associated with a specific transaction type. It is also one of the predefined performance
metrics that is provided with the Synopsys AMBA ACE VIP.
This performance metric is slightly more complex than the previous example and
introduces a few new concepts related to writing performance metrics. First, this metric
demonstrates how to utilize the relationships (that is, parent-child) between transactions;

and second, it showed that SQL SELECT statements can incorporate more complex
manipulation of data.
The definition of the predefined metric called ace_trans_read_byte_count is illustrated in
the following figure:
Figure 50

Predefined Metric Definition

This performance metric computes the number of bytes associated with each ACE read.
The SQL expression is shown in the following figure:
Figure 51

SQL Expression

Similar to the previous performance metrics example, to understand this performance
metric,
* First, consider the FROM portion of the SQL expression.

For this performance metric, it is necessary to analyze data from three tables.
The names of these tables are $inst__Bus_Activity, $inst__Transaction, and
$inst__svt_axi_port_configuration, which is similar to the previous example, with the
addition of the $inst__Bus_Activity table. Note that, this table includes an AS statement
that allows the table to be referred to as activity_data in the rest of the SQL statement.
* Next, consider the WHERE portion of the SQL expression

The portion of the WHERE condition which selects only ACE instances is the same
the previous example. However, the way the desired transactions are selected is
somewhat different than the previous example. In this example, the transactions are
selected utilizing the parent-child relationships.
To provide some background, for each ACE Read transaction, there are read data
transactions that are recorded as child transactions, whose type is RDATA and are
recorded as Bus_Activity. Thus, the condition checks two things:
Firstly, the condition checks the database for any transactions in the Bus_Activity
table whose type is RDATA
Secondly, the condition limits the result to transactions in the Bus_Activity table that
have a parent-child relationship with a transaction in the Transaction table. This is
accomplished using the event and parent_event attributes that are automatically
generated by Performance Analyzer when the SQL tables are constructed.
* Finally, consider the SELECT portion of the SQL statement.

As previously mentioned, the goal of the metric is to extract the number of bytes
associated with each ACE Read transaction. Consider the following screenshot from
Protocol Analyzer:
Figure 52

Protocol Analyzer Screenshot

In the above figure, an ACE Read transaction is selected. In addition, the filter
capability of the Details tab is used to show the value of the burst_size attribute.
The value of that attribute for the selected transaction is BURST_SIZE_64BIT,
which is a string. However, the metric needs to extract an integer value. This can
be accomplished by using some of the more advanced capabilities of the SQLite

language. The SQL language provides many built-in functions that can be utilized in
SQL expressions. This expression uses two of these functions: substr and cast.
The substr function is used to transform the string BURST_SIZE_64BIT to 64BIT. This
new string can then be transformed to an integer using the cast function. The result
is 64, but this is the number of bits associated with the transaction. To compute the
number of bytes, this value (which is now an integer) can be divided by 8 to calculate
the number of bytes associated with the transaction.
Performance Analyzer supports all the built-in functions available with SQLite. There
are many on-line resources that list these functions and provide examples of their
usage. For additional information about the built-in functions available with SQLite, see
https://sqlite.org/lang_corefunc.html
In addition to the built-in functions that are available with SQLite, Performance Analyzer
provides four extended functions, which are described in the following table:

Instance and Multi-Instance Performance Metrics
There are two types of performance metrics:
* Performance metrics based on data from a single instance, referred to as Instance
performance metrics.
* Performance metrics based on data from multiple instances, referred to as MultiInstance performance metrics.
The difference between these two metric types is the data that is provided as input to the
metric. This difference determines what data can be referenced in the metric expression).
As the name implies, the input to an Instance performance metric is simulation data that is
associated with a single instance of a protocol. However, for a Multi-Instance performance
metric, the simulation data from multiple instances of a protocol is first aggregated and
then provided as an input to the metric.

The following figure illustrates the difference between an Instance performance metric and
a Multi-Instance performance metric. In this example, when four instances of a protocol
are applied to each metric type:
Figure 53

Instance and Multi-Instance Performance Metrics

The two examples that are described in the previous sections are both instance
performance metric. This was indicated in the perfCreateMetric Tcl command by the
-type instance argument. This means that performance metric results are generated for
each of the instances selected in Performance Analyzer, provided they match the criteria
of the specified metric.
For example, the sample FSDB file that is used for the previous examples has five ACE
Master instances (called master_0 through master_4) and four ACE Slave instances
(called slave_0 through slave_3). Therefore, if all instances are selected and the
previously described two performance metrics are to be evaluated, Performance Analyzer
performs 18 evaluations (9 instances x 2 metrics) and produces 18 results tables.
Each of the results tables are named based on the name of the instance and the name of
the metric. The name of each results table is constructed using the following pattern:
<instance_name>__<metric_name>

Note that under certain conditions, all results tables are not generated. Specifically,
for specific simulation results, it may not be possible to evaluate every performance
metric on every selected instance. This can happen when certain input tables are not
created because the simulation did not cause certain types of transactions to be recorded.

Note that the Count column on the right shows the value "N/A" for the metrics shown.

the reason for the metric not being evaluated. In the case of the ace_trans_read_latency
metric, it could not be evaluated because for this simulation data, there are no transactions
associated with the instance master_3, that is, the table master_3__Transaction cannot
be created. This does not indicate that there is anything wrong with the metric definition;
it simply indicates that the metric cannot be calculated for this instance based on the
input data provided to Performance Analyzer. A different FSDB file could yield completely
different results.

Primary and Dependent Performance Metrics
Not only does a performance metric have a type, a performance metric can be further
classified as being either a primary performance metric or a dependent performance
metric.
If the expression that is used to calculate the performance metric is described directly in
terms of protocol-related simulation data, then the metric is a primary performance metric.
However, the metric model that is used by Performance Analyzer is very flexible. The
model permits the specification of performance metrics that takes the results that are
calculated by one or more other metrics as their input. If the expression that is used to
calculate the performance metric is described in terms of one or more other performance
metric results, then the metric is a dependent performance metric.
Note that the figure from the previous sub-section illustrates only primary performance
metrics. Even though the figure shows both instance and multi-instance performance
metrics), they are all primary performance metrics. However, it is also possible to define
dependent, instance performance metrics and dependent, multi-instance performance
metrics.
As an example, consider some performance metrics that could be defined for the AMBA
ACE protocol. This document has already examined an instance performance metric that
calculates the latency of each read transaction that is processed by a single instance
of the Synopsys ACE SVT VIP. As demonstrated in the discussion of this example, the
latency of an ACE transaction is calculated by subtracting the begin time of transaction
from the end time of the transaction.
Thus, if this performance metric is applied to an instance of the ACE VIP that processes
250 transactions over the course of the simulation, the calculation of the metric produces a
result with 250 latency values , .
2. The result could contain additional information, but the main point is that the result can at least contain a
collection of latency values.
3. It is important to note that even though the result of calculation produces 250 latency values, the output of the
metric calculation is still considered a single performance metric result. If you had selected a second instance of
the ACE VIP that had calculated 100 transactions during the simulation, that can cause a second performance
metric result to be created (containing 100 latency values).

Now, consider some other performance metrics that could be defined for the AMBA
ACE protocol. One of these might be the average latency for transactions processed
by an instance of the ACE VIP. The average value can easily be calculated by taking
the average of the individual transaction latency values that were calculated by the first
example metric. This is an example of a dependent, instance performance metric.
The relationship between these performance metrics is illustrated in the following figure:

The arrow indicates that there is a dependency between these two metrics, which means
that the read latency metric must be evaluated before the average read latency metric can
be evaluated.
The following figure illustrates the processing steps (and data flow) associated with this
performance metric. This clearly shows that the input to the primary metric is protocolrelated simulation data while the input to the dependent metric is the result of a metric
evaluation.

Examples of Dependent Performance Metric Definition
This sub-section analyzes a dependent performance metric definition using the following
two examples:
Example 1
Following is an example showing a dependent performance metric definition that is used
to define one or more performance metrics:

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
This performance metric computes the average latency for all the read latencies for
each selected instance. The type of this metric is still instance (as it is for the previous
examples), as the metric calculates a value for each selected instance. However, note that
this metric definition now lists a dependent metric (specifically ace_trans_read_latency),
which is previously examined. In this example, there is only one dependent metric,
although multiple dependent metrics can be specified, if required.
The dependent metric is also utilized in the FROM portion of the SQL expression. It
is prefaced with the string $inst__ in a similar manner as the transaction tables are

referred to. When Performance Analyzer evaluates a dependent metric, the string $inst is
automatically replaced with the name of the metric for which the dependent metric is being
evaluated. For example, if the average latency value is being computed for the instance
called master_0, Performance Analyzer automatically uses the data from the results table
called master_0__ace_trans_read_latency as the input for this metric.
The SELECT statement requires some additional explanation. First, the statement utilizes
some built-in SQL functions that are previously described: round and avg. The syntax and
use of these functions is self-explanatory.
However, the use of latency may not be so obvious. To understand where that column is
defined, consider again the SQL statement for the dependent metric:

In the dependent metric, the latency value is given the name latency. This name is used
when creating the results tables for this metric. Thus, when a dependent metric needs to
reference column values in a Results table, it must use the name that is assigned to the
data in the original performance metric definition. In other words, the Results tables for the
ace_trans_read_latency performance metric contains the tables - latency, request_time,
response_time, and event.
Similar dependent metrics can be defined to calculate minimum and maximum latency for
read transactions for each instance. The definition for the minimum latency for ACE read
transactions is shown in the following figure:

The general structure of this metric is similar to the metric that calculates the average
latency for ACE read transactions, but the SELECT statement is different. There is no
specific transaction that can be identified when calculating the average latency value.
However, when calculating minimum or maximum latency values, these values can be
associated with specific transactions. Since this information might help you to track down a
problem, it is best to provide as much information as possible.
To facilitate this, the SELECT statement takes an entirely different approach to determine
the minimum latency. It does so in a manner that the other transaction-related information
can be easily extracted and placed in the Results table. One key feature of SQL is the
ability to order rows based on column values. This is accomplished using ORDER BY and
ASC (for ascending) or DESC (for descending) keywords.
This SELECT statement orders all of the items in the instance-specific
ace_trans_read_latency results tables according to the value of the latency column in
ascending order, and then selects all of the data from the first item (this is accomplished
by LIMIT 1, which limits the results to the specified number of items). The effect of LIMIT 1
is to select information from the transaction with the minimum latency value.
This metric can also be written in a manner similar to the metric that calculated the
average latency value (such as, by using the min SQL function). However, cross-selection
is not possible with such a definition, as no event is present in the Results table.
Dependent metrics can simplify the creation of performance metrics and dramatically
improve evaluation performance. However, they should be carefully considered when
designing performance metrics.
Example 2
Following is an example showing a dependent performance metric definition that counts
the number of bytes associated with each ACE read transaction. A similar dependent
performance metric can be created for this example.

Consider a dependent performance metric (called ace_ctrans_read_byte_count) that
calculates the total number of bytes associated with all of the ACE read transactions for an
instance.

This performance metric computes the total byte count for all the ACE read latencies
for each selected instance. The type of this metric is still instance (as it is for the
previous examples), as the metric calculates a value for each selected instance.
However, note that this metric definition now lists a dependent metric (specifically
ace_trans_read_byte_count), which was previously examined.
As with the prior example, the dependent metric is also utilized in the FROM portion
of the SQL expression. It is prefaced with the $inst__ string in a similar manner as the
transaction tables are referred to. The use of the byte_count column comes from the
definition of the dependent metric, whose definition is shown below for reference.

Multi-Instance Performance Metrics
This chapter so far has focused on instance performance metric definitions.
Examples calculate the latency for each ACE read transaction associated with an
instance. They also show average and minimum latency for all ACE read transactions
associated with an instance.
Other examples calculate the byte counts for each ACE read transaction associated with
an instance. They also show the total byte count for all ACE read transactions associated
with an instance.

It is useful to know the total byte count for all read transactions for all selected instances of
the ACE VIP.
The total can easily be calculated by adding together the total byte counts for the read
transactions for each instance of the ACE VIP.

the ACE VIP.
The total can easily be calculated by adding together the total byte counts for the read
transactions for each instance of the ACE VIP.
The instance-based transaction counts can be calculated using data from the previouslydescribed metric (ace_ctrans_read_byte_count). This is an example of a dependent, multiinstance performance metric.

The figure shows how a "chain" of instance-based dependent metrics can calculate a

It combines that data into a single result using a multi-instance metric.

The performance metric definition that calculates the total number of bytes associated with
all transactions for all instances is shown as follows:

Note that this performance metric definition (called ace_cinst_read_byte_count) is
similar to the previously described dependent performance metric definition (called
ace_ctrans_read_byte_count).
The metric type is defined as multi_instance instead of instance.

Performance Metric Column Data Types

Setting the type to multi_instance indicates to Performance Analyzer that $inst no longer
refers to the Results table for a single instance.
Instead, the results tables from all calculations of the dependent metrics are merged prior
to evaluating the metric.

Summary of Performance Metric Definition Types
As a quick review, there are four different types of performance metrics which differ by (a)
whether the input data is associated with a single instance or multiple instances; and (b)
whether the input data is protocol-related simulation data or is the result of evaluating a
different performance metric.
The four types of performance metrics are as follows:
* Instance, primary performance metrics
* Multi-instance, primary performance metrics
* Instance, dependent performance metrics
* Multi-instance, dependent performance metrics
The four types of performance metrics are shown in the following figure:

As illustrated in the last example, different kinds of metrics can be "chained" to create
complex relationships between performance metric definitions. Performance Analyzer
automatically keeps track of these relationships so that the metrics are evaluated in the
appropriate order to calculate the correct performance results.

Performance Metric Column Data Types
A unit must be assigned for each column that is extracted from the SQL database for a
performance metric. Consider the SQL expression for the first performance metric that
is introduced in this chapter. The user-visible data items are highlighted in red in the
following figure:

Performance Metric Column Data Types

Each of these items must be assigned a data type. This is accomplished using the
perfSetColumnType Tcl command.

The protocol suite name and the metric name must match the names that are specified in
the perfCreateMetric Tcl command.
There are four possible values for the type_string, as described in the following table:
Value

Meaning

None

The result does not require a time unit. For example, if
the performance metric produces a "count" (such as the
number of "read" transactions), no unit is required.

Time

The column represents time. When this type is
specified, the value of "unit" is almost always "fsdb time
unit", which is a special string that represents the time
unit associated with the FSDB file. In the sample SQL
above, "latency", "request_time" and "response_time"
units should all be set to "fsdb time unit".
In certain cases (which are typically rare), the column
data is extracted from an attribute that already has a
particular time unit associated with it. In such cases, the
time unit can be provided (such as, "fs", "ps", "ns" and
so on). If there is any doubt about the time unit, then
usually "fsdb time unit" should be specified.

Data

The column represents a data value. Examples of units
that can be specified with this type are: "Byte", "KB",
"MB", "GB", and "TB".

Types of Performance Metric Visualization
There are five ways in which performance metrics can be graphically displayed within
Performance Analyzer: single-value performance results, bar charts, line charts, pie
charts, and step charts.

Controlling Metric Visualization
Performance metric visualization is primarily controlled using the perfSetChart Tcl
command. The following figure illustrates the Tcl command (including all possible
command options):

The perfSetChart Tcl command has many options, but typically only a few of these
options are required.
This is the same Tcl command that can modify the chart type of predefined metrics when
running Performance Analyzer in batch mode (using the verdi_perf command).
A few options modify the visualization of a specific set of performance results (such
as -start and -end). These options are usually not used when defining a custom or
predefined performance metric.
The values for -protocol and -name options are the same as described for previous
Tcl commands (perfCreateMetric and perfSetColumnType). The other options are
described in detail in the later sections of the document.

Default Metric Visualization
If there is no perfSetChart command associated with a performance metric,
Performance Analyzer utilizes default chart types for displaying performance metric
results.

If a performance metric result contains a single row of data, the first column of that row is
displayed as a single-value metric. Following is an example:

Note that even though this is a single-value metric, the single result row includes multiple
columns.
The columns that are created in the results table for this performance metric can be
understood by examining the SQL SELECT statement that is associated with this metric:

One of the columns (that is, "event") is highlighted in red.
Even though this is a single-value metric, including this column in the result row enables
selection synchronization between Performance Analyzer and Transaction and Protocol
Analyzer windows, as shown in the following figure:

When creating custom performance metrics, consider adding any additional data in the
SELECT statement that can aid the debug process. For this metric, not only is the event
added to the results table, but also the request time and the result time.
If a performance metric result contains multiple rows of data, a bar chart is utilized.

Data in the first column of the results table is used for the y-axis. Data in the second
column is used for the x-axis. An example follows:

The results table for this performance metric also includes additional data, specifically
the response time (which is shown in the table), and the event (which is not shown in
the table, but enables selection synchronization between Performance Analyzer and
Transaction and Protocol Analyzer windows).

Simple Chart Types
For many performance metrics that produce a results table with multiple rows, the bar
chart is often a reasonable visualization choice. However, for some performance metrics,
a line chart may be more appropriate for representing the results. This may also be a
personable preference.

perfSetChart Tcl command . The following perfSetChart command is used to display

The -x and the -y options for the setPerfChart Tcl command apply to bar charts and
line charts and should be self-explanatory. These options allow you to override the default
behavior of which data to is used for x-axis and y-axis. You can recall that by default, the
data from the first column of the results table is used for the y-axis and the data from the
second column of the results table is used for the x-axis. There is one exception to this
rule: if the same column is specified for both the x-axis and the y-axis, the frequency (that
is, the count) of every distinct x value is the y value of that x value.
As previously mentioned, -start and -end options for the setPerfChart Tcl command
provide you the options to visualize a portion of the performance metric results and is
specific to a particular set of input data. Thus, these options are not applicable to general
performance metric definitions and are shown in this document for completeness.
There are two other chart types that are yet described: pie charts and step charts. Pie
charts are particularly useful for showing relative percentages. For example, in an AMBA
system, a pie chart is a good way to visualize which master instances and slave instances
are contributing to the overall transmission of bytes.
The following figure illustrates the pie chart:

The pie chart is constructed from the data in the first and second columns of the results
table. The number of "slices" in the pie is determined by the number of unique values in
the second column of the results table. Based on these "slices", the values from the first
column of the results table are added together (based on the "slices" with which they are
associated). They are then translated into percentages. From this chart, it is easy to see
that the instance called slave_0 is responsible for almost half of the byte count associated
with this particular simulation result.
The step chart is used to show count changes on the x-axis.

Aggregating Chart Data into Ranges
Currently, each row of the performance metric results data is shown as a line or a bar in
the corresponding chart. However, sometimes it is useful to split the data into ranges on
the x-axis and show only a statistical result value for every range. For example, you may
want to view how many read or write requests occur every 100 ns.
Performance Analyzer supports this capability by allowing the x-axis to be split into
ranges. For the data in each range, the y-values are calculated based on an aggregate
function that is specified in the perfSetChart Tcl command. The -x and -y options for the
Tcl command (that are previously described) can be used to specify the data to utilize for
x-axis and y-axis.
If the x-axis is split into intervals, then for every interval there may be multiple data items.
However, only one value is displayed for each interval. This value is a statistical result
of all the data items in the interval, which are specified using the -aggr option of the
perfSetChart Tcl command. The following aggregate functions are supported:

VIP Predefined Performance Metrics
Some Synopsys Verification IPs (VIPs) are shipped with predefined performance metrics.
The type and the number of metrics is protocol-specific and can vary widely from one
protocol to the other protocol.

The Synopsys AMBA VIP has one of the most extensive list of predefined performance
metric. For example, the figure below shows the predefined metrics for the AMBA ACE
protocol. There is a similar list of predefined metrics for the AMBA AXI protocol.

Directory Structure and Files
Performance metric information is stored in the same directory structure that is used to
define protocol-specific information for Protocol Analyzer. The directory structure used by
Protocol Analyzer is reviewed as follows.
For each protocol that is integrated with Protocol Analyzer, there exists information about
the protocol that needs to be captured only once. This information is stored in a collection
of files, referred as the protocol extension definition. The overall directory structure and
files that comprise a protocol extension definition are described in this section.
The purpose of a protocol extension definition is to provide Protocol Analyzer with
protocol-specific information. This enables the tool to organize and display the protocolrelated data that was generated during a simulation. This is done in a manner that is

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
se of a protocol extension definition is to provide Protocol Analyzer with
protocol-specific information. This enables the tool to organize and display the protocolrelated data that was generated during a simulation. This is done in a manner that is
most conducive to protocol-oriented debugging. The same concept applies to predefined
protocol metrics. These metrics need to be defined only once and can then be applied to
multiple designs and simulation results associated with the designs.
The extension definition for each protocol is contained in a directory structure. The
name of the top-most directory is the internal name of the protocol. This name cannot
contain any spaces or non-alphanumeric characters, with the exception of underscore
(`_') characters. For simplicity, the use of all lower-case letters is recommended. To avoid

naming collisions, consider adding a prefix or suffix that clearly differentiates the protocol
name (such as, snps_xyzbus or xyzbus_snps).
The Performance Analyzer locates protocol extension definitions using the same
mechanism as Protocol Analyzer. Specifically, if the DESIGNWARE_HOME environment
variable is defined, that directory structure is automatically scanned for protocol extension
definitions.
The Protocol extension definitions can reside in one or more custom directory locations.
These directories are specified by setting the value of the PA_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH
environment variable. Multiple directory paths can be specified using the colon character
(:) as a delimiter .
The following figure shows the overall directory structure and files that comprise a protocol
extension definition as defined for Protocol Analyzer.

The specification of predefined metrics is simply an extension of this directory structure.

Each Tcl file in the metrics directory contains Tcl commands to define the performance
metric definition and the visualization characteristics for that performance metric. The
commands are the same as those previously discussed.
