While it is not required to separate the Tcl commands for each performance metric into
a separate file, it is highly recommended for maintenance purposes. This approach also
makes it easier to locate the file that contains a performance metric of interest.
For the predefined metrics that are provided with Synopsys VIPs, the names
of the performance metrics also follow a specific naming convention. Consider
the following performance metric definitions that are discussed earlier in this
document: ace_trans_read_byte_count, ace_ctrans_read_byte_count, and
ace_cinst_read_byte_count.
* Each name begins with the string "ace" to indicate that these metrics are
associated with the AMBA ACE protocol.
* The second string indicates the kind of metric that is being defined.
* The "trans" string (shorthand for "transaction") indicates that the metric is
evaluated on multiple transactions independently, This creates a results
table that contains multiple rows (one for each transaction, as determined by
the SQL statement associated with the performance metric definition).
* The "ctrans" string (shorthand for "cross-transaction") indicates that the
metric considers all the transactions together. Again, this is determined
by the SQL statement associated with the performance metric definition.
Both "trans" and "ctrans" performance metric definitions are instance-based
performance metrics.
* The "cinst" string (shorthand for "cross-instance") indicates that the metric
considers results data from multiple instances. In other words, these are
"multi-instance" performance metric definitions.
This is a naming convention that is used by the Synopsys VIPs to make it easier to identify
performance metric definitions. It is not a requirement of the Performance Analyzer tool.
For example, to specify a predefined metric called ace_cinst_read_byte_count
(that is, the metric that was discussed in the previous section), the commands to
define the metric and the visualization characteristics are specified in a Tcl file called
ace_cinst_read_byte_count.tcl in the metrics directory.

Merging Custom Metrics With Predefined Metrics
The previous section described how to create a directory for a custom protocol that
contains performance metric definitions. However, sometimes it is desirable to merge
the predefined metrics that are shipped with a Synopsys VIP or transactor with additional
custom metrics. At other times, it is desirable to slightly modify the behavior of such
predefined metrics to satisfy specific performance measurement requirements.
To achieve this goal, it is necessary to merge the predefined metrics that are shipped with
the Synopsys tool and the custom metrics that are independently developed into a single
directory structure. Then, the PA_CUSTOM_VIP_PATH environment variable can be set to
point to this directory. As previously mentioned, multiple directory paths can be specified
using the colon character (:) as a delimiter.
This approach can be easily shown with an example. Consider the predefined
performance metrics that are shipped with the AMBA AXI VIP. The Tcl files that define
these metrics can be found in the following directory:
$DESIGNWARE_HOME/vip/svt/amba_svt/latest/pa/axi_svt/performance/metrics
To merge these predefined metrics with other metrics (or to modify these metrics), these
Tcl files must first be copied to a directory that represents a "custom" protocol definition.

section. For the AMBA AXI VIP, this task can be accomplished with the following

Introduction
As most of the designs incorporate more complex protocols, the verification engineer's
task to evaluate the performance of those designs is a challenging task. It not only takes a
significant effort but is also time-consuming.
Verdi Performance Analyzer provides a solution to this problem by enabling users to
easily analyze the performance of any design. However, many verification engineers
need access to performance parameters during the simulation run in the testbench code.
The SystemVerilog APIs described in this chapter can provide runtime access to the
Performance Data of Verdi Performance Analyzer.
Starting with Verdi N-2017.12 release, the performance analysis runtime APIs are
designed to address such challenges. Firstly, runtime performance analysis is easy to
integrate for regressions. Secondly, with the use of these APIs, the same benefits can be
extended to third party, internally developed, or other proprietary protocols.
This chapter highlights the overall runtime performance application integration process as
well as the steps that are required to use these APIs in SystemVerilog code.

Preface
(R)

Verdi Automated Debug Platform supports power-aware debug. The standard Verdi
debug capability can debug power issues detected by these visualizations.
This guide describes scenarios for using Power-Aware Debug functionality in the Verdi
Automated Debug Platform.

Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and answers to
frequently asked questions about Synopsys tools. It also provides access to Synopsys
online services, including software downloads, documentation, and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
If prompted, enter your user name and password. If you do not have a Synopsys user
name and password, follow the instructions to sign up for an account.
If you need help using the SolvNetPlus site, click REGISTRATION HELP in the top-right
menu bar.

Contacting Customer Support

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary
language from our products and customer-facing collateral.

Chapter 1: Preface
Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity

We are also removing biased language from our engineering and working environment.
This includes terms embedded in our software and IPs. At the same time, we are working
to ensure that our web content and software applications are usable to people of varying
abilities.
You may still find non-inclusive language in our software or documentation. Our IPs
implement industry-standard specifications that are currently under review to remove
exclusionary language.

Overview
The power architecture in today's designs is getting increasingly complex, and multiple
power domains with various power modes require a thorough verification method. Some
technologies are provided to define and verify the complex power domains. Among these
technologies, standard power formats, Unified Power Format (UPF - IEEE 1801-2009
standard), and power-aware simulations are widely used to ensure that low power designs
still produce a high confidence chip.
In order to support the standard power formats, and also to visualize the simulation
(R)
results, the Verdi Automated Debug Platform supports power-aware debug. The standard
Verdi debug capability can be used to debug power issues that are detected by these
visualizations.
When the RTL design is converted to a gate-level design, part of the power intent defined
in the UPF power files is synthesized either by a synthesis tool or by the designers
manually. For example, isolation or level-shifter rules are implemented by inserting
isolation or level-shifter cells during conversion from RTL to gate-level design. Along with
the conversion, the content of the UPF files should be refined by the tool or designers
respectively to reflect the changes. For the previously mentioned example, the related
isolation/level-shifter power rules should be removed from the UPF files since they are
replaced by the isolation/level-shifter cells respectively (for the flow, see Figure 1).

Chapter 2: Overview

Figure 1

UPF Refinement

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The refined UPF (UPF') files and the gate-level design need to be verified to confirm equal
functionality to the original UPF files and the RTL design. The Verdi platform provides
exactly the same power-aware debug capability as in the RTL stage, so that you can
debug inconsistencies (between RTL and gate-level) in the same Verdi environment.
Additionally, the Verdi platform can recognize and highlight power cells that are unique to
the gate-level. The Verdi platform can import the power cell information from the Synopsys
Liberty files (for usage details, see the Directly Importing Liberty Files and Displaying
Power Cell Information section) and UPF files (power cell commands). The power cells
can be highlighted that helps you to compare the inserted power cell and its related logic
with the mapping part in the RTL design. For example, you can inspect whether the
location and direction of isolation, switch, or level shifter cells is consistent with the related
power rules defined in the RTL stage.

Using Power-Aware Debug

Importing UPF Files
Select UPF 1.0 or UPF 2.0 option in the Language field and select the UPF files to load
into the Verdi platform.
Alternatively, use the -upf1.0 or -upf2.0 command-line option to import the UPF files,

Starting Verdi Power Aware Debug with UFE Flow
You must specify the -kdb option at compilation/elaboration and the +fsdb+power option
at runtime to use Verdi Power Aware capabilities with VCS under the UFE flow.
% vcs -sverilog -f run.f -upf demo.upf debug_access+all -kdb -power_top system
% simv +fsdb+power +fsdbfile+power.fsdb
% verdi -ssf power.fsdb

Power-Aware Debug support is integrated with the main nTrace window. Power-related

Power Domain List Pane
The Power Domain List pane displays all the power domains defined in the design. This
pane is docked to the same pane location as the Design Browser as a new tab. Each

power domains and power objects, see the Highlighting Power Domain, Power Objects,
and Power Signals section.
The power states for all power domains are represented by different icons. For example,
the

the related definitions can be easily found. If you load an FSDB file and click the Source
-> Active Annotation menu option, the domain status is displayed dynamically by on,

toolbar.
Some of the features for Power Domain List pane are as follows:
* The primary/default_isolation/default_retention supply set nodes appear as children
nodes for a power domain tree node.
* If a supply set node is associated with a supply set, the name of the node appears as
the supply_set_name(associate_supply_set_name) string format.
This is also illustrated in the following figure:

both Power Source Code pane and HDL source code pane, as shown in the following

The Power source code pane is displayed by default. Click the HDL source code tab, as
shown in the following figure, to view the HDL source code pane.

* By default, the isolation supply set node appears as the children node for an isolation
policy node.
For example, if the supply set is associated with some other supply set SS_ISO,
the associated supply set appears as SS_ISO, else, associated supply set
appears as domain_name.default_isolation. The supply set appears as the
policy_name.isolation_supply_set(associate_supply_set_name) string format. This is
also illustrated in the following figure.

* The retention supply set node appears as the children node for a retention policy node,
by default.
For example, if the supply set is associated with some other supply set SS_RET,
the associated supply set appears as SS_RET, else, associated supply set
appears as domain_name.default_retention. The supply set appears as the
policy_name.retention_supply_set(associate_supply_set_name) string format. This is
also illustrated in the following figure.

* The power/ground children node for a supply set node appears as
supply_set_name.power or supply_set_name.ground by default. If the power/ground
children nodes are overwritten by a supply net object, the node name appears as the
overwritten supply net object.

If set1.ground is overwritten by VSS, the child ground net node appears as VSS.

Color Coding in Power State Table
* A row highlighted with an orange background color signifies that the signal is in active
power mode.
* A row highlighted with red background color signifies that Verdi cannot find the
combination of power status to meet the predefined Power State Table in UPF.
* Multiple rows are highlighted because these modes are differentiated only in voltage.
Such modes cannot be distinguished in the Verdi platform because voltage value is not
recorded in the FSDB file (simulator dependency).
* Text in red color signifies that Verdi cannot find the exact value of a signal from FSDB.
For example, as illustrated in Figure 10, the font color for on(HV, 1.08v) is red, which
signifies that the value of VDDMS is not the exact value.
Figure 10

Color coding in Power State Table

text:
Power Source Code Pane
The source code pane of the main window shows the source code of the imported UPF
power file in a separate tab. The content is changed accordingly when double-clicking
different items in the Power Domain List pane. Enabling the Source -> Active Annotation
menu option annotates the FSDB value for signals under the source code, if the FSDB file
is loaded into the Verdi platform.
Tracing capabilities including tracing HDL driver/load and tracing power driver/load are
also available in the power source code pane:
* To trace the HDL driver/load, click the Trace -> Trace Driver/Trace Load option on the
toolbar. The traced results are displayed in the design source code pane.
* To trace the power driver/load/connectivity, select a signal in the power source code
pane, right click, and select the Trace Power Driver/Trace Power Load/Trace Power

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Connectivity option. Or, select a signal in the power source code pane, click the Trace
Power icon on the toolbar, and select Driver, Load, or Connectivity option. Refer to
the following figure:

The cursor jumps to the corresponding source code, and the traced results are displayed
in the Trace tab of the Message pane.
Definitions of the power driver/load are as follows:
* Power Driver: These commands impact the HDL signal. For example, if an HDL signal
is defined in a retention rule command, it implies that when the associated power
domain is turned off, the HDL signal becomes a retention signal (impacted). Therefore,
this retention rule is one of the traced results of the HDL signal's Power Driver.
The Power Driver trace results include the following:
UPF
create_power_domain: if the HDL signal belongs to the power domain.
set_isolation: if the HDL signal is the isolation signal of the command.
set_retention: if the HDL signal is the retention signal of the command.
set_level_shifter: if the HDL signal is the level shifter signal of the command.
* Power Load: These commands are impacted by the HDL signal. For example, if
the HDL signal is defined in a shut off condition, the signal turns off the associated
power domain when the value matches the condition. This implies the power domain
is impacted by the HDL signal. Therefore, this shut off condition is one of the traced
results of the HDL signal's Power Load.
The Power Load trace results include the following when the HDL signal is contained in
the options:
UPF
create_power_switch -control_port
set_isolation_control -isolation_signal

set_retention_control -restore_signal
set_retention_control -save_signal

Enabling UPF Commands of Inactive Power Domains in the Power
Source Code View
Verdi allows you to debug the UPF commands of inactive power domains in the Power
Source Code View. Debug functions like RMB, viewing annotations, and drag-and-drop
are supported on these commands.
The Show Previous/Show Next command searches the commands in the previous/next
line by file in the Power Source Code View.

select the Schematic -> Report Selected Impacted Signalsoption to open a form

title: Verification ContinuumTM

Figure 13

Impacted Power Signals of the Isolation Rule

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The Power Map pane can validate all signals in between power domains to be guarded
with isolation rules if a possibility exists (seeAppendix A: Power Map Validation) that the
domain a signal is coming from (from domain) is off while the domain the signal is going
to (to domain) is not. In such a case, unexpected results could propagate through such
signals from the from domain to the to domain. Similarly, signals are suggested to be
guarded with level-shifter rules if the signals' from and to domains are both on/standby
states, but the domains' voltages are different.
The checking is performed when the Power Map pane is first invoked or when the related
checking options (View -> Non-covered Signals -> Isolation Signals/Level-shifter
Signals) are turned on. The results are displayed as non-covered nets (shown by dotted
lines). A non-covered net contains all non-covered signals on the path from domain X to
domain Y. The red dotted lines represent the non-covered isolation nets (it is suggested to
apply isolation rules); the green dotted lines represent the non-covered level-shifter nets (it
is suggested to apply level-shifter rules). Refer to Figure 14.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Figure 14

Non-Covered Signals Shown by Dotted Lines

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Select any of the non-covered nets and select the Schematic -> Report Selected
Impacted Signals option to see all the non-covered signals belonging to the selected noncovered net (see Figure 15). Or select the Schematic -> Report Total Impacted Signals
option to view all impacted signals for the whole design.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Figure 15

Impacted Power Signals of Non-Covered Isolation Net

Double check the non-covered signals to decide whether you need to apply isolation or
level shifter rules accordingly (they may be missed during the power design). To turn off
the automatic non-covered nets checking, select the View -> Non-covered Signals ->
Isolation Signals/Level-shifted Signals option to toggle them off.

After invoking the Partial Power Map pane, right-click a power domain and select Show

Power network goes through the power switch and power port, and ends at the original

Show Power Network

button to redo the operation.

Power cells can be dragged and dropped to the existing Partial Power Map pane. The
following additional options are available to perform various actions in Power Map pane:
* Power Switch commands: Adds the switch and its domains to the current Power Map
pane and highlights the switch cell.
* Isolation/Level-shifter rule commands: Adds the target and source power domains of
the rule to the current Power Map pane and highlights all relative Isolation/Level-shifter
cells extracted from this rule.
* Power domain: Adds this power domain supply network to the current Power Map pane
and highlights the power domain cell.
* Power port: Finds the port in the current Power Map pane.
* Power supply net: Adds the connected power domain and power switch to the current
Power Map pane and highlights the power supply cell.

* HDL instance: Finds the power domain that the instance belongs to. If the power
domain exists in the Partial Power Map pane, it is highlighted; otherwise, a warning
message is displayed to indicate that the power domains cannot be found.
Figure 20

If the impacted cell or power domain does not exist, a warning message is displayed.
* Others: If the dropped power object cannot extract or trace any results in the Partial
Power Map pane, a warning message is displayed to indicate that adding the power
object to the Partial Power Map pane failed.
To trace the power switch, double-click the input pin or output pin. The loading result is
displayed for the output pin and the driver result is displayed for the input pin. Tracing
passes through the power port and ends at a power domain or a power switch.

Power Port
Verdi displays the power port name in the Trace tab of the message frame. The name of
the power port is displayed in the following format:
port_name(power_port)

Power Port Drivers
The following are the possible drivers for a power port:
* Connected Net (specified using connect_supply_net command)
Supply net connected to HighConn of an input or inout port
Supply net connected to LowConn of an output or inout port

* The supply_on, supply_off, and supply_partial_on functions in the testbench.
The driver statement for the specified power port is listed if the pad name of
supply_on, supply_off, or supply_partial_on is a string literal.

Otherwise, the driver statement is listed as possible result of all power ports.

* The nets and ports of electrical or functional equivalence

Power Port Loads
The following are the possible loads for a power port:
* Connected Net (specified using connect_supply_net command)
Supply net connected to LowConn of an input or inout port
Supply net connected to HighConn of an output or inout port

* The nets and ports of electrical or functional equivalence

When you trace power transition on TFV, Verdi displays the supply set cell for the power
domain if you specify the power domain. For example, as shown in the following sample
UPF code.
create_power_domain PD_TOP set_domain_supply_net PD_TOP \
-primary_power_net VDD \
-primary_ground_net VSS

Power Switch
Verdi displays only the active state ports of the power switch.
Consider the following sample UPF code:
create_power_domain PD_FSM \
-elements {CHILD1 CHILD2 CHILD3 MASTER}
create_supply_net VDD_FSM -domain PD_TOP
create_power_switch SW_FSM \
-domain PD_TOP \
-input_supply_port {vin VDD} \
-output_supply_port {vout VDD_FSM} \

-control_port {en pmc/PowerControl[0]}\
-on_state {ON_STATE vin {en}} \
-off_state {OFF_STATE {!en}}\
-ack_port {my_ack_port my_ack_net}

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
In the transition trace mode, the power switch is displayed as follows:
Figure 52

Power Switch in Transition Trace Mode

The default color of the power switch cell is light orange.
Verdi displays the acknowledge port (-ack_port) of the power switch as follows:
Figure 53

Ack_port of the Power Switch in Transition Trace Mode

All control nets of the power switch are the fanin cones of the acknowledge port. You can
enable the Power Cell Name option to mark the power cell name above the acknowledge
port.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Isolation
Verdi displays the isolation cells for the specified domain in the HDL trace path.
Consider the following sample UPF code:
set_isolation iso_ALUB \
-domain i_cpu/PD_ALUB \
-isolation_power_net VDD -isolation_ground_net VSS \

-clamp_value 0 \
-applies_to outputs
set_isolation_control iso_ALUB \
-domain i_cpu/PD_ALUB\
-isolation_signal pmc/ALUB_iso\
-isolation_sense high\
-location self

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
In the transition trace mode, the isolation cell is displayed as shown in the following figure.
For implicit supply set, Verdi displays upf_simstate connected with assigned power nets.
Figure 54

Isolation Cell in Transition Trace Mode

The default color of an isolation cell is pink.

Signal Naming
The naming of fanin/fanout signals follows the isolation naming rule. An instrumented
signal is inserted before or after the ISO cell. The naming rule is signal_name_UPF_ISO/
signal_name__UPF_ISO_PRE. The en port is also connected with the instrumented signal
isolation_enable_power_cell_name.
When the en port is true, the fanout signal value of the ISO cell is the clamp value. Verdi
also marks it as clamp value on the value label.
Figure 55

Isolation Fanout Value is the Clamp Value When the en Port is True

Retention
For the set_retention command specified in the UPF, Verdi displays the retention cells
for the specified domain register.
Consider the following sample UPF code:
set_retention gprs_ret -domain GPRS \
-retention_power_net VDDG -retention_ground_net VSS
set_retention_control gprs_ret -domain GPRS \
-save_signal {gprs_save high} \
-restore_signal {gprs_nrestore low}

For the save state of retention, a shadow register cell with label SHADOW is inserted in the
trace path to represent how the circuit holds the signal value. For the restore state, the
fanout signal value is restored from the shadow register.
Figure 56

Retention Cell in Transition Trace Mode

The default color of the retention cell is yellowish-brown. The coloring of the retention cells
and connection line is same. The color of the retention (restore) fanout signal does not
follow the preference color setting.
The naming of the fanin/fanout signals follows the power naming rule. Following is the
retention instrumented signal name:
save_signal_name

SRSN/SPA
For the set_related_supply_net or set_port_attribute command specified in the
UPF, Verdi displays the SRSN/SPA cells in the HDL trace path.

Consider the following sample UPF code:
set_related_supply_net -object_list {instA/out1 instA/in1} -power VDD
-ground VSS
set_related_supply_net -object_list {instA/out2} -power VDDA -ground VSS

In the transition trace mode, the SRSN/SPA cell is displayed as shown in the following
figure. For implicit supply set, Verdi displays upf_simstate connected with assigned
power nets.
Figure 57

SRSN Cell with Implicit Supply Set in Transition Trace Mode

The default color of the SRSN/SPA cell is greenish-blue. An instrumented signal is
inserted before the SRSN/SPA cell. The naming rule is signal_name_srsn_buffer.

Boundary Cell
For the XML flow, Verdi displays the boundary cell in the TFV window if it is instrumented.
Figure 58

The set_repeater command defines a strategy for inserting repeater cells (buffers) for
ports on the interface of a power domain. Repeater cells are placed within the domain,
driven by input ports of the domain, and driving the output ports of the domain.
Verdi supports the set_repeater command per the IEEE 1801-2015 UPF LRM. This
command lets you insert buffers inside the specified domain. You can insert a buffer with a
specific supply on the required side of the domain boundary pins.
Following is the syntax of the set_repeater command:
set_repeater strategy_name
-domain domain_name
[-elements element_list]
[-exclude_elements exclude_list]
[-applies_to <inputs | outputs | both>]
-repeater_supply supply_set_ref
[-name_prefix string] [-name_suffix string]
[-update]

Support Pass Through connect_supply_net and
connect_logic_net commands as Pass-Through Trace Result
During tracing, Verdi supports pass through connect_supply_net and connect_logic_net
commands as pass-through trace results. The trace result does not stop at every
connect_supply_net and connect_logic_net command.
This feature is controlled by the Pass Through Connect Supply/Logic Net Commands
preference option (Trace -> Pass Through Connect Supply/Logic Net Commands) in
the Preferences form. This option is off by default.
When you enable this option, the trace result passes through the connect_supply_net
and connect_logic_net commands during tracing. The setting is saved in the novas.rc
file.
This feature is not supported when the connect_supply_net and connect_logic_net
commands contain RTL signals.
For example, in the following figure, the trace driver passes through the
connect_supply_net commands. It displays the root cause as a supply function.

Power Aware Trace Driver/Load Support for SPICE Signals
For SPICE+UPF designs, Verdi power aware debug supports tracing drivers/loads for
SPICE signals. Verdi displays the SPICE signal name in the Trace tab, for example, as
shown in the following figure:
Figure 78

Tracing SPICE Signals With Power Analysis

In the above figure, the SPICE signal vdd connects to the power supply VDDH, and VDDH is
driven by the SPICE signal vdd_dig_high.
Limitations
Following are the limitations of this feature:
* In a SPICE domain, contributor analysis support is limited. For example, primitive
device ports are inout ports. They are all listed as contributors.
Contributors are listed only by judging port directions, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 79

Contributors Analysis is Limited for Primitive Gates

* Active driver analysis is not supported for analog signals with continuous waveform. In
this case, the status of drivers is "possible drivers".

Power Aware Trace Driver/Load Support for SPICE Signals

Figure 80

Contributors Analysis is Limited for Primitive Gates

* Active driver analysis is not supported for the drivers under analog block. In this case,
the status of drivers is "possible drivers". For example, in the following figure, Trace
Driver for top.MA.real_out1 lists the possible driver under analog block.
Figure 81

Tracing Drivers Under Analog Block

* Active driver analysis for analog signal with continuous waveform (driven by digital
signals) is not supported. In this case, the status of driver is "inactive".
In the following figure, the active trace is triggered at 20.00024620066 s. Verdi cannot
determine that a digital signal value change at 20 s drives the analog signal. The
waveform is continuous.

Reporting the SPICE Supply Port Connection to UPF Supply Net

Verdi cannot get the correct time of the value change. The status can be "inactive".
Figure 82
Active Driver Analysis for Analog Signal With Continuous Waveform (Driven by
Digital Signals)

* Power Map pane

* Design Browser pane

* nSchema window

* Temporal Flow View (TFV) pane

The TFV pane supports power domains highlight and RET/ISO annotation for retention/
isolation latches and flip-flops. The path shown in TFV has instances highlighted with
the color of the respective power domains and the RET/ISO annotation for retention/
isolation latches/flip-flops, if there are any in the path. The power domain name and
status is displayed on the toolbar.

Highlighting Power-Aware Objects
To highlight Power-Aware Objects, the Highlight Power Aware Design Object(s) option
(default value is on) must be turned on. Refer to the preference setting displayed in
Figure 85.
The Power-Aware Objects include Power Down Instance, Retention Object, Isolation
Object, Level Shifted Object, Power Switch Object, Always-on Object, Boundary
Port Object, Power Net, and Ground Net

Dumping PST and PSG Information
The Dump to FSDB File option supports dumping of the Power State Table (PST) and
Power State Group (PSG) information into the FSDB file. To enable dumping of the PST
and PSG information, you must redump FSDB (get PST and PSG value from FSDB
generated by VCS).
For backwards compatibility, set the VERDI_POWER_EVALUATE_VALUE_FOR_PST_AND_PSG
environment variable to TRUE. Following is the syntax of this variable:
setenv VERDI_POWER_EVALUATE_VALUE_FOR_PST_AND_PSG = TRUE|FALSE

Limitations
* Interactive console does not support drag-and-drop name change for $fsdbDumpVars.
You cannot directly use drag-and-drop result of power aware signals as parameter of
$fsdbDumpVars as drag-and-drop does not support full scope name for power aware
signals, and also $fsdbDumpVars cannot use full scope name as parameter to dump
power.
* TFV needs to know accurate value at a specific time, so it is recommended to dump
the power scope in the interactive mode.
* Dumper does not support dumping of attribute signals (for example, tb.VDD.voltage).

Reporting Impacted Signals
Typically, designers of the UPF power intent files and HDL designers are not the same.
To help HDL designers quickly grasp which signals are impacted by the power intent, the
Power -> Report Impacted Signals by Scope menu option is provided.

Reporting Impacted Signals

When the Power -> Report Impacted Signals by Scope menu option is executed, the
Scope Lists form opens. Select the required scopes in the form and click the OK button.
The Report Power Impacted Signals form opens up. The form lists all signals that are
impacted by the power intent (imported UPF files).
The Rule column lists the power rule related to each signal; the From/To Instance columns
list the driving scope and the loaded scope of each signal; and the From/To Domain lists
the power domain of the driving and loaded scope. For an example, see Figure 97.
You can sort each column of the Report Power Impacted Signals form by clicking the
heading of the column. For example, turn on the Show Full Name option to display
signals with full hierarchical names, and click the heading of the Signal column to sort.
After sorting, the list is sorted by hierarchy that makes it easy to browse by scope.

showing the connectivity of the selected signal.

Listing Power Related X
When debugging unknowns, to help you to rule out signal unknowns (X value) that are
affected by its own power domain being switched off (such unknowns are correct) and
focus on unknowns that may be real issues, use the List X (Tools -> List X) option in the
main window or nWave. This option highlights the unknowns that may be real issues (not
affected by its own power domain being switched off) in yellow.
To use the option, select several signals in the nWave signal pane, and then invoke the
Tools -> List X option from nWave or main window. The Source File to List X form is
opened as illustrated in Figure 101.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Listing Power Related X

Figure 101

Source File to List X Form

Select the Use Current Simulation Results option in the Source File Selection field.
The other two options do not contain power information.
In the List: field
* Select the Selected Signals option to list unknowns for selected signals in nWave.
* Select the All Signals option to list unknowns for all signals in the design.
Click the Next button in the Source File to List X form, to view the list of all unknowns in
the List X form, as illustrated in Figure 102.
Figure 102

List X Form

Power Sequence Checking

Click the Go to next time table or the Go to previous time table buttons to change to
next/previous time stamp. If the row number is marked in orange, it means the signal is
new compared to the previous time stamp. To mask out unknowns that are caused by the
power domain off, check the Ignore X Values Caused by Power Off check box.
To continue to trace these issues, select any row and click the Trace Active X button. This
performs the Trace Active X option using the current time of the selected signal.
For more information on tracing unknown (X) values in power-aware designs, click the
following video link.
This video focuses on tracing unknown (X) values in power-aware designs using
Verdi.

Power Sequence Checking
The Power Sequence Checking function can be used to check whether the results in the
FSDB file matches your original intention in the UPF file. The Verdi platform has defined
typical power rules for power-aware designs, and checks whether there are any violations
by analyzing the simulation results and the power intent file.
To use this function, invoke the Power -> Check Power Sequence menu option from the
main window that opens the Check Power Sequence form. There exist typical power rules
in the following three categories:
* Isolation
* Power Domain
* Power Mode
Toggle the check box in front of each rule as on to check the check box. Specify the
maximum error number in the Max. Errors field, and click the Check button to check the
power sequence, as illustrated in Figure 103.
Two rules are turned off by default as they require more time for the checking
that may impact the performance. Toggle on the check box, if you intend to
check these two rules.

Power Sequence Checking

Figure 103

Check Power Sequence Form

You can click the Check button to view the checking results in the Report tab of the Check
Power Sequence form, as shown in Figure 104. Violations are listed under each rule. Click
the plus icon to expand all violations, or click the minus icon to collapse these.
There are some icons displayed in front of each rule that represent severity and status of
each rule. The following is the list of these icons along with their meanings:
* The

icon signifies No Error

* The

icon signifies Error

* The

icon signifies Not Checked

* The

icon signifies Warning

Power Sequence Checking

Figure 104

Displaying Isolation Cell Information
When the Display Isolation Annotation Symbol option in the Power Aware ->
Miscellaneous page of the Preferences form is turned on, isolation annotation is
displayed as a symbol in the Source Code pane.
When the Display Isolation Annotation Symbol option is turned off, isolation annotation
is displayed as a string in the Source Code pane (that is, the annotation string for iso_in
signal is shown as iso_in; iso_out signal as iso_out; iso_inout signal as iso_inout). The
default is on.
The setting is saved in the novas.rc resource file and the key is ShowIsoSymbol.
This option is supported only in the XML flow.

Debugging VCS Low Power Instrumented Objects in Verdi
Verdi allows you to debug low power objects instrumented by VCS NLP. You can
use the low power debug DB, an XML format file, dumped by VCS NLP to handle all
instrumentation scenarios. The low power debug DB contains the following information:
* Instrumented objects information (For nTrace and Power Domain List debugging)
* Connection relationship information (For Trace Driver/Trace Load, nSchema, and
Power Map debugging)
This feature helps you to get consistent results between VCS NLP and the Verdi platform.
You can use VCS to generate the low power instrumented objects and reduce the
duplicate effort for the Verdi parser to create the low power instrumented objects.

Use Model
Dumping Low Power Debug DB XML File During Simulation
The following is the syntax to dump DB XML file during simulation:
% vcs <design file> -upf <upf file> -kdb -debug_access+all <compile
options>

You can also dump a compressed XML file.

Loading the Dump XML Database File in Verdi
If you have generated Verdi kdb database using vlogan/vhdlan, VCS NLP generates
the XML file. You can use the verdi -ssf novas.fsdb or simv -verdi option to
automatically load the XML file.
Following is the syntax to load the dump XML database file if the kdb is generated from
vericom/vhdlcom:
verdi -lp_xml[=file_name.xml]

Display Input or Output of the Isolation Signals

The Power Debug mode in Verdi Automated Debug Platform provides Signal List pane
right-click option: Add Instrumented Signals to Waveform to add instrumented signals
for different policies or strategies in the nWave window. The option menu includes
Isolation Signals, Retention Signals, SRSN Signals, and SPA Signals sub-options.
The following sections discuss about how to view the instrumented signals for the
respective strategies/policies:
* Isolation Signals
* Retention Signals
* SRSN Signals
* SPA Signals

Isolation Signals
The Add Instrumented Signals to Waveform -> Isolation Signals option adds the
instrumented isolation signals to the nWave window. As illustrated in the Figure 117,
right-click on a signal (for example, WrtEnbX) in the Signal List pane and click Add

Instrumented Signals to Waveform -> Isolation Signals option to add the instrumented
isolation signals to the nWave window.
Figure 117

Add Instrumented Isolation Signals to nWave

To enable tooltip for the signals appearing in the Signal List pane, right-click a signal and
select Show Tip option. The tooltip displays signal name, type and power information, as
illustrated in Figure 118
Figure 118

Tooltip for Signals in Signal List Pane

The isolation instrumented signals get added to the nWave window with the following
naming convention:
* *_UPF_ISO
* *_UPF_ISO_PRE
* isolation_*
This is illustrated in Figure 119.

Isolation Signals Added to nWave Window

Verdi supports tracing boundary MUX cells of power domain in nTrace, nWave, nSchema,
and Temporal Flow View. Verdi also allows you to,
* Perform power corruption calculation for power corrupted by a random cell value.
* Trace the root cause for power corruption using automatic power tracing.
This section consists of the following sub-sections:
* Support for Boundary MUX Cells in nTrace
* Support for Boundary MUX Cells in nWave
* Support for Boundary MUX Cells in nSchema
* Support for Boundary MUX Cells in Temporal Flow View
* Power Corruption Model in Temporal Flow View

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Support for Boundary MUX Cells in nTrace
nTrace displays boundary cells in the Hierarchy Tree tab and provide corresponding
debug functionalities. The Boundary MUX tree nodes are bit-based and are grouped
under an array node. The naming rule for Boundary MUX nodes is as follows:
PD_BOUNDRAY_out[bit_index](SNPS_UPF_Boundary_Mux)

Figure 124

Boundary MUX Nodes

Sorting and filtering applies to Boundary MUX tree nodes also. You can filter the boundary
MUX cells as shown in the following figure:
Figure 125

Filtering Boundary MUX Cells

Additionally, the boundary MUX is now integrated into nTrace driver/load results. If power
domain is modeled as a boundary MUX, then you can see "power domain" as driving
statements, related supply set, and instrumented signals as contributors. This helps you
to understand the existence of boundary MUX and you can continue to trace through the
instrumented signals.

Power Domain Not Modeled as Boundary MUX
This section illustrates the different trace driver/load behaviors when power domain is not
modeled as boundary MUX (for example, VCS NLP).
* If the traced signal is upf_simstate (instrumented signal) under HDL scope, Verdi
shows the power domain of HDL scope as driver.
* If the traced signal is not driven by SRSN, SPA, or ISO cell and related power domain
is off, Verdi shows the related power domain as driver. HDL drivers of traced signal
should be inactive at the same time.

correctness of active drivers/contributors status is not guaranteed. However, the static
drivers/contributors results (which is based on netlist) is still correct regardless of the
cycle-delay issues.
Figure 130

Trace Driver/Load Results on the Output of SRSN Cell

Known Issues
* Cycle delay issues affect the active drivers/contributors status of ISO, SRSN, and
Boundary MUX cells.
* Incorrect netlist issues affect the active drivers/contributors status of Boundary MUX
cells.
* Any missing dumped signals or incorrect dumped signals affect the active drivers/
contributors status.

title: Verification ContinuumTM

Support for Boundary MUX Cells in nWave
nWave supports power shading for Boundary MUX power designs. The shading is based
on power zero-delay, that is, once the power condition is enabled, the corresponding
shading is drawn.
nWave supports the following kinds of power shadings:
* Power Off: The power-off range for HDL signals is masked and the off range is
checked from upf_power_domain_state instead of upf_simstate.
* Isolation: The isolation range for HDL signals is masked according to the applied
isolation condition.
* Retention: The retention range for HDL signals is masked according to the applied
retention condition.
* Driving Power Off: The driving power-off ranges for HDL signals is masked and the off
range is checked from upf_power_domain_state instead of upf_simstate.
* Toggle: The range for HDL signals is masked where the scope is already in a poweroff corruption state and the input signals contain value changes. The off range is
checked from upf_power_domain_state, instead of upf_simstate.
To check what condition each shading is based on, turn on the Waveform -> View
Options -> Waveform Pane -> Enable Tip preference option (invoked using Tools ->
Preferences). The tip provides additional information.
For example, the following figure shows Power Off shading where

text:
upf_power_domain_state is CORRUPT from time 132, hence, waveform draws power off

shading immediately, but the HDL signal value is changed from time 133, hence, there is
one cycle delay.

Figure 131

Power Off Shading

The following figure shows Isolation shading, where isolation condition is enabled from
time 108, hence, waveform draws isolation shading from that time, but the HDL signal
value is changed from time 109, hence, there is one cycle delay.
Figure 132

Isolation Shading

Support for Boundary MUX Cells in nSchema
nSchema also supports the symbol boundary instrument cell as Boundary Cell (BC) type.
The usage of BC type is similar to ISO/SPA/SRSN instrument cell types. The instrument
color is same as the power domain color, as illustrated in the figure below.
In the detailed RTL mode in nSchema (enabled using the View -> Detailed RTL menu
option), all boundary cells are created. However, in the non-detailed RTL mode, same
boundary cells with different index values are merged to 1 boundary cell.

Figure 133

Boundary Instrument Cell Symbol

Figure 134

Normal -> Corrupt Boundary Instrument Cell

The Drag and Drop (DnD) functionality does not contain Power_Command; it is regarded
as a usual RTL instance. The DnD functionality between different nSchema windows has
different behavior, as follows:
* Dragging and Dropping to a full window jumps to a specific scope, whereas, dragging
and dropping to a flattened window adds or selects the boundary cell in the flattened
window.
* DnD a split boundary cell to nPowerManage shows power create domain in the UPF
file. A limitation for DnD to nPowerManage is that dragging and dropping a merged
boundary cell is not supported.
* DnD a split/merged boundary cell to nWave adds all the connected signals to nWave.

Power Corruption Model in Temporal Flow View
If the value of power corrupted cell is random, it's value is obtained from the FSDB file
directly. The automatic tracing feature supported by Temporal Flow Viewallows you to
trace this value for power net when the power is corrupted. You can use the Trace This
Value right-click option to trace the corrupted power signal's value instead of using the
Trace Active X option.
The Trace Active X right-click option is disabled in power-aware Temporal Flow
View if the signal value is not X.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
When tracing the fanout signal for which the power supply set is corrupted, the value is
obtained from the FSDB file directly, and trace is performed to the power supply set to
detect the root cause of power corruption.
For example, in the following figure, the power of the cell is corrupt.
Figure 136

Corrupted Power Cell

When the Trace This Value right-click option is used for the A_reg signal, the automatic
tracing functionality traces to the corrupted power supply set to debug the root cause of
power corruption. In this case, the root cause of power corruption is the power switch
which changes from 1 -> 0, as illustrated in the following figure:
Figure 137

Tracing Corrupted Power Supply Set

In some scenarios, even though the power model is corrupted, the output may
not be X due to which the Trace Active X option is not enabled. In such cases,
you can use the Trace This Value option instead of Trace Active X.

Limitations
The following limitations apply to this feature for Temporal Flow View:
* The following UPF types are only supported:
Power Port
Power Net
Power Logic Net
i. ack_port of power switch
ii. control_port of power switch
iii. isolation_signal of isolation
iv. save_signal/restore_signal of retention
Power Supply
Power Switch
ISO
SRSN
SPA
Retention (edge trigger only)
* The connect_logic_net power logic net and Level Shift UPF types are not supported.
* Single-pin, zero-pin, and level sensitive retention type cells are not supported.

Directly Importing Liberty Files and Displaying Power Cell Information

* When tracing is performed in Temporal Flow View with partially dumping the FSDB file,
If there is no dumping on certain signals, the value is calculated by the register
signal. If it cannot be calculated or the signal is a sync signal, such as, register
signal, then "NF" is shown in the Value pane.
When trace reaches a scope that does not contain any dumped signals, the path
stops expanding at the boundary and results in the symbol, as illustrated in the

When the mouse hovers over the symbol, the tooltip message notifies that the trace
is stopped because it traced into a scope without any dumped simulation results

Transition based mode (tracing the power corruption triggering path).

Displaying Power State Group in Power State Table Frame
Overview
The following enhancements are provided with Verdi Power-Aware Debug:
* The add_power_state command is enhanced to define a Power State Table. The
create_pst and add_pst_state commands are no longer required to create a Power
State Table.
* The power states displayed in the Power State Table are composed hierarchically to
avoid exponential explosion of the size of the Power State Table.
* The Power State Table frame and the Power Domain List frame displays the related
power states in the complete design under a single user-defined group as Power State
Group List.
* The Power State Group List supports dynamic debug functionalities like active
annotation, drag and drop, and so on.

Displaying Power State Group in Power State Table Frame

Use Model
To view the related power states in a design, create a Power State Group List for the entire
design. The Power State Table frame displays the Power State Group List as illustrated in
Figure 149.
Figure 149

Power State Group Displayed in the PST Frame

Use the create_group command to create a group of related power states and define a
group name that can be used in the add_power_state command.
Syntax:
create_group group_name

Use the add_power_state command to add power states for the functional nets (power,
ground and so on) and create power state tables and define them hierarchically.
Syntax:
add_power_state [-supply|-domain|-group] object_name [-update]
-state {[parent_state_name] state_name [-legal|illegal]
[-simstate simstate]

Displaying Power State Group in Power State Table Frame

[-supply_expr {Boolean_expression}]
[-logic_expr {Boolean_expression}]
}]*
[-complete]

The following is an example to create a group GROUP1 with RUN and SLEEP states for
SS1 and SS2 signals:
#Creating power state ON for SS1
add_power_state -supply SS1 \
-state ON {-supply_expr {(power == {FULL_ON 0.8}) && (ground == {FULL_ON
0})}}
#Creating power states ON and OFF for SS2
add_power_state -supply SS2 \
-state ON {-supply_expr {(power == {FULL_ON 0.8}) && (ground == {FULL_ON
0})}}
add_power_state -supply SS2 \
-state OFF {-supply_expr {(power == {OFF}) && (ground == {FULL_ON 0})}}
#Creating group for power states
create_group GROUP1
add_power_state -group GROUP1
-state RUN {-logic_expr {SS1 == ON && SS2 == ON}}
-state SLEEP {-logic_expr {SS1 == ON && SS2 == ON}}
The following table shows the power states for GROUP1 group created
for SS1 and SS2 signals:

Supported Features
For each power state group, the member list is displayed in the Power State Table frame.
The following features are supported for Power State Group List:
* Dynamic debug functions (like active annotation, drag-and-drop power state group
to waveform, or to debug value) are supported for power state group objects and the
member object list.
* Drag and drop action is supported for power state group object and its member object
list.
* Create Power State Group List by UPF scope, similar to creating Power State Table
List in Power Domain tree is supported. Drag-and-drop action for power state group in
power domain tree is also supported.
* Double clicking the Power State Group node highlights the related power state group
object in Power State Table frame and syncs the UPF source code to its declaration.
* Double clicking the group object syncs the source code to its declaration in the UPF
source code, and highlights the group object node in the Power Domain tree.
* Double clicking the state object syncs the source code to the declaration of its related
group in the UPF source code.
* Double clicking the member of Power State Group syncs the source code to its
reference in related Power State Group.
* In Power State Table frame, as Power State Group can be used as a member of other
Power State Group, so, for each sub power state group/table object, right-click menu is
supported as Show Definition to sync source codes to its declaration and highlight the
related power state group/table item of definition in the Power State Table frame.
* Drag and drop action for Power State Group is supported in the UPF source code view
and nWave frame.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Dumping Low Power Debug DB XML File During Compilation In
UFE Flow
Verdi allows you to debug low power objects instrumented by VCS NLP. You can
use the low power debug DB, an XML format file, dumped by VCS NLP to handle all
instrumentation scenarios.
You can use the -kdb option at compile time to dump low power debug DB file in the UFE
flow.
Following are the benefits of this feature:
* Allows you to dump low power instrument scenarios/objects with specific XML format
for every partition and reuse same information from same partition.
* Reduces the memory usage, thereby improving the compile-time performance.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Use Model
The following is the syntax to dump DB XML file for single compile:
% vcs <design file> -upf <upf file> -kdb -debug_access+all <compile
options>

The following is the syntax to dump DB XML file for partition compile:
% vcs <design file> -upf <upf file> -partcomp -kdb -debug_access+all
<compile options>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
% vlogan dut.v testbench.v design.v -sverilog -kdb
% vcs topcfg -q -upf top.upf -partcomp -kdb -lca -debug_access+all
-power=dumplpconnect

text:
Demo
The following demo illustrates how to import a UPF power file into the Verdi platform and
to use power-related panes to browse the power intent.
1. Copy the upf_demo folder located at the following path to your local directory:
$VERDI_HOME/demo/power/upf_demo

2. Load the design and the FSDB dump file into the Verdi platform using the following
command:
verdi -f run.f -ssf rtl.fsdb &

3. Load the UPF power file into the Verdi platform by invoking the File -> Import CPF/
UPF Files option to open the Import CPF/UPF Files form. Select UPF1.0 in the
Language field, double-click the demo.upf file, and click the OK button. After loading
is complete, power-related panes are opened and docked in the main window.
4. The Power Domain List pane shows all power domains with every domain marked with
a different color. All power definitions are shown under the power domain hierarchically.
The Power State/Mode Table pane is added to the middle pane. A power tab is added
to the source code pane. When you double-click on different items in the left pane, the
content in the power tab changes accordingly.
5. Double-click the PD_FSM node in the Power Domain List pane. Browse the components
of the PD_FSM power domain.
The Verdi platform with the Power-Aware Debug support can automatically extract power
state tables defined in the UPF and show the states in a table format.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
1. In the Power State Table pane, double-click VDD and the source code jumps to VDD in
the Power Source Code pane.
2. Search capability for Power-Aware Debug
a. In the main window, invoke the Source -> Find String option. The PDML-Find form
is displayed.

b. Select String in the Find Type field, and type in isolation. Click the Find All button.
c. Search results are listed in the Search tab of the Message pane. Double-click any
line to jump to the corresponding source code in the source code pane.
3. Trace driver/load of a signal
a. In the Power Domain Hierarchy pane, double-click the PD_MEM node. The cursor
jumps to the respective line in the source code in the Power Source Code pane.
b. In the Power Source Code pane, right-click the VDD_MEM signal and select the Trace
Power Driver option. Power drivers are listed in the Trace tab of the Message
pane.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
4. Report Impacted Signals by invoking the Power -> Report Impacted Signals by
Scope option to open the Scope Lists form. Use the Add button to add the scopes.
The Report Power Impacted Signals form opens up, as illustrated in the following

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
a. Select the Schematic button to open an nSchema pane displaying the connection
of the selected signal.
b. Select the Control Signals tab to browse the control signals of retention and
isolation rules.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
You can bring up a schematic view of the power design in the Power Map pane using the
following steps:
1. From the main menu, select Power -> New Power Map -> Full Power Map to invoke
the Power Map pane.
2. Observe that all power domains are shown as rectangles. Drag and drop a domain to
the Power Source Code pane to browse its definition.
3. Observe that the power switch, isolation and retention rules are presented as cells
connecting to the related power domains. Drag and drop an isolation rule to the Power
Source Code pane to browse its definition.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
4. Select the red dotted line between the domains. The red dotted line represents a noncovered isolation net.
5. To view the non-covered isolation net signals, select Schematic -> Report Selected
Impacted Signals. These signals are suggested by the Verdi platform to be guarded
with an isolation rule for protection.

Go to the nTrace window and perform the following steps to practice visualizing power
information in the window:
1. In the Design Browser pane, the instances have different colors. These colors are
assigned based on the power domain specified in the UPF. You can change the color
by performing the following steps:
a. Invoke the Power -> Highlight Power Domain option to display the Highlight
Power Domain form.
b. Select PD_TOP and change it to a different color, and then press the OK button.
A tip window is displayed for showing power information. This helps you to quickly
understand the power intent of any module or signal.
2. Put the mouse cursor on i_ALUB (under system/i_cpu) in the design hierarchy pane
to view the power domain and state condition.
3. Double-click i_ALUB to view the source code which has retention annotation on some
of the signals.
4. Double-click i_CCU (under system/i_cpu) to view more retention annotation on the
signals.
5. Put the mouse cursor on one of the retention signals to view the tip with save/restore,
and shut-off condition.
6. Select i_pram (under system) to view level shifter and isolation annotation.
7. Put the mouse cursor on one of the signals to view the tip window with isolation and
level-shifter rules.
The power content can be cross probed between panes by performing the following
steps:
8. Select i_pram in the Design Browser pane and drag-and-drop to the Power Source
Code pane.
9. Go to the Power Source Code pane to view the source code of i_pram power intent.
10. To view the rules of level shifter of this domain, double-click the ls_CPU_to_MEM node
under the Level Shifter node in the Power Domain Details pane.
11. The level shifter rule is applied to the inputs of the memory. Therefore, the source code
in nTrace has an "l" annotation on all the inputs of i_pram.

Go to the nSchema window and perform the following steps to practice visualizing power
information in the schematic window:
1. In the Design Browser pane, double-click the system node and select the New
Schematic

icon.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
In the created nSchema window, blocks are highlighted with different power domain
colors to indicate to which power domain each block belongs to. It is a quick way to see
the number of power domains at the top-level view.
2. Double-click the CPU block and see that each of the three blocks below it belong to a
different power domain.
3. Select the ALUB block to view the Power Domain information on the toolbar.
4. Double-click the ALUB block to highlight the instances below. All the instances have
the same power domain as their parent scope. The signals highlighted in red are
retention signals.
5. Select a retention signal, and notice that the information of Power Signal Type is
shown on the toolbar. If the Show Tip option in the Schematics -> Select page of the
Preferences form is turned on, hovering the mouse cursor on that information displays
a tip for Restore and Save conditions.
6. Turn on the Schematic -> Active Annotation option; to see that the power state is
annotated on schematic symbols.
7. Type in 6850 in the Cursor Time field on the toolbar, the schematic symbol with state
off is grayed out.
8. To change the highlight color for power objects in the Preferences form, invoke the
Preferences form using the Tools -> Preferences option. Select the Power Aware
folder in the left pane to view the configuration page for Power Aware Objects. Select
the Retention Object, set the color to green, and click the Apply button.
9. Toggle off the Highlight Power Aware Design Object(s) option in the Preferences
form and click the Apply button. Then, the color highlight for retention signals in
the nSchema/nTrace window is removed. Similarly, toggle off the Highlight Power
Domain option to remove the color highlight for the power domains in all panes. Now,
toggle on both Highlight Power Aware Design Object(s) and Highlight Power
Domain options and click the Apply button to resume the highlight. Alternatively, select
View -> Highlight Power Aware Object and toggle on and off the Power Domain
Color or/and Power Aware Object Color options.
Go to the nWave window and perform the following steps to practice visualizing power
information in the waveform window.

1. Click the Get Signals icon to open the Get Signals form.
2. Click the system -> i_cpu -> i_CCU node, select the signals, and click the OK button.
The signal pane shows the selected signals.
3. Drag-and-drop a node from the Design Browser pane to the nWave window. In the
nWave signal pane, added Isolation/Level-shifted signals are highlighted in yellow and
are annotated with the Iso/Lvs postfix.
To practice with Active Trace and learn how power information is visualized in the active
trace results, perform the following steps:
1. Drag-and-drop the i_ALUB scope from the Design Browser pane to the nWave window.
Select the ALU[7:0]signal in the nWave signal pane. Click the transition 3 -> 55 at time
951.
2. Double-click the transition to show the active driver in the Design Source Code pane.
3. Turn on the active annotation (Source -> Active Annotation) in the main nTrace
window.
4. Do active trace on the signal, a, by double-clicking on it.
The Power Domain field on the toolbar shows the power domain name of the signal a.
In the Message pane, each trace result is added with its corresponding power domain
name and the name is highlighted with the relevant power domain color.
Go to the Temporal Flow View pane and perform the following steps to see how power
information is visualized in the Temporal Flow View pane:
1. Select the ALU[7:0] signal in the nWave signal pane and click the transition f -> XX,
time 3900. Choose the Temporal Flow Window -> New Temporal Flow Window
option from the right click menu and click the OK button in the Create Temporal Flow
View form.
2. In the created Temporal Flow View pane, select the out[7:0] signal and select Trace
This Value (Trace -> Trace This Value) in the invoked TFV window to unroll the path.
The unrolled path shows that the cause of the value change is power isolation.

3. Drag-and-drop any pin of the power switch cell to the Power Source Code pane to
show the related power rule.
To debug power sequences, perform the following steps:
1. Go to the nWave window and zoom 100%.
Observe that there are some unknowns (X's) in the waveform.
2. Select View -> Power -> Mask Power Off to enable Verdi to automatically identify the
Xs caused by power off and mark them in a shade mask.
3. Drag and drop i_pram and i_ALUB scopes from the Design Browser
pane to the nWave window. See the waveform around time 3900ns, the
system.i_pram.data[7:0] signal has X, but does not have mask as it is not caused
by power off.
4. Right-click system.i_pram.data[7:0] in the nWave signal pane to invoke the Power
-> Add Power Domain option. This option traces the power domain and adds it under
the data[7:0] signal. As the power is on, X is not caused by power off.
Trace the active driver of X to find out why data[7:0] is X.
5. Select data[7:0]and invoke the Tools -> List X option to open the Source File to
List X form. Select the Use Current Simulation Results option in the Source File
Selection field. The other two options do not contain power information. Select the
Selected SignalsPD option in the List field.
After pressing the Next button in the Source File to List X form, the List X form displays
all unknowns.
6. Click the Go to next time table button in the upper right to change time to 3900. Click
the Trace Active X button. Click Yes, OK and Trace buttons in the following three
forms, the Trace Active X Results pane is displayed.

7. In the pane, it shows X is caused by power off. Select the Action -> Show source
code on nTrace option in the form to continue tracing.
8. Enable the Source -> Active Annotation option in the main window. In the source
code, the driving signals C1 and IDR are changed to X as their power domain
(system.PD_PCU) is switched off at the time 3900.

see what causes it to be X.
10. Right-click S1 in the nWave signal pane and select the Power -> Add Power Domain
option. This adds the PD_ALUB power domain to the waveform. This is the power
domain S1 is in. You can quickly see the power state of the S1 power domain.
11. Go back to S1 in nWave and find out what causes X. Select S1 and double-click at time
6850 to locate the active driver.
12. Go to the Design Source Code pane to view active drivers. Select CH[0] and do active
trace (double-click) to locate the next active driver.
13. Show CH has retention annotation and it is in a different power domain. (Review the
power domain on the toolbar.)
14. Hover the mouse cursor on CH to view save/restore condition. Drag-and-drop CH to
nWave.
Let's find out the reason for CH[4:0] to remain X after the power is turned on.
15. Right-click CH[4:0]and select the Power -> Add Power Domain option.
16. Trace control signals for the retention rule. Right-click CH[4:0]and select the Power ->
Retention Rules -> Add Ret Controls option. This option automatically traces save
and restore signals and adds them to nWave.

17. Let's see the source code of the UPF file. right-click CH[4:0]and select Power ->
Retention Rules -> Locate Ret. Command option. This option jumps to the Power
Source Code pane and automatically locate the rule.
18. Turn on Source -> Active Annotation. The power annotation is shown in the Power
Source Code pane.
19. The power state is also shown in the Power Mode Table pane. The Verdi platform
automatically identifies power states at any given simulation time.
Go back to nWave, check the signals added in Step 16. The CPU_restore signal tries
to restore before the power is turned on again.
20. Let's check the power domain's shut-off rule. Go to the Power Domain Details pane
and select the Shut off Condition node under the PD_CCU node to check the shut off
condition.

This leads to an unknown value being restored when power is turned on again. This
concludes that the power sequence is wrong.

Appendix A: Power Map Validation
Currently, the Power Map analyzes the power mode (or state table) definition in UPF to
determine if a possibility exists that the from domain (the domain from where a signal is
coming from) is off while the to domain (the domain the signal is going to) is not. If this is
the case, unexpected results could propagate through such signals from the from domain
to the to domain.
For example, there are three power domains A, B, and C; two power modes: 1 and 2 in
total.
Domain A

Domain B

Domain C

Mode 1

On

On

Off

Mode 2

On

Off

Off

When domain B is off, domain C is always off (both in mode 1 and mode 2). When domain
C is off, domain B could be on (mode 1) or off (mode 2). So, from domain C to domain
B, it is required to insert an isolation cell. However, from domain B to domain C, it is not
necessary to insert an isolation cell.
To skip analyze power mode, turn off the Check Power Mode option (default: on) in the
Preferences form.

text:
Data Structure 351

Preface
The Python-Based NPI Coverage Model User Guide provides information to let you
access coverage database generated by verification tools such as VCS simulator.

Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and answers to
frequently asked questions about Synopsys tools. The SolvNetPlus site also gives you
access to a wide range of Synopsys online services including software downloads,
documentation, and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
If prompted, enter your user name and password. If you do not have a Synopsys user
name and password, follow the instructions to sign up for an account.
If you need help using the SolvNetPlus site, click REGISTRATION HELP in the top-right
menu bar.

Contacting Customer Support
To contact Customer Support, go to https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com.

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary
language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also
includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working
environment, including terms that are embedded in our software and IPs. At the same
time, we are working to ensure that our Web content and software applications are usable
to people of varying abilities. You might still find examples of non-inclusive language in our
software or documentation as our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are
currently under review to remove exclusionary language.

Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support six models:
* Coverage
* Language
* Netlist
* Text
* Waveform
* Waveform Writer
Each model have their own APIs to let you be able to traverse data objects and obtain
objects' properties like the existing C-Based or Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
In this guide, the environment setting for using Python-Based NPI APIs for Coverage is
demonstrated.
* Package and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Package and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi", and it is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/
NPI/python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
There are seven modules inside the "pynpi" package: npisys, lang, netlist, text, cov
waveform and waveformw. The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization,
loading design and exit. The other modules represent language model, netlist model, text
model, coverage model, wave model and waveform writer model respectively

Module Functions and Class Objects
L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects. These
functions return a class object or a list of class objects, and they follow the specification of
the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, every module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions to
let you get advanced information based on the results obtained by L0 module functions.
These functions follows the specification of the existing L1 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The most difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl iscome class method function. These L0 APIs are
usually to get integer value, string value, one-to-one method to get a handle, and 1-tomany method to get handle iterator.

User Interface and Use Flow
Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Check your Python's version:
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Environment setting for "VERDI_HOME" is required for Python-based NPI. Ensure that
you set it up before running program.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import module "npisys" for using the function of NPI initialization and exit from pynpi
package.
from pynpi import npisys

5. Import the module you need from pynpi package. For example, if you want to use
Coverage model, you can import module like the following:
from pynpi import cov

6. Note that initialization function npisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Also, you must call npisys.end() after finishing your
code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use coverage model by
Python-Based NPI APIs.
Python program to use NPI models: (demo.py)
import sys
import os
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/"
+ arch))
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import cov
# Initialize NPI
if not npisys.init(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to initialize NPI")
assert 0
# Load design (if needed, depends on models)
if not npisys.load_design(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to load design")
assert 0
# Beginning of your code here -------------------#
# Example code can be found in later chapters
#
# End of your code ------------------------------# End NPI
npisys.end()

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

C shell script example to setup environment and execute Python program: (run_demo)
#!/bin/csh -f
# Setup your $VERDI_HOME here
setenv VERDI_HOME [YOUR_VERDI_HOME_PATH]
# run the python program
# - Input arguments depend on your program design
# - If loading design is required, you can pass the options like
[YOUR_PYTHON]./demo.py -sv demo.v

To run the files, put the above files in the same directory and execute the run_demo C
shell script.
./run_demo

Module npisys
This chapter includes the following topics:
* Overview
* L0 APIs
* NPI General Options

Overview
Module npisys is for setting Python-based NPI. You must call npisys.init() before using
any other NPI modules and call npisys.end() after using any other NPI modules.

L0 APIs
Following are the public L0 APIs for system module:

npisys.init(pyArgvList)
System initialization for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list, for example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
>>>npisys.init(sys.argv)

npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
Load design for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list. For example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.

Chapter 2: Module npisys
NPI General Options

>>>npisys.load_design(sys.argv)

npisys.end()
Clean NPI-related settings and data.
Parameters: none
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
>>>npisys.end()

NPI General Options
The following table lists the NPI general options for npisys.init(). If not specified, NPI
uses the default setting:
-quiet If specified, the banner, errors, and warnings are not shown on the

console.

Python-Based NPI Coverage Model
This chapter includes the following topics:
* Overview
* Quick Start
* Class Objects

Overview
The NPI coverage model lets you access coverage databases generated by verification
tools such as the VCS simulator.
With the coverage model, you can create custom reports and tools to display and analyze
coverage data.

Quick Start
Example Code:
import sys
import os
rel_lib_path = os.environ['VERDI_HOME'] + '/share/NPI/python'
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(rel_lib_path))
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import cov
# -- traverse coverage toggle info ------------------------------------def trv_toggle(hdl, indentCnt, test, fp_w):
childList = hdl.child_handles()
for child in childList:
for i in range(indentCnt):
fp_w.write(' ')
fp_w.write('# '+child.type()+': '+child.name()+'
cov:'+str(child.covered(test)))
fp_w.write('/'+str(child.coverable(test))+'\n')
trv_toggle(child, indentCnt+1, test, fp_w)
cov.release_handle(child)

Chapter 3: Python-Based NPI Coverage Model
Quick Start

# -- traverse coverage instances --------------------------------------def trv_cov_inst(hdl, indentCnt, test, fp_w):
instList = hdl.instance_handles()
for inst in instList:
for i in range(indentCnt):
fp_w.write(' ')
hdlType = inst.type()
fp_w.write(hdlType+': ')
if hdlType == 'npiCovDatabase':
fp_w.write(inst.name()+'\n')
else:
fp_w.write(inst.full_name()+'\n')
tm = inst.toggle_metric_handle()
if (tm):
trv_toggle(tm, indentCnt, test, fp_w)
trv_cov_inst(inst, indentCnt+1, test, fp_w)
cov.release_handle(inst)
# -- init -------------------------------------------------------------res = npisys.init(sys.argv)
if res != 1:
print('[Error] Failed to do npi init')
sys.exit(1)
# -- open log to write ------------------------------------------------fp_w = open('test.log', 'w')
vdbName = 'merged.vdb'
# -- traverse all the toggle bins and write their coverage info -------covDb = cov.open(vdbName)
if (covDb):
fp_w.write('load vdb: '+covDb.name()+'\n')
# -- merge tests --------------------------------------------------mergedTest = None
testList = covDb.test_handles()
for test in testList:
fp_w.write(test.name()+'\n')
if (mergedTest == None):
mergedTest = test
else:
mergedTest = cov.merge_test(mergedTest, test)
fp_w.write('mergedTest: '+mergedTest.name()+'\n')
trv_cov_inst(covDb, 1, mergedTest, fp_w)
covDb.close()
# -- close log and end ------------------------------------------------fp_w.close()
npisys.end()

Execution Result

Chapter 3: Python-Based NPI Coverage Model

mergedTest: merged.vdb/test
npiCovInstance: test_jukebox
npiCovInstance: test_jukebox.st0
# npiCovSignal: trki cov:4/4
# npiCovSignalBit: trki[0] cov:2/2

In the coverage module, use the C/C++-Based NPI object diagrams to see how to use
Python-Based NPI class objects.
Follow these rules:
1. Every int or string property can be called as a class function.
The function name is that property after removing the prefix "npiCov" and converting
the rest to snake case.
Here is the mapping table:
C/C++-based NPI Usage

Python-based NPI Usage

npi_cov_get_str(npiCovName, hdl)

hdl.name()

npi_cov_get(npiCovLineNo, hdl)

hdl.line_no()

2. Every one-to-one method can be called as a class function.
The function name is that method plus "_method" after removing the prefix "npiCov"
and converting the rest to snake case.
For one-to-many methods, change "_method" to "_methods".
The C/C++ API returns an iterator for 1-to-many methods. Python returns a list.

coverage class API to programmatically query and manage verification coverage data.
Key class categories include functional coverage (covergroups, coverpoints, crosses),
code coverage (branch, condition, toggle, FSM, line), assertion coverage (cover properties
and sequences), and power-domain coverage. Requires a loaded NPI coverage database.
Supports batch scripting and Verdi interactive sessions.
