Setting design_based_root_cause to False
The design_based_root_cause is set to false to root cause the differences occurred
due to compile and runtime switch changes and VCS software version changes. It
identifies the point that caused differences in the simulation results. When you set

design_based_root_cause to false the DUTRCA Root Cause Results section is

available on the RCA Manager.

The DUTRCA Root Cause Results section lists the traced out root causes. The RCA
report shows DUTRCA Root Cause Results listing the Simulation Log Analysis, Root
Cause In DUT, Root Cause Not in DUT, and Low Priority root cause groups. The
Simulation Log Analysis section lists the hit analyzed error message and error types
during the Log Analysis process.
The indicates root causes and indicates a debug entry. When you hover over the Root
Cause or Debug Entry icon, a tooltip provides its details.
Signal-Based Root Cause Format
The following is the format of each signal-based root cause:
<signal_name>#<root-cause time>(module:<module_ name>)

Signal-Based Root Cause Example
For example, in the following figure, Root Cause In DUT and Root Cause Not in
DUT groups contain one signal-based root cause and two signal-based root causes,
respectively:
Figure 79

RCA Report Example With design_based_root_cause: false

In the Root Cause In DUT group, the following signal is the signal-based root cause
whose root cause time is 4232830 and the corresponding module is uart_wb:
/minsoc_tb_top/minsoc_top_0/uart__interface/web_sel_is[3:0]

You can start debugging from the top signal-based root cause in the report. Right-click a
root cause and click Show Signal on Waveform to see the waveforms.
Figure 80

Show Signal on Waveform on GUI

Setting design_based_root_cause to True
The design_based_root_cause is set to true to root cause the design differences
in the actual source code found in the simv.daidir databases. When you set
design_based_root_cause to true, the DUTRCA Root Cause Results and Total
Source Code Changes sections are available on the RCA Manager.
The DUTRCA Root Cause Results section lists the traced out root causes. The RCA
report shows DUTRCA Root Cause Results listing the Simulation Log Analysis, Root
Cause In DUT, Root Cause Not in DUT, Mixed, and Low Priority root cause groups.
Total Source Code Changes
The Total Source Code Changes node lists the found design changes and the traced-out
root causes. It displays the file name references and the number of design differences
available in that file. When you expand one of the file references, it shows the line number
with the module name.

You can click the design change to see the unix diff differences results in the Design
Differences window, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 81

Showing Design Differences in Verdi

The following three buttons are located in the upper-right corner of the Design Differences
window:

* Minimize: It minimizes the Design Difference window. To open a minimized or hidden
Design Difference window, choose View > Design Differences.
* Undock from the RCA manager: It separates the Design Differences window from the
RCA manager.
* Show vimdiff: It issues vimdiff command and shows the differences between the
target and the reference files in the opened vim window.

Design-Change-Based Root Cause Format
When the design_based_root_cause field is set to true, the Root Cause In DUT and
Mixed root cause groups are in the format of design-change-based root cause. However,
the Root Cause Not in DUT root cause group is in the format of signal-based root cause.
Design-Change-Based Root Cause Example
For example, as shown in the following figure, there are Root Cause In DUT and Root
Cause Not in DUT root cause groups. The root cause shown in the Root Cause In DUT
group is in the design-change-based root cause format and the root cause shown in the
Root Cause Not in DUT group is in the signal-based root cause format.
Figure 82

RCA Report Example With design_based_root_cause: true

With the format of design-change-based root cause, the signal-based root causes with the
same root cause time and design change lines are grouped together in Root Cause Time
Group, and the signal-based root cause information is hidden in the report. Then, the Root
Cause Time Groups with the same design change lines are grouped together in Design
Change Line Group.
The formats of the Root Cause Time Group and Design Change Line Group are as
follows:
* Root Cause Time Group: A number with a prefix "#," for example #351000.
* Design Change Line Group: The format is
<filename>:<line_number>(module:<module_name>)

Tracing Result in TFV
The TFV tracing features are common to both the settings (True and False) of the
design_based_root_cause option, except the differences mentioned in the table
available in the Root Cause Groups section.
You can double-click a debug entry or use RMB > Show Signal on TFV to display the
tracing path in TFV. The following figure shows the tracing path in Verdi TFV:
Figure 84

Showing Tracing Path in Verdi TFV

You can select the path in the Root Cause List field and the selected path gets highlighted
in the TFV window.

Figure 85

Root Cause List Displaying the Root Causes of a Debug Entry

You can use the View > Show Single Path to Root Cause option to display only one path
on the TFV window. By default, the Show Single Path to Root Cause option is enabled.
When the Show Single Path to Root Cause option is enabled and you choose RMB >
Show Signal on TFV, the in-path root causes are listed in the Root Cause List field.
When the Show Single Path to Root Cause option is disabled and you choose RMB >
Show Signal on TFV option, all the root causes listed on the RCA Manager window and
the in-path root causes are listed in the Root Cause List field.
In TFV, all fan-ins of a given debug entry are traced by DUTRCA, but only the root-causes
that reach one or more design differences are recorded in the RCA report. Also, all the
design differences on the trace path are denoted as root-causes.

differences in Verdi TFV:

Sorting by Rank
When sorting the report, if root causes are in the format of signal-based root
cause (occur in the (1) Root Cause In DUT, Root Cause Not in DUT groups when
design_based_root_cause is set to false; (2) Root Cause Not in DUT group when
design_based_root_cause is set to true), the criterion is as follows:
The signal-based root causes within a root cause group (Root Cause In DUT or Root
Cause Not in DUT) are sorted by rank.

Figure 90

RCA Report With Sorting by Rank (Signal-Based Root Cause Format)

The following figure displays an RCA report with a list of Design Change Line Groups
containing Root Cause Time Groups.
Figure 91
RCA Report With Sorting by Rank (Design-Change-Based Root Cause Format in
In DUT Group When design_based_root_cause: true)

As shown in Figure 91, a Design Change Line Group can contain multiple Root Cause
Time Groups. For example, the Design Change Line Group, ALUB.sv:261-271 contains
four Root Cause Time Groups at 7950ns, 0ns, 5650ns, and 25ns. A Root Cause Time
Group can contain multiple signal-based root causes, however, they are hidden in the
report.

While sorting the report, when root causes are in the format of design-change-based
root cause (occur in the In DUT and/or Mixed groups when design_based_root_cause
is set to true), the criteria are as follows:
* Although signal-based root causes are hidden in the report, internally these signalbased root causes have ranks.
* A Root Cause Time Group receives the highest rank from the signal-based root
causes contained in it. Then, Root Cause Time Groups within the same Design
Change Line Group are sorted by rank.
* A Design Change Line Group receives the highest rank from the Root Cause Time
Groups contained in it. The Design Change Line Groups within the In DUT group or
Mixed group are sorted by rank.
For example, consider Design Change Group Line A has three Root Cause Time Groups
#300, #200 and #400. Design Change Group Line B has two Root Cause Time Groups,
#350 and #100. Also, consider the order of ranking of these Root Cause Time Groups
as #350>#200>#300>#100>#400. As the rank of #350>#100, #350 is sorted above #100
in the report under Line B. For Line A and Line B groups, as #350 (the highest rank
under Line B) > #200 (the highest rank under Line A), Line B is sorted above Line A. The
following figure shows the result of this example:
Figure 92

Sorting Results by Rank

Signal Match for Correlative Root Causes
After the root cause is sorted based on the waveform similarity analysis, signal match is
used to correlate root causes with the simulation log. Signal match identifies whether the
signal name relates to an error log. If the signal name relates to an error log, then that
signal name is listed at the highest rank in sorting.
Considering the root cause and its debug entries as a group, the related score can also
be calculated on the debug entry signal and root cause signal. It uses the highest score as
the root cause score. If a root cause is identified as a Correlative root cause, then it gets
the highest rank in sorting.

The feature is applied for the report with both the formats (signal-based root cause and
design-change-based root cause). However, only on signal-based root cause format, a

the highest rank in sorting.

The feature is applied for the report with both the formats (signal-based root cause and
design-change-based root cause). However, only on signal-based root cause format, a
note indicates that a signal-based root cause is a correlative root cause.
Signal match for Correlative Root Causes is applied only when the simulation
log exists.
The ranking feature comes with the Group Root Cause option.
Group Root Cause
The Group Root Cause option groups the root causes by reasons and allows you to pick
up the root cause of your interest. This option specifies the following categories in the
Root Cause In DUT and Root Cause Not in DUT root cause groups:
Root Cause In DUT
* Register output diff
* Primary input diff
* Constant value diff
* Combinational diff
* Others
Root Cause Not in DUT
* Interface
* Behavior code
* Floating
* Others

false.

Unified DUTRCA and TBRCA Report
After you run the autorca -cfg <cfg.yaml> command with enable_transaction_diff
set to true, the tool generates two XML report files. The one XML file is for DUTRCA and
the other is for TBRCA. For detailed information about TBRCA, refer to the Testbench
Root Cause Analysis (TBRCA) chapter .
Load only the DUTRCA report file (dutrca_report.xml) to Verdi GUI. When required,
the rcaReport window can automatically synchronize with TBRCA reports and load the
required information using the following command:
%> autorca -load_report dutrca_report.xml

When Verdi launches, it loads the target design file and FSDB file. The analysis report
appears in a new rcaReport window.
The unified DUTRCA and TBRCA debug flow is available only when you set
enable_transaction_diff to true.
The rcaReport window in RCA Manager consists of the Analysis details and Target Build,
or Trace result sections. You can check for any design changes and the identified root
causes in the DUTRCA Root Cause Results section. This section also classifies debug
entries based on whether their root causes are coming from the DUT scope or from
outside the DUT scope.

The debug entries under Not in DUT indicate the root causes that are coming from
outside the DUT. To narrow down the search for the root causes of the failures, RDA
provides the Testbench Root Cause Analysis (TBRCA) feature. If an error occurs in a
testbench component, TBRCA finds which testbench component has the error. It also
points to the location of the error within that component.
The report generated by the autorca command consists of the DUTRCA and TBRCA
reports. The rcaReport window lists them in a unified way. The following figure displays
how DUTRCA report gets synchronized with TBRCA:
Figure 93

Unified Debug DUTRCA And TBRCA Reports

To display TBRCA Transaction Analysis details, right-click the module listed under Not in
DUT and click Transaction Diff that opens another rcaReport tab displaying Transaction
Analysis details.
The TBRCA tool supports the Transaction Difference Analysis approach to simplify the
debug process. For more details refer to the Transaction Difference Analysis section.

The TBRCA Transaction Difference analysis flow analyzes two FSDB files -- one from
a passing case and one from a related failing case. It identifies differences between the

transactions recorded during both simulations. The transaction analysis report displays the
following information:

* The right pane provides a summary of the item selected in the left pane, as displayed

* For every stream, an interface path is available in the second column to navigate the

filter the stream report for a specific interface.
* To view the transaction mismatch in Protocol Analyzer (PA), right-click the transaction
mismatch and click Show Transaction in PA. The PA window displays both the
reference and the target case FSDBs and highlights the differences. The following

Limitations of Low-Power Debug
The following are the limitations of the Low-Power Debug feature:
* DUTRCA Design Difference Analysis does not support file name changes.
* The Low Power Debug feature for Temporal Flow View supports the following UPF
types:
Power port
Power net
Power logic net
ack_port of power switch

Power switch
ISO

Testbench Root Cause Analysis (TBRCA)
* TBRCA Application
* Transaction Difference Analysis
* Message Analysis

In a complex design environment, you construct the testbench with different components.
When an error occurs in a testbench component, finding the root cause can be difficult
and time-consuming. Testbench RCA identifies the root cause of testbench errors.
This includes identifying the specific testbench component and the region within that
component where the error occurs.
When you introduce an error into a design environment, the error can occur in the DUT
or the testbench. Testbench RCA focuses on errors in the testbench. If the tool does not
identify the root cause, Testbench RCA reports these as "items of interest" to help you to
debug.
If a design that was previously operating correctly begins to fail, it can be challenging
to identify and locate the cause of the error. This error can spread quickly through the
entire environment. Further, the error might not be reported at the simulation time where
the error occurs. You might not be able to detect and report the error immediately during
simulation. By the time the error gets detected and reported, it involves many testbench

variables and DUT signals. The following diagram shows an example for the time
difference between the cause of the error and the detection of the error:
Figure 108

Error Occurs Versus Errors Detected

Testbench RCA (TBRCA) is a component of the Regression RCA solutions. You can
choose to run TBRCA automatically as a part of the overall flow, or run TBRCA in the
standalone mode. The following figure illustrates running TBRCA in the standalone mode:
Figure 109

Testbench RCA in Standalone Mode

The overall flow of TBRCA is shown in the following figure:
Figure 110

Testbench RCA Overall Flow

TBRCA supports the following two approaches to simplify the debug process:
Transaction Difference Analysis: The first approach involves the following steps:
1. Identify the reference and target simulations that can be compared.
2. Compare the reference and target simulations to identify when and where the
transactions of the target and reference results differ.
3. Report and analyze the differing transactions to locate the cause of differences.
The following figure illustrates the first approach:

TBRCA Application

In the Figure 110 the entry point for transaction difference analysis is indicated by the
number "1."
Message Analysis: Message analysis is the second approach which requires only the
target FSDB file and the log file. It involves the following steps:
1. Analyze the first error message from the log file.
2. Identify transactions, signals, and source code related to the error message.
The following figure illustrates the second approach:

In the Figure 110, the entry point for message analysis is indicated by the number "2."

TBRCA Application
Testbench RCA operates on the design environments that use UVM or OVM testbenches.
Testbench RCA provides the following key features:
* Automatically performs Transaction Difference Analysis
Compares and analyzes the interface signals that are found in the target and
reference test cases.
Compares UVM hierarchy of the target and reference designs.
Compares the recorded transactions, both UVM transactions and Synopsys VIP
transactions.

TBRCA Application

* When the transaction differences are not found between the reference and target
simulations, TBRCA automatically performs Message Analysis.
* Message Analysis attempts to identify transactions that might be related to the first
error message to aid the debugging of the error.
* Generates report indicating whether the root-cause is due to the testbench or the other
IP. The report can be reviewed with Verdi and the related features.

You must enable recording of the following information:
* UVM (or OVM) hierarchy and structure (that is, connectivity)
* Sequencer and TLM port activity
* Signal activity of the interfaces that are used to connect the testbench and DUT
* KDB, the structure of the design
You must record the UVM (or OVM) hierarchy, structure, and transactions using the
following options:
Compilation option:
+define+UVM_VERDI_PORT_RECORDING -lca -kdb -debug_acc+all

Runtime options:
+UVM_TR_RECORD
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE=HIER+TLM

The KDB file can be created using the unified compilation flow, -kdb.

Performing Testbench RCA
You can perform TBRCA using the autorca command and can display the options
specified to TBRCA using the -help (or -h) switch. These options can also be displayed
when the option is not provided to TBRCA.
You can generate a template file for TBRCA using the following options:
%> autorca -gen_cfg_template tbrca.yaml -gen_mode tbrca

The following is an example of the Message Analysis YAML file:
usage_mode: tbrca
####################################################
# tbrca: Testbench root cause analysis options
####################################################
tbrca:
## set error case to debug ##
target_waveform: target_data/novas.fsdb # [full path], required field
target_simv_daidir: target_data/simv.daidir # [full path], required
field
target_sim_log: target_data/simv.log # [full path], required field

The TBRCA Transaction Difference Analysis flow analyzes two FSDB files - one from a
passing case and another from a related failing case. It identifies the differences between
the transactions recorded in two simulations. You can view and analyze the resulting
transaction differences and associated interface signals in the Verdi GUI.
The following are the requirements for Target and Reference Simulations and FSDB:
* Enable recording of all items associated with the UVM or OVM testbench.
* Use the same seed for both the passing and failing test cases. This avoids transaction
or sequence differences related to randomization.

The following figure displays the Transaction Difference Analysis flow:
Figure 111

Transaction Difference Analysis Flow

The Transaction Difference Analysis flow consists of the following major operations:
1. Interface analysis: The interface signals in both the passing and failing test cases are
analyzed and compared. These signals connect the testbench with the RTL code. For
more details on interface analysis, refer to Interface Analysis.
2. UVM/OVM characteristics analysis: The UVM or OVM hierarchy is compared
between the passing and failing designs. This comparison checks the basic structure
of the hierarchy, that includes comparing the number of components and their
connections. It also looks at activity of certain operations associated with the hierarchy,
such as when objections are raised and lowered. For more details on UVM/OVM
characteristics analysis, refer to UVM/OVM Characteristics Analysis.
3. Transaction comparison: Transactions recorded during the simulation of the passing
and failing tests are compared. The UVM or OVM transactions are compared. If the
design includes Synopsys VIPs that support Protocol Analyzer, these transactions are
compared and reported separately. For more details on transaction comparison, refer
to Transaction Comparison.
4. Debugging in Verdi GUI: You can view and analyze the results of comparing passing
and failing tests in the Verdi environment. Use the following command: autorca
-load_report <report_path>. For more details on debugging in Verdi GUI, refer to
Debugging in Verdi GUI.
Message Analysis is used only when the differences are not found between transactions in
the passing and failing tests. TBRCA uses message analysis to identify transactions that
might be related to the first error message. This helps in debugging the error.

The following figure displays the TBRCA options:
Figure 112

TBRCA Root Cause Analysis Options

You can run message analysis only when you pass the log file using the
target_sim_log option in the configuration file. You must include both the
reference and target FSDB files to TBRCA.
If you do not include the target_sim_log option in the configuration file,
TBRCA provides a message to run message analysis with the appropriate
options.
TBRCA Transaction Difference Analysis Invocation Example
* As the required data is recorded in the FSDB files, specify only the FSDB files for
passing and failing tests.
* If the transaction differences are not detected, you can pass the target_sim_log
option to run message analysis.
* The output transcript is written to the console.txt file in the verdiLog/tbAutoRCA/
logs directory.
Figure 113

TBRCA Transaction Difference Analysis Invocation Example

You can refer to the Transaction Difference Analysis Review With Verdi section to view all
analysis details in the report window in Verdi GUI.

Interface Analysis
Interface analysis determines which signal on the testbench/RTL boundary is the first
to differ and in which direction. When the UVM/OVM information is recorded during
simulation, details about the interfaces that are connected to the testbench are also
recorded. These interfaces are analyzed by TBRCA.
Scenarios to Perform Interface Analysis
You can come across the following scenarios while performing interface analysis:
1. When you find differences while comparing interface signals, first determine the
direction of each signal. TBRCA attempts to identify whether the interface signal is
driven by RTL code or by testbench code.
As SystemVerilog interface signals do not have an explicit direction
associated with them, TBRCA analyzes the SystemVerilog source code to
determine the direction.
2. When the first difference involves an interface signal driven from the RTL to the
testbench, the error likely exists in the RTL code (DUT). When the first difference is
associated with an interface signal driven from the testbench to the RTL, the error likely
exists in the testbench code.
3. When you find no differences while comparing the interface signals, but an error still
occurs, the error most likely exists in an internal testbench component.
4. When differences appear in both testbench inputs and outputs, and the first differences
occur at the same time, the error might exist in the DUT or the testbench. This situation
occurs because a feedback loop connects the testbench code and the RTL code.
The following figure explains all the four scenarios:

TBRCA reports differences when any of these conditions are true:
* Interface signals exist in the reference test but do not appear in the error test.
* Interface signals exist in the error test but do not appear in the reference test.
To view the interface analysis results and compare the differing signals in Verdi GUI, refer
to the Transaction Difference Analysis Review With Verdi section.

title: Appendix 257
text:
test.
* Interface signals exist in the error test but do not appear in the reference test.
To view the interface analysis results and compare the differing signals in Verdi GUI, refer
to the Transaction Difference Analysis Review With Verdi section.
Interface analysis provides insight into the source of error. However, it might not
always provide a definitive answer for the source of the error.

UVM/OVM Characteristics Analysis
The second major operation is UVM/OVM Characteristics or Hierarchy Analysis where
the following characteristics of the target testbench are compared with the reference
testbench:
* Component hierarchy
* Component connections
* UVM/OVM objections
* UVM/OVM phases
* Resources
The following figure illustrates the characteristics comparison:
Figure 114

Reference Testbench Versus Target Testbench

TBRCA displays every difference between the target and reference testbench. You can
analyze these differences to assess how they might affect simulation results.

TBRCA reports differences due to addition or removal of a component from the testbench
hierarchy. For example, consider adding new components to the error test environment
in a system. When these new components are not use in the test case that is being
examined by TBRCA, such differences might not affect the simulation results.
You can view the UVM/OVM Hierarchy Analysis report files in Verdi.

Transaction Comparison
The third major operation of TBRCA is Transaction Comparison which finds the point in
the simulation where the recorded transactions begin to diverge.
Figure 115

Transaction Comparison

To improve the accuracy of transaction and comparison of mismatched
transactions, it is recommended to use the UVM/OVM version with VERDI22.06
onwards.

Debugging in Verdi GUI
You can use the following command to view the differing signals and transactions in Verdi:
%> autorca -load_report <report.xml>

The autorca command generates the report, tbrca_report.xml, at the following
location: <working directory>/rca.work/tbAutoRCA/reports/tbrca_report.xml
If you want to load this report, you need to specify the path in the following way:
%> autorca -load_report <work directory >/rca.work/tbAutoRCA/reports/
tbrca_report.xml

The following figure displays the rcaReport window in Verdi:
Figure 116

Debugging in Verdi GUI

The rcaReport window displays the analysis details that were shown in the transcript, as
shown in the following figure:
Figure 117

Analysis Details in Verdi GUI

You can perform various actions to view additional information about each analysis stage.
Figure 118

Actions for Additional Information

Transaction Difference Analysis Review With Verdi
You can view all analysis details in the report window of the Verdi GUI. You can also
perform multiple actions on these details to view more information about each stage of the
analysis.
When you right-click the selected difference and click Show Transaction in PA (see
Figure 118), the Protocol Analyzer (PA) window appears with details, as shown in the
Figure 119

Show Transaction in Protocol Analyzer

The RMB action in the report can help you load transactions and signals into the
Transaction and Protocol Analyzer and Wave windows. To view the first transaction
difference, click the transaction identifiers shown in the tree. This loads the corresponding
stream data from the reference and target FSDB files into the Transaction and Protocol

Analyzer windows and highlights the transactions. You can see more information about the
signal differences. The following figure displays these details:
Figure 120

Displaying Transaction Differences in nWave

You can use the transaction difference as the starting point for debugging and identify
the root cause of the error. To start the debugging process and to find the source code
associated with the transaction, right-click the transaction in the target FSDB and select
View Source, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 121

View Source Code Associated With Transaction

This displays the corresponding source code in the following nTrace window:
Figure 122

Displaying Source Code in nTrace Window

The following example shows how to debug the error starting with the error or differential
transaction shown on Transaction and Protocol Analyzer. As the error is reported in the
driver, you can investigate whether the error is associated with the driver-transfer
method. Double-click the method name, as shown in the following figure:

If the first interface signal difference is associated with the sig_data_out signal, it
means that the error is likely associated with the data phase of the transfer. Based on this
explanation, you can investigate the drive_data_phase method.

This method of identifying the source of an error is called Static Analysis. You must
investigate the read_byte and write_byte. This shows that the error most likely occurred
while reading or writing a byte.
The following figure shows that the error got injected in the read_byte method:
Figure 123

Error Injected in read_byte Method

The tracking of an error through static analysis shows that Transaction Difference
Analysis correctly identifies the component where the error is located. It also highlights the
transaction value to start the debugging process.

The Testbench RCA Message Analysis flow analyzes messages using a Natural
Language Processing (NLP) algorithm. It identifies transactions and signals closely
associated with that message. The resulting transactions and signals can then be
analyzed in the Verdi GUI.
The message to be analyzed can be selected based on the options specified to TBRCA.
When you provide an error log file, TBRCA analyzes the first UVM (or OVM) error that it
finds. If you specify a particular error message, TBRCA analyzes that message instead.
The message analysis results depend on the quality of the error message. The message
analysis algorithm identifies transactions linked to a message. It parses and analyzes the

with the errors. You must check the driving of the address phase and data phase. Because

title: Appendix 257
text:
As per the static analysis, the error most likely occurred while reading or writing a byte, as
shown in the following figure:

Using static analysis, Message Analysis identifies the component where the error
happened. It also highlights the transaction of value to help you begin debugging.

Message Analysis Features
The Message Analysis approach uses log messages to identify the cause of error. The
following sections describe various features of Message Analysis:
* Log Message Callstack Details
* Matching Attributes And Values
* Matching Transaction Details
* Matching Interfaces
* Analyzing Log Message From the Extracted Log File
* Assertion Type Message Analysis
* Support for User-Defined Messages
* Time Out Related Cases Support
* Verdi Interactive Message Analysis Features
* Show All ERROR-Related Log Messages in SmartLog - Upward Track
* ERROR and GOLDEN Pattern Log Messages

Log Message Callstack Details
When the log message call stack details are not available in the simulation log file, then
you can dump the WARNING, ERROR, and FATAL messages call stack details into the
simulation log file using the following runtime options:
+UVM_STACKTRACE=warn +UVM_STACKTRACE=error +UVM_STACKTRACE=fatal

VCS dumps the log message call stack details into the log file above the ERROR/
WARNING/FATAL message. TBRCA can read these call stack details from the simulation
log file and show them to you.
The following figure displays the Message callstack details. The first column shows the
file name and the line number of each call stack, and the second column shows the scope
of the file to which the line number refers.
Figure 127

Log Message Call Stack Details

You can double-click the required call stack or use the RMB action Show in nTrace to
open the file path and the line number of the selected call stack details. The following
figure displays the Show in nTrace feature:
Figure 128

Displaying Selected Stack in the Source Window

Matching Attributes And Values
Message Analysis provides the final matching attributes and values in the RCA report.
These attributes and values are one of the criteria for the Message Analysis to find
transactions from FSDB.
Loading Search Expression Into the Transaction And Protocol Analyzer Search
Dialog Box
Select the RMB option Load Search Expression to load the attributes and values in the
expressions format into the Transaction and Protocol Analyzer (TNPA) Search dialog box.
Figure 129

Load Search Expression

You can double-click to choose the required expression and start defining to search for the
required transactions in the TNPA window.
For more details about the TNPA Search dialog box, refer to the Search Capability for
Transactions section of the Verdi Transaction and Protocol Debug User Guide.

Matching Transaction Details
The Matching Transaction Details section provides all the matching transactions
collected using different approaches for analysis. It consists of the following two groups:
* Analysis Based on Message Description
* Active Transactions at Error Time
The following figure displays the Matching Transaction Details section:
Figure 130

Matching Transaction Details

Each group contains the matching transactions. Each transaction contains the related port
or stream names and the related virtual interface.

Figure 131

Additional Details for Each Transaction

You can use the RMB option View All Transactions to add all the transactions in the
selected group.
You can use the RMB option View in nWave to add the selected interface into nWave.
Analysis Based on Message Description
The Analysis Based on Message Description group contains transactions found by
analyzing the message description. This group focuses on the listed attributes and their
values.
Figure 132

Displaying Matching Attribute and Values

Active Transactions at Error Time
The Active Transactions at Error Time section contains transactions that are active or
detected when the error occurs. This section captures transactions present at the exact
error time. The tool filters these transactions using the log message TB scope and the
ERROR message call stack.

Matching Interfaces
Matching analysis displays all the matching interfaces grouped by the sources. You can
review the matching interfaces and can get information required for debugging an issue. It
includes the following groups:
* Message Reported TB Interfaces
* Matching Transaction Related Interfaces
* Matching Interfaces by the Message Source File Name
Figure 133

Matching Interfaces

To add the interface and matching signals into nWave, click the RMB option View in
nWave. In the absence of the matching signals, TBRCA adds all the interface signals into
nWave.

Analyzing Log Message From the Extracted Log File
The simulation log file contains different types of log messages, and you can extract the
types of log messages needed for analysis into a separate file, as shown in the following
example:

With this feature, you can analyze the extracted log file using the Message Analysis
approach.
In the YAML configuration file, you can input the extracted log file to be analyzed using the
analyze_extract_msg_file option. This is shown in the following figure:
Figure 134

Analyzing the Extracted Message File

TBRCA always picks the first valid log message irrespective of the type (Fatal, Error,
Warning, or Information) from the extracted file for analysis. If the first character of a line
contains #, assuming it to be a comment, TBRCA picks the next line.
The extracted log file must contain the line number and its associated log message.
TBRCA considers colon (:) as a delimiter to differentiate line number and log message at
each line. It takes the left hand side of the colon as the line number of the log message
and the right-hand side of the colon as the log message.
In the YAML configuration file, the target_sim_log option is mandatory
and you must specify the original log file from which the log messages are
extracted.

Assertion Type Message Analysis
Message Analysis reports the number of assertion messages found from the simulation
log and analyzes the assertion message reported before the UVM_ERROR message.

Figure 135

Assertion Type Message Analysis

Before opening the RCA report, set the following environment variable to add the assertion
related signal into the nWave window:
setenv IMPST_DISABLE_MUST_EXIST_PATH 1

RCA report displays the analysis details of the assertion message under the Assertion
analysis details section, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 136

Assertion Analysis Details

The Assertion analysis details section displays details related to assertion name and the
matching interfaces.
Select the assertion name and click the RMB option Load Signals and View Source to
load the assertion property associated source into nTrace and signals into nWave. It also
adds the assertion_time marker at the assertion start time.

Figure 137

Loading Signals and Viewing Source

You can use the RMB option View in nWave to add matching interfaces and signals into
nWave as shown in the following figure:
Figure 138

Viewing Matching Interfaces into nWave

Support for User-Defined Messages
Simulation log file can contain user-defined messages along with the normal UVM/OVM
format log messages. In the following figure, the highlighted messages are dumped using
macros:

To enable TBRCA to interpret the format of user-defined log messages, create a rule file
and specify it in the YAML configuration file. Use the partition_rule_files option, as
shown in the following figure.
Figure 139

Creating the Rule File

The rule file contains details about the user-defined log messages.
The rules are provided as input to Verdi SmartLog as partition-rule files.
Therefore, it must follow the syntax and format of the Verdi SmartLog partition
rule file. Refer to the SmartLog Tutorial chapter of the Verdi User Guide and
Tutorial for more details.
You can input the user-defined log message details into the Pattern field. The Pattern
option accepts the regular expressions as shown in the following figure. TBRCA accepts
multiple rule files. To understand the user-defined message format, you must mention the
user_defined or UserDefined string as a part of the Type option. TBRCA allows the
string to be case-insensitive.
Figure 140

User-Defined Log Message Details in the Pattern Field

When TBRCA reads the simulation log files, it identifies the log message using the
rule files and collects the user-defined messages. After collecting all the user-defined

messages, TBRCA analyzes the first ERROR type message. If the first message is not an
ERROR type, then it analyzes WARNING or FATAL type user-defined message.
If TBRCA does not find any of the message types, it analyzes the log message using the
default approach.

Time Out Related Cases Support
Simulation can be timed out with or without generating a UVM_ERROR. When the
simulation generates a UVM_ERROR even after it is timed out, analyzing UVM_ERROR is
not useful. Therefore, Message Analysis provides a solution of collecting thread details to
analyze the time-out related cases.
Collecting Thread Details
To collect the thread details, you must set the time-out time when the simulation stops
responding and update the VCS runtime arguments.
Setting time-out time
To collect the thread details at a particular time, set the simulation time-out or the time
when the simulation stops responding using the following environment variable:
setenv TBRCA_COLLECT_THREAD_TIME <simulation time>

For example, setenv TBRCA_COLLECT_THREAD_TIME 20000
Consider a simulation that runs from time 0 to 100000 and the time-out starts from the
time 20000, then you can set any time between 20000 to 100000 to collect the thread
details. The time-out value helps Message Analysis to stop simulation at the given time
and collect the thread details.
Updating VCS Runtime Arguments
In addition to the setting time-out, you can also add the following VCS runtime arguments
to collect the required details:
-ucli -i <$VERDI_HOME>/etc/tbAutoRCA/scripts/log_analysis/analyzers/
tbrca_timeout_analysis.tcl

title: Appendix 257
text:
After the simulation is completed, Message Analysis collects all the active thread details
which include Running, Waiting, and Blocking.
You can run the Message Analysis and open the report to view, navigate, and search the
thread details to identify the suspicious thread causing the simulation time-out.

The following figure displays the thread details in the report:
Figure 141

Displaying Collected Thread Details

The collected threads provide the file path, line number details, and the active status about
each thread. When you double-click each thread, it points you to the source code of that
thread.

Verdi Interactive Message Analysis Features
Message analysis supports the source code analysis features using the Verdi interactive
debug mode.
During the interactive mode, you can further debug the issue using the following Verdi
interactive debug features:
* Understand the call stack details of the cause of log message.
* Analyze the runtime object information of the design.
* Other interactive Verdi features.
You must have write access to the design location to identify the design
changes.
Analyze Attribute Value Changes
During the simulation run, the transaction attribute value gets updated and changed
multiple times and at multiple places.

Some of the designs might fail due to a value mismatch of a particular attribute. In such
cases, the feature of analyzing attribute value changes provides the following details:
* Different values assigned to the attribute.
* Time when each value gets changed.
* File path and line number of each value change.
When the message analysis report opens, select the required transactions for which you
need to analyze the value changes.
Right-click the required attribute available on the Transaction And Protocol Analyzer
(TNPA) Details table, and click Analyze Value Change to analyze the value changes of
the selected attribute.
Figure 142

Transaction And Protocol Analyzer (TNPA) Details

Clicking Analyzer Value Change opens Verdi in interactive mode. The simulation runs,
checkpoints are saved at each value change, and the recent value changes for the
selected attribute are displayed.

Figure 143

Invoke New Verdi And Save Checkpoints at Different Value Changes

You can select the checkpoints to analyze the required value changes.
Run Simulation to Selected Log Message
When you debug an issue, observe any abnormal log messages or messages with
important details about the issue. Use the Run Simulation to Selected Log Message
feature to identify when and where these log messages occur. This feature displays the
file, line number, and time for each log message.
Right-click the required log message and click Run Simulation to Here.

Figure 144

Run Simulation to the Selected Log Message

When you click Run Simulation to Here, a new Verdi opens and runs the simulation to
the selected log message and time.

Show All ERROR-Related Log Messages in SmartLog - Upward
Track
The feature displays all log messages related to errors. The SmartLog Upward Track
collects every log message associated with error messages from the simulation log file.
TBRCA loads these collected log messages into the Verdi SmartLog Upward Track
window for analysis.
The SmartLog Upward Track window navigates the messages by synchronizing them
with the main log file. Using this feature, you can quickly get all the error transaction
related messages.

For collecting the error-related log messages, TBRCA only looks upward to collect the
other related messages from the ERROR message.
To enable the feature, you must set the environment variable,
TBRCA_ENABLE_MA_UPWARD_TRACK_ANALYSIS, set to 1.

ERROR and GOLDEN Pattern Log Messages
The Error and Golden Pattern Log Messages feature helps you understand any deviation
or changes in the transaction activities from the beginning to the end of the transaction.
TBRCA considers the previous successfully completed transaction log messages as the

pattern. After collecting all Error and Golden pattern log messages, you can see their
differences from the loaded report.
To enable the Error and Golden Pattern Log Messages feature, you must set

X Root Cause Analysis (XRCA)
* What is XRCA?
* XRCA Application
* XRCA Usage
* XRCA Root Cause Reasons

Traditionally, unknown values (Xs) typically propagate through the design over multiple
statements. There are many root causes of unknown values. For example, if there is an
X in the input of a logic gate, if memory is not initialized, or if there is a setup or hold time
violation.
Usually, multiple Xs occur together. When you have multiple unknowns, select one X as
the startpoint for debugging, even if it is in your log or signal list. Then, trace backward
through the driver or fan-in signals of your chosen signal until you find the earliest X. If
the signal you selected is not the only cause of unknowns, pick another X from the group
and repeat the process. This cycle involves several small, repeated steps that can be
organized and automated.
XRCA automatically scans X signals in FSDB files and traces each X signal to its root
cause. It can process many X signals together, which reduces debugging time. XRCA also
creates clear, organized reports of the root causes. You can load these reports in Verdi to
view the tracing paths.
XRCA is a useful tool for debugging X signals during the start of gate-level simulation
and for finding X signal issues during regression. XRCA supports tracing at the gatelevel netlist, RTL, and VCS X propagation. It also helps trace X signals from low power
components and can detect X-pessimism.

What is XRCA?

What is XRCA?
XRCA is a highly effective tool that helps you quickly trace the path from an unknown
signal at an observation point to the root cause signal. This saves significant manual effort.
Using the input design and FSDB, XRCA with the tracing technology automatically traces
groups of X signals to their root causes. It also has built-in knowledge of how X values are
generated. With the analyzing technology, XRCA analyzes the root causes and generates
categorized reports. These reports are text files, and you can also use the capability for
further debugging in Verdi Apex mode. After the design and FSDB are ready, all tracings
and analysis steps run automatically, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 150

XRCA Methodology

Figure 151 shows that XRCA uses the dumped waveform and design as inputs. You
can also specify a signal list to only focus on specific signals with X values. If you do not
provide a signal list, XRCA runs in auto-scan mode. In auto-scan mode, it scans and
traverses all signals of the FSDB and generates a list of signals with X values.

What is XRCA?

Figure 151

XRCA Inputs

With a signal list (provided by the user or generated in auto-scan mode), XRCA
automatically traces back step by step to the active driver of unknown values. This
process continues for each signal until the path reaches the unknown root cause or meets
the specified stop criteria
From scanning to tracing, XRCA builds a behavior model that represents the actual design
behaviors. This model enables automatic tracing of all nodes of the design based on the
behavior to guide which fan-in signals should be traced further. The following figure is an
example showing the backward path tracing of XRCA in the behavior model:
Figure 152

XRCA Behavior Model

What is XRCA?

After completing the tracing process, XRCA analyzes the tracing results and organizes the
identified root causes into distinct categories. The following figure shows scenarios before
and after XRCA analysis and categorization:

X-Pessimism Detection
XRCA helps you find out the root causes of X signals. However, some X signals might be
false alarms due to X-pessimism. To identify X, you need to check the false X manually.
This is a time-consuming process.
For example:

If A has an unknown value, the simulation value of the AND gate is X. However, you can
find out that the result of an AND gate must be 0 because A AND is always equal to 0
(zero), irrespective of the value of A.

XRCA Application

XRCA-XPESS Engine
XRCA provides an X-pessimism engine to analyze the unknown values and validate
whether an X signal is a real X, or it has a constant value. This feature first runs XRCAXPESS to find out false X, and then runs XRCA engine to analyze the remaining nonXPESS signals.
Figure 154

XRCA-XPESS Engine

The XRCA-XPESS engine has the following limitation:
* The XRCA-XPESS engine detects X-pessimism reliably only on gate-level simulation
(GLS) designs. This feature does not support RTL designs.

XRCA Application
The following are the key points that XRCA adheres to:
* With a given unknown value signal list, XRCA analyzes all these issues automatically.
* Without a given X value signal list, XRCA automatically generates a signal list with X
values, then analyzes them.
* Generates a report, which classifies unknown values of the signals to the same root
causes.
* Allows Verdi to load the report and shows the trace path in Verdi Apex mode.
* Speeds up the debug process significantly.

Stops tracing at the task boundary
when XRCA finds the traced signal
inside the task block. Set -task_stop
to true to enable the feature. By
default, it is false.

Advanced Option for Debug Entry Scanning
target_scope

[Optional] Specify the DUT hierarchy
in the target_scope option to enable
XRCA to scan for the X debug-entry
signals.

max_err_cnt

Specify the maximum count to scan X
debug entry. The default is 256. Set it to
0 for no limitation.

max_scan_level

Specify maximum scanning
level to scan X debug entry from
target_scope. The default is 3. Set it
to 0 to scan all the levels.

max_sample_per_signal

Specify maximum count of X debug
entry for each signal. The default is 1.
Set it to 0 for no limitation.

target_signal_type

Specify the type of signals to be
scanned:
* type: {boundary, register, all} or the
union of some of them.
* boundary: input/output/inout direction
signals.
* register: register type signals.
* all: all signals in the FSDB file.

begin_time [time[unit]]

Specify the begin time of scanning the
X debug entry signals in the waveform
file. The default is 1 and the default time
unit is FSDB time unit.

end_time [time[unit]]

Specify the end time of scanning the
X debug entry signals in the waveform
file. The default is waveform max time
and the default time unit is FSDB time
unit.

gen_list [true|false]

Dumps X debug entry signal list
scanned by XRCA and does not invoke
tracing. The default is false.

Tracing Specific Items at the Set Time in XRCA
The target_signal_list option of the YAML file of XRCA appends a file that lists all the
signals, scopes, and assertions that you want to trace.
You must categorize your inputs by specifying assertList, scopeList, and signalList
keywords for assertions, scopes, and signals, respectively in the following file format:
<keyword>
<full_signal_name>#<time><time_unit>

Where,
* <keyword> can be one of the following:
signalList specifies the following <full_signal_name> lines or is left empty for
debug entries.
assertList specifies the following <full_signal_name> lines for assertions.
scopeList specifies the following <full_signal_name> lines for design scopes.

* <time> specifies the time point from where the tracing starts for the specified item.
* <time_unit> specifies the units of the time point from where the tracing starts for the
specified item.
* You can specify scopeList and signalList without time using the
following file format:
<keyword>
<full_signal/scope_name>

* When the file is not specified, XRCA automatically scans the FSDB file for
signals that have X and traces Xs on those signals.
## Example 1: (debug entries)
##
system.CPU.output#100ns
##
system.CPU.output#100000ps
##
/system/CPU/output#100ns
## You can specify signals without time if the time is not available.
##
system.CPU.output
##
/system/CPU/output
## You must specify assertions with time.
## Example 2: (assertions with the same start and fail times)
##
assertList
##
system.CPU.check_reset#250ns
##
/system/CPU/check_clock#500000ps
## Example 3: (assertions with different start and fail times)
##
assertList
##
system.CPU.check_reset#200ns#250ns
##
/system/CPU/check_clock#400000ps#500000ps
## Example 4: (scopes)
##
scopeList
##
system.CPU.ALU#100ns
##
/system/CPU/PCU#20000ps
## You can specify scopes without time if the time is not available.
##
system.CPU.PCU
##
/system/CPU/PCU

Invoking XRCA and Reviewing XRCA Results in Verdi
To invoke XRCA, use the following command:
$ autorca -cfg <template_name.yaml>

While launching XRCA, XRCA finds the X signal for analysis by following the process
shown in Figure 159:
Figure 159

Flowchart to Find X Signal for Analysis

After successfully finding the X signal for analysis, XRCA performs X tracing to trace the
root cause of the found X signal. When the XRCA tracing finishes, the console displays
the following message to load the trace report:
[RCA] Load report with 'autorca -load_report xrca_report.xml'

$ autorca -load_report xrca_report.xml

XRCA GUI Report
XRCA GUI Report is integrated with the existing functions of SmartLog to help you browse
the whole XRCA report structure with a concise template. You can trace the XRCA results
using XRCA GUI Report that provides the following key features:
* Tree widget report layout
* Filtering/sorting/search function
* Four report types grouping
* Intuitive GUI interaction with TFV, nWave, and nTrace
* X-propagation flow of XRCA
The following figure displays the report loaded to Verdi:
Figure 160

GUI Window for XRCA Results

The following are the features of the XRCA GUI window:
* Loads XRCA results report to Verdi in a standalone window.
* Displays all the debug entries in one window.
* Supports collapse configuration by default.
* Adds and expands the X-pessimism Result section when there is an X-pessimism
signal in the report. However, you can collapse the merge nodes under x-pessimism
debug entry.

* The tree structure of XRCA Root Cause Results for each debug entry consists of the
following items:
Debug entry,
Root cause,
Hint (if analyzing X-propagation/NLP data)
Module, signal name (available in case of module grouping)
Reason (available in case of reason grouping)
* Allows single selection.
* Provides toolbar for interactive actions such as filtering, sorting, and searching.
Refer to the following sections for details on the XRCA GUI report layout and features:
* Tree Widget Report Layout
* Impact of X-pessimism on XRCA Report
* XRCA Report Debug View

Tree Widget Report Layout
XRCA results are displayed in a tree widget layout and provide details that include tracing
configuration, XRCA root cause results, related design, and related waveform based on
the XRCA trace result.
The following figure displays XRCA configuration, X-pessimism, and XRCA Root Cause
Results:
Figure 161

XRCA Tree Widget Report Layout

The Tree Widget view consists of the following sections:
* Configuration: The XRCA Configuration section of the Tree widget view displays the
following items:
XRCA version used to analysis
FSDB file
Time unit
Signal file (displayed when you specify the signal list)
Analysis X options (otherwise, XRCA performs auto-scan)
Trace Options
X-pessimism options (displayed for XRCA reports with the xpess:true
configuration X-Pessimism option)
* X-pessimism Result: The X-pessimism result is displayed only when XRCA has the
xpess:true configuration option. The report displays x-pessimism debug entry with its
merge nodes.
* XRCA Root Cause Results: All the debug entries and their root cause information are
displayed in the XRCA Root Cause Results section.
Hint
XRCA integrates the traditional Verdi flow for tracing X-propagation hint with the XRCA
GUI report as shown in the following figure:
Figure 162

X-Propagation Hint With XRCA GUI Report

In the report, the X-propagation signal is tagged with the prefix "hint" and has a reason
"Driven by X-propagation statement (t-merge/x-merge)."
You can check all the X-propagation signals on the path from the debug entry signal to its
root cause and can use the nTrace/nWave/TFV sync features to analyze them.

When you load the XRCA tracing report containing XPROP information, nTrace enables
the X-propagation instrument by default. An X red notation on the instance tree and a
green tag on the source view display the XPROP section.

TFV Displaying X-Propagation Signal

Impact of X-pessimism on XRCA Report
For describing the impact of X-pessimism on XRCA report, primarily the following parts of
the report are used:
* Root cause found signals
* X-pessimism signals
Following are the cases to demonstrate the XRCA report with X-pessimism included:
1. XRCA runs with X-pessimism disabled.
2. XRCA runs with X-pessimism enabled. X-pessimism signal is not specified.
3. XRCA runs with X-pessimism enabled. X-pessimism signal is specified.
Case1: XRCA runs with X-pessimism disabled
In this case, the original XRCA report is demonstrated. XRCA traces the specified signals
iteratively and arranges them by root cause. For example,
XRCA reports X at top.dut.e and top.dut.h is contributed from X at top.dut.a.

Root Cause Found:
#0 top.dut.a(X from un-initialized signal)
TM0C1 top.dut.e#3500
TM0C1 top.dut.h#3500
#0 top.dut.b(X from un-initialized signal)
TM0C1 top.dut.g#3500
TM0C1 top.dut.h#3500

Case2: XRCA runs with X-pessimism enabled
In this case, the X-pessimism signal is not specified in XRCA. If only top.dut.f signal is
verified as FalseX, XRCA removes top.dut.a as the root cause of top.dut.h because
signal top.dut.a is in the fan-in of signal top.dut.h.

Root Cause Found:
#0 top.dut.a(X from un-initialized signal)
TM0C1 top.dut.e#3500
#0 top.dut.b(X from un-initialized signal)
TM0C1 top.dut.g#3500
TM0C1 top.dut.h#3500

Case3: XRCA runs with X-pessimism enabled
In this case, the X-pessimism signal is specified in XRCA.
If three signals, top.dut.f, top.dut.g, top.dut.h, are verified as FalseX, XRCA
removes top.dut.a as the root cause of top.dut.h. All debug entries related to
top.dut.b are FalseX, so top.dut.b is removed from the root cause list. Two userdefined signals, top.dut.g and top.dut.h are verified as FalseX, so XRCA adds them in
the X-pessimism report.

Root Cause Found:
#0 top.dut.a(X from un-initialized signal)
TM0C1 top.dut.e#3500
X-pessimism:
top.dut.g#3500
top.dut.h#3500

* (Merge Node): It is present under debug entry and contains root X-pessimism signals
in the fan-in cone of this debug entry.
Click the signal hyper-link, it opens the GUI window to replay the tracing path with Xpess
notation above the gate and register. And there is a hint "(1'b1 x-pessimism)" to notify that
it is an X-pessimism with constant value 1 (or 0).
Also, there is a pair of highlighted paths. A split signal merges at the OR gate with different
polarities, and therefore, causes X-pessimism.

This case is an example of sub-node root X-pessimism signal where the debug entry is a
propagated X-pessimism.
The following figure shows another example where the debug entry signal is an Xpessimism.

XRCA Report Debug View
XRCA report debug view extends the usage of the XRCA report in SmartLog. In addition
to listing debug entry signals, root causes information, and replaying the trace paths by
clicking signals, you can also extract, sort, search, and group the GUI table. With these
new features, you can read trace reports in a concise way.

Functions Available on Toolbar
The toolbar of the XRCA Report debug view consists of multiple functions, as shown in the
Figure 166

Filter
Click Filter
to invoke the Filter dialog box. The blue dot (the annotate button,
)
on the button indicates that the filter is applied for the current view. The following figure
displays the Filter dialog box:
Figure 167

Filter Dialog Box

It consists of the following keys:
* Filtering data: Select any one of the following filtering data:
Debug entry signal: The tree widget displays all entries that match the debug entry
filtering criteria.
Root cause signal: The tree widget displays all entries that match the root cause
filtering criteria.
Module: The tree widget displays all entries that match the filtering criteria for
module.
Reason: The tree widget displays all entries that match the filtering criteria for
reason.
* Operator: It allows you to select how you want to filter your data. You can select from
these options: contains, does not contain, is, or is not.
* Text box: Enter the criteria you want to set for the selected filtering data.

Show Signal on TFV
, to
You can select a signal on the report debug view, click Show Signal on TFV,
show the signal on TFV. You can also invoke the Show Signal on TFV feature using the
keyboard shortcut Ctrl+t.
When the signal is X-pessimism type (xpess debug entry/merge node), this feature
displays all its trace path and marks the path with sm notation.
The displaying path on signal varies with grouping, as shown in the following points:
* Group by debug entry
When you select a debug entry signal, this feature displays the path from the debug
entry to its first child root cause. The path is centered and highlighted.
When you select a root cause signal, this feature displays the path from its parent
debug entry to the root cause. The path is centered and highlighted.
* Group by root cause
When you select a root cause signal, this feature displays the path from the root case
signal. It centers and highlights the selected signal.
When you select a debug entry signal in root cause group, this feature displays the
path from the debug entry signal to its parent root cause. It centers and highlights the
selected debug entry.
* When the selected signal is a Hint, the feature displays the path from its parent debug
entry to the parent root cause. It centers and highlights the Hint signal.
The following data types can invoke the TFV synchronization:
* debugEntry
* rootCause
* hint

* xpessDebugEntry
* xpessMergeNode

Grouping in XRCA GUI Layout
The data available in the XRCA GUI layout are grouped based on the multiple items,
such as debug entry, module, root cause, and reason. This section provides details on the
XRCA GUI layout.
By Debug Entry
XRCA Root Cause Results are grouped in the following steps:
1. Debug entry
2. Root cause
3. Hint (when hint is available between the debug entry and root cause)
The following figure displays grouping by debug entry:

Grouping Based on Debug Entry

By Module
XRCA Root Cause Results are grouped in the following steps:
1. Module and root cause signal name (same module same signal)
2. Root cause
3. Debug entry
4. Hint (when hint is available between the debug entry and root cause)
The following figure displays grouping by module:
Figure 173

Grouping Based on Module

By Root Cause (Default)
XRCA Root Cause Results are grouped in the following steps:
1. Root cause
2. Debug entry
3. Hint (when hint is available between the debug entry and root cause)
The following figure displays grouping by root cause:
Figure 174

Grouping Based on the Root Cause

By Reason
XRCA Root Cause Results are grouped in the following steps:
1. Reason
2. Root cause

3. Debug entry
4. Hint (when hint is available between the debug entry and root cause)
The following figure displays grouping by reason:

XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
XRCA automatically identifies cases where an X root cause is driven by a timing violation
reported in the simulation log. After running XRCA, a post-processing module performs the
following tasks:
* Scans XRCA root causes.
* Correlates them with timingviolation messages in the simulation log (VCS or thirdparty formats).
* Annotates matching root causes as timing violation and records the exact
simulation log file and line in the XRCA report.
When you load xrca_report.xml,
* For root causes that correlate to a timing violation, XRCA updates the displayed reason
text to X from timing violation.
* When a timingviolation subsection is present for a root cause, the GUI adds a
timing violation tree widget under that root cause.
* Use Show Timing Violation on SmartLog in SmartLog to open the simulation log
and jump to the recorded line. Use Show Timing Violation on Source View in
Source View to navigate to the related source location.
The following are the key features of XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation:
* It acts purely as a post process.
* It runs only when timing_violation_check is enabled and target_sim_log
specifies a readable simulation log file. For details, see Enabling XRCA TimingViolation Correlation.
The XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation section consists of the following topics:
* Enabling XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
* Post-Processing After XRCA Run
* Loading Report With XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
* Limitations of XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation

Enabling XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
The XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation feature is conditionally enabled. To use this
feature, all of the following must be true:
* The timing_violation_check option is enabled in the XRCA YAML template.
* A valid simulation log path, target_sim_log, is specified in the XRCA YAML template.
* The file at that path exists and can be opened for reading.
However, if timing_violation_check is set to false, if the target_sim_log field is
missing or empty, or if the simulation log file cannot be opened, then
* The timing-violation post process is skipped.
* No timing-violation annotation is applied.
* No change to root cause reasons.
* No additional navigation is enabled.

title: Appendix 257
text:
Post-Processing After XRCA Run
After the XRCA run completes, the tool performs the following postprocessing steps to
correlate root causes with timing violations:
1. Extracts root-cause information from the XRCA output
a. After XRCA finishes, the output file xrca_report.xml is available.
b. XRCA parses xrca_report.xml to identify all <rootCause> entries.
c. For each root cause, the tool extracts the full signal name and identifies the driven
scope instance. The tool considers cross-module references (XMRs) also.
d. XRCA builds an inmemory list of root-cause signals and scopes, to be used in
subsequent searches.
2. Correlates root causes with timing violations in the simulation log
a. The tool uses the root-cause list and the specified simulation-log file
(target_sim_log).
b. It searches the simulation log for candidate locations that match a root-cause
scope.
c. When several timing-violation candidates exist, the tool selects the violation with a
time closest to, but earlier than, the original root-cause time.
d. For each candidate location, the tool checks whether it forms a valid
timingviolation block, based on existing SmartLog rules.

title: Appendix 257
text:
It supports VCS and third-party timing-violation formats.
e. When a timing-violation block is matched, XRCA collects the following
timingviolation information:
Timing-violation type (for example, hold)
Source code file
Source code line
Simulation log file
Simulation log line
Timing-violation time
Load parse rule for the log type
3. For each root cause with a correlated timing-violation block, the tool creates a
timing-violation subsection under the related <rootCause> element in the enriched
xrca_report.xml file.
4. For each root cause, the tool performs the following:
Constructs a timing-violation subsection under root cause section.
Saves the updated xrca_report.xml (overwriting the report file).

Loading Report With XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
When you load the enriched XRCA report (xrca_report.xml) in Verdi, the GUI interprets
timing-violation data stored during post-processing. XRCA displays the reason for each
root cause entry as follows:
* For each <rootCause> entry,
Check if corresponding timing-violation subsection exists.
If the timing-violation tree subsection exists, create timing-violation tree widget
using the following format:
Timing Violation: <Timing violation type>@<Source code file>:<Source
code line>[Simulation log file:Simulation log line]

Timing Violation: hold@star79337.v:896338[sim.log:908]

Remap or override the displayed reason text for this root cause to X from timing
violation.
If the root cause does not contain timingviolation information, the GUI displays
the original reason as provided in the XRCA report.
* When you select a timing-violation tree widget under a root cause and click Show
Timing Violation on SmartLog, XRCA uses SmartLog Tcl commands to:
Open SmartLog if it is not opened.
Open the simulation log file referenced in the timing-violation tree widget (if not
already open in SmartLog).
Load the appropriate parsing rule for the simulation log. For example, a rule specific
for VCS or third-party simulator timing violations.
Move the SmartLog view cursor to the line number associated with the timing
violation. This displays the exact timing violation message.
* When you choose Show Timing Violation on Source View, XRCA automatically
navigates to the source code pane. It highlights the relevant source code line
corresponding to the timing violation, as detailed in the timing violation tree widget.

Limitations of XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
The XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation feature has the following limitations:
* It supports only VCS and third-party simulator log formats.
* It requires timing_violation_check to be enabled and a valid, readable simulation
log path (target_sim_log) from the RDA or autorca configuration.

Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis
(MCPRCA)
* MCPRCA Usage

During RTL simulation, Dynamic SDC Verification in VCS detects timing constraint bugs,
such as Multiple Cycle Path (MCP), FP, and clock group issues. SDC forms a key part of
RTL signoff. Teams use VCS with SDC (VCS-SDC) for signoff during verification. VCSSDC reduces project cycle time by several weeks.
Debugging violations detected by VCS-SDC can be difficult when MCP bugs affect many
signals. RDA offers a Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis (MCPRCA) solution. This
solution automatically groups violations into fewer categories. It provides connections to
further debug with waveform, source code, and simulation log, using Verdi.

MCPRCA helps you to debug the VCS-SDC detected violations using Verdi. After
completing simulation with VCS-SDC, MCPRCA checks the results of VCS-SDC and
helps in finding out the violations. MCPRCA uses the Violation Binning feature to group
violations from a simulation log and generate further debug entries.
RDA provides the Verdi GUI to review MCPRCA reports generated after analyzing
violations from the log file. You can also use the GUI to debug the source code, logs, and
waveform.

The following figure gives an overview of the MCPRCA debug flow:
Figure 187

MCPRCA Debug Flow

The following are the requirements for the MCPRCA setup:
* VCS compilation with SDC commands which contains MCP, FP, or clock group
property.
* Run simulation. The property can pass or fail.

The following steps are required to perform MCPRCA:
1. Prepare a configuration file for MCPRCA. Refer to the Preparing RDA Configuration
File for MCPRCA section for more details.
2. Invoke MCPRCA. Refer to the Invoking MCPRCA section for more details.
3. Review the MCPRCA results in Verdi. Refer to the Reviewing MCPRCA in Verdi GUI
section for more details.
The MCPRCA Usage section consists of the following topics:
* Preparing RDA Configuration File for MCPRCA
* Invoking MCPRCA
* Reviewing MCPRCA in Verdi GUI
* SDC Annotation
* Smart Waiver

Preparing RDA Configuration File for MCPRCA
You can generate an empty MCPRCA template for the VCS-SDC mode using the following
command:
> $VERDI_HOME/bin/autorca -gen_cfg_template <template_name.yaml>
-gen_mode mcprca

After generating the configuration file, you can see a template, <template_name.yaml>,
generated under the current directory. The following is the figure of the MCPRCA
configuration template:

more details about the waiver rules syntax and the waiver usage in GUI.

Invoking MCPRCA
You can invoke MCPRCA using the following autorca command:
> $VERDI_HOME/bin/autorca -cfg <template_name.yaml>

After MCPRCA, you can use Verdi to review and check the analysis results. Use
the following command to load the RDA tracing results into Verdi and enable the
corresponding features:
%> autorca -load_report <tracing_reports>

autorca -load_report mcprca_report.xml

After you load the MCPRCA report, Verdi displays the report results. Verdi also prepares
other debug entries, including SmartLog, Violation Waveform, Connection to SDC
command, and SDC clock annotation.

Grouping
The Grouping feature is a key feature in MCPRCA. It reviews all violations grouped into
bins with different information. That is, violations grouped in the same bin might be caused

by the same bug. Click the Group by list and select any one of the grouping rules. The
following figure displays the Group by field:
Figure 191

Selecting Grouping Rules

You can use the following grouping rules for MCP to group violations into bins with
different aspects:
* signal_to: Group violations by the same signals (TO) names.
* signal_from: Group violations by the same signals (FROM) names.
* signal_both: Group violations by the same signals (TO) and same signals (FROM)
names.
* clock_to: Group violations by the same clock names of signals (TO).
* clock_from: Group violations by the same clock names of signals (FROM).
* sdc_command: Group violations by the same SDC command.
Using the Grouping feature, you can review the results of different grouping rules
immediately in the active report window.

Smart Waiver
You can use the Smart Waiver feature to reduce noise by removing the violation indexes
that are not the real root cause from the report. You can use the waive rule to classify the
violation messages and move them to the waived folder. A waive rule consists of the rule
name, the FROM signal and the TO signal.
The following is the waive rule format of the content of the specified waiver files:
Waive violation index matches FROM signal and TO signal. Signal name is allowed to use
wildcard (* ?)
* waive -name $RuleName -to {<$ToSignalName>} -from {<$FromSignalName>}
To disable waive rule, rule names are separated with a space.
* waive -disable {$RuleName1 $RuleName2 $RuleName3}

* Waive violation index matches the FROM signal testbench.dut.mux.ff1 and to
signal testbench.dut.mux.out2.
waive -name rule1 -to {testbench.dut.mux.out2} -from
{testbench.dut.mux.ff1}

The rule1 waives index matched with the FROM signal and the TO signal.
* Waive violation index with TO signal testbench.dut.mux.out.
waive -name rule2 -to {testbench.dut.out}
waive -name rule3 -to {testbench.dut.out} -from {*}

The rule2 is equal to rule3; they waive indexes which are matched with the TO
signal.
* Waive violation index with the FROM signal testbench.dut.mux.ff1.
testbench.dut.mux.ff1.
waive -name rule4 -from {testbench.dut.mux.ff1}
waive -name rule5 -from {testbench.dut.mux.ff1} -to
{*}

The rule3 is equal to rule4; they waive indexes which are matched with the FROM
signal.
* Disable waive rule.
waive -disable {rule1 rule2 rule3}

This command disables rule1, rule2, and rule3 specified in the same file.
* Waive violation index with multiple FROM signals.
Violation index with two FROM signals and one TO signal. This index can waive.
TO signal: top.sub1.ccc
FROM signal: top.sub2.aaa
FROM signal: top.sub3.bbb
Waive with full signal specified.
waive -name rule6 -to {top.sub1.ccc} -from
{top.sub2.aaa}
waive -name rule7 -to {top.sub1.ccc} -from
{top.sub3.bbb}

Waive with TO signal specified. This rule waives other matched index.
waive -name rule8 -to {top.sub1.ccc}

or waive with both the FROM signals specified. This rule also waives other matched
index.
waive -name rule9 -from {top.sub2.aaa}
waive -name rule10 -from {top.sub3.bbb}

If the violation index matches the waiver rule then it is moved to the waived index folder on
the report.
