A feature is obsolete when the feature is no longer supported and no longer functional in
Verdi releases. This chapter mentions the obsolete features in Verdi.

Active Tracing of RTL

Active Tracing of RTL
1. In the nWave frame, select a specific signal that you want to debug.

This takes you to the line in source code that is causing the transition.
3. In the main window, invoke Source > Active Annotation.

Function Debugging
1. In the source code frame, find a signal that is driven by a function, for example, "add"
and so on.
2. Invoke Source > Function Annotation.
3. Double-click the function, for example, "add".
4. Click the function, for example. "add" to jump back.

Macro Debugging
1. In the source code frame, find a macro, for example. MACRO1(CLOCK2).
2. Put your mouse cursor on MACRO1. The tip window shows the definition of MACRO1.
3. Invoke Source -> Expand Macro.

SystemVerilog TestBench (SVTB) - FSDB Logging
1. The $fsdbLog dumping command can be used to log messages into the FSDB file.
The use of $fsdbLog is not restricted to SVTB and can be used anywhere in your
environment where you have previously used crude text logging mechanisms to log
interesting information. The flexibility of $fsdbLog allows you to capture not only
messages but also severities, variable states, and so on.
2. The messages are recorded in the msg_root scope in the FSDB file. Invoke the
Signal -> Get Signals command in nWave to get them.

Compile and Dump SystemVerilog Assertions
1. Adding dumping task to design:
$fsdbDumpSVA; command is required to dump SVA data. Only failure asserts are
dumped, the Verdi system calculates properties automatically when analyzing.
Adding the +fsdb+sva_success simulation option, if success SVA needs to be
dumped.
For VCS, include the -debug_access+<option> compile-time option on the VCS
command line.
Include the -sverilog option to enable SystemVerilog features.
2. Compiling using UFE:
Include the -kdb compile-time option to generate Verdi KDB with Unified
Compile front end and to dump the design into the libraries specified in the
synopsys_sim.setup file. For example:
// -kdb in VCS two-step flow
% vcs -kdb <compile_options> <source files> -debug_access+all
// -kdb in VCS three-step flow
%> vlogan -kdb <vlogan options> <source files>
%> vhdlan -kdb <vhdlan options> <source files>
%> vcs -kdb <top_name> -debug_access+all -lca

title: Verification ContinuumTM

Compute Newly Added SVA in Verdi Without Rerunning
Simulation
1. Load design and signal level FSDB into the Verdi system.
2. In the main window, invoke Tools -> Property Tools -> Evaluator.
a. In the Evaluate Properties form, expand the design hierarchy in the left pane, and
click the node that contains assertions.
b. Select assertions in the middle pane, and click the Add Selected Properties icon
to add assertions to the right pane.
c. Click the Evaluate button, and click Yes on the Question box.
The assertions are evaluated, and a virtual FSDB file is generated to combine the
original FSDB file and the new created one. The virtual FSDB file will be loaded into
nWave automatically.

Analyze the Reason for Assertion Failures
1. In the main window, invoke Tools -> Property Tools -> Statistics to open the
Statistics frame.
2. Double-click Assert in the FSDB Statistics section to add all assertions to the
Property Details field.
3. Then double-click an assertion failure in the Property Details field. The Analyzer frame
appears at the bottom.
4. Scroll down the Analyzer frame to view property and sequences for the specific SV
Assertion that you want to debug.
Notice the time information above and the data information below the variable signals
in the sequences.
5. Click the Expand button

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
This focuses in on the logical failures in the sequence.
6. In the nWave frame, select the SV Assertion that you want to debug and invoke
Waveform -> Property -> Expand Overlapping/Shrink Overlapping.
7. View the expanded assert at top for the specific SV assertion that you want to debug.

Compare Two FSDB Mismatches

Compare Two FSDB Mismatches
1. Open two nWave frames with different FSDB files. Ideally pass vs. fail FSDB files on
same test or RTL vs. Gate simulation on locked in signal names.
In the first nWave frame, invoke File > Open, select an FSDB file and click the Add
button, then click OK button.
In the second nWave frame, invoke File > Open, select a different FSDB file and
click the Add button, then click OK button.
2. Put the same signals to the two nWave frames. You can drag and drop signals from
one nWave frame to another.
3. Synchronize the nWave frame cursors.
In the first nWave, invoke Window > Sync Waveform View.
In the second nWave, invoke Window > Sync Waveform View.
4. Compare any parts of the signals, for example. compare all signals in each group for
both nWave frames.
a. In nWave, invoke Tools > Waveform Compare > Compare Two Groups.
b. In Compare Two Groups form, click Groups in Different Windows.
c. Select the first group name from the first Group Name selection field. And select
the second group name from the second Group Name selection field.
d. The Comparison Result form shows your comparison results for the signals in each
group.
e. To save report, click Save button to save the report as a .txt file.
5. Search by mismatches:
In the first nWave frame, make sure Search By option is set to Mismatches (/),
then click the blue horizontal arrows next to the Search By option.

Collapse Source Code
1. In the main window, enable all three options in the Automatic Source Code Folding

2. In the source code frame, you see process and while blocks with a [-] and [+] next to

nAnalyzer is an optional Verdi module.
1. In the main window, invoke Tools -> New Schematics -> Clock Tree.
2. Click the Import button to open the Import form.
3. In the Format field change to SDC, and then select a SDC (Synopsys Design

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
nAnalyzer - Switching Reports
nAnalyzer is an optional Verdi module.
1. In the main window, invoke Tools -> Switching Analysis -> New Query.
a. In Switching Analysis form, working scope should be a scope that you
want to focus on, or just use the top scope for everything, for example,
tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.i_CPU;
b. Enable Include Instances under the Hierarchy.
c. Enable Switching Activity Report for the report type.
d. Click OK.
2. Click OK on the Question box to do Behavior Analysis.
3. In the Switching Analysis Report frame,
a. In the Filters tab, enter in a module name to search for, for example, enter: *alu* in
the Module text field.
b. In the Sorting Scheme tab, select the Sort By option as Name and also enable the
Ascend option.
c. Left-click theTransition Count column to sort the results by the number of
transitions.
4. In the Switching Analysis Report frame, click the New Query button to open the
Switching Analysis form.
a. In the Switching Analysis form, you can change the working scope to another level,
for example, tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.i_CPU.i_ALUB.i_alu
b. Enable the Peak Activity Report option in the Report Type section.
c. Click OK.
The new Switching Analysis Report frame has different Time stamps with
Transition Count. Also notice the "Time Period" at the top of the window
should have some range, for example, "0 ~ 15000 x ns".
d. To find the location for the highest peak activity for an instance of time, double-click
the row in the Switching Analysis Report frame that has the time that you want to
see. This opens a new Switching Analysis Report frame but the Time Period is one
snapshot in time, for example, "3000 ~ 3000 x ns". This gives you all the locations in
that time snapshot and their Transition Counts.

nAnalyzer is an optional Verdi module.
1. In the main window, invoke File -> SDF -> Load SDF Files -> <your_sdf_file>.sdf
2. In the main window, invoke Source -> Find String; enter the name of a register where
you want to start. Select Match Case and In All Files options; double-click in the
required result in the message frame at the bottom of the main window.
3. In the main window, click New Schematic icon.
4. In the nSchema frame, invoke Trace -> Two Points.
5. In the source code frame, drag and drop starting point output pin into From field of
Trace Two Points form.
6. In the main window, invoke Source -> Find String; enter some name of a register
where you want to end; Select Match Case and In All Files options; Double-click in
the required result in the message frame at the bottom of the main window.
7. In the source code frame, drag and drop ending point output pin into To field of Trace
Two Points form.
8. In Trace Two Points form, click the Trace button.
a. In View Trace Result Schematic frame, invoke Schematic -> SDF Annotation.
b. In View Trace Result Schematic frame, invoke Schematic -> Delay Type and
Schematic -> Delay Scale.
c. In View Trace Result Schematic frame, invoke Trace -> Shortest/Longest Path
and select Longest.
d. In the nSchema frame, right-click in the cell to invoke Show Cell Delay.

-ord. Click on nSchema in Show On section, then click Show button at bottom.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Accelerate Simulation and Reduce Dumping Size with Siloti
1. Run a Siloti command as follows:
% vericom -f run.f &
% esa -lib work -top top -db es -bas top -libPath work -bdb_file work
&

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
-db: To indicate the output should be an Essential Signal Database (ESDB), and
specify the output ESDB file name.
-bas <Design Top>: Specify the design top for Behavior Analysis. If this option is
not specified, esa finds a design top automatically.
-libPath: Specify the path to store BDB (Behavior Database). If this option is not
specified, ./work is the default path.
-bdb_file: Specify the BDB file name. If this option is not specified, ./work is the
default.
2. The design has been analyzed with Behavior Analysis to generate a minimal but
sufficient set of signals to be dumped during simulation to provide 100% visibility during
debug.
3. Be sure to add the simulation runtime option +fsdb+esdb to specify the generated esa
database when running your simulation:
% ./simv +fsdb+esdb="es"

4. Load design and essential signal FSDB file into the Verdi system:
% verdi -lib work -top top -esAuto -ssf esd.fsdb -bdb_load work.lib+
+/work.bdb &

-esAuto: Perform Data Expansion setup (auto time window mode) automatically
after loading the design.
-bdb_load: Load the BDB file which has been generated by esa utility.
5. Enable Active Annotation by invoking Source -> Active Annotation in the main
window to view data expansion results. Note that the value calculated by the Data
Expansion engine is marked as purple.

Resources

6. Drag local signals to nWave. Drag an instance in the Verdi session.
7. Create a Temporal Flow View from this transition to view full capabilities of Verdi
debug.

Purpose
This document explains how to install the Verdi supplementary package. The manual
should be read from beginning to end, although you may skip any sections with which
you are already familiar. For detailed descriptions of individual commands, refer to the
appropriate chapter of the Verdi supplementary User Guide.
For detailed usage on any of the installed products, refer to the appropriate user's guide
as listed in the Related Publications section of this chapter.

Audience
The audience for this document includes engineers who are familiar with languages and
tools used in design and verification such as Verilog, VHDL, and SystemVerilog, and
typically install and set-up tool software.
This document assumes that you have a basic knowledge of the platform on which your
version of the Verdi Supplementary runs: UNIX or Linux and that you are knowledgeable in
Verilog or VHDL and digital logic design.

Chapter 1: About This Document
Book Organization

Book Organization
This Supplementary Package Installation and System Administration Guide is organized
as follows:
* About This Document provides an introduction to this document and explains how to
use it.
* Installing Verdi Supplementary Package explains how to install Verdi supplementary
package.

Conventions Used in This Book
The following conventions are used in this document:
* Italics font is used for emphasis, book titles, section names, design names, file path,
and file names within paragraphs.
* Bold is used to emphasize text, highlight titles, menu items, and other Verdi terms.
* Courier type is used for program listings. It is also used for test messages that the
Verdi platform display on the screen.
* NOTE describes important information, warnings, or unique commands.
* Menu -> Command identifies the path used to select a menu command.
* Left-click or Click means click the left mouse button on the indicated item.
* Middle-click means click the middle mouse button on the indicated item.
* Right-click means click the right mouse button on the indicated item.
* Double-click means click twice consecutively with the left mouse button.
* Shift-left-click means press and hold the <Shift> key then click the left mouse button on
the indicated item.
* Drag-left means press and hold the left mouse button, then move the pointer to the
destination and release the button.
* Drag means press and hold the middle mouse button on the indicated item then move
and drop the item to the other window.

Overview
Before installing the Verdi Supplementary package, verify that your workstation meets the
following requirements:
* Software files from the Synopsys SolvnetPlus website.
* 35 GB hard drive space (including downloaded files).
* The license file.
If VCS is installed
You can use Vericom/Vhdlcom Advanced Mode by setting VCS_HOME to the VCS
installation directory.
% setenv VCS_HOME <VCS_installed_directory>

If VCS is not installed
You need to install Verdi Supplementary package under path such as:
$VERDI_HOME/platform/

Install Verdi first, if you have not installed it
Note:
The images in this chapter are for reference only. The product version shown in
the images may differ from your release version.

1. Enter the basic information.

2. Select the source directory.

3. Select the target directory.

4. Click Next.

5. Select Product VERDI-The Industry Open Debug Platform.

6. Select all platforms.

7. Check the installation configurations, and then click Accept, Install.

Installation is in progress.

Installation is completed.

Install the Verdi Supplementary Package
1. Enter the basic information.

2. Select the source directory.

3. Select the target directory <VERDI_HOME>/platform/.

4.

Install the Verdi Supplementary Package
1. Enter the basic information.

2. Select the source directory.

3. Select the target directory <VERDI_HOME>/platform/.

4. Ignore the following warning message:

5. Select Product VERDI_SUPP.

6. Retain the default settings.

7. Check the installation configurations, and then click Accept, Install.

Installation is completed.

After installation
You will see the folder verdi_supp and a symbolic link as follows:
> ls <VERDI_HOME>/platform/LINUX64/lib/
mtrace Qt tbb vcs verdi_supp

Preface
This guide describes the Verdi supplementary package. The Verdi supplementary
package is for users who do not have VCS installed. After you install it in your Verdi
installation, you can use Vericom/Vhdlcom Advanced Mode.

Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and answers to
frequently asked questions about Synopsys tools. It also provides access to Synopsys
online services, including software downloads, documentation, and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
If prompted, enter your user name and password. If you do not have a Synopsys user
name and password, follow the instructions to sign up for an account.

What is Verdi Supplementary Package?
Verdi Supplementary Package is a special package for the users who do not have VCS
installed. You can use Vericom/Vhdlcom Advanced Mode after installing it inside Verdi
installation.

What is Vericom/Vhdlcom Advanced Mode?
Vericom/Vhdlcom Advanced Mode is for vericom/vhdlcom users to transfer parser to
vlogan with one modification in the compiling script. In Vericom/Vhdlcom Advanced
Mode, you can have privilege of getting support of features up-to-date, and it also
provides better consistency on behaviors between KDB and simulator. You can have
better performance by using Vericom/Vhdlcom Advanced Mode, one benefit is shorter
parsing time, the other important advantage is that you are able to use Verdi Smart Load
and PreLoad capabilities, which reduce lots of memory and loading time especially for a
huge design.

Release Requirement - Prerequisites
It is recommended to use Verdi and VCS (if you can access VCS in your environment)
with versions newer than below:
VCS: T-2022.06-SP2-1 ~ U-2023.03-SP1-1, Linux 64-Bit.

Who Should Download Verdi Supplementary Package?

conditions:

accessibility to VCS).

cannot be updated.

environment is the same as above.
If you have installed VCS or have the access to VCS in your environment, you can directly
use that VCS to execute the Vericom/Vhdlcom Advance Mode, there is no need to
download any extra package in this case.

title: 3 errors Errors found at first pass
text:
Re-Parsing Design with Fault Tolerance

Parsing design file 'test.v'
CPU time: .366 seconds to compile
Passed after re-compile

Limitation and Known Issues
Some syntax errors can prevent scopes from being created successfully.
1. Matching a semicolon (';') across module scopes can remove those scopes from the
skip list. If they also have critical syntax errors, they are not generated.
2. Matching brace ) for ( across module scopes, just like previous, once those module
scopes not in skip list also have vital syntax errors, they are not generated.

3. Matching 'endmodule' for `module' across module scopes, just like previous, once
those module scopes not in skip list also have vital syntax errors, they are not
generated.
4. Errors that cannot be suppressed by vlogan now, here are two examples:
a. IPD (Identifier previously declared)
b. IND (Identifier not declared)

Elaboration and Smart Load

Elaboration and Smart Load
You can use Smart Load after elaboration, smart load can save massive memory and
open design much more quickly especially for a huge design.

Before 2023.03
> setenv NOVAS_EXECUTABLE_ARCH 64
> elabcom -usevcs=adv -lib work
> verdi -usevcs=adv -smart_load_kdb -elab kdb.elab++

After 2023.03
> setenv NOVAS_EXECUTABLE_ARCH 64
> elabcom -usevcs=adv -lib work -top system
> verdi -usevcs=adv -smart_load_kdb -elab kdb.elab++
or
> verdi -usevcs=adv -smart_load_kdb -dbdir simv.daidir

After 2023.03-SP2
> setenv NOVAS_EXECUTABLE_ARCH 32/64
> elabcom -usevcs=adv -lib work -top system
> verdi -usevcs=adv -smart_load_kdb -elab kdb.elab++
or
> verdi -usevcs=adv -smart_load_kdb -dbdir simv.daidir

Elaboration and Smart Load

Elaboration and Smart Load
You can use Smart Load after elaboration, smart load can save massive memory and
open design much more quickly especially for a huge design.

Before 2023.03
> setenv NOVAS_EXECUTABLE_ARCH 64
> elabcom -usevcs=adv -lib work
> verdi -usevcs=adv -smart_load_kdb -elab kdb.elab++

After 2023.03
> setenv NOVAS_EXECUTABLE_ARCH 64
> elabcom -usevcs=adv -lib work -top system
> verdi -usevcs=adv -smart_load_kdb -elab kdb.elab++
or
> verdi -usevcs=adv -smart_load_kdb -dbdir simv.daidir

After 2023.03-SP2
> setenv NOVAS_EXECUTABLE_ARCH 32/64
> elabcom -usevcs=adv -lib work -top system
> verdi -usevcs=adv -smart_load_kdb -elab kdb.elab++
or
> verdi -usevcs=adv -smart_load_kdb -dbdir simv.daidir

Introduction
Overview
The core of Verdi SystemVerilog Testbench (SVTB) Interactive Simulation Debug is a tight
integration with the simulator. This integration enables communication between the Verdi
platform and the simulator. Verdi SVTB Interactive Simulation Debug helps you set up the
simulation environment. You can then bring up Interactive Simulation Debug mode easily
to debug SVTB in the Verdi platform.
The Interactive Simulation Debug solution in the Verdi Automated Debug Platform includes
capabilities for software interactive debugging. These capabilities are especially critical
for SystemVerilog testbench. At its core is a tight integration with the simulator. This
integration enables communication between the Verdi platform and the simulator. After you
set up the simulation environment, you can bring up Interactive Simulation Debug mode
easily. You can then use its features to debug SVTB in the Verdi platform.
The Interactive Simulation Debug solution includes the following advantages:
* Simulation control commands to operate simulation execution.
* Managing Breakpoints for managing the setting and usage of breakpoints.
* Stack and Thread View panes for viewing the call stack and executed threads.
* Watch and Local panes for checking signals, member data, and program variables.
* Class Browser and Object Browser panes for viewing the member data of class and
dynamic objects.
* Constraint debug for analyzing the solver and distribution data.
* Rewind for going back to a specific simulation point.
* Save and Restore session for the convenience of continuing the debug job.
The remaining portion of this document provides further details on how to use these
enhanced functions.

text:
Usage
To use the interactive features, Interactive Simulation Debug mode needs to be enabled
first. The following sections describe how to invoke Interactive Simulation Debug mode.
* Before Invoking Interactive Simulation Debug Mode
* Invoking Verdi Interactive Debug
* Interactive Simulation Debug Mode
* Debugging During Initialization of SystemVerilog Static Functions and Tasks
* Viewing Force/Release Information in Interactive Debug Mode
* Invoking Verdi With Existing Simulation Process

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Before Invoking Interactive Simulation Debug Mode
Before using the Interactive Simulation Debug features, the following criteria must be met:
* Design should include a SystemVerilog testbench. The design under test consists of
Verilog, SystemVerilog, or VHDL. Refer to the VHDL Support appendix for details about
the difference between VHDL and Verilog support.
* You must have a supported VCS simulator as listed in the Supported Platforms section.
* Your Interactive Simulation Debug session focuses on the SVTB portion.
After the above criteria are met, you must generate the simulation executable. Then, set
a couple of environment variables before invoking the Verdi platform and configuring the
Simulation page of the Preferences form. Finally, you are ready to start running Interactive
Debug mode. You can use the SystemVerilog example appended in Appendix A to run
through the features described in this document.

Set Environment Variables
The following environment variables must be set before compilation, elaboration, and
invoking the Verdi platform to enable Interactive Simulation Debug mode.

Before Invoking Interactive Simulation Debug Mode

setenv VCS_HOME <VCS_INST_DIR>
setenv VERDI_HOME <VERDI_INST_DIR>
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/VCS/
<PLATFORM>:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

If the version of VCS you used is prior J-14.12 VCS and your design includes FSDB
dumping commands, you can also set these variables to help facilitate the script:
# Set environment variables for FSDB dumping tasks in design
setenv tab $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/VCS/LINUXAMD64/novas.tab
setenv pli $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/VCS/LINUXAMD64/pli.a

Generate the Simulator Executable
You must generate the simv simulator executable with the command line debugging option
-debug_access+all. For example:
% vcs -sverilog example.sv -debug_access+all <compilation options>

Import SystemVerilog Design and Testbench to Verdi
Import your SystemVerilog design and testbench into the Verdi platform on the Verdi
command line. For example:
% verdi -sv example.sv &

Refer to the Import SystemVerilog Files section of the Verdi and Siloti Command
Reference manual ($VERDI_HOME/doc/reference.pdf) and the Compile and Import
SystemVerilog Code application note for details about importing SystemVerilog code.

Configure Simulation Selection
Invoke the Tools -> Preferences command in the nTrace main window and select the
Simulation page on the Preferences form.
1. Select VCS as the Simulator.
2. Type the full path of the simulator executable in the Executable Path text field.
3. Specify the interactive FSDB file name. The default value is inter.fsdb.
Figure 1

Configure Simulation Selections

Invoking Verdi Interactive Debug

Alternatively, specify the -simType, -simBin, and -simOpt options on the Verdi
command line to specify the simulation options. Refer to the Utilities: verdi
section of the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference manual ($VERDI_HOME/
doc/reference.pdf) for details.

Passing Tcl Commands at Runtime
You can pass Tcl commands from the simv command line using the -verdi_opts "-cmd"
option at runtime. Following is the syntax:
% simv -verdi -verdi_opts "-cmd '<tcl_command>'"

The -cmd option allows you to pass Tcl commands from the simv command line at runtime.
The Tcl commands can be UCLI or Verdi commands.
% simv -verdi -verdi_opts "-cmd 'puts {Hello world}'"

Invoking Verdi Interactive Debug
The following sections describe different ways to invoke Verdi Interactive Debug:
* Launching Simulation and Verdi at the Same Time
* Launching Verdi After Performing Simulation
* Invoking Verdi Using Dbdir
* Handling FSDB_GATE When Invoking Verdi Interactive Mode Using Attach and
Command Line Flows

Launching Simulation and Verdi at the Same Time
You can use either of the following ways to launch the simulation and Verdi at the same
time:
* Using simv Command Line
* Using Verdi Command Line
* Using Verdi GUI

Invoking Verdi Interactive Debug

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Using simv Command Line
In Unified Front End flow, use the -verdi runtime option to run the simulation and enable
Verdi interactive mode. Following is the use model:
% vcs -debug_access+all -kdb [compile options]
% simv -verdi [runtime options] [-verdi_opts
<verdi_options>]

Using Verdi Command Line
In the Unified Front End flow, you can use the -i runtime option to run the simulation and
enable Verdi interactive mode while invoking Verdi. Following is the use model:
% vcs -debug_access+all -kdb [compile options]
% verdi -i [verdi options] -simDelim "[vcs runtime options]"

% vcs -full64 -sverilog -debug_access+all+reverse -kdb=common_elab
-ntb_opts uvm -timescale=1ns/1ns
% verdi -dbdir ./test_simv.daidir -i +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=HIER -simDelim "
+UVM_TESTNAME=test_2m_4s +UVM_TR_RECORD"

Using Verdi GUI
You must use the -debug_access+all and -kdb options at compile time.
Perform the following steps:
1. Invoke Verdi with dbdir as follows:
% verdi -dbdir simv.daidir

2. In the Verdi GUI, click Tools -> Preferences.

Invoking Verdi Interactive Debug

In the Simulation page of the Preferences dialog box, specify simv path and
simulation options as shown in the following figure:
Figure 2

in the toolbar to invoke the Verdi simulator.

Launching Verdi After Performing Simulation
If your simulation is executing, you can enable Verdi Interactive debug by attaching Verdi
to the running simulation using the command line or Verdi GUI.
The following are the three ways to attach Verdi to a running simulation:
* Attaching Verdi to a Running Simulation
* Invoking Verdi Using UCLI Command
To enable these flows, you must specify the -debug_access+all -kdb options
at compile time and -ucli -ucli2Proc options at runtime.

Invoking Verdi Interactive Debug

Attaching Verdi to a Running Simulation
You must use the -attachSim <simv_pid> runtime option to attach Verdi to a simulation
with the Process ID (PID). There is no need to specify the -dbdir option to import the
design.
Example: % verdi -attachSim 16733
You cannot use this option with the following usages while invoking Verdi interactive mode:
* simv -verdi
* verdi -i
* start_verdi in ucli2Proc mode

Invoking Verdi Using UCLI Command
You must use the -start_verdi UCLI command as follows to launch Verdi in UCLI mode:
ucli% start_verdi

Invoking Verdi Using Dbdir
You can invoke Verdi with dbdir and then attach Verdi to a selected simulation using Verdi
GUI command as follows:
1. In Verdi GUI, select the Simulation -> Attach to Simulationcommand to open the
Attach to Simulation dialog box.
2. In the Attach to Simulation dialog box, select a simulation process and click Attach.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Handling FSDB_GATE When Invoking Verdi Interactive Mode
Using Attach and Command Line Flows
Attach Flow
The Attach flow attaches Verdi to the simulation process. In this flow, the simulation
provides the FSDB_GATE setting. By default, this setting is enabled when the dump signal is
simv. You can use the setenv FSDB_GATE 0 command to disable the default FSDB_GATE
setting.
Verdi also provides the Enable FSDB Gate preference option (Preferences ->
Simulation) to disable the FSDB_GATE setting; you must clear the checkbox of this option
to disable the setting. However, a simulation restart is required to use the preference
setting to disable FSDB_GATE.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Command Line Flow
This flow invokes Verdi interactive mode while executing simv in the command line.
In this flow, the FSDB_GATE setting keeps the original behavior. That is, FSDB_GATE is autodisabled when invoking Verdi interactive mode.
You can use the setenv INT_FSDB_GATE 1 command to enable the FSDB_GATE setting
in the interactive mode in the command line flow. Verdi also provides the Enable FSDB
Gate preference option (Preferences -> Simulation) to enable the FSDB_GATE setting;
you must select the checkbox of this option to enable the setting. However, a simulation
restart is required to use the preference setting to enable FSDB_GATE.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Interactive Simulation Debug Mode
After loading your SystemVerilog design and testbench, select the Tools -> Run
Simulation command to start Interactive Simulation Debug mode.
Figure 3

Interactive Simulation Debug Mode in Verdi Platform

Debugging During Initialization of SystemVerilog Static Functions and Tasks

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The following panes can be viewed in the Interactive Simulation Debug Mode:
* The Interactive Toolbar places the simulation command buttons. The Interactive
Browser provides the testbench architecture view.
* The Local tab automatically shows the local information in the current simulation scope.
The Member tab shows the member data of the object.
* The Interactive Console pane provides the interface to input the UCLI commands. It
shows the results of simulator execution. You can change the text font of the Interactive
Console pane in the Source Code -> Color/Font page of the Preferences form
(invoked with the Tools ' Preferences command).
* You can add variables, signals, or objects to a Watch tab of the Watch pane. This pane
contains one Watch tab by default. The maximum number of Watch tabs that you can
add using the Debug -> Add New Watch command is five.
* The simulator status is shown in the Status bar. You can place the cursor over the
Stopped field of the Status bar and hold for a couple of seconds to display a tip
window.
All Interactive Debug panes support partial match (the default setting), whole words,
regular expression, and wildcard. The find and filter functionality synchronizes with
Preferences > General> Find/Filter > Find/Filter Options. For more information, see
the Find/Filter Page section in Preference chapter of the Verdi(R) and Siloti(R) Command
Reference Guide. You can modify the match case behavior flowing from the Preferences
window by selecting the Match Case option.
Unless explicitly listed, the In All Columns preference is not supported for the Interactive
Debug panes. Only specified columns are filtered, typically Name, Scope, or Hierarchy.
Other columns remain sortable but not filterable.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Debugging During Initialization of SystemVerilog Static
Functions and Tasks
You can enable debugging when initialization begins for static SystemVerilog tasks and
functions in module definitions. Use the -ucli=init runtime option as follows:
% simv -verdi -ucli=init

This debugging capability enables you to set breakpoints during initialization.
During initialization (init mode), the -ucli=init runtime option does not support the
features mentioned in the Limitations section.

Debugging During Initialization of SystemVerilog Static Functions and Tasks

When you click the run button in the init mode, Verdi executes run0 first and then the run
command. The run0 execution runs through and exits the initialization mode. Therefore,
the FSDB file is created when the initialization mode finishes at time 0.

The following are the limitations of the -ucli=init runtime option:
* FSDB commands
* The change and value commands
* Rewind/Reverse Debug
* Save/Restore simulator states
* Dumping mechanism. For example,
If you input run 100 and the init mode is exited, then the FSDB file is created at
time 50 if there are dumping tasks in the design at that time. The FSDB is empty
during time 0~50. In addition, the environment variable FILE_NAME determines the
FSDB filename. Verdi sets this variable when you enter interactive mode.
If you input run 100 and the init mode is exited, and there are no dumping
tasks during this period, then Verdi creates the FSDB file at time 100. It uses the
fsdbDumpfiles command. The FILE_NAME and fsdbDumpfiles command use the
same filename in the above scenarios. The only difference is when the FSDB file is
created.
Verdi disables the user interface for the above restricted features in interactive mode, as
shown in the following figures. It also disables FSDB-based features (for example, dump
command, fsdbDumpvars, and so on). These features are enabled only after you exit the
init mode.
Figure 4

Run the simulation as follows:

or,

% simv -verdi -force_list=uniqueID

Invoking Verdi With Existing Simulation Process
You can use the -attachSim <sim_pid> option to invoke Verdi with an attached
simulation mode. This feature provides a simplified way to attach Verdi to the simulation
without the need to specify the -dbdir option in the same machine. The dbdir is
automatically obtained by Verdi connecting to the running VCS simulation using the
process ID, pid.
Following is the syntax:
% verdi -attachSim < sim_pid >
<sim_pid>: The simulation process ID which you want to attach.

Invoking Verdi With Existing Simulation Process

This option cannot be applied with the following usages while invoking Verdi interactive
mode:
* simv -verdi
* verdi -i
* In ucli2Proc mode, start_verdi
Key Points to Note
* Use the -debug_access+all VCS elaboration option to enable the VCS debug
features.
* The simulation must start with the -ucli -ucli2Proc VCS runtime option.
* The Restart and Restore session commands are not supported in Verdi after the
simulation is attached.
* The design used in the simulation is used for invoking Verdi, and not to specify another
design for the Verdi command.
* Using Ctrl+Z to suspend a simv process and then trying to attach Verdi to the
simulation is not supported.
* The -attachSim option supports only the following additional options in the Verdi
command line:
-Apex, -Base, -Elite, -SX, -Ultra, -apex, -base, -lca, -rcFile, and -play

Simulation Control and Local/Watch Variables
Observation
The simulation control commands are provided to control the simulation progress and
the Local and Watch tabs are used to observe the program execution and to trace
data changes. You can also use the Manage Breakpoints to control the simulation stop
locations with more variability and flexibility.

* Simulation Control Commands
* Local Tab

Simulation Control Commands
The Interactive toolbar lists the frequently used simulation control commands. These
commands direct how the simulator executes the program, as shown in the following
figure. Other commands appear in the Simulation menu. For example, the Kill Simulator
Process command is in that menu.
Figure 11

Simulation Control Commands in Toolbar

Use the Step command to advance the simulation to the statement where a function is
called. Click the Step button in the toolbar, or select the Simulation -> Step command.
The Local and Watch tabs refresh accordingly.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
To avoid confusion, simulation commands are allowed only when the simulator is not busy.
Therefore, if the simulator is running, only the Simulation -> Stop and Simulation -> Kill
Simulator Process commands are enabled. All other simulator related commands are
disabled.
When the simulation finishes, Verdi does not exit Interactive Simulation Debug mode. It
keeps the data in each frame. Use the Simulation -> Quit or Tools -> Stop Simulation
commands to exit Interactive Simulation Debug mode.
Refer to the Simulation Commands section of the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference
manual ($VERDI_HOME/doc/reference.pdf) for details about the simulation commands.
Refer to the Constraint Debug section for details about the constraints commands.

When the Next or Step simulation control commands are used and the scope of the
current simulation belongs to a testbench scope or defined class object, all variables of the
current simulation scope are shown automatically in the Local tab. Variables in the Local
tab include the following categories:
* this: Represents the current class object. It is displayed only when the simulation stops
inside a class object scope. The object ID and all member data are listed under the
"this" node.
* Local variables: All local variables in the current scope are displayed, including
function arguments, interface class objects, and constraints.
* Arguments: All arguments of the method are displayed if the simulation stops inside a
function or task.

* Global Variables: If the global variables are defined in the program, then they are

* Package: The imported packages for the current scope are displayed. You can expand
a package node to see the global variables under this package.

The annotation values are based on the cursor time in the active nWave window. The

* If the cursor time in the nWave window does not equal to the current simulation time,

Stopping the Simulator After Covergroup Sampling
You can use the Verdi GUI or the supported simulator commands to set a breakpoint or
stop point after a covergroup samples data. This allows you to pause the simulation and
inspect the coverage state immediately after sampling.
The exact method to set a stop point may depend on your simulator and
integration with Verdi.
* Stopping the Simulator Using UCLI Commands
* Stopping the Simulator Using the Verdi GUI
Stopping the Simulator Using UCLI Commands
To set a breakpoint for a covergroup, use the following commands:
stop -cov_inst <covergroup_instance_name>
stop -cov_defn <covergroup_definition_name>

Stopping the Simulator Using the Verdi GUI

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Verdi GUI
Stopping the Simulator Using UCLI Commands
To set a breakpoint for a covergroup, use the following commands:
stop -cov_inst <covergroup_instance_name>
stop -cov_defn <covergroup_definition_name>

Stopping the Simulator Using the Verdi GUI
To set a breakpoint for a covergroup using the Verdi GUI, do the following:
1. Right-click the covergroup definition or instance in the Member pane and click Set
Breakpoint.
2. Go to the Covergroup tab of the Manage Breakpoints form.

Figure 52

Covergroup Tab of Manage Breakpoints

3. In the Break after Sampling section, choose of the following:
All Instances of Covergroup Definition: Enter the covergroup type name.
This applies the breakpoint to all instances of a given covergroup definition.
Specified Covergroup Instance: Enter the hierarchical instance path.
This targets one specific covergroup instance.
4. Select Dump Coverage Database on Trigger if you want the simulator to write out the
coverage database at the moment the breakpoint hits.
5. In the Condition field, specify an optional conditional expression.
Breakpoint triggers only if this condition evaluates to true.

6. Select one of the Stop Frequency options: Once or Repeat.
7. In the Skip field, specify the number of matching events to skip before stopping.
8. Click Update.
When the breakpoint is triggered, the simulator dumps the coverage database
automatically. The breakpoint works not only for procedural sample() function call, but
also for event-triggered sample() function call.
After the simulation finishes, the correct covergroup definition or instance name
cannot be found.

covergroup instance that has not been sampled.

Changing the Radix of Data Member
Verdi applies the following changes if you change the radix for a data member of the
selected object:
* Applies the radix change for the selected data member.
* Applies the radix change for the selected data member of other objects instantiated
from the same class.
For example, consider the following code:
class A;
{
int mem_a;
int mem_b;
}

If there are three objects instantiated from class A, for example, p.A@1, p.A@2, and p.A@3.
If you change the radix for p.A@1.mem_a to binary, then Verdi changes the radixes of
p.A@2.mem_a and p.A@3.mem_a to binary. However, the radix of p.A@1.mem_b is not
changed to binary.

Support for Radix and Value Format Synchronization in Different
Views
Verdi supports radix and value format synchronization for the signals or testbench
variables that are not dumped to FSDB across all views (nSchema, nTrace, signal list,
nWave, Local Pane, Watch Pane, and Member Pane).
The radix type of the DUT signals is synchronized across all views.
For a testbench variable, the radix type is synchronized across all views except nWave.
That is, the testbench variable displayed in nWave does not synchronize with other views.

Change Sequence to Query Value When Cursor Time Equals Simulation Time

For a testbench variable, radix setting is stored based on the class. Therefore, all objects
of that class have the same radix for the member variable.

Change Sequence to Query Value When Cursor Time Equals
Simulation Time
When cursor time equals simulation time, Verdi initially queries the annotation value from
the simulator and then from the FSDB.

HDL Example

module memory (
input wire read,
input wire write,
input wire [7:0] data_in,
input wire [3:0] address,
output reg [7:0] data_out
);
reg [7:0] mem [0:15];
always @ (*)
begin
if (write) mem[address] = data_in;
end
always @ (read, address)
begin
if (read) data_out = mem[address];
end
endmodule

Depth to dump the two levels of signals for the active scope and so on. You can set
"All" in the Depth field to dump the instance to the FSDB file.
Figure 95

Dump Options

The data types of memory, MDA, packed array, structure, union, and packed structure
signals can be disabled from dumping by turning off the All option to get better
performance and prevent a larger waveform size. You can also enable the signal
categories in the Dump Options field to dump the specified signal types in the scope.

Dumping Dynamic Objects
Dumping objects and data members to an FSDB file is also available. You can directly
select a variable from the Class, Object, Member, Watch, or Local tabs and drag and drop
the variable to the nWave window with the loaded FSDB file. This dumps the variable to
inter.fsdb FSDB file and add it to the nWave window (refer to the following figure). When
the select variable is a class object, the value of the added variable will be the value of the
class pointer.

Dumping Dynamic Objects

Figure 96

Object Dumping Including Data Member

After adding objects to the nWave window, double-click the object to expand it and see
its member data (refer to the figure above). If there is a data member with class type, you
can add it as an individual variable in the nWave window. As shown in the following figure,
right-click the variable in the waveform and use the Add Object command to add this
object to the nWave window.
Figure 97

Directly Add Object in nWave

After adding the data member with class type, you can expand it as the added object
described above.

Dump Batch Signals

Dump Batch Signals
You can restore signals from the saved .rc file to automatically dump all batch signals in
one time and then add them in the nWave window automatically as follows:
* In an opened nWave window with a loaded inter.fsdb file, use the File -> Restore
Signal command to open the Restore Signal form
* Select a saved .rc file and click the OK button to load this file
After the .rc file is loaded to the nWave window, all the signals saved in the .rc file is
dumped to the FSDB file and added to the nWave window.
Dumping batch signals does not support novas.rc file. You need to save a .rc
file in the nWave window.

Restart
You can use the Simulation -> Restart command to restart the current simulation. After
invoking the Restart command, the following actions are restarted:
* Setting breakpoints.
* Dumping and adding signals in the nWave window (the signals that were previously
dumped into the inter.fsdb file are automatically dumped after restarting the
simulation).
* Issue force commands for HDL signals.
Only the force commands issued for HDL signals are applied. The force
commands from script files or Interactive Console pane are ignored.
In the Interactive Debug-> Restart page of the Preferences form (invoked with the Tools
-> Preferences command), you can also disable the options (refer to the following figure)
before restarting simulation to disable restart of these actions.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Chapter 9: Rebuild and Restart

Figure 98

Restart Options

These settings for restart options are applied after invoking the Restart
command.

When your design is modified, you can use the rebuild and restart features to rebuild the
KDB and the simv simulator executable in the Interactive Simulation Debug mode by using
the VCS script or your own custom script. Meanwhile, you can decide whether to restart
the simulation after the design rebuilt. After rebuilding the KDB and the simv simulator
executable, the KDB can be loaded automatically.
Invoke the Rebuild and Restart form by using the Simulation -> Rebuild and Restart
command to specify the configurations of rebuild and restart features.

Chapter 9: Rebuild and Restart

Figure 99

Rebuild and Restart Configurations

Where,
* Rebuild KDB and simv: Verdi uses the specified method to rebuild the KDB and the
simv simulator executable files.
* Load KDB after Design Rebuild: Verdi uses the specified method to load the KDB
after the design is rebuilt.
* Restart Simulator after Design Rebuild: When the option is enabled, Verdi restarts
the simulation after the design is rebuilt and loaded.
After completing the setting of the configuration, click OK. Verdi performs the following
actions:
1. Rebuild the KDB and the simv simulator executable files.
2. Load the KDB.
3. If the Restart Simulator after Design Rebuild option is enabled, restart the
simulation.

Chapter 9: Rebuild and Restart

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
After the simulation is rebuilt and restarted, the GUI layouts and the following data of
Interactive Simulation Debug mode is restored:
* The objects dumped in the FSDB file
* The breakpoint commands, force and release commands, and signals shown in the
nWave window.
This feature can be controlled in the Interactive Debug -> Restart page
(refer to the Restart section for details).
Limitation
* Rebuild and Restart flow is not supported for Mixed Signal Verification flow.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Configurations of Rebuild KDB and simv
You can enable the Use Custom Command to Rebuild option and type the rebuild
command directly in the field to rebuild the KDB and the simv simulator executable files.

The current working directory is used by default. If you want to run the rebuild commands
in another directory, you can specify the path in the Run Command in Directory field.

When you have your own custom script file, you can also enable this option and use the
script file to perform the rebuild.

Chapter 9: Rebuild and Restart

It is recommended to include only the compile and elaborate commands in the
scripts.
VCS generates the vcs_rebuild rebuild script (located in the simv.daidir/vcs_rebuild
path) automatically when VCS is invoked each time. You can use the commands recorded
in this file to rebuild the KDB and the simv simulator executable files by enabling the Use
Script Generated by VCS to Rebuild option.

The Use Script Generated by VCS to Rebuild method is recommended for
Verilog-only single-VCS compilation flows. It does not support UUM, MX, slave
mode, or multi-step builds. For complex compilation script, UUM, MX or multistep builds, use the Use Custom Command to Rebuild method.

Configurations of Load KDB after Design Rebuild
You can use one of the following toggle options in the Rebuild and Restart form to load the
KDB:

* Reload: When this option is enabled, the options which were used previously to load
the KDB are used to reload the KDB. This option is enabled by default.
* Load KDB from 'simv.kdb' Generated by VCS: If your KDB file is generated by the
Unified Compiler front-end flow, this option is provided to load the KDB with the options
generated in the simv.kdb file.

Chapter 9: Rebuild and Restart

* Use Custom Command: You can use custom commands or a script file to load the
KDB.
If files are added from your design, you need to use new import commands
or a new script to import those files.

Configurations of Restart Simulator after Design Rebuild
You can enable the Restart Simulator after Design Rebuild option to restart the
simulation in Verdi Interactive Simulation Debug mode after the design is rebuilt. The
option is enabled by default.

You can enable the Restart Simulator after Design Rebuild option to restart the
simulation in Interactive Simulation Debug mode after the design is rebuilt. The option is
enabled by default.

Save/Restore Simulation Session/State
During Interactive Simulation Debug mode, the Verdi platform provides the following two
types of save and restore features to save the currently ongoing debugging process or
restoring the point to continue the unfinished debugging process:
* Save/Restore Session
* Save/Restore State

Save/Restore Session
Verdi allows you to save the current state of debugging process of Verdi (that is, display
layout and design database) and restore the saved session file with a different design and
different simv, KDB, and FSDB information in both interactive and post-processing debug
mode.
The following sections describe this feature in detail:
* Saving a Session or Layout
* Restoring the Saved Session

Saving a Session or Layout
You can save the current state of debugging process of Verdi, that is, display layout and
design database path options, using the Save Session dialog box. The options that you
select in the Save Session dialog box are restored after you restart Verdi.

Chapter 11: Save/Restore Simulation Session/State
Save/Restore Session

To save a session,
1. Select File -> Save Session to open the Save Session dialog box, as shown in the
following figure:
Figure 111

Save Session Dialog Box

In the post-processing mode, you must click the Advanced button to view the
advanced settings.
2. To specify the file name, enter a file name in the File Name field or browse for the file
in your directory. The default file name is Verdi.ses.
The session (.ses) resource file stores the current Verdi information to restore window
layout, current scopes, current design, viewing options, and bookmarks. For more
information about the session file, refer to the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference
Manual.
3. Select the Save Open Database Information option if you want to save the design
database (KDB) and FSDB to the session file. By default, this option is disabled in the
interactive mode and saves only GUI status according to the Save Window Options
setting. This option is enabled by default in the post-processing mode.
The Save Simulation State option is the sub-option of the Save Open Database
Information option. This option allows you to save the simulation state to the session
file and restore it when restoring the saved session. This option is enabled only when
the Save Open Database Information option is enabled. You can clear the Save
Simulation State check box to disable this option.

Chapter 11: Save/Restore Simulation Session/State
Save/Restore Session

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
If the Save Open Database Information option is disabled or not selected, the design
database information is not saved to the session file. The restore session can be
restored with a different design, simv, FSDB and KDB. For more information, see
Disabling Database Information.
4. Select any of the following path option from the Path Option list box:
Absolute Paths -- (Default) Specifies fully qualified path for opened design database.
This allows you to reload the session file from any location, but if you move the
simulation directory, the session file does not work.
Relative Paths -- Specifies path for opened design databases (relative to the directory
where the session file is stored) or interactive design. If you move the simulation
directory, the session file still works.
5. Select any of the following window option from the options specified under the Save
Window Options section:
All Windows -- Saves the layout and contents of all windows in the current Verdi
session to the session file. The restore session restores all windows to be same as the
saved session. If the Save Simulation State option is not enabled, then the contents
of the Stack pane, Local pane, Member pane, Object view, and Constraint view are not
restored.
Single Window -- Saves the layout and contents of only a single window in the
session file and restores it in the restore session. This option is supported only for the
single waveform window. All opened waveform views are listed in the list box located in
this section. You can choose a waveform view to save from this list box.
6. Click OK to save the session.
You can place the mouse pointer over an option to view its information in a tool tip.
Disabling Database Information
If you disable the Save Open Database Information option, the design database
information is not saved to the session file. The restore session can be restored with a
different design, simv, FSDB and KDB. The following points describe this flow:
* Simulation state is not restored in this flow
* If you select the All Windows option, the content of all windows except the Stack
pane, Local pane, Member pane, Object view, and Constraint view is restored.
* If you select the Single Window option, the layout and content of the selected
waveform view is restored.

To restore the saved session,
1. Select File -> Restore Session to open the Restore Session dialog box, as shown in
the following figure:
Figure 112

2. Select a saved session and click OK.

for gate-level designs. The FSDB file is also restored, and the signals that were dumped
continue to be dumped to the FSDB file.

Constraint Debug
The Verdi platform provides the Constraints Solver engine for randomization. You can
analyze a randomized call after randomization finishes and before post-randomization
runs.
Constraints Solver is a complex engine in VCS simulation. Good debug capabilities
can greatly enhance your efficiency. Better debug capabilities help you understand the
constraints. They also help you see how a randomized call was solved, where inefficiency
comes from, and why a solver failed during Interactive Simulation Debug mode.
The Constraint Debug features are listed and described in the following sections:
* Display the constraints and random variables information in the Local pane. The
Constraint Mode and Random Mode can be enabled and disabled in the Local pane.
* Display the static constraint information in the Member pane.
* Constraint breakpoints can be set and the simulation control command is provided to
step into Constraint Debug mode.
* Show details about how the constraints were solved in the Solver tab. Show the
relationship between the variables in the Relation tab.
* Re-randomization is supported.
* Interactive rewind is supported.
* Distribution Debug is supported.
* Add new constraints on-the-fly from the Local tab.
The Name column of the Solver, Relation, Dropped_Reason, Dist_R, and Histogram_R
tabs are filterable. Other columns support only sorting.

Breakpoint Management
To be able to stop the simulation before any or certain randomize calls (for example,
obj.randomize();), the breakpoint can be set by double-clicking the line where
randomize is called (refer to the following figure) or in the Constraints page of the
Breakpoints form (invoked with the Debug -> Manage Breakpoints command).
Figure 123

Set Breakpoint for randomization

As shown in the following figure, the Break at Solver Serial field maps to the -serial
UCLI option, the Executing Frequency: Once option maps to the -once option, the

Breakpoint Management

Class Name field maps to the -class option and the Solver Condition field maps to the
-solver_cond option for the stop -solver command.
Figure 124

Set Breakpoint for Randomization in Breakpoints Form

* You can use the Active Random Object option in Verdi to allow the randomization to
stop when the randomize() method is called from the object derived from the specified
class or from the object that contains the embedded objects of the specified class type.
Use the -random_objects option along with the -class option in the stop -solver
UCLI command as shown in the following command:
stop -solver [-random_objects] [-class <class_name>]

The -random_objects option extends the -class functionality to match class names
in the set of objects that are to be randomized as a whole. The matching of class
names starts with the object that invoked the randomize() method. These class
objects are referred as the active random objects.
* In the Expression field, type the expression for the -solver_cond option. If the
expression specified by -solver_cond option is evaluated as true, then the breakpoint
is hit when any random variable of the specified class is solved.
* The Inconsistency option button represents the -inconsistency option. If you select
the Inconsistency option button, the breakpoint is hit when inconsistent constraints
are detected during randomization.

The Verdi platform lets you re-randomize multiple times after you step into the Constraint
Solver. You can then check the distribution of random variable values in a histogram. This
feature helps you understand the constraint behavior and find potential debug issues.

Distribution Re-randomized Analysis

Figure 144

Distribution Histogram

Refer to the following figure and the following explanation to analyze the histogram.
1. The variable name is displayed on the top, and its initial value is marked below the
variable name.
2. The range of the initial value is the union of the initial value ranges from N times (the
specified number) randomizations.
3. The number of values during each interval is marked at the top of the bar, if the number
is zero, it is highlighted in red.
4. By default, there are 10 columns or less if the interval is "1" already.
5. The Max value is equal to:
min_value + interval * number_of_columns

6. You can specify the min/max and interval in the respective fields on the top. Click the
Apply button, the histogram is re-plotted with the new attributes.
7. The current radix is displayed.
You can use the Reset button to re-plot the default histogram.

Reverse Debug
The following sections describe the Verdi Reverse Debug feature in Interactive Simulation
Debug Mode:
* Introduction
* Use Model
* Reverse Debug Commands
* Checkpoint Distribution
* Checkpoint Memory Profiling
* Reverse Debug Support for VHDL
* Limitations

Introduction
The reverse debug features of Interactive Simulation Debug in Verdi support interactive
debugging.
You can run the simulation backwards.
You can start debugging at the symptom of the problem. Then go back in time along the
bug propagation cause-effect chain. The divide-and-conquer debugging method is more
efficient with reverse debugging.
reverse debugging

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
For example, the simulation might stop before a function call. If you are unsure whether
the function returns the correct value, step over this function call and check the returned
result. If the result is wrong, perform the Reverse Next command. Then step into the
function and investigate what causes the wrong result. Without reverse debugging, you
must restart debugging. You must also use breakpoints to reach the same simulation
state. That process is costly.
reverse debuggingreverse next

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Following are the VCS simulation control commands for reverse executing simulation in
Verdi:
reverse debuggingsimulation control commands for reverse executing simulation

* Run/Continue Reverse
* Next Reverse
* Step Reverse
* Step Out Reverse
* Step in Thread Reverse
* Step in Testbench Reverse
* Next in Thread Reverse
You can also reverse or advance the simulation to the previous or next value assignment
of a signal or variable. Invoke a command for the selected signal or variable. For a DUT
design, dump all signals and use the traced information to figure out where to go. For a
testbench, this approach does not work. The feature should also work without all signals
traced. You can use this feature to go to the desired assignment of the object.
In addition, Verdi provides the Undo Last Simulation Control command. Use it to
quickly undo recent simulation execution commands, such as Run, Next, and Step. Verdi
also provides the Redo Last Simulation Control command to redo the corresponding
command.
The following sections provide a detailed description of these features:
* Prerequisites
* Use Model
* Limitations

Prerequisites
VCS is a prerequisite for these Reverse Debug features in Interactive Simulation Debug
mode. You must use the -debug_access+reverse VCS elaboration option. Enable
Interactive Simulation Debug mode only after you set this option.
reverse debugging-debug_access+all+reverse

These sections explain how to enable Reverse Debug features.

Before Invoking Verdi Interactive Simulation Debug Mode
You must generate the simv simulator executable with the -debug_access+reverse
debug option on the VCS command line. For example:
% vcs -sverilog example.sv -debug_access+reverse -kdb=common_elab
<compilation/elaboration options>

* Refer to the VCS User Guide for details about the -debug_access+reverse
simulation option.
* If you use interactive mode but set only -debug_access or -debug_access
+all (both without +reverse), Verdi Advisor turns on and flashes for about
1 minute. Click the Advisor icon to see the suggestion.

Enabling Verdi Reverse Interactive Simulation Debug Mode
You can invoke Verdi Interactive Simulation Debug mode by using the following command:
% simv -verdi

Using Reverse Simulation Control Commands
The reverse simulation control commands provide the ability to move to an earlier
simulation state from the current interactive simulation debugging. All commands bring

the simulation back in time to the completely functional execution state with full visibility.
The information of Interactive Simulation Debug frames (for example, the Local and Object
tabs, and so on) is reversed and updated accordingly.
As shown in the following figures, you can use the commands by clicking the command
icons or selecting them from the Simulation command menu to direct the simulator how to
reverse execute the program.

Using Undo and Redo Last Simulation Control Command
By using the Undo Last Simulation Control command, you can quickly undo effect of the
most recent simulation execution command(s) (for example, Run, Next, or Step, and so
on). For example, after you executed the Run command and the simulation stopped at a
certain breakpoint. If you want to go back to the simulation state as it was before the Run
command, use the Undo Last Simulation Control command as shown in the following

The Undo Last Simulation Control command is not fully supported in following
situations:
* When command execution is in VHDL code
* When simulation is stopped inside certain breakpoints (for example, constraint solver
or assertion breakpoint). In this case, the simulation goes to the most recently executed
source code line before the desired location. The Undo Last Simulation Control
command cannot go back to the desired execution location exactly.
To ensure the Undo Last Simulation Control command work in the above situations,
enable automatic checkpoint creation at each simulation stop with the following step:
1. Select the Interactive Debug -> Reverse Debug page from the Preferences form
opened by the Tools -> Preferences command.

Active Point Behavior
The active point is a checkpoint that is automatically created at the latest available
simulation time before going back in time. The active point allows the user to jump back to
the latest simulation time from the past.

After the active point is created automatically, whether the user run the simulation without
specifying the time or with a specified time that is later than the time of the active point, the
simulation stops upon reaching the active point.

Discarding Future Simulator Status
The Discard Future command is added to the Simulation menu. Use this command to
destroy future simulator status, including FSDB truncation.
Figure 159

Discard Future

The following actions issue a warning message. The message reminds you to select the
Discard Future command:
* Drag signals to nWave
If drag-and-drop signals are already dumped, adds them to nWave. No message is
issued in this case.
If drag-and-drop signals are not dumped, a message dialog saying Can't dump
signal `sig_name', please run `Discard Future' command and repeat the last
operation is issued.
If some drag-and-drop signals are already dumped and some are not, Verdi adds
the dumped signals. It issues a message similar to the one above for the signals
that are not dumped.

* Right-click menu commands like Add to Waveform or Add Object to waveform in
different views.
* File -> Restore Signals from nWave
* You might issue commands from Interactive Console in the past that can change future
simulator status. In that case, the console shows a message. The message asks you to
run `Discard Future' and issue the command again.
Following is the syntax to use the Discard Future command from the Interactive Console:
srcTBDiscardFuture - Discards future simulation status.

Discarding Future Automatically
You might run a simulation command in the past that can change future simulator status.
Examples include force, dump, constraint, or assertion. If so, the following message is
displayed:
Discard simulation status in future?

If you select Yes, Verdi automatically allows you to discard future status.
If you select No, Verdi cancels your command that can change future simulation status.
The following right-click menu options allow you to automatically discard future:
* Dump to FSDB/Dump in the Source Code frame, Local frame, Watch frame, Member
frame, and instance tree
* Force Signal in the Source Code frame
* Change value in Local frame/Watch frame
* Set Constraint Mode in Local frame/Watch frame
* assert on/off/kill in the nWave, nTrace and related dialogs

Saving and Restoring Session
When invoking the File -> Save Session command, turn on the Enable Reverse Debug
on Restore Session option to save all the needed data to enable reverse debug after
restoring a session.

Figure 160

Enable Reverse Debug on Restore Session in Save Session Form

Depending on the simulation memory footprint and runtime length, turn on the
Enable Reverse Debug on Restore Session option can take significant disk
space.
The Restore Session form, opened by the File -> Restore Session command, allows
to restore a saved session. If the session is saved with reverse debug enabled, it will
automatically restore all needed data.
After restoring a session, you can use all reverse debug features in the same way as in
Interactive debug.
There might be some initial wait time as data is loaded incrementally as needed
from disk.
The VCS version used to save and restore a session must be the same. Mixed
simulation versions are not allowed.

UCLI Save and Restore Session
Saving and Restoring
The UCLI checkpoint command supports saving and restoring with checkpoints.
Use the following UCLI command line to save and restore a session:
checkpoint
[ -save -session <name>] |
[ -save_add <checkpoint id> -session <name> ] |
[ -restore -session <name>]

Where, <checkpoint id> is the checkpoint number, allowing to save an individual
checkpoint to a session. To obtain a list of all existing checkpoints and their IDs, execute
the checkpoint -list command.
The default directory for a saved session is the current directory. All data is located in the
<name> and <name>.data files, and in the <name>.checkpoints directory.
To save/restore session to a different directory, specify a relative or an absolute path as a
<name>.
checkpoint
checkpoint
checkpoint
checkpoint

-save -session ./test/session1.cpdb
-save -session ~/temp/session1.cpdb
-restore -session ./test/session1.cpdb
-restore -session ~/temp/session1.cpdb

text:
Specifying Compression Level of a Save Session
You can use the following configuration setting to specify compression level when saving
checkpoints to a session:
config checkpointcompression [high | medium | low]

Default is low, which means faster runtime. When running in batch mode, if runtime is not
important, you can use high or medium to reduce disk space consumption.

Adding Virtual Checkpoints to a Session
VCS allows you to add virtual checkpoint to a session. You can create a real checkpoint
before UVM error and a virtual checkpoint at UVM error, then you can directly rewind to
UVM error and start debugging from it. Since it is a virtual checkpoint, VCS rewinds to
real checkpoint before UVM error and re-executes to the exact point where UVM error
occurred. Virtual checkpoints have little memory overhead at the expense that rewind to
them might take some more time.

To add virtual checkpoints to a session, use the following commands in your scripts:
* Add the new -virtual option to the checkpoint -add command. Following is the
syntax:
checkpoint -add [<description>] -virtual

This command creates a virtual checkpoint even if reverse debug is not enabled
and also if there is no checkpoint available before. The only requirement is that step
counter should be enabled at this point of time. Step counter is enabled as soon as a
first checkpoint is created (or reverse debug is enabled).
* Save virtual checkpoints to the session using checkpoint -save_add command.
Example
set count 1
run 900ns
# Create a real checkpoint some time before UVM error.
set id [checkpoint -add "before UVM error #$count"]
checkpoint -save_add $id -session test
checkpoint -kill $id
stop -uvm error
run
# Create a virtual checkpoint at UVM error.
set id [checkpoint -add "UVM error #$count" -virtual]
checkpoint -save_add $id -session test
checkpoint -kill $id
repeat for other time stamps

After restore, you can see the checkpoints in Verdi GUI:
1: "before UVM error #1"
2: "UVM error #1"

You can now directly rewind to UVM Error #1 and start debugging from it. Since it is a
virtual checkpoint, the tool rewinds to real checkpoint before UVM error #1 and reexecutes to the exact point where UVM error occurred.

Support for Debug Points
VCS allows you to specify the simulation events (for example, UVM error or fatal
messages) as special kind of checkpoints called "debug points" in the simulation. Autocheckpoint and session save handles the real checkpoints (a special checkpoint created
at the current simulation end before executing the reverse command) created before a
debug point in a special way to make sure rewind to the debug point is fast after session
restore. As a result, the time to start debugging after session restore can be reduced
significantly for long running simulations. The debug points are shown in Verdi GUI as
usual checkpoints and you can easily rewind to them.

Also, to prioritize debug points in a saved session (and to protect against exceeding disk
quota), you can specify maximum disk space to be occupied by the saved session.
The following sections describe the debug points feature in detail:
* Creating Debug Points
* Creating Debug Points Automatically
* Creating User-Defined Debug Points
* Breakpoints on UVM Error and Fatal Messages
* Limiting the Size of a Save Session
* Debug Point Prioritization

Creating Debug Points
To create a new debug point, use the -debug_point option with the UCLI checkpoint
command. Following is the syntax:
checkpoint -add "error_type" -debug_point

checkpoint -add "UVM Error" -debug_point

To allow fast rewind to a debug point, some real checkpoint must be kept close before it.
If the real checkpoint is too far away from the debug point, then initial rewind to the debug
point takes much time. If it is too close, then the debug range is reduced accordingly. The
following new configuration setting allows you to specify how far away (in seconds) a real
checkpoint must be kept before debug point:
config debugpointinterval 10

Default time is 10 seconds, that is, a real checkpoint should be kept at least 10 seconds
before debug point.
The checkpoints reserved for the debug points are taken from the checkpoints specified
for auto-checkpoint (config checkpointgenerate, by default 40). Therefore, it is
required to limit the number of debug points. The following new configuration setting
allows you to specify the number of debug points (default is 5):
config debugpoints 5

You cannot use more than N-2 debug points, where N is the number of automatic
checkpoints.

Creating Debug Points Automatically
VCS automatically creates checkpoints when UVM error or fatal message is produced
(when config uvmerrorcheckpoints on).
This functionality is enhanced to create checkpoints as "debug points" automatically. The
name of the configuration variable is changed to:
config uvmdebugpoints on

For backward compatibility, old usage is allowed:
config uvmerrorcheckpoints on

Creating User-Defined Debug Points
The UCLI stop command allows you to create debug points using a script file. You can
create debug points using the checkpoint command in the Tcl script file. Following is the
syntax:
stop -command {tcl_script} [-continue]

stop -command {checkpoint -add "name" -debug_point} [-continue]

Breakpoints on UVM Error and Fatal Messages
The UCLI stop breakpoint command is enhanced to stop the simulation at UVM error and
fatal messages. Following is the syntax:
stop -uvm [error | fatal]

Limiting the Size of a Save Session
You can specify maximum disk space to be occupied by the saved session to avoid
exceeding disk quota. This allows you to prioritize debug points in the saved session.
To enable this feature, a new option -max_size is added to the UCLI checkpoint
command. Following is the syntax:
checkpoint [-save | -save_add] -session <name> -max_size <Gb>

The -max_size option specifies maximum size in Gb which a saved session should not
exceed (after the save is complete).

command. Following is the syntax:
checkpoint [-save | -save_add] -session <name> -max_size <Gb>

The -max_size option specifies maximum size in Gb which a saved session should not
exceed (after the save is complete). A real number is allowed as a size, for example:
-max_size 0.5

For the -save_add option, if the existing session exceeds the specified size, an error
message is issued and the checkpoint is not saved.

Reverse Debug Commands

For the -save option, following is the order of saving checkpoints when -max_size is
provided:
* Save special checkpoints kept before debug points (starting from the first debug point).
* Save checkpoint for the simulation start.
* Save all other checkpoints in usual way starting from the end.
In the above process, if the size exceeds the maximum size, VCS stops saving and issues
a warning message.

Debug Point Prioritization
In most cases, the first UVM error/fatal is the starting point for debugging than the
following error/fatal messages. That is, when saving session by nightly run in batch mode,
more checkpoints should be saved for the first debug point rather than for the following
checkpoints. To achieve this, you can use the following script:
config endofsim noexit
config reversedebug on
stop -uvm error
stop -uvm fatal
run
stop -delete *
checkpoint -save -session "foo" -max_size 5
run
checkpoint -save -session "foo" -max_size 10
quit

The above script uses 10 Gb memory for the complete session, from which 5Gb is used
for the first debug point.
To allow this use model, the auto-checkpoint feature is enhanced for the checkpoints
already saved to the disk. When the auto-checkpoint feature detects that some
checkpoints must be deleted, the checkpoint process is killed (so that it does not consume
memory), but the checkpoint is not removed from the disk by the save session commands
of the same session.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
This command specifies the amount of time and use the Run/Continue Reverse
command (by clicking the above icon or selecting the Simulation -> Run/Continue
Reverse command) to go back in time for the specified amount of time, as the same time
entry field used by the Run/Continue command (see figure). All the current breakpoints
are respected and the simulation stops at the most recent (considered back from the
current execution state) breakpoint hit.
When the time entry field is empty and no breakpoints are hit, the simulation is rewound
back to the start. If the reverse debug feature was enabled some time after the simulation
started, using the Run/Continue Reverse command (as well as other reverse commands)
stops at this point instead. In this case, a confirmation dialog box is displayed with the
"Rewind to first checkpoint at time <time>?" message.
The run-time of executing the Run/Continue Reverse command is dependent on how far
back in time it would go. If executing the Run/Continue Reverse command takes long
time, you can interrupt it by clicking the
Stop icon in the toolbar.

Next Reverse

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
This command goes back one SystemVerilog line which steps over task/function calls.
Eventually, it might stop on a breakpoint inside the task/function called at the previous line.
