Checkpoint Distribution

Go to Active Point

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
This command allows you to quickly go to the active point.

Checkpoint Distribution
The auto-checkpoint feature uses half of the checkpoints for logarithmic distribution (near
the current simulation execution location). It uses the other half for linear distribution
(checkpoints distributed regularly over the full debug range). This distribution provides
optimal reverse debug performance with reasonable memory overhead for RTL design.
However, for gate-level designs, checkpoint memory overhead is much higher. Linear
checkpoints also cause more overhead than logarithmic ones. To keep memory overhead
low, reduce the number of used checkpoints to 10 or 5. In this case, use only logarithmic
checkpoints.
To make the auto-checkpoint feature use logarithmic checkpoints only, the following new
configuration setting is added to UCLI:
config checkpointdistribution [hybrid | log]

Default is hybrid.
Verdi Preferences form for the Reverse Debug option is enhanced with the following new
option, as shown in the following figure:
Use Half of the Checkpoints for Linear Distribution

This checkbox is checked by default. It is enabled only when the Reverse
Debug option is enabled. When this option is enabled, Verdi calls the config
checkpointdistribution hybrid UCLI command. When it is disabled, Verdi calls the
config checkpointdistribution log UCLI command.

Checkpoint Memory Profiling

Checkpoint Memory Profiling
VCS allows you to check memory overhead of checkpoints and adjusts the number of
checkpoints to be used depending on their runtime memory usage limits. To enable this
feature, a new -memory option is added to the UCLI checkpoint command. Following is
the syntax:
checkpoint -memory

This command reports the current auto-checkpoint overhead for resident memory usage.
For example:
Checkpoint proportional sizes:
* 1: 777 Mb
* 2: 769 Mb
* 3: 593 Mb
* 4: 573 Mb
* 5: 528 Mb
* 6: 351 Mb
* 7: 312 Mb
* 8: 319 Mb
* static database server: 322 Mb
Active simulation process:
* Proportional size: 394 Mb
* Resident size: 1732 Mb
Total size (active process + checkpoints):
* 4938 Mb (overhead: 3206 Mb, 2.9x)

Proportional sizes here reflect memory usage when taking page sharing into account.
For example, assume you have 5 checkpoints all sharing 100 Mb memory, and each
checkpoint has 50 Mb private memory pages. In this case, each checkpoint has
"proportional size" as 50 + 100/5 = 70 Mb.

Reverse Debug Support for VHDL

The auto-checkpoint overhead is shown relative to resident size of active simulation
process. The checkpoint -memory command can be used, for example, in the following
way:
* Run the simulation to the end with reverse debug enabled.
* Check output of checkpoint -memory.
* If memory overhead is too high, reduce the number of checkpoints, restart the
simulation, and repeat the above steps until it does not exceed the desired limit.

Reverse Debug Support for VHDL
These Verdi and UCLI commands work correctly for VHDL source code:
Verdi Commands
* Step Reverse
* Next Reverse
* Run Reverse. This command correctly handles VHDL breakpoints.
* Undo/Redo
UCLI Commands
* step -reverse
* next -reverse
* run -reverse . This command correctly handles VHDL breakpoints.
* Virtual Checkpoints (config virtualcheckpoints [on|off]). The tool creates
virtual checkpoints for VHDL locations.
The following limitations apply to the Reverse Debug feature:
* Reverse debug is not supported for pure VHDL designs.
* The Step Out Reverse command is not supported for VHDL.

For Reverse Debug:
* VCS Design Level Parallelism (DLP) is not supported
* VCS Fine-Grained parallelism (FGP) is not supported
* The following actions of PLI code are not supported:
IPC communication using sockets, pipes or shared memory
Performing the file seeking operations, and then writing at a new position (that is, it
is assumed that simulation only appends data to the output files)
* Analog-digital co-simulation (using NanoSim) is not supported
* The Reverse debug commands are not supported for pure VHDL source code.
* When the design is compiled with the -simprofile option for simulation profiling,
reverse debug will not be possible.
For Go to Previous/Next Assignment feature:
* Several object types do not allow the setting of a value change breakpoint. When the
breakpoint cannot be set, an error message is generated and the command has no
effect.

Tracing Testbench Driver in Temporal Flow View
The following sections describe this feature in Interactive Simulation Debug Mode:
* Introduction
* Viewing Testbench Frame Node on TFV
* Viewing Signal Information when Tracing on Existing Path
* Property Window for Testbench Node/Folder
* Limitations

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Introduction
Verdi provides a new tracing mechanism to trace the driver of value change on the
testbench scope using the Trace on TFV command icon
in the toolbar.
The Trace on TFV command records the tracing results and displays them in the
Temporal Flow View frame. You can use the tracing map in the Temporal Flow View frame
to figure out the relation of signal driver/load.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Introduction

Perform the following steps to enable this feature:
1. Compile your design with the -debug_access+reverse option. This option enables
reverse debug capabilities.
2. In the Verdi GUI, select the Reverse Debug option in the Preferences dialog box, as
Figure 161

Preferences Dialog

3. To perform signal tracing on the testbench scope, use either of the following methods:
a. Select a signal in the Source Code pane, as shown in Figure 162.
Figure 162

Signal Tracing

Click the Trace on TFV icon in the toolbar. The trace path is added to the Temporal
Flow View as shown in Figure 163.

Figure 163

Tracing Testbench Driver in Temporal Flow View

The icon on the trace path indicates the path traced with a single signal and
icon indicates the path traced with multiple signals.
After first tracing, the driver statements are highlighted in the Source Code pane.
b. Double-click on the hardware boundary signal.
Verdi displays the trace path connected to the testbench signal as shown in the
following figure:
Figure 164

Trace Path Connected to the Testbench Signal in the Temporal Flow View

The following topics describe this section in detail:
* Frame Node
* Stack Node
* Interface Node

* Trimmed label
* Right-Click Options

Frame Node
A signal is represented by a frame node as shown in the following figure. An empty fanin
pin is added to the frame node if it is end of the trace path.
Figure 165

Frame Node

You can click a fanin pin and then click Trace on TFV icon in the toolbar to continue signal
tracing.
If you double-click a frame node, Source Code pane shows the execution point of the
active frame.

Stack Node
If multiple frames with the same time are very close to each other in the same stack, they
are merged into a stack node as shown in the following figure:
Figure 166

Stack Node

If you double-click a frame within a stack node, the Source Code pane shows the
execution point of the frame. The clicked frame is highlighted in orange color as shown in
the following figure, and indicates the current rewind frame.

Figure 167

Frame Highlighted in Orange Color

If you execute new trace or any commands that change the simulation execution point, the
highlight color will be canceled.
The selected signal name is displayed as a pin name on the frame node. The connection
connects from start node to end node as shown in Figure 168.
Figure 168

Signal Name

If you double-click on normal frame node, Verdi rewinds to the latest trace point of the
frame.
If you double-click a testbench signal pin, the source statement is highlighted in the
Source Code pane.

Hovering the mouse pointer on a frame node highlights the frame and displays its full
name as shown in the following figure:
Figure 169

Viewing Frame Name

Hovering the mouse pointer on a trace path frame or a rewind frame shows its information
in a tooltip as shown in the following figure:
Figure 170

Viewing Frame Information in a Tooltip

Interface Node
If the trace path traces through a hardware interface, an interface node is added to the
trace path, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 171

Interface Node

An interface node indicates that the tracing happens through the hardware interface
signal.

If tracing happens directly from the interface signal, the start node is the interface node, as
Figure 172

Tracing Through Interface Signal

If tracing happens from the DUT cell, the trace path traces through the interface node and
connects to end frame, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 173

Tracing Through DUT

If tracing of the interface signal happens from testbench frame, the trace path traces
through the interface cell, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 174

Tracing from Testbench

The fanout signal connects to the start frame and fanin signal connects to the end frame.
If you double click on an interface node, Verdi does not go back to the execution point.
You can use the property window (see Property Window for Testbench Node/Folder) to go
back to the related execution point of an interface cell.

Viewing Signal Information when Tracing on Existing Path

Trimmed label
If the signal name is longer than the label space, Verdi trims off extra name and replaces it
with "^".
For a testbench signal, Verdi trims the signal from start to end. If you enable Show
Hierarchy name, Verdi trims the hierarchy name first.

Right-Click Options
You can right-click a signal on the frame node and select the Jump To Driver or Jump to
Load right-click option, as shown in the following figure, to jump to the respective driver/
load in the Source Code pane.
Figure 175

Right-click Options

Viewing Signal Information when Tracing on Existing Path
When you trace on the existing trace path, Verdi updates the trace information on the
signal label. Therefore, you can check the trace information on the TFV trace path. Verdi
adds the icon on the trace path to indicate the path traced with a single signal and adds
the
icon to indicate the path traced with multiple signals. For example, when you trace
the vif.sig_clock signal, Verdi creates a trace path as shown in the following figure:
Figure 176

Tracing on Existing Trace Path

Viewing Signal Information when Tracing on Existing Path

When you go back to the first frame and trace another signal vif.sig_grant, as the trace
path is same as vif.sig_clock, Verdi combines these two tracing results and shows the
icon above the signal pin as shown in the following figure:
Figure 177

Tracing on Existing Trace Path

Hovering the mouse pointer on the / icon displays related traced signal information in
a tooltip as shown in the following figure:

Viewing Traced Signal Information in a Tooltip

Starting with this release, you can use the Properties window in the Temporal Flow View
frame to view detailed information of the testbench trace.

Property Window for Testbench Node/Folder

In the Temporal Flow View frame, select View ->Properties to open the Properties
window as shown in the following figure:
Figure 187

Properties Window

You can also use the keyboard shortcut key Ctrl+P to turn on/off the Properties window.
The Properties window allows you to highlight and rewind check point by double-clicking a
frame item in the hierarchical tree list.
When you select a testbench folder on the TFV, the Properties window displays all the
related frames on the tree list. The first level tree node is the frame node and the related
traced signals are the sub-tree nodes.
For each traced signal, a tree node contains two sub-tree nodes, one is the start check
point of the trace and another is the end check point of the trace.
To select a fanin or fanout signal, the Properties window lists all traced signals as the first
level tree node, and also contains two fixed sub-tree nodes (start point and end point for
user to rewind check point) for each node.
The structure of the hierarchical tree list is as follows:
For the Testbench folder selected on TFV:
First level: frame node
Second level: trace signal node
Third level: two fixed entries - start point and end point

For the Testbench Node selected on TFV:
First level: trace signal node
Second level: two fixed entries - start point and end point
You can double click on a frame node to expand it, and then you can double click on a
signal node to highlight the traced path. You can double click on a start or end check point
item to rewind to check point.
The coloring of the property tree is same as the coloring of the testbench folder on the
TFV.

Following is the limitation of this feature:
* Session save/restore is not supported for Testbench path on TFV.

Appendix D: Known Problems and Limitations
* The Verdi Interactive Simulation Debug Solution only works with VCS versions
2013.06 or later. If other versions of VCS are used, the Verdi platform exits Interactive
Simulation Debug directly.
* You cannot use Verdi Interactive Simulation Debug mode and Verdi assertion tools at
the same time. These tools include Evaluator, Statistics, Analyzer, and Add Temporary
Assertions.
* With VCS versions prior to 2013.06-SP1-1, the rewind and checkpoint features cannot
be used.
* The first created checkpoint (with checkpoint id '1') cannot be removed since the
simulator limitation.
* Mailboxes, semaphore, constraint, dynamic array, associative array and queues are
not supported for dumping. The dynamic and automatic variables outside of a class are
not supported for dumping.
* The object member data with class type is not expandable in the waveform. You must
manually trigger dumping, and then add the object (member of parent object) by object
ID to the waveform as first level item.
* The inter.fsdb FSDB file generated in Interactive Simulation Debug mode is not
supported by FSDB utilities and virtual FSDB files.
* The value change of a runtime signal cannot be updated in-time when the simulation
time goes to the next one. You must reload the FSDB file for the correct value.
* The following are limitations regarding save and restore functions:
The checkpoints cannot be restored currently.
The status of the Watch pane cannot be restored.
* Annotation values are not supported for the following data types or coding styles:
Modport signals
Partial bit(s) selection, for example, Array[i], Array[CONST]

Preface
The Verdi(R) Automated Debug Platform provides debug support for mixed HDL and
SystemC designs. You can dump SystemC signals, view SystemC instances hierarchy,
step through the SystemC/C++ source code, and debug the interactions between the
SystemC code and the HDL code.
In addition, you can also debug DPI, PLI, or any other C/C++ code linked to the simulation.

Setup and Requirements
The following options must be set to use Verdi SystemC Debug features:
1. Setup simulators for enabling the SystemC flow.
Refer to the Debugger Setup With VCS, Debugger Setup With IUS, and Simulator
Setup With Questasim sections for details.
2. Generate the FSDB file (optional).
Refer to the Generate FSDB section for details.
3. Prepare the RIDB file before performing debugging.
Refer to the Create the RIDB File section for details.
The following sections describe how to:
1. Set up the environment variable.
2. Set up the requirements of the corresponding simulator.
3. Generate the FSDB and RIDB files.
Instructions to invoke Verdi with SystemC design and to invoke it with Unified Compiler
Front-end are also described.

Debugger Setup With VCS
Perform the following sections to compile the SystemC source files and any other C/C++
file that must be debugged:
* Unified Front-end Post-Process Debug
* Unified Front-end Post-Process Debug With -kdb=sysc_elab Option
* Unified Front-end Post-Process Debug With -cbug::invokeElabcom Option
* UFE Interactive Debug
* UFE Interactive Debug With -kdb=sysc_elab Option

Debugger Setup With VCS

* Unified Front-end Post-Process Debug With -kdb=sysc_blackbox_elab Option
* UFE Interactive Debug With -kdb=sysc_blackbox_elab Option

Unified Front-end Post-Process Debug
Analyze the Verilog/VHDL and System C/C++ files with the -kdb flag. Add this flag also
during VCS elaboration. This invokes Unified Compiler Front-end (UFE).
1. Add the -cflags -g option during the analysis for getting the debug information for
SystemC, C, and C++ source files.
syscan -cflags -g
2. Elaborate -kdb and -debug_access+pp options.
%
%
%
%
%

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
syscan -kdb -cflags -g <the SystemC files>
vlogan -kdb <the Verilog files>
vcs -sysc <top_module_name> -kdb -debug_access+pp
./simv -ucli -do dump.tcl
verdi -ssf novas.fsdb -dbdir simv.daidir

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The dump.tcl file contains the following commands:
fsdbDumpvars
run

Generating RIDB and elaborating the KDB database is delayed in this process
when Verdi is invoked for the first time causing a noticeable delay up to several
minutes. This delay happens only when the design contains SystemC. There
are several possible approaches to avoid this delay when you invoke Verdi for
the first time:
* Use the VCS -kdb=sysc_elab elab option (interactive and post-process)
* Use cbug::invokeElabcom command (post-process only)
* Blackbox SystemC
In the UFE flow, when SystemC related design is imported, if the runtime
database (simv.daidir/default.ridb) is not generated, then Verdi invokes
simulator to dump RIDB. In post-processing mode, the console window appears
which is the same as in interactive mode. You can see the fail reason in the
Console directly even in post-processing mode.

Debugger Setup With VCS

Unified Front-end Post-Process Debug With -kdb=sysc_elab
Option
Add the -kdb=sysc_elab option in the compilation command line. VCS triggers creating
RIDB and KDB elaboration when it is compiling simv. This makes the VCS compilation
slower but there is no delay when you later invoke Verdi.
The runtime arguments of simv, the environment variable, and the input files must be
provided accurately. If the attempt to create RIDB and KDB elaboration fails, then a
warning message is issued and you experience a delay when you invoke Verdi for the first
time.
%
%
%
%
%

syscan -kdb -cflags -g <the SystemC files>
vlogan -kdb <the Verilog files>
vcs -sysc <top_module_name> -kdb=sysc_elab -debug_access+pp
./simv -ucli -do dump.tcl
verdi -ssf novas.fsdb -dbdir simv.daidir

% vlogan -kdb -sverilog <verilog_files>
% vcs -sysc sc_main -kdb -debug_access+pp
%./simv.vdb -ucli -do invokeElab.tcl

Debugger Setup With IUS
To generate the information the Verdi platform requires, the FSDB dumper must be
enabled and the following option must be added in the compilation command line:
-Wcxx,-g: Shows and gets the file and line information for C/C++/SystemC related files in
the Verdi platform.

Set up a Directory for SystemC Database

# Enables FSDB dumper
> setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH
$VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/IUS/$platform:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
> irun -access +r -Wcxx,-g -tcl dump.tcl -top <top_module_name> <your
design files>
> verdi -ridb default.ridb -ssf novas.fsdb

The dump.tcl file contains the following commands:
call fsdbDumpvars
run
exit

If a design contains HDL and SystemC code, it is necessary to add the
following options -scAllowSCFromPLI -ncsim_args,+scgafap+off for
appropriate time sync.
With Verdi 2014.12 version, when using IUS with SystemC dumping, ensure
that the IUS library libncsctlm2_sh.so is linked into the simulation.
This occurs automatically when you compile with ncsc_run.
For example, if you use ncsim, then the library must be specified.

Set up a Directory for SystemC Database
You can specify a directory for SystemC database with the -sc_dir option if the
simv.daidir directory is not writable or the SystemC hierarchy is changed.
This directory is created so that the SystemC database can be reused when simv.daidir is
not writable or the SystemC hierarchy is changed.
The SystemC hierarchy does not change in many scenarios.
When the deign is imported, the RIDB/KDB file in the sc_dir has higher priority than the
RIDB/KDB in the simv.daidir directory.
When the simulator is invoked and the SystemC hierarchy is different between the design
and the simulator, then the RIDB file is dumped.
The KDB database is regenerated in the -sc_dir directory, and then the design is loaded
again.

Simulator Setup With Questasim

The SystemC database is updated in the directory and can be reused next time the
directory is created.

Supported TCL Command
The following TCL command is supported for the -sc_dir directory:

debImport
This command imports the design with the SystemC database in the specified sc directory.
Syntax
debImport -dbdir /remote/simv.daidir -sc_dir /local/scDir

Simulator Setup With Questasim
To generate the information, Verdi platform requires the FSDB dumper to be enabled.
Add the following option to the compilation command line:
1. Create the library by executing the following command:
> vlib work

2. Perform the common compilation on the Verilog design by executing the following
command:
> vlog +define+NEW_PLI=1 -sv *.v

3. Compile the *.cpp codes.
>sccom -g *.cpp

Generate FSDB

4. Link the libMTISC.so file to the systemc.so file.
>sccom -link $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/MODELSIM/$PLATFORM/libMTISC.so

This library is required for the new SystemC dumping.
5. Load the Verdi dumper library for FSDB dumping when running the simulation.
>vsim -pli $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/MODELSIM/$PLATFORM/novas_fli.so
sc_main -c -do "fsdbDumpfile sc.fsdb; fsdbDumpvars 0; run 1000 ns;
exit"

>verdi -ridb default.ridb -ssf novas.fsdb

Generate FSDB
The Verdi platform provides several dumping commands that can be used to generate the
FSDB files. For dumping SystemC data into the FSDB file, the main dumping command is
$fsdbDumpvars.
The following table provides the usage of the $fsdbDumpvars dumping command with
different options to dump different SystemC data types. If you do not want to dump values,
this step can be skipped.
Usage

Dump Type

$fsdbDumpvars

sc_plain")
$fsdbDumpvars("+ Default items and variables of user-defined
sc_struct")
structs/classes/union/enum

sc_fifo")

all")

usage

Generate FSDB

The FSDB dumping commands are only supported when called in the HDL
code or on the Tcl command line. The dumping commands are not supported in
the SystemC source code.
See the Linking Novas Files with Simulators and Enabling FSDB Dumping manual for a
description of all FSDB dumping commands.
The following sections describe how to dump sc_fifo and tlm_fifo to an FSDB file in
detail.

Dump FIFO to FSDB
You can dump sc_fifo and tlm_fifo to an FSDB file using the $fsdbDumpvars command.
For flexible usage (for example, for all simulations, a specific simulation, or a specific
task), the following methods are also provided to achieve the same effect:
* Environment Variable: Set the FSDB_SC_FIFO or FSDB_ALL environment variables
before executing simulations. For example:
> setenv FSDB_SC_FIFO 1

* Simulator Option: Add the +fsdb+sc_fifo or +fsdb+all options on the simulation
command line. For example:
> ./simv +fsdb+sc_fifo

* Dumping Command: Add the +sc_fifo or +all options in the dumping task. For
example:
> $fsdbDumpVars("+sc_fifo");

Dump Analog Signals in MSV
You can dump analog signals in MSV using the dumping command fsdbDumpvars.
To dump analog signals in MSV, perform the following steps:
1. Generate FSDB file for dumping SystemC data into the FSDB file, using the dumping
command fsdbDumpvars as follows:
$fsdbDumpvars("+msv+v")

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
2. Invoke Verdi using the following command:
verdi -ssf novas.fsdb -msv

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Create the RIDB File

Setting the FIFO Size Environment Variable
You can use the NOVAS_FSDB_MAX_FIFO_SIZE environment variable to specify the value
for the maximum size of the sc_fifo when the dumping option for sc_fifo is set as follows:
> setenv NOVAS_FSDB_MAX_FIFO_SIZE <num>

The num should be a positive integer.
> setenv NOVAS_FSDB_MAX_FIFO_SIZE 2000

If the size of the sc_fifo exceeds the specified value, the data numbers exceeding the
value are not dumped. If the size is less than or equal to the specified value, the sized
number of the data are dumped. The default maximum value of the environment variable
is 100,000.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Create the RIDB File
You can skip this section if you use the VCS with the UFE flow.
The RIDB file contains the SystemC hierarchy that Verdi needs to show the mixed
SystemC/HDL instance tree. The RIDB file is automatically generated in the UFE flow
(-kdb), is named "default.ridb" and stored within the "daidir" directory of the simulator.
If you not using the UFE flow, then it may be necessary to trigger creating the RIDB file
with an explicit command.
* Use the FSDB_DUMP_RIDB environment variable or the +fsdb+dump_ridb runtime
option to generate the RIDB file without modifying and re-compiling the design:
When any FSDB dumping command is used (For example, $fsdbDumpvars() is called
in the HDL code or fsdbDumpvars is called in the TCL command line), then Verdi
platform can automatically dump the RIDB file during simulation. You must add the
+fsdb+dump_ridb runtime option or set the FSDB_DUMP_RIDB environment variable
during the simulation.
> ./simv +fsdb+dump_ridb

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Or
> setenv FSDB_DUMP_RIDB 1
> ncsim [runtime_options]

Create the RIDB File

The default name of the dumped RIDB file is default.ridb. The +fsdb+ridb_file
runtime option or the FSDB_RIDB_FILE environment variable can be used to assign a
different RIDB file name.
> irun +fsdb+dump_ridb +fsdb+ridb_file=work.ridb [compile_options]
[runtime_options]

Or
> setenv FSDB_DUMP_RIDB 1
> setenv FSDB_RIDB_FILE "work.ridb"
> ./simv

* Use the dumping command or task to generate the RIDB file:
Directly use the $ridbDump(<file_name>) dumping task in the HDL code or use the
ridbDump <file_name> dumping command in the Tcl command line to dump the
RIDB file. This usage is frequently applied in the Interactive Simulation Debug mode
debugging (refer to the Interactive Simulation Debug chapter for details).
> $ridbDump(); //Call the task in Verilog Code

The default name of the dumped RIDB file is default.ridb. Optionally, you can assign the
file name for the RIDB file.
> $ridbDump("work.ridb")

When the data type of a SystemC signal, port, or plain member is class or struct, the data
members are dumped to RIDB file also. The data member of user defied class or struct
can also be dumped.
If you want to generate only the RIDB file, you can use one of the dumping
methods without running the simulation completely. For example, start a
simulation in the Interactive mode, call the ridbDump task, and exit the
simulation immediately.

Support Scopes
The Verdi platform provides the following features for SystemC debugging in the main
windows (refer to SystemC Debug Overview):
* Displays SystemC/mixed design and hierarchy in the Instance and Declaration tabs of
the Hierarchy Browser pane (refer to Hierarchy Browser View).
* Displays SystemC/mixed design and hierarchy in the Instance and Declaration tabs of
the Hierarchy Browser pane (refer to Signal List View).
* Displays Signal, port and plain members of a SystemC instance in the Signal List pane
(refer to Signal List View).
* Displays the C/C++ source file in plain text with syntax colors in the source code pane
(refer to Source Code View).
* SystemC file or module can be found using the Find Scope command.
* SystemC signal, instance, or instance port can be found using the Find Signal/
Instance/Instport command.
Objects cannot be dragged/selected/annotated in the source code pane.

OSCI-name versus Source-name
All objects derived from the sc_object base class are visible in the SystemC design
hierarchy and always have an "OSCI-name". This name is either explicitly given in a
constructor call or is assigned automatically by the SystemC kernel such as "port_0" or
"signal_0". Most objects are also members of a C++ class (usually an SC_MODULE) and
have a "source-name" that is the name of the class member in the source code.
The OSCI and source names may be identical or different.
SC_MODULE(sctop) {
sc_signal<int> A;
sc_signal<int> B;
sc_clock clock;

};

SC_CTOR(sctop) : A("A"), clock("clk") {}

The presentation is as follows:
OSCI-name

Source-name

Display in Verdi Signal List

A

A

A(A)

signal_0

signal_0(B)

clk

clock

clk(clock)

The official name of SystemC objects is always the OSCI-name. The source-name is an
optional piece of information that is used in the Signal List pane and similar places. Always
use the OSCI-name in UCLI commands, for example, get sctop.signal_0 and not get
sctop.B.

Interactive Simulation Debug
The Interactive Debug mode is provided for SystemC interactive debugging.
The following sections describe the flow of enabling Interactive Debug mode and its
supported features:
* Starting SystemC Interactive Debugging
* Invoking Verdi Interactive Debug Mode With Unified Compiler Front-End
* Opening the C Source Code File
* Enabling C/C++ Debugging in Interactive Debug Mode
* Simulation Control Commands
* Local Tab
* Watch Tab
* Stack Pane
* Dynamic Dumping
* Variable Value Tip
* Setting Value-Change Breakpoint on C Variables
The SystemC interactive debugging is provided with VCS but not with IUS or
MTI.

Starting SystemC Interactive Debugging
After the RIDB file is prepared, you can invoke the Verdi platform by specifying the
compiled design library (using the -lib option), enter the interactive debug mode (using the
-i option), and specify the executable path (using the -simBin option) and simulation type
(using the -simType option).
> ./simv -verdi

Invoking Verdi Interactive Debug Mode With Unified Compiler Front-End

It can also be accomplished through the Verdi GUI as follows:
1. Invoke the Verdi platform.
> verdi &

2. Import the design using the File > Import Design command.
3. Invoke the Preferences form using the Tools > Preferences command to open and
set the simulator option on the Simulation page (as shown in the Configure the
Simulation).
4. Turn on Interactive Debug mode using the Tools > Run Interactive Mode command.
Figure 23

Configure the Simulation

Invoking Verdi Interactive Debug Mode With Unified Compiler
Front-End
When the Verdi Knowledge Database (KDB) is generated using Unified Compiler Frontend, you can invoke Verdi with the KDB through one of the following simulator commandline options to perform interactive simulation debugging without other configurations:
* -gui=verdi
* -verdi
For example, when the following commands are used during the compilation and
elaboration:
> vlogan -sysc -kdb <your Verilog files>
> syscan -cflags -g -kdb <your SystemC files>
> vcs -sysc <top_module_name> -debug_access+r -kdb -lca

You can use one of the following commands to invoke Verdi and enable the Interactive
Simulation Debug mode:
> simv -gui=verdi
> simv -verdi

The Verdi platform is invoked in the Interactive Simulation Debug mode. If the
default.ridb file does not exist in the simv.daidir/ directory, then the default.ridb
RIDB file is automatically generated and loaded into Verdi. If the default.ridb file
already exists in the simv.daidir/ directory, it is automatically loaded into Verdi.

Simulation Control Commands
The existing commands are also supported by the simulator for both HDL and C/C++
debugging. You can click the icons shown in Simulation Control Commands Toolbar or
select the command from the Simulation menu.
* Run/Continue: Simulation stops at a breakpoint setting in the HDL code or C code.
* Restart: Restart the simulation.
* Step: Simulation steps within the HDL code, C code, and cross step from HDL code to
C function.
* Next: Simulation goes to the next executed statement within the HDL or the C code.
* Next in C/C++: Simulation continues through the HDL code and stops in the next C/C+
+/SystemC statement to be executed. If an HDL breakpoint is reached before the next
C/C++/SystemC statement, then the simulation stops at this breakpoint. This is the
same as next -lang C UCLI command.
* Step Out: Simulation steps out within the HDL code, C code, and step out to HDL code
from C function. This is the same as next -end UCLI command.
* Quit: Quit the simulation.
* Kill Simulator Process: Kill the simulator process.
* Jump to Current Debug Position: The cursor jumps to the current debug line in the
source code pane.

Simulation Control Commands Toolbar

C-Source Debugger (CBug) Functions
You also can use the C-source debugger (CBug) functions by executing UCLI commands
in the Interactive_Console window to debug the design. The following sections introduce
the features and usages of the UCLI commands.

next -hdl
When the current scope of the simulation is a task/function or in C/C++/SystemC, you
can use the next -hdl command to advance the simulation until you exit the C domain
and are back in the HDL domain. If a breakpoint in the C domain is reached first, then the
simulation stops at this breakpoint.

Cross-step into SC Processes
CBug offers specific support for stepping between SystemC or HDL processes.

Simulation Control Commands

* When you leave a function that defines a SC_METHOD process, then a Step or Next
command automatically stops in the next SystemC or HDL process, which comes next.
* When you use the Step or Next command over a 'wait' statement that belongs to an
SC_THREAD process, then you can stop in the next SystemC or HDL process, which
comes next.
* Doing a Step or Next in Verilog or VHDL automatically stops in a SystemC process if
that process occurs to be the next SystemC or HDL process to be executed.
That is, performing Step or Next repeatedly follows the flow of SystemC and HDL
processes in the exact order in which the simulator executes them.

Step Through SystemC
This is not a separate UCLI command but a CBug configuration that affects how a Step
works.
* A Step command may be required that steps through to the next line in the user code
and does not step into SystemC kernel functions such as "sc_port::read().
* Configuration: Use the following command to enable the step-through feature:
cbug::config step_through on. The feature is disabled by default but prints a
message after reaching the first situation where a stop-through might have made
sense.
* Recovering from Error Conditions: In some cases, it is possible that an automatic
step-through does not quickly stop at a statement, but triggers another step-through,
followed by another step-through, and so on. In this case, it may make the Verdi
platform appear unresponsive, but you may not be aware that the step-through is still
active. CBug recognizes this situation and takes action. If a step-through does not stop
on its own after 10 consecutive iterations of an internal finish or step, then CBug can
stop the chain of internal finish or step sequences on its own, and report a warning that
states the automatic step-through is aborted and provides instructions to disable it.

Cross-Step between SV and PLI/DPI
When you step through HDL code and come to a call of a user-provided C function,

states the automatic step-through is aborted and provides instructions to disable it.

Cross-Step between SV and PLI/DPI
When you step through HDL code and come to a call of a user-provided C function,
such as a PLI function like $myprintf, then the Next command steps over this function.
However, the Step command steps into the C source code of this function (if CBug is
already attached).
Subsequent Step/Next commands walk through the C function and finally return you to
the HDL source; therefore, seamless stepping from HDL C HDL is possible.

Simulation Control Commands

Cross-stepping is supported only for functions that meet the following criteria:
* import_DPI functions
* PLI functions that are statically registered through a TAB file. Cross-stepping into
the call function is supported, cross-stepping into the misc or check function is not
supported.
* DirectC functions
Cross-stepping into other Verilog PLI functions is not supported. However, an explicit
breakpoint can be set in these unsupported functions to achieve the same effect.

Direct GDB Commands
You can send certain commands directly to the underlying gdb through the UCLI command
cbug::gdb. The command is executed immediately and the UCLI command returns the
response from gdb.
The command is as follows:
SimCMD>cbug::gdb <gdb-cmd>

gdb-cmd is an arbitrary command accepted by gdb including an arbitrary number of
arguments, for example info sources. When the cbug::gdb command is used in the
Interactive_Console window, CBug is automatically attached and the <gdb-cmd > arbitrary
command is sent to gdb. The result of the command is returned from gdb in a similar
manner as a Tcl routine and may have one or multiple lines.
The routine returns successfully in most cases, even if gdb itself gives an error response.
The routine gives a Tcl error response only when gdb-cmd has the wrong format, for
example when it is empty.
SimCMD> cbug::gdb info sources

The returned result is:
Source files for which symbols have been read in:
../pythag.c, rmapats.c, ctype-info.c, C-ctype.c, C_name.c,

Source files for which symbols will be read in on demand:
../../ncurses/tinfo/lib_tparm.c, ../../ncurses/tty/lib_twait.c,

Some gdb commands are not allowed and trigger an error message from CBug. These
are commands that change the state of gdb or simv (for example, commands kill, restart,
break).
To enable the commands that can change the state of the gdb and simv files,
set the CBUG_ENABLE_ALL_GDBCMD environment variable before starting Verdi.

The local C/C++ variables for the current scope are shown in the Local tab, including:
* Function arguments
* "this" pointer if the function is a member function
* Local variables in current scope
As shown in Local Variable Shown in the Local Tab, the Local tab shows the variables
with the name, value, and data type. The variables are collapsed by default.
Scalar variables which are native SystemC types such as sc_lv<3> or sc_in<int> are
shown in a pretty-print form. For example, variable mux_sel in Local Variable Shown in the
Local Tab has the native SystemC type sc_signal<sc_lv<3>> and the value is shown as
3'bXXX. If you want to bypass pretty-printing and instead see the raw response from GDB,
then type the cbug::gdb print mux_sel command in the console. Expand class/struct/
unions objects to see all members also in pretty-print form.
Figure 32

Local Variable Shown in the Local Tab

When the following situations are met, the local variables of the current stack frame are
updated:
* Simulator stops in C/C++ code.
* The current stack frame of C/C++ stack (shown in the Stack window) is changed.
* The local variable value is changed (refer to the Change Value section for details)

Objects cannot be dropped (added) to the Local tab.
Pretty-printing does not support nested typedefs and displays the value in
raw GDB format.

Change Value
The Change Value command in the right-click menu is provided to change the value of
the selected variable in the Local tab.
Figure 33

Force Signal Value

As shown in Force Signal Value, enter a new value in the Force Signal Value form. The
changed value is overwritten by a subsequent driver when the Deposit option is enabled
and is frozen when the Freeze option is enabled.
When the value is changed, Verdi calls the simulator commands to change the value
and show the simulator result in the Interactive Console window. If the value is changed
successfully, the variable value is changed in the Local tab; if not, there are no further
actions.
You also can use the change UCLI command to change the values of SystemC and local
C objects. The following command describes the usage and restrictions.
CBug supports changing the value of C variables and the SystemC sc_signal. For
example:
SimCMD> change my_var 42
SimCMD> top.inst0.signal_0 "1100ZZZZ"

SystemC Variables
Only SystemC objects of types sc_signal and sc_buffer can be changed. Changing the
value of ports, sc_fifo or any other SystemC object is not supported. SystemC objects
must be addressed by their full hierarchical path name or by a name relative to the current
scope.

SimCMD> scope top.inst1.sub_inst
SimCMD> change top.inst0.signal_0 42 // correct usage
SimCMD> change signal_0 42 // wrong usage, local path is not supported for SystemC
SimCMD> scope top.inst0
SimCMD> change signal_0 43

//correct, scope and local

Only sc_signals<T> / sc_buffer<T> of certain data types T are supported:
* All kinds of ANSI integer types, for example, int, long long, unsigned char, also bool
* Native SystemC bit-vector types: sc_lv, sc_bv, sc_int, sc_uint, sc_bigint,
sc_biguint

User-defined data types are not supported.
All SystemC sc_signals follow the "Current value versus Next value" policy. Any value
change, either from the user C++ code or a change command, modifies the next-value
only but not the current-value. The current-value is updated only with the next SystemC
delta cycle.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
als follow the "Current value versus Next value" policy. Any value
change, either from the user C++ code or a change command, modifies the next-value
only but not the current-value. The current-value is updated only with the next SystemC
delta cycle. The effect of a successful change command may therefore not be directly
visible. If you query the value with the get UCLI command, the next-value is displayed.
This is because the get command retrieves the next-value, not the current-value for
sc_signals.
However, accessing the sc_signal with a read() inside the user C++ code, shows the
current-value. This remains true until the next SystemC delta cycle occurs. CBug prints a
message explaining that the assignment is delayed until the next delta cycle.
A change may compete with other accesses from inside the user C++ code. If the signal is
first modified by a change command but later a write() happens within the same deltacycle, then the write() wins. This cancels the effect of the earlier change command. A
permanent change also known as the force -freeze is not supported.
The format of the value specified with the change command is defined by the
corresponding SystemC data type of T. ANSI integer types expect decimal literals. Native
SystemC bitvector types accept integer literal and bit-string literals.
For example, if the SystemC module top.inst_0 contains the following:
sc_signal<int> sig_int
sc_signal<sc_int<8> > sig_sc_int
sc_signal<sc_lv<40> > sig_sc_lv

then, these change commands are acceptable:
SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_int 42

//assign decimal 42

//assign decimal 15

SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_sc_int 0d015

SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_sc_int 0b0111ZZXX //assign bin value
SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_sc_int 0x0ffab

//assign hex value

SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_sc_int 15

//assign decimal 15

SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_sc_int -15

//assign decimal -15

SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_sc_lv 0d015

//assign decimal 15

SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_sc_lv -0d015

//assign decimal -15

SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_sc_lv 0b0111ZZXX //assign bin value
SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_sc_lv 0x0ffab

//assign hex value

SimCMD> change top.inst_0.sig_sc_lv 0011ZZXX

//assign bin value

Local C Variables:
Local C variables are variables that are visible within the current C/C++ stack window.
This is usually the location where the simulation is stopped. However, the window can be
changed by double-clicking a specific window in the Stack window or with the UCLI 'stack
-up' or 'stack -down' commands. Local C variables are formal arguments of functions/
methods, local variables declared inside a function/method, member variables visible in
the current member function, and global C variables. All these are referred to as "local C
variables".
Support for changing local C variables is quite different from SystemC objects. The
following restrictions apply to changing local C variables:
* CBug must be attached.
* Only simple ANSI types can be changed: bool. all kinds of integers (for example,
signed char, int, long long), 'char*' and pointers. Arrays of these types are also
acceptable if only a single element is changed.
* The format of the value is defined by gdb, for example, 42, 0x2a, 'a', "this is a test".
* SystemC types are not supported. For example, no support for sc_int, sc_lv.
* STL types such as std::string, std::vector, and so on are not supported.
* Using the full path name (for example, top.inst_0.my_int) is not supported, only
local names (for example, my_int or this->my_int)
void G(int I){
char* S = strdup("abcdefg");

}
void F(){
int I=42;
G(100);

}

SimCMD>
SimCMD>
SimCMD>
SimCMD>

// change formal arg I from G defined in line 100

change I 0xFF
change S "hij kl"
change {S[1]} 'I'
scope -up

SimCMD> change I 42

// change variable I from F defined in line 108

A C-VCBP is specified with the existing UCLI stop -change command:
stop -change [-location] <expr>

The UCLI command is extended to accept local C variables or expressions - <expr>.
<expr> refers to a variable that is visible within the current C stack frame. SystemC debug

or GDB interprets it.

The simulation stops whenever the <expr> changes.
For example, in the my_dpi.c file:

int AA;
void my_DPI_func(..)
{
AA = 10;
AA = 11;
}

Variable AA is a global variable. It is always visible to SystemC Debug or GDB, even if the
simulation has currently stopped in a different C function or even in Verilog code.
Therefore, setting a VCBP is always possible.

Execution stops on reaching the next line
The execution stops when the C-VCBP reaches the next line after modifying the variables
once.
For example, in the my_dpi.c file:

int AA;
void my_DPI_func(..)
{
for (int n=0; n<3; n++) {
AA = n;
AA = n+10;
}
printf("AA=");
}

The assignment in line 5 (AA=n) changes the variable AA and stops the simv on line 6
(and not line 5). The next reachable line is frequently the next line such as line 6 in the
example.
It can also be a different line. For example, the assignment in line 6 (AA=n+10) also stops
the simv but either on line 5 if the FOR loop iterates again or on line 8 when all the FOR
loop iterations are complete.

Expressions and Runtime Overhead
The <expr> specified as part of the stop -change <expr> command can either be a
single variable or a complex arithmetic expression involving several variables.
If no hardware limitations occurs, the GDB watches the underlying base variables, stops
when the expression changes, and evaluates it and reports a breakpoint only when the
resulting expression changes. The runtime overhead depends on the frequency of the
change in the base variable.

Scope of the Expressions
The C variables for which VCBP is set can either be global variables or local variables.
When VCBP is evaluated for local variables, the scope of the variable ends when the
scope of its function ends.

C-VCBP States
State

Active

Simulation stops when the
expression changes.

State

Disabled

The Breakpoint command is disabled
by executing the stop -disable <ID>
command. The simulation does not
stop when the expression changes.

Out-of-scope

The VCBP went out of scope and is
not active.

The UCLI command watch::isOutOfScope(id) returns 1, if the C-VCBP breakpoint ID
exists and is currently out-of-scope else returns 0 for all other outcomes.
UCLI command stop -enable <id> reactivates a C-VCBP that is out-of-scope or disabled.
The command evaluates the <expr> in the current scope. On success it becomes active
again. On failure, the C-VCBP remains or goes out-of-scope.
Simulation stops for an active C-VCBP in the following scenarios:
* When the <expr> changes the simulation does not stop if the breakpoint is configured
with the stop -continue <ID> command.
* When C-CVBP goes out-of-scope and there is no associated line breakpoint that
automatically activates it at later point in time.

text:
Automatically re-activates the C-VCBP when the F1() is called again:
ucli% stop -command {catch {stop -enable $c_vcbp}} $line_bp
ucli% stop -continue $line_bp
ucli% run

The C-VCBP (Line number 2) of local variable LL is activated only as long as F1() runs.
It goes out-of-scope as soon as F1() ends. But the next call of F1() triggers the line
breakpoint (no. 1), which in turn reactivates the C-VCBP. The line breakpoint is configured
such that it does not stop the simulation when it is hit. This setting makes the C-VCBP
is activate during all the calls of F1() but goes out-of-scope between calls of F1(). The
simulation stops only when LL changes. Therefore, the C-VCBP is seemingly permanent.
Management of the C-VCBP is convenient but causes some runtime overhead with each
execution of function F1(). Stopping the simulation internally and trying to re-activate the
C-VCBP requires some CPU time and slows down the simulation.
Also note that the <expr> of the C-VCBP is evaluated each time the line breakpoint is hit
and re-activates the C-VCBP. This is beneficial in case the memory location of <expr>
keeps shifting, if for example, it is a local variable on the stack and the function is called
through different call stacks. But if you need to watch changes of a specific object (at a
stable memory location), then use the -location option .

Associated Breakpoints
A new option for the UCLI stop command associates an arbitrary breakpoint with a CVCBP.
ucli% stop -associate <bp> <vc>

Each breakpoint has at least one associated breakpoint.
Execute the following command to un-associate:
ucli% stop -associate {} <vc>

A line breakpoint may have many C-VCBP associated with it. You can set a breakpoint
on the first line of a local variable in a function for the purpose of reactivating all the CVCBPs.

Associating a breakpoint has the following effects:
* The C-VCBP is configured to make the simulation continue even after going out-ofscope.
* The breakpoint is configured to reactivate the C-VCBP and then continue.
Enabling or disabling or deleting a VCBP changes the associated breakpoints.

Creating a C-VCBP and Line Breakpoint Pair
The following UCLI routine combines creation of both the line breakpoint and C-VCBP and
creates an association between them:
watch::create_persistent_c_vcbp -change <E> -file <F> -line <L>

ucli% watch::create_persistent_c_vcbp -change LL file my_file.c -line 100

The example creates a line breakpoint at <F><L> on line 100 and creates a C-VCBP for
<expr> for the expression LL and associates both the breakpoints. The return value is a
list of both breakpoint IDs {<line-id><c-vcbp-id>}
If setting of either of the breakpoint fails, then no breakpoint is created and an error is
returned.
If there is a line breakpoint existing in the same line or file location and if it is associated
with another C-VCBP, then the existing line breakpoint is reused for the new C-VCBP.
Therefore, creating a set of C-VCBPs with different expressions on the same file or line
location results in a single breakpoint. A set of C-VCBPs gets associated with the same
line breakpoint.
Therefore, it is recommended that this routine is used only with local variables that go out
of scope. Do not use this with global variables or memory locations.
The -location option is not supported in the
watch::create_persistent_c_vcbp routine.
Automatic reactivation of C-VCBP slows down the simulation if it occurs frequently. The
SystemC Debug displays the following message in such a case:
Note-[CBUG-BP-17] Persistent C-VCBPs are active
One or more persistent C value-change breakpoints are frequently
triggering a cycle of going out of scope and re-activation by a
controlling line breakpoint. Such cycles may cause a noticeable slow
down the simulation. This message is printed only once every 1000
cycles.
If these cycles are not intentional, then type 'stop' to identify
and disable the relevant breakpoints. Look for 'controlling VCBPs'.

Change the limit to report this message by changing TCL variable
'watch::vcbp_silent_oos_limit'.

You can set the limit of automatic reactivations using the following routine:
watch::vcbp_silent_oos_limit

The default limit is 1000 cycles.
You change the limit as follows:
ucli% set watch::vcbp_silent_oos_limit 20000

-location option
The issue with C-VCBP is its tendency to get disabled when the expression goes
out-of-scope. You can either re-activate it or use the -location option. The -location
option is available only for C-VCBP and not for Verilog or HDL or SystemC signals. The
-locationoption has the following syntax:
ucli% stop-change <expr> -location

The underlying GDB command monitors a memory location and stops when the value in
that memory changes. The <expr> is evaluated in its resulting memory address. With the
-location option, <expr> is evaluated exactly once when the C-VCBP is set for the first
time. The resulting memory address is watched, <expr> is ignored thereafter.
The benefits and penalties are illustrated in the following example:
Example 1

my_file.c

struct Object {
int ID;
double A;
bool B;
Object(int id_) : ID(id_),A(0.0),B(false) {}
};

Object* lookup_entry(int key)
{
Object* P = <search list for entry matching key>
if (P)
return P;
c simulation is stopped here
else

}

Set the C-VCBP:
ucli% get key
ucli% get P -radix hex
0xffff0010

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
ucli% get &(P->B) -radix hex
0xfff0018
ucli% stop -change P->B -location
ucli%

The VCBP remains active until the simulation ends. The simulation stops when the
new value is written to memory address 0xffff0018. The expression P->B becomes
meaningless but the memory address remains under watch.
The advantages of the -location option is as follows:
* The C-VCBP is hit only when the object at the memory address 0xffff0018 is
modified, it does not stop for any other object, (assuming that the object with the
key=17 continues to exist at address 0xffff0018 through the rest of the simulation).
* The C-VCBP remains active even after the lookup_entry() function ends and P->B
goes out of scope.

-C_expression option
You can set a C-VCBP as follows:
ucli% stop -change <expr>

The <expr> refers to a Verilog/VHDL/SystemC signal and also to a plain C expression.
The ambiguity regarding the language of the expression is resolved as follows:
* If -c_expression option is present, then <expr> must refer to a C expression.
* If the <expr> matches a Verilog, VHDL or SystemC signal, then the VCBP is set on the
signal. A matching C expression, if any, is ignored.
If no -c_expression is present, <expr> does not match a Verilog, VHDL, or SystemC
signal but matches a C expression, then a C-VCBP is created.

VCBP of Memory Locations
The <expr> of a C-VCBP also refers to a memory address in which case a word (4 bytes)
starting at <expr> is watched for changes.
CBug% stop -change *0xffff0018

Setting a VCBP on an address is similar to using the -location <expr>. With the -
location option, SystemC Debug is aware of the <expr> type and the number of bytes of
memory allocated to it, hence the underlying GDB watchpoint is set precisely.
The benefit of using a memory is its robustness and availability wherever the simulation
has stopped.

C-VCBPs on memory locations can always be activated again after a restart. But this is
also a penalty because the memory may frequently be used for different purposes during
simulation startup and thus create frequent false positives. Both the approaches can be
combined with the following command:
CBug% stop -change *(my_object_type*)0xffff0018

with my_object_type referring to the type of expression lookup_entry(17)->A.

False Positives of C-VCBPs
When an object at a memory location is deleted, freed and reallocated to a another object,
VCBP remains unaware of this change and continues to function in the same manner.
This results in a false positive and it is likely to occur when a C-VCBP watches a memory
location.
In the example, object P is freed and its memory re-allocated to string STR:

Verification ContinuumTM
text:
If the object at 0xffff0010 is deleted, its memory is freed and reallocated again to some
unrelated function, the C-VCBP remains unaware of these changes. It keeps watching the
memory location 0xffff0018. Any modification, results in a C-VCBP to hit.
The C-VCBP hits in line 311 (simv stops in the next line, 312) as required when the
memory still belongs to the object with ID=17. But, the C-VCBP also gives a bogus hit at
line 332 (simv stops in 333) which is confusing. The C-VCBP is technically correct to stop
because memory location 0xffff0010 is modified and -location option specifies to watch
the memory location rather than the original expression P->A.
False positives are especially likely when a C-VCBP watches a memory location.

C-VCBP Restart Behavior
The C-VCBP behaves in the following manner, after a simulation restart:
* C-VCBP with an associated file/line breakpoint is always set to out-of-scope status.
Such a C-VCBP is used for a local variable which definitely goes out-of-scope after a
restart.
The C-VCBP is automatically enabled after the associated file/line breakpoint is hit at a
later point.

* C-VCBP with -location option remains disabled upon restart.
The -location option is used for context sensitive expressions.
Since the context is not available directly after a restart, you can manually enable the
C-VCBP again when the simulation is back in the given context.
* The system tries to enable any other type of C-VCBP. When the enabling fails, the CVCBP goes out-of-scope.

Supported Data Types and Hardware Limitations
The C-VCBP works on any type of C/C++ variable but there are hardware limits on the
number of bytes that the GDB can watch. Therefore, most native SystemC types cannot
be supported.
Native SystemC types. For example, sc_in, sc_signal, sc_int are not
supported by C-VCBPs.
Hardware Limitations
Hardware watchpoints are implemented based on hardware feature which has machine
dependent limitations. Therefore, the limit for hardware watchpoint varies with the host/
CPU being used.
If the hardware limit has reached when a C-VCBP is set, then the UCLI command fails
with the following error message:
CBUG-VCBP-C-1 cannot set C value-change breakpoint
Value-change breakpoint of expression '<expr>' cannot be set as a GDB
hardware watchpoint. The expression may be too complex or require too
many bytes in memory. If this is a single variable, then use command
'get -cbug {sizeof(<expr>)}' to see how many bytes are needed. Use a
different expression that uses fewer bytes, for example only a single
array element or only a single member of a struct.

Even though the individual watch points are small, all the watchpoints combined exceed
the limit when the simulation is about to continue because of a Run or Step command.
The following error message is displayed on encountering such a scenario:
Error-[CBUG-BP-11] Too many C value-change breakpoints
Too many value-change breakpoints of local C expressions are active
and breakpoint(s) '1 3 ' could not be activated. The simulation cannot
continue, commands such as 'step' or 'run' are not possible.
Disable/delete these or other value-change breakpoints of local C
expressions.

SystemC Data Types and Limitations
C-VCBP works with any type of C/C++ types as long as the variables are within the GDB/
CPU limitations. But in most cases, when a SystemC data type exceeds the CPU/GDB
limitation, an error message is displayed.
ucli% gdb whatis s_int
sc_core::sc_signal<int>
ucli% print s_int
ucli% stop -change s_int

The SystemC debug displays the following error message:
Warning-[CBUG-BP-16] Limited support for native SystemC types
Expression 's_int' is of native SystemC type 'sc_core::sc_signal<int>'. C
value-change breakpoints give only limited support in this case:
- SystemC ports and signals are frequently too large (CBUG-BP-11)
- Values will be printed in GDB syntax and not with the usual
pretty-print
syntax
- Several types will only show '<incomplete type>' as new value
- The simulation will also stop at destructors of base classes
If this is an SystemC port, signal or other channel, then specify the
object with its full pathname. It will implement the value-change
breakpoint by means of a callback from the SystemC kernel instead of a
GDB 'watch' command.
Error-[CBUG-BP-13] Software value-change breakpoint forbidden
Expression 's_int' is valid, however, GDB can create only a software and
not a hardware watchpoint for it. No breakpoint has been created because
software watchpoints would drastically slow-down the simulation. Use
command 'cbug::config allow_sw_vcbp on' to enable software value-change
breakpoints and try again.

Using HDL Value-Change Breakpoints to Stop a SystemC signal, Port, or Channel
To stop the simulation when a SystemC signal, port or channel changes, use an HDL
value-change breakpoint instead of C value-change breakpoint.
ucli% stop -change top.inst0.s_int

Do not use -c_expression, use the full pathname.

Known Problems and Limitations
The following are the known issues and limitations in SystemC Debug:
* Bit Field is not supported during the dumping operation.
* Verdi SystemC Debug does not support SystemC RIDB/signal dumping for VCS slave
simulations (vcs -sysc -slave ).
* The action of adding or dragging and dropping of a SystemC signal from the source
code pane into the nWave pane is not supported.
* Array in struct data type is not supported with FSDB dumping.
* If an FSDB file contains SystemC signal(s), it is not supported by FSDB utilities and
virtual FSDB files.
* If the design is a SystemC-on-top design, Verdi shows a scope sc_main in the
hierarchy tree, even if sc_main is a C function and not a SystemC instance. The
following are the limitations of the sc_main scope only for SystemC-on-top designs:
The signal list shows only sc_signals but no plain members.
Source names are not visible for SystemC objects in the sc_main scope. Only
OSCI names are visible.

Invoking Verdi from Another Tk Application
Commands cannot be sent as soon as the Verdi platform is invoked. The registration
of commands and Tk name must be completed before proceeding. Therefore, use the

following polling mechanism to check on the status of the registration process. For
example:
exec dubussy -tkName <tk name goes here> &
while {1} {
set s [winfo interps]
if {-1 != [string first <tk name goes here> $s]} {
break;
}
after 500
}
send <tk name goes here> {debRestoreSession mySession.ses}

Invoking Commands from Another Tk Application
To invoke Verdi commands from another Tk application, a Tk name for the Verdi platform
must be registered with the -tkName command line option. The syntax for registering the
Verdi platform's Tk name is as follows:
>Verdi -tkName <Tk name>

<Tk name>: Choose any name for the Tk name. However, if another Tk application
already has the same name, then a sequential numeric value is appended to the Tk name
so that it is unique. For example, "test#2" is assigned for the second Verdi Tk name of
"test" when there is already an existing Verdi platform with Tk name "test".
To send a command to the Verdi platform, use the Tk send command. The syntax of the
send command is shown below:
send <Tk name> <Verdi's Command Reference>

If a command was successfully executed by the Verdi platform, a value of
TCL_OK is returned to the calling Tcl/Tk application; otherwise, the return
value is TCL_ERROR. Each command expects a certain number and type
of arguments. Upon receiving a command, the Verdi platform checks the
command arguments; if this check fails, the command is not executed.

Adding Event Callbacks to Tk Applications
The Verdi platform can call back the invoking Tk application when specific events occur.
This is done by sending a command to the Verdi platform which registers a callback
function along with a reason used to determine when to call the callback function. A
special command AddEventCallback is used to set up the callback information.

Tk applications do not accept commands that use xhost style security
protection. For this reason, use xauth instead.
When both the Tk application and the Verdi platform run on the same computer,
and both use an xserver on that computer, you can use the xhost command
to enable access control. This setup lets the Tk application receive event
notifications from Verdi. The same rule applies if you use VNC, because the
VNC server acts as an xserver on the same computer as the Tk application and
Verdi platform. However, this method does not work if you use a UNIX server
and the display is set to an xserver on a different computer, such as a PC.
A simpler way is to compile Tk with security turned off. In this case, the Tk
application always receives event notifications, no matter which security method
you use.
AddEventCallback
AddEventCallback TkAppName CallbackFun Reason async

TkAppName

This is the name of the Tk application (which is usually the name appearing in the title).
The Verdi platform uses this name to identify the Tcl interpreter to send commands to. If
the Tk application is running under the control of a script file, it is usually the name of the
script file.
The following Tk commands can be used to get the application name:
winfo name
winfo interps
selection get APPLICATION
CallbackFunc

This is the Tk callback command/procedure.

This is the reason for the callback. The Verdi platform invokes the callback when the
specified reason occurs. Refer to the Reason Table for details.
Async

In most cases, 1 should be specified for this parameter. Synchronous event callbacks
should be used in special situations only where the server should wait for the client to

process the event before continuation (for example, before exit). If not used carefully, the
server (Verdi) may hang with synchronous events.
RemoveEventCallback
Call this function to remove a previously installed event handler. To remove an event
handler, TkAppName, CallbackFunc, and Reason fields must match the original value
passes to AddEventCallback when registering for the event.
RemoveEventCallback TkAppName CallbackFunc Reason

TkAppName

This is the name of the Tk application. The Verdi platform uses this name to identify the Tcl
interpreter to send the commands to. If the Tk application is running under the control of a
script file, it is usually the name of the script file.
CallbackFunc

This is the original Tk callback command/procedure. It should match the name of the
callback function passed to AddEventCallback.

This is the original reason for the callback. It should match the name of the reason passed
to AddEventCallback

#!wish -f
# Callback Implementation
#

puts "Received CursorTime Change Event"
puts "Parameters:"

}

# Invoke Verdi

User - Defined Event Callbacks
Sometimes it is useful for a third party tool to register for an event callback where the
reason is defined by the registering application. The Verdi.menu file can be modified to
add a user defined menu item. When activated, this menu item calls the third party tool
with the user defined reason.
Usually, event callbacks are registered using either AddEventCallback (Tcl/Tk applications)
or CmdCltAddEventCallback (C API interface). The reason field should normally reference
a pre-defined reason otherwise an error occurs. However, if the reason begins with UDR_
(User Defined Reason) then that reason is defined dynamically. The menu file can then be
modified to call back the invoking application with the new reason.
Modify the Verdi.menu file to add a user defined menu.
Menu File
{
"Test"
_s
f.tcl
UDR_MY_REASON clientdata"

}

"Test"

"EventTrigger

Tk Application: (myTkApp)
# Register Callbacks
#
send Debussy {AddEventCallback myTkApp myEventCallbackProc
UDR_MY_REASON 0}

Replaying Commands
The Verdi platform replays the commands by typing the following command when invoking
the Verdi platform:
>Verdi -play <filename>

<filename>: The name of the command file that has been programmed manually.

Tk Commands
A full set of Tk commands is available for tool customization and integration. Tk
commands allow the creation of sophisticated graphical user interfaces by using the Tcl
scripting language. The Tk commands are registered by default when the Verdi platform
starts and can be used in scripts with -play and the Tcl source commands.
If the Tk script wants to receive event notifications from the Verdi platform (see event
reason table for full list of events), then the AddEventCallback command can be used.
proc wvCreateWindowFunc args {
puts "Tk App. Received Event"
puts "Parameters:"
foreach i $args {
puts $i;
}
}
AddEventCallback [tk appname] wvCreateWindowFunc wvCreateWindow 1

Debugging
The Verdi platform can display commands to stdout as they are received by setting the
following environment variable.
To turn on the commands displaying:
>setenv CMD_TRACE 1

To turn off the commands displaying:
>setenv CMD_TRACE 0

The command and its arguments are both output.

The Verdi platform's command language interface also supports a C interface for third
party client-side integration. Third party tools can use this interface to send commands to
and receive event notifications from a command server (that is, Verdi).
The library names to link with are libnclt.a and libsys.a. These libraries are included in the
Verdi package. Shared library versions also exist. The header file cmdclt.h contains the
needed function prototypes.
This section includes the following topics:
* Overview
* Setting Up Verdi as a Server
* Setting Up a Client Process
* Application Programming Interface (API) References

Overview
The following figure depicts the Verdi Command Language Interface with C applications
(Socket Command Clients):
Figure 3

Setting Up Verdi as a Server
To start the server for accepting commands, pass the command line arguments:
-serverPort <port> for socket interface when invoking the Verdi platform.
Syntax:
>Verdi -serverPort

<port>: the port range is between 1024 and 65535.
Example:
>Verdi -serverPort 11060

Setting Up a Client Process
There are three steps to setup a client application so it can send commands to the Verdi
platform.
1. Create (CmdCltCreate)
2. Connect (CmdCltConnect)
3. Call Command (CmdCltCallCommand)
For example:
char*
result;
CmdCltConnect(cmdclt, 11060, "sps32", -1);
if (CmdCltCallCommand(cmdclt, "debImport -f run.f", 0, &result))
printf("Command successful. Result = %s\n", result);
printf("Command failed. Error = %s\n", result);

the communication protocol.

CMDCLT CmdCltCreate(char silent)
silent

If TRUE, suppresses status information from being dumped to stdout.
Pointer to a Command Client object.
Create an instance of a Command Client object. CmdCltDestroy MUST be called to free
the returned object.

void CmdCltDestroy(CMDCLT cmdclient)

Destroys a Command Client Object. This function MUST be called to free the object
returned by CmdCltCreate.

void CmdCltConnect(CMDCLT cmdclient, int port, char*
serverName, int timeout)

port

Port on which to communicate with server. 1024 > port < 65535
serverName

Server name. This can be the machine name or an IP address. A value of NULL means
the local machine.
timeout

Timeout period. If a connection cannot be made within timeout, CmdCltConnect returns. A
value of -1 means the function does not return until a connection has been established.
Connects to the server. This function does not return until a connection has been
established. The server side must be started with the command line option -serverPort
<port number> where <port number> is the same as port. It is not necessary to start the
server first.
For example,
>Verdi -serverPort 11060

CmdCltConnect(cmdclt, 11060, "sps32", -1);

void CmdCltSetAbortProc(CMDCLT cmdclient, procVoid func,
void* clientData)

func

Callback function.
clientData

Application defined data that is passed to your callback. This value can be NULL.
Can be used to set a function that is called back when the connection with the server is
broken.
Whenever CmdCltCallCommand or CmdCltAddEventCallback is called, a check of
the connection with the server is made. If the connection is broken, func is called.
CmdCltCheckConnection can be called to manually check the connection.
void AbortProc(void* clientData)
{
char* myString = (char*)clientData;
printf("%s\n", myString);
}
int main()
{
char myString[100];
CmdCltConnect(cmdclt, 11060, "sps32", -1);
strcpy(myString, "Connection broken");
CmdCltSetAbortProc(cmdclt, AbortProc, myString);

return 1;
}

char CmdCltCallCommand(CMDCLT cmdclient, char* command,
char async, char** returnString)

command

Command to call. This can be any valid Tcl command.
async

If 0, this command is executed synchronously, otherwise it is executed asynchronously.
returnString

Points to the result of the call. If return value is 0, returns an error message. Otherwise
points to the return result.
0 on error.
Used to send a command/Tcl expression to the server and retrieve the result. Sending
the command asynchronously can greatly speed up the execution of the command,
however, using asynchronous commands it is not possible to get the returnString and
CmdCltCallCommand will always return TRUE. This function calls CmdCltCheckForEvents
to check for any pending events before sending the command.
char*
result;
CmdCltConnect(cmdclt, 11060, "sps32", -1);
if (CmdCltCallCommand(cmdclt, "Test A B C", 0, &result))
printf("Command successful. Result = %s\n", result);
printf("Command failed. Error = %s\n", result);

char CmdCltAddEventCallback(CMDCLT cmdclient, char* reason,
procVoid func, void* clientData);

reason

Event notification callback reason. (See below)
func

Callback function. Must be of the form: void myEventCB(char* eventname, void*
clientData, char* callData)

0 on error.
Registers a function to be called when a particular event (reason) in the server occurs. To

title: Verification ContinuumTM

ion callback reason. (See below)
func

Callback function. Must be of the form: void myEventCB(char* eventname, void*
clientData, char* callData)

0 on error.
Registers a function to be called when a particular event (reason) in the server occurs. To
check for events CmdCltCheckForEvents MUST be called.
func should be of the following form:
void myEventCB(char* eventname, void* clientData, char* callData)

The value pointed to by callData is always a string, the value of which depends on reason.
Refer to the Reason Table in the Adding Event Callbacks to Tk Applications section of this
chapter.
Note
If you register for an event with this function, you must call CmdCltCheckForEvents at
some regular interval. See CmdCltCheckForEvents.
void CursorTimeChangeCB(void* clientData, void* callData)
{
char* cursorTime = (char*)callData;
printf("Received CursorTimeChange Event. Value = %s\n", cursorTime);
}
int main()
{

}

CmdCltConnect(cmdclt, 11060, "sps32", -1);
CmdCltAddEventCallback(cmdclient, "CursorTimeChange",
wvCursorTimeChangeCB, NULL);

return 1;

void CmdCltCheckForEvents(CMDCLT cmdclient)

Flushes all pending events. Call this function to check for any pending events and call
registered event handlers. This function should be called at some regular interval. Every

100 ~ 500 milliseconds is a good interval. For GUI based applications, a timer can be
used.
Note
If events have been registered for with CmdCltAddEventCallback, then this function
SHOULD be called, if not, then this function does nothing and does not need to be called.

char CmdCltCheckConnection(CMDCLT cmdclient, char**
errorMsg)

Use this function to test that the listening socket is still alive. It returns TRUE on
success and FALSE on error. errorString is only set if there is an error. This function
calls the function registered with CmdCltSetAbortProc, if the connection is broken.
CmdCltCallCommand and CmdCltAddEventCallback both call this function.

char* CmdCltGetDotFormat(char* machineName);
This function returns the dot notation (IP Address) given the machine name.

char* CmdCltGetLocalMachineName()
This function gets the local machine name.

int CmdCltGetFreePort()
This function gets a free port on the local machine. Returns -1 on error. After 1000 failed
attempts, returns -1.

char CmdCltIsPortFree(int port)
This function tests if the given port is free or not (local machine). It returns TRUE if the port
is free and FALSE if not free or an error occurs.

Creating and Using a Command Replay File
The command replay file contains commands that are executed when Verdi is started
with the -play command-line option. For Verdi's commands, see the Verdi Command
Language Reference chapter.
Let's create a command replay file that does the following tasks:
1. Import a design in Gate.
2. Create a new waveform window.
3. Load the FSDB file, namely verilog.fsdb.
4. Add signals in Group 1.
5. Zoom waveform's time to 300 ~ 600.
6. Create a new schematic window.
7. Push in scope system.i_cpu.
8. Push in scope system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.
9. Trace the system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.ACC_tmpreg[1] signal's drivers.
The command replay file is saved as a.cmd and is as follows:
debImport -f run.f
srcSetScope system.i_cpu
#wave
set wave1 [wvCreateWindow]
wvSetHierDelimiter -delim /
wvOpenFile -win $wave1 verilog.fsdb

wvAddSignal -win $wave1 /system/CYCLE /system/R_W /system/VMA
{/system/addr[7:0]} /system/clock {/system/data[7:0]}
wvZoom 300 600
#schema
set schema [schCreateWindow -delim . system]
schPointSelect -win $schema 7837 1434
schPushViewIn -win $schema -delim . system.i_cpu
schPointSelect -win $schema 16828 7975
schPushViewIn -win $schema -delim . system.i_cpu.i_ALUB
schZoom -win $schema 16788 46523 63701 92282
schZoom -win $schema 16951 60475 61054 85778
schPointSelect -win $schema 34229 78128
schTraceDriver -win $schema -mode oneLevel -delim .
{system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.\ACC_tmp_reg[1]}

To execute the command replay file, a.cmd, type the following on the command line when
invoking Verdi:
>verdi -play a.cmd

This tutorial shows how to send Verdi's command from a Tk application. The sample Tk
application, Signal Finder, is designed to read signals from a file, to find and trace load/
driver of the selected signals in the Tk application and to show the results in nSchema.
The subsequent sections show how to communicate the Tk application with Verdi and how
to invoke the Tk application - Signal Finder.
Use only the Tcl/Tk application and the command client library (libnclt.a) to
communicate with Verdi.
This sections consists of the following sub-sections:
* Communication Between the Tk Application and Verdi
* Invoking the Tk application
* Support Verdi Windows in Tk Containers

Communication Between the Tk Application and Verdi
To send commands to Verdi from a Tk application, you must first register a Tk name for
Verdi with the -tkName command-line option. The syntax for -tkName is as follows:
>Verdi -tkName <TK name>
