Loading Designs With Different Strategies
When you create a KDB using vcs -kdb, you have several ways to load your design into
Verdi.
To load the entire design, including all hierarchy and instances at once, use this command:
> verdi -dbdir <design.dbdir>

If your design is large or complex and may use a lot of memory, you can use Smart Load.
Smart Load loads only the first level of hierarchy at the start. When you access another
hierarchy, Verdi incrementally loads the hierarchy on demand. This saves time and
resources as they are not touched, so instances do not occupy them. Use this command:
> verdi -dbdir <design.dbdir> -smart_load_kdb

Refer to the -smart_load_kdb option description in the Verdi and Siloti Command
Reference Manual for details.
If you want to focus on specific parts of your design or exclude some modules, use
Preload. Preload lets you load selected scopes first. You can add more scopes later
without reloading everything. Use this command:
> verdi -dbdir <design.dbdir> -preload <preload_cfg_file>

For details, see the -preload option in the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual.

The Unified Compiler Flow (UFE) uses VCS with the -kdb option and the generated

Verdi supports the following use models to import design from simv.daidir related files:
* "verdi -dbdir simv.daidir"

The priority to import design from UFE is as following (from high to low):
1. Use the new -dbdir option to specify the simv.daidir directory
Similar to: dve -dbdir simv.daidir

Load simv.daidir from the same directory as simv and invoke Verdi if simv.daidir
is not available.

Smart Load
Smart Load optimizes Verdi import performance by partially loading only the required
design information at startup, allowing quicker initialization and resource management.
The remaining design is later loaded on demand during Verdi runtime. Smart Load is
enabled by default and requires no additional configuration.

Reference Source Files on the Command Line

When Smart Load is enabled, the following message appears in Verdi:
Smart-load is enabled, complete KDB is loaded on demand.

If the imported design is incompatible with Smart Load, Verdi automatically switches to a
full design load, ensuring that the verification process can process without interruption.
To skip Smart Load and load the compete KDB into the memory, use the -full_load_kdb
command-line option.
* Smart Load is not supported in the case of broken ShellDB, where ShellDB
is not generated due to failure during compilation.
* The nECO feature is not supported in Smart Load mode. You can
use the nECO feature in full load mode, if you launch Verdi with the
-full_load_kdb option.

This method loads the design directly from the source files. It is not recommended for
mixed language designs.
1. Use the following command to reference the source files on the command line:

Where, source_file_name is a file that lists all of the HDL source files.
2. Use the File -> Open Waveform File command to load the FSDB.

Loading When Design and FSDB Hierarchies do not Match
Use the following command if you have dumped the FSDB file for the entire design, but
only want to load a portion of the design for debug:
% verdi -f <source_file_name> -ssf <fsdb_file_name> -vtop <map_file_name>

Where, source_file_name is the source file name, fsdb_file_name is the name of the
FSDB file, and map_file_name is the name of the map file.
The map file is used to match the design hierarchy to the hierarchy in the FSDB file so the
simulation results are correctly annotated on the source code and schematic views. The
Verdi platform automatically generates a virtual hierarchy in the design according to the
definitions in the map file. The syntax is as follows:
design hierarchy

FSDB

module_name = hierarchical_instance_path

The map file matches the case sensitivity of the associated language. For
example, Verilog is case-sensitive so if the module definition is all capitalized,
the map file description needs to be as well (that is, cpu does not equal CPU).
VHDL is not case-sensitive (that is, cpu equals CPU).
If you incorrectly enter the module name in the map file, you may see an error similar to
the following in the compiler.log (File -> View Import Log):
*Error* view cpu is not defined for inst i_cpu
"virtual_top_autov_15123.gen:, 7:

This error needs to be eliminated. Check the module definition in the source code and
confirm that the map file matches it exactly.

Replacing the Absolute Paths in Verdi KDB

Replacing the Absolute Paths in Verdi KDB
When you copy or move compile-time files such as simv, simv.daidir, csrc, kdb, or
compile vdb to a new location, the absolute paths saved in these files may no longer
work. The original directory might not exist anymore. This can affect how the KDB works in
the new location.
Verdi stores design source files in binary format inside the KDB. Most debug operations
in Verdi use these source files directly from the KDB. However, in some cases, Verdi tries
to find source files in the compile directory using the path saved in the KDB. The following
are the cases:
* Open Source Editor within Verdi to edit the source files
* OneSearch: Search from the source files
* Coverage: Source code viewer
For the three use cases above--Verdi Editor, One Search, and Coverage Source Code
Viewer--Verdi searches for source files in the compile area where the KDB is created. If
you move the files, this search may not work.
KDB keeps the original file paths from compile time. Verdi lets you set the absolute path to
the compile directory.

Option to Retain the Paths Specified Inside the KDB
Verdi offers a compile-time command line option to save the location of your source files
using the path you provide. If you use absolute paths, Verdi keeps them as absolute paths
in the KDB. If you use relative paths, Verdi keeps them as relative paths.
For example:
vcs -preserve_path

The option -preserve_path is used to ensure that the tool does not change the userdefined path that the user has provided during vlogan/vhdlan/syscan/vcs.

Option to Specify Absolute Path to the Compile Directory
Verdi lets you specify the absolute path to the compile directory when you start the tool.
Use the Verdi command line option to set the reference compile directory for source files
that use relative paths. Make sure to enter the reference directory as an absolute path.
For example:
Verdi -comdir <absolute path of the compile dir>

Support of Incremental Dump in vlogan Without PSL

When you load the design with -comdir <absolute path of the compile dir>, Verdi
uses -comdir directory as the reference directory of the relative path in KDB to find the
location of the source files.
When you load the design without -comdir, Verdi uses the directory that contains
simv.daidir as the reference directory of the relative paths in KDB, for the following
operations:
* Open Source Editor within Verdi to edit the source files
* OneSearch: Search from the source files
* Coverage Source code viewer

The KDB relocation methodology is applicable only for 2-step flow.

Support of Incremental Dump in vlogan Without PSL
Incremental dump feature reduces the KDB memory overhead with vlogan. However,
incremental dump in KDB does not work with PSL syntax. If there is only inline PSL in
the design, -kdb=common_elab could skip the inline PSL, which allows the incremental
dump to work as expected. In other words, incremental dump occurs with -psl and
-kdb=exclude_inline_psl.
If the design consists of both inline PSL and vunit syntax, incremental dump does not
work. That is, -kdb=exclude_inline_psl fails to work with -pslfile or *.psl or *.vu or
*.vunit.

Getting Relative Path in FSDB
To ensure the correct path of simv.daidir can be found, FSDB stores the absolute path
of the working directory of simulation, as the reference directory. Verdi can transfer the
absolute paths to relative paths from the reference directory, so that the correct folder path
and the KDB can be found.

-kdb=common_elab Supports VCS Dynamic Test Loading

Required Conditions
The feature is supported under the following conditions:
* The folder simv.daidir is under working directory (working directory is the reference
directory where the simulation is executed).
For example, when you execute simulation in the /a/b/c/ path, simv.daidir should
be in the /a/b/c/simv.daidir/ or /a/b/c/../simv.daidir/ path.
* The relative path between working directory and simv.daidir is the same as the one
between the directory where users open Verdi and simv.daidir.
When you load FSDB with the -ssf option, Verdi uses working directory as a reference
directory and transfer the absolute path of simv.daidir to a relative path. Therefore, the
correct folder path and KDB can be found.
* Consider you execute simulation in the following path:/home/debug/.
* After simulation, FSDB contains absolute path to simv.daidir at /home/debug/
simv.daidir/ and to working directory at /home/debug/.

correct folder path and KDB can be found.
* Consider you execute simulation in the following path:/home/debug/.
* After simulation, FSDB contains absolute path to simv.daidir at /home/debug/
simv.daidir/ and to working directory at /home/debug/.
* After downloading it to another path, Verdi operates these two paths and finds the
relative path for simv.daidir is ./simv.daidir/.
When simv.daidir exists at both original path and download path, the one
in original path is set to use.

* You must make sure that the solution is used under the conditions described in the
Required Conditions section.
* For the solution to perform successfully, after download, the relative paths between
simv.daidir, source files, and KDB should not be changed.

-kdb=common_elab Supports VCS Dynamic Test Loading
Dynamic Test Loading (DTL) is a mechanism to load Verilog packages at any time in
the middle of a simulation. The package is dynamically loaded and can have testbench
collateral. For example, it includes UVM test classes or UVM sequence classes. This
mechanism can be used to run different UVM tests or sequences without having to
regenerate the simulator executable (simv).

-kdb=common_elab Supports VCS Dynamic Test Loading

The Save-Restore feature allows you to save the simulation state and then resume
simulation from the saved state.
The partition compiler feature allows you to compile Verdi KDB data into partition library.
The new test is compiled into partition library.

The following options are used:
* -enable_dynamic_tb: This option is used to compile and create a simulator
executable that can dynamically load a test.
* -dynamic_tb: This option is used to compile the Precompiled IP for the test package
that has to be dynamically loaded.
* -kdb=common_elab -partcomp: This option is used to create KDB related models and
enable partition compiler.
* -debug_access+all: This option is used for Verdi interactive debug in the save state
step.
Following are the steps involved in VCS common elaboration partition compiler flow:
1. Enclose all the basic test classes in a Verilog package, for example, base_test_pkg.
The following is the command used: vcs -kdb=common_elab -partcomp
-enable_dynamic_tb

These base classes may be derived from UVM classes. Compile the base_test
package using the VCS methodology. Integrate the DUT and the base_test package
together to create the simulator executable (simv).
Verdi interactive debug mode: -debug_access+all
2. Following options are used for saving simulation state after the common part of the test
is executed:
Verdi Interactive debug: -ucli2Proc
Verdi UVM Debug: +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=HIER is used to write UVM tree to FSDB.

save saveddesign; ; run}

Verdi Support for Dynamic Test Loading
Verdi features can be used to debug and trace new test in post-process mode and
interactive mode.
* Post-process mode: New test package is added into source view, instance tree, and
declaration tree.
* Interactive debug mode: Using the option +dtl_add_pkg=[new_test] -i
restore.cmds, you can debug new test package with interactive debug features.
* UVM-aware debug:
OVM/UVM hierarchy tree: New test name can be shown using OVM/UVM hierarchy
tree.
To know more about the usage of DTL, refer to the Dynamic Test Loading
chapter of the VCS LCA Features Guide.

Following are the limitations of this feature:
1. The following technologies do not support DTL:
FGP
Dynamic Reconfiguration
Debug of classes
VMC
2. Cross Modules References (XMR) from the Dynamic Test package to the DUT is not
be supported.

-kdb=common_elab Supports VCS Dynamic Test Loading

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
3. The PIP created for the Dynamic Test Package should not have any modules. Only
packages are supported.
4. If source code of the base test is changed, then the base test package needs to be
recompiled and simv needs to be regenerated. If the new test is dependent on the
base test, then the new test has to be recompiled.
5. The dynamic test package cannot be part of the simulator executable (simv).
6. Dynamically loaded UVM packages should configure the tests in the main phase and
not in the build phase.
7. In Verdi interactive debug usage, you cannot specify other script in simv -verdi -i
restore.cmds. Also, you cannot append the UCLI commands to restore.cmd.

The Verdi platform is a multi-window docking application with a flexible and easy-to-use
graphical user interface (GUI).
You can customize the Verdi platform layout by dragging a frame away from its original
position (undocking). Drop it in a new position (docking) to attach it to the left, right, above,
below, or on top of another frame. You can also move a toolbar category to the left, right,
above, or below the relevant frame. You can change the bind key of any command and
arrange toolbar categories fairly easily.
Before you begin this tutorial, follow the instructions in the Before You Begin chapter.

Start Verdi Platform

Refer to the Launching Techniques chapter for information on starting the Verdi platform.
Refer to the User Interface chapter for more details about the interface.

Start Verdi Platform
1. Change the directory to <working_dir>/demo/verilog/rtl.
% cd <working_dir>/demo/verilog/rtl

text:
Using the Welcome Page
1. Choose the Help -> Welcome command if the Welcome page is not displayed.
Figure 54

Welcome Page

2. On the Welcome page, click the What's New icon and then click the Application
Notes icon. You can see the application note files and the FAQ file here.
3. Click the Home Page icon to go back to the Welcome page and then click the Work
Modes icon.

Saving and Restoring a Session

Figure 55

Work Modes Page

4. Select the Testbench Debug Mode option and then click the Go to Work button.
The window layout of the Verdi platform adds the Constraint, Inheritance, FSDB_Msg
and the Static frames for testbench code browsing and message debugging purposes.
5. Click the Welcome icon
Welcome page.

in the lower right corner of the main window to display the

6. Click the Work Modes icon to show to the Work Modes page again.
7. Select the Hardware Debug Mode option and then click the Go to Work button.
The window layout of the Verdi platform is now optimized for Hardware Debug Mode.
The work mode may also be specified on the Verdi command line with the
-workMode option.

Saving and Restoring a Session
1. Choose the File -> Save Session command and save the current session to "my.ses".
2. Go to the Welcome page and click the History icon to show the History page.

Saving and Restoring a Session

3. Select the my.ses option on the History page. A screen shot of the session is displayed
to the right as shown in the following figure:
Figure 56

Session Preview

4. Select the novas_autosave.ses option.
The image shows the time the session was saved.
If you do not see this file, exit the Verdi session and start it again. The file is
automatically created on exit.
5. Click the Restore Session button to restore the novas_autosave.ses session.
6. Go back to the History page and restore the my.ses session.
For more information on how to save and restore a debug session in Verdi, click the
following video link:
This video explains how to save and restore a debug session in Verdi. In the
Verdi GUI, you save a session by selecting File > Save Session, enabling the
Save Simulation State and Enable Reverse Debug on Restore Session
options, specifying a file name, and clicking Save. To restore a session, select
File > Restore Session, choose the saved session file, and click OK. These
methods ensure that your simulation state, checkpoints, and GUI layout are
preserved for efficient debugging.

Changing the Default Frame Location

Changing the Default Frame Location
1. Click the New Waveform icon to open an nWave window.
The nWave frame is added as a new tab on top of the Message frame.
2. Click the frame banner of the nWave frame and drag it to the left.
The nWave frame is now floating (undocked).
3. Drag the nWave frame around and see that the dockable area (outlined with a dashed
line) is changing along with the cursor position.
4. Drop the nWave frame to dock it.
5. Undock and dock the nWave frame (or another frame) to different positions several
times to become familiar with the usage.
For more information on how to change the layout arrangement on a Verdi platform, click
the following video link:
This video demonstrates how to optimize your workflow in nTrace by mastering
layout arrangement. It covers docking, undocking, and customizing frames to
streamline navigation and improve visibility for efficient debugging.

Maximizing the Display
1. Click the

Undock icon on the nWave toolbar to make it a standalone window.

2. Click the Dock icon on the nWave standalone window.
The nWave frame is docked to the main window again.
3. Double-click the nWave frame banner. This maximizes the nWave frame size and
makes it easy to see the content of the frame more clearly.
4. Double-click the nWave frame banner again and the nWave frame goes back to its
original size.

Modifying the Menu/Toolbar

Modifying the Menu/Toolbar
1. Right-click the nWave frame banner to display the right-click command menu and
select the Menu option to hide the menu bar.
Figure 57

nWave Configuration Menu

2. After the Menu option is turned off, press the Alt key within the nWave frame's central
area to show the menu bar. Pressing the Alt key again hides the menu.
3. Turn on the Menu option in the right-click command menu.
4. On the right-click command menu, select the Open option to hide the icons associated
with the Open toolbar category.
The Open category disappears from the toolbar of the nWave frame.
5. On the right-click command menu, select the Open option again to restore the Open
toolbar category.
6. Click the left handle (vertical bar) of the Open toolbar category and drag a little. The

For each docked Verdi component, the search toolbar and spotlight search is consolidated
in the top window's spotlight search String/Signal option as the Unified Find option which
is applied in the active window.
You can invoke the Unified Find option with the Ctrl+F shortcut key, which auto switches
the spotlight search as the String/Signal option and auto-focuses in the key-in text box. If
the text box is empty then it is auto filled with the active window's selection text.
The search option is also enhanced in Verdi for the Unified Find option.
This section consists of the following subsections:
* Support for Active Window Icon With the Spotlight Icon
* Enhancement to the Search Option in the Message Frame
* Enhancement to the Search Option in the Transaction Table View, Transaction Relation
Navigator Window, and SmartSheet
* Enhancement to the Spotlight Icon
* Enhancements to the Right-Click Options
* Enhancements to the Temporal Flow View Tools Menu
* Limitations

Support for Active Window Icon With the Spotlight Icon
Verdi supports Active Window icon on the Spotlight function area as shown in the
Figure 64

Active Window Icon

Click the triangle of the Active Window icon to view the active docked windows available
as shown in the following figure:
Figure 65

Active Window Icon Options

A check mark is displayed for the current active window. You can select any other docked
active window available in the Active Window icon to change the current active window.

A tooltip is displayed which provides the active window information, as shown in the
Figure 66

Tooltip Information

In the Source Code pane for the active window, the Unified Find option
searches for the string from the cursor point. For example, if the cursor point
is at the 99th line of a 100 line source code and line 3 and line 100 has the
searched string, then since the cursor is at line 99, the first search match found
is at 100th line and then the 3rd line. Also, for the SmartLog, Console, and
OneSearch, the Unified Find option searches for the string from the viewable
content.

Enhancement to the Search Option in the Message Frame
The search and find option is enhanced in the Message frame as follows:
1. The Find String text box is available only in the OneTrace tab and Search tab.
2. The toolbar icons to find previous string and next string are removed.
3. Only support to auto-fill the selected string is available in OneTrace tab. When you
select Ctrl+F and find a text, the text field is empty.
4. The Find Whole Words Only option in the String/Signal option is disabled when the
current active window is the Message frame.

Enhancement to the Spotlight Icon
The String/Signal option is added in the Spotlight icon, as shown in the following figure.

Figure 69

Spotlight Functions

Click the triangle as shown in the figure to select String/Signal option and then specify a
string to search in the text field to dynamically search for the first object that matches in
the current pane/window.
You can click the Find Previous or Find Next icons to find the previous or next string
specified in the Spotlight text field.
Following options are available with the String/Signal Options:
* Match Case: When this option is turned on, strings or signals matching the
capitalization of the text entered in the Spotlight text field is found.
* Wildcard: When this option is turned on, the wildcard characters (* or ?) are supported
to specify the pattern-matching string. For example, if EN_A* is entered, EN_AB,
EN_AC, and En_ AD are all found.
* Regular Expression: When this option is turned on, additional regular expressions are
supported. Special keywords (*, ?, +, -, |) are treated as regular expressions.
* Find Whole Words Only: When this option is turned on, the identifiers matching the
complete word you enter in the Spotlight text field are searched. Note that this option
is disabled when the current active window is switched to the Source Code window
to avoid conflicts when the Match Whole Word Only option in selected in the nTrace
Find String form.
* Find in All Columns: When this option is turned on, the signal is searched in all the
columns available in the active tab. For example, specify a string "fsm" to search in the
text field. When the Find in All Columns option is turned on, and the Instance tab is
the active window, then "fsm" is searched in all the columns available in the Instance

tab. When the Find in All Columns option is turned off, then the tooltip is displayed
which provides information about where the search string is available, as shown in the
Figure 70

Tooltip Information

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
By default, the Find in All Columns option is turned off.
The Find in All Columns option is enabled if the current active window is one
of following:
1. Constraint Debug tab
2. Class tab
3. Object tab
4. Member pane
5. Stack pane
6. Local pane
7. Watch pane
8. Assertion Debug
9. Instance Tree (enable this option Source Code->Design Tree->Search and
Filter in Expanded Tree in the Preferences form to search for the string in
the Instance tab, instead of Declaration tab)
10. Signal List
11. Message Pane (enable this option when current tab is OneTrace and has
content available in it)

When the Wildcard, Regular Expression, Find Whole Words Only are all
turned off, it is in default mode. That is, you try to find an item that partially
matches the pattern even if wildcard characters are added.
You can also set the default option in the Find/filter page (General -> Find/
Filter -> Find Options) of the Preferences form.

Support for Active Window in Verdi
Verdi uses an active window system to determine which docked pane receives top window
commands. The active pane is indicated by a dark-blue banner, and commands are
automatically disabled when not applicable to the active window.
Verdi has multiple docked panes in the top window, each with its own selection. To switch
the active window, click on a pane, drag an item from it, or press Ctrl+Shift+Tab. Menu and
toolbar commands apply only to the active pane's selection. Commands specific to certain
views (such as source view or signal list) are enabled only when that view is active.

Support for Active Window in Verdi

To make a window active, perform either of the following options:
1. Click the mouse button (left, right, or center) on the window.
2. Click the banner on the window. The banner color changes to blue. When the docked
banner is hidden using the Hide Banners option, then a blue line appears as shown in
Figure 74

Banner Color

3. Drag an item/items from a window to make it active.
Drop operation does not make a window active.
You can also use the shortcut key Ctrl+Shift+Tab to switch active windows for visible
docked views.
Figure 75

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Scenarios of Active Window
* When the current active window is closed or hidden, then the last visible docked
window becomes the active window.
If the docked view is in the middle, then the next docked view becomes visible and
active. For example, if the docked view is in the middle (for example, nSchema6), then
next dock view (nSchema7) become visible and active.
* If the docked view is on the right, then the previous window becomes visible and active.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
This feature has the following limitations:
* When the window is undocked, then you cannot run the trace/radix/notation
command in the top window.
* When the window is docked in container window, then you cannot run the shortcut
commands in top window.
* When Signal List has different selection with source view, then some trace command
and radix/notation command are disabled.
* A shortcut is applied on an active window only if the same commands that are available
on the top window are also available in the active window.
For example, TFV does not have OneTrace commands, therefore OneTrace menu
commands and shortcuts (OneTrace -> Driver) do not apply even if TFV is the active
window and OneTrace commands are available in the top window.

The nTrace main window is a source code viewer and analyzer that operates on the KDB
to display the design hierarchy and source code (Verilog, VHDL, SystemVerilog, mixed) for
selected design blocks.
The Verdi platform quickly identifies signal connectivity information (drivers and loads)
without any simulation overhead.
With the FSDB, the simulation results can be back-annotated in the source code.
The Verdi platform can then analyze and determine a signal's active driver at a particular
simulation time.
Before you begin this tutorial, follow the instructions in the Before You Begin chapter.
Refer to the Launching Techniques chapter for more information on starting the Verdi
platform and opening the nTrace main window, which is the default window. Also refer to
the User Interface chapter for more details regarding the nTrace interface.

Traverse the Design Hierarchy in nTrace
You can traverse the design hierarchy to understand the design structure.
1. Change to the demo directory.
% cd <working_dir>/demo/verilog/cpu/src

% verdi -f run.f -workMode hardwareDebug &

This tutorial uses a Verilog design example. The same capability is available
for VHDL or mixed designs.

plus symbol to the left of the i_CPUsystem block instance name to reveal its i_CPU
and i_pram subblocks.
Figure 76

i_CCU, and i_PCU subblocks.

The plus/minus symbols to the left of the block instance names in the design browser
frame are used to expand/collapse the display of the selected block's hierarchy.

1. To access source code, double-click the i_CPUunit instance name in the design

nSchema Tutorial
* Start nSchema

* Support for Annotation and Fault Coverage on nSchema Window

nSchema is a schematic viewer and analyzer that generates interactive debug-specific
logic diagrams. These diagrams display the structure of the selected portions of a design.
RTL diagrams show the interconnection of finite state machines, storage elements, and
multiplexers. Gate-level diagrams show the interconnection of semiconductor vendor cells.
Special flattened diagrams cut through the design hierarchy to isolate connected design
elements.
nSchema dynamically generates partial schematics to focus on the circuits of interest in a
large design.
Before you begin this tutorial, follow the instructions in the Before You Begin chapter. Refer
to the User Interface chapter for general information on the nSchema window.

Start nSchema

The nSchema window is used to display auto-generated schematics and logical diagrams,
the frame can be undocked to be a standalone nSchema window, as shown in the
following example:
Figure 106

Example of nSchema Window

nSchema generates the schematic for both RTL and gate-level designs. For RTL designs,
the Verdi platform extracts certain types of synthesizeable function blocks from the HDL
code, such as registers, latches, multiplexers, pure combinatorial or sequential circuits,
and so on.
With this capability, you can get a clear picture of the design intent, especially for a design
with which you are unfamiliar.
For gate-level designs, the Verdi platform uses standard symbols, such as nand, nor,
inverter, and so on, to make the schematic more readable and understandable.
To perform certain functions, such as signal tracing or intuitive searching, you can dragand-drop items between windows to cross-link the tools.

nWave Tutorial
nWave is a state-of-the-art graphical waveform viewer and analyzer that is fully integrated
with the source code, schematic, and flow views of the Verdi platform. A waveform search
engine combined with backward and forward navigation allows you to search for signal
transitions, bus values, discrepancies, and user-defined events easily.
nWave offers the following:
* Flexible signal group management
* Customizable glitch detection
* A built-in logic analyzer
* Logical operations and events
* Display of delays back-annotated from SDF files
* Mixed analog/digital (A/D) display capabilities, including overlap, vertical zoom, delta x
and y, arithmetic operations, analog-to-digital signal conversion, and others
* Display of transactions and messages
Before you begin this tutorial, follow the instructions in the Before You Begin chapter. Refer
to the User Interface chapter for more details regarding the nWave interface.
* Add Signals
* Manipulate the Waveform View
* Change Signal/Group Attributes
* Create New Signals/Buses From Existing Signals
* Save and Restore Signals
* Group or Ungroup Multiple FSDB Files
* Calculate Toggle Coverage
* Define Events and Complex Events

* Support VHDL Fixed-point Types in nWave
* Capture and Display Frequency of a Scalar Signal as a New Signal
* Generate Dump Files From Verdi Signal RC Files

Adding Signals Using Index Wildcards
The nWave Add Signal by Name dialog box supports wildcard characters in array
indices, letting you add multiple indexed signals without specifying each index individually.
A search such as /system/a[*].data[5] adds all matching signals to the waveform
viewer. Patterns are automatically expanded to individual signals in the waveform viewer.
Wildcard

Meaning

*

Matches zero or more characters

?

Matches exactly one character

The usage is as follows:
/system/psPnl[*].Addr[51:0]

This pattern adds all psPnl array elements with their Addr signals to the waveform.
Wildcard Scope and Matching Rules
Wildcard matching in the Add Signal by Name dialog box supports the following features:
1. Index wildcard *: The * wildcard matches zero or more characters within an index
dimension. For example, /system/a[*] matches /system/a[0:9] and all signals with
any index value.
2. Index wildcard ?: The ? wildcard matches exactly one character within an index
dimension. For example, /system/a[?] matches /system/a[0] and /system/a[1],
but not /system/a[10].
3. Cross-dimension expansion for *: The * wildcard can expand across multiple
index dimensions. For example, /system/macroram[10*] can match /system/
macroram[101][7:0]. (? cannot expand across dimensions.)
4. Combined name and index wildcards: Wildcards in both signal name and index can
be used together in a single search pattern (for example, top.cpu*.data[*]).
5. Maximum signal limit: A maximum of 100 matched signals are added to the
waveform; additional matches are ignored. When a wildcard matches more than 100
signals, only the first 100 are added and nWave displays an information message
indicating that results have been truncated.

Figure 128

Information Message for Truncated Wildcard Results

6. No-match warning: When a wildcard pattern matches no signals in the design, nWave
displays a warning through the List of Signal(s) Not Found dialog box.
Figure 129

Warning When No Signals Match

You can combine wildcards for both indices and signal members. For example, /system/
a[*].data[*].
* ? matches a single character and * matches zero to n characters.
* Neither ? nor * can expand across scopes. Wildcards match signals within
the specified scope only.
* ? cannot expand across scopes and dimensions. For example, /system/
macroram[10?] cannot match /system/macroram[101][7:0].
* * can expand across dimensions. For example, /system/macroram[10*]
can match /system/macroram[101][7:0].

specified signal names.

When using index wildcard characters (* or ?) in array indices within the Add Signal by
Name dialog box:
* Array slice notation combined with an index wildcard is not supported. For example,
a[*].data[7:1] (and likewise a[?].data[7:1]) does not match. The signal cannot
be found when an array slice is used with a wildcard in the same search pattern.
Use one of the following workarounds instead:
Search using a index wildcard, such as /system/a[*].data[*].
Specify the complete index range, such as /system/a[*].data[7:0].
* Index wildcards may not be fully supported for signals in mixed-language designs.

nWave allows you to create events to help figure out complex conditions. Through
previous events, you can then capture the designated conditions clearly.
* Create a Single Event
* Save and Reload Events
* Create a Complex Event
* Create a Complex Event With a Timer
* Create Complex Event with a Counter

Create a Single Event
Simple events can be created through a fixed combination of signals. For example, to
capture a synchronous read and write cycle, you can specify the correct signals and
values. Simple events can then be used to form a complex event (for example, limit the
duration, the occurred sequence, or the number of times the event must be issued).

1. Close the previous Verdi session.
2. Change directories to the <working_dir>/demo/verilog/rtl directory and then invoke the
Verdi platform as follows.
% cd <working_dir>/demo/verilog/rtl
% verdi -f run.f -ssf rtl.fsdb -workMode hardwareDebug &

3. In the nWave window, choose the Signal -> Get Signals command to open the Get
Signals form.
4. In the Get Signals form, select the R_W, clock, and reset signals under the system/
i_cpu scope and click the OK button.
5. Choose the Waveform -> Go To -> Time command to open the Search Time form.
6. Enter 400 in the Time Value field and click the OK button.
The cursor changes to time 400 in the waveform pane.
7. With the three signals selected, choose the Signal -> Event command to open the
Event Window.
8. In the Event Window, click Insert to create event 0.
Figure 157

nWave Event Window

An event is inserted using the selected signals current values as the event conditions.
9. In the Event Window, click Edit.
10. In the Edit Event form, change the name to read_cycle in the Event Name field. Do not
change the expression which should be:
"clock"=== b1 && "reset" === b1 && "R_W" === b1

11. Click OK and the read_cycle event is added into Event Window.
12. Click Capture to view the related waveform. Leave the Event Window open.

Create a Complex Event With a Timer
Two built-in timers are provided that can be used to compose the complex event. Timers
are used to trace the period of a complex event. They can be controlled with different
options: START, STOP, PAUSE, and CONT. The timer is globally set. If no value is set for
the timer in the sub-conditions, then the value is inherited from the global setting. The subcondition can have its own setting with a priority higher than the global ones.

Example 1
1. In the Event Window, Complex Event tab, click Edit to open the Edit Complex Event
2. In the Edit Complex Event form, stay at level 0 and perform the following:
a. In the Complex Event Name field, enter level_trigger2.
b. Change the condition to IF read_cycle LASTS 25 ns THEN goto level 1 (click
trigger to change the action).
c. Leave the remaining fields unchanged.
d. Increase the level number from Level 0 to Level 1 by clicking the right-arrow.
3. In the Edit Complex Event window, stay at level 1 and perform the following:
a. Change Timer1 to START
b. Change the condition to IF timer1 == 5 ns THEN trigger
c. Leave the remaining fields unchanged.
4. Click OK to create this complex event and close the Edit Complex Event form.
5. In the Event Window, turn on the Also Capture Timer and Counter option and click
the Capture button to capture the event.
The event is added to the nWave window with signal name level_trigger2. When the
state jumps from level0 to level1, timer1 is started, and then after 5 ns, the trigger
occurs as shown as in the following figure:
Figure 160

level_trigger2 Captured in nWave

2. In the Edit Complex Event form, stay at level 0 and perform the following:

b. Change Timer1 to START.
c. Change the condition to IF read_cycle LASTS 25 ns THEN goto level 1 (click
trigger to change the action).
d. Leave the remaining fields unchanged.
e. Increase the level number from Level 0 to Level 1 by clicking the right arrow.
3. In the Edit Complex Event window, stay at level 1 and perform the following:

Verdi can show bit-vectors as signed or unsigned fixed-point values in nWave.
This section explains these features:
* Verdi automatically displays fixed-point values if the signal uses the VHDL fixed-point
standard or is a Verilog vector signal.
* You can set the radix (Binary, Octal, Decimal, or Hexadecimal) for single-bit VHDL
fixed-point signals.
* Verdi supports the new FSDB utility for VHDL fixed-point types.
* Verdi supports fixed-point display for Verilog vector signals.

Display Fixed-point Value
Verdi automatically displays fixed-point values for signals that use the VHDL fixed-point
standard.
Fixed-point signals are grouped into following two types based on their range. Each type
has its own display format.
* Signal range that contain binary point; that is, MSB -1 and LSB -1
sig1[4:-3] -> 11111.111
sig2[-1:-3] -> .111

* Signal range that does not contain binary point; that is, MSB < -1 or LSB > -1
sig3[-2:-4] -> 111 represent for 0.0111
sig4[3:1] -> 111 represent for 1110

Generate Dump Files From Verdi Signal RC Files
Verdi enables you to automatically convert simulation dump files (such as .do files) from
Verdi signal RC files using a provided Perl script. By converting the signal selections
saved in a Verdi .rc file into a format suitable for batch-mode simulation dumping, you can
efficiently prepare signal dumps for subsequent debugging and analysis.
To enabling automatic dump file generation, perform the following steps:
1. Ensure you have a Verdi signal RC file (for example, signal.rc) containing the signals
you want to dump.
2. Obtain the Perl script genDumpFileBySignalRC.pl. You get access to this script when
VERDI_HOME is set by typing the script name.
3. Run the Perl script from the command line to create the .do file.
genDumpFileBySignalRC.pl signal.rc test.do

This command reads signal.rc and generates test.do containing the appropriate
dump commands.
4. You can execute the Perl script within a simulation .do file to generate the dump file
dynamically.
my_dumping.do
Exec genDumpFileBySignalRC.pl test.rc test.do
fsdbDumpVarsByFile "$env(WORKSPACE/test.do)" test.fsdb

This approach ensures the dump file is always up to date with the latest signal selections.

A mapping rule file contains multiple mapping rule sets and a mapping rule set contains

1. patternInFileName (regular expression) or patternInLogHeader (regular expression)
a. patternInFileName: is used to match the log's file name
b. patternInLogHeader: is used to match the log's first 30 lines
2. hyperlinkRule: is applied if the pattern matches
3. partitionRules: is applied if the pattern matches
The absolute path to the mapping rule file is specified in novas.rc, and SmartLog parses
the specified file.

Predicting Mapping Rule
SmartLog predicts suitable partition rule files and hyperlink rule file for the selected log, if
the selected log does not match any mapping rule set in the mapping rule file.
The user-defined partition rule files are included in predicting a rule, if the directory which
contains the user-defined partition rule files is specified in the novas.rc file.

File View
As illustrated in Figure 179, File View displays the log text row by row, accompanied with

When you click a hyperlink, SmartLog performs the action defined in the hyperlink rule file.

Structure View
The Structure View displays the content of the log file in a spreadsheet. As illustrated in
Structure View, the content is grouped into several blocks based on attributes (such as
time, severity, file name and so on) specified in the partitioning rule file.
Each block delivers one message and contains time, severity, and entire content for the
message.
For details about the partitioning rule file, see the Applying Partitioning Rule section.

Figure 185

Structure View

The following columns are present in the Structure View:
* Time
The simulation time of a block in the log file is displayed in the Time column, when the
specified partitioning rule file contains the Time attribute.
If the partitioning rule file does not contain the Time attribute, the value 0 is displayed in
the field for each block.
The value of the Time attribute is assumed as an unsigned integral type.
The values should monotonically increase with the rows in the log file.
* Severity
The severity of a block is displayed in the Severity column.
The font color of the block is determined by the severity type, as follows:
If the severity type is Fatal or Error, the block font color is red.
If the severity type is Warning, the block font color is orange.
In other cases, the block font color is black.
You can also customize the displayed text and the text color for the severity list using
the Severity page in the SmartLog folder of the Preferences form in Verdi.

Figure 186

SmartLog Page in Preferences Form

Empty spaces cannot be entered in the Display Text field.
* Message
The entire content of a block is displayed in the Message column. The hyperlink rule is
also applied to the text.
The behavior in the Message column is the same as that in File View.
Use Time and Severity right-click options on the heading of the columns to hide or
display the corresponding column.

* Code
The code of a block in the log file is displayed in the Code column. This column is
hidden by default.
To display the column, right-click on the heading of the columns and enable the Code
option.
* Type

The type of a block in the log file is displayed in the Type column. This column is
hidden by default.
To display the column, right-click on the heading of the columns and enable the Type
option.
You can rearrange the sequence of the columns in the Structure view by

Specifying Time Unit in UVM/OVM Log File
SmartLog acquires the timing information from the following time units;
* Log Time Unit
The log time unit is applied on time without a unit and affects the time value.
For example, if the time 10 without unit is recognized by SmartLog and log time unit is
set as ns, SmartLog considers it as 10ns.
If the log time unit is not specified correctly, it breaks down the synchronization
between SmartLog, nWave, and Transaction and Protocol Analyzer.
* Display Time Unit

Using Hyperlink Rule File

The display time unit does not affect the time value, it only impacts how the time is
displayed.
For example, if the time is 1000ns, SmartLog shows 1000 with display time unit ns, and
shows 1 with display time unit ms.

Specifying the Log Time Unit
You can specify the log time unit using any of the following methods:
* Click the Time -> Setup Log Time Unit menu command.
* Specify through the partition rule. For details, see Applying Partitioning Rule.
If the log time unit is not fixed, it is recommended to always print time with unit in the log
file. For example, in SV HDL code, use $timeformat in the testbench to display time with
unit in the log file.

Specifying the Display Time Unit
You can specify the display time unit using the Time -> Setup Display Time Unit menu

nSchema is a schematic viewer and analyzer that generates interactive debug-specific
logic diagrams. These diagrams display the structure of the selected portions of a design.
RTL diagrams show the interconnection of finite state machines, storage elements, and
multiplexers. Gate-level diagrams show the interconnection of semiconductor vendor cells.
Special flattened diagrams cut through the design hierarchy to isolate connected design
elements.
nSchema dynamically generates partial schematics to focus on the circuits of interest in a
large design.
Before you begin this tutorial, follow the instructions in the Before You Begin chapter. Refer
to the User Interface chapter for general information on the nSchema window.

nWave Tutorial
nWave is a state-of-the-art graphical waveform viewer and analyzer that is fully integrated
with the source code, schematic, and flow views of the Verdi platform. A waveform search
engine combined with backward and forward navigation allows you to search for signal
transitions, bus values, discrepancies, and user-defined events easily.
nWave offers the following:
* Flexible signal group management
* Customizable glitch detection
* A built-in logic analyzer
* Logical operations and events
* Display of delays back-annotated from SDF files
* Mixed analog/digital (A/D) display capabilities, including overlap, vertical zoom, delta x
and y, arithmetic operations, analog-to-digital signal conversion, and others
* Display of transactions and messages
Before you begin this tutorial, follow the instructions in the Before You Begin chapter. Refer
to the User Interface chapter for more details regarding the nWave interface.
* Add Signals
* Manipulate the Waveform View
* Change Signal/Group Attributes
* Create New Signals/Buses From Existing Signals
* Save and Restore Signals
* Group or Ungroup Multiple FSDB Files
* Calculate Toggle Coverage
* Define Events and Complex Events

* Support VHDL Fixed-point Types in nWave
* Capture and Display Frequency of a Scalar Signal as a New Signal
* Generate Dump Files From Verdi Signal RC Files

Adding Signals Using Index Wildcards
The nWave Add Signal by Name dialog box supports wildcard characters in array
indices, letting you add multiple indexed signals without specifying each index individually.
A search such as /system/a[*].data[5] adds all matching signals to the waveform
viewer. Patterns are automatically expanded to individual signals in the waveform viewer.
Wildcard

Meaning

*

Matches zero or more characters

?

Matches exactly one character

The usage is as follows:
/system/psPnl[*].Addr[51:0]

This pattern adds all psPnl array elements with their Addr signals to the waveform.
Wildcard Scope and Matching Rules
Wildcard matching in the Add Signal by Name dialog box supports the following features:
1. Index wildcard *: The * wildcard matches zero or more characters within an index
dimension. For example, /system/a[*] matches /system/a[0:9] and all signals with
any index value.
2. Index wildcard ?: The ? wildcard matches exactly one character within an index
dimension. For example, /system/a[?] matches /system/a[0] and /system/a[1],
but not /system/a[10].
3. Cross-dimension expansion for *: The * wildcard can expand across multiple
index dimensions. For example, /system/macroram[10*] can match /system/
macroram[101][7:0]. (? cannot expand across dimensions.)
4. Combined name and index wildcards: Wildcards in both signal name and index can
be used together in a single search pattern (for example, top.cpu*.data[*]).
5. Maximum signal limit: A maximum of 100 matched signals are added to the
waveform; additional matches are ignored. When a wildcard matches more than 100
signals, only the first 100 are added and nWave displays an information message
indicating that results have been truncated.

Figure 128

Information Message for Truncated Wildcard Results

6. No-match warning: When a wildcard pattern matches no signals in the design, nWave
displays a warning through the List of Signal(s) Not Found dialog box.
Figure 129

Warning When No Signals Match

You can combine wildcards for both indices and signal members. For example, /system/
a[*].data[*].
* ? matches a single character and * matches zero to n characters.
* Neither ? nor * can expand across scopes. Wildcards match signals within
the specified scope only.
* ? cannot expand across scopes and dimensions. For example, /system/
macroram[10?] cannot match /system/macroram[101][7:0].
* * can expand across dimensions. For example, /system/macroram[10*]
can match /system/macroram[101][7:0].

When using index wildcard characters (* or ?) in array indices within the Add Signal by
Name dialog box:
* Array slice notation combined with an index wildcard is not supported. For example,
a[*].data[7:1] (and likewise a[?].data[7:1]) does not match. The signal cannot
be found when an array slice is used with a wildcard in the same search pattern.
Use one of the following workarounds instead:
Search using a index wildcard, such as /system/a[*].data[*].
Specify the complete index range, such as /system/a[*].data[7:0].
* Index wildcards may not be fully supported for signals in mixed-language designs.

Create a Complex Event With a Timer
Two built-in timers are provided that can be used to compose the complex event. Timers
are used to trace the period of a complex event. They can be controlled with different
options: START, STOP, PAUSE, and CONT. The timer is globally set. If no value is set for
the timer in the sub-conditions, then the value is inherited from the global setting. The subcondition can have its own setting with a priority higher than the global ones.

Leading Zero
When you disable the leading zero option, all leading zeros in the integer part are
removed. The fractional part keeps all its digits.
* 0011.0101 -> 11.0101: The first two zeros in the integer part are removed.
* 0000.0110 -> 0.0110: The first three zeros in the integer part are removed, but one
zero remains to show the integer value.
* ufixed (-3 downto -10): 00000110 (value equal to 0.0000000110) -> 00000110,
because it only represents the fractional part, so all digits are kept.
* ufixed (10 downto 3): 00000110 (value equal to 0000011000) -> 110 because it only
represents the integer part, the first five zeros in the integer part are removed.

Generate Dump Files From Verdi Signal RC Files
Verdi enables you to automatically convert simulation dump files (such as .do files) from
Verdi signal RC files using a provided Perl script. By converting the signal selections
saved in a Verdi .rc file into a format suitable for batch-mode simulation dumping, you can
efficiently prepare signal dumps for subsequent debugging and analysis.
To enabling automatic dump file generation, perform the following steps:
1. Ensure you have a Verdi signal RC file (for example, signal.rc) containing the signals
you want to dump.
2. Obtain the Perl script genDumpFileBySignalRC.pl. You get access to this script when
VERDI_HOME is set by typing the script name.
3. Run the Perl script from the command line to create the .do file.
genDumpFileBySignalRC.pl signal.rc test.do

This command reads signal.rc and generates test.do containing the appropriate
dump commands.
4. You can execute the Perl script within a simulation .do file to generate the dump file
dynamically.
my_dumping.do
Exec genDumpFileBySignalRC.pl test.rc test.do
fsdbDumpVarsByFile "$env(WORKSPACE/test.do)" test.fsdb

This approach ensures the dump file is always up to date with the latest signal selections.

The SmartLog engine can be used to read and traverse log files in a readable view.
SmartLog loads a log file with a specific format that shows a structured presentation of
the log contents, thus providing a flexible and convenient use model for debugging. The

connection between the log file and the Verdi platform is built according to the hyperlink
rule files and the partitioning rule files.
Click the hyperlink to the log content in the SmartLog window to link to the Verdi platform,
for example, link to the source code location. The hyperlink rule can be further customized
with Tcl commands to execute a specific action in Verdi. A partitioning rule can also be
used to group the messages in SmartLog for systematic and convenient log navigation.

* Two browsing views to display log in the following modes:
File View for sequential information
Structure View for grouped information
* Identify and filter out the required log messages
* Synchronize with the cursor in the nWave frame
* Unified usage for interactive simulation console
* Customization of hyperlink rules and partitioning rules

Auto Select Rules
This section describes the auto select rules in the following sub-sections:
* Checking Mapping Rule File
* Predicting Mapping Rule

Checking Mapping Rule File
A mapping rule file contains multiple mapping rule sets and a mapping rule set contains
the following three items:
1. patternInFileName (regular expression) or patternInLogHeader (regular expression)
a. patternInFileName: is used to match the log's file name
b. patternInLogHeader: is used to match the log's first 30 lines
2. hyperlinkRule: is applied if the pattern matches
3. partitionRules: is applied if the pattern matches
The absolute path to the mapping rule file is specified in novas.rc, and SmartLog parses
the specified file.

* If the file name of the selected log starts with "sim" and ends with ".log", for example,
"simulation.log", the following mapping rule set gets selected:

* If any line of the first 30 lines of the log file contains "listModFile", the following mapping
rule set gets selected:

Predicting Mapping Rule
SmartLog predicts suitable partition rule files and hyperlink rule file for the selected log, if
the selected log does not match any mapping rule set in the mapping rule file.
The user-defined partition rule files are included in predicting a rule, if the directory which
contains the user-defined partition rule files is specified in the novas.rc file.

Auto Select Rule Mode
You can change the auto select rule mode using the Auto Select Rule Mode field in the
Open File form.
The following options are available in the Auto Select Rule Mode field:
* Always On: Enables auto-select rule.
* Normal: Enables auto-select rule.

The Normal mode changes to the Always Off mode, if any partition rule files or
hyperlink rule file is added or removed in the Open Log form and if the Open button is
clicked in the Open Log form.
* Always Off: Disables auto select rule.

Opening a Log File Using Verdi Commands
You can use the following commands to open a log file in SmartLog:
* -smlog logfile
Loads the specified log file with SmartLog.
* -smlog_hyper | -smlog_h ruleFile
Specifies the hyperlink rule file for the specified log.
This option must be used with the -smlog option.
* -smlog_partition | -smlog_p "ruleFile1 ruleFile2ruleFileN"
Specifies the partitioning rule file(s) for the specified log. A pair of double quotes (")
must be used to enclose the partitioning rule file(s).
This option must be used with the -smlog option.

Examples
The following are some examples to demonstrate use cases to open log file(s) using Verdi
commands:
Example 1 - To open a specified log (test.log) with specified partitioning rule file
(parRule1.rc) and hyperlink rule file (hyperRule.rc), use the following command:
%> verdi -smlog test.log -smlog_hyperlink hyperRule.rc -smlog_partition
"parRule1.rc"

Example 2 - To open a specified log (test.log) with specified partitioning rule files
(parRule1.rc, parRule2.rc) and hyperlink rule file (hyperRule.rc), use the following
%> verdi -smlog test.log -smlog_hyperlink hyperRule.rc -smlog_partition
"parRule1.rc parRule2.rc"

Example 3 - To open specified log files (test1.log, test2.log) with the same specified
partitioning rule files (parRule1.rc, parRule2.rc) and hyperlink rule file (hyperRule.rc), use
the following command:
%> verdi -smlog test1.log -smlog test2.log -smlog_hyperlink hyperRule.rc
-smlog_partition "parRule1.rc parRule2.rc"

Example 4 - To open multiple log files (test1.log, test2.log) with different partitioning rule
files and hyperlink rule files, use the following command:
%> verdi -smlog test1.log -smlog_hyperlink hyperRule1.rc -smlog_partition
"parRule1.rc" -smlog test2.log -smlog_hyperlink hyperRule2.rc
-smlog_partition "parRule2.rc"

The following sections explain these views in detail:
* File View
* Structure View

File View
As illustrated in Figure 179, File View displays the log text row by row, accompanied with
some keywords as hyperlinks.
When you click a hyperlink, SmartLog performs the action defined in the hyperlink rule file.
The hyperlink rule, written in a *.rc file, tells SmartLog where to create hyperlinks and what
happens when you click them.
To set up or change a hyperlink rule, click the
icon. For details about the usage of the
hyperlink rule file, see the Using Hyperlink Rule File section).

Structure View
The Structure View displays the content of the log file in a spreadsheet. As illustrated in
Structure View, the content is grouped into several blocks based on attributes (such as
time, severity, file name and so on) specified in the partitioning rule file.
Each block delivers one message and contains time, severity, and entire content for the
message.
For details about the partitioning rule file, see the Applying Partitioning Rule section.

Figure 185

Structure View

The following columns are present in the Structure View:
* Time
The simulation time of a block in the log file is displayed in the Time column, when the
specified partitioning rule file contains the Time attribute.
If the partitioning rule file does not contain the Time attribute, the value 0 is displayed in
the field for each block.
The value of the Time attribute is assumed as an unsigned integral type.
The values should monotonically increase with the rows in the log file.
* Severity
The severity of a block is displayed in the Severity column.
The font color of the block is determined by the severity type, as follows:
If the severity type is Fatal or Error, the block font color is red.
If the severity type is Warning, the block font color is orange.
In other cases, the block font color is black.
You can also customize the displayed text and the text color for the severity list using
the Severity page in the SmartLog folder of the Preferences form in Verdi.

Figure 186

SmartLog Page in Preferences Form

Empty spaces cannot be entered in the Display Text field.
* Message
The entire content of a block is displayed in the Message column. The hyperlink rule is
also applied to the text.
The behavior in the Message column is the same as that in File View.
Use Time and Severity right-click options on the heading of the columns to hide or
display the corresponding column.

* Code
The code of a block in the log file is displayed in the Code column. This column is
hidden by default.
To display the column, right-click on the heading of the columns and enable the Code
option.
* Type

The type of a block in the log file is displayed in the Type column. This column is
hidden by default.
To display the column, right-click on the heading of the columns and enable the Type
option.
You can rearrange the sequence of the columns in the Structure view by
clicking and dragging a column.
Also, you can restore the last display settings for columns including column
width and column sequence from the novas.rc file.

Specifying Time Unit in UVM/OVM Log File
SmartLog acquires the timing information from the following time units;
* Log Time Unit
The log time unit is applied on time without a unit and affects the time value.
For example, if the time 10 without unit is recognized by SmartLog and log time unit is
set as ns, SmartLog considers it as 10ns.
If the log time unit is not specified correctly, it breaks down the synchronization
between SmartLog, nWave, and Transaction and Protocol Analyzer.
* Display Time Unit

Using Hyperlink Rule File

The display time unit does not affect the time value, it only impacts how the time is
displayed.
For example, if the time is 1000ns, SmartLog shows 1000 with display time unit ns, and
shows 1 with display time unit ms.

Specifying the Log Time Unit
You can specify the log time unit using any of the following methods:
* Click the Time -> Setup Log Time Unit menu command.
* Specify through the partition rule. For details, see Applying Partitioning Rule.
If the log time unit is not fixed, it is recommended to always print time with unit in the log
file. For example, in SV HDL code, use $timeformat in the testbench to display time with
unit in the log file.

Specifying the Display Time Unit
You can specify the display time unit using the Time -> Setup Display Time Unit menu

The OneSearch capability in Verdi works like a web search engine and helps you to
search through various aspects or domains within your design. The OneSearch interface
is simple, intuitive, and easy to use; wherein you can enter a search query and get ranked
and sorted results, view the results, modify your query, and refine your search.
OneSearch supports search in Sources, Logs, Identifiers, and Docs domains with
domain-specific search engines, generates ranked matches, and stores results in domainspecific results file.
OneSearch also supports search in DB/LOg/Doc, UI Content, and Menu Command.
OneSearch is also aware of the current Verdi Work Mode (coverage/power debug and so
on) and generates results based on the work mode. For example, the coverage search
engine is available only in the Coverage mode.

Search Domains

Search Domains
The search domains for OneSearch capability are described as follows:
* Sources
The Sources domain covers all (System)Verilog, VHDL, or other input files used in
the design. The file list is extracted from the KDB (if available) or the VCS elaboration
(if available) files. If none of these files is available, all files matching \.[ch]|\.[ch]pp|
\.[ch]xx|\.(cc|hh)|\.svh|\.pli|\.v|\.vrh|\.sv|\.sva|\.vhdl|\.vhd and Makefile|synopsys_sim
\.setup|\.tcl|\.[a-z]?sh|\.upf are searched.
To specify an additional file list, use the VERDI_SEARCH_SOURCES_FILE environment
variable.
file: and files: are the supported keywords to filter the list of files matching the specified
pattern only (such as, files:a*.sv matches only files starting with a and ending with .sv).
* Logs
The Logs domain covers log files generated from compilation and simulation matching
ucli\.key|.*\.rpt|.*\.log(\.gz).
To specify an additional file list, use the VERDI_SEARCH_LOGS_FILE environment
variable.
file: and files: are supported keywords to filter the list of files matching the specified
pattern only (such as, files:sim* matches only files starting with sim).
* Identifiers
The Identifiers domain covers HDL design and testbench elements of VCS simulation.
Any identifier (that is, anything with a name) in the design is searched.
* Docs
The Docs domain covers all Verdi documentation (PDF) files.
To specify an additional file list, use the VERDI_SEARCH_DOCS_FILE environment
variable.
file: and files: are supported keywords to filter the list of files matching the specified
pattern only (such as, files:*plan* matches only files containing plan).

Search Modes

Search Modes
OneSearch supports the following search modes that decide where to search and how to
display the search results:
* Overview Mode
* Single Domain Mode

Overview Mode
This is the default mode for OneSearch.
This mode is the starting point for searching. It gives you a quick summary of results
across your whole design.
When you scroll in the OneSearch results window, you move through groups of domains.
The matches inside each group do not move.
If you change your search query, for example by adding another pattern, and click the
search button again, OneSearch starts a new search in all domains.
Each group ends with a summary line. This line shows the total number of results, not just
the ones you can see. It also shows if a search is still running.
Figure 216

Overview Mode

Single Domain Mode
This mode is the next step for viewing more results from one domain.
To change from Overview mode to Single-domain mode, click a domain link such as
Sources, Logs, Identifiers, or Docs.

Support for Multiple Line Results

When you click a domain name, OneSearch shows results from your previous search for
that domain. It does not start a new search. All matches found in the selected domain are
displayed.
Figure 217

Single Domain Mode

Support for Multiple Line Results
OneSearch ranks documentation matches within a single line. It also combines matches

Support for Synonyms

Support for Synonyms
OneSearch automatically searches synonyms for terms in search queries based on a
predefined synonym database. This functionality provides you the capability to search
results for words with the same (or very similar) meaning.
This feature is applicable to Sources, Logs, and Docs domains.
If your search query includes words that have synonyms in OneSearch, you can see a
message in the Results pane. This message tells you that the results also include matches
for those synonyms.
To see only the exact search term and not its synonyms, put your search term inside
double quotation marks ("").
The following figure shows an example of this message.
Figure 218

Example for OneSearch Query

Quoted search terms, keywords, and their arguments are not included in
synonym searches. OneSearch gives higher ranking to results that exactly
match your search query than to results that match synonyms.

Example Use Case
If the search query is start_transaction, OneSearch looks for the synonyms of start
and transaction. If start yields the synonym begin and there is no synonym defined for
transaction, then OneSearch shows results for two query terms: start_transaction and
begin_transaction.
If additional synonyms for transaction are also found, these are searched in the same
manner.

Support for Synonyms

Specifying an Additional Synonym Database
You can add another synonym search database file by setting the
VERDI_SEARCH_SYNONYM_FILE environment variable. This file should be a text file. The
synonyms you list in this file are included with the built-in synonyms database. You cannot
remove the built-in synonyms.
Write each group of synonyms on a separate line in the text file. Use commas to separate
the words. All words in the same line are treated as synonyms and can replace each other.
For example, assume that the synonym database contains the following three lines,
which signifies that A, B, and C are synonyms to each other; B and D can be used
interchangeably; and D, E, and F can also be used interchangeably.
A,B,C
B,D
D,E,F

If your search query includes the term B, the synonym search looks through the database
one line at a time. It finds every line with B and adds all related synonyms to your search.
If your search query includes the term B, the synonym search looks through the database
one line at a time. It finds every line with B and adds all related synonyms to your search.
Thus, the search for B includes the synonyms: A, C, and D, but not E and F.

The following limitations apply to this feature:
* Synonym search only applies to alphanumeric words. Special characters, such as -, _,
!, @, #, $ are not supported.
* Stemming of search terms is not supported. This means that changes in word forms,
such as nouns, pronouns, adjectives, and articles, are not recognized. Different verb
forms are also not recognized.
* Words and sub-words are included in synonym search only if they are written in all
uppercase, all lowercase, or with only the first letter capitalized.
For example, these words and their sub-words are not included in synonym search:
BeGIn, AMbA_tRANSMISSION, pOpULate, mY_OwN_USBRegister.
* Using this feature may impact OneSearch performance.

To debug a design, you need to understand the structure and the behavior of the design.
Understanding the structure allows you to visualize the connection between blocks or
signals. Also, understanding the behavior allows you to know the relationship between
driver-signals, loader-signals, driver triggers, and the value transition. Visualizing the
structure and behavior of the design is very useful and convenient to become familiar with
the design and then debug it.
The flow views are unique temporal views and analysis tools that allow the visualization
and analysis of the design's behavior through time. The Temporal Flow View identifies
and displays causal control and data paths - the registers and signals that actually caused
the erroneous value to occur - through multi-level combinational logic within one or
more register-to-register transfer stages. The mechanism helps to quickly find the bug
without repeatedly looking at the driver or fan-in signals of the signal of interest and the
intelligently filtered temporal representation allows you to locate and identify problems
in the most efficient manner possible without going through the different source code,
schematic and waveform windows. However, the flow views also can be used to drive the
source code, nWave (waveforms), nState (state machines) and nSchema (schematics)
frames as needed.

The display in the Temporal Flow View frame is similar to the following example:
Figure 220

Example Temporal Flow View Frame With Expanded Statements

In the Temporal Flow View frame notice the following items:
* The input data signals are on the left and output data signals are on the right of the
symbol.
* On top of the gray vertical line, the number shown indicates that the clock active edge
for that signal is at that time in ns. If you click the symbol associated with the register,
the number appears in the box of the toolbar, That is, the value of the register changed
at that time.
* The input control signals are on the bottom of the symbol. (An example of a control
path is a multiplexer's select input, and an example of a data path is a multiplexer's
data signals).
* Some input ports are pink (signal is actively contributing to the output value) or gray
(signal is not actively contributing). (Turn on the View -> Signal -> Active Nodes Only
toggle command to see all nodes or just active ones).
* The red dot associated with some ports indicates that these fan-in registers have value
transition in their previous clock edges.
* The clock that drives the located register can be shown without tracing through
combinational logic cones and correlating the clocks manually.
* The annotated simulations values (blue numbers).
* The signal names.
* The bus contention and active fan-in information can be clearly viewed in a single view.
* The cause of a specific data pattern on a partial bus can also be isolated.
The Temporal Flow View traces to the root cause automatically with two major
mechanisms. That is, behavior analysis engine and automatic cause and effect tracing.

Behavior Analysis Engine
From the KDB and FSDB, Verdi builds an internal model of actual design behaviors using
the synthesis and formal technology. Traditionally, the tracing stops at the problematic
signals when debugging. If further tracing is required, then you must invoke and configure
the tracing manually. Now, with the behavior analysis engine, the Temporal Flow View
traces based on the behavior of the design automatically.
Figure 221

Temporal Flow View Traces Automatically to Debug

The following tracing features are available:
* Unrolls the function over time.
* Differentiates the data from control signals.
* Determines the clocking.
* Prunes inactive elements.

Automatic Cause and Effect Tracing
The Temporal Flow View traces not only to the problematic signal but to the root cause
of the error. The Temporal Flow View provides a complete environment that helps in
visualizing the behaviors with time and structure easily. The root cause and the trace path
can be viewed holistically.

The nCompare frame compares simulation results stored in FSDB dump files by using
flexible, user-specified comparison criteria. The frame is optimized for extremely fast
comparisons of large data sets. It is fully integrated with the Verdi platform to intuitively
display differences between runs.
The nCompare module uses the Tcl language. Further, it uses the nCompare -defined-Tclextended comparison commands for comparison rules and specific comparison options.

Refer to Appendix D in the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual for details.
